av-block.stem: ECG shows a constant PR interval with intermittent sudden failure of a P wave to conduct, and the QRS is wide. Which block, and what is the definitive treatment?
av-block.explanation: Fixed PR with sudden non-conducted P waves and a wide QRS is Mobitz II — an infranodal, unstable block that warrants a permanent pacemaker. Atropine typically fails for infranodal block.

av-block.stem: Regarding distinguishing mobitz i vs ii — which is correct?

options.text: Both are “second-degree”, so treat them the same
Mobitz I = progressive PR (AV node, benign); Mobitz II = fixed PR (infranodal, pacemaker)
Atropine helps AV-nodal (1°, Mobitz I); not infranodal (Mobitz II, 3°)
Give atropine for any AV block

av-block.explanation: The PR behaviour localizes the block — nodal blocks lengthen PR and are stable; infranodal blocks keep PR fixed and drop suddenly, risking complete block.

av-block.stem: Regarding drug response — which is correct?

options.text: Give atropine for any AV block
Mobitz I = progressive PR (AV node, benign); Mobitz II = fixed PR (infranodal, pacemaker)
Atropine helps AV-nodal (1°, Mobitz I); not infranodal (Mobitz II, 3°)
Both are “second-degree”, so treat them the same

av-block.explanation: Atropine reduces vagal tone at the AV node; infranodal His–Purkinje block will not respond and needs pacing.

av-block.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cannon A waves in the JVP (complete block)”?

options.text: Changing AV timing alters valve position at systole
Atria contract against closed AV valves during AV dissociation

av-block.explanation: Cannon A waves in the JVP (complete block) → Atria contract against closed AV valves during AV dissociation.

av-block.stem: Which should you review before “Atrioventricular (AV) Block”?

options.text: Histology of the Heart Wall & Conduction Cells

av-block.explanation: Understanding cardiac histology is essential for grasping conduction abnormalities.

atrial-fibrillation.stem: An ECG shows an irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm with no P waves. The apical rate is 110 but the radial pulse is 88. What explains the apical–radial difference?

options.text: Pulse deficit — some weak beats do not generate a palpable radial pulse

atrial-fibrillation.explanation: In AF, irregular diastolic filling means some beats are too weak to transmit to the radial artery, so the apical (auscultated) rate exceeds the radial rate — a pulse deficit.

atrial-fibrillation.stem: Regarding rhythm identification — which is correct?

options.text: Irregular, so it must be atrial flutter with variable block
AF = irregularly irregular with NO P waves; flutter = regular sawtooth (often 2:1/4:1)
Avoid AV-nodal blockers; use procainamide or cardiovert
Give an AV-nodal blocker (verapamil / digoxin / adenosine)

atrial-fibrillation.explanation: Flutter has organized sawtooth F waves and is usually regular; AF has no organized atrial activity at all.

atrial-fibrillation.stem: Regarding drug choice in pre-excited af (wpw) — which is correct?

options.text: Give an AV-nodal blocker (verapamil / digoxin / adenosine)
AF = irregularly irregular with NO P waves; flutter = regular sawtooth (often 2:1/4:1)
Avoid AV-nodal blockers; use procainamide or cardiovert
Irregular, so it must be atrial flutter with variable block

atrial-fibrillation.explanation: Blocking the AV node funnels conduction down the accessory pathway → very fast ventricular rate → VF.

atrial-fibrillation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Irregularly irregular pulse”?

options.text: Some beats too weak to transmit a palpable pulse
Random AV conduction of chaotic atrial activity
Thrombo-embolism; loss of atrial kick + tachycardia

atrial-fibrillation.explanation: Irregularly irregular pulse → Random AV conduction of chaotic atrial activity.

atrial-fibrillation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pulse deficit (apical rate > radial rate)”?

options.text: Random AV conduction of chaotic atrial activity
Thrombo-embolism; loss of atrial kick + tachycardia
Some beats too weak to transmit a palpable pulse

atrial-fibrillation.explanation: Pulse deficit (apical rate > radial rate) → Some beats too weak to transmit a palpable pulse.

atrial-fibrillation.stem: Which should you review before “Atrial Fibrillation (AF)”?
atrial-fibrillation.explanation: Understanding hormonal regulation may provide context for AF.

atrial-flutter.stem: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at exactly 150/min. Carotid sinus massage transiently slows the rate and reveals sawtooth waves at 300/min in the inferior leads. Diagnosis?
atrial-flutter.explanation: A fixed ~150/min that transiently slows to reveal 300/min sawtooth F waves is atrial flutter conducting 2:1. Increasing AV block (vagal/adenosine) exposes the flutter waves.

atrial-flutter.stem: Regarding regular narrow tachycardia at ~150 — which is correct?

options.text: Always call it sinus tachycardia or PSVT
Flutter is usually REGULAR (organized macro-reentry, sawtooth); AF is irregularly irregular (no P)

atrial-flutter.explanation: A suspiciously fixed ~150/min should prompt a search for flutter waves; vagal maneuvers/adenosine unmask them.

atrial-flutter.stem: Regarding af vs flutter — which is correct?

options.text: Flutter is usually REGULAR (organized macro-reentry, sawtooth); AF is irregularly irregular (no P)
Always call it sinus tachycardia or PSVT

atrial-flutter.explanation: Degree of organization separates them — flutter is a single reentrant circuit, AF is chaotic.

atrial-flutter.stem: Which should you review before “Atrial Flutter”?
atrial-flutter.explanation: Understanding ECG waveforms is crucial for identifying flutter.

premature-contractions.stem: An early, wide, bizarre QRS with no preceding P wave is followed by a pause such that the R–R spanning it equals two normal cycles. What is this?
premature-contractions.explanation: A wide premature QRS with no P and a full compensatory pause (the SA node keeps its timing) is a PVC. A PAC would have an early abnormal P, a narrow QRS, and usually reset the SA node.

premature-contractions.stem: Regarding type of pause — which is correct?

options.text: All premature beats give a full compensatory pause
PVC = full compensatory pause; PAC usually resets the SA node (non-compensatory)
Most PVCs are benign; the danger is R-on-T triggering VT/VF
A single PVC always needs antiarrhythmics

premature-contractions.explanation: A PVC does not reset the SA node, so the next sinus beat arrives “on schedule” → full compensatory pause; a PAC depolarizes and resets it.

premature-contractions.stem: Regarding which is dangerous — which is correct?

options.text: A single PVC always needs antiarrhythmics
PVC = full compensatory pause; PAC usually resets the SA node (non-compensatory)
Most PVCs are benign; the danger is R-on-T triggering VT/VF
All premature beats give a full compensatory pause

premature-contractions.explanation: Isolated PVCs in a normal heart rarely need treatment; the lethal scenario is a PVC landing on the T-wave vulnerable period.

premature-contractions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Palpitations / “skipped beat””?

options.text: Reduced stroke volume of the premature ventricular beat
Premature beat then a pause felt as a skip

premature-contractions.explanation: Palpitations / “skipped beat” → Premature beat then a pause felt as a skip.

premature-contractions.stem: Which should you review before “Premature Contractions (PAC & PVC)”?
premature-contractions.explanation: Understanding LDL retention is crucial for grasping the pathophysiology of cardiac arrhythmias.

ventricular-tachycardia.stem: A stable patient has a regular wide-complex tachycardia at 170/min with visible AV dissociation and occasional fusion beats. Most likely diagnosis?
ventricular-tachycardia.explanation: AV dissociation plus capture and fusion beats are hallmarks of VT. A regular wide-complex tachycardia should be treated as VT until proven otherwise.

ventricular-tachycardia.stem: Regarding wide-complex tachycardia call — which is correct?

options.text: Call it SVT with bundle branch block and give verapamil
Treat regular wide-complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise
TdP → magnesium + correct electrolytes; avoid QT-prolonging drugs

ventricular-tachycardia.explanation: Misdiagnosing VT as SVT and giving a CCB can cause collapse; AV dissociation / capture / fusion beats point to VT.

ventricular-tachycardia.stem: Regarding polymorphic vt drug — which is correct?

options.text: Treat regular wide-complex tachycardia as VT until proven otherwise
TdP → magnesium + correct electrolytes; avoid QT-prolonging drugs
Call it SVT with bundle branch block and give verapamil

ventricular-tachycardia.explanation: Torsades is driven by a long QT; QT-prolonging antiarrhythmics worsen it — magnesium is first-line.

ventricular-tachycardia.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hemodynamic compromise (hypotension, ↓consciousness)”?

options.text: Independent atrial & ventricular activity — favors VT over SVT
Loss of coordinated filling/ejection at high rate

ventricular-tachycardia.explanation: Hemodynamic compromise (hypotension, ↓consciousness) → Loss of coordinated filling/ejection at high rate.

ventricular-tachycardia.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cannon A waves / variable S1 (AV dissociation)”?

options.text: Independent atrial & ventricular activity — favors VT over SVT
Loss of coordinated filling/ejection at high rate

ventricular-tachycardia.explanation: Cannon A waves / variable S1 (AV dissociation) → Independent atrial & ventricular activity — favors VT over SVT.

ventricular-fibrillation.stem: A monitored patient collapses; the rhythm is a chaotic baseline with no identifiable QRS complexes and no pulse. Immediate treatment?
ventricular-fibrillation.explanation: Pulseless VF is treated with immediate unsynchronized defibrillation and CPR. There is no organized QRS to synchronize to, so synchronized cardioversion is not possible.

ventricular-fibrillation.stem: Regarding shock type — which is correct?

options.text: A PVC on the T wave (R-on-T) in the vulnerable period can trigger VF

ventricular-fibrillation.explanation: VF has no organized QRS to synchronize to, so the shock must be unsynchronized. Synchronized cardioversion is for organized rhythms (VT-with-pulse, AF, flutter).

ventricular-fibrillation.stem: Regarding what initiates vf — which is correct?

options.text: A PVC on the T wave (R-on-T) in the vulnerable period can trigger VF

ventricular-fibrillation.explanation: The mid-T-wave vulnerable period has maximal dispersion of refractoriness; a stimulus there can ignite re-entry.

ventricular-fibrillation.stem: Which should you review before “Ventricular Fibrillation (VF)”?

stemi-localization.stem: ST elevation in II, III, and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. Which artery, and which extra lead should you obtain?
stemi-localization.explanation: Inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF) is usually RCA. Always obtain V4R to detect RV infarction, which is preload-dependent and changes management (fluids, avoid nitrates).

stemi-localization.stem: Regarding lead territory — which is correct?

options.text: ST elevation in II, III, aVF = anterior MI
Check V4R first; if RV infarct, give fluids and avoid nitrates
Give nitrates for the chest pain

stemi-localization.explanation: Anterior is V1–V4 (LAD); the inferior leads are II, III, aVF. Mixing them up changes the artery and the management.

stemi-localization.stem: Regarding inferior stemi management — which is correct?

options.text: Give nitrates for the chest pain
Check V4R first; if RV infarct, give fluids and avoid nitrates
ST elevation in II, III, aVF = anterior MI

stemi-localization.explanation: RV infarction is preload-dependent — nitrates drop preload and cause severe hypotension.

stemi-localization.stem: What best explains the finding: “Anterior: V1–V4”?
What best explains the finding: “Inferior: II, III, aVF”?
stemi-localization.explanation: Inferior: II, III, aVF → RCA (or LCx) territory.

stemi-localization.stem: Which should you review before “STEMI Localization & Reciprocal Changes”?
stemi-localization.explanation: Understanding coronary supply is critical for localizing STEMI.

bundle-branch-block.stem: QRS is 140 ms with an rSR′ (“M”) pattern in V1 and a wide slurred S wave in V6. Which conduction abnormality?
bundle-branch-block.explanation: rSR′ (“M”) in V1 with a wide S in V6 is RBBB — MaRRoW (M in V1, W in V6). LBBB would show the “M” in V6 and a QS in V1 (WiLLiaM).

bundle-branch-block.stem: Regarding which bbb — which is correct?

options.text: New LBBB + ischemic symptoms = STEMI-equivalent → activate ACS pathway
Can’t diagnose MI with LBBB, so just observe

bundle-branch-block.explanation: RBBB makes the “M” in V1; LBBB makes the “M” in V6. WiLLiaM MaRRoW keeps them straight.

bundle-branch-block.stem: Regarding chest pain + new lbbb — which is correct?

options.text: Can’t diagnose MI with LBBB, so just observe
New LBBB + ischemic symptoms = STEMI-equivalent → activate ACS pathway

bundle-branch-block.explanation: New LBBB can represent acute proximal LAD occlusion; use Sgarbossa criteria rather than dismissing it.

bundle-branch-block.stem: What best explains the finding: “Wide QRS ≥120 ms”?

options.text: The defining criterion — delayed sequential activation

bundle-branch-block.explanation: Wide QRS ≥120 ms → The defining criterion — delayed sequential activation.

bundle-branch-block.stem: What best explains the finding: “RBBB: rSR′ in V1, wide S in V6/I”?

options.text: The defining criterion — delayed sequential activation

bundle-branch-block.explanation: RBBB: rSR′ in V1, wide S in V6/I → Late right-ventricular activation (MaRRoW).

bundle-branch-block.stem: Which should you review before “Bundle Branch Block (RBBB vs LBBB)”?
bundle-branch-block.explanation: Understanding the conduction system is essential for grasping bundle branch block mechanisms.

escape-rhythms-sinus-dysfunction.stem: After a 4-second sinus pause, a beat appears with a wide QRS at a rate of ~30/min. What is this rescue beat?
escape-rhythms-sinus-dysfunction.explanation: A wide QRS at 20–40/min emerging after the sinus fails is a ventricular escape rhythm — the lowest, slowest backup pacemaker. A junctional escape would be narrow at 40–60.

escape-rhythms-sinus-dysfunction.stem: Regarding don’t treat the escape — which is correct?

options.text: Suppress the slow wide-complex escape beats
Protect the escape rhythm; treat the underlying bradycardia (atropine / pacing)
Junctional escape = narrow QRS (40–60); ventricular escape = wide QRS (20–40)
All escape rhythms look the same

escape-rhythms-sinus-dysfunction.explanation: A ventricular escape rhythm is a life-saving backup — abolishing it causes asystole. Support the rate instead.

escape-rhythms-sinus-dysfunction.stem: Regarding narrow vs wide escape — which is correct?

options.text: All escape rhythms look the same
Protect the escape rhythm; treat the underlying bradycardia (atropine / pacing)
Junctional escape = narrow QRS (40–60); ventricular escape = wide QRS (20–40)
Suppress the slow wide-complex escape beats

escape-rhythms-sinus-dysfunction.explanation: QRS width localizes the backup pacemaker — the junction conducts via His-Purkinje (narrow); the ventricle does not (wide, slow).

options.text: Cerebral hypoperfusion during a long pause
Slow sinus rate or slow escape pacemaker

escape-rhythms-sinus-dysfunction.explanation: Bradycardia → Slow sinus rate or slow escape pacemaker.

escape-rhythms-sinus-dysfunction.stem: Which should you review before “Escape Rhythms & Sinus Node Dysfunction”?
escape-rhythms-sinus-dysfunction.explanation: Understanding the conduction system is essential for grasping escape rhythms.

vsd.stem: A 5-week-old has poor feeding and a harsh pansystolic murmur at the LLSB, plus a mid-diastolic rumble at the apex. What does the apical rumble indicate?

options.text: Large shunt with ↑flow across the mitral valve (Qp:Qs >2)

vsd.explanation: A mid-diastolic apical rumble in VSD reflects increased flow across the mitral valve from a large left-to-right shunt (Qp:Qs >2) — a sign of significant shunt size, not a second valve lesion.

vsd.stem: Regarding murmur localization & timing — which is correct?

options.text: Ejection systolic murmur at the upper sternal border
Harsh pansystolic murmur at the LLSB

vsd.explanation: VSD flows LV→RV throughout systole at the lower left sternal border — pansystolic, not an ejection murmur.

vsd.stem: Regarding murmur intensity vs defect size — which is correct?

options.text: Harsh pansystolic murmur at the LLSB
Ejection systolic murmur at the upper sternal border

vsd.explanation: A large defect equalizes ventricular pressures → little turbulence → soft murmur. Loudness is inverse to size.

vsd.stem: What best explains the finding: “Harsh pansystolic murmur at LLSB”?

options.text: ↑flow across the mitral valve — signals a large shunt (Qp:Qs >2)
High-pressure LV→RV flow through the defect, all of systole

vsd.explanation: Harsh pansystolic murmur at LLSB → High-pressure LV→RV flow through the defect, all of systole.

vsd.stem: What best explains the finding: “Mid-diastolic rumble at apex”?

options.text: High-pressure LV→RV flow through the defect, all of systole
↑flow across the mitral valve — signals a large shunt (Qp:Qs >2)

vsd.explanation: Mid-diastolic rumble at apex → ↑flow across the mitral valve — signals a large shunt (Qp:Qs >2).

vsd.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)”?
vsd.explanation: Both involve congenital conditions but in different systems.

asd.stem: A 4-year-old is asymptomatic. Exam: soft systolic ejection murmur at the LUSB and a split S2 that does not change with respiration. Best explanation for the fixed split?

options.text: RV volume overload from an atrial septal defect

asd.explanation: A widely fixed split S2 reflects RV volume overload (constant RV ejection time) from a left-to-right ASD shunt. The ejection murmur is relative pulmonary stenosis, not flow through the defect.

asd.stem: Regarding source of the murmur — which is correct?

options.text: Blood rushing through the ASD makes the murmur
Relative pulmonary stenosis (↑flow across a normal pulmonary valve)

asd.explanation: The atrial pressure gradient is tiny, so flow across the ASD is silent. The audible murmur is increased flow across the pulmonary (and tricuspid) valves.

asd.stem: Regarding physical examination finding — which is correct?

options.text: Relative pulmonary stenosis (↑flow across a normal pulmonary valve)
Blood rushing through the ASD makes the murmur

asd.explanation: RV volume overload fixes RV ejection time, so the split does not vary with respiration — the defining ASD sign.

asd.stem: What best explains the finding: “Widely fixed split S2”?

options.text: Relative/functional pulmonary stenosis (↑flow across a NORMAL pulmonary valve)
Large shunt → ↑flow across the tricuspid valve
RV volume overload keeps RV ejection time constant across respiration — the ASD signature
Low-pressure atrial shunt is well tolerated for years

asd.explanation: Widely fixed split S2 → RV volume overload keeps RV ejection time constant across respiration — the ASD signature.

asd.stem: What best explains the finding: “Systolic ejection murmur at LUSB”?

options.text: RV volume overload keeps RV ejection time constant across respiration — the ASD signature
Large shunt → ↑flow across the tricuspid valve
Low-pressure atrial shunt is well tolerated for years
Relative/functional pulmonary stenosis (↑flow across a NORMAL pulmonary valve)

asd.explanation: Systolic ejection murmur at LUSB → Relative/functional pulmonary stenosis (↑flow across a NORMAL pulmonary valve).

asd.stem: Which should you review before “Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)”?
asd.explanation: Understanding jugular venous pressure is important for assessing right heart function.

pda.stem: A preterm infant has a continuous murmur at the LUSB and bounding pulses. Absent contraindications, which drug is used to close the lesion?
pda.explanation: Indomethacin inhibits prostaglandin synthesis and closes the ductus. Prostaglandin E1 does the opposite — it keeps a duct open in duct-dependent congenital lesions.

pda.stem: Regarding murmur timing — which is correct?

options.text: Indomethacin closes; prostaglandin keeps it open
Give prostaglandin to close the PDA

pda.explanation: Aortic pressure exceeds PA pressure throughout the cycle, so the duct flows continuously — not only in systole.

pda.stem: Regarding pharmacology direction — which is correct?

options.text: Give prostaglandin to close the PDA
Indomethacin closes; prostaglandin keeps it open

pda.explanation: Prostaglandins maintain ductal patency; an inhibitor (indomethacin/ibuprofen) closes it. PGE1 is used to KEEP a duct open in duct-dependent lesions.

pda.stem: What best explains the finding: “Continuous “machinery” murmur at LUSB / left infraclavicular”?

options.text: Diastolic runoff of aortic blood into the PA
Higher neonatal PA pressure limits the diastolic component
Aortic pressure > PA pressure across the whole cardiac cycle → flow in systole AND diastole

pda.explanation: Continuous “machinery” murmur at LUSB / left infraclavicular → Aortic pressure > PA pressure across the whole cardiac cycle → flow in systole AND diastole.

pda.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bounding pulses + wide pulse pressure”?

options.text: Aortic pressure > PA pressure across the whole cardiac cycle → flow in systole AND diastole
Higher neonatal PA pressure limits the diastolic component
Diastolic runoff of aortic blood into the PA

pda.explanation: Bounding pulses + wide pulse pressure → Diastolic runoff of aortic blood into the PA.

tetralogy-of-fallot.stem: A cyanotic toddler suddenly becomes more cyanotic and lethargic, and his systolic ejection murmur becomes quieter. What is the immediate positioning maneuver?
tetralogy-of-fallot.explanation: This is a hypoxic (tet) spell. Knee–chest position raises systemic vascular resistance, reducing the right-to-left shunt. The murmur softened because less blood is crossing the obstructed RVOT.

tetralogy-of-fallot.stem: Regarding murmur intensity vs severity — which is correct?

options.text: Softer / absent murmur = more severe (worse RVOT obstruction)
TOF is cyanotic but typically WITHOUT heart failure
Cyanotic, therefore must be in heart failure

tetralogy-of-fallot.explanation: The murmur is pulmonary-stenosis flow; the worse the obstruction the less flow crosses it. In a tet spell the murmur vanishes.

tetralogy-of-fallot.stem: Regarding why no heart failure — which is correct?

options.text: Cyanotic, therefore must be in heart failure
Softer / absent murmur = more severe (worse RVOT obstruction)
TOF is cyanotic but typically WITHOUT heart failure

tetralogy-of-fallot.explanation: RVOT obstruction limits pulmonary blood flow, so the lungs are not volume-overloaded — cyanosis without CHF.

tetralogy-of-fallot.stem: What best explains the finding: “Systolic ejection murmur at LUSB”?

options.text: P2 soft/inaudible because of pulmonary stenosis
Less flow crosses the RVOT as obstruction worsens
Pulmonary stenosis — the large VSD is silent, so the murmur is NOT from the VSD

tetralogy-of-fallot.explanation: Systolic ejection murmur at LUSB → Pulmonary stenosis — the large VSD is silent, so the murmur is NOT from the VSD.

tetralogy-of-fallot.stem: What best explains the finding: “Single S2”?

options.text: Pulmonary stenosis — the large VSD is silent, so the murmur is NOT from the VSD
Less flow crosses the RVOT as obstruction worsens
P2 soft/inaudible because of pulmonary stenosis

tetralogy-of-fallot.explanation: Single S2 → P2 soft/inaudible because of pulmonary stenosis.

tetralogy-of-fallot.stem: Which should you review before “Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)”?
tetralogy-of-fallot.explanation: Understanding genetic inheritance is crucial for recognizing congenital heart defects.

antiarrhythmic-drugs.stem: A patient on a long-term antiarrhythmic develops pulmonary fibrosis, abnormal thyroid function, and corneal microdeposits. Which drug?
antiarrhythmic-drugs.explanation: This triad of multi-organ toxicity (lung, thyroid, eye, also liver and skin) is characteristic of amiodarone, a Class III drug — hence baseline and periodic TFT/LFT/CXR/eye monitoring.

antiarrhythmic-drugs.stem: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 180/min with no visible P waves (AVNRT). Vagal maneuvers fail. Best acute drug?
antiarrhythmic-drugs.explanation: IV adenosine causes transient AV nodal block that interrupts the AVNRT re-entrant circuit — the first-line acute drug after vagal maneuvers fail.

antiarrhythmic-drugs.stem: Regarding drug in structural/ischemic heart disease — which is correct?

options.text: Flecainide is a good all-round antiarrhythmic
Avoid Class IC (flecainide) in structural / ischemic heart disease — proarrhythmic

antiarrhythmic-drugs.explanation: CAST showed Class IC drugs increase mortality after MI; reserve them for structurally normal hearts.

antiarrhythmic-drugs.stem: Regarding acute avnrt drug — which is correct?

options.text: Avoid Class IC (flecainide) in structural / ischemic heart disease — proarrhythmic
Flecainide is a good all-round antiarrhythmic

antiarrhythmic-drugs.explanation: Adenosine transiently blocks the AV node to terminate the reentrant circuit — first-line acute therapy for AVNRT.

antiarrhythmic-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Procainamide → drug-induced lupus (LE-like syndrome)”?
antiarrhythmic-drugs.explanation: Procainamide → drug-induced lupus (LE-like syndrome) → Class IA chronic toxicity.

antiarrhythmic-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Amiodarone → pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction, corneal microdeposits, blue-grey skin”?
antiarrhythmic-drugs.explanation: Amiodarone → pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction, corneal microdeposits, blue-grey skin → Class III multi-organ toxicity.

antiarrhythmic-drugs.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Antiarrhythmic Drugs (Vaughan-Williams)”?
antiarrhythmic-drugs.explanation: Ion channel mechanisms directly relate to the action of antiarrhythmic drugs.

antiarrhythmic-drugs.stem: Which should you review before “Antiarrhythmic Drugs (Vaughan-Williams)”?
antiarrhythmic-drugs.explanation: Knowledge of ion channel mechanisms is crucial for understanding antiarrhythmic drug actions.

atherosclerosis.stem: Which plaque feature most predicts rupture and acute coronary syndrome?

options.text: Thin fibrous cap over a large necrotic lipid core

atherosclerosis.explanation: A thin fibrous cap over a large lipid/necrotic core is the “vulnerable plaque” that ruptures and thromboses, causing ACS — independent of overall stenosis severity.

atherosclerosis.stem: Regarding stable vs unstable plaque — which is correct?

options.text: The biggest / most stenotic plaque is the most dangerous
Thin-cap vulnerable plaque (often <70% stenosis) ruptures → ACS

atherosclerosis.explanation: Acute events come from plaque COMPOSITION (thin cap, large lipid core), not just degree of stenosis — many MIs arise from non-critical plaques.

atherosclerosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Silent until critical stenosis or an acute event”?
atherosclerosis.explanation: Silent until critical stenosis or an acute event → Slow progressive luminal narrowing.
Understanding lipoproteins is essential for grasping atherogenesis.

arteriosclerosis-patterns.stem: Onion-skin, concentric, laminated arteriolar wall thickening is characteristic of?
arteriosclerosis-patterns.explanation: Hyperplastic (“onion-skin”) arteriolosclerosis — concentric laminated SMC + reduplicated basement membrane — is the hallmark of severe/malignant hypertension. Hyaline is the smooth pink thickening of HTN/DM/aging.

arteriosclerosis-patterns.stem: Regarding which pattern is clinically significant — which is correct?

options.text: Mönckeberg medial calcific sclerosis causes ischemia
Mönckeberg is usually clinically insignificant — the lumen is preserved
Severe HTN, risk of organ rupture (brain, kidney, retina)

arteriosclerosis-patterns.explanation: Calcium deposits in the MEDIA, not the intima; the lumen stays patent, so it’s an incidental finding, not an obstructive lesion.

arteriosclerosis-patterns.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hyaline arteriolosclerosis → benign nephrosclerosis”?

options.text: Severe HTN, risk of organ rupture (brain, kidney, retina)
Medial calcium with a patent lumen

arteriosclerosis-patterns.explanation: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis → benign nephrosclerosis → HTN/DM small-vessel target-organ damage.

arteriosclerosis-patterns.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hyperplastic + fibrinoid necrosis → malignant HTN”?

options.text: Severe HTN, risk of organ rupture (brain, kidney, retina)
Medial calcium with a patent lumen

arteriosclerosis-patterns.explanation: Hyperplastic + fibrinoid necrosis → malignant HTN → Severe HTN, risk of organ rupture (brain, kidney, retina).

aortic-aneurysm.stem: A 70-year-old smoker has a pulsatile periumbilical mass. The most likely cause of this infrarenal aneurysm?
aortic-aneurysm.explanation: Abdominal aortic aneurysms are most commonly atherosclerotic and infrarenal, presenting as a pulsatile mass in an older smoker. Marfan/connective-tissue and aortitis classically cause thoracic aneurysms.

aortic-aneurysm.stem: Regarding cause by location — which is correct?

options.text: AAA = atherosclerosis; TAA = HTN + connective-tissue / medial degeneration

aortic-aneurysm.explanation: Location predicts cause: abdominal (infrarenal) is classically atherosclerotic; thoracic is HTN with cystic medial degeneration (Marfan, bicuspid valve, aortitis).

aortic-aneurysm.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pulsatile abdominal mass (AAA)”?

options.text: Compression of adjacent structures / recurrent laryngeal nerve

aortic-aneurysm.explanation: Pulsatile abdominal mass (AAA) → Dilated infrarenal aorta.

aortic-aneurysm.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sudden severe pain + hypotension”?

options.text: Compression of adjacent structures / recurrent laryngeal nerve

aortic-aneurysm.explanation: Sudden severe pain + hypotension → Rupture — surgical emergency.

aortic-aneurysm.stem: Which should you review before “Aortic Aneurysm (TAA & AAA)”?
aortic-aneurysm.explanation: Basic anatomy knowledge may help in understanding vascular structures.

aortic-dissection.stem: A patient has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back. Which physical examination finding suggests ascending aortic involvement?
aortic-dissection.explanation: Ascending/root involvement → aortic valve incompetence → acute AR → early diastolic murmur. Tachycardia is non-specific and does not localize.

aortic-dissection.stem: Regarding physical examination finding — which is correct?

options.text: False lumen occludes a branch artery

aortic-dissection.explanation: Tachycardia is a non-specific stress response. The exam sign that LOCALIZES ascending involvement is the early diastolic murmur of acute aortic regurgitation.

aortic-dissection.stem: What best explains the finding: “Early diastolic murmur (acute AR)”?

options.text: False lumen occludes a branch artery

aortic-dissection.explanation: Early diastolic murmur (acute AR) → Ascending/root involvement → aortic valve incompetence.

aortic-dissection.stem: What best explains the finding: “Inter-arm BP differential / pulse deficit”?

options.text: False lumen occludes a branch artery

aortic-dissection.explanation: Inter-arm BP differential / pulse deficit → False lumen occludes a branch artery.

aortic-dissection.stem: Which should you review before “Aortic Dissection”?
aortic-dissection.explanation: Understanding heart sounds is crucial for identifying acute aortic regurgitation.

ihd-overview.stem: Chest pain at rest, increasing in frequency and severity over days, lasting >20 min and not relieved by rest or nitrates. Which category?
ihd-overview.explanation: Rest pain, crescendo pattern, prolonged duration, and lack of relief define unstable angina — an acute coronary syndrome from an unstable plaque, not the exertional/relieved pattern of stable angina.

ihd-overview.stem: Regarding stable vs unstable angina — which is correct?

options.text: Exertional pain relieved by rest = unstable
Exertional + relieved by rest/nitrates = STABLE; rest pain, crescendo, >20 min not relieved = UNSTABLE (ACS)
Demand ischemia across a fixed stenosis

ihd-overview.explanation: Unstable angina is ACS from an unstable plaque — its hallmark is pain AT REST / crescendo not relieved by rest, which changes urgency to emergency.

ihd-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Stable angina: exertional pain relieved by rest/nitrates <5 min”?

options.text: Demand ischemia across a fixed stenosis

ihd-overview.explanation: Stable angina: exertional pain relieved by rest/nitrates <5 min → Demand ischemia across a fixed stenosis.

ihd-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Unstable angina: rest pain, crescendo, >20 min, NOT relieved”?

options.text: Demand ischemia across a fixed stenosis

ihd-overview.explanation: Unstable angina: rest pain, crescendo, >20 min, NOT relieved → Acute plaque change (ACS).

myocardial-infarction-pathology.stem: Cardiac troponin in acute MI rises at, peaks at, and remains elevated for approximately:

options.text: Rise 2–4 h, peak ~48 h, remain 7–10 days
Rise immediately, peak 6 h, gone by 24 h
Rise 12 h, peak 24 h, gone by 3 days
Rise 24 h, peak 72 h, remain 14 days

myocardial-infarction-pathology.explanation: Cardiac troponin rises within 2–4 h of myocyte necrosis, peaks around 48 h, and stays elevated for 7–10 days — useful for both early and late diagnosis.

myocardial-infarction-pathology.stem: Regarding transmural vs subendocardial — which is correct?

options.text: Total occlusion → transmural (STEMI); partial occlusion / global hypoperfusion → subendocardial (NSTEMI)

myocardial-infarction-pathology.explanation: The subendocardium is the last-perfused, most vulnerable zone, so partial occlusion or global hypoperfusion infarcts the inner third without ST elevation.

myocardial-infarction-pathology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Chest pain + rapid weak pulse + sweating”?
myocardial-infarction-pathology.explanation: Chest pain + rapid weak pulse + sweating → Ischemia + sympathetic activation.

myocardial-infarction-pathology.stem: Which should you review before “Myocardial Infarction — Pathology”?
myocardial-infarction-pathology.explanation: Understanding necrosis patterns is essential for grasping myocardial infarction pathology.

mi-complications.stem: 5 days after an MI, a patient develops sudden hypotension, a new harsh holosystolic murmur, and pulmonary edema. Most likely complication?

options.text: Papillary muscle or interventricular septal rupture

mi-complications.explanation: A new holosystolic murmur with shock on days 3–7 indicates mechanical rupture — papillary muscle (acute mitral regurgitation) or interventricular septum (VSD) — during the macrophage wall-softening phase.

mi-complications.stem: Regarding timing of complication — which is correct?

options.text: A new murmur + shock 5 days post-MI is just recurrent ischemia
Days 3–7 → mechanical rupture (papillary muscle / septum / free wall)
Papillary muscle rupture (acute MR) or septal rupture (VSD)

mi-complications.explanation: Days 3–7 is the macrophage phase of maximal wall softening; a new murmur or sudden tamponade then signals mechanical rupture — a surgical emergency.

mi-complications.stem: What best explains the finding: “New holosystolic murmur on days 3–7”?

options.text: Papillary muscle rupture (acute MR) or septal rupture (VSD)

mi-complications.explanation: New holosystolic murmur on days 3–7 → Papillary muscle rupture (acute MR) or septal rupture (VSD).

mi-complications.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pericardial friction rub days 2–3”?

options.text: Papillary muscle rupture (acute MR) or septal rupture (VSD)

mi-complications.explanation: Pericardial friction rub days 2–3 → Post-infarct fibrinous pericarditis.

mi-complications.stem: Which should you review before “Complications of Myocardial Infarction”?
mi-complications.explanation: Understanding shock mechanisms is crucial for MI complications.

antiplatelets.stem: Which antiplatelet irreversibly acetylates COX-1, reducing thromboxane A₂ for the platelet’s ~10-day lifespan?
antiplatelets.explanation: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1, abolishing thromboxane A₂ synthesis for the platelet’s ~10-day lifespan. Clopidogrel targets P2Y12; ticagrelor is reversible; abciximab blocks GP IIb/IIIa.

options.text: All antiplatelets are reversible like other NSAIDs
Aspirin & clopidogrel are IRREVERSIBLE (last the platelet’s ~10-day life); ticagrelor is reversible

antiplatelets.explanation: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1 and clopidogrel irreversibly blocks P2Y12, so the effect persists until new platelets form (~10 days) — relevant before surgery.

antiplatelets.stem: What best explains the finding: “GI bleeding / peptic ulcer”?
antiplatelets.explanation: GI bleeding / peptic ulcer → Aspirin inhibits protective COX.

antiplatelets.stem: Which should you review before “Antiplatelet Drugs”?
antiplatelets.explanation: Understanding hemostasis is essential for grasping antiplatelet mechanisms.

anticoagulants.stem: A pregnant woman needs anticoagulation for VTE. Which agent is appropriate, and how is it monitored / reversed?
anticoagulants.explanation: Warfarin is teratogenic, so heparin/LMWH is used in pregnancy — monitored by aPTT (or anti-Xa) and reversed by protamine. (Warfarin uses INR + vitamin K; the two must not be mixed up.)

anticoagulants.stem: Regarding monitoring & antidote — which is correct?

options.text: Heparin is monitored by INR and reversed by vitamin K
Heparin = aPTT + protamine; Warfarin = INR/PT + vitamin K
Mechanical valve or moderate–severe mitral stenosis → warfarin
Use a DOAC for AF with a mechanical valve

anticoagulants.explanation: Don’t swap them: heparin acts on antithrombin (aPTT, protamine antidote); warfarin blocks vitamin K–dependent factors (INR, vitamin K antidote).

anticoagulants.stem: Regarding doac vs warfarin in valvular disease — which is correct?

options.text: Use a DOAC for AF with a mechanical valve
Heparin = aPTT + protamine; Warfarin = INR/PT + vitamin K
Mechanical valve or moderate–severe mitral stenosis → warfarin
Heparin is monitored by INR and reversed by vitamin K

anticoagulants.explanation: DOACs are contraindicated/inferior for mechanical valves and significant mitral stenosis — warfarin is required there.

anticoagulants.stem: What best explains the finding: “HIT — thrombocytopenia + paradoxical thrombosis”?
anticoagulants.explanation: HIT — thrombocytopenia + paradoxical thrombosis → Immune-mediated, heparin (esp. UFH).
Understanding hemostasis is essential for grasping anticoagulant mechanisms.

fibrinolytics.stem: A STEMI patient cannot reach a PCI centre within 120 minutes and presents 3 hours after symptom onset. Best reperfusion?
fibrinolytics.explanation: Within 12 h of symptom onset, if primary PCI cannot be delivered within 120 min, fibrinolysis should be given promptly (ideally within 10 min of diagnosis) to achieve reperfusion.

fibrinolytics.stem: Regarding reperfusion choice — which is correct?

options.text: Primary PCI preferred if achievable <120 min; fibrinolysis only if PCI not timely & symptoms <12 h

fibrinolytics.explanation: PCI is the preferred reperfusion strategy; fibrinolytics are the fallback when timely PCI isn’t available, within the 12-hour window.

aortic-stenosis.stem: A 72-year-old with exertional syncope has a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right 2nd ICS radiating to the carotids and a soft S2. Diagnosis?
aortic-stenosis.explanation: Exertional syncope + an ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids + a soft S2 = aortic stenosis, with concentric LVH from chronic pressure overload.

aortic-stenosis.stem: Regarding murmur radiation — which is correct?

options.text: Systolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla
Ejection systolic murmur at the aortic area radiating to the CAROTIDS = AS
Turbulent flow across the stenotic valve

aortic-stenosis.explanation: Radiation to the carotids (not axilla) and a crescendo-decrescendo shape localize AS; radiation to the axilla suggests mitral regurgitation.

aortic-stenosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids”?

options.text: Fixed cardiac output cannot meet exercise demand
Turbulent flow across the stenotic valve

aortic-stenosis.explanation: Ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids → Turbulent flow across the stenotic valve.

aortic-stenosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Soft/absent S2 + slow-rising pulse (parvus et tardus)”?

options.text: Turbulent flow across the stenotic valve
Fixed cardiac output cannot meet exercise demand

aortic-stenosis.explanation: Soft/absent S2 + slow-rising pulse (parvus et tardus) → Reduced, delayed ejection.

aortic-stenosis.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Aortic Stenosis”?
aortic-stenosis.explanation: Physical examination techniques are crucial for diagnosing aortic stenosis.

aortic-stenosis.stem: Which should you review before “Aortic Stenosis”?
aortic-stenosis.explanation: Understanding great vessels is essential for grasping aortic stenosis.

mitral-stenosis.stem: A 50-year-old with childhood rheumatic fever has a loud S1, an opening snap, and a mid-diastolic rumble at the apex, plus atrial fibrillation and an enlarged left atrium. Diagnosis?
mitral-stenosis.explanation: Loud S1 + opening snap + mid-diastolic apical rumble with LA enlargement and AF after rheumatic fever is classic mitral stenosis from commissural fusion.

mitral-stenosis.stem: Regarding diastolic vs systolic murmur — which is correct?

options.text: Mitral valve disease always gives a systolic murmur
Mitral STENOSIS = mid-DIASTOLIC rumble + opening snap (regurgitation is systolic)
Impeded diastolic LV inflow across the stenotic valve

mitral-stenosis.explanation: Stenosis impedes diastolic inflow → a diastolic rumble; regurgitation is a systolic murmur. Loud S1 + opening snap are MS hallmarks.

mitral-stenosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Loud S1 + opening snap + mid-diastolic rumble at the apex”?

options.text: Impeded diastolic LV inflow across the stenotic valve

mitral-stenosis.explanation: Loud S1 + opening snap + mid-diastolic rumble at the apex → Impeded diastolic LV inflow across the stenotic valve.

mitral-stenosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Atrial fibrillation (irregularly irregular)”?

options.text: Impeded diastolic LV inflow across the stenotic valve

mitral-stenosis.stem: Which should you review before “Mitral Stenosis”?
mitral-stenosis.explanation: Rheumatic heart disease is the primary cause of mitral stenosis.

mitral-valve-prolapse.stem: A 19-year-old woman with a mid-systolic click and aortic root dilation dies suddenly; autopsy shows a prolapsed mitral valve with elongated, ruptured chordae tendineae. Which gene is most likely mutated?
mitral-valve-prolapse.explanation: Mid-systolic click + aortic root dilation + myxomatous mitral prolapse with chordae rupture points to Marfan syndrome — a fibrillin-1 (FBN1) mutation.

mitral-valve-prolapse.stem: Regarding genetic association — which is correct?

options.text: MVP is due to a beta-myosin mutation (HCM)
MVP (myxomatous degeneration) is linked to fibrillin-1 (Marfan)

mitral-valve-prolapse.explanation: Fibrillin-1 defects (Marfan) cause myxomatous valve degeneration; beta-myosin/sarcomere mutations cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — a different disease.

mitral-valve-prolapse.stem: What best explains the finding: “Mid-systolic click ± late systolic murmur at the apex”?
mitral-valve-prolapse.explanation: Mid-systolic click ± late systolic murmur at the apex → Sudden tensing of prolapsing leaflet/chordae.

mitral-valve-prolapse.stem: What best explains the finding: “Click earlier/louder with standing or Valsalva”?
mitral-valve-prolapse.explanation: Click earlier/louder with standing or Valsalva → ↓ preload → smaller LV → earlier prolapse.

mitral-valve-prolapse.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Mitral Valve Prolapse”?
mitral-valve-prolapse.explanation: Clinical implications of mitral valve prolapse include the risk of infective endocarditis.

mitral-valve-prolapse.stem: Which should you review before “Mitral Valve Prolapse”?
mitral-valve-prolapse.explanation: Understanding heart sounds is essential for diagnosing mitral valve prolapse.

rheumatic-heart-disease.stem: A patient with chronic mitral stenosis had a childhood illness with fever, rash, migratory joint pain, and chorea. What infection precedes this disease?

options.text: Group D alpha-hemolytic streptococcal infection of the heart
Group A beta-hemolytic streptococcal infection of the pharynx
Streptococcus pyogenes infection of the skin
Staphylococcus aureus infection of the lungs

rheumatic-heart-disease.explanation: Rheumatic fever follows Group A β-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis (~2–3 weeks prior), via molecular mimicry — not a skin or staphylococcal infection.

rheumatic-heart-disease.stem: Regarding preceding infection — which is correct?

options.text: Caused by Group D / skin strep / Staphylococcus

rheumatic-heart-disease.explanation: Rheumatic fever follows Group A strep throat (not skin/impetigo, which causes post-strep glomerulonephritis); ASO titer rises.

rheumatic-heart-disease.stem: What best explains the finding: “Migratory polyarthritis, carditis (new murmur), subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea”?
rheumatic-heart-disease.explanation: Migratory polyarthritis, carditis (new murmur), subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea → Jones major criteria.

rheumatic-heart-disease.stem: What best explains the finding: “Chronic: opening snap + mid-diastolic rumble (mitral stenosis)”?
rheumatic-heart-disease.explanation: Chronic: opening snap + mid-diastolic rumble (mitral stenosis) → Healed valve scarring.

rheumatic-heart-disease.stem: Which should you review before “Rheumatic Fever & Heart Disease”?
rheumatic-heart-disease.explanation: Group A strep is the causative agent of rheumatic fever.

infective-endocarditis.stem: A 29-year-old man has 3 days of high fever, delirium, a pansystolic murmur, splenomegaly, and splinter hemorrhages under his nails. Most likely diagnosis?
infective-endocarditis.explanation: Rapid fever, a new regurgitant murmur, splenomegaly, and splinter hemorrhages indicate acute infective endocarditis — classically S. aureus on a previously normal valve.

infective-endocarditis.stem: Regarding acute vs subacute organism — which is correct?

options.text: All endocarditis is from Strep viridans
Acute, destructive on normal valves = S. aureus; subacute on damaged valves = Strep viridans

infective-endocarditis.explanation: Virulence determines the picture: S. aureus causes acute fulminant IE (also IVDU/tricuspid); viridans causes subacute IE on previously abnormal valves.

infective-endocarditis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fever + new regurgitant (pansystolic) murmur”?
infective-endocarditis.explanation: Fever + new regurgitant (pansystolic) murmur → Valve vegetation/destruction.

infective-endocarditis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Osler nodes (painful), Janeway lesions (painless), splinter hemorrhages, Roth spots”?
infective-endocarditis.explanation: Osler nodes (painful), Janeway lesions (painless), splinter hemorrhages, Roth spots → Immune complexes (Osler) & septic emboli (Janeway/Roth).

infective-endocarditis.stem: Which should you review before “Infective Endocarditis”?
infective-endocarditis.explanation: Understanding viridans strep is crucial for subacute IE.

nonbacterial-endocarditis.stem: A patient with pancreatic adenocarcinoma has a cerebral infarct; blood cultures are negative; autopsy shows a bland (sterile) valvular thrombus. Diagnosis?
nonbacterial-endocarditis.explanation: A sterile, bland valvular thrombus with negative cultures and embolic stroke in a patient with adenocarcinoma is nonbacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis — a paraneoplastic/hypercoagulable phenomenon.

nonbacterial-endocarditis.stem: Regarding cause of stroke with negative cultures — which is correct?

options.text: Nonbacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis — sterile bland thrombus in malignancy

nonbacterial-endocarditis.explanation: Negative blood cultures + embolic stroke in a cancer patient (e.g. pancreatic adenocarcinoma) points to NBTE — sterile fibrin-platelet vegetations, not infection.

nonbacterial-endocarditis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Embolic event with NEGATIVE blood cultures”?
nonbacterial-endocarditis.explanation: Embolic event with NEGATIVE blood cultures → Sterile vegetation embolizes.

nonbacterial-endocarditis.stem: What best explains the finding: “SLE features (malar rash, arthritis, nephritis, painless oral ulcers)”?
nonbacterial-endocarditis.explanation: SLE features (malar rash, arthritis, nephritis, painless oral ulcers) → Libman-Sacks underlying lupus.

nonbacterial-endocarditis.stem: Which should you review before “Marantic & Libman-Sacks Endocarditis”?
nonbacterial-endocarditis.explanation: Understanding of infective organisms is crucial for differentiating from sterile vegetations.

acs-spectrum.stem: ECG shows diffuse concave ST elevation with PR-segment depression and no reciprocal ST depression, in a patient with pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward. Most likely?
acs-spectrum.explanation: Diffuse (non-territorial) concave ST elevation with PR depression (Spodick sign) and no reciprocal changes, plus positional pleuritic pain, is acute pericarditis — not a STEMI.

acs-spectrum.stem: Regarding stemi vs mimic — which is correct?

options.text: Diffuse concave STE + PR depression (Spodick), no reciprocal change = pericarditis

acs-spectrum.explanation: Pericarditis gives widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and NO reciprocal changes; treating it as STEMI exposes the patient to thrombolysis harm.

acs-spectrum.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ischemic chest pain ± radiation, diaphoresis”?
acs-spectrum.explanation: Ischemic chest pain ± radiation, diaphoresis → Myocardial ischemia + sympathetic activation.

acs-spectrum.stem: What best explains the finding: “ST elevation in a coronary territory (+ reciprocal change)”?
acs-spectrum.explanation: ST elevation in a coronary territory (+ reciprocal change) → Transmural injury current = STEMI.

acs-spectrum.stem: Which should you review before “ACS Spectrum & Diagnosis”?

options.text: Cardiac Biomarkers in Acute Coronary Syndrome

acs-spectrum.explanation: Understanding biomarkers is essential for diagnosing ACS.

acs-management.stem: First-line immediate antiplatelet for a patient with an acute STEMI (no contraindication)?
acs-management.explanation: Chewed aspirin 150–300 mg is given immediately in suspected ACS for rapid antiplatelet effect, alongside a P2Y12 inhibitor and anticoagulation — before reperfusion.

acs-management.stem: Regarding oxygen use — which is correct?

options.text: Give high-flow O₂ to every ACS patient
Oxygen only if SpO₂ <90% (or respiratory distress)
Check V4R; if RV infarct → fluids, AVOID nitrates
Give nitrates for chest pain in inferior STEMI

acs-management.explanation: Routine hyperoxia gives no benefit and may harm; supplemental oxygen is reserved for hypoxemia.

acs-management.stem: Regarding inferior stemi drug — which is correct?

options.text: Give nitrates for chest pain in inferior STEMI
Oxygen only if SpO₂ <90% (or respiratory distress)
Check V4R; if RV infarct → fluids, AVOID nitrates
Give high-flow O₂ to every ACS patient

acs-management.explanation: RV infarction is preload-dependent — nitrates drop preload and cause profound hypotension.

acs-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “SpO₂ <90% → give oxygen”?

options.text: Oxygen only for hypoxemia, not routine

acs-management.explanation: SpO₂ <90% → give oxygen → Oxygen only for hypoxemia, not routine.

acs-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “Inferior STEMI → check V4R; RV infarct → fluids, not nitrates”?

options.text: Oxygen only for hypoxemia, not routine

acs-management.explanation: Inferior STEMI → check V4R; RV infarct → fluids, not nitrates → RV infarct is preload-dependent.

cardiomyopathy-overview.stem: By definition, cardiomyopathy is a myocardial disorder in the ABSENCE of which conditions?

options.text: CAD, hypertension, valvular, and congenital heart disease

cardiomyopathy-overview.explanation: The ESC 2008 definition labels CMP a primary myocardial disorder only when CAD, hypertension, valvular disease, and congenital heart disease have been excluded.

cardiomyopathy-overview.stem: Regarding primary cmp vs secondary mimic — which is correct?

options.text: A dilated heart in a hypertensive/ischemic patient = dilated cardiomyopathy
Primary CMP requires EXCLUDING CAD, hypertension, valvular & congenital disease

cardiomyopathy-overview.explanation: By definition cardiomyopathy is intrinsic muscle disease; if HTN/ischemia/valve disease explains it, it is a secondary mimic, not primary CMP.

cardiomyopathy-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dilated → CHF + functional mitral regurgitation”?
cardiomyopathy-overview.explanation: Dilated → CHF + functional mitral regurgitation → Chamber dilation.

cardiomyopathy-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypertrophic → ejection murmur + SCD risk”?
cardiomyopathy-overview.explanation: Hypertrophic → ejection murmur + SCD risk → LVOT obstruction / disarray.

dilated-cardiomyopathy.stem: A 30-year-old has progressive dyspnea, an S3, a displaced apex, and echo showing all-chamber dilation with EF 22%. Which cardiomyopathy?
dilated-cardiomyopathy.explanation: All-chamber dilation with a markedly reduced EF and an S3 is dilated cardiomyopathy (systolic dysfunction).

dilated-cardiomyopathy.stem: Regarding inheritance of genetic dcm — which is correct?

options.text: All genetic DCM is autosomal dominant
Cytoskeletal mutations are usually AD, but dystrophin (Duchenne/Becker) is X-linked
Annular dilation stretches the mitral valve

dilated-cardiomyopathy.explanation: Most familial DCM is AD (cytoskeletal genes), but dystrophin-related muscular dystrophies cause X-linked DCM.

dilated-cardiomyopathy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Displaced diffuse apex + S3 gallop”?

options.text: Annular dilation stretches the mitral valve

dilated-cardiomyopathy.explanation: Displaced diffuse apex + S3 gallop → Dilated, volume-overloaded LV.

dilated-cardiomyopathy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Apical pansystolic murmur (functional MR)”?

options.text: Annular dilation stretches the mitral valve

dilated-cardiomyopathy.explanation: Apical pansystolic murmur (functional MR) → Annular dilation stretches the mitral valve.

hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy.stem: A young athlete collapses; echo shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy with SAM, and his ejection murmur gets LOUDER on standing. Which gene class is mutated?
hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy.explanation: HCM is caused by sarcomere-gene mutations (commonly β-myosin heavy chain and myosin-binding protein C); the murmur louder with reduced preload is the dynamic LVOT obstruction signature.

hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy.stem: Regarding effect of preload on the murmur — which is correct?

options.text: Standing/Valsalva softens the murmur (like aortic stenosis)
The HOCM murmur gets LOUDER with ↓preload (Valsalva, standing)
Less LV volume → more outflow obstruction

hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy.explanation: Less LV volume brings the septum and mitral leaflet closer → more outflow obstruction → louder murmur; AS and MR murmurs soften with reduced preload.

hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Harsh mid-systolic ejection murmur, LOUDER with ↓preload (Valsalva, standing)”?

options.text: Less LV volume → more outflow obstruction

hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy.explanation: Harsh mid-systolic ejection murmur, LOUDER with ↓preload (Valsalva, standing) → Less LV volume → more outflow obstruction.

hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Exertional syncope”?

options.text: Less LV volume → more outflow obstruction

hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy.explanation: Exertional syncope → Dynamic LVOT obstruction / arrhythmia.

hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy.stem: Which should you review before “Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM)”?
hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy.explanation: Understanding genetic mutations is crucial for HCM.

restrictive-cardiomyopathy.stem: Endomyocardial biopsy shows amorphous pink deposits that stain with Congo red and show apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Diagnosis?
restrictive-cardiomyopathy.explanation: Apple-green birefringence on Congo red staining is pathognomonic of amyloid — the most common infiltrative cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy.

restrictive-cardiomyopathy.stem: Regarding rcm vs constrictive pericarditis — which is correct?

options.text: Right HF with a normal-size heart = constrictive pericarditis
Restrictive CMP mimics constrictive pericarditis — biopsy/imaging distinguishes (amyloid infiltration)

restrictive-cardiomyopathy.explanation: Both present with right HF and normal-size ventricles; restrictive CMP is intrinsic myocardial stiffening (often amyloid), constriction is pericardial — management differs.

restrictive-cardiomyopathy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Right-sided HF: ↑JVP, hepatomegaly, edema, ascites”?
restrictive-cardiomyopathy.explanation: Right-sided HF: ↑JVP, hepatomegaly, edema, ascites → Elevated filling pressures.

restrictive-cardiomyopathy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Signs of systemic amyloidosis”?
restrictive-cardiomyopathy.explanation: Signs of systemic amyloidosis → Underlying infiltrative disease.

arvc.stem: A young athlete has exertional VT; cardiac MRI shows fibrofatty replacement of the RV free wall, and he has woolly hair and thick palms and soles. Diagnosis?
arvc.explanation: RV fibrofatty replacement with exertional VT plus palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and woolly hair is ARVC in the setting of Naxos syndrome (a desmosomal disease).

arvc.stem: Regarding which cmp causes scd via the rv — which is correct?

options.text: Sudden death in a young athlete is always HCM
ARVC (RV fibrofatty replacement, desmosomal) also causes exertional VT / SCD

arvc.explanation: HCM is the commonest cause of young-athlete SCD, but ARVC is a key differential — RV-predominant, desmosomal, with LBBB-morphology VT and the Naxos association.

arvc.stem: What best explains the finding: “Palpitations, syncope, VT in a young person”?
arvc.explanation: Palpitations, syncope, VT in a young person → RV electrical instability.

arvc.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sudden cardiac death (often on exertion)”?
arvc.explanation: Sudden cardiac death (often on exertion) → Ventricular fibrillation.

myocarditis.stem: A 23-year-old, 2 weeks after a viral illness, has chest pain, heart failure, and tachycardia out of proportion to a low-grade fever; troponin is mildly elevated and persistent. Most likely diagnosis?
myocarditis.explanation: A post-viral picture with heart failure, tachycardia out of proportion to fever, and a slow/persistent troponin rise is classic for myocarditis.

myocarditis.stem: Regarding troponin pattern — which is correct?

options.text: Troponin behaves the same as in acute MI
Myocarditis troponin rises slower and stays elevated longer than AMI

myocarditis.explanation: AMI gives a sharp rise-and-fall; myocarditis shows a slower, more prolonged troponin elevation, with tachycardia out of proportion to fever.

myocarditis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Tachycardia out of proportion to fever”?
myocarditis.explanation: Tachycardia out of proportion to fever → Myocardial irritation.

myocarditis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Heart failure / chest pain / arrhythmia after a viral prodrome”?
myocarditis.explanation: Heart failure / chest pain / arrhythmia after a viral prodrome → Myocyte injury.

cardiogenic-shock.stem: After a large anterior MI, a patient is hypotensive (SBP 80), cold and clammy, with raised JVP and pulmonary edema. Type of shock?
cardiogenic-shock.explanation: Pump failure after a large MI with hypotension, cold/clammy skin, and congestion (raised JVP, pulmonary edema) is cardiogenic shock.

cardiogenic-shock.stem: Regarding type of shock — which is correct?

options.text: Hypotension + cold clammy skin must be hypovolemic shock
Cold/clammy + ↑JVP + pulmonary edema + a cardiac cause = cardiogenic shock
Low CO with reflex sympathetic drive

cardiogenic-shock.explanation: Both cardiogenic and hypovolemic shock are cold (vasoconstricted), but cardiogenic shock has congestion (↑JVP, edema) and a cardiac cause; hypovolemia has LOW filling pressures.

cardiogenic-shock.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cold, clammy, mottled skin; weak thready pulse”?

options.text: Low CO with reflex sympathetic drive

cardiogenic-shock.explanation: Cold, clammy, mottled skin; weak thready pulse → Intense vasoconstriction + low output.

cardiogenic-shock.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypotension (SBP <90) + tachycardia”?

options.text: Low CO with reflex sympathetic drive

cardiogenic-shock.explanation: Hypotension (SBP <90) + tachycardia → Low CO with reflex sympathetic drive.

scai-shock-classification.stem: A patient has SBP 85 and HR 110 but normal mentation, a clear lactate, and good urine output. SCAI stage?
scai-shock-classification.explanation: Hemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia) WITHOUT evidence of hypoperfusion is SCAI stage B; hypoperfusion markers would push it to stage C.

scai-shock-classification.stem: Regarding when perfusion is compromised — which is correct?

options.text: Hypotension alone means classic shock (stage C)
Hypotension WITHOUT hypoperfusion = stage B; with hypoperfusion (lactate↑, end-organ) = stage C

scai-shock-classification.explanation: Stage B is hemodynamic instability without hypoperfusion; only when perfusion markers (lactate, urine, mentation) deteriorate is it “classic” shock (C) — important for escalation.

scai-shock-classification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Lactate >2 + cold/mottled + altered mentation”?
scai-shock-classification.explanation: Lactate >2 + cold/mottled + altered mentation → Hypoperfusion = stage C onward.

scai-shock-classification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Near-pulselessness, lactate >5, pH <7.2”?
Which should you review before “SCAI Shock Classification & Support”?
scai-shock-classification.explanation: Understanding shock mechanisms is essential for SCAI classification.

cardiac-arrest.stem: A patient in PEA arrest has distended neck veins and absent breath sounds on one side after central-line placement. Which reversible cause should you treat immediately?
cardiac-arrest.explanation: Distended neck veins with unilateral absent breath sounds after a central-line attempt indicates tension pneumothorax — needle decompression is the immediate reversible-cause treatment.

cardiac-arrest.stem: Regarding pea / asystole management — which is correct?

options.text: Defibrillate a PEA or asystole arrest
Non-shockable (PEA/asystole) → CPR + epinephrine + reverse the Hs/Ts (do NOT shock)

cardiac-arrest.explanation: Only VF and pulseless VT are shockable; PEA and asystole need CPR, epinephrine, and correction of the underlying reversible cause.

cardiac-arrest.stem: What best explains the finding: “Unresponsive, pulseless, apneic”?
cardiac-arrest.explanation: Unresponsive, pulseless, apneic → No cardiac output.

cardiac-arrest.stem: What best explains the finding: “Distended neck veins ± unilateral absent breath sounds”?
cardiac-arrest.explanation: Distended neck veins ± unilateral absent breath sounds → Tension pneumothorax / tamponade clue.

cardiac-arrest.stem: Which should you review before “Cardiac Arrest & Reversible Causes”?
cardiac-arrest.explanation: Understanding cell injury mechanisms is crucial for grasping cardiac arrest causes.

heart-failure-overview.stem: Which finding best confirms systemic venous congestion in heart failure?

options.text: Positive hepatojugular reflux with raised JVP

heart-failure-overview.explanation: A positive hepatojugular reflux with elevated JVP demonstrates systemic venous congestion (backward right-heart failure).

heart-failure-overview.stem: Regarding hfref vs hfpef — which is correct?

options.text: All heart failure has a low ejection fraction
HFpEF (≥50%) has a PRESERVED EF — failure is diastolic (stiff ventricle)

heart-failure-overview.explanation: About half of HF has preserved EF; the problem is impaired filling (diastolic dysfunction), not pump weakness — the EF can be normal.

heart-failure-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pulmonary rales + ↑JVP + positive hepatojugular reflux”?
heart-failure-overview.explanation: Pulmonary rales + ↑JVP + positive hepatojugular reflux → Pulmonary & systemic venous congestion.

heart-failure-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Peripheral edema, congestive hepatomegaly, ascites”?
heart-failure-overview.explanation: Peripheral edema, congestive hepatomegaly, ascites → Systemic venous backpressure.

heart-failure-overview.stem: Which should you review before “Heart Failure — Overview & Classification”?

hfref-systolic.stem: Which drug class is a cornerstone of HFrEF therapy because it interrupts maladaptive neurohormonal remodeling?
hfref-systolic.explanation: Neurohormonal blockade (ACEi/ARB, beta-blockers, MRAs, and SGLT2 inhibitors) interrupts the RAAS/SNS-driven remodeling cycle and improves survival in HFrEF.

hfref-systolic.stem: Regarding why block raas / sympathetic in hf — which is correct?

options.text: Sympathetic & RAAS activation are helpful compensation, so don’t block them
Chronic RAAS/SNS activation is MALADAPTIVE → remodeling; blocking them (ACEi, BB, MRA) improves survival

hfref-systolic.explanation: Acutely they maintain BP, but chronically they drive remodeling and progression — neurohormonal blockade is the cornerstone of HFrEF therapy and reverse-remodels the heart.

hfref-systolic.stem: What best explains the finding: “S3 gallop, displaced apex”?
hfref-systolic.explanation: S3 gallop, displaced apex → Dilated, volume-overloaded LV.

hfref-systolic.stem: What best explains the finding: “↑ BNP / NT-proBNP”?
Which should you review before “HFrEF — Systolic Heart Failure”?
hfref-systolic.explanation: Understanding heart failure classification is essential for grasping HFrEF.

hfpef-diastolic.stem: A hypertensive patient has dyspnea, an S4 gallop, a sustained apex, and echo showing concentric LVH with EF 60%. Type of heart failure?
hfpef-diastolic.explanation: Preserved EF with concentric LVH, an S4, and a sustained apex in a hypertensive patient is HFpEF — diastolic dysfunction from a stiff hypertrophied ventricle.

hfpef-diastolic.stem: Regarding gallop sound — which is correct?

options.text: A gallop in HF is always S3 (volume overload)
HFpEF (stiff hypertrophied LV) gives an S4; S3 suggests volume overload / systolic HF
Atrium contracting against a stiff ventricle

hfpef-diastolic.explanation: S4 = atrium contracting against a stiff ventricle (diastolic dysfunction/LVH); S3 = rapid filling into a dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle (systolic HF).

hfpef-diastolic.stem: What best explains the finding: “S4 gallop”?

options.text: Atrium contracting against a stiff ventricle

hfpef-diastolic.explanation: S4 gallop → Atrium contracting against a stiff ventricle.

hfpef-diastolic.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sustained (non-displaced) apex + congestion”?

options.text: Atrium contracting against a stiff ventricle

hfpef-diastolic.explanation: Sustained (non-displaced) apex + congestion → Concentric LVH; backward failure.

hfpef-diastolic.stem: Which should you review before “HFpEF — Diastolic Heart Failure”?
hfpef-diastolic.explanation: Understanding heart sounds is crucial for identifying S4 gallop in HFpEF.

right-sided-hf.stem: What is the most common cause of right-sided heart failure?
right-sided-hf.explanation: Left-sided heart failure raises pulmonary venous and arterial pressures, overloading the RV — the most common cause of right-sided heart failure.

right-sided-hf.stem: Regarding commonest cause of right hf — which is correct?

options.text: Right heart failure is usually due to lung disease (cor pulmonale)
The most common cause of right HF is LEFT heart failure

right-sided-hf.explanation: Left HF raises pulmonary pressures that overload the RV; isolated right HF from lung disease (cor pulmonale) is less common.

right-sided-hf.stem: What best explains the finding: “↑JVP, hepatojugular reflux, hepatomegaly, peripheral edema, ascites”?
right-sided-hf.explanation: ↑JVP, hepatojugular reflux, hepatomegaly, peripheral edema, ascites → Systemic venous backpressure.

right-sided-hf.stem: What best explains the finding: “Acute PE: sudden dyspnea, ↑JVP, hypotension (acute cor pulmonale)”?
right-sided-hf.explanation: Acute PE: sudden dyspnea, ↑JVP, hypotension (acute cor pulmonale) → Acute RV pressure overload.

right-sided-hf.stem: Which should you review before “Right-sided Heart Failure”?
right-sided-hf.explanation: Overview provides foundational knowledge on heart failure types.

antianginal-principles.stem: The primary pharmacologic strategy in chronic stable angina is to:

options.text: Increase coronary oxygen supply with drugs
Reduce myocardial oxygen demand (preload / afterload / HR / contractility)

antianginal-principles.explanation: Antianginal drugs primarily reduce myocardial oxygen demand by lowering preload, afterload, heart rate, and contractility; raising supply is mainly achieved by revascularization.

antianginal-principles.stem: Regarding determinants of o₂ demand — which is correct?

options.text: Antianginals work mainly by increasing oxygen supply
They mainly REDUCE oxygen demand (preload, afterload, HR, contractility)

antianginal-principles.explanation: Pharmacologic therapy primarily lowers myocardial O₂ demand; increasing supply is largely mechanical (PCI/CABG).

organic-nitrates.stem: Why must organic nitrates never be co-administered with sildenafil (a PDE5 inhibitor)?

options.text: Both raise cGMP, causing severe hypotension

organic-nitrates.explanation: Nitrates increase cGMP via NO, and PDE5 inhibitors prevent cGMP breakdown; together they cause profound vasodilation and life-threatening hypotension.

organic-nitrates.stem: Regarding drug interaction — which is correct?

options.text: Nitrates can be given with PDE5 inhibitors for chest pain
NEVER combine nitrates with PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil) → life-threatening hypotension

organic-nitrates.explanation: Both raise cGMP; together they cause profound vasodilation and hypotension — a contraindicated combination.

organic-nitrates.stem: What best explains the finding: “Relief of anginal pain within minutes (sublingual)”?
organic-nitrates.explanation: Relief of anginal pain within minutes (sublingual) → Rapid venodilation.

organic-nitrates.stem: What best explains the finding: “Headache, flushing, postural hypotension”?
organic-nitrates.explanation: Headache, flushing, postural hypotension → Systemic vasodilation.

organic-nitrates.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Organic Nitrates”?
organic-nitrates.explanation: Erectile dysfunction treatments often involve nitrates and PDE5 inhibitors.

organic-nitrates.stem: Which should you review before “Organic Nitrates”?
organic-nitrates.explanation: Understanding nitrate contraindications is essential for managing patients with cardiovascular issues.

beta-blockers-ccb-angina.stem: Which antianginal class is particularly useful (and beta-blockers relatively avoided) in vasospastic / variant angina?
beta-blockers-ccb-angina.explanation: Calcium channel blockers relieve and prevent coronary vasospasm and are particularly useful in variant angina; beta-blockers can worsen spasm via unopposed alpha vasoconstriction.

beta-blockers-ccb-angina.stem: Regarding drug choice in vasospastic angina — which is correct?

options.text: Give a beta-blocker for vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina
Vasospastic angina → calcium channel blocker; beta-blockers can WORSEN spasm

beta-blockers-ccb-angina.explanation: Beta-blockade leaves unopposed alpha-mediated coronary vasoconstriction, worsening spasm; CCBs relieve and prevent vasospasm.

beta-blockers-ccb-angina.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bradycardia (beta-blocker, non-DHP CCB)”?
What best explains the finding: “DHP CCB: flushing, pedal edema, reflex tachycardia”?
beta-blockers-ccb-angina.explanation: DHP CCB: flushing, pedal edema, reflex tachycardia → Potent arteriolar vasodilation.

beta-blockers-ccb-angina.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Beta-blockers & CCBs in Angina”?
beta-blockers-ccb-angina.explanation: Beta-blockers are also used in migraine prophylaxis, linking pharmacological principles.

beta-blockers-ccb-angina.stem: Which should you review before “Beta-blockers & CCBs in Angina”?
beta-blockers-ccb-angina.explanation: Understanding preload and afterload is essential for grasping the mechanisms of beta-blockers and CCBs.

hf-pathology-overview.stem: A patient has structural heart disease (prior MI, reduced EF) but NO symptoms. ACC/AHA stage?
hf-pathology-overview.explanation: Stage B = structural heart disease without symptoms or signs of HF. Symptoms would make it Stage C; at-risk without structural disease is Stage A.

hf-pathology-overview.stem: Regarding hf vs cardiac dysfunction — which is correct?

options.text: Any reduced EF / cardiac dysfunction = heart failure
HF is a clinical SYNDROME (symptoms + signs); asymptomatic LV dysfunction is Stage B, not HF

hf-pathology-overview.explanation: Cardiac dysfunction can be asymptomatic (Stage B); HF requires the clinical syndrome of symptoms and signs.

hf-pathology-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, fatigue, edema”?
hf-pathology-overview.explanation: Dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, fatigue, edema → Congestion + low output.

hf-pathology-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “↑JVP, hepatojugular reflux, S3 gallop, displaced apex”?
hf-pathology-overview.explanation: ↑JVP, hepatojugular reflux, S3 gallop, displaced apex → Volume overload / LV dysfunction.

hf-pathology-overview.stem: Which should you review before “Heart Failure — Definition & Staging”?
hf-pathology-overview.explanation: Overview provides foundational knowledge on heart failure classification.

cardiac-hypertrophy-remodeling.stem: A long-standing hypertensive patient's heart shows a thick LV wall with a small cavity. Pattern and cause?
cardiac-hypertrophy-remodeling.explanation: Chronic pressure overload (hypertension) produces concentric hypertrophy — a thickened wall with a small cavity. Volume overload (regurgitation) gives eccentric, dilated hypertrophy.

cardiac-hypertrophy-remodeling.stem: Regarding hypertrophy pattern by overload — which is correct?

options.text: Pressure overload (HTN, AS) → CONCENTRIC; volume overload (AR, MR) → ECCENTRIC

cardiac-hypertrophy-remodeling.explanation: Pressure overload thickens the wall (concentric, small cavity); volume overload dilates the chamber (eccentric).

cardiac-hypertrophy-remodeling.stem: What best explains the finding: “Concentric LVH: sustained heaving apex, S4”?
cardiac-hypertrophy-remodeling.explanation: Concentric LVH: sustained heaving apex, S4 → Stiff hypertrophied LV.

cardiac-hypertrophy-remodeling.stem: What best explains the finding: “Eccentric/dilated: displaced apex, S3”?
cardiac-hypertrophy-remodeling.explanation: Eccentric/dilated: displaced apex, S3 → Volume-overloaded dilated LV.

cardiac-hypertrophy-remodeling.stem: Which should you review before “Cardiac Hypertrophy & Remodeling”?
cardiac-hypertrophy-remodeling.explanation: Understanding hypertrophy is essential for grasping cardiac remodeling.

hf-organ-pathology.stem: Lung histology shows hemosiderin-laden macrophages ('heart failure cells') in alveoli. This indicates?

options.text: Chronic left heart failure with pulmonary congestion

hf-organ-pathology.explanation: "Heart failure cells" are hemosiderin-laden macrophages from chronic pulmonary venous congestion — a hallmark of chronic left-sided heart failure.

hf-organ-pathology.stem: Regarding hemosiderin macrophages in lung — which is correct?

options.text: Alveolar hemosiderin macrophages = a primary lung disease
Heart failure cells (hemosiderin-laden macrophages) indicate chronic LEFT heart failure / pulmonary congestion

hf-organ-pathology.explanation: Chronic pulmonary congestion from left HF causes alveolar microhemorrhages; macrophages phagocytose RBCs → hemosiderin = "heart failure cells".

hf-organ-pathology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Left: bibasal crepitations, orthopnea, PND”?
hf-organ-pathology.explanation: Left: bibasal crepitations, orthopnea, PND → Pulmonary congestion.

hf-organ-pathology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Right: ↑JVP, tender hepatomegaly, pitting edema, ascites”?
hf-organ-pathology.explanation: Right: ↑JVP, tender hepatomegaly, pitting edema, ascites → Systemic venous backpressure.

hf-organ-pathology.stem: Which should you review before “HF — Organ Pathology (Left vs Right)”?
hf-organ-pathology.explanation: Understanding edema and congestion is essential for grasping heart failure pathology.

hf-pharmacology-pillars.stem: Which combination of drug classes forms the survival-improving 'four pillars' of HFrEF therapy?
hf-pharmacology-pillars.explanation: The four pillars — ARNi (or ACEi/ARB), beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitor — each improve survival in HFrEF and are started/titrated early.

hf-pharmacology-pillars.stem: Regarding acei + arni combination — which is correct?

options.text: Add an ACEi to an ARNi for extra RAAS blockade

hf-pharmacology-pillars.explanation: Both raise bradykinin; combining (or overlapping without washout) markedly increases angioedema risk.

hf-pharmacology-pillars.stem: What best explains the finding: “ACEi: dry cough, angioedema, hyperkalemia”?
hf-pharmacology-pillars.explanation: ACEi: dry cough, angioedema, hyperkalemia → Bradykinin; aldosterone suppression.

hf-pharmacology-pillars.stem: What best explains the finding: “Beta-blocker: bradycardia — start low when euvolemic/stable”?
hf-pharmacology-pillars.explanation: Beta-blocker: bradycardia — start low when euvolemic/stable → Negative chronotropy.

digoxin-inotropes.stem: An elderly HF patient on digoxin develops nausea, yellow-green visual halos, and a new arrhythmia. Which electrolyte abnormality worsens this toxicity?
digoxin-inotropes.explanation: Hypokalemia potentiates digoxin toxicity because low extracellular K⁺ leaves more Na/K-ATPase available for digoxin binding — keep K⁺ in the normal range.

digoxin-inotropes.stem: Regarding digoxin & potassium — which is correct?

options.text: HYPOkalemia potentiates digoxin toxicity (competes at Na/K-ATPase)

digoxin-inotropes.explanation: Low K⁺ frees the Na/K-ATPase binding site for digoxin, worsening toxicity — keep potassium normal.

digoxin-inotropes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Yellow-green vision / halos”?
digoxin-inotropes.explanation: Yellow-green vision / halos → Digoxin visual toxicity.
