digoxin-inotropes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Anorexia, nausea, vomiting”?
digoxin-inotropes.explanation: Anorexia, nausea, vomiting → GI digoxin toxicity.

digoxin-inotropes.stem: Which should you review before “Digoxin & Inotropes”?

hf-other-drugs.stem: A HFrEF patient (EF 30%) in sinus rhythm has HR 85 despite a maximally tolerated beta-blocker. Which agent adds further heart-rate control?
hf-other-drugs.explanation: Ivabradine inhibits the SA-node If current to slow heart rate in patients in sinus rhythm with HR ≥70 on a maximally tolerated beta-blocker (EF ≤35%).

hf-other-drugs.stem: Regarding what improves survival — which is correct?

options.text: Loop diuretics improve survival in HFrEF
Diuretics relieve congestion (symptoms) but don't improve survival — the four pillars do

hf-other-drugs.explanation: Diuretics are essential for symptom control, but the mortality benefit in HFrEF comes from neurohormonal blockade + SGLT2 inhibitors.

hf-other-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Diuretic response: ↓edema, ↓dyspnea”?

htn-classification.stem: A patient's clinic BP is normal but home and ambulatory readings are consistently ≥135/85. This pattern is?
htn-classification.explanation: Normal office BP with elevated out-of-office (home/ambulatory) BP defines masked hypertension — it carries real cardiovascular risk despite normal clinic readings.

htn-classification.stem: Regarding masked vs white coat — which is correct?

options.text: Normal office BP rules out hypertension
Masked HTN = normal office but high home/ambulatory BP — still at risk

htn-classification.explanation: Masked hypertension has normal clinic readings but elevated out-of-office BP, carrying cardiovascular risk — confirm with HBPM/ABPM.

htn-classification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Wide pulse pressure (≥60) in the elderly”?
htn-classification.explanation: Wide pulse pressure (≥60) in the elderly → Arterial stiffness → isolated systolic HTN.

htn-classification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Usually asymptomatic”?
Which should you review before “Hypertension — Definition & Classification”?
htn-classification.explanation: Understanding BP measurement is essential for classifying hypertension.

htn-pathophysiology.stem: A young woman has resistant hypertension; renal angiography shows a 'string of beads' appearance. Cause?
htn-pathophysiology.explanation: A "string of beads" on renal angiography in a young woman is fibromuscular dysplasia — a non-atherosclerotic cause of renovascular hypertension.

htn-pathophysiology.stem: Regarding htn + hypokalemia — which is correct?

options.text: Hypokalemia in a hypertensive is just a diuretic effect
Hypertension + spontaneous hypokalemia → screen for primary aldosteronism (Conn)

htn-pathophysiology.explanation: Unprovoked hypokalemia with hypertension suggests primary aldosteronism — check the aldosterone-to-renin ratio.

htn-pathophysiology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Abdominal bruit, FMD “string of beads” (young female)”?
htn-pathophysiology.explanation: Abdominal bruit, FMD “string of beads” (young female) → Renovascular hypertension.

htn-pathophysiology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypertension + spontaneous hypokalemia”?
Which should you review before “Hypertension — Pathophysiology & Secondary Causes”?

hypertensive-target-organ-damage.stem: Early hypertensive heart disease most characteristically causes:

options.text: Concentric LVH with diastolic dysfunction (preserved EF)

hypertensive-target-organ-damage.explanation: Chronic pressure overload produces concentric LV hypertrophy with diastolic dysfunction (HFpEF) first; eccentric dilation and systolic failure are late features.

hypertensive-target-organ-damage.stem: Regarding htn heart disease pattern — which is correct?

options.text: Hypertension first causes a dilated, low-EF heart
HTN causes CONCENTRIC LVH → diastolic dysfunction (HFpEF) first; dilation/systolic failure is late

hypertensive-target-organ-damage.explanation: Pressure overload produces concentric hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction (HFpEF) early; eccentric dilation with systolic failure occurs only in late/decompensated disease.

hypertensive-target-organ-damage.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sustained (heaving) apex + S4”?
hypertensive-target-organ-damage.explanation: Sustained (heaving) apex + S4 → Concentric LVH, diastolic dysfunction.

hypertensive-target-organ-damage.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypertensive retinopathy (AV nicking, hemorrhages)”?
hypertensive-target-organ-damage.explanation: Hypertensive retinopathy (AV nicking, hemorrhages) → Retinal vascular damage.

hypertensive-target-organ-damage.stem: Which should you review before “Hypertensive Target-Organ Damage”?

shock-mechanisms-types.stem: A febrile patient is hypotensive but warm, flushed, with bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure. Type of shock?
shock-mechanisms-types.explanation: Warm, flushed skin with bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure reflects low systemic vascular resistance — distributive (here septic) shock.

shock-mechanisms-types.stem: Regarding warm vs cold shock — which is correct?

options.text: All shock presents cold and clammy
Distributive shock (early septic, neurogenic, anaphylactic) is WARM/vasodilated; hypovolemic & cardiogenic are cold/vasoconstricted

shock-mechanisms-types.explanation: Distributive shock has low SVR (warm, flushed, bounding pulses); hypovolemic/cardiogenic compensate with vasoconstriction (cold, clammy).

shock-mechanisms-types.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypotension + tachycardia + ↑lactate + oliguria + altered mentation”?
shock-mechanisms-types.explanation: Hypotension + tachycardia + ↑lactate + oliguria + altered mentation → Global hypoperfusion.

shock-mechanisms-types.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cold/clammy (hypovolemic/cardiogenic) vs warm/flushed (distributive)”?
shock-mechanisms-types.explanation: Cold/clammy (hypovolemic/cardiogenic) vs warm/flushed (distributive) → High vs low SVR.

shock-mechanisms-types.stem: Which should you review before “Shock — Mechanisms & Types”?
shock-mechanisms-types.explanation: Understanding coronary circulation is essential for grasping cardiac insufficiency in shock.

vasopressors-inotropes.stem: After adequate fluid resuscitation, a patient in septic shock remains hypotensive. First-line vasopressor?
vasopressors-inotropes.explanation: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock after fluids — it reliably raises MAP with a lower arrhythmia risk than dopamine.

vasopressors-inotropes.stem: Regarding first vasopressor in septic shock — which is correct?

options.text: Use dopamine first in septic shock
Norepinephrine is first-line (better survival, fewer arrhythmias than dopamine)

vasopressors-inotropes.explanation: Surviving Sepsis guidelines make norepinephrine the first-choice vasopressor; dopamine causes more tachyarrhythmia.

vasopressors-inotropes.stem: What best explains the finding: “NE: ↑MAP, reflex bradycardia; digital ischemia/gangrene with extravasation”?
vasopressors-inotropes.explanation: NE: ↑MAP, reflex bradycardia; digital ischemia/gangrene with extravasation → Potent α1 vasoconstriction.

vasopressors-inotropes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Epinephrine: ↑HR, tremor, hyperglycemia”?
Which should you review before “Vasopressors & Inotropes”?

options.text: Inferential Statistics: CIs, p-values & Choosing a Test

vasopressors-inotropes.explanation: Basic understanding of statistics may aid in interpreting clinical studies on vasopressors.

antihypertensive-overview.stem: A 35-year-old non-Black man needs first-line antihypertensive monotherapy. Best initial class?
antihypertensive-overview.explanation: In younger, non-Black patients the renin-angiotensin system is more active, so an ACE inhibitor/ARB (“A”) is preferred first-line over C/D agents.

antihypertensive-overview.stem: Regarding first-line in a young patient — which is correct?

options.text: Start a thiazide for a young non-Black hypertensive
Young/non-Black → ACEi/ARB (A) first; older/Black → CCB or diuretic (C/D)

antihypertensive-overview.explanation: RAAS is more active in younger patients (A works best); Black/elderly patients respond better to C/D as RAAS is less dominant.

antihypertensive-overview.stem: Which should you review before “Antihypertensive Drugs — Classes & A/C/D”?

options.text: Literature Review: Purpose, Sources & Search Strategy

antihypertensive-overview.explanation: Understanding literature review aids in grasping antihypertensive studies.

htn-diuretics-raas.stem: A patient on an ACE inhibitor develops a persistent dry cough. Best management?
htn-diuretics-raas.explanation: ACE-inhibitor cough is bradykinin-mediated; switching to an ARB (which blocks AT1 without raising bradykinin) relieves it while maintaining RAAS blockade.

htn-diuretics-raas.stem: Regarding acei cough management — which is correct?

options.text: Add an antitussive and continue the ACEi
ACEi-induced dry cough → switch to an ARB (no bradykinin-mediated cough)

htn-diuretics-raas.explanation: The dry cough is bradykinin-mediated; ARBs do not raise bradykinin, so switching resolves it.

htn-diuretics-raas.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thiazide: hypokalemia + hyperuricemia (gout flare)”?
htn-diuretics-raas.explanation: Thiazide: hypokalemia + hyperuricemia (gout flare) → Distal K⁺ wasting; urate retention.

htn-diuretics-raas.stem: What best explains the finding: “Spironolactone: gynecomastia”?
Which should you review before “Diuretics & RAAS Inhibitors in HTN”?

options.text: Hormonal Control of Volume & Water Balance

htn-diuretics-raas.explanation: Understanding hormonal control is essential for grasping diuretic mechanisms.

htn-ccb-sympatholytics.stem: A patient on amlodipine develops bilateral ankle edema with no other signs of heart failure. Best explanation?
htn-ccb-sympatholytics.explanation: Dihydropyridine CCBs dilate precapillary arterioles, raising capillary hydrostatic pressure and causing peripheral edema — not fluid overload, so diuretics are ineffective.

htn-ccb-sympatholytics.stem: Regarding dhp-ccb side effect — which is correct?

options.text: Ankle edema from a DHP-CCB means heart failure → give a diuretic
DHP-CCB pedal edema is precapillary vasodilation, not volume overload — diuretics don’t help; reduce dose / add an ACEi

htn-ccb-sympatholytics.explanation: Dihydropyridine edema is local (arteriolar dilation raises capillary pressure), not fluid overload — diuretics are ineffective.

htn-ccb-sympatholytics.stem: What best explains the finding: “DHP-CCB: bilateral pedal edema”?
htn-ccb-sympatholytics.explanation: DHP-CCB: bilateral pedal edema → Precapillary arteriolar vasodilation (not fluid overload).

htn-ccb-sympatholytics.stem: What best explains the finding: “α-blocker: first-dose syncope/postural hypotension”?
htn-ccb-sympatholytics.explanation: α-blocker: first-dose syncope/postural hypotension → Abrupt venodilation.

vasculitis-overview.stem: A patient with sinusitis, lung nodules, and crescentic glomerulonephritis has a positive c-ANCA (anti-PR3). Diagnosis?
vasculitis-overview.explanation: Upper + lower respiratory granulomas with crescentic GN and PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA) is granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener).

vasculitis-overview.stem: Regarding anca association — which is correct?

options.text: c-ANCA (PR3) → GPA (Wegener); p-ANCA (MPO) → microscopic polyangiitis / Churg-Strauss
Luminal narrowing / thrombosis of inflamed vessels

vasculitis-overview.explanation: Match the antibody: PR3/c-ANCA with granulomatosis with polyangiitis; MPO/p-ANCA with MPA and eosinophilic GPA.

vasculitis-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fever, fatigue, weight loss, myalgia”?

options.text: Luminal narrowing / thrombosis of inflamed vessels

vasculitis-overview.explanation: Fever, fatigue, weight loss, myalgia → Systemic inflammation.

vasculitis-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Organ-specific ischemia”?

options.text: Luminal narrowing / thrombosis of inflamed vessels

vasculitis-overview.explanation: Organ-specific ischemia → Luminal narrowing / thrombosis of inflamed vessels.

large-medium-vasculitis.stem: A 70-year-old has new temporal headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and ESR 90. Most urgent action?
large-medium-vasculitis.explanation: Suspected giant cell arteritis is treated with immediate high-dose corticosteroids to prevent irreversible blindness; temporal artery biopsy can follow.

large-medium-vasculitis.stem: Regarding suspected gca management — which is correct?

options.text: Wait for temporal artery biopsy before treating GCA
Start high-dose corticosteroids IMMEDIATELY in suspected GCA to prevent blindness (biopsy can follow)

large-medium-vasculitis.explanation: Vision loss is irreversible; steroids are started on clinical suspicion, and biopsy stays positive for days after starting.

large-medium-vasculitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “GCA: tender temporal artery, jaw claudication, visual loss, ↑ESR”?
large-medium-vasculitis.explanation: GCA: tender temporal artery, jaw claudication, visual loss, ↑ESR → Granulomatous temporal arteritis.

large-medium-vasculitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Takayasu: absent/weak upper-limb pulses, inter-arm BP differential”?
large-medium-vasculitis.explanation: Takayasu: absent/weak upper-limb pulses, inter-arm BP differential → Aortic-arch branch stenosis.

large-medium-vasculitis.stem: Which should you review before “Large & Medium Vessel Vasculitis”?
large-medium-vasculitis.explanation: Granulomatous inflammation is key in large and medium vessel vasculitis.

small-vessel-and-venous.stem: A patient has recurrent migratory superficial thrombophlebitis appearing at different sites over weeks. What should be excluded?
small-vessel-and-venous.explanation: Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis (Trousseau sign of malignancy) is a paraneoplastic hypercoagulable state classically linked to pancreatic and other visceral cancers.

small-vessel-and-venous.stem: Regarding migratory thrombophlebitis — which is correct?

options.text: Superficial migratory thrombophlebitis is just from IV cannulas
Migratory (Trousseau) thrombophlebitis suggests occult visceral malignancy (esp. pancreatic head)
Upper resp + lung + renal granulomatous vasculitis

small-vessel-and-venous.explanation: Recurrent migratory superficial thrombophlebitis (Trousseau sign) is a paraneoplastic hypercoagulable phenomenon — search for cancer.

small-vessel-and-venous.stem: What best explains the finding: “GPA: chronic sinusitis, saddle-nose, hemoptysis, hematuria”?

options.text: Upper resp + lung + renal granulomatous vasculitis

small-vessel-and-venous.explanation: GPA: chronic sinusitis, saddle-nose, hemoptysis, hematuria → Upper resp + lung + renal granulomatous vasculitis.

small-vessel-and-venous.stem: What best explains the finding: “Raynaud: tri-color digital change with cold”?

options.text: Upper resp + lung + renal granulomatous vasculitis

small-vessel-and-venous.explanation: Raynaud: tri-color digital change with cold → Cold-induced vasospasm.

small-vessel-and-venous.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Small-vessel Vasculitis & Venous Disease”?
small-vessel-and-venous.explanation: Chest radiographs may show lung involvement in small-vessel vasculitis.

cardiac-tumors-overview.stem: What is the most common cardiac malignancy?
cardiac-tumors-overview.explanation: Metastatic spread (lung, breast, melanoma, leukemia, lymphoma) is the most common cardiac malignancy. Among primary tumors, angiosarcoma is the most common malignant one, but primaries overall are rare and mostly benign.

cardiac-tumors-overview.stem: Regarding most common cardiac tumor / malignancy — which is correct?

options.text: Myxoma is the most common cardiac malignancy
Metastatic (secondary) tumors are the most common cardiac MALIGNANCY; myxoma is the most common primary (benign) tumor

cardiac-tumors-overview.explanation: Primary cardiac tumors are rare and mostly benign (myxoma leads). Malignancy of the heart is far more often metastatic than primary; among primaries, angiosarcoma is the most common malignant one.

cardiac-tumors-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Embolic phenomena, obstruction, or constitutional symptoms”?

options.text: Many are asymptomatic until they obstruct or embolize

cardiac-tumors-overview.explanation: Embolic phenomena, obstruction, or constitutional symptoms → Fragmentation, ball-valve blockage, cytokines.

cardiac-tumors-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pericardial effusion / tamponade”?

options.text: Many are asymptomatic until they obstruct or embolize

cardiac-tumors-overview.explanation: Pericardial effusion / tamponade → Metastatic pericardial spread (lymphatic obstruction).

cardiac-tumors-overview.stem: Which should you review before “Cardiac Masses & Tumors — Overview”?
cardiac-tumors-overview.explanation: Understanding cardiac muscle is essential for grasping cardiac tumors.

cardiac-myxoma.stem: A 55-year-old woman has 4 months of dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, PND, and pulmonary edema, and now presents with dizziness, syncope, and fatigue. She is diagnosed with a primary heart tumor. The most likely tumor is:
cardiac-myxoma.explanation: A left-atrial myxoma acts as a ball-valve, intermittently obstructing the mitral orifice — producing mitral-stenosis-like congestion (dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, pulmonary edema) plus positional syncope. It is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults.

cardiac-myxoma.stem: Regarding cause of positional mitral obstruction — which is correct?

options.text: Diastolic murmur + LA obstruction = rheumatic mitral stenosis
A mobile LA mass causing POSITIONAL/intermittent obstruction with a tumor plop = atrial myxoma
Mobile mass intermittently obstructs the mitral orifice

cardiac-myxoma.explanation: Myxoma mimics mitral stenosis, but the obstruction is positional/intermittent (ball-valve) with a "tumor plop" plus constitutional and embolic features — echo shows a mass at the fossa ovalis rather than a fibrosed valve.

cardiac-myxoma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Positional dyspnea / syncope + a "tumor plop" (early-diastolic sound)”?

options.text: Mobile mass intermittently obstructs the mitral orifice

cardiac-myxoma.explanation: Positional dyspnea / syncope + a "tumor plop" (early-diastolic sound) → Mobile mass intermittently obstructs the mitral orifice.

cardiac-myxoma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Diastolic murmur mimicking mitral stenosis”?

options.text: Mobile mass intermittently obstructs the mitral orifice

cardiac-myxoma.explanation: Diastolic murmur mimicking mitral stenosis → Ball-valve obstruction of LV inflow.

cardiac-myxoma.stem: Which should you review before “Cardiac Myxoma”?
cardiac-myxoma.explanation: Understanding heart sounds is crucial for diagnosing myxoma-related murmurs.

rhabdomyoma-and-tumors.stem: An infant is found to have multiple cardiac rhabdomyomas. Which associated genetic condition is most likely?
rhabdomyoma-and-tumors.explanation: Cardiac rhabdomyomas are the most common heart tumor of infancy and are strongly associated with tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2 mutations). They are hamartomas with "spider cells" and often regress spontaneously.

rhabdomyoma-and-tumors.stem: Regarding pediatric cardiac tumor + syndrome — which is correct?

options.text: The commonest childhood cardiac tumor is myxoma
In infants/children it is rhabdomyoma, associated with tuberous sclerosis (TSC1/TSC2)

rhabdomyoma-and-tumors.explanation: Myxoma is the commonest adult primary tumor; in children it is rhabdomyoma — a hamartoma with spider cells, strongly linked to tuberous sclerosis and often regressing spontaneously.

rhabdomyoma-and-tumors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Infant with obstruction/arrhythmia + tuberous sclerosis stigmata”?
rhabdomyoma-and-tumors.explanation: Infant with obstruction/arrhythmia + tuberous sclerosis stigmata → Rhabdomyoma (ash-leaf spots, seizures, angiofibromas).

rhabdomyoma-and-tumors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Embolic stroke from a valve lesion”?
rhabdomyoma-and-tumors.explanation: Embolic stroke from a valve lesion → Papillary fibroelastoma fragments.

pericardial-effusion.stem: A pericardial effusion has a fluid/serum protein ratio of 0.7 and a fluid LDH of 400 U/L. This effusion is best classified as:
pericardial-effusion.explanation: Both values meet Light’s criteria (protein ratio >0.5 and LDH >300 U/L), so this is an exudate — pointing to inflammation, infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease rather than a pressure/oncotic (transudative) cause.

pericardial-effusion.stem: Regarding transudate vs exudate — which is correct?

options.text: Any inflammatory-looking effusion is a transudate
Exudate = protein/LDH-rich (Light’s criteria positive); transudate = CHF/hypoalbuminemia/renal
Compression of esophagus / recurrent laryngeal nerve / diaphragm / lung

pericardial-effusion.explanation: Light’s criteria separate them: an exudate (fluid/serum protein >0.5, LDH >0.6, or LDH >300) points to inflammation/infection/malignancy, whereas a transudate reflects raised hydrostatic or low oncotic pressure.

pericardial-effusion.stem: What best explains the finding: “Muffled heart sounds; pericardial friction rub”?

options.text: Compression of esophagus / recurrent laryngeal nerve / diaphragm / lung
Insulating fluid; heart swinging in fluid

pericardial-effusion.explanation: Muffled heart sounds; pericardial friction rub → Fluid between the layers.

pericardial-effusion.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dysphagia, hoarseness, hiccups, dyspnea”?

options.text: Compression of esophagus / recurrent laryngeal nerve / diaphragm / lung
Insulating fluid; heart swinging in fluid

pericardial-effusion.explanation: Dysphagia, hoarseness, hiccups, dyspnea → Compression of esophagus / recurrent laryngeal nerve / diaphragm / lung.

pericardial-effusion.stem: Which should you review before “Pericardial Effusion”?
pericardial-effusion.explanation: Understanding inflammation is crucial for differentiating transudate from exudate.

cardiac-tamponade.stem: A stabbed patient is hypotensive with distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds. The most appropriate immediate management is:
cardiac-tamponade.explanation: Hypotension + distended neck veins + muffled heart sounds is Beck’s triad of cardiac tamponade. In a penetrating-trauma patient this is acute tamponade from a small, rapidly accumulating effusion — the immediate treatment is pericardiocentesis (or surgical drainage).

cardiac-tamponade.stem: Regarding volume vs rate of effusion — which is correct?

options.text: RATE matters more than volume — a rapidly accumulating SMALL effusion (trauma, rupture) can cause tamponade
Interventricular dependence in a fixed pericardial volume

cardiac-tamponade.explanation: The stiff pericardium cannot stretch acutely, so a small rapid effusion tamponades, whereas a slowly enlarging effusion may reach a large volume without compromise.

cardiac-tamponade.stem: What best explains the finding: “Beck triad: hypotension + ↑ JVP + muffled heart sounds”?

options.text: Interventricular dependence in a fixed pericardial volume
Compensating for a fixed low stroke volume

cardiac-tamponade.explanation: Beck triad: hypotension + ↑ JVP + muffled heart sounds → Compressed chambers, insulating fluid.

cardiac-tamponade.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg inspiratory SBP fall)”?

options.text: Interventricular dependence in a fixed pericardial volume
Compensating for a fixed low stroke volume

cardiac-tamponade.explanation: Pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg inspiratory SBP fall) → Interventricular dependence in a fixed pericardial volume.

pericarditis.stem: Which morphological type of pericarditis is the most common, seen in uremia, post-MI, and rheumatoid arthritis?
pericarditis.explanation: Fibrinous (and serofibrinous) pericarditis is the most common morphology — the classic "bread-and-butter" appearance — and is typical of uremia, post-MI states, and rheumatoid arthritis. Caseous pericarditis suggests tuberculosis.

pericarditis.stem: Regarding st elevation: pericarditis vs stemi — which is correct?

options.text: Diffuse ST elevation must be a STEMI
Diffuse concave ST elevation + PR depression with NO reciprocal changes = pericarditis

pericarditis.explanation: Pericarditis gives widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal ST depression, unlike the territorial, convex ST elevation with reciprocal changes of a STEMI.

pericarditis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pleuritic chest pain, better sitting forward, worse supine”?
pericarditis.explanation: Pleuritic chest pain, better sitting forward, worse supine → Inflamed pericardial layers.

pericarditis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pericardial friction rub”?
pericarditis.explanation: Pericardial friction rub → Roughened visceral & parietal surfaces rubbing.

pericarditis.stem: Which should you review before “Acute Pericarditis”?
pericarditis.explanation: Understanding acute inflammation is essential for grasping pericarditis pathophysiology.

constrictive-tuberculous-pericarditis.stem: A patient has right heart failure with an elevated JVP that rises on inspiration, a pericardial knock, and pericardial calcification on chest X-ray. The most likely diagnosis is:
constrictive-tuberculous-pericarditis.explanation: Kussmaul sign, a pericardial knock, and pericardial calcification point to constrictive pericarditis — a rigid fibrocalcific pericardium impairing diastolic filling (often post-TB or post-radiation). It mimics restrictive cardiomyopathy but is frequently curable with pericardiectomy.

constrictive-tuberculous-pericarditis.stem: Regarding constrictive pericarditis vs restrictive cardiomyopathy — which is correct?

options.text: Right HF with a normal-size heart = restrictive cardiomyopathy
Pericardial calcification + Kussmaul + pericardial knock = CONSTRICTIVE pericarditis (pericardial, often curable by pericardiectomy)
Fixed pericardium can’t accommodate inspiratory venous return
Abrupt halt to ventricular filling by rigid pericardium

constrictive-tuberculous-pericarditis.explanation: Both cause right-heart congestion with a non-dilated heart, but constriction is a pericardial problem (calcification, knock, surgically curable) whereas restrictive cardiomyopathy is myocardial (e.g. amyloid) — the distinction changes management entirely.

constrictive-tuberculous-pericarditis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Kussmaul sign (JVP rises with inspiration)”?

options.text: Abrupt halt to ventricular filling by rigid pericardium
Fixed pericardium can’t accommodate inspiratory venous return

constrictive-tuberculous-pericarditis.explanation: Kussmaul sign (JVP rises with inspiration) → Fixed pericardium can’t accommodate inspiratory venous return.

constrictive-tuberculous-pericarditis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pericardial knock (early-diastolic sound)”?

options.text: Abrupt halt to ventricular filling by rigid pericardium
Fixed pericardium can’t accommodate inspiratory venous return

constrictive-tuberculous-pericarditis.explanation: Pericardial knock (early-diastolic sound) → Abrupt halt to ventricular filling by rigid pericardium.

neuro-localization-framework.stem: A patient has leg weakness with increased tone, brisk knee jerks, ankle clonus, and an up-going plantar response. This pattern indicates:
neuro-localization-framework.explanation: Spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and a Babinski sign are the hallmarks of an upper motor neuron (corticospinal) lesion. LMN, muscle, and NMJ disorders give flaccid weakness with normal or reduced reflexes.

neuro-localization-framework.stem: Regarding umn vs lmn weakness — which is correct?

options.text: Weakness + reduced reflexes must be an UMN (brain/cord) lesion
Flaccid weakness with areflexia, atrophy and fasciculations is an LMN lesion

neuro-localization-framework.explanation: UMN lesions give spasticity, hyperreflexia and an up-going toe; LMN lesions give flaccidity, areflexia, wasting and fasciculation — the reflex/tone pattern separates them.

neuro-localization-framework.stem: What best explains the finding: “Babinski sign, clonus, hyperreflexia, spasticity”?
neuro-localization-framework.explanation: Babinski sign, clonus, hyperreflexia, spasticity → Corticospinal (UMN) lesion.

neuro-localization-framework.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fasciculations, atrophy, areflexia, flaccidity”?
neuro-localization-framework.explanation: Fasciculations, atrophy, areflexia, flaccidity → Anterior horn / peripheral (LMN) lesion.

neuro-localization-framework.stem: Which should you review before “Neuro Localization Framework”?
neuro-localization-framework.explanation: Understanding reflexes is essential for neuro localization.

spinal-cord-syndromes.stem: After a stab wound, a patient has right-leg spastic weakness with loss of vibration sense on the right, and loss of pain and temperature on the left below the umbilicus. This is:
spinal-cord-syndromes.explanation: Ipsilateral motor + dorsal-column loss with contralateral spinothalamic (pain/temperature) loss is Brown-Séquard hemicord syndrome — classically from a penetrating injury.

spinal-cord-syndromes.stem: Regarding side of pain/temperature loss — which is correct?

options.text: In hemicord (Brown-Séquard), all deficits are on the side of the lesion
Pain/temperature loss is CONTRALateral and begins a couple of levels below; motor and touch/vibration loss are ipsilateral

spinal-cord-syndromes.explanation: Spinothalamic fibers cross within 1–2 segments of entry, so a hemicord lesion drops pain/temp on the opposite side, while the still-uncrossed corticospinal and dorsal-column deficits stay ipsilateral.

spinal-cord-syndromes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Contralateral pain/temperature loss a few levels below the lesion”?

options.text: Central/commissural lesion hits crossing spinothalamic fibers

spinal-cord-syndromes.explanation: Contralateral pain/temperature loss a few levels below the lesion → Spinothalamic fibers already crossed.

spinal-cord-syndromes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ipsilateral vibration/proprioception loss + weakness”?

options.text: Central/commissural lesion hits crossing spinothalamic fibers

spinal-cord-syndromes.explanation: Ipsilateral vibration/proprioception loss + weakness → Dorsal column + corticospinal (uncrossed at cord).

brainstem-syndromes.stem: A patient has loss of pain and temperature on the right side of the face and the left side of the body, plus hoarseness, ipsilateral Horner syndrome, and vertigo. The lesion is:
brainstem-syndromes.explanation: Crossed pain/temp loss (ipsilateral face, contralateral body) with Horner, dysphagia/hoarseness and vertigo is the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome from PICA/vertebral occlusion — on the side of the facial deficit.

brainstem-syndromes.stem: Regarding localizing a crossed deficit — which is correct?

options.text: Ipsilateral face numbness and contralateral body numbness means two separate lesions
That crossed pattern is a single lateral brainstem (medullary) lesion

brainstem-syndromes.explanation: The spinal trigeminal tract carries ipsilateral facial pain/temp while the spinothalamic tract carries already-crossed body pain/temp — one lateral medullary lesion produces both, as in Wallenberg syndrome.

brainstem-syndromes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Crossed pain/temp: ipsilateral face + contralateral body”?

options.text: Descending sympathetic, nucleus ambiguus, vestibular nuclei

brainstem-syndromes.explanation: Crossed pain/temp: ipsilateral face + contralateral body → Spinal trigeminal (ipsi) + spinothalamic (contra) both hit.

brainstem-syndromes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Tongue deviates toward the lesion + contralateral arm/leg weakness”?

options.text: Descending sympathetic, nucleus ambiguus, vestibular nuclei

brainstem-syndromes.explanation: Tongue deviates toward the lesion + contralateral arm/leg weakness → Medial medullary CN XII + pyramid.

brainstem-syndromes.stem: Which should you review before “Brainstem Syndromes”?
brainstem-syndromes.explanation: Understanding descending motor pathways is essential for localizing brainstem lesions.

cortex-and-stroke.stem: A right-handed patient suddenly cannot produce fluent speech but comprehends well, and has right face and arm weakness. The lesion localizes to:

options.text: Left frontal cortex, dominant MCA territory

cortex-and-stroke.explanation: Non-fluent (Broca) aphasia with preserved comprehension plus contralateral face/arm weakness localizes to the dominant (left) frontal cortex in the MCA territory.

cortex-and-stroke.stem: Regarding mca vs aca weakness pattern — which is correct?

options.text: A dense hemiparesis affecting the leg most = MCA stroke
Leg-predominant weakness points to the ACA (medial homunculus); MCA weakness is face/arm-predominant

cortex-and-stroke.explanation: The motor homunculus puts the leg on the medial surface (ACA territory) and the face/hand on the lateral surface (MCA territory) — the body part most affected tells you the artery.

cortex-and-stroke.stem: What best explains the finding: “Contralateral face + arm weakness with aphasia”?
cortex-and-stroke.explanation: Contralateral face + arm weakness with aphasia → Dominant MCA territory.

cortex-and-stroke.stem: What best explains the finding: “Contralateral leg weakness > arm”?
cortex-and-stroke.explanation: Contralateral leg weakness > arm → ACA territory (medial motor strip).

cortex-and-stroke.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Cerebral Cortex & Stroke Syndromes”?
Which should you review before “Cerebral Cortex & Stroke Syndromes”?
cortex-and-stroke.explanation: Understanding higher cortical functions is essential for grasping stroke syndromes.

basal-ganglia-cerebellum.stem: A patient develops sudden, violent, large-amplitude flinging movements of the left arm and leg. The most likely lesion is in the:
basal-ganglia-cerebellum.explanation: Hemiballismus — violent flinging of the contralateral limbs — classically results from a lesion (often lacunar stroke) of the subthalamic nucleus on the opposite side.

basal-ganglia-cerebellum.stem: Regarding tremor type localization — which is correct?

options.text: Any tremor points to the cerebellum
A resting tremor is basal-ganglia (parkinsonian); an intention tremor (worse approaching a target) is cerebellar

basal-ganglia-cerebellum.explanation: Resting pill-rolling tremor that eases with movement is nigrostriatal; a tremor that appears/worsens on reaching a target with dysmetria is cerebellar — opposite behaviors localize to different systems.

basal-ganglia-cerebellum.stem: What best explains the finding: “Resting (pill-rolling) tremor + cogwheel rigidity + bradykinesia”?
basal-ganglia-cerebellum.explanation: Resting (pill-rolling) tremor + cogwheel rigidity + bradykinesia → Nigrostriatal dopamine loss.

basal-ganglia-cerebellum.stem: What best explains the finding: “Intention tremor, dysmetria, ipsilateral limb ataxia”?
basal-ganglia-cerebellum.explanation: Intention tremor, dysmetria, ipsilateral limb ataxia → Neocerebellar (posterior lobe) lesion.

basal-ganglia-cerebellum.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Basal Ganglia & Cerebellum”?
basal-ganglia-cerebellum.explanation: Motor posturing and reflexes are clinically relevant to basal ganglia function.

basal-ganglia-cerebellum.stem: Which should you review before “Basal Ganglia & Cerebellum”?
basal-ganglia-cerebellum.explanation: Understanding circuitry is essential for grasping basal ganglia functions.

limbic-hypothalamus.stem: A chronic heavy-alcohol user has profound difficulty forming new memories and fills gaps with fabricated stories. The structures classically damaged are the:
limbic-hypothalamus.explanation: Anterograde amnesia with confabulation is Korsakoff syndrome — thiamine-deficiency damage to the mammillary bodies and dorsomedial thalamus (Papez circuit nodes).

limbic-hypothalamus.stem: Regarding hypothalamic feeding nuclei — which is correct?

options.text: A lesion causing obesity must be in the lateral (hunger) hypothalamus
Obesity/hyperphagia follows a ventromedial (satiety) lesion; lateral lesions cause anorexia

limbic-hypothalamus.explanation: The ventromedial nucleus is the satiety centre — destroy it and the patient overeats; the lateral nucleus is the feeding/hunger centre — destroy it and the patient stops eating.

limbic-hypothalamus.stem: What best explains the finding: “Anterograde amnesia with confabulation”?

options.text: Pituitary/suprasellar mass on the optic chiasm

limbic-hypothalamus.explanation: Anterograde amnesia with confabulation → Mammillary/thalamic (Papez) damage — Korsakoff.

limbic-hypothalamus.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hyperphagia and obesity”?

options.text: Pituitary/suprasellar mass on the optic chiasm

limbic-hypothalamus.explanation: Hyperphagia and obesity → Ventromedial (satiety) hypothalamic lesion.

limbic-hypothalamus.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Limbic System & Hypothalamus”?
limbic-hypothalamus.explanation: Clinical implications of hypothalamic control over pituitary hormones.

limbic-hypothalamus.stem: Which should you review before “Limbic System & Hypothalamus”?
limbic-hypothalamus.explanation: Understanding hypothalamic nuclei is essential for grasping their functions.

extraocular-muscles.stem: A patient reports vertical diplopia worse when reading or descending stairs and tilts the head to one side to compensate. The affected nerve/muscle is:
extraocular-muscles.explanation: Vertical diplopia worse on down-gaze (reading, stairs) with a compensatory contralateral head tilt is a superior oblique (CN IV) palsy — the SO depresses the adducted eye.

extraocular-muscles.stem: Regarding testing the superior oblique — which is correct?

options.text: Ask the patient to look down and out to test the superior oblique
Test SO depression with the eye ADducted (looking down-and-in); SR/IR are tested in abduction
CN III palsy (unopposed LR + SO; loss of parasympathetic)

extraocular-muscles.explanation: A muscle’s pure vertical action is only isolated when the eye is rotated so its axis aligns with the pull — obliques in adduction, recti in abduction.

extraocular-muscles.stem: What best explains the finding: ““Down-and-out” eye with ptosis and dilated pupil”?

options.text: CN III palsy (unopposed LR + SO; loss of parasympathetic)

extraocular-muscles.explanation: “Down-and-out” eye with ptosis and dilated pupil → CN III palsy (unopposed LR + SO; loss of parasympathetic).

extraocular-muscles.stem: What best explains the finding: “Vertical diplopia + head tilt to the opposite shoulder”?

options.text: CN III palsy (unopposed LR + SO; loss of parasympathetic)

extraocular-muscles.explanation: Vertical diplopia + head tilt to the opposite shoulder → CN IV (SO) palsy — Bielschowsky.

extraocular-muscles.stem: Which should you review before “Extraocular Muscles & Actions”?
extraocular-muscles.explanation: Directly related to the innervation of extraocular muscles.

gaze-pathways-ino.stem: A 28-year-old woman cannot adduct her left eye on right gaze, and her right eye shows nystagmus while abducting; convergence is normal. The lesion is the:
gaze-pathways-ino.explanation: Impaired adduction of the left eye with abducting nystagmus of the right and preserved convergence is a left internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF lesion) — in a young woman, think multiple sclerosis.

gaze-pathways-ino.stem: Regarding localizing failed adduction — which is correct?

options.text: An eye that won’t adduct means a CN III (medial rectus) palsy
If convergence is intact and the other eye shows abducting nystagmus, it is an internuclear ophthalmoplegia (MLF lesion), not a CN III palsy

gaze-pathways-ino.explanation: A CN III palsy also affects convergence, lid, and pupil; an INO spares convergence and the pupil because the CN III nucleus is intact — the defect is in the MLF connecting it to the abducens nucleus.

gaze-pathways-ino.stem: What best explains the finding: “Failure of adduction of one eye + nystagmus of the abducting eye”?

options.text: CN III nucleus intact — localizes to the MLF

gaze-pathways-ino.explanation: Failure of adduction of one eye + nystagmus of the abducting eye → Ipsilateral MLF lesion (INO).

gaze-pathways-ino.stem: What best explains the finding: “Both eyes cannot look toward one side”?

options.text: CN III nucleus intact — localizes to the MLF

gaze-pathways-ino.explanation: Both eyes cannot look toward one side → PPRF / abducens-nucleus (gaze-centre) lesion.

vestibular-system-reflexes.stem: In an unconscious patient, turning the head to the right makes both eyes move conjugately to the left. This Doll's-eye response indicates:
vestibular-system-reflexes.explanation: A positive (intact) oculocephalic/Doll's-eye reflex — eyes moving opposite to head turn — means the vestibulo-ocular pathway through the brainstem tegmentum is intact. Its absence suggests a midbrain/pontine lesion.

vestibular-system-reflexes.stem: Regarding peripheral vs central vertigo — which is correct?

options.text: Severe vertigo with nystagmus is always a benign peripheral (inner-ear) problem
Direction-changing or vertical nystagmus, absent skew/other neuro signs, or a normal head-impulse test point to a central (brainstem/cerebellar) cause

vestibular-system-reflexes.explanation: Peripheral vertigo gives unidirectional, fatigable, horizontal nystagmus with an abnormal head-impulse test; central vertigo can look identical but shows direction-changing/vertical nystagmus and additional neurologic signs — missing it can mean a cerebellar stroke.

vestibular-system-reflexes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Positional vertigo with fatigable nystagmus (Dix-Hallpike)”?
vestibular-system-reflexes.explanation: Positional vertigo with fatigable nystagmus (Dix-Hallpike) → Peripheral (BPPV) canalith stimulation.

vestibular-system-reflexes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Absent Doll's-eye in a comatose patient”?
vestibular-system-reflexes.explanation: Absent Doll's-eye in a comatose patient → Brainstem (midbrain/pons) lesion.

vestibular-system-reflexes.stem: Which should you review before “Vestibular System & Reflexes”?
vestibular-system-reflexes.explanation: Understanding vestibular physiology is essential for grasping reflex mechanisms.

pupillary-reflexes-horner.stem: A patient has a small right pupil, mild right upper-lid droop, and decreased sweating on the right face. The lesion involves the:
pupillary-reflexes-horner.explanation: Miosis + partial ptosis + anhidrosis is Horner syndrome from interruption of the oculosympathetic pathway. A CN III lesion would instead give a dilated pupil and marked ptosis.

pupillary-reflexes-horner.stem: Regarding ptosis + pupil size — which is correct?

options.text: Ptosis with a small pupil is a CN III palsy
Ptosis with a MIOTIC pupil (± anhidrosis) is Horner syndrome; CN III palsy gives ptosis with a DILATED pupil

pupillary-reflexes-horner.explanation: Sympathetic (Horner) loss gives a small pupil and mild ptosis; CN III (parasympathetic + levator) loss gives a large pupil and severe ptosis — the pupil size flips the diagnosis.

pupillary-reflexes-horner.stem: What best explains the finding: “Affected pupil dilates on the swinging-light test (RAPD)”?
pupillary-reflexes-horner.explanation: Affected pupil dilates on the swinging-light test (RAPD) → Afferent (optic nerve) defect.

pupillary-reflexes-horner.stem: What best explains the finding: “Miosis + partial ptosis + facial anhidrosis”?
pupillary-reflexes-horner.explanation: Miosis + partial ptosis + facial anhidrosis → Horner (oculosympathetic) lesion.

hearing-balance-basics.stem: On the left ear, Rinne shows bone conduction louder than air conduction, and Weber lateralizes to the left. This indicates:
hearing-balance-basics.explanation: BC > AC (Rinne negative) plus Weber lateralizing to the same ear indicates a conductive hearing loss on the left.

hearing-balance-basics.stem: Regarding interpreting weber lateralization — which is correct?

options.text: Weber always lateralizes toward the healthy ear
Weber lateralizes to the affected ear in conductive loss and to the better ear in sensorineural loss
Conductive loss (bad ear hears bone conduction better)

hearing-balance-basics.explanation: In conductive loss the affected ear is shielded from ambient noise and detects bone conduction better, so Weber goes to the bad ear; in SNHL the cochlea is the problem, so sound is heard in the good ear.

hearing-balance-basics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Weber lateralizes to the bad ear”?

options.text: Sensorineural loss in the affected ear
Conductive loss (bad ear hears bone conduction better)

hearing-balance-basics.explanation: Weber lateralizes to the bad ear → Conductive loss (bad ear hears bone conduction better).

hearing-balance-basics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rinne negative (BC > AC) in the affected ear”?

options.text: Conductive loss (bad ear hears bone conduction better)
Sensorineural loss in the affected ear

hearing-balance-basics.explanation: Rinne negative (BC > AC) in the affected ear → Conductive loss on that side.

hearing-balance-basics.stem: Which should you review before “Hearing, Balance & Tuning-Fork Tests”?
hearing-balance-basics.explanation: Foundational knowledge of ear anatomy is essential for understanding hearing and balance.

external-ear-disorders.stem: A poorly controlled diabetic has severe, unrelenting ear pain, purulent discharge, and granulation tissue in the ear canal. The most likely diagnosis and organism are:
external-ear-disorders.explanation: Severe pain with granulation tissue in a diabetic/immunocompromised patient is necrotizing (malignant) otitis externa — a Pseudomonas skull-base osteomyelitis requiring systemic anti-pseudomonal therapy.

external-ear-disorders.stem: Regarding facial palsy with an ear rash — which is correct?

options.text: A facial nerve palsy with an ear rash is just Bell’s palsy plus incidental dermatitis
Vesicles in the ear with facial palsy = Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus), not idiopathic Bell’s palsy

external-ear-disorders.explanation: Ramsay Hunt is VZV reactivation in the geniculate ganglion — the vesicles distinguish it from Bell’s palsy and it warrants antivirals plus steroids for a chance at facial recovery.

external-ear-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pain on tragal pressure / pinna traction + otorrhea”?
external-ear-disorders.explanation: Pain on tragal pressure / pinna traction + otorrhea → Otitis externa (canal inflammation).

external-ear-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Vesicles on the auricle + facial palsy”?
external-ear-disorders.explanation: Vesicles on the auricle + facial palsy → Ramsay Hunt (VZV, geniculate ganglion).

external-ear-disorders.stem: Which should you review before “External Ear Disorders”?
external-ear-disorders.explanation: Basic biochemistry knowledge may be helpful but is not directly related to ear disorders.

middle-ear-disorders.stem: A child with acute otitis media develops fever, postauricular swelling that pushes the ear forward, and tenderness over the mastoid. The most likely complication is:
middle-ear-disorders.explanation: Postauricular swelling displacing the pinna with mastoid tenderness after AOM is acute mastoiditis — a suppurative complication of otitis media that can progress to abscess or intracranial spread.

middle-ear-disorders.stem: Regarding conductive loss with a normal drum — which is correct?

options.text: Conductive hearing loss must mean wax, effusion, or a perforation on otoscopy
A young adult with progressive conductive loss and a normal tympanic membrane suggests otosclerosis (stapes fixation)

middle-ear-disorders.explanation: Otosclerosis fixes the stapes footplate while the drum looks normal — the audiogram (with a Carhart notch) reveals the conductive loss that otoscopy cannot.

middle-ear-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bulging, erythematous, immobile tympanic membrane”?
middle-ear-disorders.explanation: Bulging, erythematous, immobile tympanic membrane → AOM with middle-ear pus.

middle-ear-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Conductive hearing loss with a normal-looking drum”?
middle-ear-disorders.explanation: Conductive hearing loss with a normal-looking drum → Otosclerosis (stapes fixation).

middle-ear-disorders.stem: Which should you review before “Middle Ear Disorders”?
middle-ear-disorders.explanation: Understanding auditory physiology is crucial for grasping the mechanisms of hearing loss in middle ear disorders.

inner-ear-disorders.stem: A patient has recurrent episodes of spinning vertigo lasting hours, with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and a sense of fullness in one ear. The diagnosis is:
inner-ear-disorders.explanation: Episodic vertigo (hours) with fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness is the classic Ménière triad from idiopathic endolymphatic hydrops.

inner-ear-disorders.stem: Regarding vertigo ± hearing loss — which is correct?

options.text: Acute vertigo lasting days with hearing loss is vestibular neuritis
Vestibular neuritis spares hearing; vertigo WITH hearing loss is labyrinthitis (or a central cause)

inner-ear-disorders.explanation: Vestibular neuritis affects only the vestibular nerve (no cochlear symptoms), whereas labyrinthitis involves the whole labyrinth and adds SNHL — the presence of hearing loss separates them.

inner-ear-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Brief positional vertigo + fatigable nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike”?
inner-ear-disorders.explanation: Brief positional vertigo + fatigable nystagmus on Dix-Hallpike → Posterior-canal BPPV.

inner-ear-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Vertigo + fluctuating SNHL + tinnitus/fullness”?
inner-ear-disorders.explanation: Vertigo + fluctuating SNHL + tinnitus/fullness → Ménière (endolymphatic hydrops).

inner-ear-disorders.stem: Which should you review before “Inner Ear Disorders & Temporal Bone”?
inner-ear-disorders.explanation: Understanding the anatomy of the parotid and temporal regions aids in grasping ear disorders.

visual-pathway-fields.stem: A patient with a pituitary macroadenoma is most likely to show which visual field defect?

options.text: Right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing

visual-pathway-fields.explanation: A pituitary tumor compresses the optic chiasm, damaging the crossing nasal fibers and producing a bitemporal (heteronymous) hemianopia.

visual-pathway-fields.stem: Regarding bitemporal vs homonymous — which is correct?

options.text: Any hemianopia points to an occipital stroke
Bitemporal (heteronymous) hemianopia localizes to the optic chiasm; a homonymous hemianopia is retrochiasmal

visual-pathway-fields.explanation: Only a chiasmal lesion splits the two temporal (crossing nasal) fibers to give a bitemporal pattern; any lesion behind the chiasm produces a same-sided (homonymous) defect in both eyes.

visual-pathway-fields.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bitemporal hemianopia”?
What best explains the finding: “Congruous homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing”?
visual-pathway-fields.explanation: Congruous homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing → Occipital (PCA) lesion.

visual-pathway-fields.stem: Which should you review before “Visual Pathway & Field Defects”?

options.text: Outbreak Investigation: Steps, Epidemic Curve & the Box Jellyfish Case

visual-pathway-fields.explanation: Basic understanding of investigation steps may aid in clinical context.

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: A 68-year-old with hypertension has sudden, painless, complete loss of vision in one eye. Fundus shows a pale retina with a cherry-red spot. The diagnosis is:
retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: Sudden painless monocular loss with a pale retina and cherry-red spot is central retinal artery occlusion — a retinal stroke requiring urgent management and vascular workup.

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: Regarding painless vs painful acute visual loss — which is correct?

options.text: Sudden monocular visual loss needs urgent steroids for optic neuritis
Painless sudden loss with a cherry-red spot is CRAO (a retinal stroke); optic neuritis is painful and occurs in young women

retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: CRAO/CRVO are painless vascular events; optic neuritis and acute angle-closure glaucoma are painful — the pain history and fundus findings separate vascular from inflammatory causes.

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pale retina with a cherry-red spot + RAPD”?
retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: Pale retina with a cherry-red spot + RAPD → CRAO (inner-retinal infarction).

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Diffuse retinal hemorrhages + dilated tortuous veins”?
retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: Diffuse retinal hemorrhages + dilated tortuous veins → CRVO (“blood-and-thunder” fundus).

retinal-vascular-occlusions.stem: Which should you review before “Retinal Vascular Occlusions”?
retinal-vascular-occlusions.explanation: Understanding ocular anatomy is essential for grasping retinal vascular occlusions.

amd-diabetic-retinopathy.stem: A long-standing diabetic develops new vessels on the optic disc and a vitreous hemorrhage. Beyond glycemic control, the key retinal treatment is:
amd-diabetic-retinopathy.explanation: Neovascularization defines proliferative diabetic retinopathy; panretinal photocoagulation (with anti-VEGF) ablates ischemic retina and reduces the VEGF drive, treating the new vessels and their complications.

amd-diabetic-retinopathy.stem: Regarding cause of vision loss in diabetic retinopathy — which is correct?

options.text: Vision loss in diabetic retinopathy is mainly from the new vessels themselves
Diabetic macular edema is the leading cause of vision loss; neovascularization causes loss via hemorrhage, traction, and neovascular glaucoma

amd-diabetic-retinopathy.explanation: Macular edema directly blurs central vision, while PDR threatens sight through its complications — both are treated, but the mechanisms of vision loss differ.

amd-diabetic-retinopathy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Central scotoma + metamorphopsia (Amsler grid)”?
amd-diabetic-retinopathy.explanation: Central scotoma + metamorphopsia (Amsler grid) → Macular (AMD) involvement.

amd-diabetic-retinopathy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, hard exudates”?
amd-diabetic-retinopathy.explanation: Microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages, hard exudates → NPDR microvascular damage.

pediatric-infective-retina.stem: A 2-year-old is brought in because a photograph showed a white reflex in one eye instead of red. The most important diagnosis to exclude is:
pediatric-infective-retina.explanation: Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in a young child must prompt urgent evaluation to exclude retinoblastoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy of childhood (RB1, 13q14).

pediatric-infective-retina.stem: Regarding leukocoria in a young child — which is correct?

options.text: A white pupil in a child is usually a congenital cataract to be scheduled electively
Leukocoria must be worked up urgently — retinoblastoma (a life-threatening malignancy) is the key diagnosis to exclude

pediatric-infective-retina.explanation: Although cataract, ROP and others cause leukocoria, retinoblastoma is a childhood cancer that can be fatal if missed — any white pupil warrants prompt fundus examination.

pediatric-infective-retina.stem: What best explains the finding: “Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in a young child”?
pediatric-infective-retina.explanation: Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in a young child → Retinoblastoma / ROP / other.

pediatric-infective-retina.stem: What best explains the finding: “Painful red eye + hypopyon after surgery/trauma”?
pediatric-infective-retina.explanation: Painful red eye + hypopyon after surgery/trauma → Endophthalmitis.

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: A 30-year-old woman has subacute loss of vision in one eye with pain on eye movement, an RAPD, and reduced color vision. The most likely diagnosis is:
optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: Painful (worse on eye movement) subacute monocular loss with an RAPD and color desaturation in a young woman is optic neuritis, strongly associated with demyelination/MS.

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: Regarding painful visual loss with a swollen disc — which is correct?

options.text: An older patient with sudden painless visual loss and a swollen disc just needs blood-pressure control
Check ESR/CRP — arteritic AION from giant cell arteritis needs immediate steroids to protect the fellow eye

optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: Non-arteritic AION relates to vascular risk factors, but arteritic AION (GCA) can rapidly blind the other eye; the inflammatory markers (and jaw claudication, scalp tenderness) mandate urgent steroids.

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: What best explains the finding: “RAPD + pain on eye movement + red desaturation”?
optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: RAPD + pain on eye movement + red desaturation → Optic neuritis.

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bilateral disc swelling + headache + CN VI palsy”?
optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: Bilateral disc swelling + headache + CN VI palsy → Raised ICP → papilledema.

optic-nerve-disc-edema.stem: Which should you review before “Optic Nerve Disorders & Disc Edema”?
optic-nerve-disc-edema.explanation: Understanding edema mechanisms is crucial for optic nerve disc edema.

cns-cellular-reactions.stem: Twelve hours after a cardiac arrest, cortical neurons show shrinkage, nuclear pyknosis, and bright cytoplasmic eosinophilia. These “red neurons” indicate:
cns-cellular-reactions.explanation: Red neurons — eosinophilic, shrunken, pyknotic cells appearing 6–12 h after irreversible injury — are the earliest morphologic marker of acute hypoxic-ischemic neuronal necrosis.

cns-cellular-reactions.stem: Regarding marker of cns injury — which is correct?

options.text: A fibroblastic/collagen scar forms after CNS injury as in other tissues
The CNS heals by gliosis (reactive astrocytosis), not by fibroblastic scarring

cns-cellular-reactions.explanation: Astrocytes, expressing GFAP, hypertrophy and proliferate to form the glial scar — gliosis is the universal histologic footprint of CNS injury, unlike the collagenous scars of peripheral tissues.

cns-cellular-reactions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Eosinophilic shrunken neurons (“red neurons”)”?
cns-cellular-reactions.explanation: Eosinophilic shrunken neurons (“red neurons”) → Acute hypoxic-ischemic necrosis.

cns-cellular-reactions.stem: What best explains the finding: “GFAP-positive hypertrophic astrocytes (gliosis)”?
cns-cellular-reactions.explanation: GFAP-positive hypertrophic astrocytes (gliosis) → Non-specific marker of CNS injury.

cns-cellular-reactions.stem: Which should you review before “CNS Cellular Reactions to Injury”?
cns-cellular-reactions.explanation: Understanding neuronal and glial structures is essential for grasping CNS cellular reactions.

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.stem: A person falls backward and strikes the occiput. Besides bruising at the impact site, injury is found in the frontal and temporal poles. This anterior damage is called:
traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.explanation: Damage opposite the impact site, as the brain rebounds against the skull, is a contrecoup contusion — classically at the frontal/temporal poles after an occipital blow.

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.stem: Regarding concussion vs contusion — which is correct?

options.text: Any post-traumatic loss of consciousness means structural brain damage
Concussion is a transient, reversible functional disturbance with no structural lesion; a contusion is a visible parenchymal bruise

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.explanation: Concussion produces temporary neurologic dysfunction that recovers fully, whereas a contusion is direct tissue injury (coup/contrecoup) seen on imaging/pathology.

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.stem: What best explains the finding: “Transient loss of consciousness with full recovery”?
traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.explanation: Transient loss of consciousness with full recovery → Concussion.

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sensorimotor level on the trunk after spinal trauma”?
traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.explanation: Sensorimotor level on the trunk after spinal trauma → Cord injury at that segment.

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.stem: Which should you review before “Traumatic Brain & Spinal Injury”?

options.text: Trauma, Acute Stress, PTSD & Psychological First Aid

traumatic-brain-spinal-injury.explanation: Psychological effects of trauma are closely related to brain injury outcomes.

raised-icp-herniation.stem: A patient with a large hemispheric mass develops a fixed, dilated right pupil and left-sided weakness with declining consciousness. This indicates:
raised-icp-herniation.explanation: An ipsilateral blown pupil (CN III compression) with contralateral hemiparesis and depressed consciousness is classic uncal (transtentorial) herniation — a neurosurgical emergency.

raised-icp-herniation.stem: Regarding vasogenic vs cytotoxic edema — which is correct?

options.text: All cerebral edema comes from blood-brain-barrier leakage
Vasogenic edema is extracellular (BBB breakdown, tumor/inflammation); cytotoxic edema is intracellular (cell-membrane failure in ischemia)
Uncal herniation compressing CN III (and cerebral peduncle)

raised-icp-herniation.explanation: The two mechanisms differ in compartment and cause — vasogenic responds to steroids (tumor edema), whereas cytotoxic (ischemic) edema does not.

raised-icp-herniation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil + contralateral hemiparesis”?

options.text: Uncal herniation compressing CN III (and cerebral peduncle)

raised-icp-herniation.explanation: Ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil + contralateral hemiparesis → Uncal herniation compressing CN III (and cerebral peduncle).

raised-icp-herniation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypertension + bradycardia + irregular breathing”?

options.text: Uncal herniation compressing CN III (and cerebral peduncle)

raised-icp-herniation.explanation: Hypertension + bradycardia + irregular breathing → Cushing response to raised ICP.

raised-icp-herniation.stem: Which should you review before “Raised ICP, Edema & Herniation”?
raised-icp-herniation.explanation: Understanding edema types is crucial for grasping raised ICP.

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: A young man is struck in the temple, briefly loses consciousness, wakes and talks, then rapidly deteriorates. CT shows a biconvex hyperdensity that does not cross suture lines. The diagnosis is:
epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: A lucid interval after temporal trauma with a biconvex (lens-shaped) collection that respects suture lines is an epidural hematoma from middle meningeal artery rupture — a neurosurgical emergency.

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: Regarding distinguishing extra-axial bleeds — which is correct?

options.text: A crescent-shaped bleed that crosses a suture line is an epidural hematoma
A crescent collection crossing suture lines (but not the midline) is a SUBDURAL; epidurals are biconvex and stop at sutures

epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: The epidural is bound by dural attachments at sutures (biconvex), while the subdural spreads in the subdural space across sutures but is halted by midline dural reflections (crescent).

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Lucid interval then rapid decline after temporal trauma”?
epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: Lucid interval then rapid decline after temporal trauma → Arterial epidural hematoma.

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Gradual confusion/headache in an elderly or alcoholic patient”?
epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: Gradual confusion/headache in an elderly or alcoholic patient → Chronic subdural (bridging-vein) hematoma.

epidural-subdural-hematoma.stem: Which should you review before “Epidural & Subdural Hematoma”?
epidural-subdural-hematoma.explanation: Understanding the anatomy of the meninges is crucial for grasping hematoma formation.

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.stem: A 50-year-old suddenly collapses with the “worst headache of my life” and neck stiffness. Non-contrast CT shows blood in the basal cisterns. The most likely cause is:
sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.explanation: A thunderclap “worst headache of life” with subarachnoid blood in the basal cisterns is a subarachnoid hemorrhage, most often from a ruptured berry aneurysm at the Circle of Willis.

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.stem: Regarding location of hypertensive hemorrhage — which is correct?

options.text: A lobar hemorrhage in an elderly patient is from chronic hypertension
Hypertensive bleeds are typically DEEP (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum); lobar hemorrhages in the elderly suggest cerebral amyloid angiopathy

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.explanation: Hypertension damages small penetrating vessels deep in the brain (Charcot-Bouchard aneurysms), whereas amyloid deposition in cortical vessels causes superficial lobar bleeds — location points to the cause.

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sudden “worst headache of life” + meningismus”?
sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.explanation: Sudden “worst headache of life” + meningismus → Aneurysmal SAH.

sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.stem: What best explains the finding: “Deep (basal ganglia/thalamic) hemorrhage in a hypertensive”?
sah-aneurysm-avm-iph.explanation: Deep (basal ganglia/thalamic) hemorrhage in a hypertensive → Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm rupture.

altered-mental-status-coma.stem: A comatose patient has symmetric pupils, intact brainstem reflexes, no focal weakness, and no meningismus. The most likely category of cause is:
altered-mental-status-coma.explanation: A non-focal, symmetric exam with preserved brainstem reflexes and no meningismus points to a diffuse metabolic or toxic encephalopathy — the third and most common category of altered mental status.

altered-mental-status-coma.stem: Regarding coma from a single lesion — which is correct?

options.text: A single unilateral hemispheric stroke explains the coma
Coma requires bilateral hemispheric dysfunction or a brainstem (ARAS) lesion — a unilateral hemisphere lesion alone does not cause coma unless it raises ICP and compresses the brainstem

altered-mental-status-coma.explanation: Wakefulness depends on the brainstem ARAS projecting to both hemispheres; one hemisphere can be lost without coma unless mass effect secondarily compresses the brainstem.

altered-mental-status-coma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Symmetric exam, preserved brainstem reflexes, no focal signs”?
altered-mental-status-coma.explanation: Symmetric exam, preserved brainstem reflexes, no focal signs → Metabolic/toxic encephalopathy.

altered-mental-status-coma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Focal weakness, gaze deviation, or cranial-nerve signs”?
altered-mental-status-coma.explanation: Focal weakness, gaze deviation, or cranial-nerve signs → Structural (stroke/mass) cause.

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: A malnourished patient with chronic alcohol use is confused, with nystagmus and an unsteady gait. The immediate treatment priority is:
wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: This is Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion + ophthalmoplegia + ataxia). Give IV thiamine before any glucose, because a glucose load can precipitate or worsen the encephalopathy.

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: Regarding order of thiamine vs glucose — which is correct?

options.text: Give IV dextrose first to a confused, malnourished alcoholic patient
Give thiamine before (or with) glucose — a glucose load in thiamine deficiency can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy

wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: Glucose metabolism consumes thiamine; loading glucose into a depleted patient can trigger or worsen Wernicke, so thiamine must come first.

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: What best explains the finding: “Confusion + horizontal nystagmus/ophthalmoplegia + ataxic gait”?
wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: Confusion + horizontal nystagmus/ophthalmoplegia + ataxic gait → Wernicke (midline diencephalic/brainstem necrosis).

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dense anterograde amnesia with confabulation”?
wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: Dense anterograde amnesia with confabulation → Korsakoff (mammillary/Papez damage).

wernicke-korsakoff.stem: Which should you review before “Wernicke Encephalopathy & Korsakoff”?
wernicke-korsakoff.explanation: Directly addresses thiamine deficiency and its role in Wernicke's.

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: A cirrhotic patient becomes drowsy and confused with a flapping tremor after a gastrointestinal bleed. The best initial management is:

options.text: Lactulose plus treatment of the GI bleed (the precipitant)

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: Confusion with asterixis in a cirrhotic after a GI bleed is hepatic encephalopathy. Lower ammonia with lactulose (± rifaximin) and treat the precipitant (the GI hemorrhage).

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: Regarding managing hepatic encephalopathy — which is correct?

options.text: Treat hepatic encephalopathy by restricting protein and lowering ammonia only
Always search for and treat the precipitant (GI bleed, infection, hypokalemia, constipation, sedatives) alongside lactulose/rifaximin

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: Most episodes of HE are triggered by an identifiable precipitant; correcting it is as important as lowering ammonia, and prolonged protein restriction worsens malnutrition.

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Asterixis (flapping tremor) + confusion in a cirrhotic”?
hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: Asterixis (flapping tremor) + confusion in a cirrhotic → Hepatic encephalopathy.

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Multifocal myoclonus ± seizures in renal failure”?
hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: Multifocal myoclonus ± seizures in renal failure → Uremic encephalopathy.

hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.stem: Which should you review before “Hepatic & Uremic Encephalopathy”?
hepatic-uremic-encephalopathy.explanation: Understanding liver function and cirrhosis is essential for hepatic encephalopathy.

periodic-paralysis.stem: A 25-year-old man has recurrent attacks of limb weakness after heavy dessert meals or stress; eye, bulbar, and breathing muscles are spared, and his father is similarly affected. The most likely diagnosis is:
periodic-paralysis.explanation: Episodic flaccid weakness triggered by carbohydrate load/stress, sparing ocular/bulbar/respiratory muscles, with autosomal-dominant inheritance is hypokalemic periodic paralysis — check potassium during an attack.

periodic-paralysis.stem: Regarding episodic weakness workup — which is correct?

options.text: Recurrent limb weakness in a young man is a psychiatric or non-organic problem
Episodic flaccid weakness with a potassium shift (and often thyrotoxicosis or family history) is periodic paralysis — check K⁺ during the attack and thyroid function

periodic-paralysis.explanation: PP is a real channelopathy/electrolyte disorder; measuring potassium during an attack and screening for thyrotoxicosis identifies a treatable cause and prevents dangerous arrhythmia (Andersen-Tawil).

periodic-paralysis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Episodic flaccid limb weakness sparing eyes/bulbar/respiration”?
periodic-paralysis.explanation: Episodic flaccid limb weakness sparing eyes/bulbar/respiration → Periodic paralysis (channelopathy).

periodic-paralysis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Attacks after heavy carbohydrate meals + family history”?
periodic-paralysis.explanation: Attacks after heavy carbohydrate meals + family history → Hypokalemic PP.

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: A neurotransmitter binds a receptor that directly opens a chloride channel within milliseconds, hyperpolarizing the postsynaptic membrane. This is:
cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: Direct, millisecond-scale opening of a Cl⁻ channel producing hyperpolarization (IPSP) is an ionotropic inhibitory receptor such as GABA_A — the target of benzodiazepines and barbiturates.

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: Regarding why give l-dopa instead of dopamine — which is correct?

options.text: Just give dopamine to replace the deficient neurotransmitter in Parkinson disease
Dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier; its precursor L-DOPA uses the amino-acid transporter to enter the brain

cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: The BBB excludes the polar dopamine molecule, so the lipophilic/transportable precursor L-DOPA is given and then decarboxylated to dopamine centrally.

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rapid (ms) inhibitory response = GABA_A opening Cl⁻ channels”?
cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: Rapid (ms) inhibitory response = GABA_A opening Cl⁻ channels → Ionotropic receptor (fast IPSP).

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: What best explains the finding: “Slow, lasting modulation (seconds) via second messengers”?
cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: Slow, lasting modulation (seconds) via second messengers → Metabotropic GPCR (cAMP/IP₃/DAG).

cns-pharmacology-foundations.stem: Which should you review before “CNS Pharmacology Foundations”?
cns-pharmacology-foundations.explanation: Understanding EPSPs/IPSPs is essential for grasping CNS drug mechanisms.

cns-neurotransmitters.stem: A patient on a typical antipsychotic develops a resting tremor and rigidity plus galactorrhea. These effects are explained by dopamine blockade in which pathways?
cns-neurotransmitters.explanation: Nigrostriatal D2 blockade produces extrapyramidal (parkinsonian) symptoms, and tuberoinfundibular D2 blockade removes dopamine’s inhibition of prolactin, causing hyperprolactinemia (galactorrhea).

cns-neurotransmitters.stem: Regarding antipsychotic side effects by pathway — which is correct?

options.text: A D2 blocker only affects the reward (mesolimbic) pathway targeted for psychosis
D2 blockade also hits the nigrostriatal pathway (→ extrapyramidal symptoms) and tuberoinfundibular pathway (→ hyperprolactinemia)

cns-neurotransmitters.explanation: Non-selective D2 antagonism affects all dopaminergic pathways, so blocking mesolimbic dopamine for psychosis unavoidably risks EPS and raised prolactin.

cns-neurotransmitters.stem: What best explains the finding: “Extrapyramidal symptoms on an antipsychotic”?
cns-neurotransmitters.explanation: Extrapyramidal symptoms on an antipsychotic → Nigrostriatal D2 blockade.

cns-neurotransmitters.stem: What best explains the finding: “Galactorrhea/amenorrhea on a D2 antagonist”?
cns-neurotransmitters.explanation: Galactorrhea/amenorrhea on a D2 antagonist → Tuberoinfundibular D2 block → hyperprolactinemia.

cns-stimulants.stem: A stimulant increases synaptic dopamine primarily by reversing the dopamine transporter and inhibiting vesicular storage and MAO. This describes:
cns-stimulants.explanation: Amphetamine raises dopamine by reversing DAT/NET, blocking VMAT storage, and inhibiting MAO — actively releasing catecholamines, unlike cocaine which blocks reuptake.

cns-stimulants.stem: Regarding amphetamine vs cocaine mechanism — which is correct?

options.text: Amphetamine works mainly by blocking dopamine reuptake like cocaine
Amphetamine actively RELEASES catecholamines (reverses transporters, blocks VMAT/MAO); cocaine BLOCKS reuptake (DAT > NET)

cns-stimulants.explanation: Both raise synaptic dopamine, but amphetamine drives release from the terminal while cocaine simply prevents reuptake — a classic mechanism distinction.

cns-stimulants.stem: What best explains the finding: “Euphoria, hyperactivity, mydriasis, tachycardia, hyperthermia”?
cns-stimulants.explanation: Euphoria, hyperactivity, mydriasis, tachycardia, hyperthermia → Central + peripheral catecholamine excess.

cns-stimulants.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nasal septal perforation”?

aeds-principles-targets.stem: A patient in status epilepticus is brought to the ED. The correct first-line pharmacologic treatment is:
aeds-principles-targets.explanation: Status epilepticus is first treated with a benzodiazepine (lorazepam, diazepam, or midazolam) to abort the seizure, followed by a longer-acting agent (phenytoin, valproate, or levetiracetam).

aeds-principles-targets.stem: Regarding drug choice in absence epilepsy — which is correct?

options.text: Carbamazepine is a good broad first choice for any seizure, including absence
Carbamazepine (and phenytoin, gabapentin, etc.) WORSEN absence seizures — use ethosuximide or valproate

aeds-principles-targets.explanation: Sodium-channel/GABAergic agents like carbamazepine can aggravate absence seizures; ethosuximide (T-type Ca²⁺) and valproate are the appropriate choices.

aeds-principles-targets.stem: What best explains the finding: “Brief staring spells with 3-Hz spike-wave”?
aeds-principles-targets.explanation: Brief staring spells with 3-Hz spike-wave → Absence seizure (T-type Ca²⁺, thalamocortical).

aeds-principles-targets.stem: What best explains the finding: “Generalized convulsion >5 min or recurrent without recovery”?
aeds-principles-targets.explanation: Generalized convulsion >5 min or recurrent without recovery → Status epilepticus.

aeds-principles-targets.stem: Which should you review before “Antiepileptic Drugs — Principles & Targets”?

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.stem: Before starting carbamazepine in a Thai patient, which test best reduces the risk of a life-threatening cutaneous reaction?
aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.explanation: HLA-B*1502 (common in Southeast Asians) strongly predicts carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN, so screening is recommended before starting the drug.

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.stem: Regarding phenytoin dosing kinetics — which is correct?

options.text: Doubling the phenytoin dose will roughly double the serum level
Phenytoin shows zero-order (saturable) kinetics at therapeutic doses — small dose increases can cause disproportionately large level rises and toxicity

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.explanation: Once the metabolizing enzymes saturate, phenytoin clearance becomes constant, so level rises nonlinearly — a classic cause of unexpected toxicity.

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.stem: What best explains the finding: “Gingival hyperplasia + hirsutism”?
What best explains the finding: “Hyponatremia + rash in an Asian patient on carbamazepine”?
aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.explanation: Hyponatremia + rash in an Asian patient on carbamazepine → SIADH; HLA-B*1502 SJS risk.

aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.stem: Which should you review before “AEDs — Sodium Channel Blockers”?
aeds-sodium-channel-blockers.explanation: Understanding sodium balance is crucial for grasping sodium channel blockers' effects.

aeds-gaba-and-absence.stem: A child with pure absence epilepsy is best treated first-line with a drug that blocks thalamic T-type calcium channels, namely:
