aeds-gaba-and-absence.explanation: Ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons and is the classic drug for absence seizures; carbamazepine, phenytoin, and vigabatrin can worsen absence.

aeds-gaba-and-absence.stem: Regarding gabapentin mechanism — which is correct?

options.text: Gabapentin, being a GABA analog, works by activating GABA receptors
Gabapentin/pregabalin act on the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, NOT on GABA receptors

aeds-gaba-and-absence.explanation: Despite the name and structure, they do not bind GABA receptors — their anticonvulsant and analgesic effects come from reducing Ca²⁺-dependent neurotransmitter release via α2δ.

aeds-gaba-and-absence.stem: What best explains the finding: “Absence controlled by ethosuximide”?
aeds-gaba-and-absence.explanation: Absence controlled by ethosuximide → T-type Ca²⁺ channel block.

aeds-gaba-and-absence.stem: What best explains the finding: “Peripheral visual field constriction on an AED”?
aeds-gaba-and-absence.explanation: Peripheral visual field constriction on an AED → Vigabatrin.

aeds-broad-spectrum.stem: Which antiepileptic drug is broad-spectrum (effective across absence, myoclonic, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures) but is strongly teratogenic and hepatotoxic?
aeds-broad-spectrum.explanation: Valproate acts at multiple targets and covers all major seizure types (plus bipolar disorder and migraine), but carries hepatotoxicity and teratogenicity (neural tube defects), so it is avoided in pregnancy.

aeds-broad-spectrum.stem: Regarding aed choice in a woman of childbearing age — which is correct?

options.text: Valproate is broad-spectrum, so it is the safe default for any young woman with generalized epilepsy
Avoid valproate in women who may become pregnant — it is highly teratogenic (neural tube defects); prefer lamotrigine or levetiracetam

aeds-broad-spectrum.explanation: Valproate’s broad efficacy is offset by strong teratogenicity and hepatotoxicity, so safer alternatives are chosen when pregnancy is possible.

aeds-broad-spectrum.stem: What best explains the finding: “Weight gain, alopecia, tremor, high ammonia on an AED”?
aeds-broad-spectrum.explanation: Weight gain, alopecia, tremor, high ammonia on an AED → Valproate.

aeds-broad-spectrum.stem: What best explains the finding: “Kidney stones + word-finding difficulty + weight loss”?
aeds-broad-spectrum.explanation: Kidney stones + word-finding difficulty + weight loss → Topiramate (carbonic anhydrase inhibition).

aeds-broad-spectrum.stem: Which should you review before “AEDs — Broad-Spectrum & Glutamate Agents”?
aeds-broad-spectrum.explanation: Understanding neurotransmission is essential for grasping AED mechanisms.

levodopa-and-adjuncts.stem: Levodopa is combined with carbidopa in Parkinson disease primarily to:

options.text: Inhibit peripheral DOPA-decarboxylase, increasing CNS delivery and reducing side effects

levodopa-and-adjuncts.explanation: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral DOPA-decarboxylase, so more levodopa reaches the brain and there is less peripheral dopamine causing nausea and orthostatic hypotension.

levodopa-and-adjuncts.stem: Regarding purpose of carbidopa — which is correct?

options.text: Carbidopa is added to help levodopa cross the blood-brain barrier
Carbidopa inhibits PERIPHERAL DOPA-decarboxylase, so more levodopa survives to reach the brain and peripheral side effects fall — it does not itself enter the CNS

levodopa-and-adjuncts.explanation: Carbidopa cannot cross the BBB; by blocking peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine, it increases central delivery and reduces nausea and hypotension.

levodopa-and-adjuncts.stem: What best explains the finding: “Improvement of bradykinesia/rigidity on levodopa”?
levodopa-and-adjuncts.explanation: Improvement of bradykinesia/rigidity on levodopa → Central dopamine repletion.

levodopa-and-adjuncts.stem: What best explains the finding: “End-of-dose “wearing-off” and involuntary dyskinesias”?
levodopa-and-adjuncts.explanation: End-of-dose “wearing-off” and involuntary dyskinesias → Fluctuating levodopa levels.

dopamine-agonists-antimuscarinics.stem: A patient on haloperidol develops rigidity and bradykinesia. The most appropriate management is to reduce/stop the antipsychotic and add:
dopamine-agonists-antimuscarinics.explanation: Drug-induced parkinsonism results from dopamine (D2) receptor blockade; a central antimuscarinic such as benztropine is the treatment of choice, alongside reducing the causative drug. Levodopa is ineffective when receptors are blocked.

dopamine-agonists-antimuscarinics.stem: Regarding treating drug-induced parkinsonism — which is correct?

options.text: Add levodopa to treat parkinsonism caused by an antipsychotic
Drug-induced parkinsonism is from D2 blockade — treat by stopping/reducing the offending drug and using a central antimuscarinic (e.g. benztropine), not levodopa

dopamine-agonists-antimuscarinics.explanation: Because the receptors are blocked, adding levodopa is ineffective; antimuscarinics rebalance the ACh–dopamine ratio and relieve the parkinsonism.

dopamine-agonists-antimuscarinics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sudden sleep attacks / new gambling on therapy”?
dopamine-agonists-antimuscarinics.explanation: Sudden sleep attacks / new gambling on therapy → Dopamine-agonist effect.

dopamine-agonists-antimuscarinics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Parkinsonism after starting an antipsychotic/metoclopramide”?
dopamine-agonists-antimuscarinics.explanation: Parkinsonism after starting an antipsychotic/metoclopramide → Drug-induced (D2 blockade) — treat with antimuscarinic.

dopamine-agonists-antimuscarinics.stem: Which should you review before “Dopamine Agonists, Amantadine & Antimuscarinics”?
dopamine-agonists-antimuscarinics.explanation: Understanding agonists and antagonists is essential for grasping dopamine agonists.

astrocytoma-glioblastoma.stem: A 62-year-old presents with a rapidly enlarging hemispheric mass. Histology shows a GFAP-positive astrocytic tumor with microvascular proliferation and pseudopalisading necrosis, IDH-wildtype. The diagnosis is:
astrocytoma-glioblastoma.explanation: Pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation in an IDH-wildtype astrocytic tumor of an older adult define glioblastoma, WHO grade 4 — the most common CNS malignancy.

astrocytoma-glioblastoma.stem: Regarding metastatic potential of cns tumors — which is correct?

options.text: A high-grade brain malignancy like glioblastoma commonly metastasizes to lungs and liver
Primary CNS malignancies rarely spread outside the CNS; they cause harm by local infiltration and compression

astrocytoma-glioblastoma.explanation: Unlike systemic cancers, gliomas almost never metastasize beyond the neuraxis — their lethality comes from infiltration of vital brain structures, not distant spread.

astrocytoma-glioblastoma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Progressive headache, new seizures, focal deficit in an adult”?
astrocytoma-glioblastoma.explanation: Progressive headache, new seizures, focal deficit in an adult → Expanding infiltrating hemispheric glioma.

astrocytoma-glioblastoma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ring-enhancing mass crossing the corpus callosum”?
astrocytoma-glioblastoma.explanation: Ring-enhancing mass crossing the corpus callosum → Butterfly glioblastoma.

other-gliomas.stem: A frontal-lobe tumor in an adult with a long seizure history shows cells with perinuclear halos (“fried-egg”) and a delicate “chicken-wire” vasculature with calcification. The defining molecular finding is:
other-gliomas.explanation: The fried-egg cells and chicken-wire capillaries describe oligodendroglioma, which is defined by an IDH mutation together with 1p/19q whole-arm codeletion.

other-gliomas.stem: Regarding circumscribed vs diffuse glioma prognosis — which is correct?

options.text: All gliomas are aggressive, infiltrative, and carry a poor prognosis
Pilocytic astrocytoma is a well-circumscribed WHO grade 1 tumor (Rosenthal fibers) that is often curable by resection

other-gliomas.explanation: Unlike diffuse (infiltrating) astrocytomas, the pilocytic astrocytoma is discrete and low-grade — an important benign exception with an excellent prognosis.

other-gliomas.stem: What best explains the finding: “Frontal calcified tumor with seizures”?
other-gliomas.explanation: Frontal calcified tumor with seizures → Oligodendroglioma.

other-gliomas.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cerebellar cyst + mural nodule in a child”?
other-gliomas.explanation: Cerebellar cyst + mural nodule in a child → Pilocytic astrocytoma (grade 1).

pediatric-embryonal-tumors.stem: A 7-year-old has ataxia and a cerebellar midline mass composed of small round blue cells with Homer-Wright rosettes; spinal MRI shows nodular deposits along the cauda equina. The diagnosis is:
pediatric-embryonal-tumors.explanation: A cerebellar small-round-blue-cell tumor with Homer-Wright rosettes and CSF “drop metastases” to the cauda equina in a child is medulloblastoma (embryonal, WHO grade 4).

pediatric-embryonal-tumors.stem: Regarding spread pattern of medulloblastoma — which is correct?

options.text: A malignant brain tumor in a child metastasizes hematogenously to the lungs
Medulloblastoma disseminates via the CSF, producing “drop metastases” along the neuraxis (e.g. cauda equina)

pediatric-embryonal-tumors.explanation: CNS tumors rarely leave the neuraxis; medulloblastoma’s characteristic spread is through CSF pathways, so staging includes the whole spine and CSF cytology.

pediatric-embryonal-tumors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Child with ataxia, morning headache, vomiting”?
pediatric-embryonal-tumors.explanation: Child with ataxia, morning headache, vomiting → Cerebellar mass + obstructive hydrocephalus.

pediatric-embryonal-tumors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Drug-resistant temporal-lobe epilepsy in a young patient”?
pediatric-embryonal-tumors.explanation: Drug-resistant temporal-lobe epilepsy in a young patient → Ganglioglioma.

pediatric-embryonal-tumors.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Medulloblastoma, Ganglioglioma & Choroid Plexus”?
pediatric-embryonal-tumors.explanation: Both involve pediatric conditions but in different systems.

pediatric-embryonal-tumors.stem: Which should you review before “Medulloblastoma, Ganglioglioma & Choroid Plexus”?

meningioma-schwannoma-pituitary.stem: A dura-based, well-demarcated extra-axial mass in a middle-aged woman shows cellular whorls and psammoma bodies on histology. The diagnosis is:
meningioma-schwannoma-pituitary.explanation: A dura-based extra-axial tumor with whorls and psammoma bodies, more common in women, is a meningioma — the most common primary brain tumor, usually benign (WHO grade 1).

meningioma-schwannoma-pituitary.stem: Regarding bilateral acoustic neuromas — which is correct?

options.text: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are just sporadic tumors
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are essentially diagnostic of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)

meningioma-schwannoma-pituitary.explanation: Sporadic schwannomas are unilateral; bilateral CN VIII schwannomas signal the NF2 tumor-suppressor syndrome and warrant genetic evaluation.

meningioma-schwannoma-pituitary.stem: What best explains the finding: “Slow-growing dura-based mass with a “tail” on MRI”?
meningioma-schwannoma-pituitary.explanation: Slow-growing dura-based mass with a “tail” on MRI → Meningioma.

meningioma-schwannoma-pituitary.stem: What best explains the finding: “Unilateral SNHL + tinnitus + imbalance”?
meningioma-schwannoma-pituitary.explanation: Unilateral SNHL + tinnitus + imbalance → Vestibular schwannoma (CN VIII, CPA).

meningioma-schwannoma-pituitary.stem: Which should you review before “Meningioma, Schwannoma & Pituitary Adenoma”?

options.text: MSK Embryology: Somites & the Axial Skeleton

cns-lymphoma-metastases.stem: An AIDS patient has a solitary periventricular enhancing brain mass; biopsy shows perivascular sheets of EBV-positive large B-cells. The diagnosis is:
cns-lymphoma-metastases.explanation: A periventricular EBV-associated diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with perivascular clustering in an immunosuppressed patient is primary CNS lymphoma — the most common CNS neoplasm in immunosuppression.

cns-lymphoma-metastases.stem: Regarding steroids before cns lymphoma biopsy — which is correct?

options.text: Give corticosteroids up front for any enhancing brain mass with edema, then biopsy
If CNS lymphoma is suspected, avoid steroids before biopsy — they can rapidly shrink the tumor and obscure the diagnosis

cns-lymphoma-metastases.explanation: Lymphoma is exquisitely steroid-sensitive; premature steroids may cause the lesion to “disappear” and yield a non-diagnostic biopsy, delaying correct treatment.

cns-lymphoma-metastases.stem: What best explains the finding: “Periventricular mass in an AIDS/transplant patient”?
cns-lymphoma-metastases.explanation: Periventricular mass in an AIDS/transplant patient → Primary CNS lymphoma (EBV, DLBCL).

cns-lymphoma-metastases.stem: What best explains the finding: “Multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the gray-white junction”?
cns-lymphoma-metastases.explanation: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the gray-white junction → Hematogenous metastases.

cns-lymphoma-metastases.stem: Which should you review before “CNS Lymphoma & Metastases”?
cns-lymphoma-metastases.explanation: Understanding differentiation and invasion is crucial for grasping CNS lymphoma pathology.

ototopical-drugs.stem: A patient with otitis externa and a possibly perforated eardrum needs antibiotic drops. The safest choice regarding inner-ear toxicity is:
ototopical-drugs.explanation: Fluoroquinolone ear drops (ofloxacin, ciprofloxacin) lack inner-ear toxicity and are approved for middle-ear use, making them the safe choice when the tympanic membrane may be perforated. Aminoglycosides and chloramphenicol are potentially ototoxic.

ototopical-drugs.stem: Regarding choosing ear drops with a possible perforation — which is correct?

options.text: Any antibiotic ear drop is fine as long as it covers the likely organisms
If the tympanic membrane may be perforated, avoid ototoxic (aminoglycoside/chloramphenicol) and wax-softening drops — use a non-ototoxic quinolone

ototopical-drugs.explanation: With a perforation, ototoxic drops reach the inner ear and can cause permanent cochleovestibular damage; quinolones are the safe choice for middle-ear exposure.

ototopical-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Painful, swollen, discharging canal (bacterial OE)”?
ototopical-drugs.explanation: Painful, swollen, discharging canal (bacterial OE) → Pseudomonas/S. aureus otitis externa.

ototopical-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Itchy, damp ear with fungal debris”?
ototopical-drugs.explanation: Itchy, damp ear with fungal debris → Otomycosis (Aspergillus).

ototopical-drugs.stem: Which should you review before “Ototopical Drugs”?
ototopical-drugs.explanation: Understanding external ear disorders is essential for applying ototopical drugs.

vertigo-vestibular-drugs.stem: Which drug, a histamine analog acting as an H3 antagonist to increase inner-ear blood flow, is used for maintenance therapy of Ménière disease?
vertigo-vestibular-drugs.explanation: Betahistine (an H3 antagonist/weak H1 agonist) increases inner-ear microcirculation and reduces vestibular activity, and is the mainstay for Ménière disease. Meclizine/scopolamine are acute suppressants; ondansetron is an antiemetic.

vertigo-vestibular-drugs.stem: Regarding duration of vestibular suppressant use — which is correct?

options.text: Keep a patient on daily meclizine long-term to prevent all vertigo
Use vestibular suppressants only short-term — chronic use impairs central vestibular compensation and prolongs disability

vertigo-vestibular-drugs.explanation: Suppressants blunt the vestibular signal that the brain needs to recalibrate; prolonged use prevents compensation, so they are for acute symptom relief only.

vertigo-vestibular-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Acute spinning vertigo with nausea”?
vertigo-vestibular-drugs.explanation: Acute spinning vertigo with nausea → Vestibular imbalance (treat short-term with suppressants).

vertigo-vestibular-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Recurrent vertigo + fluctuating SNHL + tinnitus/fullness”?
vertigo-vestibular-drugs.explanation: Recurrent vertigo + fluctuating SNHL + tinnitus/fullness → Ménière (endolymphatic hydrops) → betahistine.

vertigo-vestibular-drugs.stem: Which should you review before “Vertigo & Vestibular Drugs”?
vertigo-vestibular-drugs.explanation: Understanding vestibular physiology is essential for grasping drug mechanisms.

cognitive-domains-dementia-workup.stem: A 78-year-old develops acute confusion that fluctuates over hours, with marked inattention and drowsiness, two days after surgery. The most likely diagnosis is:
cognitive-domains-dementia-workup.explanation: Acute-onset, fluctuating inattention with altered consciousness — especially post-operatively — is delirium, a reversible condition that must be excluded before diagnosing dementia.

cognitive-domains-dementia-workup.stem: Regarding mci vs dementia — which is correct?

options.text: Any objective cognitive impairment on testing means dementia
Mild cognitive impairment has measurable cognitive decline but PRESERVED activities of daily living; dementia requires functional (ADL) impairment

cognitive-domains-dementia-workup.explanation: The defining line between MCI and dementia is functional independence — MCI patients still manage daily activities, whereas dementia impairs them.

cognitive-domains-dementia-workup.stem: What best explains the finding: “Acute, fluctuating inattention with clouded consciousness”?
cognitive-domains-dementia-workup.explanation: Acute, fluctuating inattention with clouded consciousness → Delirium (not dementia).

cognitive-domains-dementia-workup.stem: What best explains the finding: “Impaired instrumental ADLs (finances, medications)”?
cognitive-domains-dementia-workup.explanation: Impaired instrumental ADLs (finances, medications) → Progression from MCI to dementia.

cognitive-domains-dementia-workup.stem: Which should you review before “Cognitive Domains & Dementia Workup”?
cognitive-domains-dementia-workup.explanation: Basic understanding of cellular structures may aid in understanding brain pathology.

alzheimer-and-dementias.stem: A 72-year-old with progressive short-term memory loss has symmetric hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy on MRI. First-line pharmacologic therapy is:
alzheimer-and-dementias.explanation: This is Alzheimer disease; cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) are first-line symptomatic therapy, with memantine added in moderate–severe disease.

alzheimer-and-dementias.stem: Regarding apoe4 and alzheimer risk — which is correct?

options.text: Carrying an APOE4 allele means the patient will definitely develop Alzheimer disease
APOE4 is a risk factor (heterozygous ~2–3×, homozygous ~10×), not a deterministic mutation; the deterministic genes are PSEN1/PSEN2/APP in early-onset AD

alzheimer-and-dementias.explanation: APOE4 raises probability of late-onset AD but many carriers never develop it and many patients lack it; only the autosomal-dominant early-onset genes are causative.

alzheimer-and-dementias.stem: What best explains the finding: “Early episodic (short-term) memory loss”?
alzheimer-and-dementias.explanation: Early episodic (short-term) memory loss → Hippocampal/medial temporal involvement.

alzheimer-and-dementias.stem: What best explains the finding: “Symmetric hippocampal/temporoparietal atrophy on MRI”?
alzheimer-and-dementias.explanation: Symmetric hippocampal/temporoparietal atrophy on MRI → AD neurodegeneration.

alzheimer-and-dementias.stem: Which should you review before “Alzheimer Disease & Dementia Subtypes”?
alzheimer-and-dementias.explanation: Understanding protein misfolding is essential for grasping the pathology of Alzheimer's disease.

disorders-of-consciousness.stem: A febrile patient with reduced consciousness has marked neck stiffness but no focal neurological deficit. The most appropriate initial concern is:
disorders-of-consciousness.explanation: Altered consciousness with neck stiffness points to meningeal irritation — meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage — mandating urgent imaging and lumbar puncture.

disorders-of-consciousness.stem: Regarding what produces coma — which is correct?

options.text: Any large stroke in one hemisphere will render a patient comatose
Coma requires the brainstem ARAS or bilateral hemispheric involvement; a unilateral hemispheric lesion causes coma only if it produces mass effect that compresses the brainstem
Midbrain / CN III dysfunction (e.g. uncal herniation)

disorders-of-consciousness.explanation: Wakefulness depends on the ascending reticular activating system projecting bilaterally, so one hemisphere can be damaged without coma unless herniation secondarily involves the brainstem.

disorders-of-consciousness.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fixed dilated pupil”?

options.text: Midbrain / CN III dysfunction (e.g. uncal herniation)

disorders-of-consciousness.explanation: Fixed dilated pupil → Midbrain / CN III dysfunction (e.g. uncal herniation).

disorders-of-consciousness.stem: What best explains the finding: “Neck stiffness with reduced consciousness”?

options.text: Midbrain / CN III dysfunction (e.g. uncal herniation)

disorders-of-consciousness.explanation: Neck stiffness with reduced consciousness → Meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage.

disorders-of-consciousness.stem: Which should you review before “Disorders of Consciousness”?
disorders-of-consciousness.explanation: Directly related to understanding coma and altered consciousness.

migraine-pathophysiology-acute.stem: A 55-year-old with known coronary artery disease has frequent severe migraines. Which acute therapy is safest regarding cardiovascular risk?
migraine-pathophysiology-acute.explanation: Triptans and ergots cause coronary vasoconstriction and are contraindicated in coronary artery disease. Gepants (CGRP-receptor antagonists) and lasmiditan (a 5-HT1F ditan) relieve migraine without vasoconstriction.

migraine-pathophysiology-acute.stem: Regarding acute migraine drug in a patient with heart disease — which is correct?

options.text: Use a triptan for any moderate–severe migraine regardless of cardiac history
Triptans and ergots cause coronary vasoconstriction and are contraindicated in coronary artery disease/uncontrolled hypertension — use a gepant or ditan (no vasoconstriction) instead

migraine-pathophysiology-acute.explanation: 5-HT1B receptors on coronary arteries mediate vasospasm, so triptans/ergots are unsafe in vascular disease; CGRP antagonists and lasmiditan relieve migraine without constricting vessels.

migraine-pathophysiology-acute.stem: What best explains the finding: “Unilateral throbbing headache + nausea + photophobia”?
migraine-pathophysiology-acute.explanation: Unilateral throbbing headache + nausea + photophobia → Trigeminovascular activation.

migraine-pathophysiology-acute.stem: What best explains the finding: “Preceding scintillating scotoma / zigzag lines”?
migraine-pathophysiology-acute.explanation: Preceding scintillating scotoma / zigzag lines → Cortical spreading depression (aura).

migraine-prophylaxis.stem: A hypertensive patient with frequent migraines needs preventive therapy but also has asthma. Which first-line prophylactic should be AVOIDED?
migraine-prophylaxis.explanation: Beta-blockers such as propranolol are effective migraine prophylaxis (especially with hypertension) but are contraindicated in asthma; an alternative like topiramate or a CGRP mAb should be chosen.

migraine-prophylaxis.stem: Regarding preventive vs acute migraine therapy — which is correct?

options.text: Prophylactic drugs like propranolol or topiramate can be taken at headache onset to abort an attack
Preventives are taken daily to reduce attack frequency and take weeks to work — they do not abort an acute attack (use NSAIDs/triptans for that)

migraine-prophylaxis.explanation: Migraine prophylaxis modifies attack frequency over time; acute (abortive) therapy is a separate category taken during an attack.

migraine-prophylaxis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Migraine + hypertension”?
What best explains the finding: “Migraine + depression/insomnia”?
Which should you review before “Migraine Prophylaxis”?
migraine-prophylaxis.explanation: Understanding genetics may provide context for migraine susceptibility.

sedative-hypnotics-benzodiazepines.stem: Benzodiazepines and barbiturates both act at the GABA_A receptor. The key mechanistic difference is that benzodiazepines increase the ____ of chloride channel opening, whereas barbiturates increase the ____.
sedative-hypnotics-benzodiazepines.explanation: Benzodiazepines increase the frequency of GABA-mediated Cl⁻ channel opening, while barbiturates increase the duration of opening (and at high doses can open the channel directly).

sedative-hypnotics-benzodiazepines.stem: Regarding benzodiazepine choice in liver disease/elderly — which is correct?

options.text: Any benzodiazepine is equally safe in an elderly patient with hepatic impairment
Prefer lorazepam, oxazepam, or estazolam (LEO) — they undergo only glucuronidation with no active metabolites, so they don’t accumulate

sedative-hypnotics-benzodiazepines.explanation: Benzodiazepines metabolized by CYP oxidation to long-acting active metabolites accumulate in the elderly and in liver disease, causing excessive sedation; LEO agents avoid this.

sedative-hypnotics-benzodiazepines.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sedation + anterograde amnesia after a benzodiazepine”?
sedative-hypnotics-benzodiazepines.explanation: Sedation + anterograde amnesia after a benzodiazepine → GABA_A potentiation.

sedative-hypnotics-benzodiazepines.stem: What best explains the finding: “Reversal of benzodiazepine sedation by flumazenil”?
sedative-hypnotics-benzodiazepines.explanation: Reversal of benzodiazepine sedation by flumazenil → Competitive GABA_A benzodiazepine-site antagonist.

sedative-hypnotics-benzodiazepines.stem: Which should you review before “Sedative-Hypnotics & Benzodiazepines”?
sedative-hypnotics-benzodiazepines.explanation: Understanding pain modulation can provide context for sedative effects.

barbiturates-and-anxiolytics.stem: A patient with generalized anxiety disorder and a history of alcohol dependence needs an anxiolytic with no sedation or dependence potential. The best choice is:
barbiturates-and-anxiolytics.explanation: Buspirone, a 5-HT1A partial agonist, treats GAD without sedation, dependence, or additive CNS depression, making it well suited to patients with a substance-use history (though it takes 2–4 weeks to work).

barbiturates-and-anxiolytics.stem: Regarding reversing sedative-hypnotic overdose — which is correct?

options.text: Flumazenil can reverse both benzodiazepine and barbiturate overdoses
Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and Z-drugs only — there is NO antidote for barbiturates (supportive/ventilatory care)

barbiturates-and-anxiolytics.explanation: Barbiturates act partly by directly opening the Cl⁻ channel independent of the benzodiazepine site, so flumazenil is ineffective; management of barbiturate overdose is supportive.

barbiturates-and-anxiolytics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Respiratory/cardiac depression from overdose, no reversal agent”?
barbiturates-and-anxiolytics.explanation: Respiratory/cardiac depression from overdose, no reversal agent → Barbiturate (low therapeutic index).

barbiturates-and-anxiolytics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Acute porphyria attack triggered by a sedative”?
barbiturates-and-anxiolytics.explanation: Acute porphyria attack triggered by a sedative → Barbiturate induces ALA synthase.

barbiturates-and-anxiolytics.stem: Which should you review before “Barbiturates & Non-Benzodiazepine Anxiolytics”?
barbiturates-and-anxiolytics.explanation: Understanding dose-response is crucial for grasping barbiturate effects.

opioid-receptors-mechanism.stem: Which opioid receptor is responsible for most of the analgesic effect as well as respiratory depression and physical dependence?
opioid-receptors-mechanism.explanation: The μ (mu) receptor mediates most analgesia along with euphoria, respiratory depression, miosis, constipation, and physical dependence.

opioid-receptors-mechanism.stem: Regarding adding a partial agonist to a full agonist — which is correct?

options.text: Adding buprenorphine to a patient already on a full μ agonist will boost analgesia
A partial agonist (buprenorphine) can displace the full agonist and precipitate acute withdrawal / reduce analgesia

opioid-receptors-mechanism.explanation: Because the partial agonist has high affinity but lower efficacy, it competes off the full agonist and drops net receptor activation — triggering withdrawal in a dependent patient.

opioid-receptors-mechanism.stem: What best explains the finding: “Analgesia with euphoria, miosis, constipation”?
opioid-receptors-mechanism.explanation: Analgesia with euphoria, miosis, constipation → μ-receptor activation.

opioid-receptors-mechanism.stem: What best explains the finding: “Withdrawal precipitated by adding buprenorphine to a full agonist”?
opioid-receptors-mechanism.explanation: Withdrawal precipitated by adding buprenorphine to a full agonist → Partial agonist displaces full agonist.

opioid-effects-toxicity.stem: An unresponsive patient has pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 4/min. The immediate antidote is:
opioid-effects-toxicity.explanation: The opioid overdose triad (respiratory depression, pinpoint miosis, coma) is reversed with naloxone, a competitive opioid antagonist; because naloxone is short-acting, repeat dosing may be required.

opioid-effects-toxicity.stem: Regarding tolerance to opioid side effects — which is correct?

options.text: With chronic use, patients become tolerant to all opioid effects including constipation
Tolerance develops to analgesia, euphoria, and respiratory depression, but NOT to miosis or constipation

opioid-effects-toxicity.explanation: Constipation persists throughout therapy (so a bowel regimen is always needed), and miosis remains — which is why these are reliable clinical markers of opioid effect even in chronic users.

opioid-effects-toxicity.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pinpoint pupils + slow shallow breathing + coma”?
opioid-effects-toxicity.explanation: Pinpoint pupils + slow shallow breathing + coma → Opioid overdose triad.

opioid-effects-toxicity.stem: What best explains the finding: “Constipation persisting despite chronic use”?
opioid-effects-toxicity.explanation: Constipation persisting despite chronic use → No tolerance to GI effect.

opioid-effects-toxicity.stem: Which should you review before “Opioid Effects, Toxicity & Uses”?
opioid-effects-toxicity.explanation: Understanding acetaminophen overdose is crucial for differentiating from opioid toxicity.

antipsychotics-dopamine-eps.stem: Two days after starting haloperidol, a young man develops sustained involuntary contraction of the neck muscles and an upward deviation of the eyes. This is:
antipsychotics-dopamine-eps.explanation: Acute dystonia (including oculogyric crisis) occurs within hours to days of starting a high-potency antipsychotic and is treated with anticholinergics such as benztropine or diphenhydramine.

antipsychotics-dopamine-eps.stem: Regarding nms vs serotonin syndrome — which is correct?

options.text: Fever with rigidity on a psychiatric drug is always serotonin syndrome
Fever + lead-pipe rigidity + ↑CK after a dopamine-blocking (antipsychotic) drug is neuroleptic malignant syndrome; serotonin syndrome (from serotonergic drugs) shows hyperreflexia and clonus instead

antipsychotics-dopamine-eps.explanation: NMS follows dopamine antagonists and features rigidity with bradyreflexia, whereas serotonin syndrome follows serotonergic drugs and features neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia).

antipsychotics-dopamine-eps.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sustained muscle contraction / oculogyric crisis soon after starting”?
antipsychotics-dopamine-eps.explanation: Sustained muscle contraction / oculogyric crisis soon after starting → Acute dystonia (EPS).

antipsychotics-dopamine-eps.stem: What best explains the finding: “Involuntary lip-smacking/tongue movements after long use”?
antipsychotics-dopamine-eps.explanation: Involuntary lip-smacking/tongue movements after long use → Tardive dyskinesia.

atypical-antipsychotic-agents.stem: A patient with schizophrenia refractory to two adequate antipsychotic trials is started on clozapine. Which monitoring is mandatory because of a potentially fatal adverse effect?
atypical-antipsychotic-agents.explanation: Clozapine is used for treatment-resistant schizophrenia but can cause agranulocytosis, so regular CBC monitoring is mandatory (it also carries risks of seizures, myocarditis, and metabolic effects).

atypical-antipsychotic-agents.stem: Regarding clozapine monitoring — which is correct?

options.text: Clozapine is a safe first-line antipsychotic since it has minimal EPS
Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia and requires regular CBC monitoring because of the risk of agranulocytosis (plus seizures, myocarditis, metabolic effects)

atypical-antipsychotic-agents.explanation: Despite superior efficacy and minimal EPS, clozapine’s potentially fatal agranulocytosis mandates blood-count monitoring and restricts it to refractory cases.

atypical-antipsychotic-agents.stem: What best explains the finding: “Improvement in treatment-resistant psychosis + neutropenia”?
atypical-antipsychotic-agents.explanation: Improvement in treatment-resistant psychosis + neutropenia → Clozapine (agranulocytosis risk).

atypical-antipsychotic-agents.stem: What best explains the finding: “Weight gain, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia”?
atypical-antipsychotic-agents.explanation: Weight gain, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia → Olanzapine/clozapine metabolic effects.

atypical-antipsychotic-agents.stem: Which should you review before “Antipsychotic Agents & Their Profiles”?
atypical-antipsychotic-agents.explanation: Knowledge of neurotransmitter types is essential for understanding antipsychotic mechanisms.

antidepressants-ssri-snri.stem: A patient on an MAOI is given an SSRI and develops agitation, fever, tremor, hyperreflexia, and clonus. The diagnosis is:
antidepressants-ssri-snri.explanation: Combining serotonergic agents (here an MAOI + SSRI) can cause serotonin syndrome — autonomic instability plus neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia) and altered mental status.

antidepressants-ssri-snri.stem: Regarding timing of antidepressant response — which is correct?

options.text: If an SSRI hasn’t improved mood within a few days it has failed and should be switched
Antidepressants require ~2–4 weeks for full therapeutic effect — early lack of response does not mean failure

antidepressants-ssri-snri.explanation: Although synaptic serotonin rises immediately, the mood benefit depends on slower downstream neuroadaptation, so adequate trials last several weeks before judging efficacy.

antidepressants-ssri-snri.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nausea and sexual dysfunction early in therapy”?
antidepressants-ssri-snri.explanation: Nausea and sexual dysfunction early in therapy → Serotonergic (5-HT3) side effects.

antidepressants-ssri-snri.stem: What best explains the finding: “Clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, fever”?
antidepressants-ssri-snri.explanation: Clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, fever → Serotonin syndrome.

antidepressants-ssri-snri.stem: Which should you review before “Antidepressants — SSRIs & SNRIs”?
antidepressants-ssri-snri.explanation: Knowledge of drug interactions is crucial for safe antidepressant prescribing.

tca-maoi-atypical-antidepressants.stem: A patient on phenelzine develops a severe headache and hypertensive crisis after eating aged cheese and cured meats. The mechanism is:

options.text: Tyramine-induced hypertensive crisis from MAO inhibition

tca-maoi-atypical-antidepressants.explanation: MAOIs prevent breakdown of dietary tyramine (a sympathomimetic), so tyramine-rich foods trigger a hypertensive crisis — the reason MAOIs require strict dietary restriction.

tca-maoi-atypical-antidepressants.stem: Regarding bupropion contraindication — which is correct?

options.text: Bupropion’s lack of sexual side effects makes it a good choice for any depressed patient
Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in seizure disorders and in patients with bulimia/anorexia

tca-maoi-atypical-antidepressants.explanation: Its dopaminergic/noradrenergic action increases seizure risk, so despite its favorable sexual/weight profile it must be avoided where seizure risk is already elevated.

tca-maoi-atypical-antidepressants.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dry mouth, urinary retention, sedation, QT on ECG”?
tca-maoi-atypical-antidepressants.explanation: Dry mouth, urinary retention, sedation, QT on ECG → TCA receptor blockade + cardiotoxicity.

tca-maoi-atypical-antidepressants.stem: What best explains the finding: “Severe hypertension after aged cheese on an MAOI”?
tca-maoi-atypical-antidepressants.explanation: Severe hypertension after aged cheese on an MAOI → Tyramine hypertensive crisis.

tca-maoi-atypical-antidepressants.stem: Which should you review before “TCAs, MAOIs & Atypical Antidepressants”?

options.text: Long-Term Depression & the Basis of Memory

tca-maoi-atypical-antidepressants.explanation: Understanding memory mechanisms aids in grasping antidepressant effects.

mood-stabilizers-bipolar.stem: A 28-year-old with a current manic episode (elevated mood, decreased need for sleep, grandiosity) and a prior depressive episode is diagnosed with bipolar I disorder. The most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy is:
mood-stabilizers-bipolar.explanation: Acute mania in bipolar disorder is treated with a mood stabilizer such as lithium (or valproate, ± an antipsychotic); antidepressant monotherapy is avoided because it can precipitate mania.

mood-stabilizers-bipolar.stem: Regarding treating bipolar depression — which is correct?

options.text: A patient with bipolar disorder who is depressed should be started on an SSRI as monotherapy
Antidepressant monotherapy can precipitate a manic switch — bipolar disorder is managed with a mood stabilizer (e.g. lithium, lamotrigine, or an atypical antipsychotic)

mood-stabilizers-bipolar.explanation: Because the underlying disorder cycles into mania, giving an antidepressant alone can trigger or worsen manic episodes; mood stabilization is the foundation of treatment.

mood-stabilizers-bipolar.stem: What best explains the finding: “Tremor, polyuria, weight gain, hypothyroidism”?
mood-stabilizers-bipolar.explanation: Tremor, polyuria, weight gain, hypothyroidism → Chronic lithium.

mood-stabilizers-bipolar.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nausea, ataxia, confusion, seizures”?
mood-stabilizers-bipolar.explanation: Nausea, ataxia, confusion, seizures → Lithium toxicity.

bacterial-meningitis.stem: A febrile patient with neck stiffness has CSF showing 2,000 WBC/mm³ (90% neutrophils), protein 200 mg/dL, and glucose 25 mg/dL (serum 100). The most likely diagnosis is:
bacterial-meningitis.explanation: Neutrophil-predominant pleocytosis with high protein and low glucose (CSF:serum ratio <0.4) is the classic profile of acute bacterial meningitis — treat empirically without delay.

bacterial-meningitis.stem: Regarding csf glucose interpretation — which is correct?

options.text: A low CSF glucose confirms bacterial (not tuberculous or fungal) meningitis
Low CSF glucose occurs in BOTH bacterial and TB/fungal meningitis; the cell type separates them — neutrophils (bacterial) vs lymphocytes (TB/fungal)

bacterial-meningitis.explanation: Organisms that consume glucose lower it in bacterial, tuberculous, and fungal meningitis alike, so the predominant white-cell type (and clinical tempo) is what distinguishes them.

bacterial-meningitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fever + neck stiffness + altered mental status”?
bacterial-meningitis.explanation: Fever + neck stiffness + altered mental status → Meningeal inflammation (classic triad).

bacterial-meningitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “CSF: neutrophils, high protein, low glucose”?
bacterial-meningitis.explanation: CSF: neutrophils, high protein, low glucose → Bacterial meningitis.

subacute-chronic-meningitis.stem: An HIV-positive patient has subacute headache and a very high CSF opening pressure. CSF shows lymphocytes and low glucose. Which test is most sensitive/specific for the diagnosis?
subacute-chronic-meningitis.explanation: Cryptococcal antigen testing (blood/CSF) exceeds 99% sensitivity and specificity for cryptococcal meningitis, which classically causes very high intracranial pressure in immunocompromised patients.

subacute-chronic-meningitis.stem: Regarding managing cryptococcal meningitis — which is correct?

options.text: Antifungal therapy alone is enough in cryptococcal meningitis
You must also aggressively manage the raised intracranial pressure (serial LPs/drainage) — high ICP is a major cause of death even with antifungals

subacute-chronic-meningitis.explanation: Cryptococcal meningitis often produces very high opening pressures that cause visual loss and death independent of the infection, so pressure control is as important as amphotericin/flucytosine.

subacute-chronic-meningitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Subacute meningitis + cranial nerve palsies + hydrocephalus”?
subacute-chronic-meningitis.explanation: Subacute meningitis + cranial nerve palsies + hydrocephalus → Tuberculous (basal) meningitis.

subacute-chronic-meningitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Meningitis with very high opening pressure in HIV”?
subacute-chronic-meningitis.explanation: Meningitis with very high opening pressure in HIV → Cryptococcal meningitis.

subacute-chronic-meningitis.stem: Which should you review before “TB, Cryptococcal & Eosinophilic Meningitis”?
subacute-chronic-meningitis.explanation: Knowledge of eosinophilic meningitis is crucial for differential diagnosis.

encephalitis-myelitis.stem: A previously well adult presents with fever, confusion, and seizures; MRI shows temporal-lobe abnormality. The best immediate management is:

options.text: Await CSF PCR before any treatment

encephalitis-myelitis.explanation: Temporal-lobe encephalitis suggests HSV-1; empiric IV acyclovir should be started immediately because HSV encephalitis is lethal if untreated and early PCR can be falsely negative.

encephalitis-myelitis.stem: Regarding when to start acyclovir in encephalitis — which is correct?

options.text: Wait for the CSF HSV PCR result before starting acyclovir
Start empiric IV acyclovir immediately in suspected encephalitis — HSV encephalitis is treatable but rapidly fatal, and early PCR can be falsely negative

encephalitis-myelitis.explanation: Delaying antiviral therapy for a confirmatory test risks irreversible damage or death; PCR within 48–72 h of onset may be negative, so treat on suspicion.

encephalitis-myelitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fever, confusion, seizures + temporal-lobe MRI change”?
encephalitis-myelitis.explanation: Fever, confusion, seizures + temporal-lobe MRI change → HSV-1 encephalitis.

encephalitis-myelitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Young patient: psychosis + movement disorder + seizures”?
encephalitis-myelitis.explanation: Young patient: psychosis + movement disorder + seizures → Anti-NMDAR autoimmune encephalitis.

neurotoxins-facial-palsy.stem: A patient develops symmetric descending weakness with ptosis, diplopia, and dysphagia after eating home-canned food; there is no fever and sensation is intact. The toxin responsible acts by:

options.text: Blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction

neurotoxins-facial-palsy.explanation: Botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release at the NMJ, producing a symmetric descending flaccid paralysis with oculobulbar signs, no fever, and intact sensation — the opposite of tetanus.

neurotoxins-facial-palsy.stem: Regarding forehead in facial weakness — which is correct?

options.text: Facial droop with a spared forehead is Bell’s palsy
Bell’s palsy is a LOWER motor neuron lesion that involves the WHOLE half of the face including the forehead; forehead SPARING indicates an upper motor neuron (central) lesion such as a stroke

neurotoxins-facial-palsy.explanation: The upper face receives bilateral cortical input, so a central (UMN) lesion spares the forehead, whereas the peripheral CN VII lesion of Bell’s palsy weakens the entire ipsilateral face.

neurotoxins-facial-palsy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Lockjaw, risus sardonicus, opisthotonus, spasms”?
neurotoxins-facial-palsy.explanation: Lockjaw, risus sardonicus, opisthotonus, spasms → Tetanus (loss of inhibition).

neurotoxins-facial-palsy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Symmetric descending weakness + ptosis/diplopia, no fever, alert”?
neurotoxins-facial-palsy.explanation: Symmetric descending weakness + ptosis/diplopia, no fever, alert → Botulism (blocked ACh).

neurotoxins-facial-palsy.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Tetanus, Botulism & Bell’s Palsy”?
neurotoxins-facial-palsy.explanation: Links basic science of muscle mechanics to clinical manifestations of tetanus.

neurotoxins-facial-palsy.stem: Which should you review before “Tetanus, Botulism & Bell’s Palsy”?
neurotoxins-facial-palsy.explanation: Essential for understanding tetanus and botulism.

amino-acids-proteins-structure.stem: Which level of protein structure is defined by the pattern of α-helices and β-sheets formed through backbone hydrogen bonds?
amino-acids-proteins-structure.explanation: Secondary structure (α-helix, β-sheet) arises from hydrogen bonding along the peptide backbone. Primary is the sequence, tertiary is the 3-D fold, and quaternary is the assembly of subunits.

amino-acids-proteins-structure.stem: Regarding what denaturation changes — which is correct?

options.text: Denaturing a protein breaks its peptide bonds and changes the primary sequence
Denaturation disrupts the non-covalent 2°/3°/4° structure but leaves the primary sequence (peptide bonds) intact
Acidic/basic R groups give net charge at a given pH

amino-acids-proteins-structure.explanation: Heat, pH, or chaotropes unfold a protein by breaking H-bonds and hydrophobic interactions; the covalent backbone sequence is unchanged, which is why some proteins can refold.

amino-acids-proteins-structure.stem: What best explains the finding: “Charge-based separation of proteins (electrophoresis)”?

options.text: Acidic/basic R groups give net charge at a given pH

amino-acids-proteins-structure.explanation: Charge-based separation of proteins (electrophoresis) → Acidic/basic R groups give net charge at a given pH.

collagen-elastin.stem: A young non-smoker develops panlobular emphysema and is found to have liver disease. The most likely underlying defect is:
collagen-elastin.explanation: α1-antitrypsin deficiency leaves neutrophil elastase unopposed (→ emphysema), while misfolded α1-AT accumulates in hepatocytes (→ cirrhosis) — a combined lung and liver disease.

collagen-elastin.stem: Regarding vitamin c and collagen — which is correct?

options.text: Vitamin C is needed to synthesize the collagen amino-acid sequence itself
Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl (and lysyl) hydroxylase — it enables the post-translational hydroxylation that stabilizes the triple helix, not the sequence

collagen-elastin.explanation: Without hydroxyproline, interchain hydrogen bonds fail and the collagen triple helix is unstable, producing the fragile connective tissue of scurvy.

collagen-elastin.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bleeding gums, poor wound healing, perifollicular hemorrhage”?
collagen-elastin.explanation: Bleeding gums, poor wound healing, perifollicular hemorrhage → Vitamin C deficiency → defective collagen (scurvy).

collagen-elastin.stem: What best explains the finding: “Early-onset panlobular emphysema in a non-smoker (or young smoker)”?
collagen-elastin.explanation: Early-onset panlobular emphysema in a non-smoker (or young smoker) → α1-antitrypsin deficiency (unopposed elastase).

collagen-elastin.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Collagen & Elastin”?
collagen-elastin.explanation: Both modules can be linked through the importance of protein structure in function.

collagen-elastin.stem: Which should you review before “Collagen & Elastin”?
collagen-elastin.explanation: Understanding amino acids is essential for grasping collagen and elastin structure.

hemoglobin-myoglobin.stem: Sickle-cell disease results from which molecular change in the β-globin chain?

options.text: A frameshift causing a premature stop codon
A missense mutation replacing glutamate with valine at position 6
Deletion of the entire β-globin gene

hemoglobin-myoglobin.explanation: HbS arises from a single missense mutation (Glu→Val at β6), replacing a polar with a nonpolar residue; deoxygenated HbS polymerizes, sickling the red cell.

hemoglobin-myoglobin.stem: Regarding why hemoglobin is cooperative — which is correct?

options.text: Myoglobin binds O₂ cooperatively because it has high affinity
Cooperativity requires multiple interacting subunits — only the hemoglobin tetramer is cooperative (sigmoidal); myoglobin is a single subunit (hyperbolic)
Cooperative binding by the hemoglobin tetramer

hemoglobin-myoglobin.explanation: Cooperative (sigmoidal) binding depends on subunit-to-subunit communication (T↔R), which a monomeric protein like myoglobin cannot show.

hemoglobin-myoglobin.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sigmoidal O₂-dissociation curve”?

options.text: Cooperative binding by the hemoglobin tetramer

hemoglobin-myoglobin.explanation: Sigmoidal O₂-dissociation curve → Cooperative binding by the hemoglobin tetramer.

hemoglobin-myoglobin.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sickled red cells / vaso-occlusive pain”?

options.text: Cooperative binding by the hemoglobin tetramer

hemoglobin-myoglobin.explanation: Sickled red cells / vaso-occlusive pain → Deoxygenated HbS polymerization.

hemoglobin-myoglobin.stem: Which should you review before “Hemoglobin, Myoglobin & Sickle Cell”?
hemoglobin-myoglobin.explanation: Understanding protein structure is essential for grasping hemoglobin and myoglobin functions.

protein-misfolding-amyloid.stem: A misfolded protein propagates disease by converting normally folded copies of the same protein into a β-sheet-rich, aggregation-prone form, without any nucleic acid. This describes:
protein-misfolding-amyloid.explanation: Prions are protein-only infectious agents: the misfolded PrPˢᶜ templates conversion of normal PrP into the pathogenic β-sheet form, causing transmissible spongiform encephalopathies such as CJD.

protein-misfolding-amyloid.stem: Regarding mechanism of prion disease — which is correct?

options.text: Prion diseases are caused by a virus or a mutation in a nucleic acid
Prions are misfolded proteins (PrPˢᶜ) that template the misfolding of normal PrP — no nucleic acid is involved

protein-misfolding-amyloid.explanation: The infectious agent is protein-only: a β-sheet-rich conformer converts normal cellular prion protein, propagating the disease and making it transmissible without DNA or RNA.

protein-misfolding-amyloid.stem: What best explains the finding: “Progressive dementia with cerebral β-amyloid plaques”?
protein-misfolding-amyloid.explanation: Progressive dementia with cerebral β-amyloid plaques → Alzheimer amyloidosis.

protein-misfolding-amyloid.stem: What best explains the finding: “Restrictive cardiomyopathy / proteinuria + monoclonal light chains”?
protein-misfolding-amyloid.explanation: Restrictive cardiomyopathy / proteinuria + monoclonal light chains → AL amyloidosis (myeloma).

protein-misfolding-amyloid.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Protein Misfolding & Amyloid”?
Which should you review before “Protein Misfolding & Amyloid”?
protein-misfolding-amyloid.explanation: Understanding protein structure is essential for grasping misfolding mechanisms.

enzyme-catalysis-classification.stem: A kinase transfers a phosphate group from ATP to glucose. This enzyme belongs to which EC class?
enzyme-catalysis-classification.explanation: Kinases move a functional (phosphate) group from one molecule to another, so they are transferases (EC class 2).

enzyme-catalysis-classification.stem: Regarding what an enzyme changes — which is correct?

options.text: Enzymes make an unfavorable reaction favorable by shifting the equilibrium
Enzymes only lower the activation energy (speed the rate); they do not change ΔG or the position of equilibrium

enzyme-catalysis-classification.explanation: A catalyst accelerates forward and reverse rates equally, so it reaches equilibrium faster but cannot alter the thermodynamics (ΔG) of the reaction.

enzyme-catalysis-classification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Reaction accelerated without altering ΔG/equilibrium”?
enzyme-catalysis-classification.explanation: Reaction accelerated without altering ΔG/equilibrium → Catalyst lowers activation energy only.

enzyme-catalysis-classification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Loss of activity when a cofactor is removed”?
enzyme-catalysis-classification.explanation: Loss of activity when a cofactor is removed → Apoenzyme alone is inactive.

enzyme-kinetics.stem: Enzyme X has a Km of 2 µM and enzyme Y has a Km of 50 µM for the same substrate. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Enzyme Y has higher affinity for the substrate
Enzyme X has higher affinity for the substrate
Km tells us nothing about affinity

enzyme-kinetics.explanation: Km is inversely related to affinity, so the lower Km (enzyme X, 2 µM) indicates tighter substrate binding (higher affinity).

enzyme-kinetics.stem: Regarding meaning of km — which is correct?

options.text: A high Km means the enzyme binds its substrate tightly
Km is inversely related to affinity — a HIGH Km means LOW affinity (needs more substrate to reach ½Vmax)

enzyme-kinetics.explanation: Km is the substrate concentration giving half-maximal velocity; the more substrate required, the weaker the binding, so high Km = low affinity.

enzyme-kinetics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hyperbolic v vs [S] plot”?
enzyme-kinetics.explanation: Hyperbolic v vs [S] plot → Michaelis-Menten kinetics.

enzyme-kinetics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Half-maximal velocity at a given [S]”?
enzyme-kinetics.explanation: Half-maximal velocity at a given [S] → That [S] equals Km.

enzyme-kinetics.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Enzyme Kinetics”?

options.text: Cardiac Biomarkers in Acute Coronary Syndrome

enzyme-kinetics.explanation: Enzyme kinetics is relevant in interpreting cardiac biomarkers in clinical settings.

enzyme-inhibition-regulation.stem: A drug inhibits an enzyme; kinetic analysis shows increased Km with unchanged Vmax, and the inhibition is reversed by high substrate concentrations. This is:
enzyme-inhibition-regulation.explanation: Increased Km with unchanged Vmax, overcome by excess substrate, is the signature of competitive inhibition (the inhibitor and substrate compete for the active site).

enzyme-inhibition-regulation.stem: Regarding competitive vs noncompetitive inhibition — which is correct?

options.text: Adding more substrate will overcome any enzyme inhibitor
Only competitive inhibition is overcome by excess substrate (↑Km, Vmax unchanged); noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax and is NOT reversed by more substrate

enzyme-inhibition-regulation.explanation: Competitive inhibitors vie for the active site so substrate can outcompete them, whereas noncompetitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and reduce Vmax regardless of substrate concentration.

enzyme-inhibition-regulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Inhibition overcome by adding more substrate”?
enzyme-inhibition-regulation.explanation: Inhibition overcome by adding more substrate → Competitive inhibitor (↑Km).

enzyme-inhibition-regulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Inhibition NOT overcome by more substrate”?
enzyme-inhibition-regulation.explanation: Inhibition NOT overcome by more substrate → Noncompetitive inhibitor (↓Vmax).

coenzymes-cofactors.stem: A malnourished patient has a megaloblastic anemia. A deficiency of which coenzyme precursors is most likely responsible?
coenzymes-cofactors.explanation: Folate (as tetrahydrofolate) and B12 are required for one-carbon transfer in nucleotide synthesis; their deficiency impairs DNA synthesis and causes megaloblastic anemia.

coenzymes-cofactors.stem: Regarding cofactor vs coenzyme vs prosthetic group — which is correct?

options.text: A cofactor and a coenzyme are exactly the same thing
Cofactor is the umbrella term; coenzymes are the ORGANIC (often vitamin-derived) subset, distinct from inorganic metal-ion cofactors
Folate (B9) or B12 deficiency → impaired DNA synthesis

coenzymes-cofactors.explanation: All coenzymes are cofactors, but not all cofactors are coenzymes — metal ions (Zn²⁺, Mg²⁺) are inorganic cofactors, while NAD⁺, TPP, and PLP are organic coenzymes.

coenzymes-cofactors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Megaloblastic anemia”?

options.text: Folate (B9) or B12 deficiency → impaired DNA synthesis

coenzymes-cofactors.explanation: Megaloblastic anemia → Folate (B9) or B12 deficiency → impaired DNA synthesis.

coenzymes-cofactors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia (pellagra)”?

options.text: Folate (B9) or B12 deficiency → impaired DNA synthesis

nucleotides-structure-roles.stem: Which set correctly lists the purine bases?
nucleotides-structure-roles.explanation: Adenine and guanine are the double-ringed purines; cytosine, thymine, and uracil are the single-ringed pyrimidines.

nucleotides-structure-roles.stem: Regarding nucleoside vs nucleotide — which is correct?

options.text: Nucleoside and nucleotide are interchangeable terms
A nucleoTide has a phosphaTe; a nucleoside is base + sugar only (no phosphate)

nucleotides-structure-roles.explanation: The phosphate group is the distinguishing feature — nucleotides are phosphorylated nucleosides and are the building blocks of nucleic acids.

nucleotides-structure-roles.stem: What best explains the finding: “Purine vs pyrimidine identification”?
nucleotides-structure-roles.explanation: Purine vs pyrimidine identification → Two rings (A/G) vs one ring (C/T/U).

nucleotides-structure-roles.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Nucleotides — Structure & Roles”?
nucleotides-structure-roles.explanation: Nucleotides play a role in gene expression relevant to adrenal cortex function.

dna-structure-forms.stem: Two DNA fragments of equal length are compared. Fragment 1 is 70% G-C; fragment 2 is 30% G-C. Which has the higher melting temperature and why?

options.text: Fragment 2, because A-T pairs are more stable
Fragment 1, because G-C pairs have three hydrogen bonds
Both melt at the same temperature
Fragment 2, because it has fewer hydrogen bonds

dna-structure-forms.explanation: G-C pairs are held by three hydrogen bonds versus two for A-T, so higher GC content raises the melting temperature.

dna-structure-forms.stem: Regarding determinant of dna melting temperature — which is correct?

options.text: A longer DNA sequence always melts at a higher temperature than a shorter one
Tm is driven mainly by G-C content (three H-bonds) — GC-rich DNA melts at a higher temperature regardless of comparable length

dna-structure-forms.explanation: Each G-C pair contributes three hydrogen bonds versus two for A-T, so base composition (GC%) is the dominant determinant of duplex thermal stability.

dna-structure-forms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Higher melting temperature for GC-rich DNA”?
dna-structure-forms.explanation: Higher melting temperature for GC-rich DNA → Three H-bonds per G-C pair.

dna-structure-forms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Increased A260 on heating (hyperchromicity)”?
dna-structure-forms.explanation: Increased A260 on heating (hyperchromicity) → Strand separation exposes bases.

dna-structure-forms.stem: Which is a clinical application of “DNA Structure & Forms”?

chromatin-packaging.stem: The histone octamer around which DNA wraps to form a nucleosome consists of two copies each of:
chromatin-packaging.explanation: The nucleosome core is an octamer of two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4; H1 is the separate linker histone.

chromatin-packaging.stem: Regarding histone content of the nucleosome core — which is correct?

options.text: The nucleosome core octamer includes histone H1
The core octamer is two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4; H1 is the LINKER histone, not part of the core

chromatin-packaging.explanation: H1 sits outside the core, binding linker DNA to compact nucleosomes into the 30-nm fiber — it is not one of the eight core histones.

chromatin-packaging.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nucleosome “beads-on-a-string” on EM”?
chromatin-packaging.explanation: Nucleosome “beads-on-a-string” on EM → DNA + histone octamer repeating unit.

chromatin-packaging.stem: What best explains the finding: “Silenced genes in condensed regions”?
chromatin-packaging.explanation: Silenced genes in condensed regions → Heterochromatin.

rna-types.stem: Which feature distinguishes RNA from DNA?

options.text: RNA contains thymine; DNA contains uracil
RNA contains ribose and uracil and is usually single-stranded
RNA is always double-stranded like DNA

rna-types.explanation: RNA uses ribose (with a 2′-OH) and uracil in place of thymine and is typically single-stranded, folding into hairpins via self-complementary regions.

rna-types.stem: Regarding most abundant rna in the cell — which is correct?

options.text: mRNA is the most abundant RNA because it carries all the genetic messages
rRNA is the most abundant cellular RNA (it forms the bulk of ribosomes); mRNA is relatively scarce

rna-types.explanation: Although mRNA carries the coding information, ribosomal RNA constitutes the majority of a cell’s RNA because ribosomes are numerous and rRNA-rich.

rna-types.stem: What best explains the finding: “Uracil instead of thymine in a nucleic acid”?
rna-types.explanation: Uracil instead of thymine in a nucleic acid → RNA.

rna-types.stem: Which is a clinical application of “RNA Types & DNA vs RNA”?
Which should you review before “RNA Types & DNA vs RNA”?
rna-types.explanation: Understanding nucleotides is essential for grasping RNA structure.

purine-pyrimidine-synthesis.stem: Which molecule donates the ribose-5-phosphate used in both de novo synthesis and salvage of nucleotides?
purine-pyrimidine-synthesis.explanation: PRPP is the activated ribose-5-phosphate donor for de novo purine/pyrimidine synthesis and for salvage reactions (via HGPRT/APRT).

purine-pyrimidine-synthesis.stem: Regarding order of ring vs sugar assembly — which is correct?

options.text: Both purine and pyrimidine rings are built while already attached to the ribose sugar
Purine rings are built ON PRPP (sugar first); pyrimidine rings are built FIRST (as orotate) and then joined to PRPP
IMP branch uses GTP for AMP and ATP for GMP + feedback
THF donates the methyl for dUMP → dTMP

purine-pyrimidine-synthesis.explanation: The two pathways differ in sequence — purines assemble the base directly on the ribose-phosphate, whereas pyrimidines make the free ring (orotate) before attaching it to ribose.

purine-pyrimidine-synthesis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Balanced AMP:GMP pools”?

options.text: THF donates the methyl for dUMP → dTMP
IMP branch uses GTP for AMP and ATP for GMP + feedback

purine-pyrimidine-synthesis.explanation: Balanced AMP:GMP pools → IMP branch uses GTP for AMP and ATP for GMP + feedback.

purine-pyrimidine-synthesis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thymidylate synthesis depends on folate”?

options.text: THF donates the methyl for dUMP → dTMP
IMP branch uses GTP for AMP and ATP for GMP + feedback

purine-pyrimidine-synthesis.explanation: Thymidylate synthesis depends on folate → THF donates the methyl for dUMP → dTMP.

nucleotide-degradation-gout.stem: Allopurinol lowers serum uric acid in gout by inhibiting which enzyme?
nucleotide-degradation-gout.explanation: Allopurinol (and febuxostat) inhibit xanthine oxidase, reducing conversion of hypoxanthine/xanthine to uric acid; the accumulated precursors are more soluble.

nucleotide-degradation-gout.stem: Regarding commonest cause of hyperuricemia — which is correct?

options.text: Most gout is caused by overproduction of uric acid
Underexcretion of urate (renal) is the most common cause of hyperuricemia; overproduction (e.g. HGPRT deficiency) is less common

nucleotide-degradation-gout.explanation: Although enzyme defects overproduce urate in a minority, the majority of hyperuricemia results from reduced renal excretion — relevant to choosing allopurinol vs a uricosuric.

nucleotide-degradation-gout.stem: What best explains the finding: “Acute monoarthritis of the first MTP (podagra)”?
nucleotide-degradation-gout.explanation: Acute monoarthritis of the first MTP (podagra) → Monosodium urate crystal deposition.

nucleotide-degradation-gout.stem: What best explains the finding: “Negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals”?
nucleotide-degradation-gout.explanation: Negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals → Urate in joint fluid.

nucleotide-degradation-gout.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Nucleotide Degradation & Gout”?
Which should you review before “Nucleotide Degradation & Gout”?
nucleotide-degradation-gout.explanation: Understanding purine metabolism is essential for grasping nucleotide degradation.

nucleotide-drugs-disorders.stem: An infant has severe combined immunodeficiency. Enzyme testing shows deficient adenosine deaminase. The mechanism of immune failure is:

options.text: Excess uric acid crystallizing in lymph nodes
dATP accumulation inhibiting ribonucleotide reductase, blocking DNA synthesis in lymphocytes
Failure of purine salvage via HGPRT

nucleotide-drugs-disorders.explanation: ADA deficiency causes dATP to accumulate, which inhibits ribonucleotide reductase; without dNTPs, DNA synthesis stalls, and proliferating lymphocytes are especially affected — producing SCID.

nucleotide-drugs-disorders.stem: Regarding orotic aciduria differential — which is correct?

options.text: Any orotic aciduria is due to UMP synthase deficiency
Hereditary orotic aciduria (UMP synthase deficiency) gives megaloblastic anemia WITHOUT hyperammonemia; ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency also raises orotate but WITH hyperammonemia

nucleotide-drugs-disorders.explanation: Both raise urinary orotate, but the urea-cycle (OTC) defect adds hyperammonemia and no megaloblastic anemia — the associated features distinguish them.

nucleotide-drugs-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Recurrent infections from birth (SCID)”?
nucleotide-drugs-disorders.explanation: Recurrent infections from birth (SCID) → ADA deficiency → dATP → RNR inhibition.

nucleotide-drugs-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Megaloblastic anemia unresponsive to B12/folate + orotic acid in urine”?
nucleotide-drugs-disorders.explanation: Megaloblastic anemia unresponsive to B12/folate + orotic acid in urine → Orotic aciduria (UMP synthase deficiency).

nucleotide-drugs-disorders.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Nucleotide Drugs & Disorders”?
nucleotide-drugs-disorders.explanation: Some nucleotide drugs are used in dermatologic conditions.

nucleotide-drugs-disorders.stem: Which should you review before “Nucleotide Drugs & Disorders”?
nucleotide-drugs-disorders.explanation: Understanding nucleotide synthesis is essential for grasping drug mechanisms.

dna-replication-machinery.stem: Which enzyme uses its 3′→5′ exonuclease activity to remove a mismatched nucleotide during replication?
dna-replication-machinery.explanation: DNA polymerase’s 3′→5′ exonuclease provides proofreading, excising an incorrectly paired nucleotide and greatly lowering the error rate.

dna-replication-machinery.stem: Regarding direction of dna synthesis — which is correct?

options.text: On the lagging strand, DNA polymerase synthesizes in the 3′→5′ direction to follow the fork
DNA polymerase ALWAYS synthesizes 5′→3′; the lagging strand is made in short 5′→3′ Okazaki fragments away from the fork, then joined
Leading vs lagging (Okazaki) at the fork

dna-replication-machinery.explanation: No DNA polymerase can add nucleotides 3′→5′; the lagging-strand discontinuity (Okazaki fragments) is the cell’s solution to building a strand whose template runs the “wrong” way.

dna-replication-machinery.stem: What best explains the finding: “Continuous vs discontinuous strand synthesis”?

options.text: DNA Pol cannot initiate de novo
Leading vs lagging (Okazaki) at the fork

dna-replication-machinery.explanation: Continuous vs discontinuous strand synthesis → Leading vs lagging (Okazaki) at the fork.

dna-replication-machinery.stem: What best explains the finding: “Proofreading corrects a misincorporated base”?

options.text: Leading vs lagging (Okazaki) at the fork
DNA Pol cannot initiate de novo

dna-replication-machinery.explanation: Proofreading corrects a misincorporated base → 3′→5′ exonuclease of DNA polymerase.

dna-replication-machinery.stem: Which is a clinical application of “DNA Replication Machinery”?

options.text: Child Sexual Abuse: Trauma-informed Clinical Response

dna-replication-machinery.explanation: Understanding DNA replication can be relevant in discussions of genetic factors in trauma responses.

eukaryotic-replication-telomeres.stem: How do cancer cells overcome the progressive telomere shortening that limits the replicative lifespan of normal somatic cells?

options.text: They reactivate telomerase to extend telomeres
They lose all origins of replication

eukaryotic-replication-telomeres.explanation: Most cancers reactivate telomerase (TERT + RNA template) to rebuild telomeres, escaping replicative senescence — a hallmark of cellular immortalization.

eukaryotic-replication-telomeres.stem: Regarding why telomeres shorten — which is correct?

options.text: Telomeres shorten because nucleases actively chew the chromosome ends each division
Shortening is due to the end-replication problem — the lagging-strand terminus cannot be primed/filled after primer removal, not active degradation

eukaryotic-replication-telomeres.explanation: DNA polymerase requires a 5′ primer and synthesizes only 5′→3′, so once the terminal RNA primer is removed there is no upstream 3′ end to extend, leaving the very end uncopied.

eukaryotic-replication-telomeres.stem: What best explains the finding: “Progressive telomere shortening in somatic cells”?
eukaryotic-replication-telomeres.explanation: Progressive telomere shortening in somatic cells → End-replication problem without telomerase.

eukaryotic-replication-telomeres.stem: What best explains the finding: “Telomerase reactivation in tumor cells”?
eukaryotic-replication-telomeres.explanation: Telomerase reactivation in tumor cells → Immortalization (cancer hallmark).

eukaryotic-replication-telomeres.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Eukaryotic Replication & Telomeres”?
eukaryotic-replication-telomeres.explanation: Understanding telomeres may indirectly relate to cellular aging in clinical contexts.

eukaryotic-replication-telomeres.stem: Which should you review before “Eukaryotic Replication & Telomeres”?
eukaryotic-replication-telomeres.explanation: Understanding DNA replication machinery is essential for grasping telomere function.

mutations-dna-damage.stem: Ultraviolet light most characteristically produces which type of DNA lesion?
mutations-dna-damage.explanation: UV light forms covalent pyrimidine (thymine) dimers that distort the helix and block replication/transcription; these are repaired by nucleotide-excision repair.

mutations-dna-damage.stem: Regarding silent vs missense mutation — which is correct?

options.text: Any single-base change alters the encoded protein
A silent mutation changes the codon but not the amino acid (degenerate code); a missense mutation changes the amino acid

mutations-dna-damage.explanation: Because the genetic code is degenerate, some base substitutions (especially in the third position) leave the amino acid unchanged — those are silent, not missense.

mutations-dna-damage.stem: What best explains the finding: “Skin lesions after UV exposure”?
mutations-dna-damage.explanation: Skin lesions after UV exposure → Pyrimidine dimers.

mutations-dna-damage.stem: What best explains the finding: “G→T transversions”?
Which is a clinical application of “Mutations & DNA Damage”?
mutations-dna-damage.explanation: Mutations can be relevant in genetic conditions like HCM.

dna-repair-mechanisms.stem: A child with extreme sensitivity to sunlight develops multiple skin cancers early in life due to an inability to remove UV-induced pyrimidine dimers. The defective repair pathway is:
dna-repair-mechanisms.explanation: Xeroderma pigmentosum results from defective nucleotide-excision repair, which normally removes bulky UV-induced pyrimidine dimers; patients are extremely photosensitive and cancer-prone.

dna-repair-mechanisms.stem: Regarding hr vs nhej for double-strand breaks — which is correct?

options.text: Both double-strand-break pathways repair the DNA equally accurately
Homologous recombination is accurate (uses the sister chromatid in S/G2); non-homologous end-joining is error-prone and operates in G1

dna-repair-mechanisms.explanation: HR copies from an intact template so it restores the sequence faithfully, whereas NHEJ simply ligates the broken ends and often introduces small insertions/deletions.

dna-repair-mechanisms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Severe sunburn, freckling, skin cancers in childhood”?
dna-repair-mechanisms.explanation: Severe sunburn, freckling, skin cancers in childhood → Xeroderma pigmentosum (NER defect).

dna-repair-mechanisms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Early colorectal cancer with microsatellite instability”?
dna-repair-mechanisms.explanation: Early colorectal cancer with microsatellite instability → Lynch syndrome (MMR defect: MSH2/MLH1).

human-genome-organization.stem: Regions of a gene that are transcribed but removed by splicing and therefore absent from the mature mRNA are called:
human-genome-organization.explanation: Introns are transcribed into pre-mRNA but excised by RNA splicing, so only the exons remain in the mature mRNA.

human-genome-organization.stem: Regarding snp vs mutation — which is correct?

options.text: Any single-base difference between two people is a mutation
A single-base variant present in >1% of the population is called a polymorphism (SNP); the term mutation is reserved for variants at <1% frequency
mtDNA passed only from the mother

human-genome-organization.explanation: The distinction is by population frequency, not by mechanism — common single-base variants are SNPs (useful in association studies), while rare ones are termed mutations.

human-genome-organization.stem: What best explains the finding: “Maternal (mitochondrial) inheritance pattern”?

options.text: mtDNA passed only from the mother

human-genome-organization.explanation: Maternal (mitochondrial) inheritance pattern → mtDNA passed only from the mother.

human-genome-organization.stem: What best explains the finding: “STR/microsatellite profile unique per person”?

options.text: mtDNA passed only from the mother

human-genome-organization.explanation: STR/microsatellite profile unique per person → Variable tandem-repeat number.

human-genome-organization.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Human Genome Organization”?

options.text: Differences of Sex Development & Reproductive Anomalies

human-genome-organization.explanation: Genetic variations can lead to reproductive anomalies.

transcription-mechanism.stem: A toxin from the death-cap mushroom (α-amanitin) blocks messenger RNA synthesis. Its target is:
transcription-mechanism.explanation: α-amanitin inhibits RNA polymerase II, which transcribes mRNA (and RNA pol III at high concentrations), halting protein-coding gene expression.

transcription-mechanism.stem: Regarding template vs coding strand — which is correct?

options.text: The RNA transcript has the same sequence as the template strand it is read from
RNA is complementary to the TEMPLATE strand and therefore identical (with U for T) to the CODING (sense) strand
Template strand is copied; coding strand matches RNA

transcription-mechanism.explanation: Because RNA polymerase base-pairs with the template, the product matches the opposite (coding) strand — a frequent source of confusion when writing an mRNA sequence.

transcription-mechanism.stem: What best explains the finding: “RNA sequence identical to the coding strand (with U)”?

options.text: Template strand is copied; coding strand matches RNA

transcription-mechanism.explanation: RNA sequence identical to the coding strand (with U) → Template strand is copied; coding strand matches RNA.

transcription-mechanism.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rifampin stops bacterial (not human) transcription”?

options.text: Template strand is copied; coding strand matches RNA

transcription-mechanism.explanation: Rifampin stops bacterial (not human) transcription → Bacterial RNA polymerase β subunit.

transcription-mechanism.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Transcription Mechanism”?
transcription-mechanism.explanation: Understanding transcription is crucial for developing antiviral strategies targeting viral RNA synthesis.

rna-processing.stem: Which structure carries out the removal of introns from eukaryotic pre-mRNA?
rna-processing.explanation: The spliceosome, composed of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (U1, U2, U4, U5, U6), recognizes consensus sequences at intron boundaries and excises introns while joining exons.

rna-processing.stem: Regarding what splicing removes — which is correct?

options.text: Splicing removes exons and keeps introns in the mature mRNA
Splicing removes INTRONS (intervening, non-coding) and joins the EXONS (expressed sequences)

rna-processing.explanation: Only exons remain in the mature mRNA; a mutation that creates or destroys a splice site (as in HbE/β-thalassemia) disrupts this and alters the protein produced.

rna-processing.stem: What best explains the finding: “Reduced β-globin from a mutation creating an extra splice site”?
rna-processing.explanation: Reduced β-globin from a mutation creating an extra splice site → HbE / β-thalassemia (aberrant splicing).

genetic-code-translation.stem: Aminoglycoside and tetracycline antibiotics inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding which ribosomal subunit?
genetic-code-translation.explanation: Aminoglycosides and tetracyclines act on the 30S subunit of the bacterial ribosome; macrolides and chloramphenicol act on the 50S subunit.

genetic-code-translation.stem: Regarding which enzyme forms the peptide bond — which is correct?

options.text: A protein enzyme in the ribosome catalyzes peptide-bond formation
Peptide-bond formation is catalyzed by the peptidyltransferase activity of the large-subunit rRNA — a ribozyme, not a protein
