genetic-code-translation.explanation: The ribosome’s catalytic core is RNA; recognizing that rRNA is the peptidyltransferase explains why several antibiotics that bind rRNA block protein synthesis.

genetic-code-translation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Single-base change altering one amino acid vs a stop”?
genetic-code-translation.explanation: Single-base change altering one amino acid vs a stop → Missense vs nonsense mutation.

genetic-code-translation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Antibiotic halting bacterial protein synthesis”?
genetic-code-translation.explanation: Antibiotic halting bacterial protein synthesis → 30S or 50S ribosomal target.

protein-targeting-ptm.stem: A newborn has coarse facial features and elevated lysosomal enzymes in the blood but deficient enzymes within lysosomes. The defect is in:

options.text: The phosphotransferase that adds mannose-6-phosphate (I-cell disease)

protein-targeting-ptm.explanation: I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II) is caused by defective phosphotransferase, so lysosomal enzymes lack the mannose-6-phosphate tag and are secreted instead of delivered to lysosomes.

protein-targeting-ptm.stem: Regarding i-cell disease mechanism — which is correct?

options.text: I-cell disease is caused by a deficiency of a single lysosomal enzyme
I-cell disease results from a phosphotransferase defect that fails to add the mannose-6-phosphate tag, so ALL lysosomal enzymes are mis-sorted (secreted) — not a single enzyme deficiency

protein-targeting-ptm.explanation: Without the M6P sorting signal, lysosomal hydrolases are secreted rather than delivered, so multiple enzymes are missing from lysosomes — a trafficking, not an enzyme-synthesis, defect.

protein-targeting-ptm.stem: What best explains the finding: “Lysosomal enzymes found in blood, not lysosomes”?
protein-targeting-ptm.explanation: Lysosomal enzymes found in blood, not lysosomes → I-cell disease (M6P phosphotransferase defect).

protein-targeting-ptm.stem: What best explains the finding: “Progressive chorea + autosomal-dominant CAG expansion”?
protein-targeting-ptm.explanation: Progressive chorea + autosomal-dominant CAG expansion → Huntington disease (toxic polyQ HTT).

protein-targeting-ptm.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Protein Targeting & Post-translational Modification”?
protein-targeting-ptm.explanation: Protein targeting and modification are relevant in glandular secretion.

epigenetics-transcriptional-control.stem: Which of the following best describes epigenetic regulation of gene expression?

options.text: It requires editing of the DNA base sequence
It is reversible and can be influenced by environmental factors such as diet
It occurs only during embryonic development
It affects only translation, not transcription

epigenetics-transcriptional-control.explanation: Epigenetic mechanisms (DNA methylation, histone modification) are heritable but reversible changes in expression that do not alter the DNA sequence and can be modulated by the environment.

epigenetics-transcriptional-control.stem: Regarding epigenetic vs genetic change — which is correct?

options.text: Epigenetic gene silencing requires a change in the underlying DNA base sequence
Epigenetic regulation (methylation, histone modification) is reversible and does NOT alter the DNA sequence

epigenetics-transcriptional-control.explanation: Unlike a mutation, epigenetic marks change gene accessibility without editing the code, which is why they are heritable yet reversible and influenced by environment/diet.

epigenetics-transcriptional-control.stem: What best explains the finding: “Gene silenced by promoter CpG hypermethylation”?
epigenetics-transcriptional-control.explanation: Gene silenced by promoter CpG hypermethylation → DNA methylation → heterochromatin.

epigenetics-transcriptional-control.stem: What best explains the finding: “Reactivation of expression by an HDAC inhibitor”?
epigenetics-transcriptional-control.explanation: Reactivation of expression by an HDAC inhibitor → Histone acetylation opens chromatin.

post-transcriptional-translational-contr.stem: When cellular iron is low, aconitase (IRP) binds the iron-response element in the 5′UTR of ferritin mRNA. The effect on ferritin is to:
post-transcriptional-translational-contr.explanation: Aconitase binding the 5′UTR IRE of ferritin mRNA blocks its translation, so less iron-storage protein is made when iron is scarce (while it stabilizes transferrin-receptor mRNA to boost uptake).

post-transcriptional-translational-contr.stem: Regarding mirna vs sirna — which is correct?

options.text: siRNA and miRNA both bind with partial complementarity and only repress translation
siRNA has 100% complementarity and cleaves its single target mRNA; miRNA binds partially and represses/destabilizes multiple targets

post-transcriptional-translational-contr.explanation: The degree of base-pairing distinguishes them — perfect matching (siRNA) triggers cleavage with tight specificity, while partial matching (miRNA) lets one miRNA regulate many mRNAs.

post-transcriptional-translational-contr.stem: What best explains the finding: “Tissue-specific protein isoforms from one gene”?
post-transcriptional-translational-contr.explanation: Tissue-specific protein isoforms from one gene → Alternative splicing.

post-transcriptional-translational-contr.stem: What best explains the finding: “Intestinal ApoB-48 vs hepatic ApoB-100”?
post-transcriptional-translational-contr.explanation: Intestinal ApoB-48 vs hepatic ApoB-100 → RNA editing (cytidine deaminase).

post-transcriptional-translational-contr.stem: Which should you review before “Post-transcriptional & Translational Control”?
post-transcriptional-translational-contr.explanation: Understanding transcriptional control is essential for grasping post-transcriptional mechanisms.

cloning-pcr-sequencing.stem: Which technique is required to detect and quantify an RNA virus such as SARS-CoV-2 from a swab?
cloning-pcr-sequencing.explanation: Real-time RT-PCR reverse-transcribes the viral RNA into cDNA and then amplifies it with fluorescent detection each cycle, allowing quantification (Ct value).

cloning-pcr-sequencing.stem: Regarding detecting rna by pcr — which is correct?

options.text: Standard PCR can directly amplify an RNA virus genome
RNA must first be reverse-transcribed into cDNA (RT-PCR); standard PCR only amplifies DNA

cloning-pcr-sequencing.explanation: DNA polymerase used in PCR needs a DNA template, so detecting RNA (e.g. SARS-CoV-2) requires reverse transcriptase to make cDNA before amplification.

cloning-pcr-sequencing.stem: What best explains the finding: “Millions of DNA copies from a tiny sample in hours”?
cloning-pcr-sequencing.explanation: Millions of DNA copies from a tiny sample in hours → PCR amplification.

cloning-pcr-sequencing.stem: What best explains the finding: “Viral load reported as a cycle threshold (Ct)”?
cloning-pcr-sequencing.explanation: Viral load reported as a cycle threshold (Ct) → Real-time RT-PCR.

cloning-pcr-sequencing.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Cloning, PCR & Sequencing”?

options.text: ECG in Clinical Practice: A Systematic Approach

cloning-pcr-sequencing.explanation: Understanding molecular techniques can aid in interpreting genetic markers related to cardiac conditions.

gene-therapy-crispr.stem: In CRISPR-Cas9 editing, after Cas9 creates a double-strand break, which repair pathway is typically exploited to create a gene KNOCK-OUT?
gene-therapy-crispr.explanation: Error-prone non-homologous end joining introduces small insertions/deletions that disrupt the gene (knock-out); precise homology-directed repair is used for knock-in but is less efficient.

gene-therapy-crispr.stem: Regarding somatic vs germline gene therapy — which is correct?

options.text: All gene therapy changes are passed on to the patient’s children
Only germline editing is heritable; somatic gene therapy alters body cells and is NOT transmitted to offspring

gene-therapy-crispr.explanation: Somatic edits affect only the treated tissues of one individual, whereas germline edits enter the reproductive lineage and are inherited — the source of the major ethical debate.

gene-therapy-crispr.stem: What best explains the finding: “Gene knock-out from error-prone end-joining”?
gene-therapy-crispr.explanation: Gene knock-out from error-prone end-joining → NHEJ after Cas9 cut.

gene-therapy-crispr.stem: What best explains the finding: “Precise single-base correction without a double-strand break”?
gene-therapy-crispr.explanation: Precise single-base correction without a double-strand break → Base editing (deaminase + nickase).

gene-therapy-crispr.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Gene Therapy & CRISPR”?
Which should you review before “Gene Therapy & CRISPR”?
gene-therapy-crispr.explanation: Understanding gene editing techniques requires knowledge of cloning and sequencing methods.

carbohydrate-structure-isomerism.stem: Glucose and mannose have the same structure except for the configuration at carbon 2. They are best described as:
carbohydrate-structure-isomerism.explanation: Sugars differing at a single asymmetric carbon are epimers; glucose and mannose differ at C2, so they are C2 epimers (glucose and galactose are C4 epimers).

carbohydrate-structure-isomerism.stem: Regarding epimer vs enantiomer — which is correct?

options.text: Glucose and galactose are enantiomers because they are different sugars
Glucose and galactose are EPIMERS — they differ at a single carbon (C4); enantiomers are complete mirror images (like D- vs L-glucose)

carbohydrate-structure-isomerism.explanation: Epimers differ at only one chiral center, whereas enantiomers differ at every chiral center; conflating them is a common carbohydrate-chemistry error.

carbohydrate-structure-isomerism.stem: What best explains the finding: “Glucose and galactose differ only at C4”?
carbohydrate-structure-isomerism.explanation: Glucose and galactose differ only at C4 → C4 epimers.

carbohydrate-structure-isomerism.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sucrose does not reduce Benedict’s reagent”?
carbohydrate-structure-isomerism.explanation: Sucrose does not reduce Benedict’s reagent → No free anomeric carbon (non-reducing).

glycosidic-bonds-polysaccharides.stem: Starch and cellulose are both polymers of glucose, yet humans can digest starch but not cellulose. The reason is that:

options.text: Cellulose is made of galactose, not glucose
Cellulose uses β-1,4 linkages that human enzymes cannot cleave

glycosidic-bonds-polysaccharides.explanation: Human amylases cleave the α-1,4 bonds of starch but not the β-1,4 bonds of cellulose, so cellulose passes through undigested as dietary fiber.

glycosidic-bonds-polysaccharides.stem: Regarding why cellulose is indigestible — which is correct?

options.text: Humans cannot digest cellulose because it is a different sugar than starch
Cellulose and starch are both glucose polymers; humans lack an enzyme to hydrolyze the β-1,4 linkage of cellulose (but can digest the α-1,4 of starch)
No enzyme for β-1,4 glucose bonds

glycosidic-bonds-polysaccharides.explanation: The difference is the bond configuration (β vs α), not the monomer — amylase cleaves α-1,4 but not β-1,4, so cellulose passes as fiber.

glycosidic-bonds-polysaccharides.stem: What best explains the finding: “Humans cannot digest cellulose”?

options.text: No enzyme for β-1,4 glucose bonds

glycosidic-bonds-polysaccharides.explanation: Humans cannot digest cellulose → No enzyme for β-1,4 glucose bonds.

glycosidic-bonds-polysaccharides.stem: What best explains the finding: “Heparin used clinically as an anticoagulant”?

options.text: No enzyme for β-1,4 glucose bonds

glycosidic-bonds-polysaccharides.explanation: Heparin used clinically as an anticoagulant → A sulfated glycosaminoglycan.

fatty-acids-membranes.stem: Compared with a saturated fatty acid of the same length, a cis-unsaturated fatty acid has a:

options.text: Higher melting point because it packs more tightly
Lower melting point because the cis double bond kink prevents tight packing
Higher melting point because it has more hydrogen

fatty-acids-membranes.explanation: A cis double bond creates a kink that disrupts packing, lowering the melting point — which is why unsaturated fats (oils) are liquid and increase membrane fluidity.

fatty-acids-membranes.stem: Regarding why unsaturated fats are more fluid — which is correct?

options.text: Unsaturated fats are liquid because they have fewer carbons than saturated fats
Cis double bonds introduce kinks that prevent tight packing, lowering the melting point — independent of chain length
Cis double bonds lower melting point

fatty-acids-membranes.explanation: The kink from a cis double bond disrupts van der Waals packing, so unsaturated fats stay fluid at room temperature and increase membrane fluidity.

fatty-acids-membranes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Oils (unsaturated) liquid vs fats (saturated) solid at room temp”?

options.text: Cis double bonds lower melting point

fatty-acids-membranes.explanation: Oils (unsaturated) liquid vs fats (saturated) solid at room temp → Cis double bonds lower melting point.

fatty-acids-membranes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dietary requirement for linoleic/linolenic acid”?

options.text: Cis double bonds lower melting point

fatty-acids-membranes.explanation: Dietary requirement for linoleic/linolenic acid → Essential fatty acids (ω-6/ω-3).

fatty-acids-membranes.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Fatty Acids, Triglycerides & Membranes”?
fatty-acids-membranes.explanation: Understanding membrane composition is key in skin biology.

cholesterol-steroids-lipoproteins.stem: Which lipoprotein is chiefly responsible for delivering cholesterol to peripheral tissues and, when elevated, promotes atherosclerosis?
cholesterol-steroids-lipoproteins.explanation: LDL (“bad” cholesterol) delivers cholesterol to tissues; elevated LDL drives atherosclerotic plaque formation, whereas HDL performs protective reverse cholesterol transport.

cholesterol-steroids-lipoproteins.stem: Regarding lipoprotein density — which is correct?

options.text: HDL is the lowest-density lipoprotein because it carries cholesterol
Density rises with protein content: chylomicrons (most lipid) are LOWEST density and HDL (most protein) is HIGHEST density

cholesterol-steroids-lipoproteins.explanation: Lipoprotein density tracks the protein-to-lipid ratio, so the triglyceride-rich chylomicron is least dense and the protein-rich HDL is most dense — the basis for their names.

cholesterol-steroids-lipoproteins.stem: What best explains the finding: “Emulsification of dietary fat for absorption”?
cholesterol-steroids-lipoproteins.explanation: Emulsification of dietary fat for absorption → Bile acids (amphipathic cholesterol derivatives).

cholesterol-steroids-lipoproteins.stem: What best explains the finding: “High LDL cholesterol → atherosclerotic plaque”?
cholesterol-steroids-lipoproteins.explanation: High LDL cholesterol → atherosclerotic plaque → LDL delivers cholesterol to vessels.

cholesterol-steroids-lipoproteins.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Cholesterol, Steroids & Lipoproteins”?

options.text: Sex Steroid Synthesis, Transport & Receptor Action

developmental-anatomy-periods-terms.stem: Which prenatal period extends from the third through eighth week after fertilization?
developmental-anatomy-periods-terms.explanation: The embryonic period is weeks 3-8 and contains the core events of organogenesis.

developmental-anatomy-periods-terms.stem: Regarding developmental dating — which is correct?

options.text: A 10-week gestational-age pregnancy contains a 10-week-old embryo from fertilization
Fertilization age is usually about 8 weeks when gestational age is 10 weeks
Gestational dating starts at the LMP
Weeks 3-8 are the organogenetic embryonic period

developmental-anatomy-periods-terms.explanation: Obstetric dating begins at the LMP, roughly 2 weeks before ovulation and fertilization.

developmental-anatomy-periods-terms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Gestational age exceeds fertilization age by about 2 weeks”?

options.text: Weeks 3-8 are the organogenetic embryonic period
Gestational dating starts at the LMP

developmental-anatomy-periods-terms.explanation: Gestational age exceeds fertilization age by about 2 weeks → Gestational dating starts at the LMP.

developmental-anatomy-periods-terms.stem: What best explains the finding: “A major structural defect after a week-5 exposure”?

options.text: Weeks 3-8 are the organogenetic embryonic period
Gestational dating starts at the LMP

developmental-anatomy-periods-terms.explanation: A major structural defect after a week-5 exposure → Weeks 3-8 are the organogenetic embryonic period.

developmental-anatomy-periods-terms.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Developmental Anatomy: Terms & Periods”?
developmental-anatomy-periods-terms.explanation: Knowledge of developmental anatomy can provide context for understanding complications arising from congenital issues.

developmental-genetic-regulation.stem: Which change most directly makes chromatin more accessible to transcription factors?
developmental-genetic-regulation.explanation: Histone acetylation loosens nucleosome packing and generally promotes access to transcriptional machinery.

developmental-genetic-regulation.stem: Regarding epigenetic versus genetic change — which is correct?

options.text: Any inherited change in gene expression must alter the DNA base sequence
Epigenetic marks can transmit an expression state without changing nucleotide sequence

developmental-genetic-regulation.explanation: DNA methylation and histone modification regulate chromatin accessibility rather than gene sequence.

developmental-genetic-regulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Normal DNA sequence with heritable transcriptional silencing”?
developmental-genetic-regulation.explanation: Normal DNA sequence with heritable transcriptional silencing → Epigenetic methylation/chromatin compaction.

developmental-genetic-regulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “46,XX testicular development after SRY translocation”?
developmental-genetic-regulation.explanation: 46,XX testicular development after SRY translocation → SRY initiates the testis-determining pathway.

developmental-genetic-regulation.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Genes, Signaling & Developmental Control”?

gametogenesis-female-tract.stem: At which stage is the human oocyte normally arrested at ovulation?
gametogenesis-female-tract.explanation: The secondary oocyte is ovulated in metaphase II and completes the division only after fertilization.

gametogenesis-female-tract.stem: Regarding identity of the ovulated female gamete — which is correct?

options.text: Ovulation releases a fully mature ovum that has completed meiosis II
Ovulation releases a secondary oocyte arrested in metaphase II
Secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II until fertilization

gametogenesis-female-tract.explanation: Meiosis II finishes only when fertilization activates the oocyte.

gametogenesis-female-tract.stem: What best explains the finding: “Primary oocyte present at birth”?

options.text: Secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II until fertilization
Fertilization normally occurs in the ampulla before transport to the uterus

gametogenesis-female-tract.explanation: Primary oocyte present at birth → Prenatal oogenesis with prophase-I arrest.

gametogenesis-female-tract.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ovulated cell has not completed meiosis II”?

options.text: Secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II until fertilization
Fertilization normally occurs in the ampulla before transport to the uterus

gametogenesis-female-tract.explanation: Ovulated cell has not completed meiosis II → Secondary oocyte is arrested in metaphase II until fertilization.

gametogenesis-female-tract.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Gametogenesis & Female Reproductive Tract”?
gametogenesis-female-tract.explanation: Understanding reproductive physiology can aid in recognizing complications during pregnancy.

gametogenesis-female-tract.stem: Which should you review before “Gametogenesis & Female Reproductive Tract”?
gametogenesis-female-tract.explanation: Understanding developmental terms is essential for grasping gametogenesis.

capacitation-fertilization.stem: Which event most directly prevents polyspermy after the first sperm fuses with the oocyte?
capacitation-fertilization.explanation: Cortical granule release modifies the zona pellucida and blocks further sperm penetration.

capacitation-fertilization.stem: Regarding function of the cortical reaction — which is correct?

options.text: The cortical reaction helps the first sperm digest the zona
It modifies the zona after fusion to prevent additional sperm entry

capacitation-fertilization.explanation: Acrosomal enzymes aid penetration; cortical granules create the polyspermy block.

capacitation-fertilization.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sperm reaches the oocyte but cannot penetrate the zona”?
capacitation-fertilization.explanation: Sperm reaches the oocyte but cannot penetrate the zona → Failed capacitation or acrosomal reaction.

capacitation-fertilization.stem: What best explains the finding: “More than one sperm enters the oocyte”?
capacitation-fertilization.explanation: More than one sperm enters the oocyte → Failure of cortical/zona polyspermy block.

capacitation-fertilization.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Capacitation & Fertilization”?

cleavage-blastocyst-implantation.stem: Which blastocyst component gives rise primarily to the embryo proper?
cleavage-blastocyst-implantation.explanation: The inner cell mass becomes the embryo proper; the trophoblast contributes mainly to the fetal-maternal interface.

cleavage-blastocyst-implantation.stem: Regarding growth during cleavage — which is correct?

options.text: The embryo enlarges with every cleavage division
Cell number rises while total conceptus size stays constrained by the zona pellucida

cleavage-blastocyst-implantation.explanation: Cleavage partitions the zygote cytoplasm into progressively smaller blastomeres.

cleavage-blastocyst-implantation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Blastocyst remains enclosed by zona pellucida”?
cleavage-blastocyst-implantation.explanation: Blastocyst remains enclosed by zona pellucida → Hatching failure prevents endometrial attachment.

cleavage-blastocyst-implantation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Endometrial stromal cells enlarge around implant”?
cleavage-blastocyst-implantation.explanation: Endometrial stromal cells enlarge around implant → Decidualization supports and regulates implantation.

cleavage-blastocyst-implantation.stem: Which should you review before “Cleavage, Blastocyst & Implantation”?
cleavage-blastocyst-implantation.explanation: Understanding fertilization is essential for grasping cleavage.

bilaminar-disc-week-two.stem: Which week-two cell layer is the invasive, multinucleated source of hCG?
bilaminar-disc-week-two.explanation: Syncytiotrophoblast invades the endometrium, opens lacunae, and secretes hCG.

bilaminar-disc-week-two.stem: Regarding origin of the bilaminar disc — which is correct?

options.text: Cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast form the embryonic disc
Epiblast and hypoblast form the bilaminar disc; cyto- and syncytiotrophoblast are trophoblast layers
Cytotrophoblast supplies cells to the syncytium

bilaminar-disc-week-two.explanation: Embryoblast and trophoblast undergo separate week-two differentiations.

bilaminar-disc-week-two.stem: What best explains the finding: “Multinucleated invasive trophoblast without cell boundaries”?

options.text: Cytotrophoblast supplies cells to the syncytium

bilaminar-disc-week-two.explanation: Multinucleated invasive trophoblast without cell boundaries → Syncytiotrophoblast.

bilaminar-disc-week-two.stem: What best explains the finding: “Mitotically active mononuclear trophoblast layer”?

options.text: Cytotrophoblast supplies cells to the syncytium

bilaminar-disc-week-two.explanation: Mitotically active mononuclear trophoblast layer → Cytotrophoblast supplies cells to the syncytium.

bilaminar-disc-week-two.stem: Which should you review before “Second Week: Bilaminar Disc & Cavities”?
bilaminar-disc-week-two.explanation: Understanding fertilization is essential for grasping the formation of the bilaminar disc.

preembryonic-clinical-applications.stem: What is the most common site of an ectopic pregnancy?
preembryonic-clinical-applications.explanation: Most ectopic pregnancies are tubal, reflecting failed transport from the normal ampullary fertilization site to the uterine cavity.

preembryonic-clinical-applications.stem: Regarding interpreting a positive pregnancy test — which is correct?

options.text: Positive urine hCG confirms a normal intrauterine pregnancy
It confirms trophoblast-derived hCG; location and viability require clinical follow-up and ultrasound

preembryonic-clinical-applications.explanation: Ectopic and molar pregnancies can both produce hCG.

preembryonic-clinical-applications.stem: What best explains the finding: “Positive hCG with no intrauterine pregnancy and pelvic pain”?
preembryonic-clinical-applications.explanation: Positive hCG with no intrauterine pregnancy and pelvic pain → Ectopic pregnancy until excluded.

preembryonic-clinical-applications.stem: What best explains the finding: “Triploid conceptus with abnormal villi and fetal tissue”?
preembryonic-clinical-applications.explanation: Triploid conceptus with abnormal villi and fetal tissue → Partial hydatidiform mole.

preembryonic-clinical-applications.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Pre-embryonic Clinical Applications”?

options.text: Uterine Tubes, Ovaries, Lymphatics & Clinical Anatomy

preembryonic-clinical-applications.explanation: Knowledge of uterine tubes is crucial for understanding ectopic pregnancies.

preembryonic-clinical-applications.stem: Which should you review before “Pre-embryonic Clinical Applications”?
preembryonic-clinical-applications.explanation: Understanding fertilization is essential for pre-embryonic applications.

gastrulation-body-axis.stem: Which embryonic cell population gives rise to all three primary germ layers?
gastrulation-body-axis.explanation: During gastrulation, migrating and remaining epiblast cells generate endoderm, mesoderm, and ectoderm.

gastrulation-body-axis.stem: Regarding origin of definitive endoderm — which is correct?

options.text: Epiblast cells replace hypoblast to form definitive endoderm
Completed gastrulation establishes ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm
Ectoderm and endoderm remain apposed at future openings

gastrulation-body-axis.explanation: All three germ layers of the embryo proper originate from epiblast.

gastrulation-body-axis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Trilaminar embryonic disc”?

options.text: Ectoderm and endoderm remain apposed at future openings
Completed gastrulation establishes ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm

gastrulation-body-axis.explanation: Trilaminar embryonic disc → Completed gastrulation establishes ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.

gastrulation-body-axis.stem: What best explains the finding: “No mesoderm at buccopharyngeal or cloacal membrane”?

options.text: Ectoderm and endoderm remain apposed at future openings
Completed gastrulation establishes ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm

gastrulation-body-axis.explanation: No mesoderm at buccopharyngeal or cloacal membrane → Ectoderm and endoderm remain apposed at future openings.

gastrulation-body-axis.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Gastrulation & Body-axis Formation”?
gastrulation-body-axis.explanation: Understanding embryonic development is essential for grasping cardiac development.

notochord-neurulation-neural-crest.stem: Which adult structure is derived from the notochord?
notochord-neurulation-neural-crest.explanation: The notochord regresses except for remnants within the nucleus pulposus.

notochord-neurulation-neural-crest.stem: Regarding embryologic origin of the nucleus pulposus — which is correct?

options.text: It comes from sclerotome like the rest of the vertebral column
The nucleus pulposus is a notochord remnant

notochord-neurulation-neural-crest.explanation: Sclerotome surrounds the notochord, but the central gelatinous nucleus retains notochordal origin.

notochord-neurulation-neural-crest.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nucleus pulposus in an intervertebral disc”?
notochord-neurulation-neural-crest.explanation: Nucleus pulposus in an intervertebral disc → Persistent notochord remnant.

notochord-neurulation-neural-crest.stem: What best explains the finding: “Absent dorsal neural-tube closure”?
notochord-neurulation-neural-crest.explanation: Absent dorsal neural-tube closure → Failed caudal neuropore closure.

notochord-neurulation-neural-crest.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Notochord, Neurulation & Neural Crest”?
notochord-neurulation-neural-crest.explanation: Neuroblastoma originates from neural crest cells.

notochord-neurulation-neural-crest.stem: Which should you review before “Notochord, Neurulation & Neural Crest”?
notochord-neurulation-neural-crest.explanation: Gastrulation is essential for understanding notochord formation.

germ-layer-derivatives-folding.stem: Which mesodermal subdivision gives rise to most of the urogenital system?
germ-layer-derivatives-folding.explanation: Intermediate mesoderm generates much of the urinary and genital systems.

germ-layer-derivatives-folding.stem: Regarding origin of a mixed organ — which is correct?

options.text: Every component of an endoderm-lined organ must be endodermal
The epithelial lining may be endodermal while muscle, connective tissue, and vessels are mesodermal

germ-layer-derivatives-folding.explanation: Organogenesis combines tissues from different germ layers.

germ-layer-derivatives-folding.stem: What best explains the finding: “Vertebral cartilage or skeletal muscle derivative”?
germ-layer-derivatives-folding.explanation: Vertebral cartilage or skeletal muscle derivative → Paraxial mesoderm / somite.

germ-layer-derivatives-folding.stem: What best explains the finding: “Kidney and gonadal duct derivative”?
germ-layer-derivatives-folding.explanation: Kidney and gonadal duct derivative → Intermediate mesoderm.

germ-layer-derivatives-folding.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Germ-layer Derivatives & Embryonic Folding”?

gastrulation-clinical-stem-cells.stem: A cell can generate derivatives of ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm but not an entire placenta. Its potency is:
gastrulation-clinical-stem-cells.explanation: Pluripotent cells can generate all three embryonic germ layers but lack the full extraembryonic capacity of totipotent cells.

gastrulation-clinical-stem-cells.stem: Regarding totipotent versus pluripotent — which is correct?

options.text: A pluripotent cell can independently form an entire conceptus including placenta
Totipotent cells can form embryonic and extraembryonic tissues; pluripotent cells form all embryonic germ-layer derivatives
Caudal regression from abnormal caudal mesoderm

gastrulation-clinical-stem-cells.explanation: Extraembryonic capacity is the key boundary between the terms.

gastrulation-clinical-stem-cells.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sacrococcygeal mass containing tissues from three germ layers”?

options.text: Caudal regression from abnormal caudal mesoderm

gastrulation-clinical-stem-cells.explanation: Sacrococcygeal mass containing tissues from three germ layers → Primitive-streak remnant teratoma.

gastrulation-clinical-stem-cells.stem: What best explains the finding: “Lower-limb and lumbosacral defects with urogenital/anorectal anomalies”?

options.text: Caudal regression from abnormal caudal mesoderm

gastrulation-clinical-stem-cells.explanation: Lower-limb and lumbosacral defects with urogenital/anorectal anomalies → Caudal regression from abnormal caudal mesoderm.

gastrulation-clinical-stem-cells.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Gastrulation Defects & Stem-cell Potency”?
gastrulation-clinical-stem-cells.explanation: Understanding of embryonic development aids in comprehending midgut issues.

congenital-anomaly-classification.stem: A limb forms normally and is later damaged by an amniotic band. This anomaly is classified as:
congenital-anomaly-classification.explanation: Disruption is extrinsic destruction of a structure that was initially developing normally.

congenital-anomaly-classification.stem: Regarding malformation versus disruption — which is correct?

options.text: Every congenital structural defect is a malformation
A disruption is extrinsic damage to tissue that had begun normal development

congenital-anomaly-classification.explanation: The same final missing structure can arise from failure to form or later destruction.

congenital-anomaly-classification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Amniotic band removes part of a previously formed limb”?

options.text: Syndrome with a defined chromosomal cause

congenital-anomaly-classification.explanation: Amniotic band removes part of a previously formed limb → Disruption.

congenital-anomaly-classification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Potter facies and limb positioning after oligohydramnios”?

options.text: Syndrome with a defined chromosomal cause

congenital-anomaly-classification.explanation: Potter facies and limb positioning after oligohydramnios → Mechanical deformation sequence.

congenital-anomaly-classification.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Classifying Congenital Anomalies”?
congenital-anomaly-classification.explanation: Birthmarks can be considered a type of congenital anomaly.

congenital-anomaly-classification.stem: Which should you review before “Classifying Congenital Anomalies”?
congenital-anomaly-classification.explanation: Understanding teratogenesis is essential for classifying congenital anomalies.

teratogenesis-critical-periods.stem: During which interval is an embryo generally most vulnerable to major structural malformations?

options.text: The final week before birth only

teratogenesis-critical-periods.explanation: Weeks 3-8 encompass organogenesis, when disruption of organ primordia produces major structural anomalies.

teratogenesis-critical-periods.stem: Regarding predicting teratogenic outcome — which is correct?

options.text: A known teratogen always produces the same anomaly
Outcome depends on developmental timing, effective dose, and embryonic genotype
CNS remains developmentally vulnerable beyond initial organ formation

teratogenesis-critical-periods.explanation: Teratogenesis is an interaction, not a fixed one-exposure/one-defect rule.

teratogenesis-critical-periods.stem: What best explains the finding: “Major organ malformation after exposure in weeks 3-8”?

options.text: CNS remains developmentally vulnerable beyond initial organ formation
Dose, timing, and embryonic genotype differ

teratogenesis-critical-periods.explanation: Major organ malformation after exposure in weeks 3-8 → Organogenesis is maximally sensitive.

teratogenesis-critical-periods.stem: What best explains the finding: “Different outcomes after the same maternal exposure”?

options.text: Dose, timing, and embryonic genotype differ
CNS remains developmentally vulnerable beyond initial organ formation

teratogenesis-critical-periods.explanation: Different outcomes after the same maternal exposure → Dose, timing, and embryonic genotype differ.

placenta-development-circulation.stem: What distinguishes a tertiary chorionic villus from a secondary villus?

options.text: Direct mixing of maternal and fetal blood

placenta-development-circulation.explanation: A secondary villus has a mesodermal core; fetal vessels developing in that core create a tertiary villus.

placenta-development-circulation.stem: Regarding maternal versus fetal placental component — which is correct?

options.text: Decidua basalis is the fetal side because it lies beneath the embryo
Decidua basalis is maternal; chorion frondosum is fetal
Decidual septa partition the maternal placenta

placenta-development-circulation.explanation: Decidua is transformed endometrium, while chorion derives from the conceptus.

placenta-development-circulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Smooth shiny fetal surface with chorionic vessels and cord”?

options.text: Decidual septa partition the maternal placenta

placenta-development-circulation.explanation: Smooth shiny fetal surface with chorionic vessels and cord → Amnion-covered chorionic plate.

placenta-development-circulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Villus with mesoderm and fetal capillaries”?

options.text: Decidual septa partition the maternal placenta

placenta-development-circulation.explanation: Villus with mesoderm and fetal capillaries → Tertiary chorionic villus.

placenta-development-circulation.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Placental Development & Circulation”?

options.text: hPL, Placental GH, CRH & Maternal Metabolic Adaptation

extraembryonic-membranes-cord.stem: The urachus normally becomes which adult structure?
extraembryonic-membranes-cord.explanation: The allantois becomes the urachus, which obliterates as the median umbilical ligament.

extraembryonic-membranes-cord.stem: Regarding umbilical vessel oxygenation — which is correct?

options.text: A vessel called an artery must carry oxygenated blood
Umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated fetal blood to placenta; the umbilical vein returns oxygenated blood

extraembryonic-membranes-cord.explanation: Artery and vein are named by direction relative to the heart, not oxygen content.

extraembryonic-membranes-cord.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cord with one vein and two arteries in Wharton jelly”?

options.text: Patent urachus between bladder and umbilicus

extraembryonic-membranes-cord.explanation: Cord with one vein and two arteries in Wharton jelly → Normal umbilical-cord anatomy.

extraembryonic-membranes-cord.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ileal diverticulum at antimesenteric border”?

options.text: Patent urachus between bladder and umbilicus

extraembryonic-membranes-cord.explanation: Ileal diverticulum at antimesenteric border → Persistent vitelline duct (Meckel diverticulum).

extraembryonic-membranes-cord.stem: Which should you review before “Amnion, Umbilical Cord, Yolk Sac & Allantois”?
extraembryonic-membranes-cord.explanation: Understanding body membranes is foundational for grasping extraembryonic membranes.

placenta-clinical-abnormalities.stem: Placental tissue extends through the full myometrial thickness and reaches the uterine serosa. This is:
placenta-clinical-abnormalities.explanation: Percreta is the deepest accreta-spectrum lesion, penetrating through myometrium to serosa and sometimes adjacent organs.

placenta-clinical-abnormalities.stem: Regarding interpreting nipt — which is correct?

options.text: A positive cell-free-DNA screen is a definitive fetal karyotype
NIPT is a screening test and should be confirmed by diagnostic sampling when management depends on it

placenta-clinical-abnormalities.explanation: Cell-free DNA is largely placental and has false-positive/discordant possibilities.

placenta-clinical-abnormalities.stem: What best explains the finding: “Painless third-trimester bleeding”?
placenta-clinical-abnormalities.explanation: Painless third-trimester bleeding → Placenta previa until excluded.

placenta-clinical-abnormalities.stem: What best explains the finding: “Placenta invades through myometrium to serosa/adjacent organ”?
placenta-clinical-abnormalities.explanation: Placenta invades through myometrium to serosa/adjacent organ → Placenta percreta.

placenta-clinical-abnormalities.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Placental, Cord & Amniotic Abnormalities”?
placenta-clinical-abnormalities.explanation: Links basic science of placental function to clinical implications.

chromosome-structure-chromatin.stem: Which histones form the core octamer of a nucleosome?

options.text: Two each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4

chromosome-structure-chromatin.explanation: The core octamer contains two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, and H4; H1 binds linker DNA.

chromosome-structure-chromatin.stem: Regarding chromosome versus chromatid count — which is correct?

options.text: DNA replication doubles the chromosome number
Replication doubles chromatids/DNA content, but chromosome number stays the same until centromeres separate
Short arms carry repeated rRNA-gene regions

chromosome-structure-chromatin.stem: What best explains the finding: “Open, gene-rich, transcriptionally active chromatin”?

options.text: Short arms carry repeated rRNA-gene regions

chromosome-structure-chromatin.explanation: Open, gene-rich, transcriptionally active chromatin → Euchromatin.

chromosome-structure-chromatin.stem: What best explains the finding: “Two identical DNA structures joined at centromere”?

options.text: Short arms carry repeated rRNA-gene regions

chromosome-structure-chromatin.explanation: Two identical DNA structures joined at centromere → Sister chromatids after S phase.

mitosis-cell-cycle-checkpoints.stem: Which checkpoint prevents anaphase until every chromosome is properly attached to the mitotic spindle?
mitosis-cell-cycle-checkpoints.explanation: The spindle-assembly checkpoint monitors kinetochore attachment and delays chromatid separation until alignment is safe.

mitosis-cell-cycle-checkpoints.stem: Regarding spindle checkpoint — which is correct?

options.text: Anaphase begins as soon as one chromosome attaches to spindle fibers
All chromosomes must be correctly attached before sister-chromatid separation

mitosis-cell-cycle-checkpoints.explanation: The metaphase checkpoint prevents unequal chromosome segregation.

mitosis-cell-cycle-checkpoints.stem: What best explains the finding: “Chromosomes aligned at equatorial plate”?
mitosis-cell-cycle-checkpoints.explanation: Chromosomes aligned at equatorial plate → Metaphase.

mitosis-cell-cycle-checkpoints.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sister chromatids moving to opposite poles”?
mitosis-cell-cycle-checkpoints.explanation: Sister chromatids moving to opposite poles → Anaphase after centromere separation.

meiosis-recombination.stem: During which prophase-I stage does crossing over primarily occur?
meiosis-recombination.explanation: Homologs are fully synapsed in pachytene, allowing crossing over between nonsister chromatids.

meiosis-recombination.stem: Regarding what separates in meiosis i — which is correct?

options.text: Sister chromatids separate at anaphase I just as in mitosis
Homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I; sisters remain joined until meiosis II

meiosis-recombination.explanation: This is what makes meiosis I the reduction division.

meiosis-recombination.stem: What best explains the finding: “Chiasmata visible between homologs”?
meiosis-recombination.explanation: Chiasmata visible between homologs → Diplotene after pachytene crossing over.

meiosis-recombination.stem: What best explains the finding: “Homologs move apart but centromeres remain intact”?
meiosis-recombination.explanation: Homologs move apart but centromeres remain intact → Anaphase I.

meiosis-recombination.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Meiosis, Synapsis & Recombination”?

karyotype-chromosome-analysis.stem: Why is colcemid added during conventional chromosome preparation?

options.text: To arrest cells in metaphase by disrupting spindle formation

karyotype-chromosome-analysis.explanation: Colcemid interferes with spindle microtubules and enriches cells in metaphase, when chromosomes are maximally condensed.

karyotype-chromosome-analysis.stem: Regarding limits of a normal karyotype — which is correct?

options.text: A normal karyotype excludes every genetic disorder
Karyotyping misses small copy-number changes and sequence variants below its resolution
Normal male chromosome count and sex-chromosome complement
Chromosome 5, short arm, region 1, band 5, sub-band 2

karyotype-chromosome-analysis.explanation: A normal chromosome silhouette does not prove normal DNA sequence.

options.text: Normal male chromosome count and sex-chromosome complement
Alternative banding patterns identify the same chromosome regions
Chromosome 5, short arm, region 1, band 5, sub-band 2

karyotype-chromosome-analysis.explanation: 5p15.2 → Chromosome 5, short arm, region 1, band 5, sub-band 2.

karyotype-chromosome-analysis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bright Q band corresponding to dark G band”?

options.text: Alternative banding patterns identify the same chromosome regions
Normal male chromosome count and sex-chromosome complement
Chromosome 5, short arm, region 1, band 5, sub-band 2

karyotype-chromosome-analysis.explanation: Bright Q band corresponding to dark G band → Alternative banding patterns identify the same chromosome regions.

karyotype-chromosome-analysis.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Karyotype, Banding & Chromosome Analysis”?

numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.stem: Which gamete pattern follows nondisjunction in meiosis II?

options.text: Two normal, one disomic, one nullisomic
Two disomic and two nullisomic only

numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.explanation: Only the affected meiosis-II daughter mis-segregates sisters, leaving two normal products from the other meiosis-I daughter.

numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.stem: Regarding meiosis-i versus meiosis-ii nondisjunction — which is correct?

options.text: Both errors produce the same four gametes
Meiosis I produces two disomic and two nullisomic gametes; meiosis II produces two normal, one disomic, and one nullisomic

numerical-chromosome-abnormalities.explanation: The first error affects homolog segregation; the second affects only one pair of sister chromatids.

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.stem: A chromosome consists of two copies of its long arm and no short arm. This is:
chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.explanation: An isochromosome contains mirror-image copies of one arm with loss of the other.

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.stem: Regarding isochromosome dosage — which is correct?

options.text: An isochromosome is balanced because it still has two arms
It duplicates one arm and deletes the other, causing partial trisomy plus partial monosomy

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.explanation: Arm count is preserved, but genetic content is not.

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.stem: What best explains the finding: “Terminal loss from 5p”?
chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.explanation: Terminal loss from 5p → Deletion causing partial monosomy (cri-du-chat pattern).

chromosome-copy-structure-abnormalities.stem: What best explains the finding: “Mirror-image chromosome arms”?
Which is a clinical application of “Deletion, Duplication, Ring & Isochromosome”?

translocations-inversions.stem: Which segregation pattern in a reciprocal-translocation carrier can produce normal or balanced gametes?
translocations-inversions.explanation: Alternate segregation sends the two normal chromosomes together and the two translocation derivatives together, preserving balance.

translocations-inversions.stem: Regarding balanced robertsonian carrier — which is correct?

options.text: A person with 45 chromosomes must have monosomy and a severe phenotype
A balanced Robertsonian carrier can be healthy because the fused long arms preserve essential unique material
Possible balanced translocation carrier producing unbalanced gametes

translocations-inversions.explanation: Chromosome count and genetic dosage are related but not identical.

translocations-inversions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Phenotypically normal adult with recurrent miscarriage”?

options.text: Possible balanced translocation carrier producing unbalanced gametes

translocations-inversions.explanation: Phenotypically normal adult with recurrent miscarriage → Possible balanced translocation carrier producing unbalanced gametes.

translocations-inversions.stem: What best explains the finding: “45 chromosomes with fused 14q and 21q”?

options.text: Possible balanced translocation carrier producing unbalanced gametes

translocations-inversions.explanation: 45 chromosomes with fused 14q and 21q → Balanced Robertsonian translocation.

translocations-inversions.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Translocations, Insertions & Inversions”?
translocations-inversions.explanation: Basic science concepts may relate to clinical reflexes but are not directly linked.

translocations-inversions.stem: Which should you review before “Translocations, Insertions & Inversions”?
translocations-inversions.explanation: Aneuploidy is a key concept related to chromosome aberrations.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: Two genetically distinct cell lines arise after mitotic nondisjunction in a single early embryo. This is:
mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: Both cell lines descend from one zygote, so the condition is mosaicism.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: Regarding mosaicism versus chimerism — which is correct?

options.text: Any person with two genotypes is a mosaic
Mosaicism arises from one zygote; chimerism combines cell lines from more than one zygote
Mosaic Turner pattern from postzygotic error

mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: The number of cell lines is shared; their developmental origin distinguishes the terms.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: What best explains the finding: “45,X/46,XX cell lines in one person”?

options.text: Mosaic Turner pattern from postzygotic error

mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: 45,X/46,XX cell lines in one person → Mosaic Turner pattern from postzygotic error.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: What best explains the finding: “46,XX/46,XY tissues after fusion of two embryos”?

options.text: Mosaic Turner pattern from postzygotic error

mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: 46,XX/46,XY tissues after fusion of two embryos → Tetragametic chimerism.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Mosaicism & Chimerism”?
mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: Some AEDs may have effects related to chromosomal abnormalities.

mosaicism-chimerism.stem: Which should you review before “Mosaicism & Chimerism”?
mosaicism-chimerism.explanation: Understanding aneuploidy is essential for grasping mosaicism and chimerism.

options.text: A male with a deletion of 21

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.explanation: 47 chromosomes, XY (male), +21 (an extra chromosome 21) = a male with trisomy 21, i.e. Down syndrome. The + precedes the gained chromosome.

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.stem: Regarding where the + or − sign goes — which is correct?

options.text: The sign precedes the chromosome for whole-chromosome changes: 47,XY,+21 (a trailing sign after a band would instead refer to arm gain/loss in older shorthand, which ISCN discourages)

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.explanation: ISCN puts +/− before the chromosome number for aneuploidy; "21q+" style shorthand is not used in a formal karyotype.

options.text: Mosaic: trisomy 21 in 10 cells, normal in 5
Mosaic: trisomy 21 in 10 cells, normal in 5

cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.stem: Which is a clinical application of “ISCN Nomenclature: Symbols & Numerical Karyotypes”?
cytogenetic-nomenclature-basics.explanation: Understanding karyotypes can aid in interpreting genetic conditions that may affect blood gas levels.

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.stem: A phenotypically normal woman has the karyotype 45,XX,der(14;21)(q10;q10). What is she?
structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.explanation: A Robertsonian fusion of chromosomes 14 and 21 gives 45 total chromosomes with balanced material — a phenotypically normal carrier who has an increased risk of a child with translocation Down syndrome.

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.stem: Regarding chromosome count of a balanced robertsonian carrier — which is correct?

options.text: A translocation carrier must have 46 chromosomes
A balanced Robertsonian carrier has 45 chromosomes — two acrocentrics fuse into one derivative, so the count drops by one while the genetic material is balanced

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.explanation: Robertsonian fusion physically merges two chromosomes into one, lowering the total count even though the carrier is phenotypically normal.

structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.stem: Which is a clinical application of “ISCN Nomenclature: Structural Rearrangements & Mosaicism”?
Which should you review before “ISCN Nomenclature: Structural Rearrangements & Mosaicism”?
structural-rearrangement-nomenclature.explanation: Understanding basic symbols and karyotypes is essential for grasping structural rearrangements.

autosomal-trisomies.stem: A newborn has hypotonia, a flat facial profile, upslanting palpebral fissures, Brushfield spots, and a single palmar crease. Karyotype shows 46,XY,der(14;21)(q10;q10),+21. What counseling point is most important?

options.text: This is translocation Down syndrome — test parents, as recurrence risk may be high

autosomal-trisomies.explanation: The karyotype shows Down syndrome from a Robertsonian (14;21) translocation. Unlike free trisomy 21 (~1% recurrence), a translocation may be inherited from a balanced-carrier parent with substantial recurrence risk, so parental karyotyping is essential.

autosomal-trisomies.stem: Regarding recurrence risk in down syndrome — which is correct?

options.text: Every Down syndrome pregnancy carries a high recurrence risk
Only translocation Down syndrome (e.g. a carrier parent with rob(14;21)) has a high recurrence risk; free trisomy 21 (95%) recurs at only ≈1%

autosomal-trisomies.explanation: Recurrence counseling hinges on the karyotype — a Robertsonian carrier parent changes the risk dramatically, so parental testing is essential.

autosomal-trisomies.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypotonia + flat facies + single palmar crease + Brushfield spots”?
autosomal-trisomies.explanation: Hypotonia + flat facies + single palmar crease + Brushfield spots → Down syndrome (trisomy 21).

autosomal-trisomies.stem: What best explains the finding: “Clenched fists with overlapping fingers + rocker-bottom feet + micrognathia”?
autosomal-trisomies.explanation: Clenched fists with overlapping fingers + rocker-bottom feet + micrognathia → Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18).

autosomal-trisomies.stem: Which should you review before “Autosomal Trisomies: Down, Edwards, Patau”?
autosomal-trisomies.explanation: Understanding aneuploidy is essential for grasping trisomy mechanisms.

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.stem: An infant has a distinctive high-pitched, cat-like cry, microcephaly, hypertelorism, and severe developmental delay. Which chromosomal abnormality is responsible?
autosomal-deletion-syndromes.explanation: The mewing cat-like cry with microcephaly and hypertelorism is cri-du-chat syndrome, a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p−), critical region 5p15.

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.stem: Regarding chromosome arm in cri-du-chat — which is correct?

options.text: Cri-du-chat is a deletion of the long arm of chromosome 5
It is a deletion of the SHORT arm of chromosome 5 (5p−), critical region 5p15

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.explanation: Both classic deletion syndromes here (cri-du-chat 5p, Wolf-Hirschhorn 4p) involve the short (p) arm — a common point tested.

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.stem: What best explains the finding: “High-pitched cat-like cry + microcephaly + hypertelorism”?

options.text: Consider a balanced translocation carrier parent

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.explanation: High-pitched cat-like cry + microcephaly + hypertelorism → Cri-du-chat (5p−).

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.stem: What best explains the finding: “"Greek warrior helmet" facies + seizures + growth failure”?

options.text: Consider a balanced translocation carrier parent

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.explanation: "Greek warrior helmet" facies + seizures + growth failure → Wolf-Hirschhorn (4p−).

autosomal-deletion-syndromes.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Autosomal Deletion Syndromes: Cri-du-chat & Wolf-Hirschhorn”?

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.stem: A child with severe intellectual disability, an ataxic gait, seizures, absent speech, and frequent inappropriate laughter has a 15q11-q13 abnormality. What is the parent-of-origin mechanism?
microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.explanation: Angelman syndrome results from loss of the maternally expressed 15q11-q13 (deletion, paternal UPD, imprinting defect, or UBE3A mutation), giving the ataxic "happy puppet" phenotype. Loss of the paternal copy causes Prader-Willi.

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.stem: Regarding prader-willi vs angelman — which is correct?

options.text: Prader-Willi and Angelman come from deletions on different chromosomes
Both involve the SAME 15q11-q13 region — Prader-Willi is loss of the PATERNAL copy, Angelman is loss of the MATERNAL copy (genomic imprinting)

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.explanation: The parent of origin, not the location, decides the phenotype — the classic teaching example of imprinting.

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Neonatal hypotonia → childhood hyperphagia, obesity, hypogonadism”?
microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.explanation: Neonatal hypotonia → childhood hyperphagia, obesity, hypogonadism → Prader-Willi (paternal 15q loss).

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ataxic gait, seizures, absent speech, inappropriate laughter”?
microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.explanation: Ataxic gait, seizures, absent speech, inappropriate laughter → Angelman (maternal 15q loss).

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Microdeletion & Imprinting Syndromes”?

options.text: Sex Steroid Synthesis, Transport & Receptor Action

microdeletion-imprinting-syndromes.explanation: Both modules involve genetic mechanisms but in different contexts.

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: How many Barr bodies are present in a somatic cell with a 47,XXX karyotype?
x-inactivation-sex-determination.explanation: The number of Barr bodies equals the number of X chromosomes minus one. With three X chromosomes, two are inactivated → 2 Barr bodies.

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: Regarding barr body count — which is correct?

options.text: A 47,XXY (Klinefelter) male has no Barr body because he is male
Barr bodies depend on X count, not sex: 47,XXY has two X chromosomes → ONE Barr body
SRY is sufficient for testis determination

x-inactivation-sex-determination.explanation: One X stays active and the rest are inactivated regardless of sex, so the count is (X − 1).

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: What best explains the finding: “47,XXY has one Barr body”?

options.text: SRY is sufficient for testis determination

x-inactivation-sex-determination.explanation: 47,XXY has one Barr body → Barr bodies = X − 1.

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: What best explains the finding: “SRY translocated to an X → 46,XX male”?

options.text: SRY is sufficient for testis determination

x-inactivation-sex-determination.explanation: SRY translocated to an X → 46,XX male → SRY is sufficient for testis determination.

x-inactivation-sex-determination.stem: Which is a clinical application of “X-Inactivation, Barr Bodies & Sex Determination”?

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.stem: A short 15-year-old girl has not started menstruating; exam shows a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, and a history of coarctation repair. FSH and LH are elevated. What is the karyotype?
sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.explanation: Turner syndrome (45,X): short stature, webbed neck, coarctation of the aorta, and ovarian dysgenesis causing primary amenorrhea with elevated (hypergonadotropic) FSH/LH.

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.stem: Regarding gonadotropin levels in turner/klinefelter — which is correct?

options.text: Hypogonadism in these syndromes means low FSH/LH
Both are PRIMARY (hypergonadotropic) hypogonadism — the gonad fails, so FSH/LH are HIGH with low sex steroids

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.explanation: The defect is at the gonad, not the pituitary, so feedback drives gonadotropins up (unlike central/secondary hypogonadism).

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.stem: What best explains the finding: “Short female, webbed neck, coarctation, primary amenorrhea”?
sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.explanation: Short female, webbed neck, coarctation, primary amenorrhea → Turner syndrome (45,X).

sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.stem: What best explains the finding: “Tall male, small firm testes, gynecomastia, ↑FSH/LH”?
sex-chromosome-aneuploidies.explanation: Tall male, small firm testes, gynecomastia, ↑FSH/LH → Klinefelter (47,XXY).

dsd-fragile-x.stem: A phenotypic 17-year-old female presents with primary amenorrhea. She has normal breasts, scant pubic hair, a short blind-ending vagina, no uterus, and 46,XY karyotype with intra-abdominal testes. What is the defect?
dsd-fragile-x.explanation: Complete androgen insensitivity: a 46,XY individual with an X-linked androgen-receptor mutation. Testes make testosterone and AMH, so the uterus is absent, but androgen resistance yields female external genitalia and scant sexual hair.

dsd-fragile-x.stem: Regarding uterus in complete androgen insensitivity — which is correct?

options.text: A 46,XY person raised female should have a uterus
In CAIS the uterus is ABSENT — the testes secrete AMH, which regresses the Müllerian ducts, while androgen resistance produces female external genitalia

dsd-fragile-x.explanation: AMH still works even though the androgen receptor does not, so Müllerian structures involute despite the female phenotype.

dsd-fragile-x.stem: What best explains the finding: “46,XY girl, primary amenorrhea, no uterus, testes in inguinal canal”?
dsd-fragile-x.explanation: 46,XY girl, primary amenorrhea, no uterus, testes in inguinal canal → Complete androgen insensitivity (AR mutation).

dsd-fragile-x.stem: What best explains the finding: “Boy with intellectual disability, long face, large ears, macro-orchidism”?
dsd-fragile-x.explanation: Boy with intellectual disability, long face, large ears, macro-orchidism → Fragile X (FMR1 CGG expansion).

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: A pedigree shows affected males in several generations, all connected through unaffected females, with no instance of an affected father having an affected son. What is the inheritance pattern?
mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: Affected males transmitted through carrier females with no male-to-male transmission is classic X-linked recessive inheritance (e.g. hemophilia, G6PD deficiency).

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: Regarding distinguishing x-linked from autosomal dominant — which is correct?

options.text: A disease affecting mostly males in a family must be X-linked
Look for male-to-male (father→son) transmission — its PRESENCE excludes X-linked inheritance (a father gives his son a Y, not his X)

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: Sex bias alone is not enough; father-to-son transmission is the decisive feature that rules out X-linkage.

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: What best explains the finding: “Disease in every generation, both sexes, father→son transmission”?
mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: Disease in every generation, both sexes, father→son transmission → Autosomal dominant.

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: What best explains the finding: “Affected males linked through unaffected carrier females; no father→son”?
mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: Affected males linked through unaffected carrier females; no father→son → X-linked recessive.

mendelian-inheritance-patterns.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Mendelian Inheritance Patterns”?
mendelian-inheritance-patterns.explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot has genetic components that may involve Mendelian inheritance patterns.

inheritance-modifiers.stem: In a family with an autosomal dominant disease, one man clearly transmitted the mutant allele from his affected father to his affected son but shows no symptoms himself. This best illustrates:
inheritance-modifiers.explanation: An obligate carrier who is phenotypically normal demonstrates incomplete (reduced) penetrance — the disease genotype is present but the phenotype is not expressed.

inheritance-modifiers.stem: Regarding penetrance vs expressivity — which is correct?

options.text: Incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity are the same thing
Penetrance is whether the phenotype appears at all (all-or-none); expressivity is how severe it is when it does appear

inheritance-modifiers.explanation: They are separate modifiers — a mutation can be fully penetrant yet variably expressed, or incompletely penetrant.

inheritance-modifiers.stem: What best explains the finding: “Unaffected obligate carrier between two affected relatives”?
inheritance-modifiers.explanation: Unaffected obligate carrier between two affected relatives → Incomplete penetrance (nonpenetrance).

inheritance-modifiers.stem: What best explains the finding: “One mutation → lens, skeleton, and aortic disease”?
inheritance-modifiers.explanation: One mutation → lens, skeleton, and aortic disease → Pleiotropy (Marfan).

inheritance-modifiers.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Complications of Single-Gene Inheritance”?
inheritance-modifiers.explanation: Single-gene inheritance concepts may relate to congenital heart defects.

inheritance-modifiers.stem: Which should you review before “Complications of Single-Gene Inheritance”?
inheritance-modifiers.explanation: Understanding Mendelian patterns is essential for grasping inheritance modifiers.

multifactorial-population-genetics.stem: An autosomal recessive disease has an incidence of 1 in 10,000. Approximately what is the carrier frequency in this population?
Regarding meaning of q² in hardy-weinberg — which is correct?

options.text: The carrier frequency equals the disease incidence
q² is the disease (homozygote) incidence; the CARRIER frequency is 2pq ≈ 2q ≈ 2√incidence — much larger than the disease rate

multifactorial-population-genetics.explanation: Carriers (2pq) vastly outnumber affected homozygotes (q²) for rare recessive diseases, which is why carrier screening matters.

multifactorial-population-genetics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Recurrence ~2–4% in first-degree relatives of a cleft-lip/NTD proband”?
multifactorial-population-genetics.explanation: Recurrence ~2–4% in first-degree relatives of a cleft-lip/NTD proband → Multifactorial inheritance.

multifactorial-population-genetics.stem: What best explains the finding: “CF incidence 1/2500 → carrier frequency 1/25”?
Which is a clinical application of “Multifactorial Inheritance & Population Genetics”?

options.text: Drugs for Urinary Frequency, Incontinence & Enuresis

multifactorial-population-genetics.stem: Which should you review before “Multifactorial Inheritance & Population Genetics”?
multifactorial-population-genetics.explanation: Understanding Mendelian patterns is essential for grasping multifactorial inheritance.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: A pregnant woman at 12 weeks has a positive cell-free DNA (NIPT) result for trisomy 21. What is the appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed directly to a decision based on the NIPT
Confirm with a diagnostic test such as CVS or amniocentesis

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: NIPT is a highly sensitive screen but not diagnostic; a positive result should be confirmed with an invasive diagnostic test (CVS or amniocentesis) that provides a fetal karyotype.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: Regarding acting on a screening result — which is correct?

options.text: A positive NIPT or quad screen confirms fetal Down syndrome
These are SCREENS — a positive result raises risk and must be confirmed by a diagnostic test (amniocentesis or CVS karyotype) before any irreversible decision

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: Screening tests have false positives; a definitive karyotype is required to diagnose aneuploidy.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Quad screen: ↓AFP, ↓uE3, ↑hCG, ↑inhibin A”?
prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: Quad screen: ↓AFP, ↓uE3, ↑hCG, ↑inhibin A → Down syndrome risk pattern.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Elevated maternal serum AFP”?
prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: Elevated maternal serum AFP → Neural tube / abdominal wall defect.

prenatal-screening-diagnosis.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Prenatal Screening & Diagnosis”?
prenatal-screening-diagnosis.explanation: Gestational diabetes is a key aspect of prenatal diagnosis and care.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: A couple is screened before pregnancy. Both have low MCV; PCR confirms both carry α-thalassemia-1 (SEA deletion). What severe fetal condition is this pregnancy at risk for?
thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: Two α-thalassemia-1 carriers risk a fetus with all four α-globin genes deleted (--/--), causing Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis, which is lethal in utero — the couple should be offered prenatal diagnosis.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: Regarding interpreting a low mcv in screening — which is correct?

options.text: A low MCV in a prospective parent just means iron deficiency
In thalassemia screening a low MCV flags a possible thalassemia trait and triggers confirmatory testing (α-thal-1 PCR, HbA₂/Hb typing) — iron deficiency must be excluded but not assumed
α-thalassemia-1 trait (risk of Hb Bart's hydrops)

thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: Microcytosis is the entry point of the screening algorithm; missing a thalassemia trait risks an affected fetus if the partner is also a carrier.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: What best explains the finding: “Low MCV with normal iron studies + positive α-thal-1 PCR”?

options.text: α-thalassemia-1 trait (risk of Hb Bart's hydrops)

thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: Low MCV with normal iron studies + positive α-thal-1 PCR → α-thalassemia-1 trait (risk of Hb Bart's hydrops).

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: What best explains the finding: “HbA₂ > 4% on Hb typing”?

options.text: α-thalassemia-1 trait (risk of Hb Bart's hydrops)

thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: HbA₂ > 4% on Hb typing → β-thalassemia trait.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Thalassemia Carrier Screening & Prevention”?
thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: Both involve screening during pregnancy, but focus on different conditions.

thalassemia-prevention-screening.stem: Which should you review before “Thalassemia Carrier Screening & Prevention”?
thalassemia-prevention-screening.explanation: Foundational knowledge on prenatal screening is essential for understanding thalassemia screening.

fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.stem: Which macronutrient provides the greatest energy per gram?
fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.explanation: Triacylglycerol yields about 9 kcal/g, compared with about 4 kcal/g from carbohydrate or protein.

fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.stem: Regarding energy density — which is correct?

options.text: Protein gives more energy per gram because it is structurally complex
Protein and carbohydrate each yield about 4 kcal/g; fat yields about 9 kcal/g
Highly reduced carbon and anhydrous storage

fuel-nutrients-energy-balance.explanation: Energy yield depends on chemical reduction and storage hydration, not structural complexity.

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.stem: Which transporter mediates apical fructose uptake into an enterocyte?
carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.explanation: Fructose enters through apical GLUT5; glucose and galactose use SGLT1, then all exit through GLUT2.

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.stem: Regarding apical intestinal transport — which is correct?

options.text: Glucose/galactose use apical SGLT1, fructose uses apical GLUT5, and basolateral GLUT2 exports all three
Unabsorbed lactose retains water and is fermented
Intact Na⁺-glucose cotransport drives water absorption

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.explanation: The apical transporter depends on the identity of the monosaccharide.

carbohydrate-digestion-absorption.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Carbohydrate Digestion & Monosaccharide Absorption”?

protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.stem: Loss of brush-border enteropeptidase most directly prevents activation of which enzyme?
protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.explanation: Enteropeptidase converts trypsinogen to trypsin, which then activates the other pancreatic protease zymogens.

protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.stem: Regarding protease activation — which is correct?

options.text: Enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen; trypsin then activates the other pancreatic zymogens
Reduced delivery of proteases and other digestive enzymes

protein-digestion-amino-acid-absorption.explanation: The key small-intestinal activation cascade begins at the brush border.

lipid-digestion-chylomicrons.stem: Which apolipoprotein is required for intestinal chylomicron assembly?
lipid-digestion-chylomicrons.explanation: ApoB-48 is the structural apolipoprotein assembled with dietary lipid in enterocytes.

lipid-digestion-chylomicrons.stem: Regarding what enters the enterocyte — which is correct?

options.text: The whole mixed micelle is endocytosed
Lipid products leave the micelle and enter; bile salts remain luminal and are reclaimed in terminal ileum

lipid-digestion-chylomicrons.explanation: Micelles are delivery vehicles, not absorbed particles.

lipid-digestion-chylomicrons.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Lipid Digestion, Micelles & Chylomicrons”?

malabsorption-patterns.stem: Which deficiency pattern is most characteristic of chronic severe fat malabsorption?

options.text: Vitamins B1, B2, B3, and B6
Vitamins A, D, E, and K

malabsorption-patterns.explanation: Micelle-dependent absorption is required for the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K.

malabsorption-patterns.stem: Regarding maldigestion versus malabsorption — which is correct?

options.text: All nutrient loss means an enterocyte transporter is defective
Pancreatic or bile failure can prevent luminal digestion before nutrients ever reach the transporter
Selective carbohydrate malabsorption and bacterial fermentation

malabsorption-patterns.explanation: Localizing the failed step narrows both testing and treatment.

malabsorption-patterns.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Clinical Patterns of Maldigestion & Malabsorption”?

options.text: Pepsin, Intrinsic Factor & Gastric Mucosal Defense

malabsorption-patterns.explanation: Gastric enzymes play a role in the initial digestion process.

free-energy-atp-coupling.stem: An enzyme catalyzes a reaction with a negative ΔG. What does the enzyme change?
free-energy-atp-coupling.explanation: Enzymes lower activation energy and increase rate without changing ΔG or the equilibrium constant.

free-energy-atp-coupling.stem: Regarding thermodynamics versus kinetics — which is correct?

options.text: A negative ΔG means the reaction must be fast
A negative ΔG makes a reaction thermodynamically favorable, but the activation barrier can still make it slow
Thermodynamic favorability does not determine activation energy
Forward and reverse fluxes are equal and ΔG = 0

free-energy-atp-coupling.explanation: ΔG predicts direction; activation energy determines rate.

free-energy-atp-coupling.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Free Energy, ATP & Reaction Coupling”?
free-energy-atp-coupling.explanation: ATP is vital for cardiac function, including in conditions like atrial fibrillation.

pdh-tca-cycle.stem: Which set correctly lists the products of one TCA-cycle turn per acetyl-CoA?
pdh-tca-cycle.explanation: Each acetyl-CoA yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP, and 2 CO₂.

pdh-tca-cycle.stem: Regarding tca oxygen dependence — which is correct?

options.text: The TCA cycle directly consumes molecular oxygen
TCA does not directly use O₂, but it stops without O₂ because NADH/FADH₂ cannot be reoxidized by the ETC
PDH deficiency diverts pyruvate to lactate
Ketones bypass the blocked pyruvate-to-acetyl-CoA step

pdh-tca-cycle.explanation: Its oxygen dependence is indirect through regeneration of oxidized cofactors.

electron-transport-oxphos.stem: Which respiratory-chain complex transfers electrons to CoQ without pumping protons?
electron-transport-oxphos.explanation: Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) feeds FADH₂-derived electrons to CoQ but does not pump H⁺.

electron-transport-oxphos.stem: Regarding electron carriers versus complexes — which is correct?

options.text: CoQ and cytochrome c pump protons
CoQ and cytochrome c are mobile electron carriers; complexes I, III, and IV are the proton pumps
Succinate dehydrogenase transfers electrons to CoQ without pumping H⁺
NADH uses one additional proton-pumping complex

electron-transport-oxphos.explanation: Mobility and proton pumping are separate roles.

etc-inhibitors-uncoupling-shuttles.stem: A mitochondrial toxin increases oxygen consumption and heat production while decreasing ATP. What is its action?
etc-inhibitors-uncoupling-shuttles.explanation: Uncoupling allows protons to bypass ATP synthase, so respiration accelerates but energy is released as heat.

etc-inhibitors-uncoupling-shuttles.stem: Regarding inhibitor versus uncoupler — which is correct?

options.text: ETC inhibitors decrease O₂ use; uncouplers generally increase O₂ use while reducing ATP production
Cyanide blocks complex IV, preventing tissue oxygen use

etc-inhibitors-uncoupling-shuttles.explanation: An uncoupler removes back-pressure from the proton gradient rather than blocking electron flow.

etc-inhibitors-uncoupling-shuttles.stem: Which is a clinical application of “ETC Inhibitors, Uncoupling & NADH Shuttles”?
Which should you review before “ETC Inhibitors, Uncoupling & NADH Shuttles”?
etc-inhibitors-uncoupling-shuttles.explanation: Essential for understanding the role of ETC in ATP synthesis.

tca-amphibolic-anaplerosis.stem: Which reaction is the major anaplerotic source of oxaloacetate in human mitochondria?
tca-amphibolic-anaplerosis.explanation: Biotin-dependent pyruvate carboxylase replenishes oxaloacetate and is activated by acetyl-CoA.

tca-amphibolic-anaplerosis.stem: Regarding acetyl-coa entry into tca — which is correct?

options.text: Abundant acetyl-CoA guarantees rapid TCA oxidation
Acetyl-CoA oxidation also requires enough oxaloacetate and other TCA intermediates
Signals the need for oxaloacetate to support TCA flux or gluconeogenesis
Pyruvate carboxylase is a biotin-dependent carboxylase

tca-amphibolic-anaplerosis.explanation: During fasting, oxaloacetate withdrawal for gluconeogenesis helps divert acetyl-CoA toward ketogenesis.

tca-amphibolic-anaplerosis.stem: Which should you review before “TCA Cycle as an Amphibolic & Anaplerotic Hub”?
tca-amphibolic-anaplerosis.explanation: Understanding pyruvate dehydrogenase is essential for grasping TCA cycle entry.

glucose-transport-glycolysis.stem: Which metabolite most strongly activates hepatic PFK-1 after a carbohydrate-rich meal?
glucose-transport-glycolysis.explanation: Insulin raises F-2,6-BP, which strongly activates PFK-1 and promotes glycolysis.

glucose-transport-glycolysis.stem: Regarding insulin-dependent glucose entry — which is correct?

options.text: Insulin is required for glucose uptake into every tissue
