soft-tissue-tumors.explanation: Malignant nerve-sheath tumor in an NF1 patient → MPNST.

soft-tissue-tumors.stem: Which should you review before “Soft Tissue Tumors”?
soft-tissue-tumors.explanation: Understanding tumor nomenclature is essential for classifying soft tissue tumors.

bone-tumors.stem: A 15-year-old has a painful mass at the distal femur metaphysis; X-ray shows a mixed lytic-blastic lesion with cortical destruction and a Codman triangle. Biopsy shows malignant cells producing osteoid. The diagnosis is:
bone-tumors.explanation: A metaphyseal tumor around the knee in a teenager with a Codman triangle and osteoid-producing malignant cells is osteosarcoma — the most common primary malignant bone tumor.

bone-tumors.stem: Regarding most common malignant bone tumor — which is correct?

options.text: Osteosarcoma is the most common malignant tumor found in bone
Metastasis is the most common malignant bone tumor overall; osteosarcoma is the most common PRIMARY malignant bone tumor

bone-tumors.explanation: Metastatic carcinoma (breast, lung, prostate, etc.) far outnumbers primary bone sarcomas — “most common primary” and “most common overall” are different answers.

bone-tumors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Codman triangle / sunburst on X-ray in a teenager”?
bone-tumors.explanation: Codman triangle / sunburst on X-ray in a teenager → Osteosarcoma (metaphysis).

bone-tumors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Onion-skin periosteal reaction, diaphysis, child”?
bone-tumors.explanation: Onion-skin periosteal reaction, diaphysis, child → Ewing sarcoma.

pituitary-adenomas-hyperpituitarism.stem: A 28-year-old woman has 8 months of amenorrhea and milky nipple discharge. Prolactin is markedly elevated and MRI shows a 6-mm pituitary lesion. What is the best initial treatment?
pituitary-adenomas-hyperpituitarism.explanation: A prolactinoma — the most common functional pituitary adenoma — is treated first with a dopamine agonist (cabergoline/bromocriptine), which both normalizes prolactin and shrinks the tumor. Surgery is reserved for drug failure or apoplexy.

pituitary-adenomas-hyperpituitarism.stem: A 45-year-old man has enlarging hands, a protruding jaw, and new hypertension and diabetes. Which single test best confirms the diagnosis?

options.text: IGF-1 with an oral glucose GH-suppression test

pituitary-adenomas-hyperpituitarism.explanation: Acromegaly is confirmed by an elevated IGF-1 plus failure of GH to suppress after an oral glucose load. A single random GH is unreliable because of pulsatile secretion.

pituitary-adenomas-hyperpituitarism.stem: Regarding first-line treatment of a prolactinoma — which is correct?

options.text: It is a tumor, so resect it surgically first
A dopamine agonist (cabergoline/bromocriptine) is first-line — it lowers prolactin AND shrinks the tumor; surgery is reserved for failure/apoplexy
It causes BItemporal hemianopsia — the chiasm crossing fibers (nasal retina) are compressed
A pituitary mass causes homonymous hemianopsia

pituitary-adenomas-hyperpituitarism.explanation: Lactotrophs are dopamine-responsive, so unlike most tumors the prolactinoma is managed medically before surgery.

pituitary-adenomas-hyperpituitarism.stem: Regarding visual field pattern — which is correct?

options.text: A pituitary mass causes homonymous hemianopsia
A dopamine agonist (cabergoline/bromocriptine) is first-line — it lowers prolactin AND shrinks the tumor; surgery is reserved for failure/apoplexy
It causes BItemporal hemianopsia — the chiasm crossing fibers (nasal retina) are compressed
It is a tumor, so resect it surgically first

pituitary-adenomas-hyperpituitarism.explanation: Homonymous defects come from retrochiasmal (tract/radiation) lesions; the chiasm gives the classic bitemporal (tunnel) pattern.

pituitary-adenomas-hyperpituitarism.stem: What best explains the finding: “Young woman: amenorrhea + galactorrhea + ↑prolactin”?
pituitary-adenomas-hyperpituitarism.explanation: Young woman: amenorrhea + galactorrhea + ↑prolactin → Prolactinoma (lactotroph adenoma).

pituitary-adenomas-hyperpituitarism.stem: What best explains the finding: “Coarse features, enlarged hands/feet, prognathism, ring/shoe no longer fits”?
pituitary-adenomas-hyperpituitarism.explanation: Coarse features, enlarged hands/feet, prognathism, ring/shoe no longer fits → Acromegaly (adult GH excess).

pituitary-adenomas-hyperpituitarism.stem: Which should you review before “Pituitary Adenomas & Hyperpituitarism”?
pituitary-adenomas-hyperpituitarism.explanation: Understanding growth hormone and IGF-1 is essential for grasping the effects of somatotroph adenomas.

hypopituitarism.stem: A woman who had a severe postpartum hemorrhage cannot breastfeed and later develops amenorrhea, fatigue, and loss of axillary/pubic hair. What is the diagnosis?
hypopituitarism.explanation: Sheehan syndrome is postpartum ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary; failure of lactation is the earliest sign, followed by loss of other anterior hormones.

hypopituitarism.stem: Regarding order of hormone replacement in panhypopituitarism — which is correct?

options.text: Start levothyroxine for the low T4 right away
Give glucocorticoid first; thyroid hormone raises metabolic clearance of cortisol and can trigger an adrenal crisis if cortisol is not replaced

hypopituitarism.explanation: A classic sequencing trap — the low-cortisol state must be covered before thyroid replacement is started.

hypopituitarism.stem: What best explains the finding: “New mother who cannot breastfeed, then amenorrhea + loss of body hair”?
hypopituitarism.explanation: New mother who cannot breastfeed, then amenorrhea + loss of body hair → Sheehan syndrome.

hypopituitarism.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fatigue, cold intolerance, hypotension, hyponatremia after head injury”?
hypopituitarism.explanation: Fatigue, cold intolerance, hypotension, hyponatremia after head injury → Panhypopituitarism (secondary hypothyroid + hypoadrenal).

posterior-pituitary-syndromes.stem: A patient with small-cell lung carcinoma has Na⁺ 122, serum osmolality 255, and an inappropriately concentrated urine while euvolemic. What is the mechanism?
posterior-pituitary-syndromes.explanation: SIADH — most often from ectopic ADH by small-cell lung carcinoma — causes water retention with dilutional hyponatremia, low serum osmolality, and inappropriately concentrated urine.

posterior-pituitary-syndromes.stem: Regarding sodium direction in di vs siadh — which is correct?

options.text: Diabetes insipidus causes low sodium because of all that water loss
DI raises serum sodium (free-water loss → hypernatremia); SIADH is the one that causes hyponatremia

posterior-pituitary-syndromes.explanation: The name "insipidus" refers to dilute urine, not dilute blood — the blood becomes concentrated.

posterior-pituitary-syndromes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Massive dilute polyuria + hypernatremia after neurosurgery”?
posterior-pituitary-syndromes.explanation: Massive dilute polyuria + hypernatremia after neurosurgery → Central DI.

posterior-pituitary-syndromes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hyponatremia + concentrated urine + euvolemia in a lung-cancer patient”?
posterior-pituitary-syndromes.explanation: Hyponatremia + concentrated urine + euvolemia in a lung-cancer patient → SIADH (ectopic ADH).

posterior-pituitary-syndromes.stem: Which should you review before “Posterior Pituitary Syndromes: DI & SIADH”?
posterior-pituitary-syndromes.explanation: Understanding body fluid compartments is essential for grasping the effects of ADH on water balance.

craniopharyngioma.stem: A 9-year-old has headaches, poor growth, and bitemporal vision loss. Imaging shows a calcified cystic suprasellar mass; histology shows squamous nests with peripheral palisading and compact lamellar "wet" keratin. The diagnosis is:
craniopharyngioma.explanation: Craniopharyngioma arises from Rathke-pouch remnants; the adamantinomatous variant (children) shows peripheral palisading, wet keratin, cholesterol clefts, and calcification, and compresses the chiasm and pituitary.

craniopharyngioma.stem: Regarding suprasellar mass in a child — which is correct?

options.text: A sellar/suprasellar tumor in a child must be a pituitary adenoma
A calcified cystic suprasellar mass in a child is a craniopharyngioma (Rathke-pouch remnant); pituitary adenomas are rare in children and usually not calcified

craniopharyngioma.explanation: Calcification + cystic change + childhood age points to craniopharyngioma, not adenoma.

craniopharyngioma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Child with short stature, headache, and bitemporal hemianopsia + calcified suprasellar cyst”?
craniopharyngioma.explanation: Child with short stature, headache, and bitemporal hemianopsia + calcified suprasellar cyst → Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma.

craniopharyngioma.stem: What best explains the finding: “"Wet keratin" and cholesterol clefts on histology”?
craniopharyngioma.explanation: "Wet keratin" and cholesterol clefts on histology → Adamantinomatous variant.

craniopharyngioma.stem: Which should you review before “Craniopharyngioma & Suprasellar Tumors”?
craniopharyngioma.explanation: Knowledge of calcification processes is crucial for interpreting imaging findings.

gnrh-gonadotropin-drugs.stem: A man with metastatic prostate cancer is started on continuous leuprolide. What is the intended endocrine effect, and what early complication should be anticipated?

options.text: Sustained rise in testosterone; no early risk
Suppression of testosterone after an initial testosterone flare

gnrh-gonadotropin-drugs.explanation: Continuous GnRH-agonist dosing downregulates receptors and suppresses LH/testosterone, but causes an initial flare that can transiently worsen the tumor — an antiandrogen is often co-given. (Degarelix, an antagonist, avoids the flare.)

gnrh-gonadotropin-drugs.stem: Regarding why a gnrh agonist lowers hormones — which is correct?

options.text: Leuprolide is a GnRH agonist so it must raise LH and testosterone
Given continuously it downregulates GnRH receptors and SUPPRESSES LH/FSH — that is why it treats prostate cancer and endometriosis (after a transient flare)
GnRH antagonist blocks premature LH surge

gnrh-gonadotropin-drugs.explanation: The agonist only stimulates when pulsatile; sustained exposure desensitizes the gonadotroph.

gnrh-gonadotropin-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Leuprolide used to LOWER testosterone in prostate cancer”?

options.text: GnRH antagonist blocks premature LH surge

gnrh-gonadotropin-drugs.explanation: Leuprolide used to LOWER testosterone in prostate cancer → Continuous GnRH-agonist downregulates receptors.

gnrh-gonadotropin-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ganirelix/cetrorelix during IVF”?

options.text: GnRH antagonist blocks premature LH surge

gnrh-gonadotropin-drugs.explanation: Ganirelix/cetrorelix during IVF → GnRH antagonist blocks premature LH surge.

gnrh-gonadotropin-drugs.stem: Which should you review before “GnRH & Gonadotropin Drugs”?

options.text: Male HPG Axis, Leydig & Sertoli Regulation

gnrh-gonadotropin-drugs.explanation: Understanding the male HPG axis is essential for grasping GnRH's role.

growth-hormone-prolactin-drugs.stem: A patient with acromegaly has residual GH excess after transsphenoidal surgery. Which drug is a somatostatin analog that inhibits GH release?
growth-hormone-prolactin-drugs.explanation: Octreotide is a somatostatin analog that inhibits GH release; pegvisomant (a GH-receptor antagonist) is an alternative. Somatropin and mecasermin are replacements (GH and IGF-1), which would worsen acromegaly.

growth-hormone-prolactin-drugs.stem: Regarding cause of new galactorrhea — which is correct?

options.text: Galactorrhea always means a prolactinoma needing imaging
Check the medication list first — dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) are a common cause of hyperprolactinemia
Somatostatin analog / GH-receptor antagonist for acromegaly

growth-hormone-prolactin-drugs.explanation: Blocking dopamine removes the tonic brake on prolactin; the fix may be stopping the offending drug, not surgery.

growth-hormone-prolactin-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Octreotide or pegvisomant prescribed for enlarging jaw/hands”?

options.text: Somatostatin analog / GH-receptor antagonist for acromegaly

growth-hormone-prolactin-drugs.explanation: Octreotide or pegvisomant prescribed for enlarging jaw/hands → Somatostatin analog / GH-receptor antagonist for acromegaly.

growth-hormone-prolactin-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Galactorrhea/amenorrhea appearing after starting risperidone”?

options.text: Somatostatin analog / GH-receptor antagonist for acromegaly

growth-hormone-prolactin-drugs.explanation: Galactorrhea/amenorrhea appearing after starting risperidone → Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia (D2 blockade).

growth-hormone-prolactin-drugs.stem: Which should you review before “GH, IGF-1 & Prolactin Drugs”?
growth-hormone-prolactin-drugs.explanation: Understanding agonists and antagonists is crucial for GH and prolactin drug mechanisms.

posterior-pituitary-drugs.stem: A hospitalized patient with SIADH and symptomatic hyponatremia is not improving with fluid restriction. Which drug promotes free-water excretion by blocking renal V2 receptors?
posterior-pituitary-drugs.explanation: Vaptans (tolvaptan, conivaptan) block V2 receptors to cause aquaresis, raising serum sodium in SIADH. Desmopressin is a V2 agonist and would worsen hyponatremia.

posterior-pituitary-drugs.stem: Regarding desmopressin in nephrogenic di — which is correct?

options.text: Give desmopressin for any diabetes insipidus
Desmopressin works only in CENTRAL DI; nephrogenic DI is ADH-resistant and needs cause removal, thiazide, and salt restriction
Selective V2 agonist; nephrogenic tubules are resistant

posterior-pituitary-drugs.explanation: The defect in nephrogenic DI is downstream of the V2 receptor, so a V2 agonist has little effect.

posterior-pituitary-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Oxytocin infusion for labor induction / postpartum hemorrhage”?

options.text: Selective V2 agonist; nephrogenic tubules are resistant

posterior-pituitary-drugs.explanation: Oxytocin infusion for labor induction / postpartum hemorrhage → Uterine smooth-muscle contraction.

posterior-pituitary-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Desmopressin corrects polyuria in central DI but not nephrogenic”?

options.text: Selective V2 agonist; nephrogenic tubules are resistant

posterior-pituitary-drugs.explanation: Desmopressin corrects polyuria in central DI but not nephrogenic → Selective V2 agonist; nephrogenic tubules are resistant.

posterior-pituitary-drugs.stem: Which should you review before “Oxytocin & Vasopressin Drugs”?
posterior-pituitary-drugs.explanation: Understanding oxytocin's role in milk ejection and parturition is essential.

hyperaldosteronism.stem: A 40-year-old man has BP 150/100, generalized weakness, Na⁺ 144, K⁺ 2.0, and HCO₃⁻ 35. Plasma aldosterone is high with suppressed renin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
hyperaldosteronism.explanation: Hypertension with hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, high aldosterone, and suppressed renin is primary hyperaldosteronism. Renal artery stenosis would raise renin (secondary).

hyperaldosteronism.stem: Regarding renin level in primary hyperaldosteronism — which is correct?

options.text: High aldosterone should go with high renin
In PRIMARY hyperaldosteronism renin is LOW (suppressed) — the adrenal makes aldosterone autonomously; high renin indicates a SECONDARY cause

hyperaldosteronism.explanation: The ARR works precisely because primary disease uncouples aldosterone from renin.

hyperaldosteronism.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypertension + spontaneous hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis”?
hyperaldosteronism.explanation: Hypertension + spontaneous hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis → Primary hyperaldosteronism.

hyperaldosteronism.stem: What best explains the finding: “High aldosterone with SUPPRESSED renin (high ARR)”?
hyperaldosteronism.explanation: High aldosterone with SUPPRESSED renin (high ARR) → Autonomous adrenal aldosterone.

hyperaldosteronism.stem: Which should you review before “Hyperaldosteronism (Primary vs Secondary)”?
hyperaldosteronism.explanation: Understanding aldosterone synthesis and RAAS control is essential for grasping hyperaldosteronism.

adrenal-cushing-pathology.stem: A 55-year-old woman on long-term corticosteroids for rheumatoid arthritis develops central obesity, a moon face, and abdominal striae. What best explains her presentation?
adrenal-cushing-pathology.explanation: Exogenous glucocorticoid therapy is the most common cause of Cushing syndrome; her ACTH and endogenous cortisol would be suppressed and the adrenals atrophic. "Cushing disease" is reserved for a pituitary ACTH adenoma.

adrenal-cushing-pathology.stem: Regarding cushing syndrome vs cushing disease — which is correct?

options.text: Cushing syndrome and Cushing disease are the same thing
Cushing SYNDROME is hypercortisolism from any cause; Cushing DISEASE specifically means an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma

adrenal-cushing-pathology.explanation: Exam stems reward the distinction — "disease" points to the pituitary source, not iatrogenic or adrenal causes.

adrenal-cushing-pathology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Moon face, buffalo hump, purple abdominal striae, central obesity”?
adrenal-cushing-pathology.explanation: Moon face, buffalo hump, purple abdominal striae, central obesity → Cortisol-driven fat redistribution + collagen loss.

adrenal-cushing-pathology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Proximal muscle weakness + osteoporosis + easy bruising”?
adrenal-cushing-pathology.explanation: Proximal muscle weakness + osteoporosis + easy bruising → Glucocorticoid catabolic effect.

adrenal-cushing-pathology.stem: Which should you review before “Hypercortisolism: Causes & Adrenal Pathology”?
adrenal-cushing-pathology.explanation: Understanding cortisol's actions is essential for grasping hypercortisolism.

adrenal-insufficiency.stem: A 35-year-old woman has fatigue, weight loss, BP 90/60, and hyperpigmentation of the palmar creases and oral mucosa. Which electrolyte/acid-base pattern is most consistent?
adrenal-insufficiency.explanation: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison) loses both cortisol and aldosterone → hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, and a mild metabolic acidosis; hyperpigmentation reflects high ACTH/MSH.

adrenal-insufficiency.stem: Regarding primary vs secondary adrenal insufficiency — which is correct?

options.text: All adrenal insufficiency causes hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia
Only PRIMARY (Addison) does — high ACTH/MSH gives pigmentation and aldosterone loss gives hyperkalemia; SECONDARY (low ACTH) has neither

adrenal-insufficiency.explanation: Aldosterone is RAAS-driven, so it is preserved in ACTH deficiency, and low ACTH cannot cause MSH-mediated pigmentation.

adrenal-insufficiency.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation of palmar creases/oral mucosa, hypotension”?
adrenal-insufficiency.explanation: Fatigue, weight loss, hyperpigmentation of palmar creases/oral mucosa, hypotension → Primary (Addison) — high ACTH/MSH.

adrenal-insufficiency.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hyponatremia + hyperkalemia + hypoglycemia”?
adrenal-insufficiency.explanation: Hyponatremia + hyperkalemia + hypoglycemia → Combined cortisol + aldosterone deficiency.

adrenal-insufficiency.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison & Crisis)”?
adrenal-insufficiency.explanation: Hypoglycemia is a common symptom in both conditions.

adrenal-insufficiency.stem: Which should you review before “Adrenal Insufficiency (Addison & Crisis)”?
adrenal-insufficiency.explanation: Understanding aldosterone's role is crucial for adrenal insufficiency.

congenital-adrenal-hyperplasia.stem: A newborn with ambiguous genitalia becomes hypotensive on day 5 with Na⁺ 122 and K⁺ 6.8. Markedly elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone confirms the diagnosis. Which enzyme is deficient?
congenital-adrenal-hyperplasia.explanation: 21-hydroxylase deficiency (CYP21A2) is the most common CAH: low cortisol and aldosterone (salt-wasting), androgen excess (virilization), and elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone.

congenital-adrenal-hyperplasia.stem: Regarding direction of androgens in 21-hydroxylase deficiency — which is correct?

options.text: An enzyme deficiency should lower all adrenal steroids including androgens
Cortisol and aldosterone fall, but androgens RISE — blocked precursors are shunted into the intact androgen pathway, causing virilization

congenital-adrenal-hyperplasia.explanation: The block is upstream of cortisol/aldosterone but the androgen branch is open, so it is over-fed.

congenital-adrenal-hyperplasia.stem: What best explains the finding: “Newborn girl with ambiguous genitalia + salt-wasting crisis”?
congenital-adrenal-hyperplasia.explanation: Newborn girl with ambiguous genitalia + salt-wasting crisis → Classic salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

congenital-adrenal-hyperplasia.stem: What best explains the finding: “Young child with precocious puberty and rapid growth then short stature”?
congenital-adrenal-hyperplasia.explanation: Young child with precocious puberty and rapid growth then short stature → Androgen excess → early epiphyseal fusion.

congenital-adrenal-hyperplasia.stem: Which should you review before “Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (Adrenogenital Syndrome)”?
congenital-adrenal-hyperplasia.explanation: Understanding cellular adaptations is essential for grasping adrenal hyperplasia mechanisms.

pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma.stem: A patient has recurrent episodes of severe headache, palpitations, sweating, and spikes of hypertension. Imaging shows an adrenal-medulla mass. Which laboratory finding confirms the diagnosis?

options.text: Failure of cortisol to suppress on dexamethasone

pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma.explanation: Pheochromocytoma secretes catecholamines; diagnosis rests on elevated plasma/urinary metanephrines and VMA. Biopsy is avoided, and α-blockade precedes β-blockade before resection.

pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma.stem: Regarding order of adrenergic blockade before surgery — which is correct?

options.text: Start a beta-blocker to control the tachycardia and hypertension
Give an alpha-blocker (phenoxybenzamine) FIRST; starting a beta-blocker alone leaves unopposed alpha vasoconstriction → hypertensive crisis

pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma.explanation: Blocking β2-mediated vasodilation while α is intact worsens vasoconstriction — a classic and dangerous sequencing error.

pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Episodic headache + palpitations + diaphoresis + paroxysmal hypertension”?
pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma.explanation: Episodic headache + palpitations + diaphoresis + paroxysmal hypertension → Catecholamine surges from a pheochromocytoma.

pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Zellballen nests + salt-and-pepper chromatin”?
pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma.explanation: Zellballen nests + salt-and-pepper chromatin → Chromaffin-cell tumor histology.

pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma.stem: Which should you review before “Pheochromocytoma & Paraganglioma”?
pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma.explanation: Understanding catecholamine synthesis is crucial for grasping pheochromocytoma pathology.

neuroblastoma.stem: An 18-month-old has a large abdominal mass crossing the midline, elevated urinary VMA and HVA, and biopsy showing small round blue cells forming Homer-Wright rosettes. The diagnosis is:
neuroblastoma.explanation: Neuroblastoma — the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood — is a neural-crest small round blue cell tumor with Homer-Wright rosettes and elevated VMA/HVA; MYCN amplification predicts poor prognosis.

neuroblastoma.stem: Regarding wilms tumor vs neuroblastoma — which is correct?

options.text: A child’s abdominal mass is a Wilms tumor
Neuroblastoma typically CROSSES the midline, elevates VMA/HVA, and shows Homer-Wright rosettes; Wilms tumor is intrarenal, usually does not cross midline, and does not raise catecholamines

neuroblastoma.explanation: The midline-crossing and catecholamine metabolites distinguish the sympathetic neuroblastoma from a renal Wilms tumor.

neuroblastoma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Infant with a firm abdominal mass crossing the midline”?
neuroblastoma.explanation: Infant with a firm abdominal mass crossing the midline → Adrenal/sympathetic neuroblastoma.

neuroblastoma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Homer-Wright rosettes; small round blue cells”?
neuroblastoma.explanation: Homer-Wright rosettes; small round blue cells → Neuroblastic differentiation.
Neuroblastoma arises from neural crest cells.

multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.stem: A 40-year-old man has a thyroidectomy showing medullary thyroid carcinoma, plus parathyroid hyperplasia. Which tumor should be excluded next, and what gene is implicated?
multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.explanation: Medullary thyroid carcinoma + parathyroid hyperplasia is MEN 2A (RET proto-oncogene); a pheochromocytoma must be excluded before surgery. Prolactinoma/insulinoma belong to MEN 1.

multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.stem: Regarding next tumor to look for after medullary thyroid ca + parathyroid disease — which is correct?

options.text: Order a pituitary MRI for a prolactinoma
This is MEN 2A (RET) — screen for PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA (plasma metanephrines) before any surgery; prolactinoma belongs to MEN 1

multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.explanation: Missing a coexisting pheochromocytoma risks a lethal intra-operative catecholamine crisis.

multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypercalcemia + gastrinoma + prolactinoma in one patient”?
multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.explanation: Hypercalcemia + gastrinoma + prolactinoma in one patient → MEN 1 (3 P’s).

multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.stem: What best explains the finding: “Medullary thyroid carcinoma + parathyroid hyperplasia”?
multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.explanation: Medullary thyroid carcinoma + parathyroid hyperplasia → MEN 2A → look for pheochromocytoma next.

multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.stem: Which should you review before “Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN)”?
multiple-endocrine-neoplasia.explanation: Familiarity with neoplasia terminology is crucial for discussing MEN.

cushing-diagnosis-workup.stem: A patient with Cushing syndrome has: 8 AM cortisol high, LDDST — not suppressed, HDDST — suppressed, ACTH — high. What is the source?
cushing-diagnosis-workup.explanation: High ACTH with suppression on high-dose (but not low-dose) dexamethasone indicates a pituitary ACTH adenoma — Cushing disease. Ectopic and adrenal causes fail to suppress on both; exogenous shows low ACTH and low cortisol.

cushing-diagnosis-workup.stem: Regarding interpreting the high-dose dexamethasone test — which is correct?

options.text: If cortisol suppresses at all, the patient does not have Cushing syndrome
Suppression on the HIGH-dose test points to a pituitary source (Cushing disease); ectopic and adrenal causes fail to suppress on both low and high doses

cushing-diagnosis-workup.explanation: Pituitary adenomas retain partial glucocorticoid feedback, so they suppress at high dose — that is the whole point of the HDDST.

cushing-diagnosis-workup.stem: What best explains the finding: “Loss of diurnal rhythm — elevated late-night salivary cortisol”?
cushing-diagnosis-workup.explanation: Loss of diurnal rhythm — elevated late-night salivary cortisol → Autonomous cortisol secretion.

cushing-diagnosis-workup.stem: What best explains the finding: “High ACTH, cortisol suppresses on HIGH-dose but not low-dose dex”?
cushing-diagnosis-workup.explanation: High ACTH, cortisol suppresses on HIGH-dose but not low-dose dex → Cushing disease (pituitary adenoma retains feedback).

cushing-diagnosis-workup.stem: Which should you review before “Cushing Syndrome: Diagnostic Workup”?
cushing-diagnosis-workup.explanation: Understanding cortisol regulation is essential for diagnosing Cushing syndrome.

cushing-management-steroid-withdrawal.stem: After successful transsphenoidal removal of an ACTH-secreting adenoma, what is the expected early postoperative state and its management?

options.text: Cortisol excess persists; give a steroidogenesis inhibitor
Transient cortisol deficiency; give hydrocortisone cover and taper as the HPA axis recovers
No hormonal change; no treatment needed

cushing-management-steroid-withdrawal.explanation: Removing the cortisol source leaves the chronically suppressed normal corticotrophs unable to respond, causing transient adrenal insufficiency; patients need perioperative hydrocortisone with a taper guided by recovering morning cortisol.

cushing-management-steroid-withdrawal.stem: Regarding stopping long-term glucocorticoids — which is correct?

options.text: The Cushing features are from the steroid, so just stop the drug
Taper gradually — chronic suppression atrophies the adrenals, and abrupt withdrawal precipitates an adrenal crisis; cover extra during illness/surgery
Successful removal of the cortisol source

cushing-management-steroid-withdrawal.explanation: The HPA axis needs weeks–months to recover; sudden withdrawal leaves the patient unable to mount a cortisol response.

cushing-management-steroid-withdrawal.stem: What best explains the finding: “9 AM cortisol <1.8 µg/dL after omitting hydrocortisone post-op”?

options.text: Recovered HPA axis — can stop steroids
Successful removal of the cortisol source

cushing-management-steroid-withdrawal.explanation: 9 AM cortisol <1.8 µg/dL after omitting hydrocortisone post-op → Successful removal of the cortisol source.

cushing-management-steroid-withdrawal.stem: What best explains the finding: “Shock/hypoglycemia after stopping long-term prednisolone”?

options.text: Successful removal of the cortisol source
Recovered HPA axis — can stop steroids

cushing-management-steroid-withdrawal.explanation: Shock/hypoglycemia after stopping long-term prednisolone → Adrenal crisis from HPA suppression.

cushing-management-steroid-withdrawal.stem: Which should you review before “Cushing Management & Steroid Withdrawal”?
cushing-management-steroid-withdrawal.explanation: Understanding cortisol's actions is essential for managing Cushing syndrome.

corticosteroid-pharmacology.stem: By what primary mechanism do glucocorticoids exert their broad anti-inflammatory effect?

options.text: Inhibition of phospholipase A₂, reducing both prostaglandins and leukotrienes

corticosteroid-pharmacology.explanation: Glucocorticoids act via intracellular receptors to inhibit phospholipase A₂ at the top of the arachidonic-acid cascade, suppressing both the COX (prostaglandin) and LOX (leukotriene) arms — a broader effect than NSAIDs, which block only COX.

corticosteroid-pharmacology.stem: Regarding anti-inflammatory site of steroids vs nsaids — which is correct?

options.text: Steroids and NSAIDs both just block cyclooxygenase
Glucocorticoids inhibit phospholipase A₂ (upstream), suppressing BOTH prostaglandins and leukotrienes; NSAIDs act downstream at COX only

corticosteroid-pharmacology.explanation: The upstream PLA₂ block explains the broader anti-inflammatory effect (and why leukotriene-driven asthma responds to steroids but not to NSAIDs).

corticosteroid-pharmacology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cushingoid features (moon face, striae, hyperglycemia) on chronic steroids”?
corticosteroid-pharmacology.explanation: Cushingoid features (moon face, striae, hyperglycemia) on chronic steroids → Iatrogenic glucocorticoid excess.

corticosteroid-pharmacology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Osteoporotic fracture in a long-term steroid user”?
corticosteroid-pharmacology.explanation: Osteoporotic fracture in a long-term steroid user → Osteoblast apoptosis + ↑bone resorption.

corticosteroid-pharmacology.stem: Which should you review before “Corticosteroid Pharmacology”?
corticosteroid-pharmacology.explanation: Understanding cortisol's actions is essential for grasping corticosteroid pharmacology.

corticosteroid-antagonists.stem: A patient with Cushing syndrome cannot undergo curative surgery. Which drug lowers cortisol by inhibiting adrenal steroidogenesis, and what is its key toxicity?
corticosteroid-antagonists.explanation: Ketoconazole inhibits steroidogenic enzymes to lower cortisol in Cushing syndrome; its notable toxicity is hepatotoxicity. Mifepristone blocks the receptor, and spironolactone is a mineralocorticoid antagonist.

corticosteroid-antagonists.stem: Regarding spironolactone adverse effects — which is correct?

options.text: A potassium-sparing diuretic only risks lowering potassium
Spironolactone causes HYPERkalemia (it blocks aldosterone) plus antiandrogen effects like gynecomastia; eplerenone is the more selective alternative
Antiandrogen effect of the mineralocorticoid antagonist

corticosteroid-antagonists.explanation: Blocking aldosterone spares potassium (retains it) → hyperkalemia, and cross-reactivity at sex-steroid receptors gives gynecomastia.

corticosteroid-antagonists.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ketoconazole/metyrapone used to lower cortisol in Cushing”?

options.text: Antiandrogen effect of the mineralocorticoid antagonist

corticosteroid-antagonists.explanation: Ketoconazole/metyrapone used to lower cortisol in Cushing → Steroidogenesis inhibition.

corticosteroid-antagonists.stem: What best explains the finding: “Gynecomastia developing on spironolactone”?

options.text: Antiandrogen effect of the mineralocorticoid antagonist

corticosteroid-antagonists.explanation: Gynecomastia developing on spironolactone → Antiandrogen effect of the mineralocorticoid antagonist.

corticosteroid-antagonists.stem: Which should you review before “Corticosteroid Antagonists”?
corticosteroid-antagonists.explanation: Knowledge of cortisol's actions aids in understanding the effects of antagonists.

hyperthyroidism-graves.stem: A 30-year-old woman has weight loss, palpitations, a diffuse goiter, exophthalmos, and pretibial non-pitting edema. TSH is low and radioiodine uptake is diffusely increased. What is the mechanism?

options.text: Autoantibody against the TSH receptor (Graves disease)

hyperthyroidism-graves.explanation: Graves disease is caused by stimulating anti-TSH-receptor antibodies, producing diffuse goiter, ophthalmopathy, dermopathy, and diffusely increased radioiodine uptake with suppressed TSH.

hyperthyroidism-graves.stem: Regarding distinguishing hyperthyroid causes — which is correct?

options.text: All hyperthyroidism has increased radioiodine uptake
Thyroiditis (and exogenous thyroid hormone) causes hyperthyroidism with LOW uptake — preformed hormone leaks out; Graves and toxic adenoma have high uptake

hyperthyroidism-graves.explanation: The RAIU pattern separates gland-driven overproduction (high uptake) from hormone leakage/exogenous sources (low uptake).

hyperthyroidism-graves.stem: What best explains the finding: “Exophthalmos + diffuse goiter + pretibial myxedema”?

options.text: Sympathetic overstimulation of the superior tarsal muscle

hyperthyroidism-graves.explanation: Exophthalmos + diffuse goiter + pretibial myxedema → Graves triad (TSH-receptor antibody).

hyperthyroidism-graves.stem: What best explains the finding: “New atrial fibrillation with weight loss and tremor”?

options.text: Sympathetic overstimulation of the superior tarsal muscle

hyperthyroidism-graves.explanation: New atrial fibrillation with weight loss and tremor → Thyrotoxic cardiac effect.

hyperthyroidism-graves.stem: Which should you review before “Hyperthyroidism & Graves Disease”?
hyperthyroidism-graves.explanation: Graves disease is an autoimmune condition.

hypothyroidism-goiter.stem: A euthyroid patient from an iodine-deficient region has a diffusely enlarged thyroid without nodules. What is the mechanism of the enlargement?

options.text: Compensatory TSH rise causing follicular hypertrophy and hyperplasia

hypothyroidism-goiter.explanation: Iodine deficiency impairs hormone synthesis; the compensatory rise in TSH drives follicular hypertrophy and hyperplasia (diffuse nontoxic/colloid goiter), usually keeping the patient euthyroid.

hypothyroidism-goiter.stem: Regarding thyroid status in a simple goiter — which is correct?

options.text: A big goiter must mean the patient is hypothyroid
Most simple/colloid goiters are EUTHYROID — the compensatory TSH-driven hyperplasia maintains adequate hormone output; hypothyroidism appears only if the underlying defect is severe

hypothyroidism-goiter.explanation: The goiter itself is the compensation, so gland size does not equal functional status.

hypothyroidism-goiter.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, slow mentation”?
hypothyroidism-goiter.explanation: Cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, slow mentation → Myxedema (adult hypothyroidism).

hypothyroidism-goiter.stem: What best explains the finding: “Diffusely enlarged thyroid in an iodine-poor region, euthyroid”?
hypothyroidism-goiter.explanation: Diffusely enlarged thyroid in an iodine-poor region, euthyroid → Simple (colloid) goiter — compensatory TSH.

hypothyroidism-goiter.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Hypothyroidism & Goiter”?
hypothyroidism-goiter.explanation: Both conditions involve endocrine glands but are not directly related.

hypothyroidism-goiter.stem: Which should you review before “Hypothyroidism & Goiter”?
hypothyroidism-goiter.explanation: Understanding thyroid histology is essential for grasping goiter pathology.

thyroiditis.stem: A 50-year-old woman has painless goiter, fatigue, and hypothyroidism; biopsy shows dense lymphocytic infiltrate with germinal centers and Hürthle cell change. Which antibody is most characteristic?
thyroiditis.explanation: Hashimoto thyroiditis — the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas — shows lymphocytic infiltrate with germinal centers and Hürthle cells, with anti-TPO (and anti-thyroglobulin) antibodies.

thyroiditis.stem: Regarding painful vs painless thyroiditis — which is correct?

options.text: All thyroiditis is painless and autoimmune
Subacute granulomatous (De Quervain) thyroiditis is PAINFUL and post-viral with granulomas; Hashimoto and the postpartum/painless variant are painless and autoimmune

thyroiditis.explanation: Pain plus a preceding viral illness and granulomatous histology is the De Quervain signature, distinct from the painless autoimmune types.

thyroiditis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Painless goiter + hypothyroidism + anti-TPO antibodies”?
thyroiditis.explanation: Painless goiter + hypothyroidism + anti-TPO antibodies → Hashimoto thyroiditis.

thyroiditis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Tender/painful thyroid after a viral URI”?
thyroiditis.explanation: Tender/painful thyroid after a viral URI → Subacute granulomatous (De Quervain).
Basic anatomy knowledge may help in understanding thyroiditis presentations.

thyroid-neoplasms.stem: A thyroid nodule biopsy shows nests of cells with an amyloid-containing stroma; serum calcitonin is elevated. From which cell does this tumor arise, and what syndrome should be considered?
thyroid-neoplasms.explanation: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, secretes calcitonin (deposited as amyloid), and may be part of MEN 2 (RET proto-oncogene).

thyroid-neoplasms.stem: Regarding why fna cannot diagnose follicular carcinoma — which is correct?

options.text: FNA can distinguish follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma
It cannot — the diagnosis of follicular carcinoma requires seeing CAPSULAR or VASCULAR invasion, which needs the whole capsule (surgical excision), not a cytology sample

thyroid-neoplasms.explanation: Papillary carcinoma is defined by nuclear features (visible on FNA), but follicular carcinoma is defined by invasion, which FNA cannot assess.

thyroid-neoplasms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cold thyroid nodule with Orphan-Annie nuclei + psammoma bodies”?
thyroid-neoplasms.explanation: Cold thyroid nodule with Orphan-Annie nuclei + psammoma bodies → Papillary carcinoma.

thyroid-neoplasms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thyroid tumor with amyloid stroma + high calcitonin”?
thyroid-neoplasms.explanation: Thyroid tumor with amyloid stroma + high calcitonin → Medullary carcinoma (C cells).

thyroid-neoplasms.stem: Which should you review before “Thyroid Neoplasms”?

hyperparathyroidism.stem: A patient has hypercalcemia, kidney stones, bone pain, and constipation. Serum PTH is elevated. What is the most likely underlying lesion?

options.text: Squamous cell lung carcinoma secreting PTHrP

hyperparathyroidism.explanation: Hypercalcemia with an elevated PTH and the "stones, bones, groans, and psychic moans" picture is primary hyperparathyroidism, most often a solitary parathyroid adenoma. Malignancy (PTHrP) would suppress PTH.

hyperparathyroidism.stem: Regarding hypercalcemia of malignancy vs primary hyperparathyroidism — which is correct?

options.text: Any hypercalcemia means overactive parathyroid glands
Malignancy causes hypercalcemia via PTHrP with SUPPRESSED (low) PTH; primary hyperparathyroidism has HIGH PTH — you must measure PTH to tell them apart

hyperparathyroidism.explanation: PTHrP mimics PTH at the receptor but is a different molecule, so measured PTH is low — the opposite of primary disease.

hyperparathyroidism.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypercalcemia + high PTH + kidney stones + bone pain”?
hyperparathyroidism.explanation: Hypercalcemia + high PTH + kidney stones + bone pain → Primary hyperparathyroidism (adenoma).

hyperparathyroidism.stem: What best explains the finding: “Brown tumor / osteitis fibrosa cystica on imaging”?
hyperparathyroidism.explanation: Brown tumor / osteitis fibrosa cystica on imaging → PTH-driven bone resorption.

hyperparathyroidism.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Hyperparathyroidism”?
hyperparathyroidism.explanation: Calcitonin is directly involved in calcium homeostasis.

hypoparathyroidism.stem: Two days after a total thyroidectomy, a patient develops perioral numbness and carpopedal spasm; tapping the facial nerve produces a twitch. What is the underlying disturbance?
hypoparathyroidism.explanation: Inadvertent parathyroid injury during thyroidectomy causes hypoparathyroidism and hypocalcemia, producing neuromuscular irritability — perioral numbness, carpopedal spasm, and a positive Chvostek sign.

hypoparathyroidism.stem: Regarding most common cause of hypoparathyroidism — which is correct?

options.text: It must be an autoimmune or genetic disease
The most common cause is SURGICAL — accidental removal or devascularization of the parathyroids during thyroid/neck surgery

hypoparathyroidism.explanation: Postoperative hypocalcemia after thyroidectomy is a classic and common scenario; autoimmune (APS1) and congenital (DiGeorge) causes are much rarer.

hypoparathyroidism.stem: What best explains the finding: “Perioral numbness, carpopedal spasm, positive Chvostek/Trousseau”?
hypoparathyroidism.explanation: Perioral numbness, carpopedal spasm, positive Chvostek/Trousseau → Hypocalcemic neuromuscular irritability.

hypoparathyroidism.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypocalcemia after recent thyroidectomy”?
hypoparathyroidism.explanation: Hypocalcemia after recent thyroidectomy → Surgical hypoparathyroidism.

type1-diabetes-pathogenesis.stem: A child has two islet autoantibodies but normal fasting and post-load glucose. Which stage of type 1 diabetes is present?
type1-diabetes-pathogenesis.explanation: Stage 1 T1DM is islet autoimmunity with normoglycemia. Stage 2 adds dysglycemia; stage 3 is overt clinical diabetes.

type1-diabetes-pathogenesis.stem: Regarding staging presymptomatic t1dm — which is correct?

options.text: Autoantibodies alone mean the patient already has clinical diabetes
Multiple islet autoantibodies with normal glucose define stage 1 T1DM; overt symptomatic hyperglycemia is stage 3
Glucosuria with osmotic diuresis plus cellular fuel starvation
Absolute insulin deficiency permits unopposed lipolysis and ketogenesis

type1-diabetes-pathogenesis.explanation: Autoimmunity begins before dysglycemia and symptoms, so antibody status and glucose status must be read separately.

type1-diabetes-pathogenesis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, and weight loss”?

options.text: Absolute insulin deficiency permits unopposed lipolysis and ketogenesis
Glucosuria with osmotic diuresis plus cellular fuel starvation

type1-diabetes-pathogenesis.explanation: Polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, and weight loss → Glucosuria with osmotic diuresis plus cellular fuel starvation.

type1-diabetes-pathogenesis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ketonemia or DKA at first presentation”?

options.text: Absolute insulin deficiency permits unopposed lipolysis and ketogenesis
Glucosuria with osmotic diuresis plus cellular fuel starvation

type1-diabetes-pathogenesis.explanation: Ketonemia or DKA at first presentation → Absolute insulin deficiency permits unopposed lipolysis and ketogenesis.

type1-diabetes-pathogenesis.stem: Which should you review before “Type 1 Diabetes: Autoimmune Beta-cell Failure”?
type1-diabetes-pathogenesis.explanation: Understanding islet hormones is crucial for grasping beta-cell function.

insulin-resistance-type2-diabetes.stem: Which event most directly explains the transition from compensated insulin resistance to overt type 2 diabetes?
insulin-resistance-type2-diabetes.explanation: Compensatory hyperinsulinemia initially offsets insulin resistance. Overt T2DM appears as beta-cell reserve progressively fails.

insulin-resistance-type2-diabetes.stem: Regarding natural history of t2dm — which is correct?

options.text: Hyperglycemia begins as soon as insulin resistance develops
Beta cells initially compensate with hyperinsulinemia; glucose rises when compensation becomes inadequate
Hyperinsulinemia stimulates growth-factor receptors in skin

insulin-resistance-type2-diabetes.explanation: Insulin resistance precedes clinical diabetes, often by years.

insulin-resistance-type2-diabetes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Central obesity with high triglycerides, hypertension, and low HDL”?

options.text: Hyperinsulinemia stimulates growth-factor receptors in skin
Long compensatory phase before beta-cell reserve fails

insulin-resistance-type2-diabetes.explanation: Central obesity with high triglycerides, hypertension, and low HDL → Insulin resistance / metabolic syndrome.

insulin-resistance-type2-diabetes.stem: Which should you review before “Insulin Resistance & Type 2 Diabetes”?
insulin-resistance-type2-diabetes.explanation: Understanding the differences in diabetes pathogenesis is crucial for grasping T2DM.

diabetes-complications-overview.stem: Which set contains only chronic microvascular complications of diabetes?
diabetes-complications-overview.explanation: Retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy are the classic microvascular triad. MI, stroke, and PAD are macrovascular.

diabetes-complications-overview.stem: Regarding classifying diabetic complications — which is correct?

options.text: Peripheral arterial disease is a microvascular complication because it affects the distal limb
Peripheral arterial disease is macrovascular atherosclerosis; neuropathy is the microvascular contributor to the diabetic foot
Peripheral neuropathy removes protective pain sensation

diabetes-complications-overview.explanation: Classify by the injured vessel/pathway, not by the anatomic size of the affected body part.

diabetes-complications-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Reduced monofilament sensation with a painless foot wound”?

options.text: Peripheral neuropathy removes protective pain sensation

diabetes-complications-overview.explanation: Reduced monofilament sensation with a painless foot wound → Peripheral neuropathy removes protective pain sensation.

options.text: Peripheral neuropathy removes protective pain sensation

thyroid-hormone-replacement.stem: A patient starts levothyroxine today. When should thyroid function usually be rechecked to guide dose adjustment?
thyroid-hormone-replacement.explanation: The 6-8 day half-life of T4 means several weeks are needed to approach steady state; dose response is usually assessed after about 6-8 weeks.

thyroid-hormone-replacement.stem: Regarding timing a levothyroxine dose adjustment — which is correct?

options.text: Increase the dose after a few days if TSH remains high
Wait about 6-8 weeks after a dose change before interpreting the new steady-state thyroid function
Food, iron, antacid, or sequestrant interference may reduce absorption

thyroid-hormone-replacement.explanation: Levothyroxine has a long half-life, so early testing can provoke unnecessary dose stacking and over-replacement.

thyroid-hormone-replacement.stem: What best explains the finding: “Palpitations or atrial fibrillation after dose escalation”?

options.text: Food, iron, antacid, or sequestrant interference may reduce absorption

thyroid-hormone-replacement.explanation: Palpitations or atrial fibrillation after dose escalation → Excess thyroid-hormone replacement.

thyroid-hormone-replacement.stem: What best explains the finding: “Persistently high TSH despite reported adherence”?

options.text: Food, iron, antacid, or sequestrant interference may reduce absorption

thyroid-hormone-replacement.explanation: Persistently high TSH despite reported adherence → Food, iron, antacid, or sequestrant interference may reduce absorption.

thyroid-hormone-replacement.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Thyroid Hormone Replacement”?
thyroid-hormone-replacement.explanation: Thyroid hormone replacement is a key treatment in thyroid disease management.

thyroid-hormone-replacement.stem: Which should you review before “Thyroid Hormone Replacement”?
thyroid-hormone-replacement.explanation: Understanding drug absorption and metabolism is crucial for levothyroxine dosing.

thioamides-antithyroid-drugs.stem: Which action distinguishes high-dose PTU from methimazole and helps explain its use in thyroid storm?

options.text: Destruction of thyroid tissue by beta radiation

thioamides-antithyroid-drugs.explanation: Both thioamides inhibit thyroid peroxidase, but high-dose PTU also inhibits peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion, useful when rapid T3 reduction is needed.

thioamides-antithyroid-drugs.stem: Regarding why thioamides have a delayed onset — which is correct?

options.text: They block synthesis but not release, so preformed thyroid hormone must first be depleted

thioamides-antithyroid-drugs.explanation: Both drugs are absorbed rapidly; the delay is physiological storage, not pharmacokinetic absorption.

thioamides-antithyroid-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fever and sore throat while taking a thioamide”?

options.text: PTU is preferred during this limited period

thioamides-antithyroid-drugs.explanation: Fever and sore throat while taking a thioamide → Possible agranulocytosis.

thioamides-antithyroid-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Severe hepatitis on antithyroid therapy”?

options.text: PTU is preferred during this limited period

thioamides-antithyroid-drugs.explanation: Severe hepatitis on antithyroid therapy → Characteristic major toxicity of PTU.

iodide-radioiodine-thyrotoxicosis.stem: Which is the correct sequence for thioamide and iodide during treatment of thyroid storm?
iodide-radioiodine-thyrotoxicosis.explanation: Block new hormone synthesis with a thioamide before giving iodide to block release; otherwise the iodide load may be used as substrate.

iodide-radioiodine-thyrotoxicosis.stem: Regarding drug sequence in thyroid storm — which is correct?

options.text: Give iodide first because it acts fastest
Give a thioamide first, then iodide after synthesis is blocked
Synthesis must be blocked before the iodide load

iodide-radioiodine-thyrotoxicosis.explanation: The fast drug is not automatically the first drug: iodide loading before synthesis blockade can worsen hormone production.

iodide-radioiodine-thyrotoxicosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thioamide followed by iodide in thyroid storm”?

options.text: Expected common consequence of I-131 ablation
Synthesis must be blocked before the iodide load

iodide-radioiodine-thyrotoxicosis.explanation: Thioamide followed by iodide in thyroid storm → Synthesis must be blocked before the iodide load.

iodide-radioiodine-thyrotoxicosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Late hypothyroidism after definitive hyperthyroidism therapy”?

options.text: Expected common consequence of I-131 ablation
Synthesis must be blocked before the iodide load

iodide-radioiodine-thyrotoxicosis.explanation: Late hypothyroidism after definitive hyperthyroidism therapy → Expected common consequence of I-131 ablation.

iodide-radioiodine-thyrotoxicosis.stem: Which should you review before “Iodide, Radioiodine & Thyrotoxicosis Adjuncts”?
iodide-radioiodine-thyrotoxicosis.explanation: Understanding thyroid hormone synthesis is essential for grasping iodide's role.

severe-hypercalcemia-therapy.stem: Which drug lowers calcium within hours but loses effectiveness after 2-3 days because of tachyphylaxis?
severe-hypercalcemia-therapy.explanation: Calcitonin is the rapid bridge therapy for severe hypercalcemia, but receptor tachyphylaxis limits its useful duration.

severe-hypercalcemia-therapy.stem: Regarding initial therapy in dehydrated severe hypercalcemia — which is correct?

options.text: Start furosemide before fluids to force calcium excretion
Restore intravascular volume with normal saline first; use a loop only in a well-hydrated patient when indicated
Renal concentrating defect with volume loss

severe-hypercalcemia-therapy.explanation: Hypercalcemic patients are often volume depleted, and premature diuresis worsens renal perfusion and calcium clearance.

severe-hypercalcemia-therapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dehydration and polyuria in severe hypercalcemia”?

options.text: Renal concentrating defect with volume loss

severe-hypercalcemia-therapy.explanation: Dehydration and polyuria in severe hypercalcemia → Renal concentrating defect with volume loss.

severe-hypercalcemia-therapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Calcium falls rapidly then rebounds after calcitonin”?

options.text: Renal concentrating defect with volume loss

severe-hypercalcemia-therapy.explanation: Calcium falls rapidly then rebounds after calcitonin → Short action and tachyphylaxis.

severe-hypercalcemia-therapy.stem: Which should you review before “Severe Hypercalcemia: Drug Therapy”?
severe-hypercalcemia-therapy.explanation: Calcitonin's role in mineral homeostasis is crucial for understanding its therapeutic use.

secondary-hyperparathyroidism-ckd.stem: Which laboratory pattern best fits CKD-associated secondary hyperparathyroidism?

options.text: High PTH, high calcium, low phosphate
High PTH, low/normal calcium, high/normal phosphate
Low PTH, low calcium, high phosphate
Low PTH, high calcium, low phosphate

secondary-hyperparathyroidism-ckd.explanation: CKD retains phosphate and reduces calcitriol, keeping calcium low/normal and stimulating secondary PTH elevation.

secondary-hyperparathyroidism-ckd.stem: Regarding primary versus secondary hyperparathyroidism — which is correct?

options.text: A high PTH level always means primary hyperparathyroidism
In CKD, high PTH with low/normal calcium and high/normal phosphate indicates secondary hyperparathyroidism
Appropriate secondary response to mineral imbalance
CKD-mineral and bone disorder with sustained PTH excess

secondary-hyperparathyroidism-ckd.explanation: PTH must be interpreted with calcium, phosphate, and renal function.

secondary-hyperparathyroidism-ckd.stem: What best explains the finding: “High PTH with low/normal calcium in CKD”?

options.text: CKD-mineral and bone disorder with sustained PTH excess
Vitamin D increases intestinal calcium absorption
Appropriate secondary response to mineral imbalance

secondary-hyperparathyroidism-ckd.explanation: High PTH with low/normal calcium in CKD → Appropriate secondary response to mineral imbalance.

secondary-hyperparathyroidism-ckd.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypercalcemia after calcitriol escalation”?

options.text: Vitamin D increases intestinal calcium absorption
Appropriate secondary response to mineral imbalance
CKD-mineral and bone disorder with sustained PTH excess

secondary-hyperparathyroidism-ckd.explanation: Hypercalcemia after calcitriol escalation → Vitamin D increases intestinal calcium absorption.

secondary-hyperparathyroidism-ckd.stem: Which should you review before “Secondary Hyperparathyroidism in CKD”?
secondary-hyperparathyroidism-ckd.explanation: The kidney's endocrine functions are crucial for understanding secondary hyperparathyroidism.

hypoparathyroidism-treatment.stem: A patient develops carpopedal spasm and stridor after thyroid surgery. Calcium is low and phosphate is high. What is the immediate treatment?
hypoparathyroidism-treatment.explanation: Postoperative hypoparathyroidism can cause severe hypocalcemic tetany and laryngospasm; slow IV calcium gluconate is the immediate therapy.

hypoparathyroidism-treatment.stem: Regarding emergency treatment of hypocalcemic tetany — which is correct?

options.text: Start oral calcium and wait for absorption
Give slow IV calcium gluconate for immediate control of severe symptomatic hypocalcemia
Carpal spasm after inflating a BP cuff above systolic pressure

hypoparathyroidism-treatment.explanation: Airway compromise, seizure, and arrhythmia make tetany an intravenous-calcium emergency.

hypoparathyroidism-treatment.stem: What best explains the finding: “Trousseau sign”?

options.text: Carpal spasm after inflating a BP cuff above systolic pressure

hypoparathyroidism-treatment.explanation: Trousseau sign → Carpal spasm after inflating a BP cuff above systolic pressure.

hypoparathyroidism-treatment.stem: What best explains the finding: “Laryngospasm, stridor, or seizure”?

options.text: Carpal spasm after inflating a BP cuff above systolic pressure

hypoparathyroidism-treatment.explanation: Laryngospasm, stridor, or seizure → Severe hypocalcemic tetany.

hypoparathyroidism-treatment.stem: Which should you review before “Hypoparathyroidism: Recognition & Treatment”?
hypoparathyroidism-treatment.explanation: Understanding hypoparathyroidism is essential for recognizing its treatment.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: An asymptomatic adult has a fasting plasma glucose of 120 mg/dL. How should this be classified?
diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.explanation: FPG 100-125 mg/dL is impaired fasting glucose/prediabetes; diabetes begins at 126 mg/dL and generally requires confirmation if asymptomatic.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: Regarding confirming diabetes — which is correct?

options.text: Any single abnormal screening value permanently establishes diabetes
Confirm an abnormal result in an asymptomatic patient unless hyperglycemia is unequivocal; symptomatic random glucose >=200 or crisis is diagnostic
Classic symptoms plus random glucose >=200 establish diabetes
Impaired fasting glucose / prediabetes, not diabetes

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.explanation: Biologic and preanalytic variation matter when the clinical picture is not definitive.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: What best explains the finding: “Polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss with random glucose 220 mg/dL”?

options.text: Impaired fasting glucose / prediabetes, not diabetes
One abnormal one-step threshold is enough for GDM
Classic symptoms plus random glucose >=200 establish diabetes

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.explanation: Polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss with random glucose 220 mg/dL → Classic symptoms plus random glucose >=200 establish diabetes.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: What best explains the finding: “FPG 120 mg/dL without symptoms”?

options.text: Impaired fasting glucose / prediabetes, not diabetes
Classic symptoms plus random glucose >=200 establish diabetes
One abnormal one-step threshold is enough for GDM

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.explanation: FPG 120 mg/dL without symptoms → Impaired fasting glucose / prediabetes, not diabetes.

diabetes-diagnostic-criteria-gdm.stem: Which should you review before “Diabetes Diagnosis, Screening & GDM”?

glucose-specimens-monitoring.stem: Why can glucose be falsely low when whole blood remains at room temperature before plasma separation?

options.text: Blood cells continue consuming glucose by glycolysis
The kidney clears glucose from the tube

glucose-specimens-monitoring.explanation: RBCs and WBCs remain metabolically active in vitro and consume glucose; prompt separation or an antiglycolytic tube limits the fall.

glucose-specimens-monitoring.stem: Regarding using a portable glucose meter for diagnosis — which is correct?

options.text: A home meter value alone can establish diabetes
Portable meters guide monitoring; diagnosis requires accepted laboratory plasma glucose or standardized HbA1c testing
Ongoing leukocyte/RBC glycolysis in the tube

glucose-specimens-monitoring.explanation: Point-of-care meter error is too variable for formal diagnosis and screening.

glucose-specimens-monitoring.stem: What best explains the finding: “Unexpectedly low laboratory glucose after delayed separation”?

options.text: Ongoing leukocyte/RBC glycolysis in the tube

glucose-specimens-monitoring.explanation: Unexpectedly low laboratory glucose after delayed separation → Ongoing leukocyte/RBC glycolysis in the tube.

glucose-specimens-monitoring.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypoglycemic symptoms despite a normal CGM reading during rapid change”?

options.text: Ongoing leukocyte/RBC glycolysis in the tube

glucose-specimens-monitoring.explanation: Hypoglycemic symptoms despite a normal CGM reading during rapid change → Interstitial sensor lag.

glucose-specimens-monitoring.stem: Which should you review before “Glucose Specimens, SMBG & CGM”?
glucose-specimens-monitoring.explanation: Understanding glucose transport is essential for glucose monitoring.

hba1c-fructosamine.stem: Which marker best reflects glycemic control over the preceding 2-3 weeks when HbA1c is unreliable because of hemolysis?
hba1c-fructosamine.explanation: Fructosamine reflects glycated serum proteins, mainly albumin, over about 2-3 weeks and is independent of RBC survival.

hba1c-fructosamine.stem: Regarding interpreting hba1c in hemolysis — which is correct?

options.text: A normal HbA1c always proves average glucose is normal
Hemolysis can falsely lower HbA1c because RBCs are removed before accumulating their expected glycation
Shortened RBC survival reduces time available for glycation
Altered/older RBC population can falsely elevate HbA1c

hba1c-fructosamine.explanation: HbA1c measures glycemia filtered through erythrocyte lifespan.

hba1c-fructosamine.stem: What best explains the finding: “Low HbA1c despite frequent high glucose in hemolytic anemia”?

options.text: Altered/older RBC population can falsely elevate HbA1c
Fructosamine has the shorter integration window
Shortened RBC survival reduces time available for glycation

hba1c-fructosamine.explanation: Low HbA1c despite frequent high glucose in hemolytic anemia → Shortened RBC survival reduces time available for glycation.

hba1c-fructosamine.stem: What best explains the finding: “High HbA1c in iron-deficiency anemia”?

options.text: Altered/older RBC population can falsely elevate HbA1c
Shortened RBC survival reduces time available for glycation
Fructosamine has the shorter integration window

hba1c-fructosamine.explanation: High HbA1c in iron-deficiency anemia → Altered/older RBC population can falsely elevate HbA1c.

hba1c-fructosamine.stem: Which should you review before “HbA1c & Fructosamine”?
hba1c-fructosamine.explanation: Foundational knowledge on HbA1c and its role in diabetes.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: Why can a urine nitroprusside ketone test underestimate DKA severity?

options.text: It is positive only when pH is normal
It detects albumin rather than ketones

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: Nitroprusside detects mainly acetoacetate. BHB is the dominant ketone in DKA, so direct blood BHB is preferred.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: Regarding using urine ketones to follow dka — which is correct?

options.text: A urine nitroprusside strip quantifies the major circulating ketone
It detects acetoacetate but not BHB; use blood BHB with acid-base data for diagnosis and monitoring

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: BHB predominates in DKA, so urine strips can understate the active ketone burden.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: What best explains the finding: “Kussmaul breathing, abdominal pain, fruity breath”?

options.text: Possible transient albuminuria requiring repeat confirmation

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: Kussmaul breathing, abdominal pain, fruity breath → Ketotic high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: What best explains the finding: “Profound dehydration and altered consciousness without marked ketones”?

options.text: Possible transient albuminuria requiring repeat confirmation

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: Profound dehydration and altered consciousness without marked ketones → HHS with hyperosmolar neuronal dehydration.

diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.stem: Which should you review before “Ketones, Albuminuria & Metabolic Complications”?
diabetes-ketone-albuminuria-tests.explanation: Understanding glycemic markers is essential for interpreting ketone levels in emergencies.

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: A patient with diabetes has glucose 180 mg/dL, BHB 4.5 mmol/L, pH 7.20, and bicarbonate 12 mmol/L. What is the best diagnosis?

options.text: No diabetic emergency because glucose is below 200

dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: The patient has diabetes, significant ketonemia, and metabolic acidosis. DKA can occur with glucose below 200 mg/dL.

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: Regarding recognizing euglycemic dka — which is correct?

options.text: Glucose below 200 mg/dL rules out DKA
Ketosis plus metabolic acidosis can be DKA even with glucose below 200 mg/dL
Respiratory compensation plus ketones in DKA

dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: The diagnosis depends on all three components, and euglycemic DKA is a recognized presentation.

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: What best explains the finding: “Kussmaul breathing with fruity breath and abdominal pain”?

options.text: Acidosis and insulin lack shift K out of cells while urine loses K
Respiratory compensation plus ketones in DKA

dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: Kussmaul breathing with fruity breath and abdominal pain → Respiratory compensation plus ketones in DKA.

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: What best explains the finding: “Profound dehydration with delirium or focal neurologic signs”?

options.text: Respiratory compensation plus ketones in DKA
Acidosis and insulin lack shift K out of cells while urine loses K

dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: Profound dehydration with delirium or focal neurologic signs → Hyperosmolar neuronal dehydration in HHS.

dka-hhs-recognition.stem: Which should you review before “DKA & HHS: Recognition and Diagnosis”?
dka-hhs-recognition.explanation: Understanding glycemic markers is essential for diagnosing DKA and HHS.

dka-hhs-management.stem: A patient with DKA has serum potassium 3.1 mmol/L. What is the next treatment priority?

options.text: Give routine bicarbonate regardless of pH

dka-hhs-management.explanation: With K <3.5 mmol/L, potassium must be replaced before insulin because insulin will shift K intracellularly and can provoke life-threatening hypokalemia.

dka-hhs-management.stem: Regarding starting insulin in dka with hypokalemia — which is correct?

options.text: Insulin is always the first infusion because it reverses DKA
If K is <3.5 mmol/L, replace potassium and delay insulin until K is safely above 3.5
Glycemia corrects before DKA resolves; insulin must continue with dextrose
Rapid intracellular K shift causing treatment-induced hypokalemia

dka-hhs-management.explanation: Insulin can abruptly shift potassium into cells and cause fatal arrhythmia or respiratory-muscle weakness.

dka-hhs-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “Falling glucose but persistent BHB/acidosis”?

options.text: Rapid intracellular K shift causing treatment-induced hypokalemia
Fluid strategy must be reduced/monitored in cardiac compromise
Glycemia corrects before DKA resolves; insulin must continue with dextrose

dka-hhs-management.explanation: Falling glucose but persistent BHB/acidosis → Glycemia corrects before DKA resolves; insulin must continue with dextrose.

dka-hhs-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “Weakness or arrhythmia after insulin starts”?

options.text: Rapid intracellular K shift causing treatment-induced hypokalemia
Glycemia corrects before DKA resolves; insulin must continue with dextrose
Fluid strategy must be reduced/monitored in cardiac compromise

dka-hhs-management.explanation: Weakness or arrhythmia after insulin starts → Rapid intracellular K shift causing treatment-induced hypokalemia.

dka-hhs-management.stem: Which is a clinical application of “DKA & HHS: Fluids, Insulin & Potassium”?
dka-hhs-management.explanation: Clinical application of DKA management principles.

dka-hhs-management.stem: Which should you review before “DKA & HHS: Fluids, Insulin & Potassium”?
dka-hhs-management.explanation: Understanding fluid compartments is essential for managing DKA.

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.stem: A thyrotoxic patient has fever, agitation, HR 145/min, and pulmonary edema. What is the correct early antithyroid sequence?

options.text: Thioamide, then iodide at least 1 hour later
Iodide, then thioamide the next day

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.explanation: In thyroid storm, block new synthesis with a thioamide before giving iodide to acutely block hormone release.

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.stem: Regarding diagnosing and sequencing therapy in thyroid storm — which is correct?

options.text: Wait for a very high free T4, then give iodide before the thioamide
Treat on clinical multiorgan decompensation; give thioamide first and iodide at least 1 hour later
Multiorgan decompensation distinguishes storm from uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.explanation: Hormone level does not grade severity, and iodide must follow synthesis blockade.

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fever, HR >=130, agitation/delirium, heart failure, or GI/hepatic dysfunction”?

options.text: Severity is clinical and tissue-response driven, not concentration driven
Multiorgan decompensation distinguishes storm from uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.explanation: Fever, HR >=130, agitation/delirium, heart failure, or GI/hepatic dysfunction → Multiorgan decompensation distinguishes storm from uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis.

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “Severe storm despite only modest FT4/FT3 elevation”?

options.text: Severity is clinical and tissue-response driven, not concentration driven
Multiorgan decompensation distinguishes storm from uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.explanation: Severe storm despite only modest FT4/FT3 elevation → Severity is clinical and tissue-response driven, not concentration driven.

thyroid-storm-recognition-management.stem: Which should you review before “Thyroid Storm: Recognition & Management”?

insulin-therapy-regimens.stem: Which insulin component primarily covers fasting and between-meal glucose production?
insulin-therapy-regimens.explanation: Basal insulin restrains background hepatic glucose output; prandial insulin covers carbohydrate absorbed from meals.

insulin-therapy-regimens.stem: Regarding role of basal versus prandial insulin — which is correct?

options.text: Basal insulin should be increased to correct every post-meal spike
Basal insulin controls fasting/inter-meal glucose; prandial insulin targets meal excursions
Insulin-associated lipohypertrophy/lipoatrophy from poor site rotation

insulin-therapy-regimens.explanation: Using basal insulin to chase meals causes overnight or fasting hypoglycemia.

insulin-therapy-regimens.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, then confusion”?

options.text: Insulin-associated lipohypertrophy/lipoatrophy from poor site rotation
Marked insulin deficiency requiring insulin initiation

insulin-therapy-regimens.explanation: Sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, then confusion → Adrenergic followed by neuroglycopenic hypoglycemia.

insulin-therapy-regimens.stem: What best explains the finding: “Weight loss, ketosis, and glucose >=300 mg/dL in T2DM”?

options.text: Marked insulin deficiency requiring insulin initiation
Insulin-associated lipohypertrophy/lipoatrophy from poor site rotation

insulin-therapy-regimens.explanation: Weight loss, ketosis, and glucose >=300 mg/dL in T2DM → Marked insulin deficiency requiring insulin initiation.

insulin-therapy-regimens.stem: Which should you review before “Insulin Therapy & Regimens”?
insulin-therapy-regimens.explanation: Understanding ketogenesis is crucial for managing insulin therapy.

insulin-secretagogues.stem: Sulfonylureas increase insulin secretion by which beta-cell action?
insulin-secretagogues.explanation: KATP-channel closure depolarizes the beta cell, opens voltage-gated calcium channels, and triggers insulin exocytosis.

insulin-secretagogues.stem: Regarding why secretagogues do not treat t1dm — which is correct?

options.text: Any drug that increases insulin can replace injected insulin
Secretagogues can only release insulin from functioning beta cells; T1DM has absolute beta-cell failure
Accumulation of a secretagogue, especially glyburide
Increased endogenous insulin from a sulfonylurea/meglitinide

insulin-secretagogues.explanation: The mechanism depends on a cellular reserve that T1DM lacks.

insulin-secretagogues.stem: What best explains the finding: “Prolonged hypoglycemia in renal impairment”?

options.text: Increased endogenous insulin from a sulfonylurea/meglitinide
There are too few functioning beta cells to stimulate
Accumulation of a secretagogue, especially glyburide

insulin-secretagogues.explanation: Prolonged hypoglycemia in renal impairment → Accumulation of a secretagogue, especially glyburide.

insulin-secretagogues.stem: What best explains the finding: “No useful response in T1DM”?

options.text: There are too few functioning beta cells to stimulate
Accumulation of a secretagogue, especially glyburide
Increased endogenous insulin from a sulfonylurea/meglitinide

insulin-secretagogues.explanation: No useful response in T1DM → There are too few functioning beta cells to stimulate.

insulin-secretagogues.stem: Which should you review before “Insulin Secretagogues”?
insulin-secretagogues.explanation: Knowledge of insulin synthesis and secretion is critical for understanding how secretagogues work.

incretin-based-therapy.stem: Which diabetes drug class increases glucose-dependent insulin secretion, slows gastric emptying, and commonly causes weight loss?
incretin-based-therapy.explanation: GLP-1 receptor agonists combine glucose-dependent islet effects with satiety and delayed gastric emptying, producing weight loss.

incretin-based-therapy.stem: Regarding glp-1 ra versus dpp-4 inhibitor — which is correct?

options.text: Both incretin classes produce the same weight loss
GLP-1 receptor agonists produce meaningful weight loss; DPP-4 inhibitors are generally weight neutral

incretin-based-therapy.explanation: Direct pharmacologic receptor agonism is stronger than preservation of endogenous GLP-1.

incretin-based-therapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nausea with marked weight loss after a weekly injection”?

options.text: DPP-4 inhibitor rather than GLP-1 receptor agonist

incretin-based-therapy.explanation: Nausea with marked weight loss after a weekly injection → GLP-1 receptor agonist effect.

incretin-based-therapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Severe persistent abdominal pain”?

options.text: DPP-4 inhibitor rather than GLP-1 receptor agonist

incretin-based-therapy.explanation: Severe persistent abdominal pain → Possible pancreatitis on incretin-based therapy.

incretin-based-therapy.stem: Which should you review before “Incretin-based Therapy”?
incretin-based-therapy.explanation: Understanding insulin secretion is crucial for grasping incretin effects.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: A patient with T2DM and symptomatic heart failure should generally avoid which insulin-sensitizing class?
metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: TZDs activate PPAR-gamma but cause sodium/fluid retention, edema, weight gain, and can worsen heart failure.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: Regarding choosing a sensitizer in heart failure — which is correct?

options.text: Pioglitazone is safe because it does not directly depress contractility
Avoid TZDs in heart failure because fluid retention can precipitate or worsen congestion

metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: The relevant toxicity is volume retention, not negative inotropy.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: What best explains the finding: “Neuropathy with macrocytic anemia on long-term metformin”?
metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: Neuropathy with macrocytic anemia on long-term metformin → Vitamin B12 deficiency.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: What best explains the finding: “Edema and heart-failure worsening after pioglitazone”?
metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: Edema and heart-failure worsening after pioglitazone → TZD-associated fluid retention.

metformin-thiazolidinediones.stem: Which should you review before “Insulin Sensitizers: Metformin & TZDs”?
metformin-thiazolidinediones.explanation: Gluconeogenesis is directly affected by metformin's mechanism.

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.stem: A patient with T2DM and heart failure needs another glucose-lowering drug. Which class is specifically prioritized in the lecture algorithm?
sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors are prioritized for T2DM with heart failure. TZDs can worsen fluid retention and are a poor fit.

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.stem: Regarding selecting therapy when a major comorbidity is present — which is correct?

options.text: Always choose the drug with the largest HbA1c reduction
In heart failure, CKD, or ASCVD, prioritize agents with outcome benefit even when another class lowers HbA1c more
Glucosuria plus osmotic diuresis from SGLT2 inhibition
Alpha-glucosidase inhibition leaves carbohydrate for colonic fermentation

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.explanation: Modern diabetes pharmacotherapy treats cardiorenal risk as well as glucose.

sglt2-alpha-glucosidase-selection.stem: What best explains the finding: “Genital infection with polyuria and dizziness after a -gliflozin”?

options.text: Alpha-glucosidase inhibition leaves carbohydrate for colonic fermentation
Comorbidity pattern favoring an SGLT2 inhibitor
Glucosuria plus osmotic diuresis from SGLT2 inhibition
