inguinal-canal-hernias.explanation: Groin bulge that descends into the scrotum, controlled by pressure over the deep ring → Indirect inguinal hernia (lateral to epigastric).

inguinal-canal-hernias.stem: What best explains the finding: “Groin bulge medial to the epigastric vessels through the posterior wall”?
inguinal-canal-hernias.explanation: Groin bulge medial to the epigastric vessels through the posterior wall → Direct inguinal hernia (Hesselbach triangle).

inguinal-canal-hernias.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Inguinal Canal & Hernias”?
Which should you review before “Inguinal Canal & Hernias”?
inguinal-canal-hernias.explanation: Understanding the abdominal wall anatomy is essential for grasping inguinal canal structures.

peritoneum-stomach.stem: The entire arterial supply of the stomach is derived from branches of which vessel?
peritoneum-stomach.explanation: The stomach (a foregut derivative) is supplied entirely by branches of the celiac trunk: left/right gastric arteries (lesser curvature), left/right gastro-omental arteries (greater curvature), and short gastric arteries (fundus).

peritoneum-stomach.stem: Regarding duodenum peritoneal status — which is correct?

options.text: Only the 1st (superior) part is intraperitoneal; the 2nd–4th parts are RETROperitoneal (SAD PUCKER)
Lowest point of the supine peritoneal cavity
Foregut (celiac) visceral afferents refer to the epigastrium

peritoneum-stomach.explanation: The duodenal cap (1st part) has mesentery, but the rest becomes fixed retroperitoneally — relevant to perforation and imaging.

peritoneum-stomach.stem: What best explains the finding: “Free fluid/pus collecting in the hepatorenal recess (Morison pouch)”?

options.text: Foregut (celiac) visceral afferents refer to the epigastrium
Lowest point of the supine peritoneal cavity

peritoneum-stomach.explanation: Free fluid/pus collecting in the hepatorenal recess (Morison pouch) → Lowest point of the supine peritoneal cavity.

peritoneum-stomach.stem: What best explains the finding: “Epigastric pain from a gastric ulcer”?

options.text: Foregut (celiac) visceral afferents refer to the epigastrium
Lowest point of the supine peritoneal cavity

peritoneum-stomach.explanation: Epigastric pain from a gastric ulcer → Foregut (celiac) visceral afferents refer to the epigastrium.

peritoneum-stomach.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Peritoneum & Stomach”?
peritoneum-stomach.explanation: Links to the vascular supply and anatomical relations in the abdominal cavity.

posterior-abdominal-wall-diaphragm.stem: At which vertebral level does the esophagus (with the vagal trunks) pass through the diaphragm?
posterior-abdominal-wall-diaphragm.explanation: The esophageal hiatus is at T10 (esophagus + anterior/posterior vagal trunks). The caval opening is at T8 and the aortic hiatus at T12.

posterior-abdominal-wall-diaphragm.stem: Regarding level of the caval opening — which is correct?

options.text: The IVC passes through the diaphragm at T10 with the esophagus
The IVC (caval opening) is at T8; the ESOPHAGUS passes at T10 and the AORTA at T12
Psoas irritation on the posterior wall

posterior-abdominal-wall-diaphragm.explanation: Each aperture has its own vertebral level — mixing T8/T10/T12 is the classic error.

posterior-abdominal-wall-diaphragm.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pulsatile expansile central abdominal mass + back pain in an older man”?

options.text: Psoas irritation on the posterior wall

posterior-abdominal-wall-diaphragm.explanation: Pulsatile expansile central abdominal mass + back pain in an older man → Abdominal aortic aneurysm (infrarenal).

posterior-abdominal-wall-diaphragm.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Posterior Abdominal Wall, Aorta & Diaphragm”?

options.text: Pudendal Neurovasculature, Erectile Tissues & External Genitalia

posterior-abdominal-wall-diaphragm.explanation: Understanding the diaphragm's role in respiration is crucial for pelvic floor function.

lumbar-plexus.stem: A patient has weak knee extension and a lost patellar reflex after a psoas abscess. Which nerve is affected?
lumbar-plexus.explanation: The femoral nerve (L2–L4) supplies the quadriceps (knee extension) and carries the afferent/efferent limbs of the patellar reflex; because it runs within/adjacent to psoas, a psoas abscess can compress it.

lumbar-plexus.stem: Regarding femoral vs obturator function — which is correct?

options.text: The femoral nerve supplies the thigh adductors
The FEMORAL nerve supplies knee EXTENSORS (quadriceps); the OBTURATOR nerve supplies the thigh ADDUCTORS

lumbar-plexus.explanation: Femoral (anterior compartment, lateral to psoas) = extension; obturator (medial compartment, medial to psoas) = adduction.

lumbar-plexus.stem: What best explains the finding: “Weak knee extension + absent patellar reflex”?
lumbar-plexus.explanation: Weak knee extension + absent patellar reflex → Femoral nerve (L2–L4) lesion.

lumbar-plexus.stem: What best explains the finding: “Weak thigh adduction”?
lumbar-plexus.explanation: Weak thigh adduction → Obturator nerve (L2–L4) lesion.

kidney-ureter-anatomy.stem: A patient with severe loin-to-groin pain has a ureteric stone. At which of the following normal constrictions are stones LEAST likely to be trapped?

options.text: Mid-ureter over the psoas muscle (no constriction)
Where the ureter crosses the pelvic brim/iliac vessels

kidney-ureter-anatomy.explanation: Stones lodge at the three normal constrictions — the ureteropelvic junction, the pelvic brim (crossing the iliac vessels), and the ureterovesical junction (narrowest). The mid-ureter over psoas is not a constriction.

kidney-ureter-anatomy.stem: Regarding renal segmental arteries — which is correct?

options.text: The renal segmental arteries anastomose freely, so blocking one is harmless
Segmental renal arteries are END arteries with NO anastomoses — occluding one causes a segmental infarct of that region

kidney-ureter-anatomy.explanation: The lack of collateral flow is why renal artery embolism produces wedge-shaped infarcts.

kidney-ureter-anatomy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, patient writhing”?
kidney-ureter-anatomy.explanation: Severe colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, patient writhing → Ureteric stone (renal colic, T11–L2).

kidney-ureter-anatomy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Stone lodged where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels”?
kidney-ureter-anatomy.explanation: Stone lodged where the ureter crosses the iliac vessels → Pelvic-brim constriction.

kidney-ureter-anatomy.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Kidney & Ureter”?
kidney-ureter-anatomy.explanation: Understanding the anatomy helps in diagnosing and managing urinary stones.

kidney-ureter-anatomy.stem: Which should you review before “Kidney & Ureter”?
kidney-ureter-anatomy.explanation: Understanding the anatomy of the posterior abdominal wall is essential for kidney and ureter anatomy.

bladder-urethra.stem: Which autonomic input contracts the detrusor muscle to produce voiding?
bladder-urethra.explanation: Parasympathetic fibres from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) contract the detrusor and relax the internal urethral sphincter to void; sympathetic input (T11–L2) promotes storage.

bladder-urethra.stem: Regarding autonomic control of the bladder — which is correct?

options.text: PARASYMPATHETIC (S2–S4, pelvic splanchnics) contracts the detrusor to VOID; sympathetic promotes STORAGE (relaxes detrusor, closes the internal sphincter)

bladder-urethra.explanation: "Parasympathetic = Pee, Sympathetic = Store" — a frequently reversed exam point.

bladder-urethra.stem: What best explains the finding: “Recurrent UTIs in a woman”?
bladder-urethra.explanation: Recurrent UTIs in a woman → Short female urethra.

bladder-urethra.stem: What best explains the finding: “Urinary retention + high-riding prostate after pelvic fracture”?
bladder-urethra.explanation: Urinary retention + high-riding prostate after pelvic fracture → Membranous urethral rupture.

bladder-urethra.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Urinary Bladder & Urethra”?

options.text: Histology of the Ureter, Bladder & Urethra

bladder-urethra.explanation: Histological understanding is crucial for bladder and urethra pathology.

bladder-urethra.stem: Which should you review before “Urinary Bladder & Urethra”?
bladder-urethra.explanation: Understanding kidney and ureter anatomy is essential for bladder and urethra function.

small-large-intestine.stem: Which set of features is characteristic of the LARGE intestine and distinguishes it from the small intestine?

options.text: Plicae circulares, villi, and Peyer patches
Teniae coli, haustra, and omental appendices
Long vasa recta and few arcades

small-large-intestine.explanation: The large intestine is recognized by teniae coli (three longitudinal muscle bands), haustra (sacculations), and omental appendices (fatty tags); the small intestine has plicae circulares, villi, and (in the ileum) Peyer patches.

small-large-intestine.stem: Regarding sensation above vs below the dentate line — which is correct?

options.text: Internal hemorrhoids (above the dentate line) are very painful
ABOVE the dentate line is visceral/INSENSATE (internal hemorrhoids are typically painless); BELOW it is somatic (pudendal) and PAINFUL (external hemorrhoids/fissures hurt)
Somatic (pudendal) innervation of the lower anal canal

small-large-intestine.explanation: The dentate line marks the switch from visceral (autonomic, insensate) to somatic (pain-sensitive) innervation.

small-large-intestine.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pain starting periumbilical then localizing to McBurney's point (RLQ)”?

options.text: Somatic (pudendal) innervation of the lower anal canal

small-large-intestine.explanation: Pain starting periumbilical then localizing to McBurney's point (RLQ) → Appendicitis (midgut referral → local peritoneal irritation).

small-large-intestine.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bright-red bleeding + pain from a lesion below the dentate line”?

options.text: Somatic (pudendal) innervation of the lower anal canal

small-large-intestine.explanation: Bright-red bleeding + pain from a lesion below the dentate line → Somatic (pudendal) innervation of the lower anal canal.

small-large-intestine.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Small & Large Intestine”?
small-large-intestine.explanation: Vasculitis can affect the blood supply to the intestines, leading to clinical implications.

liver-biliary-pancreas.stem: During a laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the surgeon dissects the hepatocystic (Calot) triangle to safely identify and ligate which artery?
liver-biliary-pancreas.explanation: The cystic artery (usually from the right hepatic artery) lies within the hepatocystic (Calot) triangle — bounded by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and inferior liver edge — which is dissected to avoid bile-duct injury.

liver-biliary-pancreas.stem: Regarding ligamentum teres vs ligamentum venosum — which is correct?

options.text: The ligamentum teres is the remnant of the ductus venosus
The ligamentum TERES (round ligament, in the falciform ligament) is the remnant of the left UMBILICAL VEIN; the ligamentum VENOSUM is the remnant of the ductus venosus

liver-biliary-pancreas.explanation: Teres = umbilical vein (recanalizes in portal hypertension → caput medusae); venosum = ductus venosus.

liver-biliary-pancreas.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bile-duct injury during cholecystectomy”?

options.text: Recanalized paraumbilical veins along the ligamentum teres

liver-biliary-pancreas.explanation: Bile-duct injury during cholecystectomy → Misidentified structures in Calot triangle.

liver-biliary-pancreas.stem: What best explains the finding: “Obstructive jaundice from a stone/tumor at the ampulla”?

options.text: Recanalized paraumbilical veins along the ligamentum teres

liver-biliary-pancreas.explanation: Obstructive jaundice from a stone/tumor at the ampulla → Blockage at the hepatopancreatic ampulla.

liver-biliary-pancreas.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Liver, Biliary Tract & Pancreas”?
liver-biliary-pancreas.explanation: Clinical applications regarding liver and gallbladder diseases are directly linked to this module.

liver-biliary-pancreas.stem: Which should you review before “Liver, Biliary Tract & Pancreas”?
liver-biliary-pancreas.explanation: Understanding the liver's blood supply is essential for grasping its anatomy and function.

gi-blood-supply-portal-system.stem: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies which segment of the gut, and where is its visceral pain typically referred?

options.text: Hindgut (distal 1/3 transverse colon to upper rectum); suprapubic region

gi-blood-supply-portal-system.explanation: The IMA supplies the hindgut (distal third of the transverse colon to the upper rectum); its visceral afferents refer pain to the suprapubic (hypogastric) region.

gi-blood-supply-portal-system.stem: Regarding referred pain of early appendicitis — which is correct?

options.text: Appendicitis pain starts in the right lower quadrant
It classically starts PERIUMBILICALLY (midgut visceral referral, SMA territory) and only later localizes to the RLQ when the parietal peritoneum is irritated

gi-blood-supply-portal-system.explanation: Midgut structures refer visceral pain to the periumbilical region before somatic (parietal) pain localizes it.

gi-blood-supply-portal-system.stem: What best explains the finding: “Periumbilical pain that migrates to the RLQ”?
gi-blood-supply-portal-system.explanation: Periumbilical pain that migrates to the RLQ → Midgut (SMA) referral → local peritoneal irritation (appendicitis).

gi-blood-supply-portal-system.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hematemesis from esophageal varices”?
gi-blood-supply-portal-system.explanation: Hematemesis from esophageal varices → Left gastric ↔ azygos portosystemic anastomosis.

gi-blood-supply-portal-system.stem: Which is a clinical application of “GI Blood Supply & Portal System”?
gi-blood-supply-portal-system.explanation: Liver lobules are directly involved in the hepatic blood supply.

gi-blood-supply-portal-system.stem: Which should you review before “GI Blood Supply & Portal System”?
gi-blood-supply-portal-system.explanation: The liver's blood supply is integral to its function and pathology.

lower-limb-bones-hip-joint.stem: Why does an intracapsular femoral neck fracture in an elderly patient carry a high risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head?

options.text: It disrupts the artery of the ligamentum teres, the main adult supply
It disrupts the retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery, the dominant supply
The femoral head has no arterial supply

lower-limb-bones-hip-joint.explanation: The femoral head is supplied mainly by retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery running along the neck; an intracapsular neck fracture tears these vessels, risking avascular necrosis.

lower-limb-bones-hip-joint.stem: Regarding blood supply of the femoral head — which is correct?

options.text: The artery of the ligamentum teres is the main supply to the femoral head in adults
In adults the MEDIAL CIRCUMFLEX FEMORAL artery (via retinacular vessels) is the dominant supply; the ligamentum teres artery is minor — hence a neck fracture risks avascular necrosis

lower-limb-bones-hip-joint.explanation: The retinacular branches run along the neck, so an intracapsular fracture cuts off the head's main blood supply.

lower-limb-bones-hip-joint.stem: What best explains the finding: “Elderly fall: leg shortened + externally rotated, unable to weight-bear”?

options.text: Posterior hip dislocation (sciatic nerve at risk)

lower-limb-bones-hip-joint.explanation: Elderly fall: leg shortened + externally rotated, unable to weight-bear → Femoral neck fracture.

lower-limb-bones-hip-joint.stem: What best explains the finding: “AVN of the femoral head after an intracapsular fracture”?

options.text: Posterior hip dislocation (sciatic nerve at risk)

lower-limb-bones-hip-joint.explanation: AVN of the femoral head after an intracapsular fracture → Disrupted medial circumflex femoral supply.

lower-limb-bones-hip-joint.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Lower Limb Bones & Hip Joint”?

options.text: MSK Embryology: Limb Development, Ossification & Joints

lower-limb-bones-hip-joint.explanation: Embryological development of limb joints provides insight into hip joint formation.

lower-limb-bones-hip-joint.stem: Which should you review before “Lower Limb Bones & Hip Joint”?
lower-limb-bones-hip-joint.explanation: Understanding the pectoral girdle aids in comprehending limb mechanics.

femoral-triangle-anterior-thigh.stem: Listed from lateral to medial, what are the contents of the femoral triangle?

options.text: Femoral Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space (canal), Lymphatics

femoral-triangle-anterior-thigh.explanation: From lateral to medial the femoral triangle contains the femoral Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space (femoral canal), and Lymphatics ("NAVEL"). The femoral nerve lies outside the femoral sheath.

femoral-triangle-anterior-thigh.stem: Regarding femoral vs inguinal hernia location — which is correct?

options.text: A femoral hernia lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle
A FEMORAL hernia is BELOW and LATERAL to the pubic tubercle (through the femoral canal); an INGUINAL hernia is above and medial to it

femoral-triangle-anterior-thigh.explanation: The pubic tubercle is the reference: femoral hernias emerge below the inguinal ligament through the narrow femoral ring, which is why they strangulate readily.

femoral-triangle-anterior-thigh.stem: What best explains the finding: “Groin lump BELOW & lateral to the pubic tubercle, often strangulating”?
femoral-triangle-anterior-thigh.explanation: Groin lump BELOW & lateral to the pubic tubercle, often strangulating → Femoral hernia (femoral canal).

femoral-triangle-anterior-thigh.stem: What best explains the finding: “Weak knee extension + absent patellar reflex”?
femoral-triangle-anterior-thigh.explanation: Weak knee extension + absent patellar reflex → Femoral nerve lesion (quadriceps).

femoral-triangle-anterior-thigh.stem: Which should you review before “Femoral Triangle & Anterior Thigh”?
femoral-triangle-anterior-thigh.explanation: Understanding the femoral triangle requires knowledge of the hip joint and lower limb bones.

medial-thigh-adductors.stem: The femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery as it passes through which structure?
medial-thigh-adductors.explanation: The femoral vessels pass from the adductor canal through the adductor hiatus (a gap in adductor magnus) to enter the popliteal fossa, where the femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery.

medial-thigh-adductors.stem: Regarding innervation of adductor magnus — which is correct?

options.text: Adductor magnus is supplied entirely by the obturator nerve
It has DUAL innervation: the adductor part by the obturator nerve and the hamstring (ischiocondylar) part by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve

medial-thigh-adductors.explanation: Its hamstring part behaves like the posterior-thigh muscles (hip extension), so it shares their tibial nerve supply.

medial-thigh-adductors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Weak thigh adduction + medial-thigh numbness”?
medial-thigh-adductors.explanation: Weak thigh adduction + medial-thigh numbness → Obturator nerve lesion.

medial-thigh-adductors.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Medial Thigh: Adductors & Obturator Nerve”?
medial-thigh-adductors.explanation: Obturator nerve injury can be relevant in surgical contexts like aortic aneurysm repair.

medial-thigh-adductors.stem: Which should you review before “Medial Thigh: Adductors & Obturator Nerve”?
medial-thigh-adductors.explanation: Understanding the hip joint is essential for grasping the function of adductors.

gluteal-region-nerves.stem: A patient with a superior gluteal nerve injury stands on the affected leg. What is observed?

options.text: The pelvis drops on the same side as the injury
The pelvis drops on the opposite (unsupported) side (positive Trendelenburg)

gluteal-region-nerves.explanation: The superior gluteal nerve supplies the hip abductors (gluteus medius/minimus, TFL); their weakness means the pelvis is not held level and drops on the opposite, unsupported side — a positive Trendelenburg sign.

gluteal-region-nerves.stem: Regarding side the pelvis drops in trendelenburg — which is correct?

options.text: In a positive Trendelenburg the pelvis drops on the same (affected) side
The pelvis drops on the OPPOSITE (unsupported) side — the weak abductors on the stance (affected) leg cannot hold the pelvis level

gluteal-region-nerves.explanation: Hip abductors act on the stance side to keep the contralateral pelvis up; their weakness lets the swing-side pelvis sag.

gluteal-region-nerves.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on the affected leg”?
gluteal-region-nerves.explanation: Pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on the affected leg → Superior gluteal nerve (abductor) palsy — Trendelenburg.

gluteal-region-nerves.stem: What best explains the finding: “Waddling gait”?

posterior-thigh-sciatic.stem: Which nerve supplies the three "true" hamstring muscles (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, long head of biceps femoris)?

options.text: Common fibular division of the sciatic nerve
Tibial division of the sciatic nerve

posterior-thigh-sciatic.explanation: The hamstrings are supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve; only the short head of biceps femoris is supplied by the common fibular division.

posterior-thigh-sciatic.stem: Regarding which sciatic division is more often injured — which is correct?

options.text: The tibial division is the part usually damaged in the leg
The COMMON FIBULAR (peroneal) division is more commonly injured because it wraps superficially around the neck of the fibula → foot drop

posterior-thigh-sciatic.explanation: Its exposed position at the fibular neck makes it vulnerable to fractures, casts, and compression.

posterior-thigh-sciatic.stem: What best explains the finding: “Foot drop after a fibular-neck injury or tight cast”?
posterior-thigh-sciatic.explanation: Foot drop after a fibular-neck injury or tight cast → Common fibular (peroneal) nerve palsy.

posterior-thigh-sciatic.stem: What best explains the finding: “Weak knee flexion + hip extension + sensory loss below the knee”?
posterior-thigh-sciatic.explanation: Weak knee flexion + hip extension + sensory loss below the knee → Complete sciatic nerve lesion.

popliteal-fossa.stem: In the popliteal fossa, which structure lies deepest (against the joint capsule) and is therefore most at risk in a knee dislocation?
popliteal-fossa.explanation: The popliteal artery is the deepest content, lying against the knee-joint capsule; its tethered deep position makes it vulnerable to injury in knee dislocations and supracondylar femoral fractures.

popliteal-fossa.stem: Regarding depth of the popliteal artery — which is correct?

options.text: The popliteal artery is the most superficial structure in the fossa, so it is easy to feel
The popliteal artery is the DEEPEST structure (against the joint capsule) and is hard to palpate; the tibial nerve is most superficial

popliteal-fossa.explanation: Its deep, tethered position explains both the difficulty palpating it and its vulnerability in knee dislocation.

popliteal-fossa.stem: What best explains the finding: “Absent distal pulses after a knee dislocation”?
popliteal-fossa.explanation: Absent distal pulses after a knee dislocation → Popliteal artery injury (deepest, tethered).

popliteal-fossa.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pulsatile mass behind the knee”?
popliteal-fossa.explanation: Pulsatile mass behind the knee → Popliteal artery aneurysm.

popliteal-fossa.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Popliteal Fossa”?
popliteal-fossa.explanation: Understanding vascular anatomy can aid in recognizing complications related to cardiovascular conditions.

popliteal-fossa.stem: Which should you review before “Popliteal Fossa”?
popliteal-fossa.explanation: Understanding nerve pathways is crucial for comprehending the popliteal fossa.

leg-compartments.stem: A fibular-neck fracture causes weakness of both dorsiflexion and eversion with foot drop. Which nerve is injured?
leg-compartments.explanation: The common fibular nerve wraps around the fibular neck and divides into the deep (dorsiflexors) and superficial (evertors) branches; injuring it there weakens both dorsiflexion and eversion, causing foot drop.

leg-compartments.stem: Regarding earliest sign of compartment syndrome — which is correct?

options.text: Compartment syndrome is diagnosed by a loss of the distal pulse
Pulselessness is a LATE sign — the earliest is severe PAIN out of proportion, worse on passive stretch of the compartment muscles; act before pulses disappear

leg-compartments.explanation: Waiting for pulselessness means irreversible muscle/nerve ischemia — fasciotomy should be done on clinical suspicion.

leg-compartments.stem: What best explains the finding: “Foot drop + high-stepping gait after a fibular-neck injury”?
leg-compartments.explanation: Foot drop + high-stepping gait after a fibular-neck injury → Common fibular (peroneal) nerve palsy.

leg-compartments.stem: What best explains the finding: “Severe pain worse on passive stretch, tense compartment”?
leg-compartments.explanation: Severe pain worse on passive stretch, tense compartment → Acute compartment syndrome.

leg-compartments.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Compartments of the Leg”?
leg-compartments.explanation: While not directly related, understanding compartment syndrome may aid in recognizing complications in pediatric cases.

ankle-foot-bones-arches.stem: A player "rolls" the ankle inward and has swelling over the lateral ankle. Which ligament is most likely injured?
ankle-foot-bones-arches.explanation: An inversion injury most commonly sprains the lateral ligament complex, and the anterior talofibular ligament is the weakest/most frequently torn; the medial deltoid ligament is strong and rarely injured.

ankle-foot-bones-arches.stem: Regarding which ankle ligament is most commonly sprained — which is correct?

options.text: The deltoid (medial) ligament is the one usually torn in ankle sprains
The LATERAL ligament — especially the anterior talofibular ligament — is most commonly sprained in an INVERSION injury; the strong deltoid (medial) ligament is rarely torn
Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction (acquired pes planus)

ankle-foot-bones-arches.explanation: Most ankle injuries are inversion, stressing the weaker lateral ligaments; forced eversion tends to avulse the medial malleolus rather than tear the deltoid.

ankle-foot-bones-arches.stem: What best explains the finding: “Lateral ankle swelling after "rolling" (inverting) the ankle”?

options.text: Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction (acquired pes planus)

ankle-foot-bones-arches.explanation: Lateral ankle swelling after "rolling" (inverting) the ankle → Anterior talofibular ligament sprain.

ankle-foot-bones-arches.stem: What best explains the finding: “Progressive flat foot with a "too many toes" sign”?

options.text: Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction (acquired pes planus)

ankle-foot-bones-arches.explanation: Progressive flat foot with a "too many toes" sign → Posterior tibial tendon dysfunction (acquired pes planus).

sole-of-foot.stem: Which structures pass through the tarsal tunnel behind the medial malleolus, in order from anterior to posterior?

options.text: Tibialis anterior, EHL, dorsalis pedis artery, deep fibular nerve
Tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, posterior tibial artery + tibial nerve, flexor hallucis longus
Peroneus longus, peroneus brevis, sural nerve
Great saphenous vein and saphenous nerve only

sole-of-foot.explanation: The tarsal tunnel transmits (anterior→posterior) "Tom, Dick, ANd Harry": Tibialis posterior tendon, flexor Digitorum longus, posterior tibial Artery and tibial Nerve, and flexor Hallucis longus, under the flexor retinaculum.

sole-of-foot.stem: Regarding which nerve supplies most sole intrinsics — which is correct?

options.text: The medial plantar nerve supplies most of the intrinsic foot muscles
The LATERAL plantar nerve supplies MOST intrinsics (like the ulnar in the hand); the medial plantar nerve supplies only the "LAFF" muscles

sole-of-foot.explanation: The medial/lateral plantar nerves mirror the hand's median/ulnar split — the lateral (ulnar-equivalent) does the bulk of the intrinsic work.

sole-of-foot.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sharp heel pain on the first steps in the morning”?
sole-of-foot.explanation: Sharp heel pain on the first steps in the morning → Plantar fasciitis (calcaneal origin).

sole-of-foot.stem: What best explains the finding: “Burning sole paresthesia + weak toe flexors after ankle trauma”?
sole-of-foot.explanation: Burning sole paresthesia + weak toe flexors after ankle trauma → Tarsal tunnel syndrome (tibial nerve).

sole-of-foot.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Sole of the Foot”?
sole-of-foot.explanation: Links the neurovascular supply of the sole to clinical implications in the pelvis.

sole-of-foot.stem: Which should you review before “Sole of the Foot”?
sole-of-foot.explanation: Understanding the anatomy of the foot is essential for grasping the sole's structure.

history-ancient-to-renaissance.stem: Which figure is credited with shifting medicine toward natural (rather than supernatural) causes and codifying medical ethics?
history-ancient-to-renaissance.explanation: Hippocrates is the "Father of Medicine": natural causes of disease, careful observation/prognosis, and the Hippocratic Oath. Galen systematised humoral theory; Vesalius founded anatomy; Harvey proved circulation.

history-ancient-to-renaissance.stem: Galen’s anatomical errors persisted for over a thousand years mainly because:

options.text: He performed thousands of accurate human dissections
His work was lost until the Renaissance
He extrapolated from animal dissection and his authority went unchallenged
The microscope had not been invented

history-ancient-to-renaissance.explanation: Human dissection was banned, so Galen dissected animals and extrapolated. His authority became dogma until Vesalius returned to direct human dissection — a lesson in authority vs evidence.

history-ancient-to-renaissance.stem: Regarding who founded modern anatomy? — which is correct?

options.text: Galen — he wrote the anatomy textbooks
Vesalius (1543) founded modern anatomy by dissecting humans and correcting Galen’s animal-based errors
First codified medical ethics — "do no harm"

history-ancient-to-renaissance.explanation: Galen’s prestige made his errors persist; the Renaissance advance was returning to *direct human observation*.

history-ancient-to-renaissance.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hippocratic Oath”?

options.text: Human dissection banned → errors persisted as dogma
First codified medical ethics — "do no harm"
Direct human dissection + experiment overturned Galen

history-ancient-to-renaissance.explanation: Hippocratic Oath → First codified medical ethics — "do no harm".

history-ancient-to-renaissance.stem: What best explains the finding: “4 humors (blood, phlegm, yellow + black bile)”?

options.text: First codified medical ethics — "do no harm"
Human dissection banned → errors persisted as dogma
Direct human dissection + experiment overturned Galen

history-ancient-to-renaissance.explanation: 4 humors (blood, phlegm, yellow + black bile) → Balance = health; imbalance = disease.

history-germ-theory-modern-medicine.stem: Koch’s postulates are best described as:

options.text: Criteria to establish that a specific microorganism causes a specific disease

history-germ-theory-modern-medicine.explanation: Koch’s postulates provide the causal logic linking a microbe to a disease (isolate from diseased hosts, culture, reproduce disease, re-isolate). Ethics = Belmont/Nuremberg; sterilisation = Lister.

history-germ-theory-modern-medicine.stem: Which development marks the birth of modern Evidence-Based Medicine?

options.text: Discovery of the DNA double helix

history-germ-theory-modern-medicine.explanation: Bradford Hill’s 1948 streptomycin trial is the archetypal modern RCT — randomisation to control confounding — and anchors the evidence hierarchy that defines EBM.

history-germ-theory-modern-medicine.stem: Regarding first antibiotic vs first vaccine — which is correct?

options.text: Fleming discovered penicillin (first antibiotic, 1928); Jenner made the first vaccine (smallpox, 1796)
Criteria to prove a specific microbe causes a specific disease

history-germ-theory-modern-medicine.explanation: Vaccine = prevention by immunity (Jenner). Antibiotic = kills established bacteria (Fleming). Don’t conflate them.

history-germ-theory-modern-medicine.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cowpox protects against smallpox”?

options.text: Criteria to prove a specific microbe causes a specific disease

history-germ-theory-modern-medicine.explanation: Cowpox protects against smallpox → Cross-immunity → Jenner’s first vaccine (1796).

history-germ-theory-modern-medicine.stem: What best explains the finding: “Koch’s postulates”?

options.text: Criteria to prove a specific microbe causes a specific disease

history-germ-theory-modern-medicine.explanation: Koch’s postulates → Criteria to prove a specific microbe causes a specific disease.

research-question-finer-pico.stem: In the FINER criteria, the "E" stands for:
research-question-finer-pico.explanation: FINER = Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant. "Ethical" means an ethics committee would approve the study.

research-question-finer-pico.stem: In the question "Among adults with hypertension, does telmisartan vs amlodipine reduce stroke at 3 years?", "amlodipine" corresponds to which PICO element?
research-question-finer-pico.explanation: Telmisartan is the Intervention; amlodipine is the Comparison (comparator/control); stroke is the Outcome; 3 years is the Time frame; adults with hypertension is the Population.

research-question-finer-pico.stem: Regarding finer vs pico — which is correct?

options.text: FINER and PICO are interchangeable checklists
FINER judges whether a question is *worth asking*; PICO *structures* the question into components
Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant — is the question worth doing?
Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Time — how to build the question

research-question-finer-pico.explanation: One is a quality filter, the other is a construction template. Exams pair "Novel/Feasible" with FINER and "Comparison/Outcome" with PICO.

options.text: Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Time — how to build the question
It is a descriptive question (prevalence/incidence), not analytic
Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant — is the question worth doing?

research-question-finer-pico.explanation: FINER → Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant — is the question worth doing?.

options.text: Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Time — how to build the question
Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant — is the question worth doing?
It is a descriptive question (prevalence/incidence), not analytic

research-question-finer-pico.explanation: PICO(T) → Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, Time — how to build the question.

hypothesis-objectives.stem: The null hypothesis (H₀) in a two-group drug trial states that:

options.text: The drug is superior to placebo
There is no difference between drug and placebo

hypothesis-objectives.explanation: H₀ is the "no difference/no effect" default that we try to reject. The alternative (H₁) states there IS a difference.

hypothesis-objectives.stem: Which objective is written in SMART, measurable form?

options.text: To appreciate the value of screening
To determine the prevalence of hypertension among Year-1 students in 2026
To know more about blood pressure

hypothesis-objectives.explanation: Only (c) is specific, measurable (prevalence), and time-bound. "Understand/appreciate/know" are not measurable Bloom’s verbs.

hypothesis-objectives.stem: Regarding what does a significant p-value prove? — which is correct?

options.text: It proves the alternative hypothesis is true
It gives evidence to *reject the null*; it never "proves" H₁ and cannot prove H₀ either
The hypothesis we attempt to reject with data

hypothesis-objectives.explanation: Statistics quantify evidence against H₀. "Fail to reject" ≠ "H₀ is true"; "reject" ≠ "H₁ proven."

hypothesis-objectives.stem: What best explains the finding: “H₀ = no difference / no association”?

options.text: Not measurable — rewrite with a Bloom’s action verb
The hypothesis we attempt to reject with data

hypothesis-objectives.explanation: H₀ = no difference / no association → The hypothesis we attempt to reject with data.

hypothesis-objectives.stem: What best explains the finding: “H₁ / Hₐ = there is a difference”?

options.text: The hypothesis we attempt to reject with data
Not measurable — rewrite with a Bloom’s action verb

hypothesis-objectives.explanation: H₁ / Hₐ = there is a difference → Supported *indirectly* by rejecting H₀.

literature-review-purpose-search.stem: A systematic review of RCTs is best classified as which type of source?
literature-review-purpose-search.explanation: A systematic review analyses/summarises primary studies → secondary source. The individual RCT is primary; a textbook chapter is tertiary.

literature-review-purpose-search.stem: To retrieve articles containing either "myocardial infarction" or "heart attack", you should combine the terms with:
literature-review-purpose-search.explanation: OR captures either synonym, broadening the search. AND would require both phrases in the same article; NOT excludes.

literature-review-purpose-search.stem: Regarding boolean operators — which is correct?

options.text: Using OR narrows the search to fewer, more relevant results
OR *broadens* (captures any synonym); AND *narrows* (requires all terms together)
Boolean operators shape search sensitivity vs specificity
Source hierarchy by proximity to original data

literature-review-purpose-search.explanation: OR = union of sets (more results); AND = intersection (fewer, more specific results).

literature-review-purpose-search.stem: What best explains the finding: “AND narrows, OR broadens, NOT excludes”?

options.text: Source hierarchy by proximity to original data
Boolean operators shape search sensitivity vs specificity

literature-review-purpose-search.explanation: AND narrows, OR broadens, NOT excludes → Boolean operators shape search sensitivity vs specificity.

literature-review-purpose-search.stem: What best explains the finding: “RCT report = primary; systematic review = secondary; textbook = tertiary”?

options.text: Boolean operators shape search sensitivity vs specificity
Source hierarchy by proximity to original data

literature-review-purpose-search.explanation: RCT report = primary; systematic review = secondary; textbook = tertiary → Source hierarchy by proximity to original data.

citation-synthesis-conceptual-framework.stem: Reusing substantial portions of your own previously published paper without citation is:

options.text: Acceptable, because it is your own work

citation-synthesis-conceptual-framework.explanation: Recycling your own text without citing it is self-plagiarism. Fabrication = inventing data; falsification = altering data.

citation-synthesis-conceptual-framework.stem: The conceptual framework of a study is best described as:

options.text: The list of all references cited
A literature-derived map of the study variables and their relationships

citation-synthesis-conceptual-framework.explanation: The conceptual framework diagrams the variables (exposure, outcome, confounders, mediators) and how they relate, built from the reviewed literature.

citation-synthesis-conceptual-framework.stem: Regarding conceptual framework — which is correct?

options.text: The conceptual framework is just the reference list
It is a literature-derived diagram/model of the study variables and how they relate (exposure, outcome, confounders)
Organises studies by theme to enable comparison, not just listing
Every citation must pair with a reference — common error

citation-synthesis-conceptual-framework.explanation: It operationalises the hypothesis and tells you what to measure — it is not a bibliography.

citation-synthesis-conceptual-framework.stem: What best explains the finding: “Matrix / synthesis table”?

options.text: Every citation must pair with a reference — common error
Organises studies by theme to enable comparison, not just listing
Literature-derived map of study variables and their relationships

citation-synthesis-conceptual-framework.explanation: Matrix / synthesis table → Organises studies by theme to enable comparison, not just listing.

citation-synthesis-conceptual-framework.stem: What best explains the finding: “In-text citation with no reference entry (or vice versa)”?

options.text: Organises studies by theme to enable comparison, not just listing
Literature-derived map of study variables and their relationships
Every citation must pair with a reference — common error

citation-synthesis-conceptual-framework.explanation: In-text citation with no reference entry (or vice versa) → Every citation must pair with a reference — common error.

study-designs-hierarchy.stem: Researchers want to study risk factors for a very rare cancer quickly and cheaply. The most appropriate design is:
study-designs-hierarchy.explanation: For a rare disease, start from cases and controls and look back for exposures (case-control) → Odds Ratio. A cohort would need an enormous sample and long follow-up.

study-designs-hierarchy.stem: Which design provides the strongest evidence for causation because it balances unknown confounders?
study-designs-hierarchy.explanation: Randomisation distributes both known and unknown confounders equally between groups, which is why the RCT sits above observational designs (below only systematic reviews/meta-analyses).

study-designs-hierarchy.stem: Regarding which measure does the design give? — which is correct?

options.text: A case-control study can report the relative risk
Case-control gives the *Odds Ratio* (no denominators for incidence); RR comes from cohort/RCT
Efficiency: start from whichever is scarce
Only forward designs give incidence → RR

study-designs-hierarchy.explanation: Case-control starts from diseased/non-diseased, so you cannot compute incidence → only odds → OR (≈RR only if disease is rare).

study-designs-hierarchy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rare disease → case-control; rare exposure → cohort”?

options.text: Only forward designs give incidence → RR
Classic weakness of retrospective case-control studies
Efficiency: start from whichever is scarce
Group-level (ecological) association wrongly applied to individuals

study-designs-hierarchy.explanation: Rare disease → case-control; rare exposure → cohort → Efficiency: start from whichever is scarce.

study-designs-hierarchy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cohort/RCT → Relative Risk; case-control → Odds Ratio”?

options.text: Efficiency: start from whichever is scarce
Classic weakness of retrospective case-control studies
Group-level (ecological) association wrongly applied to individuals
Only forward designs give incidence → RR

study-designs-hierarchy.explanation: Cohort/RCT → Relative Risk; case-control → Odds Ratio → Only forward designs give incidence → RR.

sampling-methods.stem: A researcher divides students into strata by year of study and randomly samples from each stratum. The main advantage is:

options.text: Lower cost than any other method
Guaranteed representation of each subgroup and greater precision
It eliminates the need for a sampling frame

sampling-methods.explanation: Stratified sampling ensures every subgroup is represented and reduces variance (↑precision). Cost reduction and no-frame are advantages of cluster sampling.

sampling-methods.stem: Surveying only patients who happen to be in the clinic waiting room today is an example of:
sampling-methods.explanation: Taking whoever is readily available is convenience (non-probability) sampling — cheap but highly prone to selection bias.

sampling-methods.stem: Regarding stratified vs cluster — which is correct?

options.text: Stratified and cluster sampling are basically the same thing
Stratified samples from EVERY subgroup (↑precision); cluster samples only SOME whole groups (↓cost)
Sampling each stratum guarantees representation & reduces variance
Sample whole clusters when a full unit list is impractical

sampling-methods.explanation: Strata are homogeneous within/heterogeneous between and all are sampled; clusters are heterogeneous within/homogeneous between and only a random subset is taken.

sampling-methods.stem: What best explains the finding: “Stratified: homogeneous within, heterogeneous between → ↑precision”?

options.text: Sample whole clusters when a full unit list is impractical
Simple; biased only if the list has hidden periodicity
Sampling each stratum guarantees representation & reduces variance
Participants recruit peers — reaches hidden/hard-to-find populations (non-probability)

sampling-methods.explanation: Stratified: homogeneous within, heterogeneous between → ↑precision → Sampling each stratum guarantees representation & reduces variance.

sampling-methods.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cluster: heterogeneous within, homogeneous between → ↓cost”?

options.text: Sampling each stratum guarantees representation & reduces variance
Simple; biased only if the list has hidden periodicity
Participants recruit peers — reaches hidden/hard-to-find populations (non-probability)
Sample whole clusters when a full unit list is impractical

sampling-methods.explanation: Cluster: heterogeneous within, homogeneous between → ↓cost → Sample whole clusters when a full unit list is impractical.

variables-confounding-bias.stem: Which set of features defines a confounder?

options.text: It lies on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome
It is associated with the exposure, is a risk factor for the outcome, and is not on the causal pathway
It changes the effect size across its levels

variables-confounding-bias.explanation: A confounder satisfies all three: associated with exposure, independent cause of outcome, NOT on the pathway. On-pathway = mediator; changes effect by level = effect modifier.

variables-confounding-bias.stem: The only method that controls for BOTH known and unknown confounders is:
variables-confounding-bias.explanation: Regression, restriction, and matching can only handle confounders you measured/anticipated. Randomisation distributes even unmeasured/unknown confounders equally — the strength of the RCT.

variables-confounding-bias.stem: Regarding confounder vs mediator — which is correct?

options.text: Any variable associated with both exposure and outcome should be adjusted for
Adjust confounders (off the pathway); do NOT adjust mediators (on the pathway) if you want the total causal effect
Definition of a confounder → adjust for it
M is a mediator (on the pathway) — do not adjust if you want the total effect

variables-confounding-bias.explanation: Adjusting a mediator removes part of the very effect you are trying to measure ("over-adjustment bias").

variables-confounding-bias.stem: What best explains the finding: “Variable linked to exposure, causes outcome, off the pathway”?

options.text: M is a mediator (on the pathway) — do not adjust if you want the total effect
Effect modification → analyse by stratum, report it
Definition of a confounder → adjust for it
Design-stage control unique to the RCT

variables-confounding-bias.explanation: Variable linked to exposure, causes outcome, off the pathway → Definition of a confounder → adjust for it.

variables-confounding-bias.stem: What best explains the finding: “X → M → Y”?

options.text: Definition of a confounder → adjust for it
Effect modification → analyse by stratum, report it
Design-stage control unique to the RCT
M is a mediator (on the pathway) — do not adjust if you want the total effect

variables-confounding-bias.explanation: X → M → Y → M is a mediator (on the pathway) — do not adjust if you want the total effect.

outbreak-investigation.stem: An epidemic curve shows a single sharp peak with all cases occurring within one incubation period. This pattern indicates:
outbreak-investigation.explanation: A single tight peak within one incubation period points to one common exposure = point source. Successive rising waves suggest propagated spread.

outbreak-investigation.stem: Which is the correct early step, done BEFORE generating a hypothesis about the source?

options.text: Establish a case definition and describe cases by person, place, and time

outbreak-investigation.explanation: Descriptive epidemiology (case definition + person/place/time, including the epidemic curve) precedes and generates the hypothesis, which is then tested with an analytic study.

outbreak-investigation.stem: Regarding when to start control measures — which is correct?

options.text: You must finish the analytic study before implementing any control measures
Control measures can and should begin as soon as a plausible source is identified — especially when severe/fatal

outbreak-investigation.explanation: Outbreak investigation and control run in parallel; delaying action to "finish the study" costs lives (a core field-epidemiology principle).

outbreak-investigation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Single sharp peak within one incubation period”?

options.text: Compares exposure groups to find the source

outbreak-investigation.explanation: Single sharp peak within one incubation period → Point-source outbreak (one common exposure).

outbreak-investigation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Successive taller waves ~1 incubation apart”?

options.text: Compares exposure groups to find the source

outbreak-investigation.explanation: Successive taller waves ~1 incubation apart → Propagated (person-to-person) spread.

data-types-descriptive-stats.stem: A histogram of hospital length-of-stay is strongly right-skewed. The most appropriate summary is:
data-types-descriptive-stats.explanation: Skewed data are best summarised by the median (IQR), which is robust to the long tail. The mean would be pulled up by outliers.
Cancer stage has a natural order but unequal/undefined intervals → ordinal. Blood group is nominal; temperature is continuous; number of siblings is discrete numerical.

data-types-descriptive-stats.stem: Regarding sd vs se — which is correct?

options.text: Standard deviation and standard error measure the same thing
SD describes spread of individual values; SE (= SD/√n) describes precision of the *mean* and shrinks with larger n
Mean dragged toward the long right tail by high outliers

data-types-descriptive-stats.explanation: Reporting SE to look "tighter" misrepresents variability. Use SD for describing data, SE/CI for describing the estimate.

data-types-descriptive-stats.stem: What best explains the finding: “Right (positive) skew → mean > median > mode”?

options.text: Data are skewed/ordinal → robust summary chosen
Mean dragged toward the long right tail by high outliers
Precision of the mean; shrinks as n grows (≠ population spread)

data-types-descriptive-stats.explanation: Right (positive) skew → mean > median > mode → Mean dragged toward the long right tail by high outliers.

data-types-descriptive-stats.stem: What best explains the finding: “Normal distribution: mean = median = mode”?

options.text: Mean dragged toward the long right tail by high outliers
Data are skewed/ordinal → robust summary chosen
Precision of the mean; shrinks as n grows (≠ population spread)

data-types-descriptive-stats.explanation: Normal distribution: mean = median = mode → Symmetry; 68–95–99.7% within ±1/2/3 SD.

inferential-stats-p-value.stem: A 95% confidence interval for a mean difference is −2 to +6. What can you conclude at α = 0.05?

options.text: The result is not statistically significant, because the interval includes 0
A Type I error has occurred
The sample size was too large

inferential-stats-p-value.explanation: The CI for a difference includes the null value 0, so p ≥ 0.05 — not statistically significant. (For a ratio, the null value is 1.)

inferential-stats-p-value.stem: To compare the mean blood pressure across three different treatment groups, the appropriate test is:
inferential-stats-p-value.explanation: A continuous outcome across >2 groups → ANOVA. A t-test handles only 2 groups; chi-square is for categorical data; correlation is for two continuous variables.

inferential-stats-p-value.stem: Regarding interpreting the p-value — which is correct?

options.text: p = 0.03 means there is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true
p = 0.03 means: IF H₀ were true, there’s a 3% chance of data this extreme — it says nothing directly about the probability H₀ is true
Interval estimate of the parameter; narrower with larger n
NOT P(H₀ true) and NOT "probability of chance"

inferential-stats-p-value.explanation: The p-value is conditional on H₀ being true; it is not the posterior probability of H₀. Misreading this is the single most common stats error.

inferential-stats-p-value.stem: What best explains the finding: “95% CI = mean ± 1.96 × SE”?

options.text: NOT P(H₀ true) and NOT "probability of chance"
Interval estimate of the parameter; narrower with larger n

inferential-stats-p-value.explanation: 95% CI = mean ± 1.96 × SE → Interval estimate of the parameter; narrower with larger n.

inferential-stats-p-value.stem: What best explains the finding: “p = P(data this extreme | H₀ true)”?

options.text: Interval estimate of the parameter; narrower with larger n
NOT P(H₀ true) and NOT "probability of chance"

inferential-stats-p-value.explanation: p = P(data this extreme | H₀ true) → NOT P(H₀ true) and NOT "probability of chance".

research-ethics-history-belmont.stem: In the Belmont Report, the requirement for fair selection of research participants is the application of which principle?
research-ethics-history-belmont.explanation: Justice → fair distribution of the burdens and benefits of research → fair participant selection. Respect for persons → informed consent; Beneficence → risk/benefit assessment.

research-ethics-history-belmont.stem: The Nuremberg Code was written primarily in response to:

options.text: Nazi human experimentation revealed at the Doctors’ Trial

research-ethics-history-belmont.explanation: The Nuremberg Code (1947) followed the Nuremberg Doctors’ Trial of Nazi physicians. Tuskegee later drove the US National Research Act and the Belmont Report.

research-ethics-history-belmont.stem: Regarding match principle to application — which is correct?

options.text: Informed consent is the application of Beneficence
Informed consent applies *Respect for persons*; Beneficence → risk/benefit assessment; Justice → fair participant selection
First code — "voluntary consent is absolutely essential"

research-ethics-history-belmont.explanation: Belmont pairs each principle with a specific application — mixing them up is the most common exam trap.

research-ethics-history-belmont.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nuremberg Code (1947)”?

options.text: Untreated syphilis in Black men → drove US regulation (National Research Act)
First code — "voluntary consent is absolutely essential"
WMA physicians’ guideline; welfare of the subject over science

research-ethics-history-belmont.explanation: Nuremberg Code (1947) → First code — "voluntary consent is absolutely essential".

research-ethics-history-belmont.stem: What best explains the finding: “Belmont: Respect → consent; Beneficence → risk/benefit; Justice → fair selection”?

options.text: First code — "voluntary consent is absolutely essential"
Untreated syphilis in Black men → drove US regulation (National Research Act)
WMA physicians’ guideline; welfare of the subject over science

research-ethics-history-belmont.explanation: Belmont: Respect → consent; Beneficence → risk/benefit; Justice → fair selection → 3 principles map to 3 applications.

informed-consent-irb.stem: A study poses no more than minimal risk to participants. Which level of IRB/REC review is appropriate?
informed-consent-irb.explanation: Minimal-risk research qualifies for expedited review (by the chair or a designee). Greater-than-minimal risk requires full board review.

informed-consent-irb.stem: Which trio constitutes the essential elements of valid informed consent?
informed-consent-irb.explanation: Valid consent requires adequate information, comprehension of it, and voluntary agreement. The other trios are the Belmont principles, risk domains, and benefit types respectively.

informed-consent-irb.stem: Regarding assent vs consent — which is correct?

options.text: A child’s assent alone is enough to enrol them in research
Minors give *assent* (agreement) but cannot give legal consent — parental/guardian *permission* is also required
All three needed for valid informed consent
Minors cannot consent; assent = the child’s own agreement

informed-consent-irb.explanation: Assent respects the child’s developing autonomy but does not replace the legally required parental permission.

informed-consent-irb.stem: What best explains the finding: “Consent = Information + Comprehension + Voluntariness”?

options.text: Minors cannot consent; assent = the child’s own agreement
Full board reserved for greater-than-minimal risk
All three needed for valid informed consent

informed-consent-irb.explanation: Consent = Information + Comprehension + Voluntariness → All three needed for valid informed consent.

informed-consent-irb.stem: What best explains the finding: “Child: parental permission + assent”?

options.text: All three needed for valid informed consent
Full board reserved for greater-than-minimal risk
Minors cannot consent; assent = the child’s own agreement

informed-consent-irb.explanation: Child: parental permission + assent → Minors cannot consent; assent = the child’s own agreement.

publication-types-imrad.stem: Which publication type is a PRIMARY source reporting the authors’ own empirical study?
publication-types-imrad.explanation: The original research article reports the authors’ own study (primary source, IMRaD). Reviews and textbooks are secondary/tertiary; editorials are opinion.

publication-types-imrad.stem: In IMRaD, statistical pooling of results from multiple studies would appear in which type of paper?
publication-types-imrad.explanation: A meta-analysis statistically combines results from multiple studies, usually within a systematic review — the highest tier of the evidence hierarchy.

publication-types-imrad.stem: Regarding where does interpretation go? — which is correct?

options.text: You can interpret and explain your findings in the Results section
Results = findings only; interpretation, implications, and limitations belong in the Discussion
Standard anatomy of an original article (+ Title/Abstract/References)
Reproducible search + statistical pooling → top of evidence hierarchy

publication-types-imrad.explanation: Mixing interpretation into Results is a classic manuscript error — IMRaD deliberately separates "what we found" from "what it means".

publication-types-imrad.stem: What best explains the finding: “IMRaD = Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion”?

options.text: Reproducible search + statistical pooling → top of evidence hierarchy
Low on the evidence hierarchy, but flags the novel
Standard anatomy of an original article (+ Title/Abstract/References)
Interpretation belongs in the Discussion, not Results

publication-types-imrad.explanation: IMRaD = Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion → Standard anatomy of an original article (+ Title/Abstract/References).

publication-types-imrad.stem: What best explains the finding: “Systematic review + meta-analysis”?

options.text: Standard anatomy of an original article (+ Title/Abstract/References)
Low on the evidence hierarchy, but flags the novel
Interpretation belongs in the Discussion, not Results
Reproducible search + statistical pooling → top of evidence hierarchy

publication-types-imrad.explanation: Systematic review + meta-analysis → Reproducible search + statistical pooling → top of evidence hierarchy.

peer-review-journal-metrics.stem: A journal that charges a publication fee but performs little or no genuine peer review and spams authors with invitations is best described as:
peer-review-journal-metrics.explanation: Predatory journals exploit pay-to-publish while skipping real peer review, using spam solicitation and false metrics/indexing claims.

peer-review-journal-metrics.stem: The journal impact factor is best understood as:

options.text: A measure of an individual article’s quality
The number of authors on a paper
A journal-level average of recent citations, not a per-paper quality metric
The rejection rate of a journal

peer-review-journal-metrics.explanation: Impact factor ≈ average citations to the journal’s articles from the previous two years — a journal-level influence proxy, not a per-article quality guarantee.

peer-review-journal-metrics.stem: Regarding what does impact factor measure? — which is correct?

options.text: A high journal impact factor means each individual paper in it is high quality
Impact factor is a *journal-level* average of citations — it says nothing guaranteed about any single article
Independent expert evaluation before acceptance — quality control
Journal-level influence proxy, NOT single-paper quality

peer-review-journal-metrics.explanation: Papers in high-IF journals vary widely; appraise each paper by its own methods, not by where it was published.

peer-review-journal-metrics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Peer review”?

options.text: Journal-level influence proxy, NOT single-paper quality
Independent expert evaluation before acceptance — quality control
Basic legitimacy signal for a journal

peer-review-journal-metrics.explanation: Peer review → Independent expert evaluation before acceptance — quality control.

peer-review-journal-metrics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Impact factor = citations to last 2 yrs’ articles”?

options.text: Independent expert evaluation before acceptance — quality control

peer-review-journal-metrics.explanation: Impact factor = citations to last 2 yrs’ articles → Journal-level influence proxy, NOT single-paper quality.

academic-authorship.stem: A senior professor is added as a co-author solely because they head the department, without any contribution to the study. This is:
academic-authorship.explanation: Crediting a non-contributor for prestige is gift/honorary authorship — unethical. Ghost authorship is the opposite: a real contributor left off the list.

academic-authorship.stem: Which contribution, on its own, satisfies the ICMJE criteria for authorship?

options.text: Only general supervision of the group
None alone — all four ICMJE criteria (contribution, drafting/revising, final approval, accountability) must be met

academic-authorship.explanation: ICMJE requires ALL four criteria together. Funding, supervision, or data collection alone are insufficient and warrant Acknowledgement rather than authorship.

academic-authorship.stem: Regarding does funding earn authorship? — which is correct?

options.text: Providing the grant money or being the department head automatically makes you an author
Funding or supervision alone does NOT meet ICMJE criteria; without intellectual contribution + drafting + approval + accountability, that person belongs in Acknowledgements
ALL four required to be listed as an author
Named without contributing (e.g. head of department) — unethical

academic-authorship.explanation: Adding a non-contributor for status is gift/honorary authorship — explicitly unethical under ICMJE.

academic-authorship.stem: What best explains the finding: “ICMJE = contribution + drafting/revising + final approval + accountability”?

options.text: Named without contributing (e.g. head of department) — unethical
Real contributor deliberately left off the author list — unethical
ALL four required to be listed as an author

academic-authorship.explanation: ICMJE = contribution + drafting/revising + final approval + accountability → ALL four required to be listed as an author.

academic-authorship.stem: What best explains the finding: “Gift/honorary authorship”?

options.text: ALL four required to be listed as an author
Real contributor deliberately left off the author list — unethical
Named without contributing (e.g. head of department) — unethical

academic-authorship.explanation: Gift/honorary authorship → Named without contributing (e.g. head of department) — unethical.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: Which cell is the principal "bridge" that links the innate and adaptive immune responses by presenting antigen to naïve T cells?
immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: Dendritic cells capture antigen, mature, migrate to lymph nodes, and present it on MHC to naïve T cells — bridging innate and adaptive immunity. They are the most potent antigen-presenting cells.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: The surface phenotype CD4⁺CD25⁺FoxP3⁺ identifies which cell?
immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: Regulatory T cells are CD4⁺CD25⁺ and express the master transcription factor FoxP3; they suppress immune responses and maintain self-tolerance.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: Regarding which arm has memory? — which is correct?

options.text: Innate immunity develops memory after repeated exposure
Only ADAPTIVE immunity (lymphocytes) has classical memory; innate responds identically each time

immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: Memory = faster/stronger secondary response, a defining feature of B/T lymphocytes, not neutrophils/macrophages.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: What best explains the finding: “CD3 on a lymphocyte”?
immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: CD3 on a lymphocyte → Pan-T-cell marker.

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: What best explains the finding: “CD4⁺CD25⁺FoxP3⁺ T cell”?
immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: CD4⁺CD25⁺FoxP3⁺ T cell → Regulatory T cell (self-tolerance).

immune-system-overview-cells.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells”?
immune-system-overview-cells.explanation: Skin immune cells are part of the innate immune response.

lymphoid-organs.stem: In a lymph node, the paracortex is populated predominantly by:
lymphoid-organs.explanation: The paracortex is the T-cell zone (with dendritic cells presenting antigen). B cells reside in cortical follicles; plasma cells accumulate in the medulla.

lymphoid-organs.stem: A splenectomised patient is at particularly high risk of overwhelming infection by:
lymphoid-organs.explanation: The spleen clears encapsulated bacteria and supports antibody responses to them, so asplenia predisposes to overwhelming pneumococcal/meningococcal/Haemophilus sepsis — hence vaccination.

lymphoid-organs.stem: Regarding where do b cells mature? — which is correct?

options.text: B cells mature in the thymus like T cells
B cells mature in the BONE MARROW; the thymus is for T-cell maturation

lymphoid-organs.explanation: Both begin in marrow, but only T cells migrate to the thymus to mature. "B = Bone marrow, T = Thymus."

lymphoid-organs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Germinal centre in a lymphoid follicle”?

options.text: Loss of splenic clearance of encapsulated bacteria

lymphoid-organs.explanation: Germinal centre in a lymphoid follicle → Active B-cell response (affinity maturation/class switch).

lymphoid-organs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Overwhelming pneumococcal sepsis post-splenectomy”?

options.text: Loss of splenic clearance of encapsulated bacteria

lymphoid-organs.explanation: Overwhelming pneumococcal sepsis post-splenectomy → Loss of splenic clearance of encapsulated bacteria.

lymphoid-organs.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Lymphoid Organs: Primary & Secondary”?

options.text: Pudendal Neurovasculature, Erectile Tissues & External Genitalia

lymphoid-organs.explanation: Understanding lymphoid organs can provide context for immune responses in genitalia.

lymphoid-organs.stem: Which should you review before “Lymphoid Organs: Primary & Secondary”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

lymphoid-organs.explanation: Understanding immune cells is essential for grasping lymphoid organ functions.

innate-barriers-prr.stem: Which Toll-like receptor recognises lipopolysaccharide (LPS) of Gram-negative bacteria?
innate-barriers-prr.explanation: TLR4 (cell surface) recognises LPS; TLR3 = dsRNA, TLR7 = ssRNA, TLR9 = CpG DNA (all endosomal nucleic-acid sensors).

innate-barriers-prr.stem: Pattern-recognition receptors differ from antibodies and T-cell receptors in that they are:

options.text: Germline-encoded and recognise conserved microbial patterns
Specific for a single unique epitope

innate-barriers-prr.explanation: PRRs are germline-encoded, non-clonal, and recognise conserved PAMPs/DAMPs. Antigen-specific diversity via somatic recombination is unique to the adaptive BCR/TCR.

innate-barriers-prr.stem: Regarding are prrs specific/clonal like antibodies? — which is correct?

options.text: Each PRR is clonally rearranged to recognise one unique antigen
PRRs are germline-encoded and recognise conserved shared PATTERNS (PAMPs) — not somatically rearranged like BCR/TCR

innate-barriers-prr.explanation: Innate receptors are fixed and pattern-based; only adaptive receptors (Ig/TCR) are diverse and antigen-specific via V(D)J recombination.

innate-barriers-prr.stem: What best explains the finding: “TLR4 recognising bacterial LPS”?
innate-barriers-prr.explanation: TLR4 recognising bacterial LPS → Surface PRR for Gram-negative endotoxin.

innate-barriers-prr.stem: What best explains the finding: “TLR9 recognising CpG DNA in an endosome”?
innate-barriers-prr.explanation: TLR9 recognising CpG DNA in an endosome → Endosomal nucleic-acid sensing (viral/bacterial).

innate-barriers-prr.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Innate Immunity: Barriers, PRRs & Inflammation”?
innate-barriers-prr.explanation: Renal defense mechanisms involve innate immune responses relevant to inflammation.

innate-barriers-prr.stem: Which should you review before “Innate Immunity: Barriers, PRRs & Inflammation”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

innate-barriers-prr.explanation: Understanding innate immunity requires knowledge of the overall immune system.

innate-nk-interferon.stem: A virus down-regulates MHC class I on infected cells to evade cytotoxic T cells. Which innate cell is specifically triggered to kill these cells?
innate-nk-interferon.explanation: Loss of MHC I removes the inhibitory signal to NK cells ("missing self"), triggering NK killing via perforin/granzyme — complementing CTLs, which require MHC I.

innate-nk-interferon.stem: Which cytokines are the principal ANTIVIRAL interferons that induce an antiviral state in neighbouring cells?
innate-nk-interferon.explanation: Type I interferons (α/β) are produced by virus-infected cells and induce an antiviral state. IFN-γ (type II) mainly activates macrophages and is made by Th1/NK cells.

innate-nk-interferon.stem: Regarding nk cell target recognition — which is correct?

options.text: NK cells kill cells that display high levels of MHC class I
NK cells kill cells that LOSE/down-regulate MHC I ("missing self"); MHC I on healthy cells INHIBITS them

innate-nk-interferon.explanation: This is the mirror image of CTLs (which require MHC I) — NK cells cover the viral immune-evasion escape route.

innate-nk-interferon.stem: What best explains the finding: “NK kills a cell that has lost MHC class I”?

options.text: Type II IFN (Th1/NK) — distinct from antiviral IFN-α/β

innate-nk-interferon.explanation: NK kills a cell that has lost MHC class I → "Missing self" removes inhibitory signal.

innate-nk-interferon.stem: What best explains the finding: “NK kills an IgG-coated target via CD16”?

options.text: Type II IFN (Th1/NK) — distinct from antiviral IFN-α/β

innate-nk-interferon.explanation: NK kills an IgG-coated target via CD16 → ADCC (FcγRIII).

innate-nk-interferon.stem: Which is a clinical application of “NK Cells, Interferons & Innate Effectors”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

innate-nk-interferon.explanation: NK cells can be involved in skin immune responses, linking basic science to clinical applications.

antibody-structure.stem: The antigen-binding specificity of an antibody is determined primarily by the:

options.text: Hypervariable (CDR) loops of the variable regions

antibody-structure.explanation: The complementarity-determining regions (CDRs/hypervariable regions) of the heavy and light variable domains form the antigen-binding pocket. The Fc/constant region governs effector function.

antibody-structure.stem: Which region of the immunoglobulin molecule determines its isotype (class) and effector functions such as complement activation?

options.text: The variable region of the light chain

antibody-structure.explanation: The Fc — formed by the heavy-chain constant region — defines the isotype (γ/α/μ/ε/δ) and mediates effector functions (complement, Fc-receptor binding, placental transfer).

antibody-structure.stem: Regarding what determines antibody class? — which is correct?

options.text: The light chain (kappa/lambda) determines the antibody class
The HEAVY-chain constant region (γ/α/μ/ε/δ) determines the isotype/class; light chains are only κ or λ
Fab, formed by variable regions of heavy + light chains (CDRs)
Fc (heavy-chain constant region) determines effector function

antibody-structure.explanation: Class = heavy-chain constant region. The variable region sets specificity; light-chain type does not define IgG vs IgA etc.

antibody-structure.stem: What best explains the finding: “Antigen-binding site location”?

options.text: Fc (heavy-chain constant region) determines effector function
Fab, formed by variable regions of heavy + light chains (CDRs)

antibody-structure.explanation: Antigen-binding site location → Fab, formed by variable regions of heavy + light chains (CDRs).

antibody-structure.stem: What best explains the finding: “Complement/Fc-receptor binding”?

options.text: Fab, formed by variable regions of heavy + light chains (CDRs)
Fc (heavy-chain constant region) determines effector function

antibody-structure.explanation: Complement/Fc-receptor binding → Fc (heavy-chain constant region) determines effector function.

antibody-structure.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Immunoglobulin Structure & Diversity”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

antibody-structure.explanation: Antibodies may play a role in neurodegenerative diseases.
