antibody-structure.explanation: Understanding B-cell development is crucial for grasping antibody structure.

antibody-classes-functions.stem: Which immunoglobulin isotype is the only one that crosses the placenta to provide passive immunity to the fetus?
antibody-classes-functions.explanation: IgG is the only isotype transported across the placenta (via FcRn), giving the newborn passive humoral immunity. IgA is provided postnatally via breast milk.

antibody-classes-functions.stem: A pentameric antibody that is the first produced in a primary response and the most efficient complement activator is:
antibody-classes-functions.explanation: IgM is a pentamer (with J chain), appears first in the primary response, and with 10 binding sites is the best classical-pathway complement activator (though of lower affinity than switched IgG).

antibody-classes-functions.stem: Regarding first vs main antibody — which is correct?

options.text: IgG is the first antibody produced in a primary immune response
IgM is FIRST (primary response); IgG dominates later and in the secondary response

antibody-classes-functions.explanation: IgM appears first (pentamer, good complement); class switching to IgG follows and gives the durable, high-affinity secondary response.

antibody-classes-functions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Only antibody crossing the placenta”?
antibody-classes-functions.explanation: Only antibody crossing the placenta → IgG (neonatal passive immunity).

antibody-classes-functions.stem: What best explains the finding: “First antibody in a primary response; best complement activator”?
antibody-classes-functions.explanation: First antibody in a primary response; best complement activator → IgM (pentamer, 10 binding sites).

complement-pathways.stem: The classical complement pathway is initiated by:

options.text: Antibody (IgM/IgG) bound to antigen activating C1
Spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 on a microbial surface

complement-pathways.explanation: The classical pathway starts when C1 binds the Fc of antigen-bound IgM/IgG. MBL/mannose = lectin pathway; spontaneous C3 tickover + properdin = alternative pathway.

complement-pathways.stem: All three complement activation pathways converge on the formation of:

options.text: A C3 convertase that cleaves C3

complement-pathways.explanation: Each pathway generates a C3 convertase (classical/lectin C4b2a; alternative C3bBb) that cleaves C3 into C3a + C3b — the central convergence step leading to C5 convertase and the MAC.

complement-pathways.stem: Regarding convergence point of complement — which is correct?

options.text: The three complement pathways stay separate through to lysis
They CONVERGE at C3 (all form a C3 convertase); downstream (C5 → MAC) is shared

complement-pathways.explanation: Different triggers, same hub — that is why C3 deficiency cripples all three pathways and causes severe pyogenic infections.

complement-pathways.stem: What best explains the finding: “Antibody–antigen complex activating complement”?
complement-pathways.explanation: Antibody–antigen complex activating complement → Classical pathway (C1 binds Fc).

complement-pathways.stem: What best explains the finding: “MBL binding mannose on a microbe”?
complement-pathways.explanation: MBL binding mannose on a microbe → Lectin pathway (MASP → C4/C2).

complement-pathways.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Complement: The Three Activation Pathways”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

complement-pathways.explanation: While not directly related, understanding complement can aid in grasping immune-related drug effects.

complement-pathways.stem: Which should you review before “Complement: The Three Activation Pathways”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

complement-pathways.explanation: Understanding hemolysis is crucial for grasping complement's role in immune responses.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: A young adult presents with a second episode of meningococcal meningitis. Which immune defect is most likely?
complement-functions-regulation.explanation: Recurrent Neisseria infection is the hallmark of terminal complement (MAC, C5–C9) deficiency, because MAC-mediated lysis is the key defence against Neisseria.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: Hereditary angioedema, presenting as recurrent non-pruritic swelling without urticaria, is caused by deficiency of:
complement-functions-regulation.explanation: C1-inhibitor deficiency leads to unregulated activation of the classical/contact pathways with excess bradykinin, causing recurrent angioedema. DAF/CD59 loss causes PNH.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: Regarding recurrent neisseria — which deficiency? — which is correct?

options.text: Recurrent Neisseria infection indicates an antibody (B-cell) deficiency
Recurrent Neisseria points to TERMINAL COMPLEMENT (C5–C9/MAC) deficiency — MAC lysis is essential against Neisseria

complement-functions-regulation.explanation: Neisseria are uniquely susceptible to MAC-mediated lysis; recurrent neisserial disease is the classic clue to terminal complement deficiency.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Recurrent Neisseria (meningococcal) infections”?

options.text: PNH — loss of DAF/CD59 (GPI anchor defect)

complement-functions-regulation.explanation: Recurrent Neisseria (meningococcal) infections → Terminal complement (C5–C9 / MAC) deficiency.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “SLE-like immune-complex disease + pyogenic infections”?

options.text: PNH — loss of DAF/CD59 (GPI anchor defect)

complement-functions-regulation.explanation: SLE-like immune-complex disease + pyogenic infections → Early classical component deficiency (C1/C2/C4).

complement-functions-regulation.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Complement: Functions, Regulation & Deficiencies”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

complement-functions-regulation.explanation: Links complement deficiencies to immune-mediated kidney diseases.

complement-functions-regulation.stem: Which should you review before “Complement: Functions, Regulation & Deficiencies”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

complement-functions-regulation.explanation: Basic understanding of biochemical processes is helpful.

t-cell-activation.stem: Full activation of a naïve T cell requires TCR–peptide-MHC engagement plus a second signal delivered by:
t-cell-activation.explanation: Co-stimulation via CD28–B7 is signal 2. CTLA-4 binding B7 is inhibitory (a checkpoint), and CD8–MHC I is part of signal 1 for cytotoxic T cells.

t-cell-activation.stem: A T cell receives antigen recognition (signal 1) but no co-stimulation. The likely outcome is:

options.text: Differentiation into a cytotoxic T cell

t-cell-activation.explanation: Signal 1 without signal 2 induces anergy — a peripheral-tolerance mechanism that prevents responses to self-antigens presented without co-stimulation.

t-cell-activation.stem: Regarding consequence of signal 1 alone — which is correct?

options.text: A T cell that recognises antigen (signal 1) is always fully activated
Antigen recognition WITHOUT co-stimulation (signal 2) → anergy/tolerance, not activation

t-cell-activation.explanation: The two-signal requirement prevents activation against self-antigens presented in the absence of "danger"/co-stimulation.

t-cell-activation.stem: What best explains the finding: “CD28–B7 engagement”?
t-cell-activation.explanation: CD28–B7 engagement → Co-stimulation (signal 2) — required for full activation.

t-cell-activation.stem: What best explains the finding: “IL-2 autocrine loop”?
t-cell-activation.explanation: IL-2 autocrine loop → Drives T-cell clonal proliferation.

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: Which CD4⁺ subset secretes IFN-γ to activate macrophages for defence against intracellular pathogens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: Th1 cells (driven by IL-12, master TF T-bet) secrete IFN-γ to activate macrophages and support CD8 CTLs — the arm against intracellular microbes and the basis of granuloma formation.

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: A mutation in FoxP3 causes severe multi-organ autoimmunity (IPEX) because it impairs which cell?
cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: FoxP3 is the master transcription factor of regulatory T cells; its loss abolishes Treg-mediated suppression → the fatal autoimmune syndrome IPEX.

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: Regarding th1 vs th2 target — which is correct?

options.text: Th2 cells are the main defence against intracellular bacteria like TB
Th1 (IFN-γ, macrophage activation) handles intracellular microbes; Th2 handles helminths/allergy (IgE, eosinophils)

cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: Th1 = intracellular + macrophages; Th2 = parasites/allergy. Swapping them is a classic error.

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: What best explains the finding: “IFN-γ activating macrophages”?
cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: IFN-γ activating macrophages → Th1 (intracellular defence, granulomas).

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: What best explains the finding: “IL-4/5/13 driving IgE + eosinophils”?
cd4-helper-subsets.explanation: IL-4/5/13 driving IgE + eosinophils → Th2 (helminths, allergy).

cd4-helper-subsets.stem: Which is a clinical application of “CD4⁺ Helper T-Cell Subsets”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells
Muscle Contraction: The Sliding Filament & Cross-Bridge Cycle

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: A cytotoxic CD8⁺ T cell induces apoptosis in a virus-infected cell primarily by:

options.text: Releasing perforin and granzymes (and FasL–Fas signalling)

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: CTLs kill via perforin (pore formation) + granzymes (caspase-mediated apoptosis) and the FasL–Fas death-receptor pathway. They recognise viral peptide on MHC I.

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: Formation of a tuberculous granuloma depends on Th1 cells activating macrophages via:
cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: Th1 cells secrete IFN-γ and express CD40L to activate macrophages, enhancing killing of intracellular microbes and forming granulomas. This axis (IL-12/IFN-γ) is essential against mycobacteria.

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: Regarding which mhc do ctls use? — which is correct?

options.text: Cytotoxic CD8 T cells recognise antigen presented on MHC class II
CD8 CTLs recognise antigen on MHC class I (on all nucleated cells); CD4 helpers use MHC II

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: Rule of 8: CD8 × MHC I = 8. MHC I displays endogenous/viral peptides for CTL surveillance.

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Target-cell apoptosis via pore + protease”?

options.text: Presented on MHC class I of the infected cell

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: Target-cell apoptosis via pore + protease → Perforin + granzyme (CTL/NK).

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: What best explains the finding: “FasL–Fas engagement killing a target”?

options.text: Presented on MHC class I of the infected cell

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: FasL–Fas engagement killing a target → Death-receptor apoptosis pathway.

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.stem: Which should you review before “CD8 Cytotoxic T Cells & Effector Mechanisms”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

cd8-ctl-nk-effectors.explanation: NK cells provide backup to CTLs in immune response.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: MHC class II molecules are expressed on:

options.text: Only professional antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells)

mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: MHC II is limited to professional APCs and presents exogenous antigen to CD4⁺ T cells. MHC I (with β2-microglobulin) is on all nucleated cells and presents to CD8⁺ T cells.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: Which HLA allele is most classically associated with ankylosing spondylitis?
mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: HLA-B27 is strongly associated with ankylosing spondylitis and other seronegative spondyloarthropathies. DQ2/DQ8 → coeliac; B*57:01 → abacavir hypersensitivity.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: Regarding where is mhc ii expressed? — which is correct?

options.text: MHC class II is expressed on all nucleated cells like MHC I
MHC II is restricted to professional APCs (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells); MHC I is on all nucleated cells

mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: Only APCs present exogenous antigen to CD4 helpers on MHC II; MHC I surveillance covers every nucleated cell.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: What best explains the finding: “MHC I associates with β2-microglobulin”?
mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: MHC I associates with β2-microglobulin → Structural requirement for surface expression.

mhc-structure-genetics.stem: What best explains the finding: “MHC II expressed only on APCs”?
mhc-structure-genetics.explanation: MHC II expressed only on APCs → Dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: A viral protein synthesised in the cytosol of an infected cell is presented to T cells via:

options.text: MHC class II to CD4⁺ T cells
The proteasome/TAP pathway on MHC class I to CD8⁺ T cells
The invariant chain pathway to CD4⁺ T cells

antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: Endogenous cytosolic antigen is degraded by the proteasome, transported by TAP into the ER, loaded on MHC I, and presented to CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: Cross-presentation by dendritic cells refers to:

options.text: Presenting endogenous antigen on MHC II
Loading exogenous (engulfed) antigen onto MHC I to prime CD8⁺ T cells

antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: Cross-presentation lets dendritic cells place exogenous antigen onto MHC I to prime CD8⁺ CTLs against pathogens/tumours that do not directly infect the DC.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: Regarding which pathway presents cytosolic viral protein? — which is correct?

options.text: Viral proteins made inside the cell are presented on MHC class II to CD4 cells
Endogenous (cytosolic) antigen → proteasome/TAP → MHC class I → CD8 T cells
Prevents premature loading until the endosome

antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: Internally synthesised (endogenous) antigen goes on MHC I. MHC II handles engulfed (exogenous) antigen. Cross-presentation is the special DC exception.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Proteasome + TAP loading peptide onto MHC I”?

options.text: Prevents premature loading until the endosome

antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: Proteasome + TAP loading peptide onto MHC I → Endogenous (cytosolic) pathway → CD8.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Invariant chain / CLIP on MHC II”?

options.text: Prevents premature loading until the endosome

antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: Invariant chain / CLIP on MHC II → Prevents premature loading until the endosome.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Antigen Processing & Presentation Pathways”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: Understanding immune response is relevant for diagnosing chronic infections.

antigen-processing-presentation.stem: Which should you review before “Antigen Processing & Presentation Pathways”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

antigen-processing-presentation.explanation: Understanding CD4 T cell function is essential for MHC II pathway.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: An immature B cell in the bone marrow that strongly binds a self-antigen can avoid deletion by further light-chain rearrangement. This process is called:
b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: Receptor editing rearranges a new light chain to change the BCR specificity away from self — a central-tolerance mechanism. Somatic hypermutation/class switching occur later in germinal centres.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: During B-cell development, which event occurs first?

options.text: Heavy-chain V(D)J rearrangement forming the pre-BCR

b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: The heavy chain rearranges first and pairs with a surrogate light chain to form the pre-BCR checkpoint, before light-chain rearrangement completes the IgM receptor.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: Regarding order of chain rearrangement — which is correct?

options.text: The light chain rearranges before the heavy chain in B-cell development
The HEAVY chain rearranges first (forming the pre-BCR checkpoint); the light chain follows

b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: Heavy-chain success (pre-BCR) licenses progression before light-chain rearrangement completes the IgM BCR.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: What best explains the finding: “Heavy chain rearranges before light chain”?
b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: Heavy chain rearranges before light chain → Ordered V(D)J; pre-BCR checkpoint.

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: What best explains the finding: “Immature B cell edits its receptor to lose self-reactivity”?
b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: Immature B cell edits its receptor to lose self-reactivity → Receptor editing (central tolerance).

b-cell-development-tolerance.stem: Which should you review before “B-Cell Development & Central Tolerance”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

b-cell-development-tolerance.explanation: Understanding B-cell receptors requires knowledge of immunoglobulin structure.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: Negative selection of thymocytes, occurring mainly in the thymic medulla, serves to:

options.text: Retain cells that can bind self-MHC
Delete thymocytes that bind self-antigen too strongly (central tolerance)
Convert CD8 cells to CD4 cells

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: Negative selection deletes strongly self-reactive thymocytes (central tolerance), aided by AIRE-driven tissue-antigen expression. Positive selection (cortex) retains MHC-restricted cells.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: Mutation of the AIRE gene causes multi-organ autoimmunity (APECED) because AIRE normally:

options.text: Drives expression of tissue-specific self-antigens in the thymus for negative selection

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: AIRE enables medullary thymic epithelial cells to express peripheral tissue antigens so that autoreactive T cells against them are deleted. Its loss lets self-reactive T cells escape → APECED/APS-1.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: Regarding positive vs negative selection — which is correct?

options.text: Positive selection deletes self-reactive T cells
POSITIVE selection KEEPS cells that recognise self-MHC (cortex); NEGATIVE selection DELETES strongly self-reactive cells (medulla)

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: Positive = survival of MHC-restricted cells; negative = removal of autoreactive ones. Reversing them is a top exam trap.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thymocyte survives by binding self-MHC (cortex)”?

options.text: Enables negative selection to tissue-specific self

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: Thymocyte survives by binding self-MHC (cortex) → Positive selection → MHC restriction.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thymocyte deleted for strong self-antigen reactivity (medulla)”?

options.text: Enables negative selection to tissue-specific self

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: Thymocyte deleted for strong self-antigen reactivity (medulla) → Negative selection → central tolerance.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: Which is a clinical application of “T-Cell Development & Thymic Selection”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells
GnRH, FSH/LH Feedback & the Midcycle Surge

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: Basic science of feedback mechanisms may have indirect relevance.

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.stem: Which should you review before “T-Cell Development & Thymic Selection”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

t-cell-development-thymic-selection.explanation: T-cell activation is essential for understanding T-cell function post-selection.

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: A 9-month-old boy has recurrent pyogenic infections, undetectable B cells, and very low levels of all immunoglobulin classes. The most likely diagnosis is:
primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: A BTK defect blocks B-cell maturation → absent B cells and panhypogammaglobulinaemia in a male infant after maternal IgG wanes. DiGeorge is a T-cell defect; CGD is a phagocyte defect.

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: A boy has hypocalcaemic tetany, a conotruncal cardiac defect, and a T-cell deficiency. Which deletion is responsible?
primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) causes thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia (T-cell deficiency + hypocalcaemia) with conotruncal heart defects — "CATCH-22".

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: Regarding selective iga deficiency reaction — which is correct?

options.text: IgA deficiency is always symptomatic with severe infections
Most selective IgA deficiency is asymptomatic; a classic clue is ANAPHYLAXIS to blood products/IVIG (anti-IgA antibodies)

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: It is the commonest and often silent PID; the exam hook is transfusion anaphylaxis, not overwhelming infection.

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: What best explains the finding: “Boy with recurrent pyogenic infections, absent B cells, all Ig low”?
primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: Boy with recurrent pyogenic infections, absent B cells, all Ig low → X-linked agammaglobulinaemia (BTK).

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: What best explains the finding: “High IgM, low IgG/A/E, PCP”?
primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: High IgM, low IgG/A/E, PCP → Hyper-IgM (CD40L defect → no class switch).

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.stem: Which should you review before “Primary Immunodeficiency: Antibody, T-Cell & Combined”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

primary-immunodeficiency-antibody-t.explanation: Understanding antigen processing is crucial for grasping immunodeficiencies.

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: A child with recurrent Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus infections, granulomas, and an abnormal dihydrorhodamine (DHR) test most likely has:
primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: CGD is a defect of NADPH oxidase → no respiratory burst → infections with catalase-positive organisms and granulomas; the DHR/NBT test is abnormal.

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: A neonate has delayed separation of the umbilical cord, recurrent bacterial infections without pus formation, and a markedly elevated neutrophil count. The defect involves:
primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 results from defective β2-integrin (CD18) → neutrophils cannot adhere and transmigrate, causing pus-free infections, delayed cord separation, and blood neutrophilia.

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: Regarding why catalase-positive organisms in cgd? — which is correct?

options.text: CGD patients get infected by all bacteria equally
CGD specifically → CATALASE-POSITIVE organisms, because catalase-negative bacteria supply their own H₂O₂ that the phagocyte can still use

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: Without NADPH oxidase, phagocytes borrow H₂O₂ from catalase-negative microbes; catalase-positive organisms destroy their own H₂O₂, escaping killing.

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: What best explains the finding: “Recurrent Staph/Aspergillus infections + granulomas”?
primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: Recurrent Staph/Aspergillus infections + granulomas → CGD (NADPH oxidase defect, catalase⁺ organisms).

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: What best explains the finding: “Abnormal DHR/NBT test”?
primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: Abnormal DHR/NBT test → Confirms absent respiratory burst (CGD).

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.stem: Which should you review before “Primary Immunodeficiency: Phagocyte & Complement Defects”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

primary-immunodeficiency-phagocyte-compl.explanation: Understanding complement defects is crucial for grasping primary immunodeficiencies.

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.stem: HIV causes progressive immunodeficiency principally by:

options.text: Depleting CD4⁺ helper T cells via gp120 binding

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.explanation: HIV gp120 binds CD4 (with CCR5/CXCR4 co-receptors) and progressively depletes CD4⁺ T cells, collapsing cell-mediated immunity and leading to opportunistic infections (AIDS at CD4 <200).

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.stem: A patient with a CD4 count of 120/µL develops a subacute pneumonia with diffuse infiltrates and marked hypoxia. The most likely opportunistic organism is:
secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.explanation: At CD4 <200/µL, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is a classic AIDS-defining opportunistic infection reflecting loss of cell-mediated immunity; prophylaxis is co-trimoxazole.

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.stem: Regarding primary vs secondary immunodeficiency frequency — which is correct?

options.text: Primary (genetic) immunodeficiencies are the most common cause of immunodeficiency
SECONDARY (acquired) immunodeficiency is far commoner — malnutrition worldwide, and HIV/drugs/malignancy clinically

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.explanation: Primary defects are rare and usually present in childhood; most immunodeficiency encountered clinically is acquired.
CD4 <200/µL → AIDS threshold → high opportunistic-infection risk.

secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.stem: What best explains the finding: “PCP, oesophageal candidiasis, CMV retinitis”?
secondary-immunodeficiency-hiv.explanation: PCP, oesophageal candidiasis, CMV retinitis → CD4/T-cell (cell-mediated) collapse in HIV.

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: A vaccine made of pure bacterial capsular polysaccharide induces mainly low-affinity IgM with poor memory, especially in infants. This is because the antigen is:
humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: Polysaccharides are T-independent antigens: they cross-link BCRs but recruit no T-cell help, so the response is IgM-dominant with little class switching or memory. Conjugation to a protein makes it T-dependent.

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: In a T-dependent antibody response, the critical "second signal" delivered from the follicular helper T cell to the B cell is:
humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: Tfh cells deliver help via CD40L–CD40 (plus cytokines), licensing the germinal-centre reaction. CD28–B7 co-stimulates the T cell itself; Fas–FasL is a cytotoxic pathway.

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: Regarding why polysaccharide vaccines fail in infants — which is correct?

options.text: Infants fail to respond to polysaccharide vaccines because they cannot make any antibody
Polysaccharides are T-INDEPENDENT antigens → poor, memory-less responses in infants; conjugating to protein makes them T-dependent

humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: The problem is lack of T-cell help/memory for polysaccharides, solved by protein conjugation — not a global inability to make antibody.

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Protein antigen → high-affinity IgG + memory”?

options.text: Protein carrier recruits T-cell help (linked recognition)

humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: Protein antigen → high-affinity IgG + memory → T-dependent (Tfh help, germinal centre).

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Polysaccharide antigen → mainly IgM, no memory”?

options.text: Protein carrier recruits T-cell help (linked recognition)

humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: Polysaccharide antigen → mainly IgM, no memory → T-independent (no T-cell help).

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Humoral Response: B-Cell Activation (T-dependent vs T-independent)”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: Cushing's syndrome may affect immune responses but is not directly related.

humoral-response-b-activation.stem: Which should you review before “Humoral Response: B-Cell Activation (T-dependent vs T-independent)”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

humoral-response-b-activation.explanation: Understanding antibody classes is essential for grasping B-cell activation.

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: Compared with the primary response, the secondary antibody response to the same antigen is:
germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: Memory B cells produce a faster, larger, class-switched (IgG), higher-affinity secondary response — the basis of vaccination and boosters. The primary response is slow and IgM-dominant.

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: Affinity maturation of antibodies occurs in the germinal centre through:

options.text: V(D)J recombination in the bone marrow
Somatic hypermutation of the variable region followed by selection of high-affinity clones
Class switching of the heavy-chain constant region

germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: Affinity maturation results from somatic hypermutation (AID) of the V region plus selection of the highest-affinity B cells by Tfh/follicular dendritic cells in the germinal centre.

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: Regarding what changes in class switching? — which is correct?

options.text: Class switching changes the antigen specificity of the antibody
Class switching changes only the HEAVY-chain constant region (isotype/function); the variable region and specificity are unchanged
Class switching (constant region changes, not variable)

germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: Switching alters effector class (IgM→IgG/A/E), not what the antibody binds. Affinity maturation refines binding via variable-region mutation.

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rising affinity of antibody over weeks”?

options.text: Class switching (constant region changes, not variable)

germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: Rising affinity of antibody over weeks → Somatic hypermutation + selection (affinity maturation).

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: What best explains the finding: “IgM → IgG switch with same antigen specificity”?

options.text: Class switching (constant region changes, not variable)

germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: IgM → IgG switch with same antigen specificity → Class switching (constant region changes, not variable).

germinal-center-antibody-response.stem: Which should you review before “Germinal Centre, Affinity Maturation & the Memory Response”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

germinal-center-antibody-response.explanation: Understanding antibody classes is essential for grasping class switching.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: The principal adaptive defence against an extracellular, toxin-producing bacterium is:
immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Extracellular bacteria are countered by humoral immunity — antibody neutralises toxins, opsonises for phagocytosis, and activates complement. Cell-mediated immunity handles intracellular organisms.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: Granuloma formation in tuberculosis primarily reflects which type of immune response?
immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Th1 cells (IFN-γ, CD40L) activate macrophages to contain intracellular bacteria in granulomas. This cell-mediated axis is why anti-TNF therapy can reactivate latent TB.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: Regarding defence against intracellular bacteria — which is correct?

options.text: Antibody is the main defence against intracellular bacteria like Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Intracellular bacteria need CELL-MEDIATED immunity (Th1/IFN-γ macrophage activation, CTL) — antibody cannot reach them
Humoral defence vs extracellular bacteria (e.g. tetanus antitoxin)
Th1/IFN-γ cell-mediated response to intracellular bacteria

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Antibody works on extracellular targets; intracellular pathogens require T-cell-driven macrophage activation and cytotoxicity.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: What best explains the finding: “Antibody neutralising a bacterial exotoxin”?

options.text: Th1/IFN-γ cell-mediated response to intracellular bacteria
Humoral defence vs extracellular bacteria (e.g. tetanus antitoxin)

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Antibody neutralising a bacterial exotoxin → Humoral defence vs extracellular bacteria (e.g. tetanus antitoxin).

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: What best explains the finding: “Granuloma with activated macrophages (TB)”?

options.text: Humoral defence vs extracellular bacteria (e.g. tetanus antitoxin)
Th1/IFN-γ cell-mediated response to intracellular bacteria

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Granuloma with activated macrophages (TB) → Th1/IFN-γ cell-mediated response to intracellular bacteria.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Immunity to Bacteria: Extracellular vs Intracellular”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Histological understanding may aid in recognizing immune responses in tissues.

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.stem: Which should you review before “Immunity to Bacteria: Extracellular vs Intracellular”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

immunity-bacteria-extracellular-intracel.explanation: Understanding complement is crucial for grasping humoral immunity.

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: The immune response responsible for defence against helminth (worm) parasites is characterised by:

options.text: Th2 cytokines (IL-4/5/13) driving IgE and eosinophils

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: Helminth defence is a Th2 response: IL-4/5/13 promote IgE, eosinophils, mast cells, and alternatively activated macrophages. Th1 handles intracellular bacteria.

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: Antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), classically seen in severe secondary dengue infection, occurs when:

options.text: Non-neutralising antibody facilitates viral entry into Fc-receptor-bearing cells
T cells kill all infected cells

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: In ADE, cross-reactive non-neutralising antibody binds virus and promotes its uptake via Fc receptors into cells, enhancing infection — the basis of more severe secondary dengue.

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: Regarding antibody in dengue — which is correct?

options.text: Antibody from a prior dengue infection always protects against the next infection
Non-neutralising cross-reactive antibody can ENHANCE a second (different serotype) dengue infection via ADE → severe dengue

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: Antibody-dependent enhancement is the exception where pre-existing antibody worsens disease — a key exam and vaccine-safety point.

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: What best explains the finding: “Type I IFN + CTL clearing a virus”?
immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: Type I IFN + CTL clearing a virus → Innate antiviral state + MHC-I-restricted killing.

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: What best explains the finding: “Severe dengue on second infection”?
immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.explanation: Severe dengue on second infection → Antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE).

immunity-viruses-fungi-parasites.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Immunity to Viruses, Fungi & Parasites + Microbial Evasion”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

mucosal-immune-system.stem: The specialised epithelial cell that samples luminal antigen and delivers it to dendritic cells in a Peyer's patch is the:
mucosal-immune-system.explanation: M cells overlie Peyer's patches and transcytose luminal antigen to underlying immune cells; some pathogens (e.g. Salmonella) exploit them to invade.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: Dimeric IgA is delivered into mucosal secretions by transcytosis across the epithelium via:

options.text: The polymeric Ig receptor (pIgR), leaving the secretory component

mucosal-immune-system.explanation: pIgR transports dimeric IgA across the epithelium; cleavage leaves the secretory component bound, protecting sIgA from gut proteases. FcRn transports IgG across the placenta.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: Regarding which antibody dominates mucosal defence? — which is correct?

options.text: IgG is the main antibody protecting mucosal surfaces
Secretory IgA (dimeric, with secretory component) is the dominant mucosal antibody — the most abundantly produced immunoglobulin
M (microfold) cell over a Peyer's patch

mucosal-immune-system.explanation: sIgA provides non-inflammatory immune exclusion at mucosae; IgG dominates serum/systemic immunity.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: What best explains the finding: “Specialised epithelial cell sampling gut antigen”?

options.text: M (microfold) cell over a Peyer's patch
Loss of secretory IgA barrier defence

mucosal-immune-system.explanation: Specialised epithelial cell sampling gut antigen → M (microfold) cell over a Peyer's patch.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: What best explains the finding: “Secretory component attached to luminal IgA”?

options.text: M (microfold) cell over a Peyer's patch
Loss of secretory IgA barrier defence

mucosal-immune-system.explanation: Secretory component attached to luminal IgA → pIgR-mediated transcytosis (protects from proteases).

mucosal-immune-system.stem: Which is a clinical application of “The Mucosal Immune System & Secretory IgA”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

mucosal-immune-system.explanation: MALT lymphoma is directly related to mucosal immune dysfunction.

mucosal-immune-system.stem: Which should you review before “The Mucosal Immune System & Secretory IgA”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

mucosal-immune-system.explanation: Understanding antibody production is crucial for grasping mucosal immunity.

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: Oral tolerance to ingested food antigens is mediated primarily by:

options.text: Regulatory T cells and tolerogenic cytokines (TGF-β, IL-10)

oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: Oral tolerance is an active, Treg-driven suppression of responses to ingested antigens (with TGF-β/IL-10 and tolerogenic dendritic cells); its failure contributes to food allergy and coeliac disease.

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: A patient develops severe Clostridioides difficile colitis after broad-spectrum antibiotics. The key predisposing change is:

options.text: Dysbiosis with loss of colonisation resistance

oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: Antibiotics disrupt the protective commensal microbiota (dysbiosis), removing colonisation resistance and allowing C. difficile overgrowth — sometimes treated by restoring flora (faecal transplant).

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: Regarding default mucosal immune state — which is correct?

options.text: The healthy gut mounts an active inflammatory response to all bacteria it contains
The default mucosal state toward commensals/food is regulated TOLERANCE (Tregs), not inflammation

oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: Constant inflammation against the trillions of commensals would be harmful; tolerance is actively maintained and only overridden for true pathogens.

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: What best explains the finding: “Immune non-response to ingested food antigen”?
oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: Immune non-response to ingested food antigen → Oral tolerance (Treg-mediated).

oral-tolerance-microbiota.stem: What best explains the finding: “Commensals outcompeting a pathogen”?
oral-tolerance-microbiota.explanation: Commensals outcompeting a pathogen → Colonisation resistance (healthy microbiota).

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: Rheumatic heart disease following group A streptococcal pharyngitis is a classic example of:

options.text: Direct bacterial invasion of the heart

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: Antibodies/T cells against streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac antigens (molecular mimicry), causing immune-mediated valvular damage after the organism is cleared.

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: Which genetic defect causes fatal early-onset multi-organ autoimmunity (IPEX) by abolishing regulatory T-cell function?
tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: FoxP3 is the master transcription factor of Tregs; its loss abolishes peripheral suppression → IPEX. AIRE loss (central tolerance) causes APECED.

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: Regarding molecular mimicry — which is correct?

options.text: Rheumatic fever damages the heart by direct streptococcal infection of the myocardium
It is molecular MIMICRY — antibodies/T cells against streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac antigens (immune-mediated, not direct infection)

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: The organism is cleared; the damage is autoimmune cross-reactivity, illustrating how infection triggers autoimmunity.

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rheumatic fever after strep pharyngitis”?
tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: Rheumatic fever after strep pharyngitis → Molecular mimicry (M protein ↔ cardiac antigen).

tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Multi-organ autoimmunity from AIRE mutation”?
tolerance-autoimmunity-mechanisms.explanation: Multi-organ autoimmunity from AIRE mutation → Central-tolerance failure (APECED).

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: Graves disease causes hyperthyroidism because the autoantibody:

options.text: Destroys thyroid follicular cells by complement
Forms immune complexes in the thyroid

autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Graves disease features a stimulating anti-TSH-receptor antibody (type II, activating) that drives thyroid hormone overproduction — contrast with the blocking anti-AChR antibody of myasthenia gravis.

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: Which autoantibody is most specific for systemic lupus erythematosus?
autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Anti-dsDNA (and anti-Sm) are specific for SLE and anti-dsDNA correlates with disease activity/nephritis. ANA is sensitive but not specific.

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: Regarding type ii activating vs blocking — which is correct?

options.text: All type II antibody-mediated autoimmune diseases destroy the target cell
Type II can also modulate receptors: Graves = STIMULATING anti-TSH-R (hyperfunction); myasthenia = BLOCKING anti-AChR (hypofunction) — no cell destruction required

autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Antibody against a receptor can activate or block it, not just trigger lysis — a favourite distinction (Graves vs MG).

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: What best explains the finding: “Anti-dsDNA / anti-Sm”?

options.text: Myasthenia gravis (type II, blocking) → fatigable weakness

autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Anti-dsDNA / anti-Sm → Specific for SLE (systemic, type III).

autoimmune-disease-examples.stem: What best explains the finding: “Stimulating anti-TSH-receptor antibody”?

options.text: Myasthenia gravis (type II, blocking) → fatigable weakness

autoimmune-disease-examples.explanation: Stimulating anti-TSH-receptor antibody → Graves disease (type II, activating) → hyperthyroidism.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: Anaphylaxis occurring within minutes of a bee sting in a sensitised person is which type of hypersensitivity?
hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Immediate reactions from allergen cross-linking IgE on mast cells (histamine release) are type I hypersensitivity; systemic form = anaphylaxis, treated with adrenaline.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: A positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia indicates which hypersensitivity mechanism?

options.text: Type II (antibody against a fixed cell antigen)

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is type II: IgG/IgM coats red cells (detected by the direct Coombs test), causing complement lysis and splenic phagocytosis.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: Regarding type ii vs type iii antibody target — which is correct?

options.text: Type II and type III hypersensitivity both involve soluble antigen–antibody complexes
Type II antibody targets a FIXED antigen on a specific cell/tissue; type III involves SOLUBLE circulating immune complexes that deposit

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Location of the antigen distinguishes them: fixed/cell-bound (II) vs soluble/deposited (III).

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: What best explains the finding: “Wheal-and-flare within minutes of allergen”?

options.text: Type II — antibody coating red cells
Type II — maternal anti-Rh IgG crosses placenta

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Wheal-and-flare within minutes of allergen → Type I — mast-cell histamine (IgE).

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: What best explains the finding: “Anaphylaxis: hypotension + bronchospasm + urticaria”?

options.text: Type II — antibody coating red cells
Type II — maternal anti-Rh IgG crosses placenta

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Anaphylaxis: hypotension + bronchospasm + urticaria → Systemic type I → give adrenaline.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Hypersensitivity Types I & II”?

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Clinical manifestations of hypersensitivity are explored in cutaneous immunology.

hypersensitivity-type-1-2.explanation: Understanding autoimmune diseases is essential for grasping Type II hypersensitivity.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: The tuberculin (Mantoux) skin test read at 48–72 hours is an example of which hypersensitivity type?
hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: The delayed (48–72 h), antibody-independent, T-cell-mediated reaction to intradermal tuberculin is the prototypical type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and serum sickness are caused by:
hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: These are type III reactions: soluble immune complexes deposit in tissues (glomeruli, vessels), activating complement and recruiting neutrophils to cause damage.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: Regarding timing of type iv — which is correct?

options.text: All hypersensitivity reactions occur within minutes
Type IV is DELAYED — it peaks at 48–72 hours because it requires T-cell recruitment (no antibody involved)

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Only type I is immediate (minutes). Type IV is cell-mediated and delayed, which is why the tuberculin test is read at 2–3 days.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: What best explains the finding: “Immune-complex deposition in glomeruli/vessels”?
hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Immune-complex deposition in glomeruli/vessels → Type III (soluble antigen + IgG + complement/neutrophils).

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: What best explains the finding: “Positive tuberculin (Mantoux) test at 48–72 h”?
hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Positive tuberculin (Mantoux) test at 48–72 h → Type IV delayed T-cell response.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Hypersensitivity Types III & IV”?

options.text: Overview: Innate vs Adaptive Immunity & Immune Cells

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Type III hypersensitivity is directly related to immune mechanisms in glomerular diseases.

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.stem: Which should you review before “Hypersensitivity Types III & IV”?

hypersensitivity-type-3-4.explanation: Understanding types I and II is essential for distinguishing them from types III and IV.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: The total binding strength of a multivalent antibody (all its antigen-binding sites acting together) is termed:
antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: Avidity is the sum of all binding-site interactions; affinity is the strength of a single site–epitope bond. IgM has high avidity despite low per-site affinity.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: Blood typing by mixing red cells with anti-A/anti-B sera relies on which antigen–antibody reaction?
antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: Antibody cross-links particulate red cells into visible clumps (haemagglutination), the basis of ABO/Rh blood typing. Precipitation involves soluble antigens.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: Regarding affinity vs avidity — which is correct?

options.text: IgM binds poorly overall because each of its sites has low affinity
IgM has LOW per-site affinity but HIGH avidity (10 sites) → strong overall binding and good agglutination/complement activation
10 binding sites sum to strong total binding

antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: Avidity is the sum of all binding sites; multivalency compensates for low per-site affinity — the key affinity-vs-avidity point.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: What best explains the finding: “IgM has high avidity but low per-site affinity”?

options.text: 10 binding sites sum to strong total binding

antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: IgM has high avidity but low per-site affinity → 10 binding sites sum to strong total binding.

antigen-antibody-principles.stem: What best explains the finding: “Haemagglutination for ABO blood typing”?

options.text: 10 binding sites sum to strong total binding

antigen-antibody-principles.explanation: Haemagglutination for ABO blood typing → Antibody cross-links (particulate) red cells.

immunoassays-techniques.stem: Measuring a patient's CD4⁺ T-lymphocyte count in HIV infection is performed by:
immunoassays-techniques.explanation: Flow cytometry stains cells with fluorochrome-labelled anti-CD antibodies and counts them individually — used for CD4 counts and immunophenotyping.

immunoassays-techniques.stem: In the standard HIV testing algorithm, a sensitive ELISA screen is followed by which specific confirmatory test?
immunoassays-techniques.explanation: A positive sensitive ELISA screen is confirmed by a specific Western blot showing antibody bands to key viral proteins — screen sensitive, confirm specific.

immunoassays-techniques.stem: Regarding screen vs confirm — which is correct?

options.text: A confirmatory Western blot is used first because it is the most sensitive test
Screen with the SENSITIVE test (ELISA) first, then CONFIRM positives with the SPECIFIC test (Western blot)

immunoassays-techniques.explanation: Sensitive screening catches all true positives (few false negatives); specific confirmation removes false positives — the standard testing algorithm (e.g. HIV).

immunoassays-techniques.stem: What best explains the finding: “Colour change proportional to analyte in a microplate”?
immunoassays-techniques.explanation: Colour change proportional to analyte in a microplate → ELISA (enzyme-linked).

immunoassays-techniques.stem: What best explains the finding: “Positive HIV screen confirmed by band pattern”?
immunoassays-techniques.explanation: Positive HIV screen confirmed by band pattern → ELISA screen → Western blot confirmation.

immunoassays-techniques.stem: Which should you review before “Immunoassays: ELISA, Blotting, Flow Cytometry”?

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: A transplanted kidney turns dusky and thromboses within minutes of reperfusion. This hyperacute rejection is due to:

options.text: Pre-existing recipient antibodies against donor ABO/HLA antigens

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: Hyperacute rejection results from pre-formed antibodies binding graft endothelium → complement activation and thrombosis in minutes; it is prevented by ABO matching and a pre-transplant crossmatch.

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: A patient develops skin rash, diarrhoea, and cholestatic jaundice after an allogeneic bone-marrow transplant. This is:
transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: In GVHD, immunocompetent donor T cells attack the immunosuppressed host — classically targeting skin, gut, and liver — a complication of bone-marrow/HSCT.

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: Regarding cause of hyperacute rejection — which is correct?

options.text: Hyperacute rejection is caused by newly activated alloreactive T cells
Hyperacute rejection is caused by PRE-EXISTING recipient antibodies (ABO/anti-HLA) → immediate thrombosis; prevented by crossmatch

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: It happens in minutes — far too fast for a new T-cell response; it requires antibody that is already present.

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: What best explains the finding: “Graft thrombosis within minutes of reperfusion”?

options.text: GVHD (donor T cells attack host skin/gut/liver)

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: Graft thrombosis within minutes of reperfusion → Hyperacute rejection (pre-existing antibody).

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cellular rejection at 1–2 weeks, reversible with steroids”?

options.text: GVHD (donor T cells attack host skin/gut/liver)

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: Cellular rejection at 1–2 weeks, reversible with steroids → Acute rejection (alloreactive T cells).

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.stem: Which should you review before “Transplantation: Allorecognition & Rejection”?

transplant-allorecognition-rejection.explanation: Understanding hypersensitivity is crucial for grasping transplant rejection mechanisms.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: Calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus and ciclosporin prevent rejection mainly by:

options.text: Blocking IL-2 production and T-cell activation

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: Calcineurin inhibitors block the calcineurin–NFAT pathway, reducing IL-2 transcription and hence T-cell activation/proliferation — a cornerstone of maintenance immunosuppression.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: Before a kidney transplant, a positive complement-dependent cytotoxicity crossmatch indicates:

options.text: Recipient antibodies against donor cells → high risk of hyperacute rejection
Donor T cells will attack the host

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: A positive crossmatch shows pre-formed recipient anti-donor antibodies that would cause hyperacute rejection — a contraindication to proceeding with that donor.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: Regarding meaning of a positive crossmatch — which is correct?

options.text: A positive crossmatch means the donor is a good HLA match and transplant should proceed
A POSITIVE crossmatch means recipient antibodies react with donor cells → high hyperacute-rejection risk → do NOT transplant

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: The crossmatch must be negative; a positive result reveals pre-formed donor-reactive antibody, contraindicating the transplant.

transplant-matching-immunosuppression.stem: What best explains the finding: “Positive pre-transplant crossmatch”?
transplant-matching-immunosuppression.explanation: Positive pre-transplant crossmatch → Contraindication — predicts hyperacute rejection.

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: The three sequential phases of cancer immunoediting are:
tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: Immunoediting proceeds Elimination (surveillance kills tumour cells) → Equilibrium (immune pressure selects variants) → Escape (edited tumour evades immunity → clinical cancer).

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: A mutated protein expressed only by a patient's tumour cells and presented on MHC I is best classified as a:
tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: A mutation-derived neoantigen unique to the tumour is a tumour-specific antigen (TSA). TAAs are normal self-proteins that are over-expressed or aberrantly expressed.

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: Regarding evidence for immunosurveillance — which is correct?

options.text: Immunosuppression has no effect on cancer risk
Immunosuppressed patients (transplant, HIV) have markedly INCREASED cancer risk — strong evidence that the immune system normally controls tumours

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: The rise in (especially virus-related) cancers with immunosuppression demonstrates active immunosurveillance.

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: What best explains the finding: “Mutated neoantigen or viral protein on a tumour”?
tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.explanation: Mutated neoantigen or viral protein on a tumour → Tumour-specific antigen (TSA).

tumor-antigens-immunosurveillance.stem: What best explains the finding: “Over-expressed self-protein (e.g. CEA)”?
Which should you review before “Tumour Antigens & Cancer Immunosurveillance”?

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: Pembrolizumab, an anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody, treats cancer by:

options.text: Blocking the PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitory checkpoint to reactivate anti-tumour T cells

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: Anti-PD-1 blocks the PD-1/PD-L1 brake that tumours use to switch off T cells, restoring T-cell-mediated tumour killing — a checkpoint-blockade immunotherapy.

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: CAR-T cell therapy for B-cell malignancies most commonly targets which antigen?
tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: CAR-T cells for B-cell leukaemia/lymphoma are typically engineered to target CD19; a major toxicity is cytokine release syndrome from massive T-cell activation.

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: Regarding how checkpoint inhibitors work — which is correct?

options.text: Checkpoint inhibitors directly kill tumour cells like chemotherapy
They BLOCK inhibitory checkpoints (PD-1/PD-L1, CTLA-4) to "release the brake" on the patient's own T cells, which then attack the tumour
Engages PD-1 → switches off T cells (evasion)
Checkpoint blockade releases exhausted T cells

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: Checkpoint inhibitors work indirectly by reactivating T cells, not by direct cytotoxicity — hence their autoimmune-type side effects.

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Tumour expressing PD-L1”?

options.text: Checkpoint blockade releases exhausted T cells
Engineered T cells target tumour antigen
Engages PD-1 → switches off T cells (evasion)

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: Tumour expressing PD-L1 → Engages PD-1 → switches off T cells (evasion).

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Response to anti-PD-1 (pembrolizumab)”?

options.text: Engages PD-1 → switches off T cells (evasion)
Engineered T cells target tumour antigen
Checkpoint blockade releases exhausted T cells

tumor-evasion-immunotherapy.explanation: Response to anti-PD-1 (pembrolizumab) → Checkpoint blockade releases exhausted T cells.

vaccines-immunization.stem: Administering preformed antitoxin (immunoglobulin) after a tetanus-prone wound is an example of:
vaccines-immunization.explanation: Giving preformed antibody provides immediate but short-lived protection with no memory — passive immunisation. Active immunisation (toxoid) would stimulate the host's own response.

vaccines-immunization.stem: Which vaccine type is generally contraindicated in a significantly immunocompromised patient?
vaccines-immunization.explanation: Live-attenuated vaccines can cause disease in immunocompromised hosts (and are avoided in pregnancy). Inactivated, toxoid, and subunit vaccines are non-replicating and safer.

vaccines-immunization.stem: Regarding live vaccines and immunosuppression — which is correct?

options.text: Live-attenuated vaccines are safe to give to immunocompromised patients because they are weakened
Live-attenuated vaccines are CONTRAINDICATED in significant immunocompromise/pregnancy — the attenuated organism can cause disease

vaccines-immunization.explanation: Without adequate immunity, even a weakened organism can replicate and cause infection; inactivated/subunit vaccines are used instead.

vaccines-immunization.stem: What best explains the finding: “Immediate protection but no memory”?

options.text: Risk of disease from the attenuated organism

vaccines-immunization.explanation: Immediate protection but no memory → Passive immunisation (preformed antibody).

vaccines-immunization.stem: What best explains the finding: “Strong lifelong immunity from one/two doses”?

options.text: Risk of disease from the attenuated organism

vaccines-immunization.explanation: Strong lifelong immunity from one/two doses → Live-attenuated vaccine.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: Before starting an anti-TNF biologic for rheumatoid arthritis, it is essential to screen for:
immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: TNF maintains granuloma integrity, so anti-TNF therapy can reactivate latent TB. Screening (and treating) latent TB before starting is standard practice.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: A therapeutic monoclonal antibody with the suffix "-umab" indicates it is:
immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: The suffix ladder is -omab (murine) → -ximab (chimeric) → -zumab (humanised) → -umab (fully human); more human sequence means lower immunogenicity.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: Regarding screening before anti-tnf therapy — which is correct?

options.text: Anti-TNF biologics can be started without any infection screening
Screen for latent TB (and hepatitis) BEFORE anti-TNF — TNF maintains granulomas, so blockade can reactivate TB
mAb for lymphoma and autoimmune disease

immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: TNF is essential for granuloma integrity (immunity bacteria extracellular intracellular); blocking it can reactivate latent tuberculosis.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Anti-CD20 (rituximab) depleting B cells”?

options.text: mAb for lymphoma and autoimmune disease

immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: Anti-CD20 (rituximab) depleting B cells → mAb for lymphoma and autoimmune disease.

immunotherapy-modulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Anti-TNF biologic for rheumatoid arthritis”?

options.text: mAb for lymphoma and autoimmune disease

immunotherapy-modulation.explanation: Anti-TNF biologic for rheumatoid arthritis → Cytokine blockade (risk: TB reactivation).
