histology-methods-staining.stem: A cell with abundant rough ER (e.g. a plasma cell) shows strongly basophilic cytoplasm on H&E because:

options.text: The rRNA of ribosomes is acidic and binds haematoxylin

histology-methods-staining.explanation: Ribosomal RNA on the RER is negatively charged (acidic) and binds the basic dye haematoxylin → basophilic cytoplasm (Nissl bodies in neurons, "clock-face" plasma cells).

histology-methods-staining.stem: To highlight the glomerular basement membrane, the best stain is:
histology-methods-staining.explanation: PAS stains carbohydrate-rich structures magenta, including basement membranes, glycogen, and mucin. Osmium is for lipid; cresyl violet for Nissl.

histology-methods-staining.stem: Regarding which dye stains the nucleus? — which is correct?

options.text: The nucleus is acidic so it must stain with the acidic dye (eosin)
DNA is acidic → it binds the BASIC dye haematoxylin → blue (basophilic)

histology-methods-staining.explanation: Acidic components bind basic dyes and vice versa. "Basophilic" describes the target loving the basic dye, not being basic itself.

histology-methods-staining.stem: What best explains the finding: “Blue cytoplasm in a plasma cell / neuron”?
histology-methods-staining.explanation: Blue cytoplasm in a plasma cell / neuron → Abundant RER (rRNA) → basophilic (Nissl bodies).

histology-methods-staining.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pink cytoplasm in muscle / RBC”?
histology-methods-staining.explanation: Pink cytoplasm in muscle / RBC → Protein-rich (actin/myosin, haemoglobin) → eosinophilic.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: On transmission electron microscopy the plasma membrane appears trilaminar because:

options.text: The two electron-dense phospholipid heads flank an electron-lucent lipid tail core
Integral proteins stain in three bands

plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: Osmium binds the polar heads, giving two dense outer lines with a lucent centre (the hydrophobic tails) — the "railroad track" trilaminar appearance.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: Which is an example of secondary active transport?

options.text: SGLT moving glucose using the Na⁺ gradient

plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: SGLT couples "downhill" Na⁺ entry (gradient set by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) to "uphill" glucose entry — secondary active transport. The ATPase itself is primary active; O₂ and K⁺-leak are passive.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: Regarding facilitated diffusion vs active transport — which is correct?

options.text: Any transport that needs a protein carrier uses ATP
Facilitated diffusion uses a carrier/channel but NO ATP (moves down-gradient); active transport uses ATP to move against the gradient
Two dense phosphate lines + lucent lipid core

plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: Carrier involvement ≠ energy use. Only active transport (or secondary active) works against the concentration gradient.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: What best explains the finding: “Trilaminar "railroad track" on TEM”?

options.text: Two dense phosphate lines + lucent lipid core

plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: Trilaminar "railroad track" on TEM → Two dense phosphate lines + lucent lipid core.

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: What best explains the finding: “Integral protein cannot be washed off”?

options.text: Two dense phosphate lines + lucent lipid core

plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: Integral protein cannot be washed off → It spans the hydrophobic core (transmembrane).

plasma-membrane-transport.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport”?
plasma-membrane-transport.explanation: Transport mechanisms are critical for glucose monitoring in clinical settings.

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: A cell specialised for steroid hormone synthesis would be expected to have abundant:
cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: SER synthesises lipids and steroids (and detoxifies) — abundant in adrenal cortex, Leydig cells, and hepatocytes. RER dominates protein-secreting cells.

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: Which organelle contains catalase and oxidises very-long-chain fatty acids, and is NOT derived from the Golgi?
cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: Peroxisomes use catalase to detoxify H₂O₂ and β-oxidise VLCFA; they arise by growth/division of existing peroxisomes, not from the Golgi (unlike lysosomes).

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: Regarding organelle vs inclusion — which is correct?

options.text: Glycogen and lipid droplets are organelles
They are INCLUSIONS — non-membranous stored material, not metabolically active organelles

cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: Organelles (mito, ER, Golgi, lysosome) carry out functions; inclusions (glycogen, lipid, pigment) are stored products or waste.

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: What best explains the finding: “Basophilic granular cytoplasm (Nissl bodies)”?

options.text: Mitochondria — inner-membrane folds house the ETC

cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: Basophilic granular cytoplasm (Nissl bodies) → Abundant RER (neurons, plasma cells).

cytoplasmic-organelles.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pale/eosinophilic cytoplasm in steroid cells”?

options.text: Mitochondria — inner-membrane folds house the ETC

cytoplasmic-organelles.explanation: Pale/eosinophilic cytoplasm in steroid cells → Abundant SER (adrenal cortex, Leydig, hepatocyte).

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: A hepatocyte shows a large, pale, vesicular nucleus with a prominent nucleolus. This indicates:

options.text: An actively transcribing, protein-synthesising cell (euchromatin + high rRNA output)

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Open euchromatin (pale) plus a prominent nucleolus (rRNA/ribosome production) marks a metabolically active, synthesising cell. Dense hyperchromatic nuclei indicate quiescence.

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: How many Barr bodies are present in a somatic cell with a 47,XXY karyotype?
nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Barr bodies = (number of X chromosomes − 1). With two X chromosomes, one is inactivated → 1 Barr body.

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: Regarding which chromatin is active? — which is correct?

options.text: The dark, dense heterochromatin must be the busy, active part
EUchromatin (pale, dispersed) is transcriptionally ACTIVE; heterochromatin (dark, condensed) is inactive
Euchromatin dominant → active protein synthesis (neuron, hepatocyte)

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Condensed = packed away/silenced. Active genes need open, accessible euchromatin — which looks pale on H&E.

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pale vesicular nucleus + big nucleolus”?

options.text: Euchromatin dominant → active protein synthesis (neuron, hepatocyte)

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Pale vesicular nucleus + big nucleolus → Euchromatin dominant → active protein synthesis (neuron, hepatocyte).

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: What best explains the finding: “Small dense hyperchromatic nucleus”?

options.text: Euchromatin dominant → active protein synthesis (neuron, hepatocyte)

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Small dense hyperchromatic nucleus → Heterochromatin dominant → inactive (lymphocyte).

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: Which is a clinical application of “The Nucleus: Envelope, Chromatin & Nucleolus”?
nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Nuclear features are relevant in thyroid histology.

nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.stem: Which should you review before “The Nucleus: Envelope, Chromatin & Nucleolus”?
nucleus-chromatin-nucleolus.explanation: Understanding chromatin structure is essential for grasping nuclear function.

actin-microfilaments.stem: The core of an intestinal microvillus is composed of:
actin-microfilaments.explanation: Microvilli have a core of bundled actin filaments (with villin/fimbrin) anchored in the terminal web — non-motile absorptive projections. The 9+2 microtubule core belongs to motile cilia.

actin-microfilaments.stem: The contractile ring that divides a cell during cytokinesis is made of:
actin-microfilaments.explanation: The cleavage furrow is generated by an actin–myosin II contractile ring. Microtubules form the mitotic spindle that separates chromosomes, not the furrow.

actin-microfilaments.stem: Regarding which filament cores microvilli? — which is correct?

options.text: Microvilli and cilia both have a microtubule core
Microvilli have an ACTIN core (non-motile); cilia have a MICROTUBULE 9+2 core (motile)
Bundled actin + villin, anchored in terminal web

actin-microfilaments.explanation: Do not conflate the two apical projections — actin = microvilli/stereocilia, microtubules = cilia/flagella.

actin-microfilaments.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thinnest filament (~6–8 nm)”?

options.text: Bundled actin + villin, anchored in terminal web

actin-microfilaments.stem: What best explains the finding: “Brush border / microvillus core”?

options.text: Bundled actin + villin, anchored in terminal web

actin-microfilaments.explanation: Brush border / microvillus core → Bundled actin + villin, anchored in terminal web.

actin-microfilaments.stem: Which should you review before “Microfilaments: Actin, Myosin & Cell Motility”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

actin-microfilaments.explanation: Actin is crucial for the structure and function of cell junctions.

microtubules-motors-centrosome.stem: A cross-section of a motile cilium shows a microtubule arrangement of:

options.text: A single central bundle of actin

microtubules-motors-centrosome.explanation: The motile ciliary axoneme is 9+2 (nine outer doublets + a central pair), with dynein arms driving bending. The basal body/centriole is 9+0 triplets.

microtubules-motors-centrosome.stem: Fast anterograde axonal transport of vesicles from the neuronal soma to the synapse is powered by:
microtubules-motors-centrosome.explanation: Kinesin walks toward the microtubule plus end (anterograde: soma → terminal). Dynein handles retrograde transport back to the soma.

microtubules-motors-centrosome.stem: Regarding kinesin vs dynein direction — which is correct?

options.text: Kinesin moves cargo toward the cell body (retrograde)
Kinesin = anterograde (toward the + end / axon terminal); dynein = retrograde (toward the − end / soma)

microtubules-motors-centrosome.explanation: Reversing them is a classic error. Anchor it: Kinesin "Kicks out," Dynein "Drags back."

microtubules-motors-centrosome.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thickest filament (~25 nm), hollow”?
What best explains the finding: “9+2 axoneme on cross-section”?

intermediate-filaments.stem: A poorly differentiated malignant tumour stains positive for vimentin and negative for keratin. The most likely category is:
intermediate-filaments.explanation: Vimentin marks mesenchymal cells → sarcoma. Keratin would indicate carcinoma; GFAP a glioma. IF immunohistochemistry reveals the tumour's tissue of origin.

intermediate-filaments.stem: Which intermediate filament is characteristic of astrocytes?
intermediate-filaments.explanation: Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) is the astrocyte IF and marks astrocytic tumours (gliomas). Desmin = muscle, keratin = epithelium, neurofilament = neurons.

intermediate-filaments.stem: Regarding are intermediate filaments dynamic like actin? — which is correct?

options.text: All cytoskeletal filaments use motor proteins and treadmill
IFs are stable, non-polar, and have NO motor proteins — they bear tension, unlike actin/microtubules

intermediate-filaments.explanation: IFs are the mechanical scaffold; only actin (myosin) and microtubules (kinesin/dynein) have motors and polarity.

intermediate-filaments.stem: What best explains the finding: “Keratin-positive tumour”?
What best explains the finding: “Vimentin-positive tumour”?
Which should you review before “Intermediate Filaments: Tissue-Specific Cytoskeleton”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

intermediate-filaments.explanation: Basic understanding of cellular metabolism may support knowledge of tissue-specific functions.

epithelial-classification.stem: The epithelium lining the trachea, in which all cells contact the basement membrane but nuclei lie at different levels, is:
epithelial-classification.explanation: The respiratory tract is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells — one layer that only appears stratified because of staggered nuclei.

epithelial-classification.stem: Simple squamous epithelium lining the pleural, peritoneal, and pericardial cavities is specifically called:
epithelial-classification.explanation: Mesothelium lines the serous body cavities; endothelium is the simple squamous lining of blood/lymphatic vessels. Urothelium is transitional epithelium of the urinary tract.

epithelial-classification.stem: Regarding pseudostratified vs stratified — which is correct?

options.text: Pseudostratified epithelium is a true multilayered (stratified) epithelium
It is a SINGLE layer — every cell touches the basement membrane, but nuclei at different heights create a layered illusion

epithelial-classification.explanation: The defining feature is BM contact by all cells. Stratified epithelia have upper cells that do NOT touch the BM.

epithelial-classification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Flat single layer lining a blood vessel”?
epithelial-classification.explanation: Flat single layer lining a blood vessel → Simple squamous = endothelium.

epithelial-classification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cuboidal cells around a colloid-filled follicle”?
epithelial-classification.explanation: Cuboidal cells around a colloid-filled follicle → Simple cuboidal = thyroid follicle.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: The brush (striated) border of the intestinal and proximal-tubule epithelium is composed of:
epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: The brush/striated border is a dense array of actin-cored microvilli that maximise absorptive surface. Cilia (microtubule, motile) belong to the airway/uterine tube.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: The lamina densa of the basal lamina is composed chiefly of:

options.text: Type III (reticular) collagen made by fibroblasts

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: The lamina densa is a network of type IV collagen with perlecan (heparan sulfate), produced by the epithelium. Type III collagen forms the reticular lamina made by fibroblasts.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: Regarding microvilli vs cilia core — which is correct?

options.text: Both microvilli and cilia are motile and share a microtubule core
Microvilli = ACTIN core, non-motile (absorption); cilia = MICROTUBULE 9+2, motile (movement)

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: Same "hair-like" look under LM, but opposite cytoskeleton and function — a very common exam distractor.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: What best explains the finding: “Striated/brush border in gut & PCT”?
epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: Striated/brush border in gut & PCT → Dense actin-cored microvilli (absorption).

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: What best explains the finding: “Motile hairs moving mucus in the airway”?
epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: Motile hairs moving mucus in the airway → Cilia (9+2 microtubule axoneme).

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Apical Specializations & the Basement Membrane”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: Basement membrane's role in placental barrier relates to epithelial function.

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.stem: Which should you review before “Apical Specializations & the Basement Membrane”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia

epithelial-surface-basement-membrane.explanation: Understanding cilia requires knowledge of microtubule structure and function.

cell-junctions.stem: Autoantibodies against desmoglein-3 (pemphigus vulgaris) disrupt which junction, causing keratinocytes to separate?
cell-junctions.explanation: Desmoglein is a desmosomal cadherin; anti-desmoglein antibodies break desmosomes → intraepidermal acantholytic blisters. Anti-hemidesmosome antibodies cause bullous pemphigoid (subepidermal).

cell-junctions.stem: Direct electrical coupling between cardiac muscle cells occurs through:
cell-junctions.explanation: Gap junctions of connexons allow ions to pass cell-to-cell, synchronising cardiac contraction (part of the intercalated disc, along with desmosomes for mechanical strength).

cell-junctions.stem: Regarding which filament anchors the desmosome? — which is correct?

options.text: Both adherens junctions and desmosomes anchor to actin
Adherens junction → ACTIN; desmosome → KERATIN (intermediate filaments)

cell-junctions.explanation: Both use Ca²⁺-dependent cadherins, but the intracellular anchor differs — actin (belt) vs keratin IF (spot-weld).

cell-junctions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Occludin/claudin apical seal”?
cell-junctions.explanation: Occludin/claudin apical seal → Tight junction (blocks paracellular leak).

cell-junctions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cadherin linked to actin”?
cell-junctions.explanation: Cadherin linked to actin → Zonula adherens.

cell-junctions.stem: Which should you review before “Cell Junctions: The Junctional Complex”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia

cell-junctions.explanation: Desmosomes anchor to keratin intermediate filaments.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: A gland in which the entire secretory cell disintegrates and becomes the secretory product uses which mode?
glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Holocrine secretion (sebaceous gland) sacrifices the whole cell. Merocrine = exocytosis with an intact cell; apocrine = apical cytoplasm pinched off.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: Serous secretory cells (e.g. pancreatic acini) are recognised histologically by:

options.text: Pale, foamy cytoplasm with a flattened basal nucleus
Basophilic cytoplasm, a round nucleus, and apical zymogen granules

glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Serous (protein-secreting) cells have basophilic RER-rich cytoplasm, a round central nucleus, and apical zymogen granules. Pale foamy cells with basal nuclei are mucous cells.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: Regarding secretion mode of sebaceous glands — which is correct?

options.text: Sebaceous glands secrete sebum by apocrine (pinching off the apex)
Sebaceous glands are HOLOCRINE — the entire cell disintegrates to form the secretion
Holocrine — entire cell disintegrates into sebum

glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Apocrine sheds only apical cytoplasm (mammary/axillary sweat); holocrine sacrifices the whole cell (sebaceous).

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sebaceous gland secretion”?

options.text: Holocrine — entire cell disintegrates into sebum

glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Sebaceous gland secretion → Holocrine — entire cell disintegrates into sebum.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: What best explains the finding: “Salivary/pancreatic secretion”?

options.text: Holocrine — entire cell disintegrates into sebum

glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Salivary/pancreatic secretion → Merocrine — exocytosis, cell preserved.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Glands: Exocrine vs Endocrine & Modes of Secretion”?

Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Clinical relevance of skin glands relates to their exocrine functions.

glands-exocrine-endocrine.stem: Which should you review before “Glands: Exocrine vs Endocrine & Modes of Secretion”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

glands-exocrine-endocrine.explanation: Understanding gland structure requires knowledge of connective tissue.

connective-tissue-cells.stem: A connective-tissue cell with an eccentric "clock-face" nucleus and deeply basophilic cytoplasm is a:
connective-tissue-cells.explanation: The clock-face (cartwheel) heterochromatin and RER-rich basophilic cytoplasm identify a plasma cell, which secretes antibodies (derived from B lymphocytes).

connective-tissue-cells.stem: Which connective-tissue cell releases histamine and heparin from metachromatic granules during allergic reactions?
connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Mast cells degranulate on IgE cross-linking, releasing histamine (vasodilation) and heparin — driving immediate hypersensitivity and inflammation.

connective-tissue-cells.stem: Regarding origin of the plasma cell vs macrophage — which is correct?

options.text: Plasma cells and macrophages both come from monocytes
Plasma cells derive from B LYMPHOCYTES (antibodies); macrophages derive from MONOCYTES (phagocytosis)

connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Different lineages: B-cell → plasma cell (humoral), monocyte → macrophage (innate/APC).

connective-tissue-cells.stem: What best explains the finding: “Spindle cell making fibres”?
connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Spindle cell making fibres → Fibroblast (most common CT cell).

connective-tissue-cells.stem: What best explains the finding: “Metachromatic granular cell releasing histamine”?
connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Metachromatic granular cell releasing histamine → Mast cell (allergy/inflammation).

connective-tissue-cells.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Connective Tissue Cells”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Connective tissue cells are directly involved in the pathology of cutaneous diseases.

connective-tissue-cells.stem: Which should you review before “Connective Tissue Cells”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

connective-tissue-cells.explanation: Understanding connective tissue cells requires knowledge of the types of fibers they produce.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: The delicate branching fibres that form the supporting stroma of a lymph node and stain with silver but poorly with H&E are composed of:
connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Reticular fibres are type III collagen — fine, argyrophilic (silver-staining), forming the stroma of lymphoid organs, liver, and bone marrow.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: A tendon, which must resist strong tension in one direction, is made of:
connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Tendons and ligaments are dense regular connective tissue — parallel type I collagen bundles aligned for unidirectional tensile strength. The dermis is dense irregular.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: Regarding reticular fibre composition — which is correct?

options.text: Reticular fibres are made of elastin
Reticular fibres are type III COLLAGEN (argyrophilic mesh); elastic fibres are elastin + fibrillin

connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Reticular = collagen III (fine branching scaffold of lymphoid/marrow); do not confuse with elastic fibres.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thick eosinophilic parallel bundles in a tendon”?
connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Thick eosinophilic parallel bundles in a tendon → Dense regular type I collagen.

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fine branching silver-stained mesh in a lymph node”?
connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Fine branching silver-stained mesh in a lymph node → Reticular fibres (type III collagen).

connective-tissue-fibers-types.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Connective Tissue Fibres & Tissue Types”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

connective-tissue-fibers-types.explanation: Clinical relevance in understanding diseases affecting connective tissues.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: Which epidermal cell produces melanin and transfers it to surrounding keratinocytes?
membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: Melanocytes (in the stratum basale) synthesise melanin in melanosomes and transfer it to keratinocytes for UV protection. Langerhans = immune APC; Merkel = touch receptor.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: Which membrane consists of connective tissue lined by cells but has NO epithelium?
membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: The synovial membrane lining joint cavities is made of connective tissue with synoviocytes but lacks a true epithelium. Mucous, serous, and cutaneous membranes all have an epithelial layer.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: Regarding which layer divides? — which is correct?

options.text: The stratum corneum actively divides to renew the skin
The stratum BASALE contains the dividing stem cells; the corneum is dead, anucleate keratin

membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: Renewal is bottom-up: mitosis at the base, cells mature and die as they ascend to form the surface barrier.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Anucleate flattened keratin scales at the surface”?
membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: Anucleate flattened keratin scales at the surface → Stratum corneum (keratinized barrier).

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Clear cells in the basal layer”?
membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: Clear cells in the basal layer → Melanocytes (melanin) or Merkel cells.

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Body Membranes & the Epidermis”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

membranes-and-epidermis.stem: Which should you review before “Body Membranes & the Epidermis”?

Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

membranes-and-epidermis.explanation: Understanding cell junctions is essential for grasping the structural integrity of the epidermis.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: A lamellated "onion-ring" mechanoreceptor in the deep dermis that senses vibration and deep pressure is a:
dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: The Pacinian corpuscle has concentric lamellae ("onion") and detects vibration/deep pressure. Meissner corpuscles in dermal papillae detect light touch.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: The reticular layer of the dermis is composed predominantly of:
dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: The reticular dermis is dense irregular connective tissue (type I collagen + elastic fibres) providing strength. The papillary dermis is loose CT; the epidermis is epithelium.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: Regarding meissner vs pacinian — which is correct?

options.text: Pacinian corpuscles detect fine light touch in the fingertips
Pacinian = deep pressure/VIBRATION (deep dermis, lamellated); Meissner = light touch (dermal papillae)

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: Location and modality differ: superficial Meissner for fine touch vs deep onion-ring Pacinian for vibration.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: What best explains the finding: “Onion-ring lamellated corpuscle in deep dermis”?
dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: Onion-ring lamellated corpuscle in deep dermis → Pacinian corpuscle (pressure/vibration).

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: What best explains the finding: “Encapsulated receptor in a dermal papilla”?
dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: Encapsulated receptor in a dermal papilla → Meissner corpuscle (light touch).

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Dermis, Sensory Receptors & Skin Appendages”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: Skin conditions like melasma can involve dermal changes.

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.stem: Which should you review before “Dermis, Sensory Receptors & Skin Appendages”?

options.text: Histology Methods: H&E Staining, Microscopy & Basophilia
Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

dermis-sensory-skin-appendages.explanation: Understanding the epidermis is essential for grasping dermal functions.

cartilage-types.stem: Which cartilage type lacks a perichondrium and is rich in type I collagen?
cartilage-types.explanation: Fibrocartilage (intervertebral disc, meniscus, pubic symphysis) has type I collagen and no perichondrium. Hyaline and elastic cartilage are type II with a perichondrium (articular hyaline is the exception with no perichondrium but still type II).

cartilage-types.stem: Growth of cartilage by division of chondrocytes within existing lacunae is termed:
cartilage-types.explanation: Interstitial growth expands cartilage from within (chondrocytes dividing in lacunae). Appositional growth adds new cartilage at the perichondrial surface.

cartilage-types.stem: Regarding collagen type in cartilage — which is correct?

options.text: All cartilage is made of type I collagen
Hyaline and elastic cartilage = type II collagen; only FIBROcartilage = type I

cartilage-types.explanation: Type II is the default cartilage collagen; fibrocartilage is the tough type-I exception (and lacks a perichondrium).

cartilage-types.stem: What best explains the finding: “Glassy matrix, chondrocytes in isogenous groups, on a joint surface”?
cartilage-types.explanation: Glassy matrix, chondrocytes in isogenous groups, on a joint surface → Hyaline cartilage (type II).

cartilage-types.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cartilage with a dark network of elastic fibres in the ear”?
cartilage-types.explanation: Cartilage with a dark network of elastic fibres in the ear → Elastic cartilage.

cartilage-types.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Cartilage: Hyaline, Elastic & Fibrocartilage”?

cartilage-types.explanation: Cartilage plays a crucial role in limb development and joint formation.

Plasma Membrane: Fluid Mosaic, Glycocalyx & Transport

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: A large multinucleated bone cell derived from the monocyte–macrophage lineage that resorbs bone matrix is the:
bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: Osteoclasts are multinucleate, monocyte-derived cells that resorb bone via a ruffled border and acid hydrolases. Osteoblasts build matrix; osteocytes maintain it.

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: In compact bone, the central canal of an osteon that carries blood vessels and nerves along the long axis is the:
bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: The Haversian canal runs along the long axis at the centre of each osteon. Volkmann canals run transversely to connect osteons; canaliculi link osteocyte lacunae.

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: Regarding origin of the osteoclast — which is correct?

options.text: Osteoclasts and osteoblasts both come from the same osteoprogenitor stem cell
Osteoblasts/osteocytes come from mesenchymal osteoprogenitors; OSTEOCLASTS come from the monocyte/macrophage (haematopoietic) lineage

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: Different lineages — that is why anti-RANKL/monocyte-targeting therapies specifically hit osteoclasts.

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: What best explains the finding: “Large multinucleated cell in a resorption (Howship) lacuna”?
bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: Large multinucleated cell in a resorption (Howship) lacuna → Osteoclast (bone resorption).

bone-tissue-cells-osteon.stem: What best explains the finding: “Plump basophilic cells lining new bone surface”?
bone-tissue-cells-osteon.explanation: Plump basophilic cells lining new bone surface → Osteoblasts (matrix deposition).

ossification.stem: The flat bones of the cranial vault form by:
ossification.explanation: Cranial vault (and clavicle/mandible) bone forms directly from mesenchyme = intramembranous ossification. Long bones use endochondral ossification (cartilage model).

ossification.stem: Achondroplasia, the commonest form of short-limbed dwarfism, results from a gain-of-function mutation affecting:
ossification.explanation: Constitutively active FGFR3 suppresses proliferation-zone chondrocytes at the growth plate → reduced endochondral bone lengthening → short limbs with a relatively normal trunk.

ossification.stem: Regarding which ossification makes flat skull bones? — which is correct?

options.text: All bones form by replacing a cartilage model (endochondral)
Flat skull bones (and the clavicle, mandible) form by INTRAMEMBRANOUS ossification — directly from mesenchyme, no cartilage template

ossification.explanation: Endochondral (cartilage-model) makes long bones and the skull base; intramembranous makes the flat cranial vault.

ossification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Skull/flat bone forming without a cartilage precursor”?
ossification.explanation: Skull/flat bone forming without a cartilage precursor → Intramembranous ossification.

ossification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Long bone lengthening at a cartilage plate”?
ossification.explanation: Long bone lengthening at a cartilage plate → Endochondral ossification (growth plate).

ossification.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Ossification: Intramembranous vs Endochondral”?

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.stem: During skeletal muscle contraction, which of the following remains constant in length?
skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: The A band equals the thick (myosin) filament length, which does not change. The I band, H zone, and overall sarcomere all shorten as thin filaments slide inward.

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.stem: The skeletal muscle triad consists of:

options.text: One T-tubule and one cisterna of sarcoplasmic reticulum
One T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of sarcoplasmic reticulum

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: The triad = one T-tubule + two terminal SR cisternae, positioned at the A–I junction, coupling depolarisation to Ca²⁺ release. Cardiac muscle has a dyad (T-tubule + one SR).

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.stem: Regarding what shortens during contraction? — which is correct?

options.text: The A band shortens as the muscle contracts
The A band stays CONSTANT; the I band and H zone shorten as thin filaments slide inward

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: Filaments do not shorten — they slide. The A band = thick filament length, which is unchanged.

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.stem: What best explains the finding: “Peripheral, multiple nuclei; cross-striations”?

options.text: Ca²⁺-release apparatus at the A–I junction

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: Peripheral, multiple nuclei; cross-striations → Skeletal muscle fibre.

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.stem: What best explains the finding: “A band constant on contraction; I band shortens”?

options.text: Ca²⁺-release apparatus at the A–I junction

skeletal-muscle-sarcomere.explanation: A band constant on contraction; I band shortens → Sliding filament (thin slides over thick).

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: The intercalated disc of cardiac muscle provides electrical coupling between cells through its:
cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: Gap junctions in the intercalated disc allow ions to pass cell-to-cell, letting the myocardium contract as a functional syncytium. Desmosomes/fascia adherens provide the mechanical coupling.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: Which feature is characteristic of smooth muscle?

options.text: Peripheral multiple nuclei and visible striations
A single central nucleus, no striations, and contraction via calmodulin/MLCK
A triad at the A–I junction

cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: Smooth muscle is spindle-shaped with one central nucleus, no striations, dense bodies instead of sarcomeres, and Ca²⁺–calmodulin–MLCK contraction. Intercalated discs and triads belong to cardiac/skeletal muscle.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: Regarding regulatory protein of smooth muscle — which is correct?

options.text: Smooth muscle contraction is triggered by Ca²⁺ binding troponin, like skeletal muscle
Smooth muscle has NO troponin — Ca²⁺ binds CALMODULIN → activates MLCK → myosin phosphorylation

cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: Only striated (skeletal/cardiac) muscle uses troponin. Smooth muscle uses the calmodulin–MLCK pathway.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: What best explains the finding: “Branched striated cells joined by dark step-lines”?
cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: Branched striated cells joined by dark step-lines → Cardiac muscle intercalated discs.

cardiac-smooth-muscle.stem: What best explains the finding: “Central single nucleus, no striations, spindle shape”?
cardiac-smooth-muscle.explanation: Central single nucleus, no striations, spindle shape → Smooth muscle.

neuron-structure-types.stem: The sensory neurons of the dorsal root ganglion are:
neuron-structure-types.explanation: Dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons are pseudounipolar — a single process leaves the soma and splits into peripheral and central branches. Bipolar = special senses; multipolar = most motor/CNS neurons.

neuron-structure-types.stem: Nissl bodies, seen as basophilic clumps in the neuronal soma, correspond ultrastructurally to:
neuron-structure-types.explanation: Nissl substance = rough ER plus free ribosomes (rRNA), hence its basophilia and role in protein synthesis. It is absent from the axon hillock and axon.

neuron-structure-types.stem: Regarding where are nissl bodies? — which is correct?

options.text: Nissl bodies extend throughout the neuron, including the axon
Nissl bodies are in the soma and dendrites but ABSENT from the axon hillock and axon

neuron-structure-types.explanation: The axon has no protein-synthesis machinery — it depends on transport from the soma; a classic identifying feature.

neuron-structure-types.stem: What best explains the finding: “Basophilic clumps in the soma (Nissl substance)”?

options.text: Single process splits into central + peripheral branch

neuron-structure-types.explanation: Basophilic clumps in the soma (Nissl substance) → RER + ribosomes → high protein synthesis.

neuron-structure-types.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pseudounipolar neuron in a dorsal root ganglion”?

options.text: Single process splits into central + peripheral branch

neuron-structure-types.explanation: Pseudounipolar neuron in a dorsal root ganglion → Single process splits into central + peripheral branch.

neuron-structure-types.stem: Which is a clinical application of “The Neuron: Structure & Morphological Types”?

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: Which glial cell myelinates multiple axons in the central nervous system?
neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: One oligodendrocyte myelinates several CNS axons. In the PNS, each Schwann cell myelinates a single internode of one axon.

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: Which neuroglial cell is derived from mesoderm (monocyte lineage) rather than neuroectoderm?
neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: Microglia are the CNS resident macrophages, derived from the mesodermal/monocyte lineage. Astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and ependymal cells are neuroectodermal.

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: Regarding cns vs pns myelination — which is correct?

options.text: One Schwann cell myelinates many axons like an oligodendrocyte
Schwann cell = ONE internode of ONE axon (PNS); oligodendrocyte = MANY axons (CNS)

neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: One-to-one (Schwann) vs one-to-many (oligodendrocyte) — and it determines which disease affects which system.

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: What best explains the finding: “GFAP-positive star-shaped cell with vascular end-feet”?
neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: GFAP-positive star-shaped cell with vascular end-feet → Astrocyte (BBB, support).

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: What best explains the finding: “CNS cell myelinating several axons at once”?
neuroglia-cns-pns.explanation: CNS cell myelinating several axons at once → Oligodendrocyte.

neuroglia-cns-pns.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Neuroglia: CNS & PNS Support Cells”?

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: Rapid saltatory conduction along a myelinated axon depends on the presence of:

options.text: Nodes of Ranvier where the action potential regenerates

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: The action potential jumps between nodes of Ranvier (gaps in myelin with clustered Na⁺ channels), speeding conduction. Continuous myelin without nodes would prevent regeneration of the impulse.

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: The connective-tissue layer that surrounds an individual nerve fascicle and forms the blood–nerve barrier is the:
nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: The perineurium wraps each fascicle and forms the blood–nerve barrier. Epineurium wraps the whole nerve; endoneurium surrounds individual axons (epimysium is a muscle sheath).

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: Regarding nerve connective-tissue layers — which is correct?

options.text: The endoneurium wraps the entire nerve
Epineurium wraps the WHOLE nerve; perineurium wraps each FASCICLE; endoneurium surrounds each AXON

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: Outer-to-inner order (Epi → Peri → Endo) is a favourite exam item — endoneurium is the innermost, around single axons.

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: What best explains the finding: “Gap in the myelin sheath with clustered Na⁺ channels”?
nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: Gap in the myelin sheath with clustered Na⁺ channels → Node of Ranvier (saltatory conduction).

nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.stem: What best explains the finding: “Faster conduction in a thicker, more myelinated axon”?
nerve-fiber-myelin-synapse.explanation: Faster conduction in a thicker, more myelinated axon → Myelination + diameter increase velocity.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: Which collagen type forms the network of the basement membrane?
ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: Type IV collagen forms the non-fibrillar network of basement membranes. Type I = bone/tendon/skin, II = cartilage, III = reticular fibres.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: The property of cartilage ground substance to resist compression is due mainly to:
ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: Sulfated GAGs on aggrecan core proteins are strongly anionic and trap water, generating turgor that resists compression. Collagen provides tensile (not compressive) strength.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: Regarding basement membrane collagen — which is correct?

options.text: Basement membranes are made of type I collagen
Basement membranes = type IV collagen (a network, non-fibrillar); type I is bone/tendon/skin

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: Type IV forms sheets, not fibres. "Floor/four" = basement membrane; type III = reticular mesh.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: What best explains the finding: “Basement membrane collagen”?

options.text: Vitamin-C-dependent proline hydroxylation fails → weak collagen

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: Basement membrane collagen → Type IV (network, non-fibrillar).

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: What best explains the finding: “Reticular fibre mesh in a lymph node”?

options.text: Vitamin-C-dependent proline hydroxylation fails → weak collagen

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: Reticular fibre mesh in a lymph node → Type III collagen.

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Extracellular Matrix: Fibres & Ground Substance”?

ecm-fibers-ground-substance.explanation: ECM components are relevant in thyroid tissue structure.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: The transmembrane receptors that mechanically and chemically link the extracellular matrix to the intracellular cytoskeleton are:
ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: Integrins bridge ECM (laminin/fibronectin) to the actin/keratin cytoskeleton and transduce signals (survival, migration). Cadherins mediate cell–cell adhesion; connexins form gap junctions.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: A rising serum C-telopeptide (CTX-1) level in a postmenopausal woman most directly reflects:

options.text: Increased osteoclastic bone resorption (type I collagen breakdown)

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: CTX-1 is a type I collagen crosslink released when osteoclasts resorb bone; elevated levels indicate increased bone turnover/resorption, useful in monitoring osteoporosis.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: Regarding fibronectin vs laminin location — which is correct?

options.text: Laminin is the main adhesive protein of general connective tissue
Laminin = basal LAMINA adhesive; fibronectin = general connective-tissue adhesion (cell ↔ collagen)

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: Match the name: Laminin → basal Lamina; fibronectin → the fibrous connective-tissue matrix.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: What best explains the finding: “Adhesive glycoprotein of the basal lamina”?
ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: Adhesive glycoprotein of the basal lamina → Laminin (binds integrins + type IV collagen).

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: What best explains the finding: “Carcinoma breaching the basement membrane”?
ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.explanation: Carcinoma breaching the basement membrane → MMP-mediated invasion → malignancy.

ecm-adhesion-integrins-clinical.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Cell–Matrix Adhesion, Integrins & Collagen Turnover”?

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: Chronic alcohol intake causes which adaptive subcellular change in hepatocytes?
subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Alcohol and drugs induce detoxifying enzymes, expanding the smooth ER — an adaptive, reversible hyperplasia. Megamitochondria may also appear in alcoholic liver disease.

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: Parakeratosis, seen in conditions such as psoriasis, refers to:

options.text: Retention of nuclei in the stratum corneum due to abnormal keratinocyte proliferation

subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Parakeratosis = retained nuclei in the normally anucleate stratum corneum, reflecting accelerated/abnormal keratinocyte turnover — an example of the "proliferation" pattern of altered histology.

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: Regarding is ser hyperplasia irreversible damage? — which is correct?

options.text: Smooth ER proliferation in hepatocytes is a sign of irreversible cell death
It is an ADAPTIVE, reversible response to drug/alcohol metabolism (enzyme induction), not lethal injury

subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Many subcellular changes are adaptive/homeostatic; distinguish reversible adaptation from lethal injury (blebbing with loss of viability, karyolysis).

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hepatocyte SER hyperplasia in a chronic drinker”?
subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Hepatocyte SER hyperplasia in a chronic drinker → Adaptive enzyme induction (detoxification).

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: What best explains the finding: “Parakeratosis (nuclei retained in stratum corneum)”?
subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Parakeratosis (nuclei retained in stratum corneum) → Abnormal keratinocyte proliferation (e.g. psoriasis).

subcellular-pathology-alterations.stem: Which should you review before “Clinical Cell Biology: Subcellular Alterations in Disease”?
subcellular-pathology-alterations.explanation: Understanding nuclear alterations is essential for grasping subcellular pathology.

intermediate-filaments-clinical.stem: Immunohistochemistry of an undifferentiated tumour is strongly positive for cytokeratin. This indicates the tumour is a:
intermediate-filaments-clinical.explanation: Cytokeratin marks epithelial cells, so keratin positivity identifies a carcinoma. Vimentin → sarcoma, GFAP → glioma; IF immunostaining reveals a tumour's tissue of origin.

intermediate-filaments-clinical.stem: The Mallory body ("alcoholic hyalin") seen in hepatocytes in alcoholic liver disease is composed of aggregated:
intermediate-filaments-clinical.explanation: Mallory bodies are clumped keratin intermediate filaments within hepatocytes — a hallmark of alcoholic liver disease (also seen in NASH).

intermediate-filaments-clinical.stem: Regarding mallory body composition — which is correct?

options.text: Mallory bodies (alcoholic hyalin) are made of collagen or amyloid
Mallory bodies are aggregated KERATIN intermediate filaments in hepatocytes

intermediate-filaments-clinical.explanation: They are a cytoskeletal (keratin) inclusion, not an extracellular deposit — a classic alcoholic liver disease finding.

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: According to Fick's law, the rate of simple diffusion across a membrane is INCREASED by:
diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: Diffusion rate rises with a steeper concentration gradient, larger surface area, higher temperature, and lipid solubility; it falls with larger molecular size and greater membrane thickness/distance.

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: Osmosis is best defined as the movement of:

options.text: Solute from high to low concentration
Water across a semipermeable membrane toward higher solute concentration
Ions against their gradient using ATP

diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: Osmosis is the passive diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane from low solute (high water) toward high solute (low water) concentration.

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: Regarding direction of osmosis — which is correct?

options.text: In osmosis, water moves toward the compartment with lower solute concentration
Water moves toward the compartment with HIGHER solute concentration (lower water concentration)

diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: Water follows solute: it diffuses down its own gradient, from high water (dilute) to low water (concentrated).

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: What best explains the finding: “O₂ and CO₂ crossing the alveolar membrane”?
diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: O₂ and CO₂ crossing the alveolar membrane → Simple diffusion (lipid-soluble gases, down gradient).

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Water moving toward the saltier compartment”?
diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: Water moving toward the saltier compartment → Osmosis (toward higher solute concentration).

diffusion-osmosis-basics.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Diffusion & Osmosis: Movement of Solutes and Water”?
diffusion-osmosis-basics.explanation: Fluid balance can impact neurological function, linking basic science to clinical scenarios.

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: Red blood cells placed in an iso-osmotic solution of urea (which freely penetrates the membrane) will:

options.text: Swell and lyse (the solution is effectively hypotonic)

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: Urea penetrates and equilibrates, contributing to osmolarity but NOT tonicity. The solution is iso-osmotic but hypotonic, so water enters and the cells swell/lyse.

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: A cell placed in a hypertonic solution will:
osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: A hypertonic solution has a higher effective solute concentration outside the cell, so water moves out and the cell shrinks (crenates).

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: Regarding iso-osmotic vs isotonic — which is correct?

options.text: A solution that is iso-osmotic to plasma is always isotonic (no volume change)
Not necessarily — if the solute PENETRATES the cell (e.g. urea), an iso-osmotic solution is actually HYPOTONIC and cells swell

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: Only non-penetrating solutes contribute to tonicity; penetrating solutes equilibrate and don't hold water out.

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: What best explains the finding: “RBCs placed in distilled water swell and lyse”?

options.text: Hypertonic, non-penetrating → draws water out of cells

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: RBCs placed in distilled water swell and lyse → Hypotonic → water enters (haemolysis).

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cells shrink (crenate) in concentrated saline”?

options.text: Hypertonic, non-penetrating → draws water out of cells

osmolarity-tonicity-cell-volume.explanation: Cells shrink (crenate) in concentrated saline → Hypertonic → water leaves.

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: Which is an example of POSITIVE feedback?

options.text: Oxytocin-driven intensification of uterine contractions during labour

homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: Oxytocin release intensifies contractions, which release more oxytocin — a self-amplifying positive-feedback loop that ends with delivery. The others are negative-feedback loops.

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: In a homeostatic control system, the structure that compares the sensed value to the set point and coordinates the response is the:
homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: The control centre (integrator) compares the sensor's input to the set point and directs the effector. The sensor detects the variable; the effector produces the response.

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: Regarding positive feedback and homeostasis — which is correct?

options.text: Positive feedback maintains homeostasis by opposing change
NEGATIVE feedback maintains homeostasis (opposes change); POSITIVE feedback amplifies a change to drive a process to completion (e.g. labour, clotting)

homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: Positive feedback is destabilising by design and is used for discrete "all-the-way" events, not for maintaining a steady state.

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: What best explains the finding: “Insulin lowering high blood glucose”?
homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: Insulin lowering high blood glucose → Negative feedback (opposes the rise).

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: What best explains the finding: “Oxytocin intensifying labour contractions”?
homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: Oxytocin intensifying labour contractions → Positive feedback (amplifies until birth).

homeostasis-feedback-control.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Homeostasis & Feedback Control”?

homeostasis-feedback-control.explanation: Breathing control is a key physiological process regulated by homeostatic feedback.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: Using the "60-40-20" rule, the intracellular fluid represents approximately what fraction of total body water?
body-fluid-compartments.explanation: ICF (~40% of body weight) is two-thirds of total body water (~60%); ECF (~20%) is one-third, subdivided into interstitial fluid (~15%) and plasma (~5%).

body-fluid-compartments.stem: The high intracellular potassium and high extracellular sodium concentrations are maintained primarily by:
body-fluid-compartments.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase actively pumps Na⁺ out and K⁺ in, establishing the characteristic ICF (high K⁺) vs ECF (high Na⁺) gradients that underlie the resting membrane potential.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: Regarding icf vs ecf proportion — which is correct?

options.text: Most body water is in the extracellular fluid
Most body water is INTRACELLULAR (ICF ≈ two-thirds of total body water); ECF is only one-third

body-fluid-compartments.explanation: The 60-40-20 rule: ICF 40% of body weight vs ECF 20% — the majority of water is inside cells.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: What best explains the finding: “High intracellular K⁺, high extracellular Na⁺”?

options.text: Low ECF osmolality → water enters brain cells

body-fluid-compartments.explanation: High intracellular K⁺, high extracellular Na⁺ → Maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: What best explains the finding: “ICF is two-thirds of total body water”?

options.text: Low ECF osmolality → water enters brain cells

body-fluid-compartments.explanation: ICF is two-thirds of total body water → 60-40-20 rule.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Body Fluid Compartments & Electrolyte Distribution”?

options.text: Diffusion & Osmosis: Movement of Solutes and Water

body-fluid-compartments.explanation: Renal function is crucial for maintaining body fluid compartments and composition.

body-fluid-compartments.stem: Which should you review before “Body Fluid Compartments & Electrolyte Distribution”?

options.text: Diffusion & Osmosis: Movement of Solutes and Water

body-fluid-compartments.explanation: Understanding body fluid compartments is essential for grasping homeostasis.

membrane-transport-passive.stem: Which feature distinguishes carrier-mediated facilitated diffusion from simple diffusion?

options.text: It moves solute against the gradient
It shows saturation (a transport maximum) and competition

membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Carrier-mediated transport saturates (limited carriers → Tm), is specific, and shows competition — unlike simple diffusion. Both are passive (down-gradient, no ATP).

membrane-transport-passive.stem: Compared with carriers, membrane ion channels transport solutes:

options.text: Much faster, through a water-filled pore

membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Channels form gated water-filled pores and conduct ions extremely rapidly (millions/sec), far faster than carriers, which must bind and change conformation. Both are passive.

membrane-transport-passive.stem: Regarding facilitated diffusion energy — which is correct?

options.text: Facilitated diffusion requires ATP because it uses a transport protein
Facilitated diffusion is PASSIVE (down-gradient, no ATP) — the protein just provides a path; only active transport uses energy

membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Protein involvement ≠ energy use. Facilitated diffusion moves solute down its gradient without ATP; active transport moves against it with ATP.

membrane-transport-passive.stem: What best explains the finding: “Transport rate plateaus at high substrate (Tm)”?
membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Transport rate plateaus at high substrate (Tm) → Carrier saturation (all carriers occupied).

membrane-transport-passive.stem: What best explains the finding: “Glucose entering cells via GLUT”?
membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Glucose entering cells via GLUT → Facilitated diffusion (carrier, down gradient).

membrane-transport-passive.stem: Which should you review before “Passive Membrane Transport: Channels & Carriers”?
membrane-transport-passive.explanation: Understanding oxygen transport is linked to passive transport mechanisms.

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: Glucose uptake by SGLT in the intestine and proximal tubule, moving glucose against its gradient using the inward Na⁺ gradient, is an example of:
membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: SGLT couples downhill Na⁺ entry (gradient set by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) to uphill glucose transport in the same direction — secondary active symport. GLUT (facilitated) moves glucose down-gradient.

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is best classified as:
membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase hydrolyses ATP directly to pump 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in against their gradients — primary active transport (and electrogenic).

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: Regarding is secondary active transport atp-free? — which is correct?

options.text: Secondary active transport requires no energy because it uses no ATP
It uses no DIRECT ATP, but it depends on the Na⁺ gradient built by the ATP-consuming Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase — so it is still energy-dependent

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: The energy is "borrowed" from the Na⁺ gradient; block the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and secondary active transport fails too.

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: What best explains the finding: “Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (3 out / 2 in) using ATP”?
membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (3 out / 2 in) using ATP → Primary active transport (electrogenic pump).

membrane-transport-active-vesicular.stem: What best explains the finding: “SGLT moving glucose uphill with Na⁺”?
membrane-transport-active-vesicular.explanation: SGLT moving glucose uphill with Na⁺ → Secondary active symport (Na⁺-coupled).

action-potential-genesis.stem: The rapid depolarising (upstroke) phase of the neuronal action potential is caused by:

options.text: K⁺ efflux through voltage-gated K⁺ channels
Na⁺ influx through voltage-gated Na⁺ channels

action-potential-genesis.explanation: Reaching threshold opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels; Na⁺ rushes in, reversing the potential toward +30 mV. Repolarisation is due to Na⁺ inactivation plus K⁺ efflux.

action-potential-genesis.stem: The "all-or-none" property of the action potential means that:

options.text: AP amplitude increases with stronger stimuli
A stimulus at or above threshold produces a full-amplitude AP, and stimulus strength is coded by frequency

action-potential-genesis.explanation: Once threshold is reached, the AP fires at full, fixed amplitude regardless of stimulus strength; a stronger stimulus increases AP frequency, not size. Sub-threshold stimuli produce no AP.

action-potential-genesis.stem: Regarding role of the na⁺/k⁺-atpase in the ap — which is correct?

options.text: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase directly produces the action potential
The AP is generated by ION FLOW through voltage-gated Na⁺ and K⁺ channels; the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase only restores the gradients afterward
Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open → Na⁺ influx

action-potential-genesis.explanation: The pump maintains the gradients over time but is not the fast event; the up/down strokes are passive ion movements through gated channels.

action-potential-genesis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rapid depolarisation to ~+30 mV”?

options.text: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open → Na⁺ influx

action-potential-genesis.explanation: Rapid depolarisation to ~+30 mV → Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open → Na⁺ influx.

action-potential-genesis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Repolarisation back toward rest”?

options.text: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open → Na⁺ influx

action-potential-genesis.explanation: Repolarisation back toward rest → Na⁺ inactivation + voltage-gated K⁺ efflux.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: During the absolute refractory period, a second action potential cannot be generated because:
action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: In the absolute refractory period the Na⁺ channels are inactivated and cannot reopen until the membrane repolarises, so no stimulus—however strong—can trigger another AP. This limits maximum firing frequency and enforces one-way conduction.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: Saltatory conduction in myelinated axons is faster because the action potential:

options.text: Decreases in amplitude as it travels
Jumps between nodes of Ranvier where Na⁺ channels are concentrated

action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: Myelin insulates the internodes, so the AP regenerates only at the nodes of Ranvier and effectively "jumps" between them (saltatory conduction), which is faster and more energy-efficient.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: Regarding why does the ap travel one way? — which is correct?

options.text: The action potential can propagate in both directions along an axon
It travels ONE way because the membrane just behind it is refractory (Na⁺ channels inactivated), so it can only depolarise the forward, non-refractory region

action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: Refractoriness enforces unidirectional (orthodromic) propagation toward the synapse.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: What best explains the finding: “AP amplitude constant along the axon”?
action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: AP amplitude constant along the axon → Regenerative (non-decremental) propagation.

action-potential-propagation-refractory.stem: What best explains the finding: “Impulse jumping node-to-node in a myelinated fibre”?
action-potential-propagation-refractory.explanation: Impulse jumping node-to-node in a myelinated fibre → Saltatory conduction (fast, efficient).

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: During the absolute refractory period, a second action potential cannot be generated because the voltage-gated sodium channels are:

options.text: In the resting (closed but ready) state
Inactivated and unable to reopen until the membrane repolarises

ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: After opening, the sodium channel's inactivation gate closes; these inactivated channels cannot reopen until repolarisation resets them, producing the absolute refractory period that ensures unidirectional propagation.

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: The two defining properties that allow ion channels to generate precise electrical signals are:
ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: Ion channels are selective (a selectivity filter admits specific ions) and gated (they open/close in response to voltage, ligands or mechanical force); together these properties let membranes produce controlled ion movements.

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: Regarding why a neuron is refractory — which is correct?

options.text: A neuron cannot re-fire immediately because the membrane potential is too high

The absolute refractory period exists because the voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are INACTIVATED (their inactivation gate is shut) and cannot reopen until the membrane REPOLARISES — it is a channel-state phenomenon, not simply a voltage level
Na⁺ channels inactivated (cannot reopen until repolarised)

ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: Refractoriness reflects the physical state of the sodium channels (inactivated, needing repolarisation to reset), which is what enforces one-way propagation and caps firing frequency.

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: What best explains the finding: “Absolute refractory period during the action potential”?

options.text: Na⁺ channels inactivated (cannot reopen until repolarised)

ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: Absolute refractory period during the action potential → Na⁺ channels inactivated (cannot reopen until repolarised).

ion-channels-structure-gating.stem: What best explains the finding: “One-way (unidirectional) impulse propagation”?

options.text: Na⁺ channels inactivated (cannot reopen until repolarised)

ion-channels-structure-gating.explanation: One-way (unidirectional) impulse propagation → Refractoriness behind the impulse.

graded-potentials-cable-properties.stem: Which property distinguishes a graded potential from an action potential?

options.text: A graded potential varies in amplitude, can summate, and decays with distance
A graded potential travels without decrement
A graded potential has a refractory period

graded-potentials-cable-properties.explanation: Graded potentials (receptor and synaptic potentials) vary in size with the stimulus, can summate, and spread passively with decay. Action potentials are all-or-none and regenerate to propagate without decrement.

graded-potentials-cable-properties.stem: A longer membrane length (space) constant, allowing a signal to spread further before decaying, results from:

options.text: Low membrane resistance and high axial resistance
High membrane resistance and low axial (internal) resistance

graded-potentials-cable-properties.explanation: The length constant increases when less current leaks across the membrane (high membrane resistance) and current flows more easily along the axon (low axial resistance, favoured by larger diameter and myelination), so the signal spreads further.

graded-potentials-cable-properties.stem: Regarding graded potentials vs action potentials — which is correct?

options.text: Graded potentials propagate long distances the same way action potentials do

Graded potentials spread PASSIVELY and DECAY with distance (they cannot travel far); only the all-or-none ACTION potential regenerates itself to travel long distances without decrement — the graded potential's job is to reach threshold locally

graded-potentials-cable-properties.explanation: Treating graded potentials as long-distance signals ignores their decremental cable behaviour; they integrate inputs to decide firing, while the action potential does the faithful long-range transmission.

graded-potentials-cable-properties.stem: What best explains the finding: “A synaptic potential that varies in size and can summate”?
graded-potentials-cable-properties.explanation: A synaptic potential that varies in size and can summate → Graded potential (EPSP/IPSP).

graded-potentials-cable-properties.stem: What best explains the finding: “Signal decaying with distance from its origin”?
graded-potentials-cable-properties.explanation: Signal decaying with distance from its origin → Passive (electrotonic) spread — cable properties.

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: The resting membrane potential of a neuron (≈ −70 mV) is closest to the equilibrium potential of which ion, and why?

options.text: Na⁺, because Na⁺ channels dominate at rest
K⁺, because the resting membrane is most permeable to K⁺
Cl⁻, because Cl⁻ is actively pumped
Ca²⁺, because of Ca²⁺ leak channels

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: Open K⁺ leak channels make the resting membrane most permeable to K⁺, so the RMP sits near E_K (≈ −90 mV), pulled slightly positive by a small Na⁺ leak.

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: The equilibrium (Nernst) potential of an ion is defined as the membrane voltage at which:

options.text: The ion is actively pumped fastest
The electrical and concentration forces on the ion are balanced, giving no net flux
All channels for the ion are closed
The ion is at its highest concentration

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: At the Nernst/equilibrium potential, the electrical gradient exactly opposes the concentration gradient, so there is no net movement of that ion.

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: Regarding what the rmp is closest to — which is correct?

options.text: The resting membrane potential lies close to the sodium equilibrium potential
The RMP lies close to the POTASSIUM equilibrium potential (E_K ≈ −90 mV) because the resting membrane is most permeable to K⁺
Resting membrane is dominated by K⁺ permeability
Nernst potential for K⁺ (its concentration gradient)

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: At rest, K⁺ leak channels dominate permeability, so the membrane potential is pulled toward E_K, not E_Na.

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: What best explains the finding: “RMP ≈ −70 mV, close to E_K”?

options.text: Nernst potential for K⁺ (its concentration gradient)
Vm (−70) far from E_Na (+60) → inward driving force
Resting membrane is dominated by K⁺ permeability
↑extracellular K⁺ → E_K less negative → RMP less negative

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: RMP ≈ −70 mV, close to E_K → Resting membrane is dominated by K⁺ permeability.

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.stem: What best explains the finding: “E_K ≈ −90 mV”?

options.text: Resting membrane is dominated by K⁺ permeability
Vm (−70) far from E_Na (+60) → inward driving force
↑extracellular K⁺ → E_K less negative → RMP less negative
Nernst potential for K⁺ (its concentration gradient)

resting-membrane-potential-nernst.explanation: E_K ≈ −90 mV → Nernst potential for K⁺ (its concentration gradient).

goldman-rmp-regulation.stem: According to the Goldman equation, the membrane potential at any moment is dominated by:

options.text: The ion with the highest intracellular concentration
The ion to which the membrane is currently most permeable
The ion pumped by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase
Whichever ion has the most negative equilibrium potential

goldman-rmp-regulation.explanation: The Goldman equation weights each ion by its permeability, so the most permeable ion dominates Vm — K⁺ at rest, Na⁺ during the AP upstroke.

goldman-rmp-regulation.stem: Hyperkalaemia (increased extracellular K⁺) affects the resting membrane potential by:

options.text: Depolarising the cell (E_K becomes less negative)

goldman-rmp-regulation.explanation: Raising extracellular K⁺ makes E_K less negative; since the RMP tracks E_K, the cell depolarises — clinically dangerous for cardiac excitability.

goldman-rmp-regulation.stem: Regarding what drives the moment-to-moment vm — which is correct?

options.text: Changes in ion CONCENTRATION cause the rapid changes in membrane potential during signalling
Rapid Vm changes are driven by changes in PERMEABILITY (channels opening/closing), not concentration — the Goldman principle
Highest resting permeability → Vm near E_K

goldman-rmp-regulation.explanation: One AP moves negligible ion amounts; it is the shift in relative permeability (to Na⁺, then K⁺) that swings Vm.

goldman-rmp-regulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Vm swings toward E_Na during the AP”?

options.text: Highest resting permeability → Vm near E_K

goldman-rmp-regulation.explanation: Vm swings toward E_Na during the AP → Na⁺ permeability transiently dominates (Goldman).

goldman-rmp-regulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “RMP set mainly by K⁺ leak channels”?

options.text: Highest resting permeability → Vm near E_K

goldman-rmp-regulation.explanation: RMP set mainly by K⁺ leak channels → Highest resting permeability → Vm near E_K.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: Neurotransmitter release from the presynaptic terminal is triggered by the entry of which ion?
neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: The action potential opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels; Ca²⁺ influx triggers synaptic vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release into the cleft.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: Acetylcholine's action at the synapse is terminated primarily by:
neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: ACh is broken down in the cleft by acetylcholinesterase; monoamines like serotonin/dopamine are instead cleared mainly by reuptake.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: Regarding is a neurotransmitter inherently excitatory? — which is correct?

options.text: Acetylcholine is always excitatory because it activates muscle
The EFFECT depends on the RECEPTOR: ACh excites skeletal muscle (nicotinic) but inhibits/slows the heart (muscarinic)
Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels at the terminal

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: A neurotransmitter's action is determined by the postsynaptic receptor and its ion channel, not the molecule alone.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ca²⁺ influx triggers NT release”?

options.text: Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels at the terminal
Main CNS excitatory vs inhibitory amino-acid NTs

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: Ca²⁺ influx triggers NT release → Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels at the terminal.

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.stem: What best explains the finding: “ACh cleared by acetylcholinesterase”?

options.text: Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels at the terminal
Main CNS excitatory vs inhibitory amino-acid NTs

neurotransmitters-types-lifecycle.explanation: ACh cleared by acetylcholinesterase → Enzymatic degradation in the cleft.

synaptic-transmission-epsp-ipsp.stem: Opening of GABA-A receptor Cl⁻ channels on a neuron produces:
synaptic-transmission-epsp-ipsp.explanation: GABA-A opens Cl⁻ channels; Cl⁻ influx hyperpolarises the cell, producing an IPSP that moves it away from threshold (inhibition). Benzodiazepines enhance this.

synaptic-transmission-epsp-ipsp.stem: A neuron fires an action potential when:

options.text: The summed EPSPs minus IPSPs depolarise the axon hillock to threshold

synaptic-transmission-epsp-ipsp.explanation: The neuron integrates excitatory and inhibitory inputs by temporal and spatial summation; only when the net depolarisation at the axon hillock reaches threshold is an AP triggered.

synaptic-transmission-epsp-ipsp.stem: Regarding epsp/ipsp vs action potential — which is correct?

options.text: Each EPSP is an all-or-none action potential
EPSPs/IPSPs are GRADED, decremental potentials that summate; an all-or-none AP is generated only when their sum reaches threshold at the axon hillock

synaptic-transmission-epsp-ipsp.explanation: Postsynaptic potentials vary in size and decay with distance; the AP is the fixed-amplitude output once threshold is crossed.

synaptic-transmission-epsp-ipsp.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fast, brief postsynaptic current”?
synaptic-transmission-epsp-ipsp.explanation: Fast, brief postsynaptic current → Ionotropic (ligand-gated ion channel).

synaptic-transmission-epsp-ipsp.stem: What best explains the finding: “Slow, prolonged, modulatory response”?
synaptic-transmission-epsp-ipsp.explanation: Slow, prolonged, modulatory response → Metabotropic (GPCR, second messenger).

neuromuscular-junction-transmission.stem: Release of acetylcholine from the motor nerve terminal is directly triggered by:

options.text: Calcium influx through voltage-gated calcium channels

neuromuscular-junction-transmission.explanation: The arriving action potential opens voltage-gated calcium channels; the resulting calcium influx triggers vesicle fusion and acetylcholine release. Without calcium entry, no transmitter is released.

neuromuscular-junction-transmission.stem: Fatigable muscle weakness that improves with an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, caused by antibodies against the postsynaptic receptor, is characteristic of:
neuromuscular-junction-transmission.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is caused by autoantibodies against the postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, producing fatigable weakness that improves when acetylcholinesterase inhibitors raise synaptic ACh. Lambert–Eaton instead targets presynaptic calcium channels.

neuromuscular-junction-transmission.stem: Regarding reliability of neuromuscular transmission — which is correct?

options.text: Like small central synapses, the neuromuscular junction often needs summation of several inputs to fire the muscle

The NMJ end-plate potential is normally LARGE and always SUPRATHRESHOLD (a high safety factor), so a single nerve impulse reliably triggers a muscle action potential — it does not depend on summation like small CNS EPSPs

neuromuscular-junction-transmission.explanation: The NMJ is built for reliability (one-to-one transmission); confusing it with the graded, summating synapses of the CNS misses why neuromuscular transmission normally never fails and why disease (myasthenia) is needed to make it fail.

neuromuscular-junction-transmission.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fatigable weakness improving with an anticholinesterase”?
neuromuscular-junction-transmission.explanation: Fatigable weakness improving with an anticholinesterase → Myasthenia gravis (anti-nicotinic-receptor antibodies).

neuromuscular-junction-transmission.stem: What best explains the finding: “Weakness that improves with repeated use”?
neuromuscular-junction-transmission.explanation: Weakness that improves with repeated use → Lambert–Eaton (anti-presynaptic Ca²⁺ channel).
