neurotransmitter-systems-catalog.stem: The principal excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters of the central nervous system are, respectively:
neurotransmitter-systems-catalog.explanation: Glutamate is the main excitatory CNS transmitter (via AMPA/NMDA receptors), and GABA is the main inhibitory transmitter of the brain (glycine predominates in the spinal cord), opening chloride channels to hyperpolarise.

neurotransmitter-systems-catalog.stem: Acetylcholine can produce different effects at different sites because it acts on:

options.text: Two receptor families — ionotropic nicotinic and G-protein-coupled muscarinic receptors

neurotransmitter-systems-catalog.explanation: Acetylcholine acts on nicotinic receptors (ligand-gated cation channels at the NMJ and autonomic ganglia) and on muscarinic receptors (G-protein-coupled, at parasympathetic targets and in the CNS); the receptor determines the response.

neurotransmitter-systems-catalog.stem: Regarding what makes a synapse excitatory or inhibitory — which is correct?

options.text: A neurotransmitter is intrinsically either excitatory or inhibitory

The SAME transmitter can be excitatory or inhibitory depending on the RECEPTOR and the ion channel it controls — e.g. acetylcholine excites at nicotinic receptors but can inhibit via certain muscarinic receptors; the postsynaptic receptor determines the effect
GABA (brain) and glycine (cord) — open Cl⁻ channels

neurotransmitter-systems-catalog.explanation: Attributing a fixed sign to the transmitter ignores receptor diversity; the ionic consequence (depolarising cation entry vs hyperpolarising Cl⁻ entry) — set by the receptor — is what makes a synapse excitatory or inhibitory.

neurotransmitter-systems-catalog.stem: What best explains the finding: “Main excitatory neurotransmitter of the CNS”?

options.text: GABA (brain) and glycine (cord) — open Cl⁻ channels
Positive modulation of the GABA-A receptor

neurotransmitter-systems-catalog.explanation: Main excitatory neurotransmitter of the CNS → Glutamate (AMPA/NMDA receptors).

neurotransmitter-systems-catalog.stem: What best explains the finding: “Main inhibitory transmitter of the brain vs spinal cord”?

options.text: Positive modulation of the GABA-A receptor
GABA (brain) and glycine (cord) — open Cl⁻ channels

neurotransmitter-systems-catalog.explanation: Main inhibitory transmitter of the brain vs spinal cord → GABA (brain) and glycine (cord) — open Cl⁻ channels.

cell-signaling-modes-receptors.stem: A lipid-soluble steroid hormone produces its effect primarily by:

options.text: Binding an intracellular (nuclear) receptor and altering gene transcription
Activating a receptor tyrosine kinase at the surface
Coupling to a G protein at the membrane

cell-signaling-modes-receptors.explanation: Being lipophilic, steroids cross the membrane and bind intracellular/nuclear receptors to modulate gene transcription — a slower, longer-lasting genomic effect than surface-receptor signalling.

cell-signaling-modes-receptors.stem: Signalling in which a cell secretes a molecule that acts on itself is termed:
cell-signaling-modes-receptors.explanation: Autocrine signalling acts on the secreting cell itself. Endocrine travels via blood to distant targets, paracrine acts on neighbours, and synaptic acts across a synapse.

cell-signaling-modes-receptors.stem: Regarding route of steroid vs peptide hormones — which is correct?

options.text: Steroid hormones act on cell-surface receptors like peptide hormones
Lipophilic steroids/thyroid hormone cross the membrane to INTRACELLULAR (nuclear) receptors → gene transcription; water-soluble peptides use SURFACE receptors

cell-signaling-modes-receptors.explanation: Solubility dictates the route: lipid-soluble → intracellular/genomic (slow, lasting); water-soluble → surface/second-messenger (fast, brief).

cell-signaling-modes-receptors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hormone acting on a distant organ via blood”?
cell-signaling-modes-receptors.explanation: Hormone acting on a distant organ via blood → Endocrine signalling.

cell-signaling-modes-receptors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Insulin binding a receptor tyrosine kinase”?
cell-signaling-modes-receptors.explanation: Insulin binding a receptor tyrosine kinase → Enzyme-linked receptor (autophosphorylation cascade).

second-messenger-systems.stem: Activation of a Gq-coupled receptor leads to phospholipase C cleaving PIP₂ into IP₃ and DAG. The role of IP₃ is to:

options.text: Release Ca²⁺ from the endoplasmic reticulum

second-messenger-systems.explanation: IP₃ diffuses to the ER and opens Ca²⁺ channels, raising cytosolic Ca²⁺; DAG activates protein kinase C. The cAMP pathway (PKA) is separate (Gs/adenylyl cyclase).

second-messenger-systems.stem: A Gs-protein-coupled receptor increases intracellular cAMP by activating:
second-messenger-systems.explanation: Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, which converts ATP to cAMP, activating PKA. Phosphodiesterase degrades cAMP; PLC/PKC belong to the Gq pathway.

second-messenger-systems.stem: Regarding what ip₃ does — which is correct?

options.text: IP₃ activates protein kinase C at the membrane
IP₃ releases Ca²⁺ from the ER; DAG is the one that activates protein kinase C (PKC)
Gq → PLC → IP₃ → ER Ca²⁺ release (+ DAG/PKC)

second-messenger-systems.explanation: From the Gq/PLC split: IP₃ → Ca²⁺ release (cytosolic), DAG → membrane-bound PKC. Don't swap their roles.

second-messenger-systems.stem: What best explains the finding: “β-adrenergic receptor raising cAMP”?

options.text: Gq → PLC → IP₃ → ER Ca²⁺ release (+ DAG/PKC)

second-messenger-systems.explanation: β-adrenergic receptor raising cAMP → Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA.

second-messenger-systems.stem: What best explains the finding: “α1/M1/M3 receptor releasing intracellular Ca²⁺”?

options.text: Gq → PLC → IP₃ → ER Ca²⁺ release (+ DAG/PKC)

second-messenger-systems.explanation: α1/M1/M3 receptor releasing intracellular Ca²⁺ → Gq → PLC → IP₃ → ER Ca²⁺ release (+ DAG/PKC).

synaptic-plasticity-ltp.stem: The NMDA receptor is described as a "coincidence detector" because it opens fully only when:

options.text: Glutamate binds, regardless of membrane potential
Glutamate binds AND the postsynaptic membrane is depolarised (expelling the Mg²⁺ block)

synaptic-plasticity-ltp.explanation: At rest Mg²⁺ blocks the NMDA channel. Only coincident glutamate binding plus depolarisation removes the Mg²⁺, allowing Ca²⁺ entry to trigger LTP — a Hebbian coincidence detector.

synaptic-plasticity-ltp.stem: The transition from early to late long-term potentiation specifically requires:

options.text: Only insertion of existing AMPA receptors
New gene transcription and protein synthesis (CREB-dependent)

synaptic-plasticity-ltp.explanation: Late LTP (maintenance) depends on CREB-driven transcription and new protein synthesis producing structural synaptic changes; early LTP relies on post-translational AMPA-receptor trafficking without new proteins.

synaptic-plasticity-ltp.stem: Regarding why nmda needs two signals — which is correct?

options.text: The NMDA receptor opens as soon as glutamate binds, like AMPA
NMDA needs glutamate AND postsynaptic depolarisation to expel the Mg²⁺ block; only then does Ca²⁺ enter to trigger LTP
Coincidence detector (Mg²⁺ block relieved by depolarisation)

synaptic-plasticity-ltp.explanation: This dual requirement makes NMDA a coincidence detector — the molecular basis of associative (Hebbian) plasticity.

synaptic-plasticity-ltp.stem: What best explains the finding: “NMDA channel needs glutamate AND depolarisation”?

options.text: Coincidence detector (Mg²⁺ block relieved by depolarisation)

synaptic-plasticity-ltp.explanation: NMDA channel needs glutamate AND depolarisation → Coincidence detector (Mg²⁺ block relieved by depolarisation).

synaptic-plasticity-ltp.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ca²⁺ influx through NMDA triggers LTP”?

options.text: Coincidence detector (Mg²⁺ block relieved by depolarisation)

synaptic-plasticity-ltp.explanation: Ca²⁺ influx through NMDA triggers LTP → Ca²⁺ → CaMKII → AMPA receptor insertion.

synaptic-plasticity-ltd-memory.stem: Whether a synapse undergoes long-term potentiation or long-term depression is determined mainly by:

options.text: The pattern and magnitude of calcium entry through NMDA receptors

synaptic-plasticity-ltd-memory.explanation: A large, rapid NMDA-receptor calcium rise favours LTP (inserting AMPA receptors), whereas a small, sustained rise favours LTD (removing AMPA receptors); the calcium signal is the switch between strengthening and weakening.

synaptic-plasticity-ltd-memory.stem: A protein-synthesis inhibitor given after learning blocks long-term memory but spares short-term memory because:

options.text: Short-term memory does not use neurons
Long-term memory consolidation requires new gene transcription and protein synthesis
Short-term memory is stored in muscle
Long-term memory does not involve synapses

synaptic-plasticity-ltd-memory.explanation: Short-term memory depends on transient changes in existing proteins, while long-term memory requires synthesis of new proteins (and structural synaptic change); blocking protein synthesis therefore prevents consolidation but not immediate recall.

synaptic-plasticity-ltd-memory.stem: Regarding requirements for short- vs long-term memory — which is correct?

options.text: All memory formation depends equally on new protein synthesis

SHORT-term memory relies on transient modification of EXISTING proteins/synaptic strength, whereas LONG-term memory (consolidation) requires NEW gene transcription and PROTEIN SYNTHESIS — which is why protein-synthesis inhibitors block long-term but not short-term memory
LTP (large NMDA Ca²⁺ → more AMPA receptors)
LTD (small sustained Ca²⁺ → fewer AMPA receptors)

synaptic-plasticity-ltd-memory.explanation: The distinction explains classic experiments and clinical consolidation: interrupting protein synthesis after learning prevents the memory from becoming permanent while leaving immediate recall intact.

synaptic-plasticity-ltd-memory.stem: What best explains the finding: “Synaptic strengthening after high-frequency stimulation”?

options.text: LTD (small sustained Ca²⁺ → fewer AMPA receptors)
LTP (large NMDA Ca²⁺ → more AMPA receptors)

synaptic-plasticity-ltd-memory.explanation: Synaptic strengthening after high-frequency stimulation → LTP (large NMDA Ca²⁺ → more AMPA receptors).

synaptic-plasticity-ltd-memory.stem: What best explains the finding: “Synaptic weakening after prolonged low-frequency stimulation”?

options.text: LTP (large NMDA Ca²⁺ → more AMPA receptors)
LTD (small sustained Ca²⁺ → fewer AMPA receptors)

synaptic-plasticity-ltd-memory.explanation: Synaptic weakening after prolonged low-frequency stimulation → LTD (small sustained Ca²⁺ → fewer AMPA receptors).

synaptic-plasticity-ltd-memory.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Long-Term Depression & the Basis of Memory”?

options.text: Diffusion & Osmosis: Movement of Solutes and Water

synaptic-plasticity-ltd-memory.explanation: Antidepressants can affect memory and synaptic plasticity.

autonomic-sympathetic-parasympathetic.stem: The parasympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system has its outflow from:

options.text: The cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and sacral segments S2–S4

autonomic-sympathetic-parasympathetic.explanation: The parasympathetic (craniosacral) outflow arises from cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and sacral segments S2–S4. The sympathetic outflow is thoracolumbar (T1–L2).

autonomic-sympathetic-parasympathetic.stem: The adrenal medulla is best described as:

options.text: A modified sympathetic ganglion that secretes adrenaline into the blood
An endocrine gland unrelated to the ANS

autonomic-sympathetic-parasympathetic.explanation: Preganglionic sympathetic fibres synapse directly on adrenal medullary cells (a modified sympathetic ganglion), which release adrenaline/noradrenaline into the blood — a systemic sympathetic response with no postganglionic neuron.

autonomic-sympathetic-parasympathetic.stem: Regarding fibre length by division — which is correct?

options.text: The sympathetic division has long preganglionic and short postganglionic fibres
Sympathetic = SHORT preganglionic / LONG postganglionic (ganglia near the cord); parasympathetic = LONG preganglionic / SHORT postganglionic (ganglia near the organ)

autonomic-sympathetic-parasympathetic.explanation: It follows from ganglion location: sympathetic chain sits near the spinal cord, parasympathetic ganglia sit in/near the target organ.

autonomic-sympathetic-parasympathetic.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sympathetic activation → ↑HR, ↑BP, dilated pupils”?
autonomic-sympathetic-parasympathetic.explanation: Sympathetic activation → ↑HR, ↑BP, dilated pupils → "Fight or flight" response.

autonomic-sympathetic-parasympathetic.stem: What best explains the finding: “Parasympathetic activation → ↓HR, ↑gut motility”?
autonomic-sympathetic-parasympathetic.explanation: Parasympathetic activation → ↓HR, ↑gut motility → "Rest and digest" response.

autonomic-sympathetic-parasympathetic.stem: Which is a clinical application of “The Autonomic Nervous System: Sympathetic vs Parasympathetic”?

Enteric Nervous System, Autonomics & GI Reflexes

autonomic-sympathetic-parasympathetic.explanation: The enteric system is influenced by both divisions of the ANS.

autonomic-sympathetic-parasympathetic.explanation: Understanding homeostasis is essential for grasping ANS functions.

autonomic-neurotransmitters-receptors.stem: The neurotransmitter released by ALL preganglionic autonomic neurons (both sympathetic and parasympathetic) acting on ganglionic receptors is:
autonomic-neurotransmitters-receptors.explanation: Every preganglionic autonomic fibre releases ACh onto nicotinic receptors in the ganglion. Parasympathetic postganglionic fibres then use ACh (muscarinic); most sympathetic postganglionic fibres use noradrenaline (adrenergic).

autonomic-neurotransmitters-receptors.stem: A β1-adrenergic receptor antagonist lowers heart rate because β1 receptors in the heart normally:

options.text: Mediate sympathetic increases in rate and force (via cAMP)

autonomic-neurotransmitters-receptors.explanation: Cardiac β1 receptors respond to sympathetic noradrenaline by raising heart rate and contractility (Gs/cAMP); blocking them slows the heart. β2 mediates bronchodilation; α1 vasoconstriction.

autonomic-neurotransmitters-receptors.stem: Regarding transmitter at sweat glands — which is correct?

options.text: All sympathetic postganglionic fibres release noradrenaline
Sympathetic fibres to SWEAT GLANDS are the exception — they release acetylcholine (sympathetic cholinergic) onto muscarinic receptors
All preganglionic fibres use ACh → nicotinic
Blocks vagal M2 → removes parasympathetic slowing

autonomic-neurotransmitters-receptors.explanation: Most sympathetic postganglionic fibres are noradrenergic, but sweat glands (and the adrenal medulla pathway) break the rule.

autonomic-neurotransmitters-receptors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ganglionic transmission blocked by a nicotinic antagonist”?

options.text: Blocks vagal M2 → removes parasympathetic slowing
Blocks sympathetic β1 (cAMP) in the SA node
All preganglionic fibres use ACh → nicotinic

autonomic-neurotransmitters-receptors.explanation: Ganglionic transmission blocked by a nicotinic antagonist → All preganglionic fibres use ACh → nicotinic.

autonomic-neurotransmitters-receptors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Atropine (muscarinic antagonist) raises heart rate”?

options.text: All preganglionic fibres use ACh → nicotinic
Blocks sympathetic β1 (cAMP) in the SA node
Blocks vagal M2 → removes parasympathetic slowing

autonomic-neurotransmitters-receptors.explanation: Atropine (muscarinic antagonist) raises heart rate → Blocks vagal M2 → removes parasympathetic slowing.

reflex-arc-stretch-withdrawal.stem: The patellar (knee-jerk) reflex is a monosynaptic stretch reflex in which the afferent signal comes from the:
reflex-arc-stretch-withdrawal.explanation: Stretching the quadriceps activates its muscle spindles; Ia afferents synapse directly on α-motor neurons (one synapse) to contract the same muscle. The Golgi tendon organ senses tension, not stretch.

reflex-arc-stretch-withdrawal.stem: In the flexor (withdrawal) reflex, contraction of the flexor muscles is accompanied by relaxation of the antagonist extensors through:

options.text: Direct α-motor neuron activation of the extensors

reflex-arc-stretch-withdrawal.explanation: The polysynaptic withdrawal reflex uses interneurons to excite flexors while reciprocally inhibiting the antagonist extensors, allowing an unopposed protective withdrawal.

reflex-arc-stretch-withdrawal.stem: Regarding spindle vs golgi tendon organ — which is correct?

options.text: The Golgi tendon organ senses muscle stretch/length like the muscle spindle
The muscle SPINDLE senses length/stretch (stretch reflex); the GOLGI TENDON ORGAN senses TENSION (inverse stretch reflex, protective inhibition)

reflex-arc-stretch-withdrawal.explanation: They are complementary proprioceptors with opposite reflex effects — spindle excites the muscle, GTO inhibits it.

reflex-arc-stretch-withdrawal.stem: What best explains the finding: “Knee-jerk (patellar) reflex”?
reflex-arc-stretch-withdrawal.explanation: Knee-jerk (patellar) reflex → Monosynaptic stretch reflex (spindle → Ia → α-motor).

reflex-arc-stretch-withdrawal.stem: What best explains the finding: “Muscle spindle detects stretch/length”?
reflex-arc-stretch-withdrawal.explanation: Muscle spindle detects stretch/length → Afferent for the stretch reflex.

reflex-arc-stretch-withdrawal.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Reflexes: The Reflex Arc, Stretch & Withdrawal”?

reflex-arc-stretch-withdrawal.explanation: Reflexes may be affected in patients undergoing steroid withdrawal.

muscle-spindle-golgi-tendon-organ.stem: The muscle spindle and the Golgi tendon organ respectively sense:
muscle-spindle-golgi-tendon-organ.explanation: The muscle spindle lies in parallel with muscle fibres and senses length/stretch (driving reflex contraction), while the Golgi tendon organ lies in series in the tendon and senses tension/force (driving reflex relaxation).

options.text: A monosynaptic reflex from the Ia afferent directly onto the α-motor neuron
Mediated by the Golgi tendon organ

muscle-spindle-golgi-tendon-organ.explanation: Tapping the tendon stretches the muscle spindle; its Ia afferent synapses directly (monosynaptically) on the α-motor neuron of the same muscle, causing reflex contraction — the deep tendon reflex tested clinically.

muscle-spindle-golgi-tendon-organ.stem: Regarding what the muscle spindle vs golgi tendon organ senses — which is correct?

options.text: The muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ both sense the same thing (muscle activity)

They sense DIFFERENT variables: the muscle SPINDLE (in parallel) senses LENGTH/stretch and drives reflex CONTRACTION, while the GOLGI TENDON ORGAN (in series) senses TENSION/force and drives reflex RELAXATION

muscle-spindle-golgi-tendon-organ.explanation: Their parallel-vs-series arrangement and length-vs-tension roles give opposite reflex effects; conflating them loses the logic of how the two feedback systems balance muscle length and load.

muscle-spindle-golgi-tendon-organ.stem: What best explains the finding: “Tendon tap → reflex muscle contraction (knee jerk)”?
muscle-spindle-golgi-tendon-organ.explanation: Tendon tap → reflex muscle contraction (knee jerk) → Monosynaptic stretch reflex (spindle → Ia → α-motor).

muscle-spindle-golgi-tendon-organ.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sudden relaxation when a muscle generates very high tension”?
muscle-spindle-golgi-tendon-organ.explanation: Sudden relaxation when a muscle generates very high tension → Golgi tendon organ (inverse myotatic reflex).

muscle-spindle-golgi-tendon-organ.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Muscle Spindles & Golgi Tendon Organs”?

options.text: Diffusion & Osmosis: Movement of Solutes and Water

muscle-spindle-golgi-tendon-organ.explanation: This module connects proprioceptors with spinal reflexes, relevant to the muscle spindle and GTO.

reflex-types-clinical-testing.stem: Increased deep tendon reflexes, clonus, spasticity and an extensor plantar (Babinski) response indicate a lesion of the:
reflex-types-clinical-testing.explanation: Loss of descending inhibition in an upper motor neuron lesion releases the stretch reflex, producing hyper-reflexia, clonus, spasticity and a Babinski sign. Lower motor neuron lesions cause the opposite (areflexia, flaccidity, wasting).

reflex-types-clinical-testing.stem: The flexor withdrawal reflex differs from the knee-jerk reflex in that it is:

options.text: Polysynaptic, involving interneurons (and a crossed-extensor component)
Mediated by the Golgi tendon organ

reflex-types-clinical-testing.explanation: The withdrawal reflex is polysynaptic: nociceptor afferents act through interneurons to flex the stimulated limb and (via the crossed-extensor reflex) extend the opposite limb for support. The stretch reflex is monosynaptic.

reflex-types-clinical-testing.stem: Regarding interpreting reflex changes — which is correct?

options.text: Weakness with absent reflexes and weakness with brisk reflexes point to the same kind of lesion

ABSENT/reduced reflexes with flaccidity, wasting and fasciculations indicate a LOWER motor neuron lesion, whereas INCREASED reflexes with spasticity, clonus and a Babinski sign indicate an UPPER motor neuron lesion — the reflex pattern localises the lesion

reflex-types-clinical-testing.explanation: Both cause weakness, but the reflex/tone pattern is what distinguishes an upper- from a lower-motor-neuron problem, directing the differential and localisation entirely differently.

reflex-types-clinical-testing.stem: What best explains the finding: “Brisk (4+) reflexes with clonus and up-going plantar”?

options.text: Segmental testing of the reflex arc

reflex-types-clinical-testing.explanation: Brisk (4+) reflexes with clonus and up-going plantar → Upper motor neuron lesion.

reflex-types-clinical-testing.stem: What best explains the finding: “Absent reflexes with flaccid, wasted, fasciculating muscle”?

options.text: Segmental testing of the reflex arc

reflex-types-clinical-testing.explanation: Absent reflexes with flaccid, wasted, fasciculating muscle → Lower motor neuron lesion.

reflex-types-clinical-testing.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Reflex Types & Clinical Testing”?

reflex-types-clinical-testing.explanation: Proprioceptors are integral to understanding reflexes and their clinical implications.

apoptosis-necrosis.stem: Which feature distinguishes apoptosis from necrosis?

options.text: Apoptosis causes cell swelling and inflammation
Apoptosis is a controlled, energy-dependent process with an intact membrane and no inflammation

apoptosis-necrosis.explanation: Apoptosis is active/programmed: the cell shrinks, forms apoptotic bodies, keeps its membrane intact, and provokes no inflammation. Necrosis is passive injury with swelling, rupture, and inflammation.

apoptosis-necrosis.stem: The intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway of apoptosis is triggered by internal stress/DNA damage and involves the release of:

options.text: Cytochrome c from mitochondria, activating caspases

apoptosis-necrosis.explanation: In the intrinsic pathway, pro-apoptotic Bax/Bak (opposing Bcl-2) permeabilise mitochondria to release cytochrome c, which activates the caspase cascade. Fas ligand drives the extrinsic pathway.

apoptosis-necrosis.stem: Regarding inflammation in cell death — which is correct?

options.text: Both apoptosis and necrosis cause inflammation
Apoptosis does NOT cause inflammation (membrane stays intact, cleanly phagocytosed); NECROSIS does (membrane ruptures, contents spill)

apoptosis-necrosis.explanation: The intact vs ruptured membrane is the key distinction — apoptosis is tidy and non-inflammatory, necrosis is messy and inflammatory.

apoptosis-necrosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cell shrinkage + apoptotic bodies, no inflammation”?
apoptosis-necrosis.explanation: Cell shrinkage + apoptotic bodies, no inflammation → Apoptosis (programmed, membrane intact).

apoptosis-necrosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cell swelling + membrane rupture + inflammation”?
apoptosis-necrosis.explanation: Cell swelling + membrane rupture + inflammation → Necrosis (injury-induced).

cellular-aging-theories.stem: Progressive shortening of telomeres with each cell division contributes to aging by:

options.text: Limiting the number of times a cell can divide (replicative senescence)
Directly causing apoptosis of all cells immediately

cellular-aging-theories.explanation: Telomeres cap chromosome ends and shorten with each division; once critically short, the cell can no longer divide (replicative senescence). Telomerase, which extends them, is largely absent in somatic cells but reactivated in cancer.

cellular-aging-theories.stem: A hallmark of cellular senescence is that the cell:

options.text: Is irreversibly arrested yet metabolically active, secreting inflammatory factors (SASP)

cellular-aging-theories.explanation: Senescent cells are permanently withdrawn from the cell cycle but remain alive and active, secreting the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) that promotes tissue inflammation ("inflammaging").

cellular-aging-theories.stem: Regarding senescence vs apoptosis — which is correct?

options.text: A senescent cell is a dead cell
A senescent cell is ALIVE but permanently unable to divide (irreversible arrest) and metabolically active — secreting inflammatory SASP factors; it is not the same as apoptotic death

cellular-aging-theories.explanation: Senescence = growth arrest (a living, non-dividing state); apoptosis = programmed death. Both limit damaged cells but differ fundamentally.

cellular-aging-theories.stem: What best explains the finding: “Telomere shortening with each division”?
cellular-aging-theories.explanation: Telomere shortening with each division → Replicative "clock" limiting cell divisions.

cellular-aging-theories.stem: What best explains the finding: “ROS-induced damage to DNA/proteins/lipids”?
cellular-aging-theories.explanation: ROS-induced damage to DNA/proteins/lipids → Free-radical (oxidative) theory of aging.

cellular-aging-theories.stem: Which should you review before “Mechanisms of Cellular Aging & Senescence”?

cellular-aging-theories.explanation: Understanding telomere shortening is crucial for grasping the genetic/telomere theory of aging.

cell-injury-free-radicals.stem: The earliest, reversible morphological manifestation of acute cell injury (e.g. from hypoxia) is:

options.text: Cellular swelling due to failure of the ATP-dependent Na⁺/K⁺ pump
Massive calcium influx with membrane rupture

cell-injury-free-radicals.explanation: ATP depletion in hypoxia disables the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, so sodium and water enter the cell, causing cellular swelling — the earliest reversible change. Membrane rupture and massive calcium influx mark irreversible injury.

cell-injury-free-radicals.stem: Free radicals (reactive oxygen species) injure cells principally by:

options.text: Lipid peroxidation of membranes, protein oxidation and DNA damage

cell-injury-free-radicals.explanation: Reactive oxygen species have unpaired electrons that damage cells through lipid peroxidation of membranes, oxidation of proteins and DNA damage; antioxidant enzymes (superoxide dismutase, catalase) and vitamins C and E defend against them.

cell-injury-free-radicals.stem: Regarding the point of irreversibility in cell injury — which is correct?

options.text: Cellular swelling means the cell is already dead

Cellular SWELLING is a REVERSIBLE change (from ATP-dependent pump failure); the cell only becomes irreversibly injured once there is severe MEMBRANE damage, massive CALCIUM influx and MITOCHONDRIAL failure — that is the point of no return

cell-injury-free-radicals.explanation: Distinguishing reversible swelling from irreversible membrane/mitochondrial collapse determines whether restoring oxygen/ATP can still save the cell — the rationale for prompt reperfusion in ischaemia.

cell-injury-free-radicals.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cellular swelling as an early injury change”?
cell-injury-free-radicals.explanation: Cellular swelling as an early injury change → ATP depletion → Na⁺/K⁺ pump failure (reversible).

cell-injury-free-radicals.stem: What best explains the finding: “Massive Ca²⁺ influx with membrane rupture”?
cell-injury-free-radicals.explanation: Massive Ca²⁺ influx with membrane rupture → Irreversible injury (point of no return).

cell-injury-free-radicals.stem: Which should you review before “Cell Injury & Free Radicals”?

options.text: Diffusion & Osmosis: Movement of Solutes and Water

cell-injury-free-radicals.explanation: Understanding metabolism is essential for grasping cell injury mechanisms.

msk-embryo-somites.stem: The vertebrae and ribs of the axial skeleton develop from which part of the somite?
msk-embryo-somites.explanation: The sclerotome gives rise to the vertebrae and ribs (axial skeleton) by endochondral ossification. The myotome forms skeletal muscle and the dermatome the dermis of the back.

msk-embryo-somites.stem: Resegmentation during vertebral development refers to:

options.text: Fusion of the caudal half of one sclerotome with the cranial half of the next, so each vertebra derives from two somites
The splitting of a single somite into ten vertebrae
Migration of neural crest into the somite
The formation of ribs from the myotome

msk-embryo-somites.explanation: Resegmentation joins the caudal half of one sclerotome to the cranial half of the adjacent one, so each vertebra forms from two somites — allowing segmental muscles and nerves to span the intervertebral joints.

msk-embryo-somites.stem: Regarding which somite part makes bone? — which is correct?

options.text: The SCLEROTOME forms the vertebrae and ribs; the myotome forms skeletal muscle
Endochondral ossification of the axial skeleton

msk-embryo-somites.explanation: "Sclero" = hard/skeleton. Sclerotome → bone, myotome → muscle, dermatome → dermis — a guaranteed exam distinction.

msk-embryo-somites.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sclerotome forms vertebrae and ribs”?

options.text: Endochondral ossification of the axial skeleton

msk-embryo-somites.explanation: Sclerotome forms vertebrae and ribs → Endochondral ossification of the axial skeleton.

msk-embryo-somites.stem: What best explains the finding: “Myotome forms skeletal muscle”?

options.text: Endochondral ossification of the axial skeleton

msk-embryo-somites.explanation: Myotome forms skeletal muscle → Myoblasts fuse into myotubes → fibres.

msk-embryo-somites.stem: Which should you review before “MSK Embryology: Somites & the Axial Skeleton”?

options.text: Muscle Contraction: The Sliding Filament & Cross-Bridge Cycle

msk-embryo-somites.explanation: Understanding ossification is crucial for grasping how somites contribute to bone formation.

msk-embryo-limb-joints.stem: The zone of polarizing activity (ZPA) patterns which limb axis, and via which signalling molecule?
msk-embryo-limb-joints.explanation: The ZPA secretes SHH to establish the anteroposterior axis; an ectopic ZPA causes mirror-image polydactyly. The AER (FGF) drives proximodistal outgrowth; dorsal ectoderm (Wnt) sets the dorsoventral axis.

msk-embryo-limb-joints.stem: A freely movable (synovial) joint develops when the mesenchymal interzone between two cartilage models:

options.text: Cavitates to form a joint cavity

msk-embryo-limb-joints.explanation: In synovial (diarthrosis) joints the interzone cavitates to form the joint cavity lined by synovium. If it becomes fibrous → synarthrosis; cartilaginous → amphiarthrosis.

msk-embryo-limb-joints.stem: Regarding aer vs zpa function — which is correct?

options.text: The apical ectodermal ridge determines the anteroposterior (thumb-to-little-finger) axis
The AER drives PROXIMODISTAL outgrowth (limb length); the ZPA (via SHH) sets the ANTEROPOSTERIOR axis
FGF signalling over the progress zone

msk-embryo-limb-joints.explanation: Two different centres, two different axes — AER = out/length, ZPA = front-to-back digit identity.

msk-embryo-limb-joints.stem: What best explains the finding: “AER drives proximodistal limb outgrowth”?

options.text: FGF signalling over the progress zone

msk-embryo-limb-joints.explanation: AER drives proximodistal limb outgrowth → FGF signalling over the progress zone.

msk-embryo-limb-joints.stem: What best explains the finding: “ZPA (SHH) sets the anteroposterior axis”?

options.text: FGF signalling over the progress zone

msk-embryo-limb-joints.explanation: ZPA (SHH) sets the anteroposterior axis → Ectopic ZPA → mirror-image polydactyly.

msk-embryo-limb-joints.stem: Which should you review before “MSK Embryology: Limb Development, Ossification & Joints”?

options.text: Muscle Contraction: The Sliding Filament & Cross-Bridge Cycle

msk-embryo-limb-joints.explanation: Understanding cartilage types is essential for grasping joint formation.

nmj-structure-transmission.stem: The depolarisation of the motor end plate produced when acetylcholine opens nicotinic receptors is called the:
nmj-structure-transmission.explanation: ACh binding opens nicotinic cation channels → Na⁺ influx → the end-plate potential (EPP), which (thanks to the safety factor) always exceeds threshold and triggers a muscle action potential.

nmj-structure-transmission.stem: Release of acetylcholine from the motor nerve terminal is directly triggered by the influx of:
nmj-structure-transmission.explanation: The nerve action potential opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels; Ca²⁺ influx triggers fusion of ACh vesicles with the presynaptic membrane (quantal release).

nmj-structure-transmission.stem: Regarding receptor type at the nmj — which is correct?

options.text: Acetylcholine acts on muscarinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction
The NMJ uses NICOTINIC (ionotropic) ACh receptors on the motor end plate; muscarinic receptors are at parasympathetic target organs
Nicotinic-receptor Na⁺ influx depolarises the end plate
Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels at the terminal

nmj-structure-transmission.explanation: Skeletal-muscle end-plate receptors are nicotinic cation channels — muscarinic (GPCR) receptors belong to the autonomic (parasympathetic) system.

nmj-structure-transmission.stem: What best explains the finding: “End-plate potential (EPP)”?

options.text: Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels at the terminal
Nicotinic-receptor Na⁺ influx depolarises the end plate

nmj-structure-transmission.explanation: End-plate potential (EPP) → Nicotinic-receptor Na⁺ influx depolarises the end plate.

nmj-structure-transmission.stem: What best explains the finding: “ACh release requires Ca²⁺ entry”?

options.text: Nicotinic-receptor Na⁺ influx depolarises the end plate
Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels at the terminal

nmj-structure-transmission.explanation: ACh release requires Ca²⁺ entry → Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels at the terminal.

nmj-drugs-disorders.stem: A patient has fatigable ptosis and diplopia that worsen through the day. The most likely cause is autoantibodies against:
nmj-drugs-disorders.explanation: Myasthenia gravis is caused by antibodies against the postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptor, reducing functional receptors and causing fatigable weakness. Anti-Ca²⁺-channel antibodies cause LEMS (which improves with use).

nmj-drugs-disorders.stem: Botulinum toxin causes flaccid paralysis by:

options.text: Preventing acetylcholine release from the nerve terminal

nmj-drugs-disorders.explanation: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins, blocking ACh vesicle release presynaptically → flaccid paralysis. Curare blocks the receptor; succinylcholine causes depolarising block; AChE inhibitors raise ACh.

nmj-drugs-disorders.stem: Regarding mg vs lems with repeated use — which is correct?

options.text: Both myasthenia gravis and Lambert-Eaton syndrome worsen with repeated muscle use
MG (postsynaptic receptor loss) gets WORSE with use (fatigable); LEMS (presynaptic Ca²⁺-channel/ACh-release defect) IMPROVES with use

nmj-drugs-disorders.explanation: In LEMS, repeated activity builds up presynaptic Ca²⁺ → more ACh release → temporary improvement; in MG the receptor deficit only fatigues further.

nmj-drugs-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fatigable ptosis/diplopia, worse with use”?

options.text: AChE inhibition raises ACh to outcompete the blocker

nmj-drugs-disorders.explanation: Fatigable ptosis/diplopia, worse with use → Myasthenia gravis (anti-nicotinic-AChR antibodies).

nmj-drugs-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Proximal weakness improving with repeated use”?

options.text: AChE inhibition raises ACh to outcompete the blocker

nmj-drugs-disorders.explanation: Proximal weakness improving with repeated use → LEMS (anti-Ca²⁺ channel; paraneoplastic, SCLC).

muscle-contraction-crossbridge.stem: In the cross-bridge cycle, the binding of a new ATP molecule to the myosin head causes:
muscle-contraction-crossbridge.explanation: ATP binding to myosin releases it from actin (detachment). Subsequent hydrolysis re-cocks the head. Rigor occurs when no ATP is available to detach the head.

muscle-contraction-crossbridge.stem: Rigor mortis develops after death because:

options.text: ATP is depleted, so cross-bridges cannot detach and remain bound
Ca²⁺ is actively pumped out of the cytosol

muscle-contraction-crossbridge.explanation: Without ATP, myosin cannot detach from actin, so the cross-bridges lock in the rigor state, producing the stiffness of rigor mortis.

muscle-contraction-crossbridge.stem: Regarding role of atp in the cross-bridge cycle — which is correct?

options.text: ATP is only needed to power contraction, not to relax the muscle
ATP is also required to DETACH myosin from actin — without it the cross-bridges cannot release (rigor)
Detachment step of the cross-bridge cycle

muscle-contraction-crossbridge.explanation: ATP binding (not hydrolysis) breaks the actin–myosin bond; this is why ATP depletion after death causes rigor mortis.

muscle-contraction-crossbridge.stem: What best explains the finding: “I band and H zone shorten; A band constant”?

options.text: Detachment step of the cross-bridge cycle
Head pivots, pulling the thin filament

muscle-contraction-crossbridge.explanation: I band and H zone shorten; A band constant → Sliding filament (thin slides over thick).

muscle-contraction-crossbridge.stem: What best explains the finding: “ATP binding needed to release myosin from actin”?

options.text: Head pivots, pulling the thin filament
Detachment step of the cross-bridge cycle

muscle-contraction-crossbridge.explanation: ATP binding needed to release myosin from actin → Detachment step of the cross-bridge cycle.

muscle-contraction-crossbridge.stem: Which should you review before “Muscle Contraction: The Sliding Filament & Cross-Bridge Cycle”?

excitation-contraction-coupling.stem: In skeletal muscle excitation–contraction coupling, cytosolic Ca²⁺ initiates contraction by binding to:

options.text: Troponin C, moving tropomyosin off the actin binding sites

excitation-contraction-coupling.explanation: Ca²⁺ binds troponin C, which shifts the troponin–tropomyosin complex to uncover myosin-binding sites on actin, allowing cross-bridge cycling. DHPR/RyR release the Ca²⁺; SERCA removes it for relaxation.

excitation-contraction-coupling.stem: Malignant hyperthermia triggered by volatile anaesthetics is caused by a mutation in the:

options.text: Ryanodine receptor (RYR1), causing uncontrolled SR Ca²⁺ release

excitation-contraction-coupling.explanation: A RYR1 mutation makes the SR Ca²⁺-release channel hypersensitive; anaesthetics/succinylcholine trigger massive Ca²⁺ release → sustained contraction and a hypermetabolic crisis, treated with dantrolene (a RyR blocker).

excitation-contraction-coupling.stem: Regarding is relaxation passive? — which is correct?

options.text: Muscle relaxation is a passive process requiring no energy
Relaxation is ACTIVE — SERCA uses ATP to pump Ca²⁺ back into the SR so tropomyosin can re-block actin
Moves tropomyosin off actin binding sites
Voltage sensor triggers SR Ca²⁺ release

excitation-contraction-coupling.explanation: Removing cytosolic Ca²⁺ against its gradient needs ATP; both contraction and relaxation are energy-dependent.

excitation-contraction-coupling.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ca²⁺ binding troponin C initiates contraction”?

options.text: Voltage sensor triggers SR Ca²⁺ release
Moves tropomyosin off actin binding sites

excitation-contraction-coupling.explanation: Ca²⁺ binding troponin C initiates contraction → Moves tropomyosin off actin binding sites.

excitation-contraction-coupling.stem: What best explains the finding: “DHPR (T-tubule) coupled to RyR (SR)”?

options.text: Moves tropomyosin off actin binding sites
Voltage sensor triggers SR Ca²⁺ release

excitation-contraction-coupling.explanation: DHPR (T-tubule) coupled to RyR (SR) → Voltage sensor triggers SR Ca²⁺ release.

muscle-twitch-tetanus-mechanics.stem: Increasing the frequency of stimulation of a skeletal muscle fibre until individual twitches fuse into a single smooth maximal contraction produces:
muscle-twitch-tetanus-mechanics.explanation: High-frequency stimulation causes temporal summation of twitches into unfused then fused (complete) tetanus — a smooth, sustained, maximal contraction.

muscle-twitch-tetanus-mechanics.stem: A muscle generates its greatest active tension when it is at a length that:

options.text: Provides optimal overlap between actin and myosin filaments

muscle-twitch-tetanus-mechanics.explanation: The length–tension relationship shows maximal force at the sarcomere length giving optimal actin–myosin overlap (most cross-bridges); over-stretch or over-shortening reduces force.

muscle-twitch-tetanus-mechanics.stem: Regarding summation vs treppe — which is correct?

options.text: Treppe and frequency summation are the same phenomenon
Summation needs INCREASING stimulus FREQUENCY (twitches overlap); treppe is a warm-up increase in force at the SAME frequency/strength

muscle-twitch-tetanus-mechanics.explanation: Summation = higher frequency adds tension toward tetanus; treppe = progressive warm-up potentiation at constant stimulation.

muscle-twitch-tetanus-mechanics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Smooth sustained maximal contraction at high frequency”?
muscle-twitch-tetanus-mechanics.explanation: Smooth sustained maximal contraction at high frequency → Fused (complete) tetanus.

muscle-twitch-tetanus-mechanics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Tension adds when stimuli arrive close together”?
muscle-twitch-tetanus-mechanics.explanation: Tension adds when stimuli arrive close together → Temporal (frequency) summation.

muscle-twitch-tetanus-mechanics.stem: Which should you review before “Muscle Mechanics: Twitch, Tetanus & Length–Tension”?

motor-unit-recruitment.stem: According to the size principle, when a muscle gradually increases its force output, motor units are recruited:

options.text: Smallest (weakest, most fatigue-resistant) first, then progressively larger

motor-unit-recruitment.explanation: The size principle recruits small, slow, fatigue-resistant (type I) units first for fine control, adding larger, fast, fatigable (type II) units as more force is needed.

motor-unit-recruitment.stem: A motor unit is defined as:

options.text: A single muscle fibre and its sarcomeres
One motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it innervates
A group of motor neurons in the spinal cord

motor-unit-recruitment.explanation: A motor unit comprises one motor neuron plus all the muscle fibres it innervates; all those fibres contract together when the neuron fires.

motor-unit-recruitment.stem: Regarding recruitment order — which is correct?

options.text: The largest, most powerful motor units are recruited first for any movement
By the SIZE PRINCIPLE, the SMALLEST (weak, fatigue-resistant) units are recruited first; larger, fatigable units are added only as more force is required
Size principle (small type I units first)

motor-unit-recruitment.explanation: Smallest-first gives fine control at low forces and reserves powerful, fatigable units for high-force demands.

motor-unit-recruitment.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fine-movement muscles have small motor units”?

options.text: Size principle (small type I units first)

motor-unit-recruitment.explanation: Fine-movement muscles have small motor units → Low innervation ratio → precise control (eye/hand).

motor-unit-recruitment.stem: What best explains the finding: “Weak, fatigue-resistant units recruited first”?

options.text: Size principle (small type I units first)

motor-unit-recruitment.explanation: Weak, fatigue-resistant units recruited first → Size principle (small type I units first).

motor-unit-recruitment.stem: Which should you review before “Motor Units & the Size Principle”?

muscle-energy-systems.stem: The energy system that provides ATP most rapidly during the first few seconds of maximal exercise is:
muscle-energy-systems.explanation: Phosphocreatine regenerates ATP instantly via creatine kinase (no oxygen), powering the first ~10 seconds. Glycolysis then predominates, followed by aerobic metabolism for sustained activity.

muscle-energy-systems.stem: The "oxygen debt" (excess post-exercise oxygen consumption) after intense exercise is used mainly to:
muscle-energy-systems.explanation: Post-exercise oxygen consumption stays elevated to regenerate phosphocreatine and ATP, oxidise/clear lactate, and restore myoglobin oxygen — repaying the anaerobic "debt."

muscle-energy-systems.stem: Regarding atp yield of anaerobic vs aerobic — which is correct?

options.text: Anaerobic glycolysis produces about the same amount of ATP as aerobic metabolism
Anaerobic glycolysis yields only ~2 ATP per glucose (+ lactate); aerobic (oxidative) metabolism yields ~30+ ATP per glucose

muscle-energy-systems.explanation: Anaerobic is fast but low-yield; aerobic is slower but vastly more efficient — hence its role in endurance.

muscle-energy-systems.stem: What best explains the finding: “First ~10 s of maximal effort”?

options.text: Oxygen debt (EPOC) — repay PCr, clear lactate

muscle-energy-systems.explanation: First ~10 s of maximal effort → Phosphocreatine system (instant, O₂-independent).

muscle-energy-systems.stem: What best explains the finding: “Lactate rises during intense exercise”?

options.text: Oxygen debt (EPOC) — repay PCr, clear lactate

muscle-energy-systems.explanation: Lactate rises during intense exercise → Anaerobic glycolysis (2 ATP, no O₂).

muscle-energy-systems.stem: Which should you review before “Energy Systems of Skeletal Muscle”?

options.text: MSK Embryology: Somites & the Axial Skeleton
MSK Embryology: Limb Development, Ossification & Joints

muscle-energy-systems.explanation: Glycolysis is a key process in anaerobic energy production.

muscle-fiber-types-fatigue.stem: Which fibre type is slow-twitch, rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, uses aerobic metabolism, and is resistant to fatigue?
muscle-fiber-types-fatigue.explanation: Type I (slow oxidative) fibres are red (high myoglobin), mitochondria-rich, aerobic, and fatigue-resistant — suited to posture and endurance. Type II fibres are fast, glycolytic, and fatigue quickly.

muscle-fiber-types-fatigue.stem: Peripheral muscle fatigue during sustained maximal contraction is primarily due to:

options.text: Complete depletion of ATP causing rigor
Accumulation of inorganic phosphate and H⁺ (lactate) plus impaired Ca²⁺ handling

muscle-fiber-types-fatigue.explanation: Fatigue is mainly metabolic: rising Pi and H⁺/lactate and impaired SR Ca²⁺ release reduce force. ATP is defended (true exhaustion would cause rigor), and central (CNS) factors also contribute.

muscle-fiber-types-fatigue.stem: Regarding cause of muscle fatigue — which is correct?

options.text: Muscle fatigue occurs because ATP is completely used up
Fatigue is mainly metabolic — accumulation of Pi, H⁺/lactate, impaired Ca²⁺ release/handling, and glycogen depletion — not complete ATP exhaustion (which would cause rigor)

muscle-fiber-types-fatigue.explanation: Cells defend ATP levels; if ATP truly ran out, cross-bridges would lock (rigor). Fatigue reflects metabolic by-products and Ca²⁺ dysfunction.

muscle-fiber-types-fatigue.stem: What best explains the finding: “Red, myoglobin-rich, mitochondria-dense fibre”?
muscle-fiber-types-fatigue.explanation: Red, myoglobin-rich, mitochondria-dense fibre → Type I (slow oxidative, fatigue-resistant).

muscle-fiber-types-fatigue.stem: What best explains the finding: “White, glycolytic, fast-fatiguing fibre”?
muscle-fiber-types-fatigue.explanation: White, glycolytic, fast-fatiguing fibre → Type IIx (fast glycolytic, power).

muscle-fiber-types-fatigue.stem: Which should you review before “Muscle Fibre Types & Fatigue”?

MSK Embryology: Limb Development, Ossification & Joints

fracture-classification.stem: A fracture in which the overlying skin is broken and the bone is exposed to the environment is termed:
fracture-classification.explanation: An open (compound) fracture breaches the skin, carrying a high infection risk and requiring urgent debridement and antibiotics. A closed fracture has intact skin.

fracture-classification.stem: Complete loss of contact between the articular surfaces of a joint is called:
fracture-classification.explanation: A dislocation is complete displacement with no contact between the joint surfaces; a subluxation is partial. A sprain injures a ligament, a strain a muscle/tendon.

fracture-classification.stem: Regarding dislocation vs subluxation — which is correct?

options.text: A subluxation and a dislocation mean the same degree of joint displacement
A dislocation is COMPLETE loss of contact between the joint surfaces; a subluxation is PARTIAL displacement (surfaces still partly in contact)

fracture-classification.explanation: Degree differs: complete (dislocation) vs partial (subluxation) — an easy exam distinction.

fracture-classification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bone protruding through the skin”?
fracture-classification.explanation: Bone protruding through the skin → Open (compound) fracture → infection risk.

fracture-classification.stem: What best explains the finding: “Incomplete bending fracture in a child”?
fracture-classification.explanation: Incomplete bending fracture in a child → Greenstick fracture (soft paediatric bone).

fracture-classification.stem: Which should you review before “Fractures & Joint Injuries: Classification”?

options.text: MSK Embryology: Somites & the Axial Skeleton

fracture-classification.explanation: Understanding humerus fractures is essential for classifying fractures.

fracture-healing.stem: Place the stages of secondary fracture healing in the correct order:

options.text: Soft callus → haematoma → remodelling → hard callus
Haematoma/inflammation → soft callus → hard callus → remodelling
Remodelling → hard callus → soft callus → haematoma
Hard callus → soft callus → haematoma → remodelling

fracture-healing.explanation: Secondary healing proceeds: haematoma/inflammation → soft (fibrocartilaginous) callus → hard (bony) callus via endochondral ossification → remodelling of woven into lamellar bone.

fracture-healing.stem: Direct (primary) bone healing with no callus formation occurs specifically when:

options.text: The fracture is left to move freely
There is rigid internal fixation with near-perfect apposition of the fragments
The fracture is comminuted and unstable

fracture-healing.explanation: Primary healing requires rigid fixation and close apposition (e.g. ORIF); bone forms directly across the gap without callus. Any movement or gap leads to secondary (callus) healing or non-union.

fracture-healing.stem: Regarding callus in primary healing — which is correct?

options.text: All fracture healing produces a visible callus
PRIMARY (direct) healing under rigid fixation produces NO callus (direct bone formation across the gap); callus is a feature of SECONDARY healing
Second stage bridging the fracture gap

fracture-healing.explanation: Rigid fixation with perfect apposition lets bone form directly; the fibrocartilaginous/bony callus is the hallmark of secondary healing, which tolerates micromotion.

fracture-healing.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus at ~2–3 weeks”?

options.text: Second stage bridging the fracture gap
Non-union (movement, poor blood supply, infection, gap)

fracture-healing.explanation: Fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus at ~2–3 weeks → Second stage bridging the fracture gap.

fracture-healing.stem: What best explains the finding: “Woven bone (hard callus) replacing soft callus”?

options.text: Second stage bridging the fracture gap
Non-union (movement, poor blood supply, infection, gap)

fracture-healing.explanation: Woven bone (hard callus) replacing soft callus → Endochondral ossification (third stage).

fracture-healing.stem: Which should you review before “Fracture Healing: Stages, Types & Complications”?

options.text: MSK Embryology: Somites & the Axial Skeleton
MSK Embryology: Limb Development, Ossification & Joints

fracture-healing.explanation: Understanding ossification is essential for grasping the healing stages.

respiratory-development-stages.stem: Surfactant, essential for extrauterine survival, is first produced in significant amounts during which stage of lung development?
respiratory-development-stages.explanation: Type II pneumocytes begin producing surfactant in the saccular stage (~wk 26 onward), reaching adequate levels ~wk 35. Its deficiency in prematurity causes neonatal RDS.

respiratory-development-stages.stem: The epithelial lining of the trachea, bronchi, and alveoli is derived embryologically from:
respiratory-development-stages.explanation: The respiratory epithelium arises from foregut endoderm (the lung bud); the surrounding cartilage, smooth muscle, connective tissue, and vessels come from splanchnic mesoderm.

respiratory-development-stages.stem: Regarding when do most alveoli form? — which is correct?

options.text: The lungs contain their full adult complement of alveoli at birth
Most alveoli form AFTER birth (the alveolar stage continues to ~8 years); a newborn has only a fraction of the adult number
Dual embryonic origin of the lung

respiratory-development-stages.explanation: Alveolarisation is largely postnatal, which is why early-life lung injury has lasting effects on alveolar number.

respiratory-development-stages.stem: What best explains the finding: “Airway epithelium from endoderm; cartilage/muscle from mesoderm”?

options.text: Dual embryonic origin of the lung

respiratory-development-stages.explanation: Airway epithelium from endoderm; cartilage/muscle from mesoderm → Dual embryonic origin of the lung.

respiratory-development-stages.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fetus at 20 weeks cannot breathe”?

options.text: Dual embryonic origin of the lung

respiratory-development-stages.explanation: Fetus at 20 weeks cannot breathe → Pseudoglandular — no gas-exchange surface yet.

respiratory-congenital-anomalies.stem: A neonate has a scaphoid abdomen, respiratory distress, and bowel sounds heard over the left chest. The most likely diagnosis is:
respiratory-congenital-anomalies.explanation: A left-sided congenital diaphragmatic hernia (foramen of Bochdalek) lets abdominal viscera enter the chest → scaphoid abdomen, bowel sounds in the thorax, and pulmonary hypoplasia causing distress.

respiratory-congenital-anomalies.stem: Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome in a premature infant is caused by:

options.text: Deficiency of surfactant from immature type II pneumocytes

respiratory-congenital-anomalies.explanation: Prematurity means insufficient surfactant (type II pneumocytes), raising alveolar surface tension and causing diffuse atelectasis (RDS) — treated with antenatal steroids and exogenous surfactant.

respiratory-congenital-anomalies.stem: Regarding consequence of congenital diaphragmatic hernia — which is correct?

options.text: The main problem in CDH is simply the herniated bowel needing repositioning
The life-threatening problem is PULMONARY HYPOPLASIA — the developing lung is compressed and underdeveloped, causing respiratory failure and pulmonary hypertension

respiratory-congenital-anomalies.explanation: Outcome depends on lung development, not just the hernia; the compressed lung can't grow, so hypoplasia (± pulmonary hypertension) dominates.

respiratory-congenital-anomalies.stem: What best explains the finding: “Polyhydramnios + choking/coughing on first feed”?
respiratory-congenital-anomalies.explanation: Polyhydramnios + choking/coughing on first feed → Oesophageal atresia ± tracheo-oesophageal fistula.

respiratory-congenital-anomalies.stem: What best explains the finding: “Scaphoid abdomen + bowel sounds in the chest”?
respiratory-congenital-anomalies.explanation: Scaphoid abdomen + bowel sounds in the chest → Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (Bochdalek).

respiratory-congenital-anomalies.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Congenital Respiratory Anomalies”?

options.text: Development of the Respiratory System: The 5 Stages

respiratory-congenital-anomalies.explanation: Directly links developmental processes to clinical outcomes in respiratory anomalies.

respiratory-congenital-anomalies.stem: Which should you review before “Congenital Respiratory Anomalies”?
respiratory-congenital-anomalies.explanation: Understanding classification aids in recognizing various congenital anomalies.

airway-conducting-respiratory-zones.stem: Which is the last, most distal airway of the CONDUCTING zone (no gas exchange)?
airway-conducting-respiratory-zones.explanation: The terminal bronchiole is the last conducting airway; the next generation, the respiratory bronchiole, is the first with alveoli and thus the start of the respiratory (gas-exchange) zone.

airway-conducting-respiratory-zones.stem: Why do the bronchioles (rather than the bronchi) narrow markedly in an asthma attack?

options.text: They lack cartilage and have relatively prominent smooth muscle, so are collapsible/constrictable
They are part of the respiratory zone

airway-conducting-respiratory-zones.explanation: Bronchioles have no cartilage to splint them open and relatively more smooth muscle, so bronchoconstriction (asthma) narrows them substantially, increasing airway resistance.

airway-conducting-respiratory-zones.stem: Regarding where does gas exchange begin? — which is correct?

options.text: Gas exchange occurs throughout the conducting airways including the terminal bronchioles
Gas exchange begins at the RESPIRATORY bronchioles (first structures with alveoli); the terminal bronchiole is the LAST purely conducting airway
Respiratory bronchiole is the first with alveoli

airway-conducting-respiratory-zones.explanation: The conducting zone (to terminal bronchioles) is dead space — no alveoli, no exchange. Alveoli first appear on respiratory bronchioles.

airway-conducting-respiratory-zones.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pseudostratified ciliated columnar + goblet cells”?

options.text: Respiratory bronchiole is the first with alveoli

airway-conducting-respiratory-zones.explanation: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar + goblet cells → Respiratory epithelium (upper conducting airway).

airway-conducting-respiratory-zones.stem: What best explains the finding: “Terminal bronchiole = last conducting airway”?

options.text: Respiratory bronchiole is the first with alveoli

airway-conducting-respiratory-zones.explanation: Terminal bronchiole = last conducting airway → Respiratory bronchiole is the first with alveoli.

airway-conducting-respiratory-zones.stem: Which should you review before “Airways: Conducting vs Respiratory Zones”?

options.text: Development of the Respiratory System: The 5 Stages

airway-conducting-respiratory-zones.explanation: Understanding the structure of the trachea and bronchi is essential for grasping the conducting zone.

alveoli-pneumocytes-respiratory-membrane.stem: Which alveolar cell produces surfactant and serves as a stem cell to regenerate the alveolar epithelium?
alveoli-pneumocytes-respiratory-membrane.explanation: Type II pneumocytes contain lamellar bodies, secrete surfactant, and act as stem cells that differentiate into type I cells to repair injury. Type I cells are thin, non-dividing gas-exchange cells.

alveoli-pneumocytes-respiratory-membrane.stem: By lowering alveolar surface tension, surfactant primarily:

options.text: Prevents alveolar collapse and increases lung compliance

alveoli-pneumocytes-respiratory-membrane.explanation: Surfactant reduces surface tension, preventing alveolar collapse at end-expiration, increasing compliance (easier inflation), and stabilising alveoli of different sizes (Laplace). Its lack causes RDS.

alveoli-pneumocytes-respiratory-membrane.stem: Regarding which pneumocyte repairs the alveolus? — which is correct?

options.text: Type I pneumocytes divide to repair damaged alveolar epithelium
Type II pneumocytes are the stem cells that proliferate and differentiate into type I cells to repair the alveolus; type I cells cannot divide

alveoli-pneumocytes-respiratory-membrane.explanation: Type I are terminally differentiated (thin exchange cells); type II both make surfactant and regenerate the epithelium.

alveoli-pneumocytes-respiratory-membrane.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thin squamous cell covering most of the alveolus”?

options.text: Type II cells differentiate into type I

alveoli-pneumocytes-respiratory-membrane.explanation: Thin squamous cell covering most of the alveolus → Type I pneumocyte (gas exchange).

alveoli-pneumocytes-respiratory-membrane.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cuboidal cell with lamellar bodies making surfactant”?

options.text: Type II cells differentiate into type I

alveoli-pneumocytes-respiratory-membrane.explanation: Cuboidal cell with lamellar bodies making surfactant → Type II pneumocyte (also stem cell).

alveoli-pneumocytes-respiratory-membrane.stem: Which should you review before “Alveoli, Pneumocytes & the Respiratory Membrane”?
alveoli-pneumocytes-respiratory-membrane.explanation: Understanding congenital anomalies aids in grasping normal alveolar function.

pulmonary-circulation-features.stem: When alveolar oxygen tension falls in one region of the lung, the local pulmonary blood vessels:

options.text: Dilate, increasing blood flow to that region
Constrict, diverting blood to better-ventilated regions

pulmonary-circulation-features.explanation: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction constricts vessels supplying poorly-ventilated alveoli, diverting blood toward well-ventilated areas to improve V/Q matching — opposite to systemic vessels.

pulmonary-circulation-features.stem: Chronic global alveolar hypoxia (e.g. in COPD) can lead to right heart failure (cor pulmonale) because widespread hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction causes:

options.text: Pulmonary hypertension, increasing right ventricular afterload

pulmonary-circulation-features.explanation: Diffuse HPV raises pulmonary vascular resistance → pulmonary hypertension → chronic right ventricular pressure overload → cor pulmonale.

pulmonary-circulation-features.stem: Regarding pulmonary vs systemic response to hypoxia — which is correct?

options.text: Hypoxia dilates blood vessels in the lungs, just as it does in systemic tissues
In the LUNGS, hypoxia causes VASOCONSTRICTION (hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction) — the opposite of the systemic circulation

pulmonary-circulation-features.explanation: This "backwards" reflex diverts pulmonary blood from poorly-ventilated to well-ventilated alveoli, improving V/Q matching.

pulmonary-circulation-features.stem: What best explains the finding: “Low alveolar O₂ → local pulmonary vasoconstriction”?
pulmonary-circulation-features.explanation: Low alveolar O₂ → local pulmonary vasoconstriction → Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (diverts blood).

pulmonary-circulation-features.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pulmonary artery pressure ~25/8 mmHg”?
pulmonary-circulation-features.explanation: Pulmonary artery pressure ~25/8 mmHg → Low-pressure circuit.

pulmonary-circulation-features.stem: Which should you review before “Pulmonary Circulation: A Low-Pressure System”?

options.text: Development of the Respiratory System: The 5 Stages

pulmonary-circulation-features.explanation: Understanding alveolar structure is essential for grasping pulmonary circulation features.

ventilation-perfusion-matching.stem: A region of lung that is perfused but not ventilated (e.g. from atelectasis) represents:
ventilation-perfusion-matching.explanation: Perfusion without ventilation is a shunt (V/Q → 0). Blood passes without being oxygenated, causing hypoxaemia that does not fully correct with supplemental O₂.

ventilation-perfusion-matching.stem: In an upright person, the ventilation–perfusion (V/Q) ratio is:

options.text: Highest at the base, lowest at the apex
Highest at the apex, lowest at the base

ventilation-perfusion-matching.explanation: Both ventilation and perfusion are greater at the base, but perfusion increases more, so the apex has the higher V/Q (dead-space-like) and the base the lower V/Q (shunt-like).

ventilation-perfusion-matching.stem: Regarding response of shunt to oxygen — which is correct?

options.text: Hypoxaemia due to a true shunt corrects fully with 100% oxygen
A true shunt does NOT correct with 100% O₂ — the oxygen can't reach the unventilated (shunted) blood; only V/Q mismatch corrects

ventilation-perfusion-matching.explanation: In shunt, blood bypasses ventilated alveoli entirely, so extra inspired O₂ never contacts it — the key distinction from V/Q mismatch.

ventilation-perfusion-matching.stem: What best explains the finding: “Highest V/Q at the lung apex”?
ventilation-perfusion-matching.explanation: Highest V/Q at the lung apex → Ventilation exceeds perfusion (gravity).

ventilation-perfusion-matching.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypoxaemia that fails to correct on 100% O₂”?
ventilation-perfusion-matching.explanation: Hypoxaemia that fails to correct on 100% O₂ → True shunt (perfused, unventilated alveoli).

ventilation-perfusion-matching.stem: Which should you review before “Ventilation–Perfusion (V/Q) Matching”?

options.text: Development of the Respiratory System: The 5 Stages

ventilation-perfusion-matching.explanation: Basic understanding of immunosuppression may aid in understanding V/Q matching in transplant patients.

lung-volumes-ventilation.stem: A patient has FEV₁/FVC of 0.55 with an increased residual volume. This pattern indicates:
lung-volumes-ventilation.explanation: A reduced FEV₁/FVC (<0.7) with air trapping (↑RV) is the obstructive pattern (asthma, COPD). Restrictive disease reduces all volumes but preserves/raises the ratio.

lung-volumes-ventilation.stem: Alveolar ventilation is best increased (for the same minute ventilation) by:

options.text: Slower, deeper breaths that reduce the dead-space fraction

lung-volumes-ventilation.explanation: Because dead space is fixed (~150 mL), deeper (larger tidal volume) breaths deliver a greater fraction of each breath to alveoli, so alveolar ventilation = (TV − dead space) × rate improves compared with rapid shallow breathing.

lung-volumes-ventilation.stem: Regarding what spirometry can measure — which is correct?

options.text: Spirometry can directly measure total lung capacity and residual volume
Spirometry CANNOT measure RV, FRC, or TLC (they contain the un-exhalable residual volume) — these need helium dilution or plethysmography

lung-volumes-ventilation.explanation: Spirometry only measures air actually moved; the residual volume never leaves the lung, so any capacity containing it can't be spirometrically measured.

options.text: It is not exhaled (needs helium dilution/plethysmography)
Higher dead-space fraction lowers alveolar ventilation

lung-volumes-ventilation.explanation: FEV₁/FVC < 0.7 → Obstructive pattern (asthma, COPD) — air trapping.

lung-volumes-ventilation.stem: What best explains the finding: “All volumes reduced, FEV₁/FVC normal/high”?

options.text: It is not exhaled (needs helium dilution/plethysmography)
Higher dead-space fraction lowers alveolar ventilation

lung-volumes-ventilation.explanation: All volumes reduced, FEV₁/FVC normal/high → Restrictive pattern (fibrosis).

lung-volumes-ventilation.stem: Which should you review before “Lung Volumes, Capacities & Alveolar Ventilation”?

options.text: Development of the Respiratory System: The 5 Stages

lung-volumes-ventilation.explanation: Thoracic anatomy is essential for understanding lung mechanics.

respiratory-mechanics-compliance.stem: The normally negative intrapleural pressure is essential because it:

options.text: Keeps the lungs expanded against their elastic recoil
Drives blood through the pulmonary circulation

respiratory-mechanics-compliance.explanation: The negative intrapleural pressure counteracts the lung's elastic recoil, holding the alveoli open. If air enters the pleural space (pneumothorax), this pressure is lost and the lung collapses.

respiratory-mechanics-compliance.stem: Pulmonary fibrosis affects lung compliance by:
respiratory-mechanics-compliance.explanation: Fibrosis deposits stiff collagen, reducing lung compliance (ΔV/ΔP) so more pressure is needed to inflate — a restrictive picture. Emphysema does the opposite (raises compliance).

respiratory-mechanics-compliance.stem: Regarding compliance in emphysema vs fibrosis — which is correct?

options.text: Emphysema makes the lungs stiff and hard to inflate (low compliance)
Emphysema INCREASES compliance (loss of elastic recoil → easy to inflate but hard to EXHALE); fibrosis DECREASES compliance (stiff, hard to inflate)
Keeps lungs expanded against elastic recoil

respiratory-mechanics-compliance.explanation: Emphysema destroys elastic tissue → floppy, high-compliance lungs with air trapping; fibrosis adds stiff collagen → low compliance.

respiratory-mechanics-compliance.stem: What best explains the finding: “Intrapleural pressure ~−5 cmH₂O”?

options.text: Loss of elastic tissue (easy to inflate, hard to exhale)
Keeps lungs expanded against elastic recoil

respiratory-mechanics-compliance.explanation: Intrapleural pressure ~−5 cmH₂O → Keeps lungs expanded against elastic recoil.

respiratory-mechanics-compliance.stem: What best explains the finding: “Lung collapse when air enters the pleural space”?

options.text: Keeps lungs expanded against elastic recoil
Loss of elastic tissue (easy to inflate, hard to exhale)

respiratory-mechanics-compliance.explanation: Lung collapse when air enters the pleural space → Pneumothorax — lost negative intrapleural pressure.

respiratory-mechanics-compliance.stem: Which should you review before “Respiratory Mechanics: Pressures, Compliance & Resistance”?

options.text: Development of the Respiratory System: The 5 Stages

respiratory-mechanics-compliance.explanation: Understanding alveolar structure is essential for grasping compliance and surface tension.

gas-exchange-diffusion.stem: According to Fick's law, the rate of gas diffusion across the respiratory membrane is DECREASED by:

options.text: An increase in membrane thickness (e.g. fibrosis, oedema)

gas-exchange-diffusion.explanation: Diffusion rate is inversely proportional to membrane thickness, so fibrosis or oedema slows gas transfer. Larger area, steeper gradient, and higher solubility all increase diffusion.

gas-exchange-diffusion.stem: Under normal resting conditions, oxygen transfer from alveolus to blood is:

options.text: Perfusion-limited (blood equilibrates with alveolar gas before leaving the capillary)

gas-exchange-diffusion.explanation: Normally O₂ equilibrates with alveolar gas about a third of the way along the capillary, so uptake depends on blood flow (perfusion-limited). A thickened membrane or very short transit time can make it diffusion-limited.

gas-exchange-diffusion.stem: Regarding which gas is affected first by a diffusion defect? — which is correct?

options.text: Impaired diffusion causes CO₂ retention (hypercapnia) before it lowers oxygen
Diffusion defects cause HYPOXAEMIA first; CO₂ (≈20× more diffusible) is usually still cleared, so hypercapnia is a late/other-mechanism feature
Gradients drive O₂ in, CO₂ out

gas-exchange-diffusion.explanation: CO₂'s high solubility lets it cross even a thickened membrane, so oxygenation fails before CO₂ elimination does.

gas-exchange-diffusion.stem: What best explains the finding: “Alveolar PO₂ 100 / PCO₂ 40; venous 40 / 46”?

options.text: Gradients drive O₂ in, CO₂ out

gas-exchange-diffusion.explanation: Alveolar PO₂ 100 / PCO₂ 40; venous 40 / 46 → Gradients drive O₂ in, CO₂ out.

gas-exchange-diffusion.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thickened membrane (fibrosis) slows O₂ transfer”?

options.text: Gradients drive O₂ in, CO₂ out

gas-exchange-diffusion.explanation: Thickened membrane (fibrosis) slows O₂ transfer → Fick — increased diffusion distance.

gas-exchange-diffusion.stem: Which should you review before “Gas Exchange: Diffusion & Partial Pressures”?

options.text: Development of the Respiratory System: The 5 Stages

gas-exchange-diffusion.explanation: Understanding the structure of the respiratory membrane is essential for gas exchange.

oxygen-transport-dissociation-curve.stem: Which change shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the RIGHT, promoting oxygen unloading to tissues?

options.text: Increased CO₂, increased H⁺ (lower pH), and increased temperature

oxygen-transport-dissociation-curve.explanation: A right shift (decreased affinity) is caused by ↑CO₂, ↑H⁺/↓pH, ↑temperature, and ↑2,3-BPG — conditions in metabolically active tissue (the Bohr effect) — enhancing O₂ delivery.

oxygen-transport-dissociation-curve.stem: In carbon monoxide poisoning, pulse oximetry can read a falsely normal oxygen saturation because:

options.text: The oximeter cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin

oxygen-transport-dissociation-curve.explanation: Standard pulse oximetry misreads carboxyhaemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin, giving a falsely reassuring SaO₂. CO also binds Hb ~250× more avidly than O₂ and left-shifts the curve — measure COHb directly.

oxygen-transport-dissociation-curve.stem: Regarding what a right shift does — which is correct?

options.text: A right shift of the oxyhaemoglobin curve means haemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly
A right shift = DECREASED affinity → Hb releases (unloads) O₂ more readily to tissues (↑P50); it is caused by ↑CO₂/H⁺/temp/2,3-BPG

oxygen-transport-dissociation-curve.explanation: Right = "release": active tissues (acidic, warm, high CO₂) shift right so more O₂ is delivered where it's needed (the Bohr effect).

oxygen-transport-dissociation-curve.stem: What best explains the finding: “Right-shifted curve (↑P50)”?
oxygen-transport-dissociation-curve.explanation: Right-shifted curve (↑P50) → ↑CO₂/H⁺/temp/2,3-BPG → O₂ unloaded to tissues (Bohr).

oxygen-transport-dissociation-curve.stem: What best explains the finding: “Left-shifted curve (↓P50)”?
oxygen-transport-dissociation-curve.explanation: Left-shifted curve (↓P50) → ↓CO₂/H⁺/temp/2,3-BPG, HbF, CO → O₂ held tightly.

oxygen-transport-dissociation-curve.stem: Which should you review before “Oxygen Transport & the Oxyhaemoglobin Curve”?

options.text: Development of the Respiratory System: The 5 Stages

oxygen-transport-dissociation-curve.explanation: Basic understanding of physiology may aid in grasping oxygen transport.

co2-transport-blood.stem: The majority of carbon dioxide is transported in the blood as:
co2-transport-blood.explanation: About 70% of CO₂ is carried as bicarbonate (formed via carbonic anhydrase in the RBC), ~23% as carbamino-haemoglobin, and ~7% dissolved. (Carboxyhaemoglobin is Hb bound to CO, unrelated.)

options.text: CO₂ and H⁺ promote oxygen release from haemoglobin
Deoxygenated haemoglobin carries CO₂ more readily than oxygenated haemoglobin
Chloride shifts into the red cell

co2-transport-blood.explanation: The Haldane effect: deoxy-Hb binds CO₂ (and buffers H⁺) better, so tissues load CO₂ as O₂ is released, and lung oxygenation of Hb releases CO₂. The Bohr effect is its O₂ counterpart (a).

co2-transport-blood.stem: Regarding main form of co₂ transport — which is correct?

options.text: Most CO₂ is carried bound to haemoglobin as carbaminohaemoglobin
Most CO₂ (~70%) is carried as BICARBONATE in plasma; carbamino-Hb is only ~23% and dissolved CO₂ ~7%

co2-transport-blood.explanation: The carbonic-anhydrase-driven conversion to bicarbonate is the dominant route; don't overstate the carbamino fraction.

co2-transport-blood.stem: What best explains the finding: “Majority of CO₂ carried as bicarbonate”?
co2-transport-blood.explanation: Majority of CO₂ carried as bicarbonate → Carbonic anhydrase → HCO₃⁻ (~70%).

co2-transport-blood.stem: What best explains the finding: “Chloride shifts into RBCs in the tissues”?
co2-transport-blood.explanation: Chloride shifts into RBCs in the tissues → Hamburger shift maintains electroneutrality.

co2-transport-blood.stem: Which should you review before “CO₂ Transport in Blood”?

options.text: Development of the Respiratory System: The 5 Stages

co2-transport-blood.explanation: Basic understanding of molecular biology is foundational.

control-of-breathing.stem: The central chemoreceptors in the medulla primarily respond to:

options.text: H⁺ in the CSF, reflecting arterial CO₂

control-of-breathing.explanation: Central chemoreceptors sense CSF H⁺, which mirrors arterial CO₂ (CO₂ crosses the BBB and generates H⁺). They provide the main drive and do NOT sense O₂ directly — that is the peripheral chemoreceptors' job.

control-of-breathing.stem: Which structures are the only receptors that sense a low arterial oxygen tension?

options.text: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies

control-of-breathing.explanation: The peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid and aortic bodies) are the only O₂ sensors, responding mainly to PaO₂ below ~60 mmHg (and also to ↑CO₂/↑H⁺). Central chemoreceptors sense only CO₂/H⁺.

control-of-breathing.stem: Regarding primary stimulus to breathe — which is correct?

options.text: Low oxygen (PaO₂) is the main minute-to-minute stimulus that controls breathing
CO₂ (via CSF H⁺, sensed by central chemoreceptors) is the PRIMARY drive; low PaO₂ only becomes a major driver below ~60 mmHg (peripheral chemoreceptors)
Central chemoreceptors sense CSF H⁺ (from CO₂)

control-of-breathing.explanation: The tightly regulated variable is PaCO₂; the hypoxic drive is a backup that matters at altitude or in blunted-central-drive states.

control-of-breathing.stem: What best explains the finding: “PaCO₂ is the main minute-to-minute breathing stimulus”?

options.text: Blunted central CO₂ response → rely on peripheral O₂
Central chemoreceptors sense CSF H⁺ (from CO₂)

control-of-breathing.explanation: PaCO₂ is the main minute-to-minute breathing stimulus → Central chemoreceptors sense CSF H⁺ (from CO₂).

control-of-breathing.stem: What best explains the finding: “Only receptors sensing low PaO₂”?

options.text: Central chemoreceptors sense CSF H⁺ (from CO₂)
Blunted central CO₂ response → rely on peripheral O₂
