control-of-breathing.explanation: Only receptors sensing low PaO₂ → Peripheral chemoreceptors (carotid/aortic bodies).

control-of-breathing.stem: Which should you review before “Control of Breathing: Centres & Chemoreceptors”?

options.text: Development of the Respiratory System: The 5 Stages

control-of-breathing.explanation: Understanding feedback mechanisms is crucial for grasping respiratory control.

abg-acid-base-interpretation.stem: An ABG shows pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 60 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 26 mEq/L. This is:
abg-acid-base-interpretation.explanation: Low pH (acidosis) with a high PaCO₂ (moving opposite to pH) and normal HCO₃⁻ = an uncompensated respiratory acidosis, typically from hypoventilation (e.g. COPD, opioids).

abg-acid-base-interpretation.stem: In a patient with a metabolic acidosis, the next step to narrow the cause is to calculate the:
abg-acid-base-interpretation.explanation: The anion gap separates high-gap metabolic acidosis (added acid: lactate, ketones, renal failure, toxins) from normal-gap (HCO₃⁻ loss: diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis).

abg-acid-base-interpretation.stem: Regarding respiratory vs metabolic on abg — which is correct?

options.text: In a respiratory acidosis, the PaCO₂ and pH change in the same direction
In RESPIRATORY disorders, PaCO₂ moves OPPOSITE to pH (↑CO₂ → ↓pH); in METABOLIC disorders, HCO₃⁻ moves in the SAME direction as pH ("ROME")

abg-acid-base-interpretation.explanation: CO₂ is an acid, so more CO₂ lowers pH — an inverse relationship. Bicarbonate is a base, so it tracks pH directly.

abg-acid-base-interpretation.stem: What best explains the finding: “↓pH with ↑PaCO₂”?
What best explains the finding: “↑pH with ↓PaCO₂”?
Which should you review before “Arterial Blood Gas & Acid–Base Interpretation”?

options.text: Development of the Respiratory System: The 5 Stages

abg-acid-base-interpretation.explanation: Understanding CO₂ transport is essential for interpreting acid-base status.

heart-anatomy-chambers-valves.stem: The left ventricular wall is considerably thicker than the right ventricular wall because it:

options.text: Pumps against the high pressure of the systemic circulation

heart-anatomy-chambers-valves.explanation: The LV ejects into the high-pressure systemic circuit, so it develops a much thicker myocardium than the RV, which pumps into the low-pressure pulmonary circuit.

heart-anatomy-chambers-valves.stem: The coronary arteries perfuse the left ventricular myocardium predominantly during:
heart-anatomy-chambers-valves.explanation: During systole the contracting myocardium compresses the coronary vessels; flow occurs mainly in diastole when the muscle relaxes (and the aortic sinuses fill). Tachycardia shortens diastole and can provoke ischaemia.

heart-anatomy-chambers-valves.stem: Regarding which valve is bicuspid? — which is correct?

options.text: The tricuspid valve is on the left and the bicuspid (mitral) valve is on the right
The MITRAL (bicuspid) valve is on the LEFT (LA→LV); the TRICUSPID valve is on the RIGHT (RA→RV)

heart-anatomy-chambers-valves.explanation: "LAB RAT": Left = Bicuspid, Right = Tricuspid. Swapping them is a classic error.

heart-anatomy-chambers-valves.stem: What best explains the finding: “LV wall much thicker than RV”?

options.text: Systolic myocardial compression + aortic valve closed

heart-anatomy-chambers-valves.explanation: LV wall much thicker than RV → Pumps against high systemic pressure.

heart-anatomy-chambers-valves.stem: What best explains the finding: “Mitral valve = bicuspid (left AV valve)”?

options.text: Systolic myocardial compression + aortic valve closed

heart-anatomy-chambers-valves.explanation: Mitral valve = bicuspid (left AV valve) → Between LA and LV.

heart-anatomy-chambers-valves.stem: Which should you review before “Heart Anatomy: Chambers, Valves & Wall”?

options.text: Blood Vessel Histology: Wall Layers & Vessel Types

heart-anatomy-chambers-valves.explanation: Understanding heart valves is essential for grasping the anatomy of the heart.

systemic-pulmonary-circulation.stem: Which vessels serve as the principal resistance vessels controlling total peripheral resistance and blood flow distribution?
systemic-pulmonary-circulation.explanation: Arterioles have a thick smooth-muscle media relative to their small lumen; adjusting their diameter is the main way the body controls total peripheral resistance, blood pressure, and regional flow.

systemic-pulmonary-circulation.stem: Because the pulmonary and systemic circuits are arranged in series, the output of the right ventricle must:

options.text: Be much greater than the left ventricle
Equal the output of the left ventricle over time
Be independent of the left ventricle
Be about half the left ventricle

systemic-pulmonary-circulation.explanation: In a series circuit, all the blood pumped by the right ventricle must pass through the left, so their outputs are equal over time; a sustained mismatch causes congestion (heart failure).

systemic-pulmonary-circulation.stem: Regarding oxygenation of pulmonary vessels — which is correct?

options.text: All arteries carry oxygenated blood and all veins carry deoxygenated blood
The PULMONARY artery carries DEOXYGENATED blood and the pulmonary vein carries OXYGENATED blood (also the umbilical vessels are reversed)

systemic-pulmonary-circulation.explanation: Arteries are defined by direction (away from the heart), not oxygen content; the pulmonary (and umbilical) vessels are the classic exceptions.

systemic-pulmonary-circulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood”?
systemic-pulmonary-circulation.explanation: Pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood → RV → lungs (the "backwards" vessel).

systemic-pulmonary-circulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Arterioles are the main resistance vessels”?
systemic-pulmonary-circulation.explanation: Arterioles are the main resistance vessels → Smooth muscle controls flow/pressure (TPR).

coronary-circulation.stem: An inferior myocardial infarction complicated by bradycardia and AV block most likely results from occlusion of the:
coronary-circulation.explanation: The right coronary artery supplies the inferior left ventricle and, in most people, both the SA and AV nodes; its occlusion causes an inferior MI often accompanied by bradyarrhythmias and AV block.

coronary-circulation.stem: Blood flow to the left ventricular myocardium occurs predominantly during diastole because:

options.text: Aortic pressure is highest in diastole
Systolic contraction compresses the intramural coronary vessels
The coronary arteries close during diastole
Oxygen demand is lowest in systole

coronary-circulation.explanation: During systole the contracting left ventricle compresses the coronary vessels running through its wall, so most left-ventricular perfusion occurs in diastole. Tachycardia and low diastolic pressure therefore reduce coronary blood flow.

coronary-circulation.stem: Regarding timing of coronary perfusion — which is correct?

options.text: The heart muscle is perfused during systole when pressure is highest

The LEFT ventricle is perfused almost entirely during DIASTOLE — systolic contraction compresses the intramural coronary vessels — which is why tachycardia (short diastole) and low diastolic pressure reduce coronary blood flow
RCA occlusion (supplies SA and AV nodes)

coronary-circulation.explanation: Intuiting that high systolic pressure drives coronary flow is backwards for the LV; recognising diastolic perfusion explains angina physiology and why heart rate and diastolic pressure matter clinically.

coronary-circulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Anterior MI with a large territory at risk”?

options.text: RCA occlusion (supplies SA and AV nodes)
Shortened diastole reduces coronary perfusion time

coronary-circulation.explanation: Anterior MI with a large territory at risk → LAD occlusion (anterior LV, apex, septum).

coronary-circulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Inferior MI with bradycardia/AV block”?

options.text: Shortened diastole reduces coronary perfusion time
RCA occlusion (supplies SA and AV nodes)

coronary-circulation.explanation: Inferior MI with bradycardia/AV block → RCA occlusion (supplies SA and AV nodes).

heart-wall-cardiac-histology.stem: The intercalated discs of cardiac muscle contain gap junctions, which:

options.text: Electrically couple cells so the myocardium acts as a functional syncytium
Insulate the atria from the ventricles

heart-wall-cardiac-histology.explanation: Gap junctions in the intercalated disc let ions pass cell-to-cell, so the impulse spreads and the myocardium contracts as a unit (functional syncytium). Desmosomes/fascia adherens provide the mechanical strength.

heart-wall-cardiac-histology.stem: Purkinje fibres are histologically recognised as:

options.text: Large, pale-staining cells rich in glycogen with few myofibrils, located subendocardially

heart-wall-cardiac-histology.explanation: Purkinje fibres are modified cardiac myocytes — large, pale, glycogen-rich, with few myofibrils — specialised for rapid conduction (not contractile force), located just under the endocardium.

heart-wall-cardiac-histology.stem: Regarding is the conduction system nervous tissue? — which is correct?

options.text: The SA node, AV node, and Purkinje fibres are nerves
They are MODIFIED CARDIAC MUSCLE cells (specialised myocytes), not neurons — the heartbeat originates within the muscle itself (myogenic)

heart-wall-cardiac-histology.explanation: The heart is myogenic: the conduction system is specialised muscle that generates/conducts the impulse; autonomic nerves only modulate it.

heart-wall-cardiac-histology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Intercalated discs between cardiac cells”?
heart-wall-cardiac-histology.explanation: Intercalated discs between cardiac cells → Desmosomes (strength) + gap junctions (coupling).

heart-wall-cardiac-histology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Central (1–2) nuclei, branched striated fibres”?
heart-wall-cardiac-histology.explanation: Central (1–2) nuclei, branched striated fibres → Cardiac (not skeletal) muscle.

heart-wall-cardiac-histology.stem: Which should you review before “Histology of the Heart Wall & Conduction Cells”?
heart-wall-cardiac-histology.explanation: Understanding cardiac muscle histology is essential for grasping heart wall structure.

blood-vessel-histology.stem: The elastic recoil of the aorta during diastole (the Windkessel effect) is possible because its tunica media is rich in:
blood-vessel-histology.explanation: Elastic (conducting) arteries like the aorta have a media dominated by elastic laminae that stretch in systole and recoil in diastole, smoothing pulsatile flow into continuous perfusion.

options.text: All three tunics with a thick muscular media
A single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane
Endothelium plus a thick elastic media

blood-vessel-histology.explanation: Capillaries are just endothelium and its basement membrane — a single-cell-thick wall optimised for exchange. Types (continuous, fenestrated, sinusoidal) differ in permeability.

blood-vessel-histology.stem: Regarding elastic vs muscular artery — which is correct?

options.text: The aorta has a media dominated by smooth muscle like a muscular artery
The aorta is an ELASTIC artery (media dominated by elastic laminae for recoil); muscular arteries have a smooth-muscle-dominated media

blood-vessel-histology.explanation: Elastic arteries store energy in systole and recoil in diastole (Windkessel); muscular arteries distribute/regulate flow. The wall composition differs.

blood-vessel-histology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Media full of elastic laminae”?
blood-vessel-histology.explanation: Media full of elastic laminae → Elastic (conducting) artery — recoil in diastole.

blood-vessel-histology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thick smooth-muscle media, small lumen”?
blood-vessel-histology.explanation: Thick smooth-muscle media, small lumen → Muscular artery / arteriole (resistance).

blood-vessel-histology.stem: Which should you review before “Blood Vessel Histology: Wall Layers & Vessel Types”?
blood-vessel-histology.explanation: Understanding blood vessel histology is essential for grasping systemic and pulmonary circulation.

heart-tube-looping-septation.stem: During normal cardiac development, the heart tube loops:
heart-tube-looping-septation.explanation: The heart tube undergoes rightward (D-) looping to position the chambers correctly. Abnormal (leftward) looping can cause dextrocardia and situs abnormalities.

heart-tube-looping-septation.stem: The truncus arteriosus is divided into the aorta and pulmonary trunk by the spiral aorticopulmonary septum, which is derived from:
heart-tube-looping-septation.explanation: Neural-crest cells form the spiral aorticopulmonary septum. Failure to spiral → transposition; unequal division → Tetralogy of Fallot; failure to divide → persistent truncus arteriosus.

heart-tube-looping-septation.stem: Regarding commonest congenital heart defect — which is correct?

options.text: The atrial septal defect is the most common congenital heart defect
The (membranous) VENTRICULAR septal defect (VSD) is the commonest congenital heart defect

heart-tube-looping-septation.explanation: VSD (usually the membranous part) is the single most common; ASD and others are less frequent.

heart-tube-looping-septation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Membranous ventricular septal defect”?

options.text: Unequal (skewed) division by the AP septum

heart-tube-looping-septation.explanation: Membranous ventricular septal defect → Commonest congenital heart defect (septation failure).

heart-tube-looping-septation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Patent foramen ovale / ASD”?

options.text: Unequal (skewed) division by the AP septum

heart-tube-looping-septation.explanation: Patent foramen ovale / ASD → Atrial septa fail to fuse.

heart-tube-looping-septation.stem: Which should you review before “Heart Development: Tube, Looping & Septation”?
heart-tube-looping-septation.explanation: Basic understanding of infections may help in understanding congenital defects.

fetal-circulation-shunts.stem: In the fetus, the ductus arteriosus shunts blood from the:

options.text: Right atrium to the left atrium
Pulmonary artery to the aorta, bypassing the lungs

fetal-circulation-shunts.explanation: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta, diverting blood away from the high-resistance fetal lungs. It closes at birth to become the ligamentum arteriosum.

fetal-circulation-shunts.stem: A patent ductus arteriosus in a newborn can often be closed pharmacologically with:

options.text: An NSAID such as indomethacin (prostaglandin inhibitor)

fetal-circulation-shunts.explanation: Prostaglandins keep the ductus open; inhibiting them with an NSAID (indomethacin/ibuprofen) closes a PDA. Conversely, PGE₁ is given to keep the duct open in duct-dependent congenital heart disease.

fetal-circulation-shunts.stem: Regarding prostaglandins and the ductus arteriosus — which is correct?

options.text: Prostaglandins close the ductus arteriosus and NSAIDs keep it open
Prostaglandins (PGE) KEEP the ductus arteriosus OPEN; NSAIDs (indomethacin) inhibit prostaglandins and CLOSE it
PGE₂ in utero; NSAIDs close it, PGE₁ keeps it open
From placenta to fetus (the reversed vessel)

fetal-circulation-shunts.explanation: This is reversed from the usual "inflammation" intuition. Clinically: PGE₁ maintains a duct-dependent lesion; NSAIDs close a PDA.

fetal-circulation-shunts.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ductus arteriosus kept open by prostaglandins”?

options.text: From placenta to fetus (the reversed vessel)
Closes as LA pressure rises after birth
PGE₂ in utero; NSAIDs close it, PGE₁ keeps it open
Remnants of ductus venosus, umbilical vein, ductus arteriosus

fetal-circulation-shunts.explanation: Ductus arteriosus kept open by prostaglandins → PGE₂ in utero; NSAIDs close it, PGE₁ keeps it open.

fetal-circulation-shunts.stem: What best explains the finding: “Umbilical vein carries the most oxygenated fetal blood”?

options.text: PGE₂ in utero; NSAIDs close it, PGE₁ keeps it open
Closes as LA pressure rises after birth
Remnants of ductus venosus, umbilical vein, ductus arteriosus
From placenta to fetus (the reversed vessel)

fetal-circulation-shunts.explanation: Umbilical vein carries the most oxygenated fetal blood → From placenta to fetus (the reversed vessel).

fetal-circulation-shunts.stem: Which should you review before “Fetal Circulation & the Three Shunts”?
fetal-circulation-shunts.explanation: Understanding placental circulation is essential for fetal circulation.

cardiac-action-potential.stem: The plateau phase (phase 2) of the ventricular action potential is produced mainly by:

options.text: Ca²⁺ influx through L-type channels balancing K⁺ efflux

cardiac-action-potential.explanation: During the plateau, inward Ca²⁺ (L-type channels) roughly balances outward K⁺, prolonging the AP and triggering Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release for contraction. Phase 0 is the Na⁺ upstroke.

cardiac-action-potential.stem: Cardiac muscle cannot undergo tetanic contraction because:

options.text: Its long action potential produces a long refractory period lasting nearly the whole contraction

cardiac-action-potential.explanation: The prolonged plateau gives cardiac muscle a long absolute refractory period, so a second AP cannot fire until the muscle has nearly relaxed — preventing tetanus and ensuring alternating contraction/filling.

cardiac-action-potential.stem: Regarding what makes the cardiac plateau? — which is correct?

options.text: The plateau of the cardiac action potential is due to continued Na⁺ influx
The plateau (phase 2) is due to Ca²⁺ influx (L-type channels) balancing K⁺ efflux — Na⁺ channels are already inactivated
L-type Ca²⁺ influx balancing K⁺ efflux

cardiac-action-potential.explanation: The fast Na⁺ current makes only the phase-0 upstroke; the sustained plateau is a Ca²⁺ phenomenon that also drives contraction.

cardiac-action-potential.stem: What best explains the finding: “Plateau phase (phase 2)”?

options.text: L-type Ca²⁺ influx balancing K⁺ efflux

cardiac-action-potential.explanation: Plateau phase (phase 2) → L-type Ca²⁺ influx balancing K⁺ efflux.

cardiac-action-potential.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cardiac muscle cannot be tetanised”?

options.text: L-type Ca²⁺ influx balancing K⁺ efflux

cardiac-action-potential.explanation: Cardiac muscle cannot be tetanised → Long absolute refractory period (long AP).

cardiac-action-potential.stem: Which should you review before “The Cardiac Action Potential”?
cardiac-action-potential.explanation: Understanding refractory periods is crucial for grasping cardiac action potential.

pacemaker-conduction-system.stem: The unstable, spontaneously depolarising phase 4 that gives SA-node cells their automaticity is driven largely by:

options.text: The "funny current" (I_f), a slow inward Na⁺ current
Fast Na⁺ channels (as in ventricular phase 0)

pacemaker-conduction-system.explanation: Pacemaker cells lack a stable resting potential; the funny current (I_f) plus Ca²⁺ currents slowly depolarise phase 4 to threshold, generating automatic rhythmic firing.

pacemaker-conduction-system.stem: Increased sympathetic (β1-adrenergic) stimulation increases heart rate by:

options.text: Decreasing the slope of pacemaker phase 4
Increasing the slope of pacemaker phase-4 depolarisation (reaching threshold sooner)

pacemaker-conduction-system.explanation: Sympathetic β1 stimulation steepens the phase-4 slope so SA-node cells reach threshold sooner (positive chronotropy). The vagus does the opposite (flattens the slope + hyperpolarises).

pacemaker-conduction-system.stem: Regarding purpose of the av nodal delay — which is correct?

options.text: The AV node delays the impulse to slow the overall heart rate
The AV delay lets the ATRIA finish contracting and FILL the ventricles before ventricular systole (optimising the "atrial kick"), not to set overall rate
Lets atria fill ventricles before systole

pacemaker-conduction-system.explanation: The delay ensures correct atrial-then-ventricular sequencing; the rate is set by the SA node's phase-4 slope.

pacemaker-conduction-system.stem: What best explains the finding: “Spontaneous phase-4 depolarisation”?

options.text: Lets atria fill ventricles before systole

pacemaker-conduction-system.explanation: Spontaneous phase-4 depolarisation → Funny current (I_f) → SA-node automaticity.

pacemaker-conduction-system.stem: What best explains the finding: “AV nodal delay (PR interval ~0.12–0.20 s)”?

options.text: Lets atria fill ventricles before systole

pacemaker-conduction-system.explanation: AV nodal delay (PR interval ~0.12–0.20 s) → Lets atria fill ventricles before systole.

pacemaker-conduction-system.stem: Which should you review before “The Pacemaker & Cardiac Conduction System”?

options.text: Nerve Fibres, Myelin, Synapses & Nerve Organization

pacemaker-conduction-system.explanation: Understanding nerve conduction is essential for grasping cardiac conduction.

cardiac-ion-currents-channels.stem: The plateau (phase 2) of the ventricular action potential is maintained primarily by:

options.text: Calcium influx through L-type channels balanced by potassium efflux

cardiac-ion-currents-channels.explanation: The plateau reflects inward L-type calcium current balanced against outward potassium current; the sustained calcium entry both prolongs the refractory period and triggers calcium-induced calcium release for contraction.

cardiac-ion-currents-channels.stem: Spontaneous phase-4 depolarisation that gives sinoatrial node cells their automaticity is driven mainly by the:
cardiac-ion-currents-channels.explanation: Pacemaker cells lack a stable resting potential; the inward funny current (I_f, an HCN-channel Na⁺ current) drives slow phase-4 depolarisation toward threshold, and its slope sets the heart rate (blocked by ivabradine).

cardiac-ion-currents-channels.stem: Regarding upstroke of the pacemaker action potential — which is correct?

options.text: The SA node action potential upstroke is caused by a fast sodium current like the ventricle

Pacemaker (SA/AV nodal) cells LACK a functional fast Na⁺ current; their phase-0 upstroke is carried by CALCIUM (L-type), and phase-4 spontaneous depolarisation is driven by the funny current (I_f) — which is why nodal conduction is slow and calcium-dependent
L-type Ca²⁺ influx balanced by K⁺ efflux (phase 2)

cardiac-ion-currents-channels.explanation: Assuming a sodium-driven upstroke everywhere misses why nodal cells are slower and calcium-dependent, and why calcium-channel blockers (not sodium blockers) slow the nodes.

cardiac-ion-currents-channels.stem: What best explains the finding: “Long plateau giving a long refractory period”?

options.text: L-type Ca²⁺ influx balanced by K⁺ efflux (phase 2)

cardiac-ion-currents-channels.explanation: Long plateau giving a long refractory period → L-type Ca²⁺ influx balanced by K⁺ efflux (phase 2).

cardiac-ion-currents-channels.stem: What best explains the finding: “Contraction triggered by the action potential”?

options.text: L-type Ca²⁺ influx balanced by K⁺ efflux (phase 2)

cardiac-ion-currents-channels.explanation: Contraction triggered by the action potential → Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release (excitation–contraction coupling).

ecg-formation-waves.stem: On the ECG, the QRS complex represents:
ecg-formation-waves.explanation: The QRS reflects ventricular depolarisation (large because of ventricular mass). The P wave = atrial depolarisation; the T wave = ventricular repolarisation.

ecg-formation-waves.stem: A prolonged PR interval on the ECG indicates:

options.text: Slowed conduction through the AV node

ecg-formation-waves.explanation: The PR interval measures the time from atrial depolarisation to ventricular depolarisation, largely the AV nodal delay; prolongation indicates slowed AV conduction (e.g. first-degree heart block).

ecg-formation-waves.stem: Regarding what the t wave represents — which is correct?

options.text: The T wave represents atrial repolarisation
The T wave represents VENTRICULAR repolarisation; atrial repolarisation is hidden within the QRS complex

ecg-formation-waves.explanation: Ventricular mass dominates the ECG, so the small atrial-repolarisation signal is masked by the QRS — the T wave is ventricular.

ecg-formation-waves.stem: What best explains the finding: “P wave”?
What best explains the finding: “QRS complex”?
Which should you review before “ECG Formation: Waves & Intervals”?
ecg-formation-waves.explanation: Understanding the conduction system is essential for grasping ECG wave formation.

cardiac-electrical-axis-vectors.stem: A wave of depolarisation travelling directly toward a positive recording electrode produces:
cardiac-electrical-axis-vectors.explanation: By convention, a depolarisation vector moving toward the positive electrode inscribes an upward deflection; moving away gives a downward deflection, and moving perpendicular gives a biphasic or flat wave.

cardiac-electrical-axis-vectors.stem: A quick way to confirm a normal mean QRS axis is to see that the QRS is net positive in:
cardiac-electrical-axis-vectors.explanation: If the QRS is predominantly positive in both lead I and lead aVF, the mean frontal-plane axis lies in the normal quadrant (roughly −30° to +90°). Discordance between these leads indicates axis deviation.

cardiac-electrical-axis-vectors.stem: Regarding interpreting the direction of an ecg deflection — which is correct?

options.text: A downward deflection means the electrical activity is weaker

Deflection DIRECTION reflects the vector's direction relative to the lead, not its strength: a depolarisation moving AWAY from the positive electrode writes a DOWNWARD deflection regardless of magnitude — amplitude reflects magnitude, direction reflects orientation

cardiac-electrical-axis-vectors.explanation: Conflating direction with strength misreads the ECG; up/down encodes whether the vector points toward or away from the electrode, while the size of the deflection encodes the magnitude.

cardiac-electrical-axis-vectors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Upward QRS deflection in a lead”?

options.text: LV hypertrophy or left anterior fascicular block
RV hypertrophy (or normal in tall/thin people, children)

cardiac-electrical-axis-vectors.explanation: Upward QRS deflection in a lead → Depolarisation moving toward that (positive) electrode.

cardiac-electrical-axis-vectors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Positive QRS in both leads I and aVF”?

options.text: LV hypertrophy or left anterior fascicular block
RV hypertrophy (or normal in tall/thin people, children)

cardiac-electrical-axis-vectors.explanation: Positive QRS in both leads I and aVF → Normal mean electrical axis.

cardiac-electrical-axis-vectors.stem: Which should you review before “Cardiac Vectors & the Electrical Axis”?
cardiac-electrical-axis-vectors.explanation: Basic understanding of data types aids in interpreting ECG data.

ecg-leads-axis.stem: ST-segment elevation seen in leads II, III, and aVF localises the infarct to the:
ecg-leads-axis.explanation: Leads II, III, and aVF view the inferior wall, usually supplied by the right coronary artery. Anterior = V1–V4 (LAD); lateral = I, aVL, V5–V6 (circumflex).

ecg-leads-axis.stem: On the ECG, lead I is predominantly negative and lead aVF is predominantly positive. This indicates:
ecg-leads-axis.explanation: Lead I negative with aVF positive means the mean vector points down-and-right → right axis deviation (e.g. RV hypertrophy, PE). Both positive = normal; I up/aVF down = left axis.

ecg-leads-axis.stem: Regarding reading axis from leads i and avf — which is correct?

options.text: If lead I is positive and aVF is negative, the axis is normal
Lead I positive with aVF NEGATIVE indicates LEFT axis deviation; normal axis has BOTH leads I and aVF predominantly positive

ecg-leads-axis.explanation: Both positive = normal; I up/aVF down = left axis; I down/aVF up = right axis. Don't call I+/aVF− normal.

ecg-leads-axis.stem: What best explains the finding: “ST changes in II, III, aVF”?
ecg-leads-axis.explanation: ST changes in II, III, aVF → Inferior territory (right coronary artery).

ecg-leads-axis.stem: What best explains the finding: “ST changes in V1–V4”?
ecg-leads-axis.explanation: ST changes in V1–V4 → Anteroseptal territory (LAD).

ecg-leads-axis.stem: Which should you review before “ECG Leads & the Cardiac Axis”?
ecg-leads-axis.explanation: Knowledge of cardiac vectors is crucial for understanding the electrical axis.

ecg-intervals-segments.stem: A PR interval consistently longer than 0.20 seconds indicates:
ecg-intervals-segments.explanation: The PR interval measures conduction from the atria through the AV node; a value persistently above 0.20 s indicates first-degree AV block. QRS width reflects ventricular conduction and ST changes reflect ischaemia.

ecg-intervals-segments.stem: Marked prolongation of the QT interval is clinically important because it predisposes to:
ecg-intervals-segments.explanation: The QT interval reflects ventricular repolarisation; prolongation (from drugs or low potassium/magnesium/calcium) predisposes to the polymorphic ventricular tachycardia torsades de pointes.

ecg-intervals-segments.stem: Regarding interpreting a wide qrs — which is correct?

options.text: A wide QRS complex simply means a strong ventricular contraction

A wide QRS (>0.12 s) reflects SLOWED ventricular DEPOLARISATION (conduction delay) — bundle branch block, a ventricular rhythm, hyperkalaemia or pre-excitation — not the strength of contraction; amplitude (not width) relates to ventricular mass
Bundle branch block or ventricular origin

ecg-intervals-segments.explanation: QRS WIDTH encodes conduction time and QRS HEIGHT encodes muscle mass; confusing the two misreads a conduction problem as a contractility finding.

ecg-intervals-segments.stem: What best explains the finding: “PR interval >0.20 s”?

options.text: Bundle branch block or ventricular origin

ecg-intervals-segments.explanation: PR interval >0.20 s → First-degree AV block (slowed AV conduction).

ecg-intervals-segments.stem: What best explains the finding: “QRS duration >0.12 s”?

options.text: Bundle branch block or ventricular origin

ecg-intervals-segments.explanation: QRS duration >0.12 s → Bundle branch block or ventricular origin.

ecg-intervals-segments.stem: Which should you review before “ECG Intervals & Segments”?
ecg-intervals-segments.explanation: Understanding wave formation is essential for interpreting intervals and segments.

blood-pressure-baroreceptor-reflex.stem: A sudden fall in arterial blood pressure (e.g. on standing) triggers the baroreceptor reflex to:

options.text: Decrease heart rate and cause vasodilation
Increase sympathetic outflow → increased heart rate, contractility, and vasoconstriction

blood-pressure-baroreceptor-reflex.explanation: Reduced baroreceptor firing (low BP) disinhibits the medullary sympathetic centres → ↑heart rate, ↑contractility, and vaso/venoconstriction, restoring blood pressure.

blood-pressure-baroreceptor-reflex.stem: Mean arterial pressure is determined by the product of:

options.text: Cardiac output and total peripheral resistance

blood-pressure-baroreceptor-reflex.explanation: MAP = cardiac output × total peripheral resistance (analogous to pressure = flow × resistance). Changes in CO or arteriolar tone (TPR) therefore alter blood pressure.

blood-pressure-baroreceptor-reflex.stem: Regarding baroreceptor response to a bp rise — which is correct?

options.text: A rise in blood pressure increases baroreceptor firing and thus increases heart rate
A BP rise increases baroreceptor firing → ↑parasympathetic/↓sympathetic → DECREASED heart rate and vasodilation (to bring BP back down)

blood-pressure-baroreceptor-reflex.explanation: It is negative feedback: the reflex opposes the change, so more stretch (higher BP) slows the heart, it doesn't speed it up.

blood-pressure-baroreceptor-reflex.stem: What best explains the finding: “MAP = CO × TPR”?

options.text: Baroreflex response to a fall in BP

blood-pressure-baroreceptor-reflex.explanation: MAP = CO × TPR → Fundamental BP equation.

blood-pressure-baroreceptor-reflex.stem: What best explains the finding: “Carotid sinus massage slows the heart”?

options.text: Baroreflex response to a fall in BP

blood-pressure-baroreceptor-reflex.explanation: Carotid sinus massage slows the heart → Baroreceptor activation → ↑vagal tone.

long-term-bp-raas.stem: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure by all of the following EXCEPT:
long-term-bp-raas.explanation: Angiotensin II RAISES BP: vasoconstriction, aldosterone (Na⁺/water retention), ADH, and thirst. Natriuresis/diuresis (lowering BP) is the action of the OPPOSING natriuretic peptides (ANP/BNP).

long-term-bp-raas.stem: Long-term regulation of arterial blood pressure is ultimately determined by:

options.text: Renal control of blood volume (salt and water balance)

long-term-bp-raas.explanation: Because neural reflexes reset over time, sustained blood pressure is set by the kidney via pressure-natriuresis and the RAAS, which control blood volume.

long-term-bp-raas.stem: Regarding short-term vs long-term bp control — which is correct?

options.text: The baroreceptor reflex is responsible for long-term blood pressure regulation
The baroreflex is SHORT-term (and resets over days); LONG-term BP is controlled by the kidney/RAAS via blood volume (pressure-natriuresis)
Response to low BP/volume, low Na⁺, or sympathetic drive

long-term-bp-raas.explanation: Neural reflexes buffer moment-to-moment changes but adapt; sustained BP is set by renal salt/water handling.

long-term-bp-raas.stem: What best explains the finding: “Renin released by the juxtaglomerular apparatus”?

options.text: Response to low BP/volume, low Na⁺, or sympathetic drive

long-term-bp-raas.explanation: Renin released by the juxtaglomerular apparatus → Response to low BP/volume, low Na⁺, or sympathetic drive.

long-term-bp-raas.stem: What best explains the finding: “ACE converts angiotensin I → II (in the lung)”?

options.text: Response to low BP/volume, low Na⁺, or sympathetic drive

long-term-bp-raas.explanation: ACE converts angiotensin I → II (in the lung) → Rate-limiting step (ACE-inhibitor target).

long-term-bp-raas.stem: Which should you review before “Long-Term BP Control: RAAS & the Kidney”?

ecg-systematic-interpretation.stem: An ECG shows an irregularly irregular rhythm with no discernible P waves. The most likely diagnosis is:
ecg-systematic-interpretation.explanation: An irregularly irregular rhythm with absent P waves is characteristic of atrial fibrillation. Sinus rhythm requires an upright P wave before each QRS in a regular pattern.

ecg-systematic-interpretation.stem: When reading an ECG systematically, sinus rhythm is confirmed by:

options.text: An upright P wave in lead II preceding every QRS with a constant PR interval

ecg-systematic-interpretation.explanation: Sinus rhythm = every QRS is preceded by an upright P wave in lead II (SA-node origin) with a constant, normal PR interval, at a regular rate.

ecg-systematic-interpretation.stem: Regarding interpreting the ecg — which is correct?

options.text: An ECG can be interpreted definitively without any clinical information
ECG interpretation must be combined with the clinical context — the same tracing (e.g. ST changes) can be normal variant, ischaemia, or pericarditis depending on the patient

ecg-systematic-interpretation.explanation: Sensitivity/specificity of ECG findings depend on pretest probability; always correlate with symptoms, history, and biomarkers.

ecg-systematic-interpretation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Irregularly irregular rhythm, no P waves”?
ecg-systematic-interpretation.explanation: Irregularly irregular rhythm, no P waves → Atrial fibrillation.

ecg-systematic-interpretation.stem: What best explains the finding: “ST-segment elevation in a coronary territory”?
ecg-systematic-interpretation.explanation: ST-segment elevation in a coronary territory → Acute STEMI (transmural injury).

ecg-systematic-interpretation.stem: Which is a clinical application of “ECG in Clinical Practice: A Systematic Approach”?

options.text: Chest X-ray for the Cardiovascular System

ecg-systematic-interpretation.explanation: Chest X-ray findings can complement ECG interpretations in cardiac assessments.

ecg-systematic-interpretation.stem: Which should you review before “ECG in Clinical Practice: A Systematic Approach”?
ecg-systematic-interpretation.explanation: Understanding wave formation is essential for ECG interpretation.

ecg-chamber-enlargement.stem: A tall, peaked P wave (greater than 2.5 mm) in lead II indicates:
ecg-chamber-enlargement.explanation: Right atrial enlargement produces a tall, peaked P wave ("P pulmonale"), classically in lead II. Left atrial enlargement instead gives a broad, notched ("M-shaped") P wave with a deep terminal negativity in V1.

ecg-chamber-enlargement.stem: Left ventricular hypertrophy on the ECG is typically suggested by:

options.text: A dominant R wave in V1 with right axis deviation
Tall R waves in the left-sided leads and deep S waves in the right-sided leads (increased voltage)
A peaked P wave in lead II

ecg-chamber-enlargement.explanation: LVH increases leftward QRS voltage — tall R waves in I/aVL/V5–6 and deep S waves in V1–2 (e.g. Sokolow–Lyon >35 mm), often with left axis deviation and a strain pattern. A dominant R in V1 with right axis suggests RVH.

ecg-chamber-enlargement.stem: Regarding reliability of ecg hypertrophy criteria — which is correct?

options.text: High QRS voltage on the ECG definitively diagnoses left ventricular hypertrophy

ECG voltage criteria are SUPPORTIVE but not definitive — they can be falsely positive (thin chest wall) or falsely negative (obesity, effusion); ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY is the confirmatory test for chamber size and hypertrophy

ecg-chamber-enlargement.explanation: Voltage on the surface ECG depends on more than muscle mass (body habitus, lead placement), so treating the ECG as definitive over/under-calls hypertrophy; it is a screening clue confirmed by imaging.

ecg-chamber-enlargement.stem: What best explains the finding: “Tall, peaked P wave in lead II”?
ecg-chamber-enlargement.explanation: Tall, peaked P wave in lead II → Right atrial enlargement (P pulmonale).

ecg-chamber-enlargement.stem: What best explains the finding: “Broad, notched (bifid) P wave with deep terminal V1 negativity”?
ecg-chamber-enlargement.explanation: Broad, notched (bifid) P wave with deep terminal V1 negativity → Left atrial enlargement (P mitrale).

ecg-chamber-enlargement.stem: Which should you review before “ECG of Chamber Enlargement”?
ecg-chamber-enlargement.explanation: Understanding electrical axis is crucial for interpreting chamber enlargement.

echocardiography-basics.stem: The ejection fraction, the principal echocardiographic measure of systolic function, is calculated as:
echocardiography-basics.explanation: EF = stroke volume ÷ end-diastolic volume (normal ~55–70%). A reduced EF indicates systolic dysfunction (HFrEF); heart failure with a preserved EF is HFpEF.

echocardiography-basics.stem: Which echocardiographic mode is used to measure the velocity and direction of blood flow (e.g. across a stenotic valve)?
echocardiography-basics.explanation: Doppler echocardiography measures blood-flow velocity/direction, used to quantify valve gradients and regurgitation. M-mode gives timing/measurements; 2-D shows real-time anatomy.

echocardiography-basics.stem: Regarding what ejection fraction measures — which is correct?

options.text: A normal ejection fraction rules out heart failure
A normal/preserved EF does NOT exclude heart failure — HFpEF has a preserved EF with impaired filling (diastolic dysfunction)

echocardiography-basics.explanation: EF measures the systolic emptying fraction; diastolic (filling) heart failure occurs with a normal EF, so echo must also assess diastolic function.

echocardiography-basics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Reduced ejection fraction (<40%)”?

options.text: Prior/current myocardial infarction in that territory

echocardiography-basics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Heart failure with preserved EF”?

options.text: Prior/current myocardial infarction in that territory

echocardiography-basics.explanation: Heart failure with preserved EF → HFpEF (diastolic/filling problem).

echocardiography-basics.stem: Which should you review before “Echocardiography: Basics”?

options.text: Cell Communication: Signalling Modes & Receptor Types
Histology of the Heart Wall & Conduction Cells

echocardiography-basics.explanation: Understanding cell signaling is essential for grasping how echocardiography assesses heart function.

chest-xray-cardiac.stem: On a standard PA chest radiograph, the upper limit of normal for the cardiothoracic ratio is approximately:
chest-xray-cardiac.explanation: A cardiothoracic ratio (cardiac width ÷ thoracic width) above 0.5 on a PA film suggests cardiomegaly. Portable/AP films magnify the heart, making the ratio unreliable.

chest-xray-cardiac.stem: Kerley B lines, upper-lobe vascular diversion, and perihilar "bat-wing" opacity on a chest X-ray indicate:

options.text: Pulmonary venous congestion from left heart failure

chest-xray-cardiac.explanation: These are radiographic signs of pulmonary venous congestion/oedema, typically from left ventricular failure raising pulmonary capillary pressure.

chest-xray-cardiac.stem: Regarding reliability of ctr on portable films — which is correct?

options.text: A cardiothoracic ratio above 0.5 always means cardiomegaly regardless of the film type
CTR is only reliable on a PA erect film; an AP/portable (supine) film magnifies the heart, so it can falsely appear enlarged

chest-xray-cardiac.explanation: On AP films the heart is farther from the detector and magnified; the >0.5 rule applies to standard PA films.

chest-xray-cardiac.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cardiothoracic ratio > 0.5 on a PA film”?
chest-xray-cardiac.explanation: Cardiothoracic ratio > 0.5 on a PA film → Cardiomegaly (or pericardial effusion).

chest-xray-cardiac.stem: What best explains the finding: “Kerley B lines + upper-lobe diversion”?
chest-xray-cardiac.explanation: Kerley B lines + upper-lobe diversion → Pulmonary venous congestion (LV failure).

chest-xray-cardiac.stem: Which should you review before “Chest X-ray for the Cardiovascular System”?

options.text: ECG in Clinical Practice: A Systematic Approach
Histology of the Heart Wall & Conduction Cells

chest-xray-cardiac.explanation: Understanding ECG is crucial for correlating with CXR findings.

cardiac-cycle-heart-sounds.stem: The first heart sound (S1) is produced by:

options.text: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
Closure of the mitral and tricuspid (AV) valves

cardiac-cycle-heart-sounds.explanation: S1 marks closure of the atrioventricular valves (mitral + tricuspid) at the onset of ventricular systole. S2 is closure of the semilunar valves at the onset of diastole.

cardiac-cycle-heart-sounds.stem: During isovolumetric contraction of the ventricle:

options.text: The aortic valve is open and blood is ejected
All four valves are closed and ventricular volume does not change while pressure rises
The mitral valve is open and the ventricle fills

cardiac-cycle-heart-sounds.explanation: Isovolumetric contraction occurs between mitral closure and aortic opening: all valves are shut, so volume is constant while pressure rises rapidly until it exceeds aortic pressure and ejection begins.

cardiac-cycle-heart-sounds.stem: Regarding what s2 represents — which is correct?

options.text: The second heart sound (S2) is produced by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves
S2 is the closure of the SEMILUNAR (aortic + pulmonary) valves at the start of DIASTOLE; S1 is AV valve closure at the start of systole
Mitral + tricuspid (AV) valve closure — start of systole
Aortic + pulmonary (semilunar) valve closure — start of diastole

cardiac-cycle-heart-sounds.explanation: S1 = AV valves (start of systole), S2 = semilunar valves (start of diastole). Don't swap them.

options.text: Aortic + pulmonary (semilunar) valve closure — start of diastole
All four valves closed, pressure rising
Mitral + tricuspid (AV) valve closure — start of systole
Rapid ventricular filling — volume overload/HF (or normal in youth)

cardiac-cycle-heart-sounds.explanation: S1 ("lub") → Mitral + tricuspid (AV) valve closure — start of systole.

options.text: Mitral + tricuspid (AV) valve closure — start of systole
All four valves closed, pressure rising
Rapid ventricular filling — volume overload/HF (or normal in youth)
Aortic + pulmonary (semilunar) valve closure — start of diastole

cardiac-cycle-heart-sounds.explanation: S2 ("dub") → Aortic + pulmonary (semilunar) valve closure — start of diastole.

hemodynamics-preload-afterload-cardiac-o.stem: According to the Frank–Starling law, increasing ventricular preload (end-diastolic stretch) will:

options.text: Increase the force of contraction and stroke volume (up to a point)
Have no effect on stroke volume

hemodynamics-preload-afterload-cardiac-o.explanation: Greater end-diastolic stretch (preload) increases the force of contraction and thus stroke volume — the intrinsic Frank–Starling mechanism that matches cardiac output to venous return.

hemodynamics-preload-afterload-cardiac-o.stem: Chronic hypertension increases which determinant of stroke volume, thereby increasing cardiac work?
hemodynamics-preload-afterload-cardiac-o.explanation: Hypertension raises the arterial pressure the ventricle must eject against (afterload), reducing stroke volume for a given contractility and increasing cardiac workload — eventually causing LV hypertrophy.

hemodynamics-preload-afterload-cardiac-o.stem: Regarding preload vs afterload — which is correct?

options.text: Afterload is the ventricular stretch at the end of filling
PRELOAD is the end-diastolic stretch/volume (venous return); AFTERLOAD is the resistance/pressure the ventricle ejects against (arterial pressure/TPR)

hemodynamics-preload-afterload-cardiac-o.explanation: Preload = "load before contraction" (filling/stretch); afterload = "load after contraction begins" (ejection resistance). Don't confuse them.

hemodynamics-preload-afterload-cardiac-o.stem: What best explains the finding: “Increased venous return → increased stroke volume”?
hemodynamics-preload-afterload-cardiac-o.explanation: Increased venous return → increased stroke volume → Frank–Starling (preload → force).

hemodynamics-preload-afterload-cardiac-o.stem: What best explains the finding: “Reduced stroke volume in aortic stenosis/hypertension”?
hemodynamics-preload-afterload-cardiac-o.explanation: Reduced stroke volume in aortic stenosis/hypertension → Increased afterload.

hemodynamics-preload-afterload-cardiac-o.stem: Which should you review before “Hemodynamics: Preload, Afterload & Cardiac Output”?
hemodynamics-preload-afterload-cardiac-o.explanation: Understanding preload and its effect on stroke volume is essential.

jugular-venous-pressure-waveform.stem: The jugular venous pressure is a useful bedside measure because it reflects:
jugular-venous-pressure-waveform.explanation: The internal jugular vein communicates with the right atrium without an intervening valve, so the JVP mirrors right atrial pressure and right-heart filling; it rises in right heart failure, volume overload and pericardial disease.

jugular-venous-pressure-waveform.stem: Intermittent giant "cannon" a waves in the JVP are characteristic of:
jugular-venous-pressure-waveform.explanation: In complete heart block the atria and ventricles beat independently; when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve, a giant "cannon" a wave is produced. Atrial fibrillation instead abolishes the a wave altogether.

jugular-venous-pressure-waveform.stem: Regarding distinguishing the jvp from the carotid pulse — which is correct?

options.text: A pulsation in the neck must be the carotid arterial pulse

The JVP is a VENOUS pulsation: it is non-palpable, has a biphasic waveform, varies with respiration and position, and is reduced by pressure — unlike the palpable, single, position-independent carotid pulse; mistaking one for the other misreads right-heart status
Elevated right atrial pressure (right heart failure/overload)

jugular-venous-pressure-waveform.explanation: The JVP's value comes from being venous (reflecting right atrial pressure); confusing it with the carotid loses the information about right-heart filling and the diagnostic waveform.

jugular-venous-pressure-waveform.stem: What best explains the finding: “Raised JVP (>3–4 cm above the sternal angle)”?

options.text: Complete heart block (atrium contracts against closed tricuspid)
Elevated right atrial pressure (right heart failure/overload)

jugular-venous-pressure-waveform.explanation: Raised JVP (>3–4 cm above the sternal angle) → Elevated right atrial pressure (right heart failure/overload).

jugular-venous-pressure-waveform.stem: What best explains the finding: “Absent a wave”?

options.text: Elevated right atrial pressure (right heart failure/overload)
Complete heart block (atrium contracts against closed tricuspid)

jugular-venous-pressure-waveform.explanation: Absent a wave → Atrial fibrillation (no coordinated atrial contraction).

frank-starling-cardiac-function.stem: The Frank–Starling mechanism states that, within physiological limits, an increase in ventricular end-diastolic volume (preload) causes:

options.text: An increase in the force of contraction and stroke volume

frank-starling-cardiac-function.explanation: Greater end-diastolic filling stretches the cardiac sarcomeres toward optimal actin–myosin overlap (and raises calcium sensitivity), increasing the force of contraction and stroke volume — an intrinsic property that also keeps the two ventricles' outputs matched.

frank-starling-cardiac-function.stem: On a cardiac function (Starling) curve, increasing contractility (e.g. sympathetic stimulation) is represented by:

options.text: Movement rightward along the same curve
An upward shift of the entire curve (greater stroke volume at any preload)
A downward shift of the curve

frank-starling-cardiac-function.explanation: Preload changes move the heart along a given curve, but increasing contractility shifts the whole curve upward so that more stroke volume is produced at any given preload; reduced contractility (heart failure) shifts it downward.

frank-starling-cardiac-function.stem: Regarding preload vs contractility on the starling curve — which is correct?

options.text: Increasing preload and increasing contractility have the same effect on the heart

Increasing PRELOAD moves the heart ALONG its existing Starling curve (more filling → more force), whereas increasing CONTRACTILITY shifts the ENTIRE curve upward (more force at ANY given preload) — they are distinct interventions

frank-starling-cardiac-function.explanation: Conflating the two obscures how inotropes (contractility, new curve) differ from fluids (preload, same curve) in managing cardiac output — a central concept in heart-failure and shock physiology.

frank-starling-cardiac-function.stem: What best explains the finding: “Stroke volume rising as end-diastolic volume rises”?
frank-starling-cardiac-function.explanation: Stroke volume rising as end-diastolic volume rises → Frank–Starling (preload → force).

frank-starling-cardiac-function.stem: What best explains the finding: “Right and left cardiac outputs staying equal”?
frank-starling-cardiac-function.explanation: Right and left cardiac outputs staying equal → Starling mechanism auto-matching the ventricles.

frank-starling-cardiac-function.stem: Which should you review before “The Frank–Starling Mechanism”?

options.text: Histology of the Heart Wall & Conduction Cells

frank-starling-cardiac-function.explanation: The Frank-Starling mechanism directly relates to the balance of outputs in systemic and pulmonary circulation.

cardiac-biomarkers-acs.stem: The preferred biomarker for diagnosing acute myocardial infarction, owing to its high sensitivity and specificity, is:
cardiac-biomarkers-acs.explanation: Cardiac troponin (I or T) is the gold-standard marker — most sensitive and specific for myocardial injury; it rises ~3–4 h after onset and remains elevated for 7–10 days.

cardiac-biomarkers-acs.stem: Three days after an MI, a patient develops recurrent chest pain. Which marker is most useful to detect re-infarction, given that troponin is still elevated?

options.text: CK-MB (which clears faster and would re-rise)

cardiac-biomarkers-acs.explanation: Because troponin stays elevated for days, a fresh CK-MB rise (CK-MB normalises in ~2–3 days) is useful to detect re-infarction on top of a recent MI.

cardiac-biomarkers-acs.stem: Regarding specificity of troponin — which is correct?

options.text: An elevated troponin always means an acute coronary syndrome (heart attack)
Troponin is sensitive for myocardial INJURY but not specific for ACS — it also rises in PE, sepsis, myocarditis, HF, and renal failure; interpret with the clinical picture and a rise/fall pattern

cardiac-biomarkers-acs.explanation: Troponin marks myocyte injury from any cause; the diagnosis of MI requires the right context (symptoms, ECG) plus a dynamic rise/fall.

cardiac-biomarkers-acs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Elevated troponin with a rise/fall pattern + chest pain + ECG changes”?
cardiac-biomarkers-acs.explanation: Elevated troponin with a rise/fall pattern + chest pain + ECG changes → Acute myocardial infarction.

cardiac-biomarkers-acs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Troponin still positive 7 days after MI”?
cardiac-biomarkers-acs.explanation: Troponin still positive 7 days after MI → Prolonged troponin elevation (7–10 days).

cardiac-biomarkers-acs.stem: Which should you review before “Cardiac Biomarkers in Acute Coronary Syndrome”?

options.text: ECG in Clinical Practice: A Systematic Approach

cardiac-biomarkers-acs.explanation: ECG interpretation is crucial for correlating troponin results with myocardial injury.

blood-pressure-measurement-abpm.stem: A patient consistently has blood pressure of 155/95 in the clinic but a normal average of 120/78 on 24-hour ambulatory monitoring. This is:
blood-pressure-measurement-abpm.explanation: High office BP with normal out-of-office (ABPM) readings defines white-coat hypertension; relying on the clinic reading alone risks unnecessary treatment.

blood-pressure-measurement-abpm.stem: Using a blood-pressure cuff that is too small for the patient's arm will typically:
blood-pressure-measurement-abpm.explanation: An undersized cuff requires more pressure to occlude the artery, falsely elevating the reading. Correct cuff size and arm position (at heart level) are essential for accuracy.

blood-pressure-measurement-abpm.stem: Regarding white-coat vs masked hypertension risk — which is correct?

options.text: Masked hypertension is harmless because the clinic reading is normal
MASKED hypertension (normal in clinic, high outside) carries real cardiovascular risk that office BP MISSES — it is arguably more dangerous than white-coat hypertension

blood-pressure-measurement-abpm.explanation: Because the clinic BP is reassuring, masked hypertension goes untreated despite genuine end-organ risk; out-of-office monitoring is needed to catch it.

blood-pressure-measurement-abpm.stem: What best explains the finding: “High BP in clinic, normal on ABPM”?

options.text: Cuff too small for arm circumference

blood-pressure-measurement-abpm.explanation: High BP in clinic, normal on ABPM → White-coat hypertension.

blood-pressure-measurement-abpm.stem: What best explains the finding: “Normal clinic BP but high on ABPM/HBPM”?

options.text: Cuff too small for arm circumference

blood-pressure-measurement-abpm.explanation: Normal clinic BP but high on ABPM/HBPM → Masked hypertension (dangerous — missed risk).

blood-pressure-measurement-abpm.stem: Which should you review before “Blood Pressure Measurement & Ambulatory Monitoring”?

options.text: Blood Pressure Determinants & the Baroreceptor Reflex

blood-pressure-measurement-abpm.explanation: Understanding baroreceptor reflex is essential for grasping blood pressure regulation.

cardiovascular-examination.stem: The mitral valve is best auscultated at the:
cardiovascular-examination.explanation: The mitral area is at the cardiac apex (5th ICS, midclavicular line). Aortic = right 2nd ICS, pulmonary = left 2nd ICS, tricuspid = left lower sternal border ("APTM").

cardiovascular-examination.stem: A murmur occurring between the first heart sound (S1) and the second heart sound (S2) is:
cardiovascular-examination.explanation: S1→S2 is systole, so a murmur there is systolic (e.g. aortic stenosis, mitral regurgitation). A murmur between S2 and the next S1 is diastolic.

cardiovascular-examination.stem: Regarding timing a murmur — which is correct?

options.text: A murmur heard between S2 and the next S1 is a systolic murmur
A murmur between S2 and S1 is DIASTOLIC (e.g. aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis); systolic murmurs fall between S1 and S2
e.g. aortic stenosis or mitral regurgitation

cardiovascular-examination.explanation: Always fix S1 and S2 first, then place the murmur: S1→S2 = systole, S2→S1 = diastole. Mis-timing changes the diagnosis entirely.

cardiovascular-examination.stem: What best explains the finding: “Apex beat in the 5th ICS, midclavicular line”?

options.text: e.g. aortic stenosis or mitral regurgitation
e.g. aortic regurgitation or mitral stenosis
A murmur intense enough to feel

cardiovascular-examination.explanation: Apex beat in the 5th ICS, midclavicular line → Normal LV apex (displaced in cardiomegaly).

cardiovascular-examination.stem: What best explains the finding: “Systolic murmur (between S1 and S2)”?

options.text: e.g. aortic regurgitation or mitral stenosis
A murmur intense enough to feel
e.g. aortic stenosis or mitral regurgitation

cardiovascular-examination.explanation: Systolic murmur (between S1 and S2) → e.g. aortic stenosis or mitral regurgitation.

cardiovascular-examination.stem: Which should you review before “The Cardiovascular Physical Examination”?

options.text: Histology of the Heart Wall & Conduction Cells

cardiovascular-examination.explanation: Understanding heart anatomy is crucial for the cardiovascular exam.

heart-sounds-murmurs-auscultation.stem: The first heart sound (S1) is produced by:

options.text: Opening of the aortic and pulmonary valves
Closure of the mitral and tricuspid (atrioventricular) valves
Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves

heart-sounds-murmurs-auscultation.explanation: S1 marks closure of the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves at the onset of ventricular systole; S2 marks closure of the semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves at its end. Valve opening is normally silent.

heart-sounds-murmurs-auscultation.stem: A harsh ejection systolic murmur best heard at the right second intercostal space and radiating to the carotids suggests:
heart-sounds-murmurs-auscultation.explanation: Aortic stenosis produces an ejection systolic murmur loudest at the aortic area (right 2nd ICS) that radiates to the carotids. Timing it between S1 and S2 confirms it is systolic, and the location/radiation identify the valve.

heart-sounds-murmurs-auscultation.stem: Regarding what produces the heart sounds — which is correct?

options.text: The heart sounds are produced when the valves open

Heart sounds are produced by valve CLOSURE (and the associated flow deceleration/vibration), not opening — S1 from AV-valve closure and S2 from semilunar-valve closure; valve opening is normally silent
Closure of AV then semilunar valves

heart-sounds-murmurs-auscultation.explanation: Attributing the sounds to opening reverses the physiology and mistimes the cycle; knowing S1/S2 mark closure is what lets you place a murmur correctly in systole or diastole.

heart-sounds-murmurs-auscultation.stem: What best explains the finding: “S1 and S2 bracketing systole”?

options.text: Closure of AV then semilunar valves

heart-sounds-murmurs-auscultation.explanation: S1 and S2 bracketing systole → Closure of AV then semilunar valves.

heart-sounds-murmurs-auscultation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids”?

options.text: Closure of AV then semilunar valves

heart-sounds-murmurs-auscultation.explanation: Systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids → Aortic stenosis.

heart-sounds-murmurs-auscultation.stem: Which should you review before “Heart Sounds & Murmurs”?
heart-sounds-murmurs-auscultation.explanation: The cardiac cycle is fundamental to understanding heart sounds and their timing.

nephron-kidney-histology.stem: Which cell type forms the outermost layer of the glomerular filtration barrier and provides the size-selective slit diaphragms?
nephron-kidney-histology.explanation: Podocytes wrap the capillaries with interdigitating foot processes; the slits between them, bridged by slit diaphragms, are the final size barrier. Endothelium is the first layer and the GBM the middle (charge) layer.

nephron-kidney-histology.stem: The macula densa, a component of the juxtaglomerular apparatus, functions as a sensor of:
nephron-kidney-histology.explanation: The macula densa is a plaque of specialised distal tubular cells that senses luminal NaCl; via the JGA it adjusts afferent arteriolar tone (tubuloglomerular feedback) and renin release.

nephron-kidney-histology.stem: Regarding distinguishing pct from dct on histology — which is correct?

options.text: Both convoluted tubules look the same
The PCT has a prominent brush border, acidophilic cytoplasm and a narrow lumen; the DCT lacks a brush border, has a wider clearer lumen and more nuclei per cross-section
Size barrier of the filtration apparatus

nephron-kidney-histology.explanation: The brush border (apical microvilli) is the single most reliable feature — it reflects the PCT's massive reabsorptive surface, which the DCT does not need.

nephron-kidney-histology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Brush border on tubular cells”?

options.text: Size barrier of the filtration apparatus

nephron-kidney-histology.explanation: Brush border on tubular cells → PCT — microvilli for bulk reabsorption.

nephron-kidney-histology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Podocytes with foot processes and slit diaphragms”?

options.text: Size barrier of the filtration apparatus

nephron-kidney-histology.explanation: Podocytes with foot processes and slit diaphragms → Size barrier of the filtration apparatus.

nephron-kidney-histology.stem: Which should you review before “Microscopic Anatomy of the Kidney & Nephron”?

options.text: Congenital Anomalies of the Kidney & Urinary Tract

nephron-kidney-histology.explanation: Basic understanding of respiratory anatomy may aid in kidney function context.

lower-urinary-tract-histology.stem: The characteristic epithelium lining the renal pelvis, ureter and bladder is:
lower-urinary-tract-histology.explanation: Urothelium (transitional epithelium) with its umbrella cells and apical plaques allows distension and forms an impermeable barrier against urine — a feature unique to the urinary passages.

lower-urinary-tract-histology.stem: Peristalsis in the ureter that actively propels urine to the bladder is generated by:

options.text: Smooth muscle in the ureteric wall

lower-urinary-tract-histology.explanation: The ureter has inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth-muscle layers that contract peristaltically; urine is actively pumped, not merely dropped, to the bladder.

lower-urinary-tract-histology.stem: Regarding interpreting urothelial thickness — which is correct?

options.text: A specimen with only 2–3 cell layers of urothelium is abnormally thin/atrophic
Urothelium normally appears thinner (flattened umbrella cells) when the organ is DISTENDED and thicker when relaxed — thickness reflects the state of filling, not pathology
Stretchable, impermeable lining of the urinary tract

lower-urinary-tract-histology.explanation: Transitional epithelium is defined by its ability to change appearance with stretch; you must know the filling state before calling it abnormal.

lower-urinary-tract-histology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Transitional epithelium (urothelium) with umbrella cells”?

options.text: Stretchable, impermeable lining of the urinary tract

lower-urinary-tract-histology.explanation: Transitional epithelium (urothelium) with umbrella cells → Stretchable, impermeable lining of the urinary tract.

lower-urinary-tract-histology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Epithelium appears thicker when empty, thinner when full”?

options.text: Stretchable, impermeable lining of the urinary tract

lower-urinary-tract-histology.explanation: Epithelium appears thicker when empty, thinner when full → Umbrella cells flatten on distension.

lower-urinary-tract-histology.stem: Which should you review before “Histology of the Ureter, Bladder & Urethra”?

options.text: Development of the Kidney & Urinary Tract
Congenital Anomalies of the Kidney & Urinary Tract

lower-urinary-tract-histology.explanation: Knowledge of kidney and ureter anatomy supports understanding of their histological features.

renal-blood-supply-vasculature.stem: Blood leaving the glomerular capillaries passes next into the:

options.text: Efferent arteriole, then a second (peritubular/vasa recta) capillary bed

renal-blood-supply-vasculature.explanation: The kidney has a portal arrangement: glomerular blood exits via the efferent arteriole into a second capillary bed (peritubular capillaries around cortical tubules, or vasa recta around medullary loops) before draining to veins.

renal-blood-supply-vasculature.stem: Which nephrons possess long loops of Henle with vasa recta and are chiefly responsible for producing concentrated urine?
renal-blood-supply-vasculature.explanation: Juxtamedullary nephrons (~15%) have glomeruli near the medulla, long loops of Henle and accompanying vasa recta; they build and use the medullary osmotic gradient to concentrate urine. Cortical nephrons have short loops and handle bulk reabsorption.

renal-blood-supply-vasculature.stem: Regarding vessel leaving the glomerulus — which is correct?

options.text: Blood leaves the glomerular capillaries through a venule like elsewhere in the body
Glomerular blood exits through an EFFERENT ARTERIOLE into a SECOND capillary bed (peritubular capillaries/vasa recta) — a portal system with two capillary beds in series, not a venule
Portal arrangement — two capillary beds in series

renal-blood-supply-vasculature.explanation: This unusual arteriole-to-capillary-to-arteriole arrangement is what lets the kidney set glomerular pressure (via efferent tone) independently of tubular perfusion — the basis of GFR autoregulation and of ACE-inhibitor effects.

renal-blood-supply-vasculature.stem: What best explains the finding: “Efferent arteriole (not venule) leaving the glomerulus”?

options.text: Portal arrangement — two capillary beds in series

renal-blood-supply-vasculature.explanation: Efferent arteriole (not venule) leaving the glomerulus → Portal arrangement — two capillary beds in series.

renal-blood-supply-vasculature.stem: What best explains the finding: “Vasa recta paralleling the long loops of Henle”?

options.text: Portal arrangement — two capillary beds in series

renal-blood-supply-vasculature.explanation: Vasa recta paralleling the long loops of Henle → Juxtamedullary nephrons — countercurrent exchange.

kidney-development-metanephros.stem: The collecting ducts, minor and major calyces, renal pelvis and ureter all develop from the:
kidney-development-metanephros.explanation: The ureteric bud (an outgrowth of the mesonephric duct) branches to form the entire collecting system; the metanephric blastema it induces forms the nephrons from glomerulus to DCT.

kidney-development-metanephros.stem: The definitive (permanent) human kidney is derived from which embryonic system?
kidney-development-metanephros.explanation: The metanephros is the third and permanent system; the pronephros regresses completely and the mesonephros is only transiently functional (its duct persists to form the ureteric bud and, in males, genital ducts).

kidney-development-metanephros.stem: Regarding origin of the collecting ducts vs nephron — which is correct?

options.text: The whole kidney, including collecting ducts, develops from one mesenchymal mass

The collecting system (collecting ducts, calyces, pelvis, ureter) comes from the URETERIC BUD, while the nephron proper (glomerulus to DCT) comes from the METANEPHRIC BLASTEMA — two different origins that induce each other

kidney-development-metanephros.explanation: The dual origin explains why a failed junction between bud-derived collecting ducts and blastema-derived nephrons causes multicystic dysplastic kidney; it is a classic exam distinction.

kidney-development-metanephros.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ureter, pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts”?
kidney-development-metanephros.explanation: Ureter, pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts → Ureteric bud derivatives.

kidney-development-metanephros.stem: What best explains the finding: “Glomerulus, PCT, loop and DCT (the nephron)”?
kidney-development-metanephros.explanation: Glomerulus, PCT, loop and DCT (the nephron) → Metanephric blastema derivatives.

kidney-development-metanephros.stem: Which should you review before “Development of the Kidney & Urinary Tract”?
kidney-development-metanephros.explanation: Understanding kidney anatomy is essential for grasping development.

kub-congenital-anomalies.stem: A horseshoe kidney sits abnormally low in the abdomen because its ascent is arrested by the:
kub-congenital-anomalies.explanation: The fused lower poles of a horseshoe kidney cannot pass beneath the inferior mesenteric artery during ascent, so the kidney remains low in the abdomen.

kub-congenital-anomalies.stem: Bilateral renal agenesis is incompatible with postnatal life primarily because the resulting oligohydramnios causes:
kub-congenital-anomalies.explanation: Fetal urine generates most amniotic fluid; its absence (oligohydramnios) prevents normal lung expansion, producing lethal pulmonary hypoplasia — the core of the Potter sequence.

kub-congenital-anomalies.stem: Regarding cause of the potter sequence — which is correct?

options.text: Potter sequence is a primary lung disease

Potter sequence is caused by OLIGOHYDRAMNIOS — usually from bilateral renal agenesis or severe obstruction — because fetal urine produces most amniotic fluid; the lung hypoplasia and limb deformities are secondary to compression
Bilateral renal agenesis/severe obstruction (fetal urine makes amniotic fluid)

kub-congenital-anomalies.explanation: It is a mechanical/fluid consequence of absent fetal urine, not an intrinsic lung defect — the kidneys are the root cause.

kub-congenital-anomalies.stem: What best explains the finding: “Low-lying midline kidney caught under the IMA”?

options.text: Bilateral renal agenesis/severe obstruction (fetal urine makes amniotic fluid)
Premature splitting of the ureteric bud

kub-congenital-anomalies.explanation: Low-lying midline kidney caught under the IMA → Horseshoe kidney (fused lower poles).

kub-congenital-anomalies.stem: What best explains the finding: “Oligohydramnios + lung hypoplasia + Potter facies”?

options.text: Premature splitting of the ureteric bud
Bilateral renal agenesis/severe obstruction (fetal urine makes amniotic fluid)

kub-congenital-anomalies.explanation: Oligohydramnios + lung hypoplasia + Potter facies → Bilateral renal agenesis/severe obstruction (fetal urine makes amniotic fluid).

kub-congenital-anomalies.stem: Which should you review before “Congenital Anomalies of the Kidney & Urinary Tract”?

options.text: Microscopic Anatomy of the Kidney & Nephron
Histology of the Ureter, Bladder & Urethra

kub-congenital-anomalies.explanation: Understanding classification aids in recognizing types of congenital anomalies.

glomerular-filtration-gfr.stem: Which substance is filtered but neither reabsorbed nor secreted, making its clearance the gold standard for measuring GFR?
glomerular-filtration-gfr.explanation: Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so all filtered inulin appears in urine and its clearance equals GFR. PAH clearance measures renal plasma flow; glucose and sodium are heavily reabsorbed.

glomerular-filtration-gfr.stem: Selective constriction of the efferent arteriole (as by angiotensin II) tends to:

options.text: Decrease GFR by lowering glomerular pressure
Increase GFR by raising glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure

glomerular-filtration-gfr.explanation: Constricting the downstream (efferent) arteriole raises pressure within the glomerular capillary (P_GC), increasing net filtration pressure and GFR — the mechanism by which angiotensin II defends GFR when renal perfusion falls.

glomerular-filtration-gfr.stem: Regarding effect of efferent arteriolar constriction on gfr — which is correct?

options.text: Constricting the EFFERENT arteriole RAISES glomerular capillary pressure and INCREASES GFR (up to a point); only afferent constriction lowers GFR

glomerular-filtration-gfr.explanation: The efferent arteriole is downstream of the glomerulus, so constricting it dams pressure back into the capillary tuft — the opposite effect of afferent constriction. This is exactly how angiotensin II preserves GFR in hypovolaemia.

glomerular-filtration-gfr.stem: What best explains the finding: “GFR ≈ 125 mL/min (~180 L/day)”?

options.text: GFR/RPF — a fifth of plasma is filtered

glomerular-filtration-gfr.explanation: GFR ≈ 125 mL/min (~180 L/day) → Bulk ultrafiltration across the barrier.

glomerular-filtration-gfr.stem: What best explains the finding: “Efferent arteriolar constriction raises GFR”?

options.text: GFR/RPF — a fifth of plasma is filtered

glomerular-filtration-gfr.explanation: Efferent arteriolar constriction raises GFR → ↑P_GC (angiotensin II effect).

glomerular-filtration-gfr.stem: Which should you review before “Glomerular Filtration & GFR”?

options.text: Histology of the Ureter, Bladder & Urethra
Development of the Kidney & Urinary Tract
Microscopic Anatomy of the Kidney & Nephron
Congenital Anomalies of the Kidney & Urinary Tract

glomerular-filtration-gfr.explanation: Understanding nephron structure is essential for grasping GFR.

renal-hemodynamics-autoregulation.stem: Renal autoregulation maintains a relatively constant GFR primarily by adjusting the tone of which vessel through myogenic and tubuloglomerular mechanisms?
renal-hemodynamics-autoregulation.explanation: Both the myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback act on the afferent arteriole to buffer GFR against changes in arterial pressure over the ~80–180 mmHg range.

renal-hemodynamics-autoregulation.stem: In a patient with bilateral renal artery stenosis, an ACE inhibitor may sharply reduce GFR because it:

options.text: Removes angiotensin II–mediated efferent constriction that was maintaining glomerular pressure

renal-hemodynamics-autoregulation.explanation: When renal perfusion is low, angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole to keep glomerular pressure (and GFR) up. Blocking its formation with an ACE inhibitor dilates the efferent arteriole and drops GFR — dramatically if the stenosis is bilateral.

renal-hemodynamics-autoregulation.stem: Regarding tubuloglomerular feedback direction — which is correct?

options.text: Increased NaCl at the macula densa dilates the afferent arteriole to increase flow
Increased NaCl delivery at the macula densa (signalling high GFR) triggers adenosine release that CONSTRICTS the afferent arteriole, REDUCING GFR back toward normal

renal-hemodynamics-autoregulation.explanation: TGF is a negative-feedback loop that stabilises GFR: high distal NaCl means GFR is too high, so the response must lower it — hence afferent constriction, not dilation.

renal-hemodynamics-autoregulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “RBF/GFR stable over MAP ~80–180 mmHg”?

options.text: Low perfusion / low macula-densa NaCl / sympathetic drive
Loss of vasodilator prostaglandins → unopposed afferent constriction

renal-hemodynamics-autoregulation.explanation: RBF/GFR stable over MAP ~80–180 mmHg → Autoregulation (myogenic + TGF).

renal-hemodynamics-autoregulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “GFR falls when MAP < ~80 mmHg”?

options.text: Low perfusion / low macula-densa NaCl / sympathetic drive
Loss of vasodilator prostaglandins → unopposed afferent constriction

renal-hemodynamics-autoregulation.explanation: GFR falls when MAP < ~80 mmHg → Autoregulation exhausted → pre-renal AKI.
