tubular-reabsorption-secretion.stem: Reabsorption of glucose, amino acids and phosphate in the proximal tubule is ultimately powered by:

options.text: ATP hydrolysis by apical glucose carriers
The sodium gradient created by the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase

tubular-reabsorption-secretion.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase keeps intracellular Na⁺ low; the inward Na⁺ gradient then drives secondary active cotransport of glucose (SGLT), amino acids and phosphate across the apical membrane. Blocking the pump halts these processes.

tubular-reabsorption-secretion.stem: Glucose begins to appear in the urine once plasma glucose exceeds the renal threshold because:

options.text: The filtered load of glucose exceeds the tubular transport maximum (Tm)
Glucose becomes too large to be filtered

tubular-reabsorption-secretion.explanation: SGLT2 carriers reabsorb all filtered glucose until they saturate at Tm; once the filtered load (plasma glucose × GFR) exceeds Tm, the excess is excreted as glucosuria.

tubular-reabsorption-secretion.stem: Regarding why glucosuria occurs in diabetes — which is correct?

options.text: The diabetic kidney is damaged and leaks glucose

Glucosuria occurs because the filtered glucose load exceeds the transport maximum (Tm) of the normal SGLT2 carriers once plasma glucose passes the renal threshold — the tubule is working normally but saturated
Filtered glucose load exceeds SGLT2 Tm (renal threshold)

tubular-reabsorption-secretion.explanation: It is a saturation phenomenon of healthy transporters, not a structural leak; the same principle (Tm) governs every carrier-mediated reabsorptive process.

tubular-reabsorption-secretion.stem: What best explains the finding: “Glucosuria once plasma glucose > ~180–200 mg/dL”?

options.text: Filtered glucose load exceeds SGLT2 Tm (renal threshold)

tubular-reabsorption-secretion.explanation: Glucosuria once plasma glucose > ~180–200 mg/dL → Filtered glucose load exceeds SGLT2 Tm (renal threshold).

tubular-reabsorption-secretion.stem: What best explains the finding: “PCT reabsorbs ~65% of filtered Na⁺ and water”?

options.text: Filtered glucose load exceeds SGLT2 Tm (renal threshold)

tubular-reabsorption-secretion.explanation: PCT reabsorbs ~65% of filtered Na⁺ and water → Isosmotic bulk reabsorption.

renal-clearance-principles.stem: The clearance of which substance is used to estimate renal plasma flow because it is both filtered and almost completely secreted?
renal-clearance-principles.explanation: PAH is filtered and nearly completely secreted, so at low plasma concentrations essentially all PAH delivered to the kidney is cleared; its clearance therefore approximates renal plasma flow (~600 mL/min).

renal-clearance-principles.stem: If a freely filtered substance has a renal clearance lower than the GFR (inulin clearance), the tubule must be:
renal-clearance-principles.explanation: A clearance below GFR means less of the substance appears in the urine than was filtered, so the tubule must be reabsorbing it. A clearance above GFR indicates net secretion.

renal-clearance-principles.stem: Regarding interpreting a normal serum creatinine — which is correct?

options.text: A serum creatinine in the normal range means kidney function is normal

Because the creatinine–GFR relationship is hyperbolic, creatinine stays near-normal until GFR has already fallen substantially — a "normal" creatinine can mask significant early loss of function, which is why eGFR/clearance is used
Freely filtered, not reabsorbed or secreted (= GFR)

renal-clearance-principles.explanation: Small early drops in GFR barely move creatinine; relying on the raw value misses early kidney disease, whereas an estimated clearance (eGFR) reveals it.

renal-clearance-principles.stem: What best explains the finding: “A solute clearance equal to inulin clearance”?

options.text: Freely filtered, not reabsorbed or secreted (= GFR)

renal-clearance-principles.explanation: A solute clearance equal to inulin clearance → Freely filtered, not reabsorbed or secreted (= GFR).

renal-clearance-principles.stem: What best explains the finding: “Creatinine clearance slightly exceeds true GFR”?

options.text: Freely filtered, not reabsorbed or secreted (= GFR)

renal-clearance-principles.explanation: Creatinine clearance slightly exceeds true GFR → Small tubular secretion of creatinine.

urine-concentration-countercurrent.stem: The high osmolality of the renal medullary interstitium is generated chiefly by the:

options.text: Countercurrent multiplier of the loop of Henle

urine-concentration-countercurrent.explanation: The loop of Henle multiplies a small transverse gradient into a large corticopapillary gradient by combining water reabsorption (descending limb) with active NaCl reabsorption (water-impermeable ascending limb); urea recycling adds the rest.

urine-concentration-countercurrent.stem: Loop diuretics produce a powerful diuresis because, by blocking NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, they:

options.text: Dissipate the medullary osmotic gradient needed to reabsorb water

urine-concentration-countercurrent.explanation: NKCC2 pumps salt into the medulla to build the concentrating gradient. Blocking it both prevents salt reabsorption and collapses the medullary gradient, so the collecting duct can no longer reabsorb water — hence the large diuresis.

urine-concentration-countercurrent.stem: Regarding which limb is the diluting segment — which is correct?

options.text: The descending limb dilutes the urine because water is leaving
The THICK ASCENDING limb is the diluting segment: it pumps NaCl out while remaining water-impermeable, so the fluid LEAVING it is dilute (hypotonic ~100 mOsm)

urine-concentration-countercurrent.explanation: The descending limb concentrates the luminal fluid (water leaves); dilution requires removing solute WITHOUT water, which only the water-impermeable thick ascending limb does — hence its diuretic-target status.

urine-concentration-countercurrent.stem: What best explains the finding: “Medullary osmolality rising ~300 → ~1200 mOsm/kg”?

options.text: NKCC2 block abolishes the medullary gradient

urine-concentration-countercurrent.explanation: Medullary osmolality rising ~300 → ~1200 mOsm/kg → Countercurrent multiplication + urea trapping.

urine-concentration-countercurrent.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypotonic fluid (~100 mOsm) leaving the loop”?

options.text: NKCC2 block abolishes the medullary gradient

urine-concentration-countercurrent.explanation: Hypotonic fluid (~100 mOsm) leaving the loop → Thick ascending limb = diluting segment.

urine-concentration-countercurrent.stem: Which should you review before “Urine Concentration: The Countercurrent Mechanism”?

adh-water-regulation.stem: ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct by:

options.text: Inserting aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane

adh-water-regulation.explanation: ADH binds the V2 receptor, raising cAMP and driving insertion of aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane of principal cells; water then follows the osmotic gradient into the hypertonic medulla, concentrating the urine.

adh-water-regulation.stem: A patient passes large volumes of dilute urine that fails to concentrate after desmopressin. This indicates:
adh-water-regulation.explanation: Failure to concentrate the urine despite exogenous ADH (desmopressin) means the collecting duct cannot respond — nephrogenic DI (e.g. lithium, hypercalcaemia, hereditary V2/AQP2 defects). Central DI would respond to desmopressin.

adh-water-regulation.stem: Regarding central vs nephrogenic diabetes insipidus — which is correct?

options.text: All diabetes insipidus improves with desmopressin (ADH)
Only CENTRAL DI (ADH deficiency) responds to desmopressin by concentrating the urine; NEPHROGENIC DI (kidney unresponsive to ADH, e.g. lithium, hypercalcaemia) does not respond

adh-water-regulation.explanation: The desmopressin response localises the lesion: if giving ADH works, the problem was a lack of ADH (central); if it fails, the receptor/channel machinery is the problem (nephrogenic).

adh-water-regulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Concentrated, low-volume urine after water deprivation”?
adh-water-regulation.explanation: Concentrated, low-volume urine after water deprivation → High ADH → AQP2 → water reabsorption.

adh-water-regulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Large volumes of dilute urine + intense thirst”?
adh-water-regulation.explanation: Large volumes of dilute urine + intense thirst → Diabetes insipidus (ADH deficiency or resistance).

adh-water-regulation.stem: Which is a clinical application of “ADH, Aquaporins & Water Balance”?

micturition-reflex.stem: Contraction of the detrusor muscle during voiding is mediated by:

options.text: Parasympathetic fibres via M3 muscarinic receptors
Somatic fibres of the pudendal nerve

micturition-reflex.explanation: Parasympathetic pelvic nerves (S2–4) release acetylcholine onto M3 receptors, contracting the detrusor while the sphincters relax — the coordinated act of micturition. Sympathetic and somatic activity favour storage.

micturition-reflex.stem: A lesion destroying the sacral micturition centre (S2–4) typically produces a bladder that is:

options.text: Flaccid/atonic with urinary retention and overflow incontinence

micturition-reflex.explanation: Loss of the sacral reflex arc (a lower motor neuron lesion) leaves the detrusor unable to contract, so the bladder becomes flaccid and distended — chronic retention with overflow incontinence. Suprasacral lesions instead cause a spastic, overactive bladder.

micturition-reflex.stem: Regarding autonomic control of voiding — which is correct?

options.text: The PARASYMPATHETIC pelvic nerve (M3) contracts the detrusor to empty the bladder; SYMPATHETIC activity promotes STORAGE (relaxes detrusor, closes the internal sphincter)

micturition-reflex.explanation: It is the reverse of a "fight-or-flight empties everything" intuition: you would not want to urinate while running from danger, so sympathetic tone favours storage, parasympathetic favours voiding.

micturition-reflex.stem: What best explains the finding: “Detrusor contraction on voiding”?

options.text: Suprasacral (UMN) lesion — loss of cortical inhibition

micturition-reflex.explanation: Detrusor contraction on voiding → Parasympathetic pelvic nerve, M3/ACh.

micturition-reflex.stem: What best explains the finding: “External sphincter under voluntary control”?

options.text: Suprasacral (UMN) lesion — loss of cortical inhibition

micturition-reflex.explanation: External sphincter under voluntary control → Somatic pudendal nerve (S2–4).

micturition-reflex.stem: Which should you review before “Micturition: Bladder Storage & Voiding”?

neurogenic-bladder-disorders.stem: A patient with a chronic spinal cord lesion above the sacral segments has a small-capacity bladder with involuntary contractions and urgency. This is a:
neurogenic-bladder-disorders.explanation: A suprasacral cord lesion removes cortical inhibition of the intact sacral reflex, producing a spastic/reflex (UMN) bladder with involuntary detrusor contractions, small capacity and urgency, often with detrusor–sphincter dyssynergia.

neurogenic-bladder-disorders.stem: Destruction of the sacral (S2–4) micturition centre or its peripheral nerves most characteristically produces:

options.text: A flaccid, atonic bladder with urinary retention and overflow incontinence

neurogenic-bladder-disorders.explanation: Loss of the sacral reflex arc (a lower motor neuron lesion) leaves the detrusor unable to contract, so the bladder becomes distended and areflexic — chronic retention with overflow incontinence.

neurogenic-bladder-disorders.stem: Regarding bladder findings immediately after spinal cord injury — which is correct?

options.text: A spinal cord injury above the sacrum immediately produces a spastic, overactive bladder
Right after acute cord injury there is SPINAL SHOCK — a temporary FLACCID, areflexic bladder — and the spastic (UMN) pattern only emerges over the following weeks as reflexes return

neurogenic-bladder-disorders.explanation: Expecting an immediate spastic bladder misreads the time course; during spinal shock the bladder is atonic and needs drainage, and management changes as the UMN pattern develops.

neurogenic-bladder-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Small, overactive bladder with urgency after cord injury”?
neurogenic-bladder-disorders.explanation: Small, overactive bladder with urgency after cord injury → Spastic (UMN) neurogenic bladder.

neurogenic-bladder-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Distended atonic bladder with overflow dribbling”?
neurogenic-bladder-disorders.explanation: Distended atonic bladder with overflow dribbling → Flaccid (LMN) bladder — retention.

neurogenic-bladder-disorders.stem: Which should you review before “Neurogenic Bladder & Voiding Disorders”?

body-fluid-compartments-renal.stem: Using the standard approximation, the intracellular and extracellular fluid compartments make up what fraction of body weight?
body-fluid-compartments-renal.explanation: Total body water is ~60% of body weight, divided into ~40% intracellular and ~20% extracellular (of which about three-quarters is interstitial and one-quarter plasma) — the 60–40–20 rule.

body-fluid-compartments-renal.stem: Rapidly infusing a large volume of pure (hypotonic) water lowers plasma osmolality and causes:

options.text: Water to move out of cells, shrinking them
Water to move into cells, causing them to swell

body-fluid-compartments-renal.explanation: A fall in ECF osmolality creates a gradient that drives water into the relatively hypertonic cells, causing them to swell — dangerous in the brain (cerebral oedema of acute hyponatraemia/water intoxication).

body-fluid-compartments-renal.stem: Regarding what determines ecf volume vs osmolality — which is correct?

options.text: Sodium concentration reflects how much salt is in the body
ECF VOLUME is set by total body SODIUM; plasma sodium CONCENTRATION (osmolality) is set by WATER balance — so hyponatraemia is usually a water problem, not a salt-deficiency problem
Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps K⁺ in, Na⁺ out
Na⁺ is the dominant ECF cation

body-fluid-compartments-renal.explanation: Because water moves freely to keep osmolality equal, the [Na⁺] you measure reflects the water-to-sodium ratio, not sodium content; separating volume (Na⁺) from concentration (water) is essential for diagnosing fluid disorders.

body-fluid-compartments-renal.stem: What best explains the finding: “ICF is the high-potassium compartment”?

options.text: Na⁺ is the dominant ECF cation
Low ECF osmolality drives water into cells
Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps K⁺ in, Na⁺ out

body-fluid-compartments-renal.explanation: ICF is the high-potassium compartment → Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps K⁺ in, Na⁺ out.

body-fluid-compartments-renal.stem: What best explains the finding: “ECF is the high-sodium compartment”?

options.text: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps K⁺ in, Na⁺ out
Low ECF osmolality drives water into cells
Na⁺ is the dominant ECF cation

body-fluid-compartments-renal.explanation: ECF is the high-sodium compartment → Na⁺ is the dominant ECF cation.

volume-water-balance-hormones.stem: In response to a fall in effective circulating volume, the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system acts to:

options.text: Retain sodium and water and raise blood pressure

volume-water-balance-hormones.explanation: RAAS retains sodium (angiotensin II proximally, aldosterone distally) and water, causes vasoconstriction, and stimulates thirst and ADH — all serving to restore ECF volume and blood pressure.

volume-water-balance-hormones.stem: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), released when the atria are stretched by volume overload, principally causes:
volume-water-balance-hormones.explanation: ANP opposes RAAS: it promotes sodium and water excretion, raises GFR, vasodilates, and inhibits renin, aldosterone and ADH — reducing an overfilled extracellular volume.

volume-water-balance-hormones.stem: Regarding volume vs osmolality regulation — which is correct?

options.text: ADH is released only when plasma osmolality is high

Although osmolality is the most SENSITIVE trigger, a large fall in effective circulating VOLUME is a powerful (if less sensitive) stimulus for ADH — the body will retain water to defend volume even when that lowers osmolality (causing hyponatraemia)
Angiotensin II + aldosterone in low-volume states

volume-water-balance-hormones.explanation: The two axes are usually separate, but when they conflict, preserving blood pressure/perfusion takes priority — explaining the hyponatraemia of severe volume depletion, heart failure and cirrhosis.

volume-water-balance-hormones.stem: What best explains the finding: “Salt and water retention with activated RAAS”?

options.text: ADH retains water to defend volume (volume > osmolality)
Angiotensin II + aldosterone in low-volume states

volume-water-balance-hormones.explanation: Salt and water retention with activated RAAS → Angiotensin II + aldosterone in low-volume states.

volume-water-balance-hormones.stem: What best explains the finding: “Natriuresis and diuresis when the atria are stretched”?

options.text: Angiotensin II + aldosterone in low-volume states
ADH retains water to defend volume (volume > osmolality)

volume-water-balance-hormones.explanation: Natriuresis and diuresis when the atria are stretched → ANP/BNP release opposing RAAS.

volume-water-balance-hormones.stem: Which should you review before “Hormonal Control of Volume & Water Balance”?

sodium-balance-ecf-volume.stem: The volume of the extracellular fluid compartment is determined principally by:
sodium-balance-ecf-volume.explanation: Sodium is the dominant extracellular solute and water follows it osmotically, so total body sodium sets ECF volume. The kidney regulates ECF volume by adjusting sodium excretion (RAAS retains, ANP excretes).

options.text: A pure water excess with normal sodium
An expansion of interstitial ECF volume from renal sodium (and water) retention

sodium-balance-ecf-volume.explanation: Oedema is expanded interstitial extracellular volume caused by inappropriate renal retention of sodium and water (e.g. in heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), which is why treatment centres on salt restriction and diuretics.

sodium-balance-ecf-volume.stem: Regarding sodium concentration vs total body sodium — which is correct?

options.text: A low plasma sodium concentration means the body is sodium-depleted (and needs salt)

Plasma [Na⁺] reflects WATER balance (osmolality), NOT total body sodium — many hyponatraemic patients (e.g. oedematous heart-failure patients) actually have EXCESS total body sodium; ECF volume, not [Na⁺], tells you the sodium status
Expanded interstitial ECF from Na⁺/water retention

sodium-balance-ecf-volume.explanation: Because water moves to keep osmolality constant, the measured concentration is a water-to-sodium ratio; treating hyponatraemia with salt when the patient is volume-overloaded worsens the oedema.

sodium-balance-ecf-volume.stem: What best explains the finding: “Low urine sodium + concentrated urine in hypovolaemia”?

options.text: Expanded interstitial ECF from Na⁺/water retention

sodium-balance-ecf-volume.explanation: Low urine sodium + concentrated urine in hypovolaemia → RAAS-driven avid Na⁺/water retention.

sodium-balance-ecf-volume.stem: What best explains the finding: “Peripheral/pulmonary oedema”?

options.text: Expanded interstitial ECF from Na⁺/water retention

sodium-balance-ecf-volume.explanation: Peripheral/pulmonary oedema → Expanded interstitial ECF from Na⁺/water retention.

sodium-balance-ecf-volume.stem: Which should you review before “Sodium Balance & ECF Volume Regulation”?

renal-potassium-handling.stem: The amount of potassium excreted in the urine is regulated mainly by:

options.text: The filtered load at the glomerulus
Secretion by principal cells of the distal nephron
Reabsorption in the loop of Henle

renal-potassium-handling.explanation: Most filtered K⁺ is reabsorbed early and fairly constantly; the regulated variable is distal secretion by collecting-duct principal cells, tuned by aldosterone, distal flow/Na⁺ delivery and plasma K⁺.

renal-potassium-handling.stem: A patient on a thiazide diuretic develops hypokalaemia. The mechanism is that increased distal delivery of sodium and fluid:

options.text: Enhances potassium secretion by principal cells

renal-potassium-handling.explanation: By delivering more Na⁺ and flow to the collecting duct, thiazides (and loop diuretics) increase Na⁺ reabsorption through ENaC, making the lumen more electronegative and driving K⁺ secretion — hence hypokalaemia.

renal-potassium-handling.stem: Regarding what determines potassium excretion — which is correct?

options.text: Potassium excretion is set by how much is filtered and reabsorbed
Because ~90% of filtered K⁺ is reabsorbed regardless, urinary K⁺ is determined mainly by SECRETION in the distal nephron (principal cells) under the control of aldosterone, distal flow and plasma K⁺
Reduced aldosterone effect → less K⁺ secretion

renal-potassium-handling.explanation: Filtration and early reabsorption are relatively fixed; the body varies excretion by dialling distal secretion up or down — which is why aldosterone and diuretics (not GFR) dominate K⁺ balance.

renal-potassium-handling.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypokalaemia on a loop or thiazide diuretic”?

options.text: Reduced aldosterone effect → less K⁺ secretion

renal-potassium-handling.explanation: Hypokalaemia on a loop or thiazide diuretic → ↑distal flow/Na⁺ delivery → ↑K⁺ secretion.

renal-potassium-handling.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hyperkalaemia with spironolactone or ACE-I”?

options.text: Reduced aldosterone effect → less K⁺ secretion

renal-potassium-handling.explanation: Hyperkalaemia with spironolactone or ACE-I → Reduced aldosterone effect → less K⁺ secretion.

renal-calcium-phosphate-handling.stem: Parathyroid hormone has which combination of effects on the kidney?

options.text: Increases calcium reabsorption and increases phosphate excretion
Decreases calcium reabsorption and decreases phosphate excretion
Increases both calcium and phosphate reabsorption

renal-calcium-phosphate-handling.explanation: PTH increases distal calcium reabsorption (raising serum Ca²⁺) while inhibiting proximal phosphate reabsorption (phosphaturia). It also stimulates 1α-hydroxylase to activate vitamin D.

renal-calcium-phosphate-handling.stem: In advanced chronic kidney disease, secondary hyperparathyroidism develops largely because of:

options.text: Phosphate retention and reduced calcitriol, causing hypocalcaemia

renal-calcium-phosphate-handling.explanation: A failing kidney excretes less phosphate (hyperphosphataemia) and activates less vitamin D (low calcitriol); the resulting hypocalcaemia drives the parathyroids to hypersecrete PTH — the mechanism of CKD-mineral and bone disorder.

renal-calcium-phosphate-handling.stem: Regarding diuretic effects on urinary calcium — which is correct?

options.text: All diuretics increase calcium excretion because they increase urine flow
LOOP diuretics increase urinary calcium (used to treat hypercalcaemia), whereas THIAZIDES DECREASE urinary calcium (used to prevent calcium stones) — opposite effects
Loss of the lumen-positive gradient in the thick ascending limb

renal-calcium-phosphate-handling.explanation: Loop diuretics abolish the lumen-positive potential in the thick ascending limb that drives paracellular Ca²⁺ reabsorption, while thiazides enhance distal Ca²⁺ reabsorption; the divergence is a classic exam point.

renal-calcium-phosphate-handling.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thiazides reduce urinary Ca²⁺ (used for Ca²⁺ stones)”?

options.text: Loss of the lumen-positive gradient in the thick ascending limb

renal-calcium-phosphate-handling.explanation: Thiazides reduce urinary Ca²⁺ (used for Ca²⁺ stones) → Enhanced distal Ca²⁺ reabsorption.

renal-calcium-phosphate-handling.stem: What best explains the finding: “Loop diuretics increase urinary Ca²⁺ (used in hypercalcaemia)”?

options.text: Loss of the lumen-positive gradient in the thick ascending limb

renal-calcium-phosphate-handling.explanation: Loop diuretics increase urinary Ca²⁺ (used in hypercalcaemia) → Loss of the lumen-positive gradient in the thick ascending limb.

renal-calcium-phosphate-handling.stem: Which should you review before “Renal Handling of Ca²⁺, PO₄, Mg²⁺, Cl⁻ & Urate”?

urinalysis-physical-chemical.stem: A urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy of the sediment shows no red blood cells. This most likely indicates:
urinalysis-physical-chemical.explanation: The blood pad detects heme; a positive pad without red cells on microscopy indicates free haemoglobin (intravascular haemolysis) or myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis) rather than true haematuria.

urinalysis-physical-chemical.stem: A urine specific gravity fixed at about 1.010 regardless of hydration status (isosthenuria) suggests:

options.text: Loss of the ability to concentrate or dilute urine (e.g. chronic kidney disease)

urinalysis-physical-chemical.explanation: A specific gravity locked near that of plasma ultrafiltrate (~1.010) means the tubules can neither concentrate nor dilute — a sign of impaired renal function such as chronic kidney disease.

urinalysis-physical-chemical.stem: Regarding interpreting a positive blood dipstick — which is correct?

options.text: A positive "blood" pad always means bleeding into the urinary tract

The dipstick blood pad detects heme, so it is positive with red cells, free HAEMOGLOBIN (haemolysis) OR MYOGLOBIN (rhabdomyolysis); microscopy showing no red cells points to haemoglobinuria/myoglobinuria
Plasma glucose exceeds the renal threshold (diabetes)

urinalysis-physical-chemical.explanation: The pad reacts to the peroxidase activity of heme regardless of source; you must correlate with microscopy to distinguish true haematuria from pigment, which have very different causes.

urinalysis-physical-chemical.stem: What best explains the finding: “Glucose on dipstick”?

options.text: Plasma glucose exceeds the renal threshold (diabetes)

urinalysis-physical-chemical.explanation: Glucose on dipstick → Plasma glucose exceeds the renal threshold (diabetes).

urinalysis-physical-chemical.stem: What best explains the finding: “Positive nitrite + leukocyte esterase”?

options.text: Plasma glucose exceeds the renal threshold (diabetes)

urinalysis-physical-chemical.explanation: Positive nitrite + leukocyte esterase → UTI (Gram-negative bacteria; pyuria).

urinalysis-physical-chemical.stem: Which should you review before “Urinalysis I: Physical & Chemical Examination”?

urinalysis-physical-chemical.explanation: Understanding ADH is crucial for interpreting urine concentration.

proteinuria-evaluation.stem: A patient with multiple myeloma has heavy proteinuria, but the urine dipstick is only trace positive. This discrepancy is because:

options.text: The dipstick detects albumin but not the filtered immunoglobulin light chains (Bence Jones protein)

proteinuria-evaluation.explanation: Overflow proteinuria in myeloma consists of free light chains (Bence Jones protein), which the albumin-sensitive dipstick largely misses; specific tests (urine protein electrophoresis/immunofixation) are needed.

proteinuria-evaluation.stem: Predominantly albuminuria (rather than low-molecular-weight proteins) indicates which mechanism of proteinuria?
proteinuria-evaluation.explanation: Albumin loss reflects a breakdown of the glomerular barrier's size/charge selectivity — glomerular proteinuria. Tubular proteinuria features low-molecular-weight proteins, and overflow proteinuria features an excess filtered protein such as light chains.

proteinuria-evaluation.stem: Regarding interpreting a negative dipstick for protein — which is correct?

options.text: A negative urine dipstick for protein rules out significant proteinuria

The dipstick mainly detects ALBUMIN and can be NEGATIVE despite heavy overflow proteinuria from immunoglobulin LIGHT CHAINS (myeloma) — if suspected, order urine protein electrophoresis/immunofixation, not just a dipstick

proteinuria-evaluation.explanation: Bence Jones light chains are not albumin, so they escape dipstick detection; relying on a negative dipstick can miss multiple myeloma presenting as renal disease.

proteinuria-evaluation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Predominantly albumin in the urine”?

options.text: Early diabetic nephropathy (and CV risk marker)

proteinuria-evaluation.explanation: Predominantly albumin in the urine → Glomerular proteinuria (barrier injury).

proteinuria-evaluation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Low-molecular-weight proteins (β2-microglobulin)”?

options.text: Early diabetic nephropathy (and CV risk marker)

proteinuria-evaluation.stem: Which should you review before “Proteinuria: Evaluation & Significance”?

proteinuria-evaluation.explanation: Understanding kidney histology is essential for evaluating proteinuria.

acute-kidney-injury-azotemia.stem: A hypovolaemic patient develops rising creatinine with a fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) of 0.5% and a BUN:creatinine ratio of 25. This indicates:
acute-kidney-injury-azotemia.explanation: A low FENa (<1%) and high BUN:creatinine ratio (>20) indicate intact tubules reabsorbing sodium avidly in response to hypoperfusion — pre-renal AKI, reversible with restored perfusion. ATN would show FENa >2% and muddy-brown casts.

acute-kidney-injury-azotemia.stem: Which finding is an indication for urgent dialysis in acute kidney injury?

options.text: Refractory hyperkalaemia or fluid overload with pulmonary oedema

acute-kidney-injury-azotemia.explanation: Uraemic emergencies — refractory hyperkalaemia, severe metabolic acidosis, fluid overload/pulmonary oedema, and uraemic pericarditis or encephalopathy — are indications for urgent dialysis (mnemonic AEIOU).

acute-kidney-injury-azotemia.stem: Regarding distinguishing pre-renal aki from atn — which is correct?

options.text: A high urine sodium and FENa always indicate the kidney is failing intrinsically

In PRE-renal AKI the tubules are intact and reabsorb Na⁺ avidly → LOW urine Na⁺, FENa <1%, BUN:Cr >20; only when tubules are DAMAGED (ATN) does FENa rise >2% — the indices distinguish a perfusion problem from intrinsic injury
Pre-renal AKI (avid Na⁺ retention, tubules intact)

acute-kidney-injury-azotemia.explanation: Pre-renal and ATN both raise creatinine, but they demand opposite actions (fluids vs supportive care); the FENa/BUN:Cr indices reveal whether the tubules are still working, guiding treatment.

acute-kidney-injury-azotemia.stem: What best explains the finding: “FENa <1%, BUN:Cr >20, concentrated urine”?

options.text: Pre-renal AKI (avid Na⁺ retention, tubules intact)

acute-kidney-injury-azotemia.explanation: FENa <1%, BUN:Cr >20, concentrated urine → Pre-renal AKI (avid Na⁺ retention, tubules intact).

acute-kidney-injury-azotemia.stem: What best explains the finding: “FENa >2% with muddy-brown granular casts”?

options.text: Pre-renal AKI (avid Na⁺ retention, tubules intact)

acute-kidney-injury-azotemia.explanation: FENa >2% with muddy-brown granular casts → Acute tubular necrosis (intrinsic).

acute-kidney-injury-azotemia.stem: Which should you review before “Acute Kidney Injury & Azotaemia”?

Histology of the Ureter, Bladder & Urethra
Development of the Kidney & Urinary Tract

acute-kidney-injury-azotemia.explanation: Understanding renal blood flow is essential for grasping AKI mechanisms.

urine-biochemical-composition.stem: The principal nitrogenous waste product excreted in normal human urine is:
urine-biochemical-composition.explanation: Urea, synthesised in the hepatic urea cycle from ammonia produced by amino-acid catabolism, is the main nitrogenous waste and the largest solute in urine by mass. Creatinine and uric acid are excreted in much smaller amounts.

urine-biochemical-composition.stem: Which of the following would be considered an ABNORMAL (pathological) constituent of urine?
urine-biochemical-composition.explanation: Glucose should be fully reabsorbed and absent from normal urine; its appearance (glucosuria) indicates plasma glucose above the renal threshold. Urea, creatinine and sodium are normal constituents.

urine-biochemical-composition.stem: Regarding why creatinine is used to normalise spot urine tests — which is correct?

options.text: Creatinine is measured because it is a toxic waste that must be tracked

Creatinine is used as a denominator (e.g. protein:creatinine ratio) because it is excreted at a fairly CONSTANT rate proportional to muscle mass, so it corrects a random sample for how dilute or concentrated it is
Main nitrogenous end-product of protein metabolism
Reflects muscle mass; basis of clearance and spot ratios

urine-biochemical-composition.explanation: Its steady excretion, not its toxicity, makes it the reference; dividing an analyte by creatinine removes the effect of variable urine concentration in a spot sample.

urine-biochemical-composition.stem: What best explains the finding: “Urea is the largest solute in urine”?

options.text: Reflects muscle mass; basis of clearance and spot ratios
Main nitrogenous end-product of protein metabolism

urine-biochemical-composition.explanation: Urea is the largest solute in urine → Main nitrogenous end-product of protein metabolism.

urine-biochemical-composition.stem: What best explains the finding: “Creatinine excretion is relatively constant”?

options.text: Main nitrogenous end-product of protein metabolism
Reflects muscle mass; basis of clearance and spot ratios

urine-biochemical-composition.explanation: Creatinine excretion is relatively constant → Reflects muscle mass; basis of clearance and spot ratios.

urine-biochemical-composition.stem: Which should you review before “Biochemistry of Normal & Abnormal Urine”?

urine-biochemical-composition.explanation: Understanding GFR is essential for interpreting urine biochemical composition.

urine-microscopy-sediment.stem: The urinary finding most specific for glomerulonephritis (a nephritic process) is:
urine-microscopy-sediment.explanation: Red cell casts form only in the tubule and contain red cells that leaked through an inflamed glomerulus — they localise bleeding to the glomerulus and are the classic marker of glomerulonephritis.

urine-microscopy-sediment.stem: Casts are not found originating from which part of the nephron?

options.text: The proximal tubule and loop of Henle

urine-microscopy-sediment.explanation: Casts form where flow slows and Tamm–Horsfall protein gels — the distal tubule and collecting duct. The proximal tubule and loop of Henle are not sites of cast formation.

urine-microscopy-sediment.stem: Regarding localising value of casts — which is correct?

options.text: Casts can come from anywhere in the urinary tract, including the bladder
Casts form only within the renal tubules (a Tamm–Horsfall protein matrix, in the distal nephron), so their presence LOCALISES disease to the KIDNEY — they never arise in the bladder or lower tract

urine-microscopy-sediment.explanation: This is what makes RBC casts so valuable: red cells alone could be from anywhere, but red cells in a cast prove glomerular bleeding, distinguishing nephritic disease from a bladder stone or tumour.

urine-microscopy-sediment.stem: What best explains the finding: “Red cell casts”?
What best explains the finding: “"Muddy-brown" granular casts”?
Which should you review before “Urinalysis II: Microscopy of the Urine Sediment”?

urine-microscopy-sediment.explanation: Understanding urine biochemistry is essential for interpreting microscopy results.

urinary-crystals-and-stones.stem: A large staghorn calculus forming in alkaline urine in a patient with recurrent Proteus urinary infections is most likely composed of:
urinary-crystals-and-stones.explanation: Urease-producing organisms such as Proteus alkalinise the urine, favouring struvite (magnesium-ammonium-phosphate) stones, which grow into large staghorn calculi — infection stones requiring treatment of the infection and stone removal.

urinary-crystals-and-stones.stem: Which stone is characteristically radiolucent and forms in acidic urine?
urinary-crystals-and-stones.explanation: Uric acid stones form in acidic urine (gout, high purine turnover) and are radiolucent on plain X-ray (visible on CT). Calcium-containing and struvite stones are radio-opaque.

urinary-crystals-and-stones.stem: Regarding radiological visibility of stones — which is correct?

options.text: All kidney stones are radio-opaque and visible on a plain X-ray
Most stones are radio-opaque, but URIC ACID stones are classically RADIOLUCENT and are missed on plain X-ray (they are seen on CT) — the acidic-urine, gout-associated stone

urinary-crystals-and-stones.explanation: Assuming a negative plain film excludes stones misses radiolucent uric acid calculi; knowing the exception directs you to CT and hints at the underlying acid urine/purine metabolism.

urinary-crystals-and-stones.stem: What best explains the finding: “Envelope-shaped crystals; commonest stone”?
urinary-crystals-and-stones.explanation: Envelope-shaped crystals; commonest stone → Calcium oxalate.

urinary-crystals-and-stones.stem: What best explains the finding: “"Coffin-lid" crystals + staghorn calculus in alkaline urine”?
urinary-crystals-and-stones.explanation: "Coffin-lid" crystals + staghorn calculus in alkaline urine → Struvite (urease-producing bacteria — infection stone).

urinary-crystals-and-stones.stem: Which should you review before “Urinary Crystals & Kidney Stones”?

options.text: Microscopic Anatomy of the Kidney & Nephron
Histology of the Ureter, Bladder & Urethra

urinary-crystals-and-stones.explanation: Anatomy is essential for understanding where stones can obstruct.

renal-metabolism-gluconeogenesis.stem: Renal oxygen consumption is most closely coupled to the rate of:
renal-metabolism-gluconeogenesis.explanation: Most renal ATP (and therefore O₂) is spent by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase driving sodium reabsorption; oxygen consumption rises and falls with the reabsorptive workload rather than tracking blood flow directly.

renal-metabolism-gluconeogenesis.stem: During a prolonged fast, the kidney contributes significantly to blood glucose through gluconeogenesis, which occurs mainly in the:
renal-metabolism-gluconeogenesis.explanation: The proximal tubule is the renal site of gluconeogenesis and can supply a substantial fraction (up to ~40%) of endogenous glucose during prolonged fasting, using substrates such as glutamine and lactate.

renal-metabolism-gluconeogenesis.stem: Regarding why the renal medulla is prone to ischaemic injury — which is correct?

options.text: The medulla is injured first because it receives the most blood flow and thus the most toxins

The medulla is vulnerable because its blood flow is deliberately LOW (to preserve the concentrating gradient) while the thick ascending limb has a HIGH oxygen demand from active transport — a supply–demand mismatch, not excess flow
Active transport is the main energy cost
High transport demand + low medullary O₂ supply

renal-metabolism-gluconeogenesis.explanation: The low medullary flow that makes urine concentration possible is exactly what starves the hard-working thick ascending limb of oxygen, so it (and the S3 proximal segment) are first to undergo acute tubular necrosis.

renal-metabolism-gluconeogenesis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Renal O₂ consumption tracks the rate of Na⁺ reabsorption”?

options.text: High transport demand + low medullary O₂ supply
Active transport is the main energy cost
Aerobic segment with low glycolytic capacity

renal-metabolism-gluconeogenesis.explanation: Renal O₂ consumption tracks the rate of Na⁺ reabsorption → Active transport is the main energy cost.

renal-metabolism-gluconeogenesis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Outer medulla (thick ascending limb, S3) dies first in ischaemia”?

options.text: Active transport is the main energy cost
Aerobic segment with low glycolytic capacity
High transport demand + low medullary O₂ supply

renal-metabolism-gluconeogenesis.explanation: Outer medulla (thick ascending limb, S3) dies first in ischaemia → High transport demand + low medullary O₂ supply.

renal-metabolism-gluconeogenesis.stem: Which should you review before “Renal Metabolism & Gluconeogenesis”?

renal-endocrine-functions.stem: The normocytic anaemia of chronic kidney disease is primarily caused by:

options.text: Reduced erythropoietin production by the diseased kidney

renal-endocrine-functions.explanation: The kidney produces erythropoietin in response to hypoxia; in CKD this falls, causing a normocytic, normochromic anaemia treated with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (with attention to iron status).

renal-endocrine-functions.stem: The kidney contributes to calcium homeostasis by:

options.text: Using 1α-hydroxylase to convert 25-OH vitamin D to active calcitriol

renal-endocrine-functions.explanation: The proximal tubule enzyme 1α-hydroxylase performs the final activation of vitamin D to calcitriol, which raises calcium and phosphate. Its loss in CKD causes hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

renal-endocrine-functions.stem: Regarding cause of anaemia in chronic kidney disease — which is correct?

options.text: Anaemia in chronic kidney disease is mainly due to blood loss or iron deficiency

The characteristic anaemia of CKD is primarily due to reduced ERYTHROPOIETIN production by the failing kidney (a normocytic, normochromic anaemia), treated with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents — though iron status must also be optimised

renal-endocrine-functions.explanation: Recognising the endocrine (EPO) cause explains why the anaemia is normocytic and responds to EPO therapy rather than to iron alone, and it reframes the kidney as an endocrine organ.

renal-endocrine-functions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Normocytic anaemia in chronic kidney disease”?

options.text: JG-cell RAAS activation (e.g. renal artery stenosis)

renal-endocrine-functions.explanation: Normocytic anaemia in chronic kidney disease → Reduced erythropoietin production.

renal-endocrine-functions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypocalcaemia + secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD”?

options.text: JG-cell RAAS activation (e.g. renal artery stenosis)

renal-endocrine-functions.explanation: Hypocalcaemia + secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD → Reduced 1α-hydroxylase → low calcitriol.

renal-endocrine-functions.stem: Which should you review before “Endocrine Functions of the Kidney”?

renal-endocrine-functions.explanation: Understanding hormonal control is essential for grasping renal endocrine functions.

chronic-kidney-disease-uremia.stem: A patient with long-standing diabetes has a persistently reduced eGFR, normocytic anaemia, hyperphosphataemia with a high PTH, and bilaterally small kidneys. The diagnosis is:
chronic-kidney-disease-uremia.explanation: Sustained reduced eGFR with anaemia (low EPO), CKD-mineral and bone disorder (high phosphate/PTH) and small scarred kidneys indicates chronic kidney disease — features that develop over time, distinguishing it from acute injury.

chronic-kidney-disease-uremia.stem: Secondary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease arises because the failing kidney:

options.text: Retains phosphate and activates less vitamin D, causing hypocalcaemia that drives PTH secretion

chronic-kidney-disease-uremia.explanation: A failing kidney excretes less phosphate (hyperphosphataemia) and produces less calcitriol; the resulting hypocalcaemia stimulates the parathyroids, causing secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal bone disease (CKD-MBD).

chronic-kidney-disease-uremia.stem: Regarding distinguishing ckd from aki — which is correct?

options.text: A raised creatinine with anaemia and small kidneys is an acute kidney injury needing fluids

Anaemia, CKD-MBD (high phosphate/PTH) and bilaterally SMALL kidneys point to CHRONIC kidney disease (chronic, usually irreversible), not acute injury — features that take time to develop distinguish it from AKI

chronic-kidney-disease-uremia.explanation: Anaemia and renal bone disease reflect long-standing loss of endocrine function, and shrunken kidneys reflect chronic scarring; mislabelling CKD as AKI leads to inappropriate expectations of recovery.

chronic-kidney-disease-uremia.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sustained low eGFR for more than 3 months”?
chronic-kidney-disease-uremia.explanation: Sustained low eGFR for more than 3 months → Chronic kidney disease (staged G1–G5).

chronic-kidney-disease-uremia.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hyperphosphataemia + hypocalcaemia + high PTH”?
chronic-kidney-disease-uremia.explanation: Hyperphosphataemia + hypocalcaemia + high PTH → CKD-mineral and bone disorder (secondary hyperparathyroidism).

chronic-kidney-disease-uremia.stem: Which should you review before “Chronic Kidney Disease & Uraemia”?

chronic-kidney-disease-uremia.explanation: Understanding CKD requires distinguishing it from AKI.

renal-bicarbonate-reabsorption.stem: Most of the filtered bicarbonate is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by a mechanism that depends on:

options.text: H⁺ secretion and carbonic anhydrase converting luminal HCO₃⁻ to CO₂

renal-bicarbonate-reabsorption.explanation: The proximal tubule secretes H⁺ (via NHE3); with luminal carbonic anhydrase, that H⁺ converts filtered HCO₃⁻ to CO₂ and water, which enter the cell and are reconverted to HCO₃⁻ that returns to the blood — reclaiming bicarbonate without net acid loss.

renal-bicarbonate-reabsorption.stem: Acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, produces an alkaline urine and a mild metabolic acidosis because it:

options.text: Blocks proximal bicarbonate reabsorption, causing bicarbonate to be lost in the urine

renal-bicarbonate-reabsorption.explanation: Inhibiting carbonic anhydrase prevents the proximal tubule from reclaiming filtered bicarbonate, so HCO₃⁻ is excreted (alkaline urine) and the loss of buffer base produces a mild metabolic acidosis.

renal-bicarbonate-reabsorption.stem: Regarding how filtered bicarbonate is reabsorbed — which is correct?

options.text: Bicarbonate is reabsorbed directly across the apical membrane like glucose

Filtered HCO₃⁻ is reclaimed INDIRECTLY: secreted H⁺ converts luminal HCO₃⁻ to CO₂ (via carbonic anhydrase), the CO₂ enters the cell and is reformed into HCO₃⁻ that leaves basolaterally — the apical membrane is relatively impermeable to HCO₃⁻ itself
Carbonic anhydrase inhibition blocks HCO₃⁻ reclamation

renal-bicarbonate-reabsorption.explanation: The bicarbonate that enters the blood is not the same molecule that was filtered; understanding the H⁺/CO₂ shuttle explains why carbonic anhydrase inhibitors block the whole process.

renal-bicarbonate-reabsorption.stem: What best explains the finding: “~85–90% of filtered HCO₃⁻ reabsorbed proximally”?

options.text: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition blocks HCO₃⁻ reclamation

renal-bicarbonate-reabsorption.explanation: ~85–90% of filtered HCO₃⁻ reabsorbed proximally → H⁺ secretion (NHE3) + carbonic anhydrase.

renal-bicarbonate-reabsorption.stem: What best explains the finding: “Acetazolamide causes alkaline urine + mild metabolic acidosis”?

options.text: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition blocks HCO₃⁻ reclamation

renal-bicarbonate-reabsorption.explanation: Acetazolamide causes alkaline urine + mild metabolic acidosis → Carbonic anhydrase inhibition blocks HCO₃⁻ reclamation.

renal-bicarbonate-reabsorption.stem: Which should you review before “Renal Acid–Base I: Bicarbonate Reabsorption”?

renal-bicarbonate-reabsorption.explanation: Understanding tubular processes is essential for grasping bicarbonate reabsorption.

renal-acid-excretion.stem: The urinary buffer that can be greatly increased to raise net acid excretion during chronic metabolic acidosis is:
renal-acid-excretion.explanation: Free H⁺ and phosphate-based titratable acid are limited/fixed; ammoniagenesis from glutamine is upregulated over days in acidosis, making ammonium the adjustable, quantitatively dominant route for excreting acid and generating new bicarbonate.

renal-acid-excretion.stem: A patient has a normal-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with an inappropriately alkaline urine, hypokalaemia and recurrent kidney stones. This is most consistent with:
renal-acid-excretion.explanation: Distal (type 1) RTA reflects failure of α-intercalated cells to secrete H⁺, so the urine cannot be acidified (inappropriately high pH); it is classically associated with hypokalaemia and calcium phosphate stones.

renal-acid-excretion.stem: Regarding which buffer lets the kidney ramp up acid excretion — which is correct?

options.text: The kidney increases acid excretion mainly by making the urine more acidic (free H⁺) or by more titratable acid
Free H⁺ is negligible and titratable acid (phosphate) is fixed; the kidney meets a large or chronic acid load by increasing AMMONIUM (NH₄⁺) excretion via upregulated glutamine ammoniagenesis
Glutamine ammoniagenesis upregulated in chronic acidosis

renal-acid-excretion.explanation: Urine pH can only fall to ~4.5, so free H⁺ carries almost no acid; phosphate buffering is capped by filtered phosphate. Only ammoniagenesis is adjustable, so it is the mechanism that adapts to chronic acidosis.

renal-acid-excretion.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ammonium is the main adjustable urinary buffer”?

options.text: Defective H⁺ secretion or HCO₃⁻ reabsorption
Glutamine ammoniagenesis upregulated in chronic acidosis

renal-acid-excretion.explanation: Ammonium is the main adjustable urinary buffer → Glutamine ammoniagenesis upregulated in chronic acidosis.

renal-acid-excretion.stem: What best explains the finding: “Titratable acid is mostly phosphate-buffered H⁺”?

options.text: Glutamine ammoniagenesis upregulated in chronic acidosis
Defective H⁺ secretion or HCO₃⁻ reabsorption

renal-acid-excretion.explanation: Titratable acid is mostly phosphate-buffered H⁺ → Fixed capacity (~85% phosphate).

renal-acid-excretion.stem: Which should you review before “Renal Acid–Base II: Acid Excretion & New Bicarbonate”?

options.text: Microscopic Anatomy of the Kidney & Nephron
Histology of the Ureter, Bladder & Urethra

renal-acid-excretion.explanation: Understanding bicarbonate reabsorption is essential for grasping acid excretion mechanisms.

acid-base-disorders-compensation.stem: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has a low pH, low bicarbonate and an anion gap of 24. This is a:
acid-base-disorders-compensation.explanation: DKA adds ketoacids, consuming bicarbonate and raising the anion gap (>12) — a high anion gap metabolic acidosis (one of the MUDPILES causes). A normal-gap acidosis instead reflects bicarbonate loss or renal tubular acidosis.

acid-base-disorders-compensation.stem: Which statement about acid–base compensation is correct?

options.text: Compensation fully returns the pH to normal
Compensation moves the secondary variable in the same direction as the primary change but does not fully normalise the pH
A normal pH always excludes an acid–base disorder

acid-base-disorders-compensation.explanation: Compensation shifts PCO₂ or HCO₃⁻ in the same direction as the primary abnormality to bring the pH toward normal, but never fully corrects it; a fully normal pH with abnormal gases suggests a mixed disorder. Renal compensation takes hours to days.

acid-base-disorders-compensation.stem: Regarding interpreting a normal ph on an abg — which is correct?

options.text: A normal blood pH means there is no acid–base disorder
Compensation NEVER fully normalises the pH, so a truly NORMAL pH with abnormal PCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ indicates a MIXED acid–base disorder (two primary processes), not the absence of one
Added acid (MUDPILES — DKA, lactate, toxins, uraemia)

acid-base-disorders-compensation.explanation: Because compensatory mechanisms only pull the pH toward normal, a normal or over-corrected pH is itself a clue to a second, opposing disorder — missing this misreads a mixed picture as normal.

acid-base-disorders-compensation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Low pH + low HCO₃⁻ with compensatory low PCO₂”?

options.text: Added acid (MUDPILES — DKA, lactate, toxins, uraemia)
Bicarbonate loss (diarrhoea) or renal tubular acidosis

acid-base-disorders-compensation.explanation: Low pH + low HCO₃⁻ with compensatory low PCO₂ → Metabolic acidosis (respiratory compensation).

acid-base-disorders-compensation.stem: What best explains the finding: “High anion gap metabolic acidosis”?

options.text: Bicarbonate loss (diarrhoea) or renal tubular acidosis
Added acid (MUDPILES — DKA, lactate, toxins, uraemia)

acid-base-disorders-compensation.explanation: High anion gap metabolic acidosis → Added acid (MUDPILES — DKA, lactate, toxins, uraemia).

acid-base-disorders-compensation.stem: Which should you review before “Acid–Base Disorders & Compensation”?

options.text: Microscopic Anatomy of the Kidney & Nephron
Histology of the Ureter, Bladder & Urethra

acid-base-disorders-compensation.explanation: Acid-base disorders are closely related to kidney function.

pharyngitis-tonsillitis-diphtheria.stem: A 10-year-old has tonsillar exudates, fever and tender cervical nodes but no cough. Prompt penicillin treatment is recommended primarily to:

options.text: Shorten the illness by several days

pharyngitis-tonsillitis-diphtheria.explanation: These Centor features suggest Group A streptococcal pharyngitis; the key reason to treat is prevention of acute rheumatic fever (and suppurative complications), as the symptomatic benefit is small.

pharyngitis-tonsillitis-diphtheria.stem: The exotoxin of Corynebacterium diphtheriae causes cell injury by:

options.text: ADP-ribosylating elongation factor EF-2, halting protein synthesis

pharyngitis-tonsillitis-diphtheria.explanation: Diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates elongation factor EF-2, blocking protein synthesis; systemic spread produces myocarditis and neuropathy, while the local effect is the grey pharyngeal pseudomembrane.

pharyngitis-tonsillitis-diphtheria.stem: Regarding why we treat streptococcal pharyngitis — which is correct?

options.text: Antibiotics are given mainly to shorten the sore throat
The primary reason to identify and treat GAS pharyngitis with penicillin is to PREVENT acute rheumatic fever (and suppurative complications); the symptomatic benefit is modest

pharyngitis-tonsillitis-diphtheria.explanation: Rheumatic fever is an immune sequela preventable by eradicating the organism early; this public-health rationale — not symptom relief — drives testing and treatment of strep throat.

pharyngitis-tonsillitis-diphtheria.stem: What best explains the finding: “Tonsillar exudate + tender cervical nodes + fever, no cough”?
pharyngitis-tonsillitis-diphtheria.explanation: Tonsillar exudate + tender cervical nodes + fever, no cough → Group A streptococcal pharyngitis (Centor).

pharyngitis-tonsillitis-diphtheria.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sandpaper rash + strawberry tongue”?
pharyngitis-tonsillitis-diphtheria.explanation: Sandpaper rash + strawberry tongue → Scarlet fever — GAS erythrogenic exotoxin.

pharyngitis-tonsillitis-diphtheria.stem: Which should you review before “Pharyngitis, Tonsillitis & Diphtheria”?
pharyngitis-tonsillitis-diphtheria.explanation: Understanding GAS is crucial for diagnosing pharyngitis.

otitis-media-sinusitis-epiglottitis.stem: Acute otitis media, acute bacterial sinusitis and (historically) epiglottitis are all commonly caused by which group of organisms?

options.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis

otitis-media-sinusitis-epiglottitis.explanation: These three encapsulated respiratory bacteria colonise the nasopharynx and cause otitis media, sinusitis and (type b H. influenzae) epiglottitis, typically after a viral URI impairs drainage.

otitis-media-sinusitis-epiglottitis.stem: A toxic-appearing child is drooling and sitting in a tripod position with stridor; lateral neck X-ray shows a "thumbprint" sign. The priority is to:

options.text: Examine the throat with a tongue depressor
Lay the child flat for IV access
Secure the airway in a controlled setting and give ceftriaxone

otitis-media-sinusitis-epiglottitis.explanation: This is epiglottitis — an airway emergency. Avoid throat examination or lying the child flat; keep them calm and upright and secure the airway before other interventions, then treat with a third-generation cephalosporin.

otitis-media-sinusitis-epiglottitis.stem: Regarding managing suspected epiglottitis — which is correct?

options.text: Examine the throat with a tongue depressor to confirm the swollen epiglottis
Do NOT examine the pharynx or lay the child flat — this can precipitate complete airway obstruction; keep the child calm/upright and secure the airway in a controlled setting first

otitis-media-sinusitis-epiglottitis.explanation: In epiglottitis the airway is critically narrowed; provoking the child or manipulating the throat can trigger laryngospasm and total obstruction, so airway safety precedes any diagnostic maneuver.

otitis-media-sinusitis-epiglottitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bulging, immobile, erythematous tympanic membrane”?
otitis-media-sinusitis-epiglottitis.explanation: Bulging, immobile, erythematous tympanic membrane → Acute otitis media with effusion.

otitis-media-sinusitis-epiglottitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Symptoms worsening after day 10 / "double sickening"”?
otitis-media-sinusitis-epiglottitis.explanation: Symptoms worsening after day 10 / "double sickening" → Acute bacterial (vs viral) rhinosinusitis.

otitis-media-sinusitis-epiglottitis.stem: Which should you review before “Otitis Media, Sinusitis & Epiglottitis”?
otitis-media-sinusitis-epiglottitis.explanation: Understanding bacterial physiology is essential for grasping the infections discussed.

nasal-sinus-inflammatory-pathology.stem: A patient with asthma and recurrent nasal polyps develops severe bronchospasm after taking ibuprofen. This triad is best explained by:
nasal-sinus-inflammatory-pathology.explanation: Asthma + nasal polyps + NSAID sensitivity is the Samter triad (AERD); COX inhibition shunts arachidonic acid toward bronchoconstrictor leukotrienes. These patients must avoid aspirin/NSAIDs.

nasal-sinus-inflammatory-pathology.stem: A saddle-nose deformity with nasal crusting, septal perforation, lung nodules and glomerulonephritis, with a positive c-ANCA, indicates:
nasal-sinus-inflammatory-pathology.explanation: This multisystem necrotising granulomatous vasculitis of the upper and lower airway plus kidney, with c-ANCA (anti-PR3), is granulomatosis with polyangiitis — an immunological disease requiring immunosuppression, not an infection.

nasal-sinus-inflammatory-pathology.stem: Regarding nature of a nasal polyp — which is correct?

options.text: A nasal polyp is a benign neoplasm arising from epithelium
Nasal polyps are inflammatory — protrusions of oedematous, chronically inflamed mucosa (rich in eosinophils), NOT true neoplasms; they reflect chronic rhinosinusitis, allergy, CF or AERD

nasal-sinus-inflammatory-pathology.explanation: Calling a polyp a tumour misframes management; they are treated as inflammatory disease (steroids, allergen/NSAID avoidance), and recurrence reflects ongoing inflammation, not neoplastic growth.

nasal-sinus-inflammatory-pathology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pale boggy nasal mucosa with eosinophils”?
nasal-sinus-inflammatory-pathology.explanation: Pale boggy nasal mucosa with eosinophils → Allergic (IgE-mediated) rhinitis.

nasal-sinus-inflammatory-pathology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Asthma + nasal polyps + aspirin sensitivity”?
nasal-sinus-inflammatory-pathology.explanation: Asthma + nasal polyps + aspirin sensitivity → Samter triad (AERD).

nasal-sinus-inflammatory-pathology.stem: Which should you review before “Rhinitis, Nasal Polyps & Sinonasal Inflammation”?
nasal-sinus-inflammatory-pathology.explanation: Sinusitis is a key component of upper respiratory tract pathology.

nasopharyngeal-laryngeal-tumors.stem: A patient from Southern China presents with a cervical lymph node mass, nasal obstruction and unilateral serous otitis media. The undifferentiated tumour is EBER-positive. The diagnosis is:
nasopharyngeal-laryngeal-tumors.explanation: EBV-associated undifferentiated nasopharyngeal carcinoma is common in Southeast/East Asia, presents with cervical nodal metastasis and Eustachian obstruction (serous otitis media), and is confirmed by EBER in situ hybridisation.

nasopharyngeal-laryngeal-tumors.stem: Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis of the larynx in a child is caused by:
nasopharyngeal-laryngeal-tumors.explanation: Laryngeal papillomas are caused by HPV 6 and 11 (the low-risk types); juvenile-onset disease can be multiple and recurrent, whereas adult lesions are often solitary. They cause hoarseness but are benign.

nasopharyngeal-laryngeal-tumors.stem: Regarding persistent hoarseness in an adult smoker — which is correct?

options.text: Persistent hoarseness in a smoker is most likely a benign vocal cord nodule

Persistent hoarseness (>2–3 weeks), especially in a smoker/drinker, must be evaluated by laryngoscopy to exclude GLOTTIC squamous cell carcinoma — benign nodules are usually bilateral and occur in voice-overusers

nasopharyngeal-laryngeal-tumors.explanation: Glottic cancer is curable when caught early precisely because it causes hoarseness early; attributing it to a benign nodule risks missing a treatable malignancy.

nasopharyngeal-laryngeal-tumors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cervical node mass + nasal obstruction + unilateral serous otitis media”?

options.text: Glottic squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise

nasopharyngeal-laryngeal-tumors.explanation: Cervical node mass + nasal obstruction + unilateral serous otitis media → Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (Eustachian blockage).

nasopharyngeal-laryngeal-tumors.stem: What best explains the finding: “EBER-positive lymphoepithelial tumour of the nasopharynx”?

options.text: Glottic squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise

nasopharyngeal-laryngeal-tumors.explanation: EBER-positive lymphoepithelial tumour of the nasopharynx → EBV-associated undifferentiated NPC.

cough-cold-allergy-drugs.stem: A patient using an oxymetazoline nasal spray for 10 days now has worse congestion than before. This is due to:

options.text: Rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) from prolonged topical decongestant use
An allergic reaction to the drug

cough-cold-allergy-drugs.explanation: Topical α-agonist decongestants used beyond ~3–5 days cause rebound vasodilation and worsening congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa). Management is to stop the spray and switch to an intranasal corticosteroid.

cough-cold-allergy-drugs.stem: Which drug class provides the most effective control of moderate-to-severe allergic rhinitis?
cough-cold-allergy-drugs.explanation: Intranasal corticosteroids are the most effective single treatment for allergic rhinitis, reducing congestion and inflammation better than antihistamines or decongestants, which are adjuncts.

cough-cold-allergy-drugs.stem: Regarding prolonged use of a topical nasal decongestant — which is correct?

options.text: If a nasal decongestant spray stops working, use it more often
Topical α-agonist decongestants cause rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa) after >3–5 days; the fix is to STOP the spray (switch to an intranasal steroid), not to use it more

cough-cold-allergy-drugs.explanation: Continued use worsens the very congestion it treated by downregulating/rebound vasodilation; recognising the self-perpetuating cycle prevents escalating misuse.

cough-cold-allergy-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sedation + dry mouth from an antihistamine”?
cough-cold-allergy-drugs.explanation: Sedation + dry mouth from an antihistamine → First-generation H1 blocker (crosses BBB, antimuscarinic).

cough-cold-allergy-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Worsening congestion after days of nasal spray”?
cough-cold-allergy-drugs.explanation: Worsening congestion after days of nasal spray → Rhinitis medicamentosa (rebound from topical decongestant).

cough-cold-allergy-drugs.stem: Which should you review before “Drugs for Cough, Cold & Allergy”?
cough-cold-allergy-drugs.explanation: Understanding drug allergies is crucial for safe pharmacological management.

mucolytics-cough-pharmacology.stem: Mucolytic drugs such as N-acetylcysteine reduce sputum viscosity by:

options.text: Cleaving the disulfide bonds that cross-link mucus glycoproteins

mucolytics-cough-pharmacology.explanation: Mucolytics such as N-acetylcysteine break the disulfide bonds that make mucus viscid, thinning secretions so they can be cleared; N-acetylcysteine is also the antidote for paracetamol overdose (glutathione repletion).

mucolytics-cough-pharmacology.stem: Which cough is most appropriately treated with an antitussive such as dextromethorphan?

options.text: A productive cough clearing purulent sputum
A cough with copious mucus in bronchiectasis
A cough due to a retained foreign body

mucolytics-cough-pharmacology.explanation: Antitussives are appropriate for a dry, unproductive cough that serves no clearance function; a productive cough should not be suppressed because it is clearing secretions.

mucolytics-cough-pharmacology.stem: Regarding when to suppress a cough — which is correct?

options.text: Any troublesome cough should be treated with a cough suppressant
Only a DRY, unproductive cough should be suppressed (dextromethorphan/codeine); a PRODUCTIVE cough is clearing secretions and should be helped to clear (expectorant/mucolytic), NOT suppressed

mucolytics-cough-pharmacology.explanation: Suppressing a productive cough traps secretions and can worsen infection; distinguishing dry from productive is the key decision that determines whether to suppress or to mobilise mucus.

mucolytics-cough-pharmacology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dextromethorphan for a dry, distressing cough”?
mucolytics-cough-pharmacology.explanation: Dextromethorphan for a dry, distressing cough → Central non-opioid cough suppression.

mucolytics-cough-pharmacology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thinner, easier-to-clear sputum on a mucolytic”?
mucolytics-cough-pharmacology.explanation: Thinner, easier-to-clear sputum on a mucolytic → Disulfide-bond cleavage (N-acetylcysteine/bromhexine).

copd-emphysema-chronic-bronchitis.stem: A 40-year-old non-smoker has lower-lobe panacinar emphysema and early cirrhosis. The most likely underlying cause is:
copd-emphysema-chronic-bronchitis.explanation: Panacinar emphysema in the lower lobes of a young non-smoker, together with liver disease, is the classic presentation of α1-antitrypsin deficiency — unopposed protease activity destroys alveolar walls and misfolded protein damages the liver.

copd-emphysema-chronic-bronchitis.stem: Which finding defines airflow obstruction on spirometry?

options.text: Reduced FVC with a normal or increased FEV₁/FVC ratio

copd-emphysema-chronic-bronchitis.explanation: Obstruction is defined by a reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio (<0.7) with air trapping (increased TLC/RV). A reduced FVC with a preserved ratio and reduced TLC instead indicates a restrictive pattern.

copd-emphysema-chronic-bronchitis.stem: Regarding diagnosing chronic bronchitis — which is correct?

options.text: Chronic bronchitis is diagnosed by lung biopsy showing mucous gland hyperplasia

Chronic bronchitis is a CLINICAL diagnosis — a productive cough for ≥3 months in ≥2 consecutive years; the mucous gland hyperplasia (raised Reid index) is the pathological correlate, not the diagnostic criterion

copd-emphysema-chronic-bronchitis.explanation: Unlike emphysema (an anatomical/structural diagnosis), chronic bronchitis is defined by symptom duration; knowing this distinction prevents mislabeling and unnecessary biopsy.

copd-emphysema-chronic-bronchitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “FEV₁/FVC < 0.7 that does not fully reverse with a bronchodilator”?
copd-emphysema-chronic-bronchitis.explanation: FEV₁/FVC < 0.7 that does not fully reverse with a bronchodilator → Fixed airflow obstruction (COPD).

copd-emphysema-chronic-bronchitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Upper-lobe centriacinar emphysema in a smoker”?
copd-emphysema-chronic-bronchitis.explanation: Upper-lobe centriacinar emphysema in a smoker → Smoking-induced protease injury.

asthma-bronchiectasis-pathology.stem: Which pathological feature distinguishes asthma from COPD?

options.text: Reversible bronchoconstriction with eosinophilic, IgE-mediated inflammation

asthma-bronchiectasis-pathology.explanation: Asthma features reversible airflow obstruction driven by type I IgE-mediated, eosinophilic inflammation (Curschmann spirals, Charcot–Leyden crystals). COPD obstruction is largely fixed and neutrophil-predominant.

asthma-bronchiectasis-pathology.stem: A young patient with situs inversus, chronic sinusitis and recurrent purulent respiratory infections with bronchiectasis most likely has:
asthma-bronchiectasis-pathology.explanation: The triad of bronchiectasis, situs inversus and chronic sinusitis is Kartagener syndrome, a form of primary ciliary dyskinesia (dynein-arm defect) that impairs mucociliary clearance and sperm/oviduct motility.

asthma-bronchiectasis-pathology.stem: Regarding interpreting a silent chest in asthma — which is correct?

options.text: Absence of wheeze in an asthmatic means the attack is improving
A "silent chest" in a distressed asthmatic is an OMINOUS sign of status asthmaticus — airflow is too low to generate a wheeze, indicating life-threatening obstruction, not improvement

asthma-bronchiectasis-pathology.explanation: Wheeze requires turbulent airflow; when obstruction is severe enough to silence the chest, the patient is peri-arrest — mistaking it for recovery is dangerous.

asthma-bronchiectasis-pathology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Reversible airflow obstruction (>12% FEV₁ gain post-bronchodilator)”?

options.text: Status asthmaticus — airflow too low to generate wheeze

asthma-bronchiectasis-pathology.explanation: Reversible airflow obstruction (>12% FEV₁ gain post-bronchodilator) → Asthma (vs fixed COPD).

asthma-bronchiectasis-pathology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Curschmann spirals + Charcot-Leyden crystals in sputum”?

options.text: Status asthmaticus — airflow too low to generate wheeze

asthma-bronchiectasis-pathology.explanation: Curschmann spirals + Charcot-Leyden crystals in sputum → Eosinophilic asthmatic airway.

asthma-bronchiectasis-pathology.stem: Which should you review before “Asthma & Bronchiectasis (Pathology)”?
asthma-bronchiectasis-pathology.explanation: Understanding sinonasal inflammation is relevant to asthma triggers.

cystic-fibrosis.stem: The diagnosis of cystic fibrosis is confirmed by:

options.text: An elevated sweat chloride concentration (plus CFTR genetic testing)

cystic-fibrosis.explanation: Defective CFTR chloride transport raises sweat chloride, so an elevated sweat chloride (with CFTR mutation analysis) is diagnostic; newborn screening uses raised immunoreactive trypsinogen.

cystic-fibrosis.stem: Chronic airway colonisation with which organism particularly marks disease progression in cystic fibrosis?
cystic-fibrosis.explanation: While S. aureus and H. influenzae predominate early, chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonisation is associated with accelerated decline in lung function and marks progression of cystic fibrosis lung disease.

cystic-fibrosis.stem: Regarding recognising cystic fibrosis as multisystem — which is correct?

options.text: Cystic fibrosis is purely a lung disease

CF is a MULTISYSTEM disease from a single CFTR defect — as well as bronchiectasis it causes pancreatic exocrine insufficiency (malabsorption, ADEK deficiency), meconium ileus, male infertility and CF-related diabetes; the sweat chloride test reflects the systemic channel defect

cystic-fibrosis.explanation: Framing CF as lung-only misses the pancreatic/GI/reproductive features that are often the presenting clues (failure to thrive, meconium ileus) and shapes the multidisciplinary management.

cystic-fibrosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Recurrent chest infections + malabsorption + failure to thrive”?

options.text: Thick intestinal secretions (often the first sign of CF)

cystic-fibrosis.explanation: Recurrent chest infections + malabsorption + failure to thrive → Multisystem cystic fibrosis.

cystic-fibrosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonisation of the airway”?

options.text: Thick intestinal secretions (often the first sign of CF)

cystic-fibrosis.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa colonisation of the airway → CF disease progression.

pulmonary-function-tests-interpretation.stem: Spirometry shows a reduced FVC, a normal FEV₁/FVC ratio and a reduced total lung capacity. This pattern is:
pulmonary-function-tests-interpretation.explanation: A restrictive pattern shows reduced lung volumes (FVC and TLC) with a preserved or increased FEV₁/FVC ratio, because both FEV₁ and FVC fall together. A reduced ratio would indicate obstruction.

pulmonary-function-tests-interpretation.stem: A patient with a restrictive spirometry pattern has a LOW DLCO. This points to:
pulmonary-function-tests-interpretation.explanation: A reduced DLCO indicates damage to the alveolar–capillary membrane, so a restrictive pattern with low DLCO points to interstitial (parenchymal) disease; a normal DLCO in restriction suggests an extrapulmonary (chest-wall/neuromuscular) cause.

pulmonary-function-tests-interpretation.stem: Regarding distinguishing obstructive from restrictive on spirometry — which is correct?

options.text: A low FEV₁ by itself means obstructive lung disease
FEV₁ falls in BOTH patterns — it is the FEV₁/FVC RATIO that distinguishes them: a LOW ratio (<0.7) = obstructive, whereas a NORMAL/HIGH ratio with reduced FVC and TLC = restrictive

pulmonary-function-tests-interpretation.explanation: Reading FEV₁ alone conflates the two patterns; the ratio (and lung volumes) is what separates airflow limitation from a small, stiff lung, which have opposite differentials.

pulmonary-function-tests-interpretation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio (<0.7)”?
pulmonary-function-tests-interpretation.explanation: Reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio (<0.7) → Obstructive pattern (COPD, asthma).

pulmonary-function-tests-interpretation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Reduced FVC and TLC with a normal/high ratio”?
pulmonary-function-tests-interpretation.explanation: Reduced FVC and TLC with a normal/high ratio → Restrictive pattern.

pulmonary-fibrosis-pneumoconioses.stem: A 65-year-old has progressive dyspnoea, dry cough, clubbing and basal "velcro" crackles; CT shows subpleural honeycombing. Spirometry most likely shows:

options.text: Reduced FEV₁/FVC ratio with increased TLC
Reduced FVC and TLC with a normal or increased FEV₁/FVC ratio

pulmonary-fibrosis-pneumoconioses.explanation: This is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (UIP pattern), a restrictive disease: FVC and TLC fall together, the FEV₁/FVC ratio is preserved or increased, and DLCO is reduced.

pulmonary-fibrosis-pneumoconioses.stem: Which pneumoconiosis is classically associated with upper-lobe nodules, eggshell calcification of hilar nodes, and an increased risk of tuberculosis?
pulmonary-fibrosis-pneumoconioses.explanation: Silicosis produces upper-lobe silicotic nodules and eggshell-calcified hilar lymph nodes, and silica impairs macrophage function, increasing susceptibility to tuberculosis.

pulmonary-fibrosis-pneumoconioses.stem: Regarding asbestos-related cancer risk — which is correct?

options.text: Asbestos exposure most commonly causes mesothelioma
Asbestos causes BRONCHOGENIC (lung) carcinoma more commonly than mesothelioma; mesothelioma is the more SPECIFIC but less common tumour, and smoking multiplies the lung-cancer risk
UIP pattern of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

pulmonary-fibrosis-pneumoconioses.explanation: Mesothelioma is the "signature" asbestos tumour, but in absolute numbers bronchogenic carcinoma is more frequent — and the smoking synergy makes lung cancer the bigger threat to an asbestos-exposed smoker.

pulmonary-fibrosis-pneumoconioses.stem: What best explains the finding: “Basal, subpleural honeycomb fibrosis with fibroblast foci”?

options.text: UIP pattern of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

pulmonary-fibrosis-pneumoconioses.explanation: Basal, subpleural honeycomb fibrosis with fibroblast foci → UIP pattern of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

pulmonary-fibrosis-pneumoconioses.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fine "velcro" inspiratory crackles + clubbing”?

options.text: UIP pattern of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis

pulmonary-fibrosis-pneumoconioses.explanation: Fine "velcro" inspiratory crackles + clubbing → Interstitial fibrosis.

pulmonary-fibrosis-pneumoconioses.stem: Which should you review before “Pulmonary Fibrosis & Pneumoconioses”?
pulmonary-fibrosis-pneumoconioses.explanation: Understanding tobacco's role in lung injury is crucial for grasping pulmonary fibrosis.

sarcoidosis-granulomatous-lung.stem: A young woman has bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum and hypercalcaemia. Biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas with negative stains for organisms. The hypercalcaemia is due to:
sarcoidosis-granulomatous-lung.explanation: In sarcoidosis, activated macrophages within granulomas express 1α-hydroxylase, converting 25-OH vitamin D to active calcitriol, which increases intestinal calcium absorption and causes hypercalcaemia/hypercalciuria.

sarcoidosis-granulomatous-lung.stem: The single most important feature distinguishing sarcoidosis from tuberculosis on a lung biopsy is:

options.text: Whether the granulomas are non-caseating (sarcoid) or caseating with acid-fast bacilli (TB)

sarcoidosis-granulomatous-lung.explanation: Sarcoid granulomas are non-caseating and organism-negative, whereas tuberculous granulomas show central caseous necrosis with acid-fast bacilli. This distinction is critical because their treatments (immunosuppression vs anti-TB drugs) are opposite.

sarcoidosis-granulomatous-lung.stem: Regarding distinguishing sarcoidosis from tuberculosis — which is correct?

options.text: A patient with lung granulomas and hilar nodes can be started on steroids for sarcoidosis

Sarcoid granulomas are NON-caseating with no organisms; you must EXCLUDE tuberculosis (caseating granulomas, AFB-positive) first, because giving immunosuppressive steroids to a TB patient can cause disseminated infection

sarcoidosis-granulomatous-lung.explanation: The two look similar radiographically but demand opposite treatments; the caseation/AFB distinction protects against immunosuppressing an occult infection.

sarcoidosis-granulomatous-lung.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray”?
sarcoidosis-granulomatous-lung.explanation: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest X-ray → Sarcoidosis (granulomatous nodal involvement).

sarcoidosis-granulomatous-lung.stem: What best explains the finding: “Non-caseating epithelioid granulomas, organisms absent”?
sarcoidosis-granulomatous-lung.explanation: Non-caseating epithelioid granulomas, organisms absent → Sarcoidosis histology.
