appendicitis-diverticular-ischemic-bowel.explanation: Left lower quadrant pain, fever, raised inflammatory markers → Acute diverticulitis.

hepatitis-liver-injury-patterns.stem: The histological hallmark of chronic hepatitis that signals progression toward cirrhosis is:

options.text: Interface hepatitis (inflammation crossing the limiting plate) with fibrosis

hepatitis-liver-injury-patterns.explanation: Chronic hepatitis is characterised by portal inflammation that spills across the limiting plate (interface hepatitis) with progressive fibrosis — the pathway toward cirrhosis. Grade reflects inflammation and stage reflects fibrosis.

hepatitis-liver-injury-patterns.stem: A patient has conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with dark urine and pale stools. This pattern indicates:
hepatitis-liver-injury-patterns.explanation: Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and appears in urine (dark urine); reduced bile flow into the gut produces pale stools — the pattern of cholestasis/obstruction. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (haemolysis, Gilbert) does not cause bilirubinuria.

hepatitis-liver-injury-patterns.stem: Regarding classifying jaundice — which is correct?

options.text: All jaundice reflects liver cell failure

Jaundice must be split by bilirubin type: UNCONJUGATED (prehepatic haemolysis or impaired conjugation, e.g. Gilbert) vs CONJUGATED (hepatocellular injury or post-hepatic obstruction) — only some reflect hepatocyte failure

hepatitis-liver-injury-patterns.explanation: The conjugated/unconjugated distinction localises the lesion (before, in, or after the hepatocyte) and directs completely different work-ups — e.g. haemolysis screen vs biliary imaging.

hepatitis-liver-injury-patterns.stem: What best explains the finding: “Raised AST/ALT with apoptotic (Councilman) bodies”?
hepatitis-liver-injury-patterns.explanation: Raised AST/ALT with apoptotic (Councilman) bodies → Acute hepatocellular injury/hepatitis.

hepatitis-liver-injury-patterns.stem: What best explains the finding: “Interface hepatitis with portal inflammation and fibrosis”?
hepatitis-liver-injury-patterns.explanation: Interface hepatitis with portal inflammation and fibrosis → Chronic hepatitis progressing to cirrhosis.

cirrhosis-fatty-liver-portal-hypertensio.stem: The two fundamental consequences of cirrhosis that produce most of its clinical features are:
cirrhosis-fatty-liver-portal-hypertensio.explanation: Cirrhosis distorts hepatic architecture, raising portal pressure (varices, ascites, splenomegaly) and reducing hepatocyte function (jaundice, hypoalbuminaemia, coagulopathy, encephalopathy). These two axes generate the clinical picture.

cirrhosis-fatty-liver-portal-hypertensio.stem: Which finding best supports alcoholic (rather than viral) hepatitis?

options.text: AST:ALT ratio greater than 2 with Mallory–Denk bodies

cirrhosis-fatty-liver-portal-hypertensio.explanation: Alcoholic hepatitis classically shows an AST:ALT ratio greater than 2 with hepatocyte ballooning, neutrophils and Mallory–Denk bodies. Anti-mitochondrial antibody indicates PBC, and Kayser–Fleischer rings indicate Wilson disease.

cirrhosis-fatty-liver-portal-hypertensio.stem: Regarding reversibility of liver disease — which is correct?

options.text: Fatty liver and cirrhosis are equally reversible if the cause is removed

Steatosis (fatty change) is REVERSIBLE if the insult is removed, but established CIRRHOSIS (diffuse fibrosis with regenerative nodules) is generally IRREVERSIBLE — the point of no return is the architectural distortion of cirrhosis

cirrhosis-fatty-liver-portal-hypertensio.explanation: Recognising that early fatty change can be reversed motivates intervention (alcohol cessation, weight loss, antivirals) before fibrosis becomes the fixed, nodular architecture of cirrhosis.

cirrhosis-fatty-liver-portal-hypertensio.stem: What best explains the finding: “Haematemesis from oesophageal varices”?
cirrhosis-fatty-liver-portal-hypertensio.explanation: Haematemesis from oesophageal varices → Portal hypertension (porto-systemic shunt).

cirrhosis-fatty-liver-portal-hypertensio.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ascites + splenomegaly + caput medusae”?
cirrhosis-fatty-liver-portal-hypertensio.explanation: Ascites + splenomegaly + caput medusae → Portal hypertension + hypoalbuminaemia.

cirrhosis-fatty-liver-portal-hypertensio.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Fatty Liver, Cirrhosis & Portal Hypertension”?
cirrhosis-fatty-liver-portal-hypertensio.explanation: Portal hypertension can lead to gastrointestinal bleeding from varices.

cirrhosis-fatty-liver-portal-hypertensio.stem: Which should you review before “Fatty Liver, Cirrhosis & Portal Hypertension”?
cirrhosis-fatty-liver-portal-hypertensio.explanation: Understanding the portal system is essential for grasping portal hypertension.

hepatocellular-carcinoma-liver-tumors.stem: A patient with long-standing hepatitis C cirrhosis develops a new hepatic mass with a rising serum alpha-fetoprotein and portal vein invasion. The diagnosis is:
hepatocellular-carcinoma-liver-tumors.explanation: HCC classically arises on cirrhosis (here HCV), with a rising AFP and a tendency for vascular (portal vein) invasion. Haemangioma and adenoma are benign and AFP-negative.

hepatocellular-carcinoma-liver-tumors.stem: Chronic hepatitis B can cause hepatocellular carcinoma even in the absence of cirrhosis because the virus:

options.text: Integrates into the host genome, promoting oncogenesis directly

hepatocellular-carcinoma-liver-tumors.explanation: Unlike most causes of HCC that act through cirrhosis, HBV DNA can integrate into the host genome and act as a direct oncogenic driver, so HBV-related HCC can occur without established cirrhosis.

hepatocellular-carcinoma-liver-tumors.stem: Regarding primary vs secondary liver tumours — which is correct?

options.text: A patient with multiple liver masses most likely has primary hepatocellular carcinoma

METASTASES are far more common than primary liver cancer; multiple masses in a NON-cirrhotic liver are usually secondaries (colon, breast, lung, pancreas), whereas HCC typically arises as a mass on a CIRRHOTIC liver with a rising AFP

hepatocellular-carcinoma-liver-tumors.explanation: Assuming multiple masses are HCC misdirects the work-up; the presence or absence of cirrhosis and the number of lesions point toward primary versus metastatic disease and change which primary to hunt for.

hepatocellular-carcinoma-liver-tumors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rising AFP + new mass in a cirrhotic liver”?
hepatocellular-carcinoma-liver-tumors.explanation: Rising AFP + new mass in a cirrhotic liver → Hepatocellular carcinoma.

hepatocellular-carcinoma-liver-tumors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Portal vein tumour thrombus”?
hepatocellular-carcinoma-liver-tumors.explanation: Portal vein tumour thrombus → HCC vascular invasion.

hepatocellular-carcinoma-liver-tumors.stem: Which should you review before “Hepatocellular Carcinoma & Liver Tumours”?
hepatocellular-carcinoma-liver-tumors.explanation: Chronic hepatitis B is a significant cause of HCC.

gallstones-cholecystitis-cholangitis.stem: A patient with gallstones presents with fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain (Charcot triad). This indicates:
gallstones-cholecystitis-cholangitis.explanation: Fever, jaundice and RUQ pain (Charcot triad) indicate ascending cholangitis — infection of an obstructed common bile duct. It is an emergency requiring antibiotics and urgent biliary drainage (ERCP); Reynolds pentad adds hypotension and confusion.

gallstones-cholecystitis-cholangitis.stem: Acute cholecystitis is distinguished from simple biliary colic mainly by the presence of:

options.text: Sustained inflammation with fever and a positive Murphy sign

gallstones-cholecystitis-cholangitis.explanation: Biliary colic is transient pain from a stone temporarily obstructing the cystic duct, without inflammation. Sustained obstruction produces acute cholecystitis with fever, constant pain and a positive Murphy sign.

gallstones-cholecystitis-cholangitis.stem: Regarding distinguishing biliary colic, cholecystitis and cholangitis — which is correct?

options.text: RUQ pain from gallstones is all the same regardless of fever or jaundice

They are distinct: biliary COLIC = transient pain, NO fever; CHOLECYSTITIS = sustained pain + fever + Murphy sign (cystic-duct level); CHOLANGITIS = fever + jaundice + RUQ pain (Charcot triad, CBD obstruction + infection) — an emergency needing duct drainage

gallstones-cholecystitis-cholangitis.explanation: The presence of fever and jaundice escalates the diagnosis from colic to cholecystitis to cholangitis, each with different urgency and management (analgesia vs cholecystectomy vs urgent ERCP).

gallstones-cholecystitis-cholangitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Episodic RUQ pain after fatty meals, no fever”?
gallstones-cholecystitis-cholangitis.explanation: Episodic RUQ pain after fatty meals, no fever → Biliary colic (transient cystic-duct obstruction).

gallstones-cholecystitis-cholangitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Constant RUQ pain + fever + positive Murphy sign”?
gallstones-cholecystitis-cholangitis.explanation: Constant RUQ pain + fever + positive Murphy sign → Acute cholecystitis.

gallstones-cholecystitis-cholangitis.stem: Which should you review before “Gallstones, Cholecystitis & Cholangitis”?

options.text: Ascending Cholangitis, Bile Flow & Fat-Soluble Vitamins

gallstones-cholecystitis-cholangitis.explanation: Understanding cholangitis is essential for grasping the complications of gallstones.

bilirubin-metabolism-jaundice.stem: A patient with obstructive jaundice from a bile-duct stone would be expected to have:

options.text: Raised unconjugated bilirubin with no bilirubin in the urine
Raised conjugated bilirubin with dark urine and pale stools
Raised unconjugated bilirubin with dark stools only

bilirubin-metabolism-jaundice.explanation: Obstruction raises conjugated (water-soluble) bilirubin, which spills into the urine (dark urine), while reduced bile flow to the gut makes stools pale; pruritus is common. Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia does not cause bilirubinuria.

bilirubin-metabolism-jaundice.stem: Unconjugated bilirubin does not appear in the urine because it is:

options.text: Fat-soluble and tightly bound to albumin (not water-soluble)

bilirubin-metabolism-jaundice.explanation: Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble and carried bound to albumin, so it is neither filtered nor excreted in urine; only conjugated (water-soluble) bilirubin appears in urine, which is why bilirubinuria indicates a conjugated cause.

bilirubin-metabolism-jaundice.stem: Regarding bilirubin in the urine — which is correct?

options.text: Any jaundice will produce bilirubin in the urine

Only CONJUGATED (water-soluble) bilirubin appears in urine; UNCONJUGATED hyperbilirubinaemia (haemolysis, Gilbert) is "acholuric" — no bilirubin in the urine — so bilirubinuria points specifically to a conjugated (hepatic/obstructive) cause

bilirubin-metabolism-jaundice.explanation: The solubility difference means the urine finding localises the jaundice: bilirubinuria excludes a pure pre-hepatic cause and points toward hepatocellular or obstructive disease.

bilirubin-metabolism-jaundice.stem: What best explains the finding: “Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with no bilirubin in the urine”?
bilirubin-metabolism-jaundice.explanation: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with no bilirubin in the urine → Pre-hepatic (haemolysis) or Gilbert syndrome.

bilirubin-metabolism-jaundice.stem: What best explains the finding: “Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia + dark urine + pale stools + pruritus”?
bilirubin-metabolism-jaundice.explanation: Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia + dark urine + pale stools + pruritus → Post-hepatic (obstructive) jaundice.

bilirubin-metabolism-jaundice.stem: Which should you review before “Bilirubin Metabolism & Jaundice”?
bilirubin-metabolism-jaundice.explanation: Understanding cholestatic patterns is essential for interpreting jaundice.

liver-function-tests-interpretation.stem: Which combination best reflects the liver's true synthetic function (and thus severity of liver failure)?

options.text: Serum albumin and the prothrombin time/INR

liver-function-tests-interpretation.explanation: Albumin and the prothrombin time/INR reflect the liver's synthetic capacity; a low albumin (chronic) and prolonged INR (acute, sensitive) indicate impaired function. Transaminases measure injury and ALP/GGT measure cholestasis, not function.

liver-function-tests-interpretation.stem: Predominantly elevated alkaline phosphatase and GGT, with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, indicate which pattern of liver test abnormality?
liver-function-tests-interpretation.explanation: A rise in ALP and GGT (with conjugated bilirubin) is a cholestatic pattern, indicating impaired bile flow (biliary obstruction or intrahepatic cholestasis); the raised GGT confirms the ALP is of hepatobiliary origin.

liver-function-tests-interpretation.stem: Regarding what "liver function tests" actually measure — which is correct?

options.text: A high AST/ALT means the liver is failing to function

AST/ALT measure hepatocyte INJURY (enzyme leak), NOT synthetic FUNCTION — true liver function is reflected by ALBUMIN and the PT/INR (and bilirubin handling); a liver can have very high transaminases yet preserved function, or normal transaminases with failing synthesis

liver-function-tests-interpretation.explanation: Confusing injury markers with function markers misjudges severity; a failing liver is identified by falling albumin and rising INR, not by how high the transaminases are.

liver-function-tests-interpretation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Predominantly raised AST and ALT”?
liver-function-tests-interpretation.explanation: Predominantly raised AST and ALT → Hepatocellular injury pattern.

liver-function-tests-interpretation.stem: What best explains the finding: “AST:ALT ratio greater than 2”?
liver-function-tests-interpretation.explanation: AST:ALT ratio greater than 2 → Alcoholic liver disease.

liver-function-tests-interpretation.stem: Which should you review before “Interpreting Liver Function Tests”?
liver-function-tests-interpretation.explanation: Understanding cholestatic patterns is essential for interpreting liver function tests.

autoimmune-metabolic-liver-disease.stem: A young adult with liver disease, a movement disorder and greenish-brown corneal rings is found to have a low serum ceruloplasmin. The diagnosis is:
autoimmune-metabolic-liver-disease.explanation: Wilson disease is copper accumulation (ATP7B mutation) causing liver and neuropsychiatric disease with Kayser–Fleischer rings and a low ceruloplasmin; it is a treatable cause of cirrhosis (copper chelation).

autoimmune-metabolic-liver-disease.stem: A middle-aged woman with pruritus and fatigue has a cholestatic LFT pattern and a positive anti-mitochondrial antibody. The most likely diagnosis is:
autoimmune-metabolic-liver-disease.explanation: Primary biliary cholangitis is an autoimmune destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts, typically in middle-aged women, with pruritus, a cholestatic pattern and a positive anti-mitochondrial antibody. PSC instead affects men with ulcerative colitis and shows beaded ducts.

autoimmune-metabolic-liver-disease.stem: Regarding distinguishing pbc from psc — which is correct?

options.text: Primary biliary cholangitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis are essentially the same disease

They differ: PBC affects middle-aged WOMEN, is ANTI-MITOCHONDRIAL antibody positive and destroys small intrahepatic ducts; PSC affects MEN with ULCERATIVE COLITIS, shows "beaded" large ducts on MRCP and carries a high cholangiocarcinoma risk

autoimmune-metabolic-liver-disease.explanation: The demographics, antibodies, duct level and cancer risk differ, driving different associations (UC in PSC) and surveillance (cholangiocarcinoma in PSC) — conflating them misses these.

autoimmune-metabolic-liver-disease.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cirrhosis + diabetes + skin pigmentation ("bronze diabetes")”?
autoimmune-metabolic-liver-disease.explanation: Cirrhosis + diabetes + skin pigmentation ("bronze diabetes") → Hereditary haemochromatosis (iron overload).

autoimmune-metabolic-liver-disease.stem: What best explains the finding: “Liver disease + movement disorder + Kayser–Fleischer rings”?
autoimmune-metabolic-liver-disease.explanation: Liver disease + movement disorder + Kayser–Fleischer rings → Wilson disease (copper; low ceruloplasmin).

autoimmune-metabolic-liver-disease.stem: Which should you review before “Autoimmune & Metabolic Liver Disease”?

options.text: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Crohn & Ulcerative Colitis

autoimmune-metabolic-liver-disease.explanation: Understanding autoimmune liver diseases requires knowledge of associated inflammatory bowel diseases.

acute-chronic-pancreatitis.stem: A patient presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and a serum lipase five times the upper limit of normal. The two most likely underlying causes are:
acute-chronic-pancreatitis.explanation: Gallstones and alcohol are the two dominant causes of acute pancreatitis. The clinical picture with a markedly raised lipase (more specific than amylase) supports the diagnosis.

acute-chronic-pancreatitis.stem: Chronic pancreatitis characteristically leads to which combination of deficiencies?
acute-chronic-pancreatitis.explanation: Progressive fibrosis destroys both acinar (exocrine) tissue, causing malabsorption and steatorrhoea, and islet (endocrine) tissue, causing diabetes — the dual insufficiency of chronic pancreatitis.

acute-chronic-pancreatitis.stem: Regarding nature of a pancreatic pseudocyst — which is correct?

options.text: A pancreatic pseudocyst is a true cyst lined by epithelium

A pancreatic PSEUDOcyst is a collection of enzyme-rich fluid walled off by granulation tissue/fibrosis WITHOUT an epithelial lining — the "pseudo" denotes the absent epithelium; it typically forms weeks after an attack

acute-chronic-pancreatitis.explanation: The lack of an epithelial lining defines it as a pseudocyst and affects management (many resolve; persistent/symptomatic ones may need drainage) — distinguishing it from true epithelial cysts and cystic neoplasms.

acute-chronic-pancreatitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back + raised lipase”?
acute-chronic-pancreatitis.explanation: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back + raised lipase → Acute pancreatitis.

acute-chronic-pancreatitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Flank (Grey Turner) / periumbilical (Cullen) bruising”?
acute-chronic-pancreatitis.explanation: Flank (Grey Turner) / periumbilical (Cullen) bruising → Haemorrhagic (necrotising) pancreatitis.

acute-chronic-pancreatitis.stem: Which should you review before “Acute & Chronic Pancreatitis”?
acute-chronic-pancreatitis.explanation: Understanding hypertriglyceridemic pancreatitis is crucial for grasping acute pancreatitis mechanisms.

pancreatic-carcinoma.stem: An older smoker presents with painless jaundice, weight loss and a palpable non-tender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign). The most likely diagnosis is:

options.text: Gallstone in the common bile duct

pancreatic-carcinoma.explanation: Painless obstructive jaundice with a palpable non-tender gallbladder (Courvoisier) in an older smoker strongly suggests a pancreatic head adenocarcinoma obstructing the common bile duct, rather than gallstones (which scar the gallbladder).

pancreatic-carcinoma.stem: Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis (Trousseau sign of malignancy) in a patient with pancreatic cancer reflects:

options.text: Direct tumour invasion of veins only

pancreatic-carcinoma.explanation: Pancreatic (and other) adenocarcinomas can induce a systemic hypercoagulable state, producing recurrent migratory thrombophlebitis — the paraneoplastic Trousseau sign of malignancy.

pancreatic-carcinoma.stem: Regarding interpreting a palpable gallbladder with jaundice — which is correct?

options.text: A palpable, distended gallbladder with jaundice is usually due to gallstones

Courvoisier law: a palpable, NON-TENDER, distended gallbladder with jaundice suggests MALIGNANT obstruction (e.g. pancreatic head cancer) rather than stones — gallstone disease typically scars the gallbladder so it cannot distend

pancreatic-carcinoma.explanation: Chronic gallstone disease fibroses the gallbladder wall, preventing distension; a distensible, palpable gallbladder therefore points away from stones and toward a malignant cause of obstruction.

pancreatic-carcinoma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Painless obstructive jaundice + weight loss in an older smoker”?
pancreatic-carcinoma.explanation: Painless obstructive jaundice + weight loss in an older smoker → Pancreatic head adenocarcinoma.

pancreatic-carcinoma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Palpable non-tender gallbladder with jaundice (Courvoisier)”?
pancreatic-carcinoma.explanation: Palpable non-tender gallbladder with jaundice (Courvoisier) → Malignant biliary obstruction.

pancreatic-carcinoma.stem: Which should you review before “Pancreatic Carcinoma”?
pancreatic-carcinoma.explanation: Understanding liver injury patterns may provide context for jaundice.

antiemetics-prokinetics.stem: Which antiemetic class is most appropriate first-line for chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting?
antiemetics-prokinetics.explanation: 5-HT3 antagonists such as ondansetron block vagal and central (CTZ) 5-HT3 receptors and are first-line for chemotherapy- and post-operative nausea (often combined with dexamethasone ± an NK1 antagonist). Antihistamines/antimuscarinics are best for motion sickness.

antiemetics-prokinetics.stem: Compared with metoclopramide, domperidone causes fewer extrapyramidal side effects because it:

options.text: Does not readily cross the blood–brain barrier

antiemetics-prokinetics.explanation: Both are D2 antagonists, but domperidone poorly penetrates the blood–brain barrier, so it produces fewer central (extrapyramidal) effects than metoclopramide, which does cross and can cause dystonia and parkinsonism.

antiemetics-prokinetics.stem: Regarding extrapyramidal effects of antiemetics — which is correct?

options.text: All dopamine-antagonist antiemetics carry the same risk of extrapyramidal side effects

METOCLOPRAMIDE crosses the blood–brain barrier and can cause extrapyramidal effects (dystonia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia), whereas DOMPERIDONE largely does not cross the BBB and has far fewer central effects (though both can prolong QT)

antiemetics-prokinetics.explanation: The BBB-penetration difference explains why domperidone is preferred when central dopamine blockade must be avoided (e.g. Parkinson patients); assuming both behave identically leads to avoidable EPS.

antiemetics-prokinetics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ondansetron chosen for chemotherapy-induced nausea”?

options.text: Domperidone does not cross the BBB

antiemetics-prokinetics.explanation: Ondansetron chosen for chemotherapy-induced nausea → 5-HT3 receptor antagonism (vagal + CTZ).

antiemetics-prokinetics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Antihistamine/antimuscarinic for motion sickness”?

options.text: Domperidone does not cross the BBB

antiemetics-prokinetics.explanation: Antihistamine/antimuscarinic for motion sickness → Vestibular (H1/muscarinic) pathway block.

laxatives-antidiarrheals-ors.stem: Oral rehydration solution remains effective even in severe secretory diarrhoea (e.g. cholera) because glucose:

options.text: Drives sodium (and therefore water) absorption via the intestinal SGLT1 cotransporter

laxatives-antidiarrheals-ors.explanation: The SGLT1 sodium–glucose cotransporter continues to absorb sodium (with water following osmotically) even when secretory toxins are active; this coupling is why ORS must contain glucose and is life-saving in cholera.

laxatives-antidiarrheals-ors.stem: In which situation is loperamide (an antimotility agent) contraindicated?

options.text: Bloody, febrile (invasive) diarrhoea or suspected EHEC infection

laxatives-antidiarrheals-ors.explanation: Antimotility drugs should be avoided in invasive/inflammatory (bloody, febrile) diarrhoea and EHEC, where slowing transit prolongs toxin exposure and increases the risk of haemolytic-uraemic syndrome and toxic megacolon.

laxatives-antidiarrheals-ors.stem: Regarding using antimotility agents in diarrhoea — which is correct?

options.text: Loperamide is a safe symptomatic treatment for all types of diarrhoea

Antimotility agents like loperamide should be AVOIDED in invasive/inflammatory (bloody, febrile) diarrhoea and in EHEC infection — slowing transit prolongs toxin/pathogen contact, increasing the risk of haemolytic-uraemic syndrome and toxic megacolon
SGLT1 Na–glucose cotransport still absorbs water

laxatives-antidiarrheals-ors.explanation: In non-inflammatory diarrhoea loperamide is helpful, but in dysentery it removes a protective clearance mechanism; recognising the bloody/febrile picture prevents a dangerous prescription.

laxatives-antidiarrheals-ors.stem: What best explains the finding: “ORS effective even in profuse cholera diarrhoea”?

options.text: SGLT1 Na–glucose cotransport still absorbs water

laxatives-antidiarrheals-ors.explanation: ORS effective even in profuse cholera diarrhoea → SGLT1 Na–glucose cotransport still absorbs water.

laxatives-antidiarrheals-ors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Loperamide reduces stool frequency in non-inflammatory diarrhoea”?

options.text: SGLT1 Na–glucose cotransport still absorbs water

laxatives-antidiarrheals-ors.explanation: Loperamide reduces stool frequency in non-inflammatory diarrhoea → Gut µ-opioid slowing of transit.

laxatives-antidiarrheals-ors.stem: Which should you review before “Laxatives, Antidiarrhoeals & Oral Rehydration”?
laxatives-antidiarrheals-ors.explanation: Understanding when to avoid antimotility agents in inflammatory diarrhoea is crucial.

ibs-functional-gi-disorders.stem: Irritable bowel syndrome is best characterised as:

options.text: A structural bowel disease with mucosal ulceration
A functional gut–brain disorder with recurrent pain and altered bowel habit but normal structure

ibs-functional-gi-disorders.explanation: IBS is a functional disorder of gut–brain interaction: recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation with altered stool frequency/form, in the absence of structural or biochemical abnormality. It is diagnosed clinically once alarm features are excluded.

ibs-functional-gi-disorders.stem: Which feature would NOT fit a diagnosis of IBS and should prompt investigation for organic disease?

options.text: Rectal bleeding with weight loss and anaemia

ibs-functional-gi-disorders.explanation: Rectal bleeding, weight loss and anaemia are alarm ("red flag") features inconsistent with IBS; they mandate investigation (e.g. colonoscopy) to exclude colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease or other organic pathology.

ibs-functional-gi-disorders.stem: Regarding diagnosing ibs safely — which is correct?

options.text: Chronic abdominal pain and altered bowel habit can be labelled IBS without further thought

IBS is a clinical diagnosis that requires the ABSENCE of alarm features (weight loss, rectal bleeding/anaemia, age >50 with new symptoms, nocturnal/progressive symptoms, family history) — these red flags mandate investigation to exclude organic disease first

ibs-functional-gi-disorders.explanation: Labelling everyone with these symptoms as IBS risks missing colorectal cancer, IBD or coeliac disease; the safe diagnosis depends on a positive pattern together with excluded red flags.

ibs-functional-gi-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Recurrent abdominal pain relieved by defecation + altered stool”?

options.text: ALARM features — investigate for organic disease

ibs-functional-gi-disorders.explanation: Recurrent abdominal pain relieved by defecation + altered stool → Irritable bowel syndrome.

ibs-functional-gi-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Normal investigations despite chronic symptoms”?

options.text: ALARM features — investigate for organic disease

ibs-functional-gi-disorders.explanation: Normal investigations despite chronic symptoms → Functional (not organic) disorder.

ibs-functional-gi-disorders.stem: Which should you review before “IBS & Functional GI Disorders”?
ibs-functional-gi-disorders.explanation: IBS diagnosis requires exclusion of colorectal cancer.

peptic-ulcer-disease.stem: A patient has epigastric pain that is relieved by eating and recurs 2–3 hours later; testing is positive for Helicobacter pylori. The most likely lesion is:
peptic-ulcer-disease.explanation: Duodenal ulcers, strongly associated with H. pylori and increased acid, classically cause pain that is relieved by food and recurs a few hours later; they are rarely malignant. Gastric ulcer pain is typically worsened by food.

peptic-ulcer-disease.stem: A posterior duodenal ulcer that erodes into a blood vessel most characteristically bleeds from the:
peptic-ulcer-disease.explanation: The gastroduodenal artery lies posterior to the first part of the duodenum, so a posterior duodenal ulcer can erode into it and cause brisk upper-GI haemorrhage. An anterior duodenal ulcer tends to perforate instead.

peptic-ulcer-disease.stem: Regarding biopsy of gastric vs duodenal ulcers — which is correct?

options.text: All peptic ulcers can be treated medically without biopsy
A GASTRIC ulcer must be BIOPSIED to exclude malignancy (gastric cancer can present as an ulcer), whereas DUODENAL ulcers are almost never malignant and do not routinely require biopsy

peptic-ulcer-disease.explanation: Malignant ulcers occur in the stomach, not the duodenum; skipping biopsy of a gastric ulcer risks missing an early gastric cancer masquerading as benign peptic disease.

peptic-ulcer-disease.stem: What best explains the finding: “Epigastric pain relieved by food, recurring hours later”?
peptic-ulcer-disease.explanation: Epigastric pain relieved by food, recurring hours later → Duodenal ulcer (H. pylori, acid).

peptic-ulcer-disease.stem: What best explains the finding: “Epigastric pain worse with food + weight loss”?
peptic-ulcer-disease.explanation: Epigastric pain worse with food + weight loss → Gastric ulcer (biopsy to exclude malignancy).

peptic-ulcer-disease.stem: Which should you review before “Peptic Ulcer Disease”?

options.text: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Crohn & Ulcerative Colitis

peptic-ulcer-disease.explanation: Understanding gastritis is essential for grasping peptic ulcer disease.

acid-suppression-h-pylori-therapy.stem: Proton pump inhibitors reduce gastric acid most effectively because they:

options.text: Irreversibly inhibit the parietal-cell H⁺/K⁺-ATPase (the final common step of acid secretion)
Neutralise acid already in the stomach

acid-suppression-h-pylori-therapy.explanation: PPIs irreversibly inhibit the H⁺/K⁺-ATPase, the final step in acid secretion regardless of the stimulus (histamine, gastrin or acetylcholine), making them more effective than H2 blockers or antacids.

acid-suppression-h-pylori-therapy.stem: Standard first-line eradication therapy for Helicobacter pylori consists of:

options.text: A proton pump inhibitor plus two antibiotics (triple therapy)

acid-suppression-h-pylori-therapy.explanation: Triple therapy — a PPI plus two antibiotics (e.g. clarithromycin and amoxicillin) for around 14 days — is standard; bismuth-based quadruple therapy is used where clarithromycin resistance is high. Eradication both heals ulcers and prevents recurrence.

acid-suppression-h-pylori-therapy.stem: Regarding treating h. pylori-positive peptic ulcers — which is correct?

options.text: A PPI alone is sufficient to cure an H. pylori-associated peptic ulcer
An H. pylori-positive ulcer needs ERADICATION (PPI + antibiotics), not acid suppression alone — a PPI heals the ulcer but leaves the organism, so ulcers recur unless H. pylori is eradicated

acid-suppression-h-pylori-therapy.explanation: H. pylori is the underlying cause; treating only the acid addresses the symptom while the infection persists, leading to relapse — hence "test and treat" for the organism.

acid-suppression-h-pylori-therapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “PPI chosen to heal a peptic ulcer or severe GERD”?
acid-suppression-h-pylori-therapy.explanation: PPI chosen to heal a peptic ulcer or severe GERD → Irreversible H⁺/K⁺-ATPase inhibition (most potent).

acid-suppression-h-pylori-therapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “B12/magnesium deficiency or C. difficile on long-term PPI”?
acid-suppression-h-pylori-therapy.explanation: B12/magnesium deficiency or C. difficile on long-term PPI → Chronic acid suppression effects.

acid-suppression-h-pylori-therapy.stem: Which should you review before “Acid Suppression & H. pylori Eradication”?

options.text: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Crohn & Ulcerative Colitis

acid-suppression-h-pylori-therapy.explanation: Understanding acid secretion is crucial for grasping acid suppression therapies.

nutrition-energy-protein-malnutrition.stem: A weaned child has generalised oedema, a distended fatty liver, skin and hair changes, and hypoalbuminaemia, with a deceptively near-normal weight. This is:
nutrition-energy-protein-malnutrition.explanation: Kwashiorkor is predominantly protein deficiency: hypoalbuminaemia causes oedema (and ascites), with fatty liver and skin/hair changes. The oedema can mask weight loss. Marasmus is total energy deficiency with wasting and no oedema.

nutrition-energy-protein-malnutrition.stem: Refeeding syndrome in a severely malnourished patient is characterised by which dangerous electrolyte shift after feeding is started?

options.text: Insulin-driven intracellular shift of phosphate, potassium and magnesium (hypophosphataemia)

nutrition-energy-protein-malnutrition.explanation: Refeeding triggers an insulin surge that drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells, causing life-threatening hypophosphataemia (and arrhythmias); thiamine demand also rises. Feed slowly and replace electrolytes and thiamine.

nutrition-energy-protein-malnutrition.stem: Regarding distinguishing kwashiorkor from marasmus — which is correct?

options.text: A malnourished child with a near-normal weight cannot be severely malnourished

KWASHIORKOR (protein deficiency) causes OEDEMA that can mask weight loss, so the weight may look deceptively normal despite severe malnutrition; MARASMUS (energy deficiency) instead causes obvious wasting without oedema

nutrition-energy-protein-malnutrition.explanation: The oedema of hypoalbuminaemia adds fluid weight, hiding tissue loss; relying on weight alone misses kwashiorkor — the oedema and low albumin are the giveaways.

nutrition-energy-protein-malnutrition.stem: What best explains the finding: “Severe muscle + fat wasting, no oedema, preserved albumin”?
nutrition-energy-protein-malnutrition.explanation: Severe muscle + fat wasting, no oedema, preserved albumin → Marasmus (total energy deficiency).

nutrition-energy-protein-malnutrition.stem: What best explains the finding: “Oedema/ascites + fatty liver + skin/hair changes”?
nutrition-energy-protein-malnutrition.explanation: Oedema/ascites + fatty liver + skin/hair changes → Kwashiorkor (protein deficiency, hypoalbuminaemia).

nutrition-energy-protein-malnutrition.stem: Which should you review before “Nutrition, Energy & Protein-Energy Malnutrition”?
nutrition-energy-protein-malnutrition.explanation: Understanding malnutrition is essential for managing pancreatic conditions.

nutritional-assessment-support.stem: When a malnourished patient has a functioning gastrointestinal tract, the preferred route of nutritional support is:
nutritional-assessment-support.explanation: The principle is "if the gut works, use it": enteral nutrition maintains gut integrity, is cheaper and has fewer complications than parenteral nutrition, which is reserved for a non-functioning or inaccessible gut.

nutritional-assessment-support.stem: Which finding indicates significant malnutrition warranting nutritional support?

options.text: A BMI below 18.5 kg/m² or unintentional weight loss greater than 10%

nutritional-assessment-support.explanation: A BMI under 18.5 kg/m² or unintentional weight loss over 10% indicates significant malnutrition and the need for nutritional support, especially in the setting of acute illness which raises requirements.

nutritional-assessment-support.stem: Regarding choosing enteral vs parenteral nutrition — which is correct?

options.text: Intravenous (parenteral) nutrition is the best, most reliable way to feed a malnourished patient

ENTERAL nutrition is preferred whenever the gut works ("if the gut works, use it") — it maintains gut integrity and has fewer complications and lower cost; PARENTERAL nutrition is reserved for a non-functioning or inaccessible gut and carries more risks (line sepsis, metabolic complications)
"If the gut works, use it" — maintains gut integrity

nutritional-assessment-support.explanation: Defaulting to parenteral nutrition exposes patients to avoidable line infections and metabolic problems and lets the gut atrophy; the functional gut should be used whenever possible.

nutritional-assessment-support.stem: What best explains the finding: “BMI <18.5 or unintentional weight loss >10%”?

options.text: "If the gut works, use it" — maintains gut integrity

nutritional-assessment-support.explanation: BMI <18.5 or unintentional weight loss >10% → Significant malnutrition (needs support).

nutritional-assessment-support.stem: What best explains the finding: “Enteral feeding chosen when the gut is functional”?

options.text: "If the gut works, use it" — maintains gut integrity

nutritional-assessment-support.explanation: Enteral feeding chosen when the gut is functional → "If the gut works, use it" — maintains gut integrity.

nutritional-assessment-support.stem: Which should you review before “Nutritional Assessment & Support”?
nutritional-assessment-support.explanation: Understanding nutritional injury is foundational for assessment.

obesity-pathophysiology.stem: The metabolic syndrome is best described as the clustering of:

options.text: Central obesity, insulin resistance/hyperglycaemia, dyslipidaemia and hypertension

obesity-pathophysiology.explanation: Metabolic syndrome clusters central (visceral) obesity, insulin resistance/hyperglycaemia, atherogenic dyslipidaemia (high triglycerides, low HDL) and hypertension — a high cardiovascular-risk state driven by visceral adiposity.

obesity-pathophysiology.stem: In common obesity, circulating leptin levels are typically:

options.text: High, but with resistance to leptin's satiety signal

obesity-pathophysiology.explanation: Leptin is secreted by adipose tissue in proportion to fat mass, so obese individuals usually have high leptin but are resistant to its central satiety effect. True leptin deficiency is a rare monogenic cause of obesity.

obesity-pathophysiology.stem: Regarding leptin levels in obesity — which is correct?

options.text: Obese people are obese because they have low leptin (the satiety hormone)
Most obese people have HIGH leptin levels but are leptin-RESISTANT — the hypothalamus no longer responds normally to the satiety signal; true leptin deficiency is a rare monogenic cause

obesity-pathophysiology.explanation: Leptin rises with fat mass, so obesity is usually a state of resistance (not deficiency); this is why leptin therapy helps only the rare deficient patient, not common obesity.

obesity-pathophysiology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Central obesity + hyperglycaemia + high TG/low HDL + hypertension”?
obesity-pathophysiology.explanation: Central obesity + hyperglycaemia + high TG/low HDL + hypertension → Metabolic syndrome.

obesity-pathophysiology.stem: What best explains the finding: “High leptin but persistent obesity”?
obesity-pathophysiology.explanation: High leptin but persistent obesity → Leptin resistance.

obesity-pathophysiology.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Obesity & Metabolic Syndrome”?
obesity-pathophysiology.explanation: Obesity is a major risk factor for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.

obesity-pathophysiology.stem: Which should you review before “Obesity & Metabolic Syndrome”?
obesity-pathophysiology.explanation: Understanding obesity's link to prediabetes is crucial.

obesity-management-bariatric-surgery.stem: In the stepped management of obesity, bariatric surgery is generally reserved for patients with:

options.text: A BMI ≥40 (or ≥35 with significant comorbidity) when lifestyle and drugs are insufficient
Any patient wishing to lose weight

obesity-management-bariatric-surgery.explanation: Bariatric surgery is the most effective, durable treatment for severe obesity and is typically offered at BMI ≥40, or ≥35 with a significant comorbidity such as type 2 diabetes, after lifestyle and pharmacotherapy.

obesity-management-bariatric-surgery.stem: A well-recognised long-term consequence of bariatric surgery that requires lifelong monitoring is:

options.text: Micronutrient deficiency (e.g. iron, B12, calcium, fat-soluble vitamins)

obesity-management-bariatric-surgery.explanation: Restrictive/malabsorptive bariatric procedures reduce absorption of iron, B12, folate, calcium and fat-soluble vitamins, so patients need lifelong supplementation and monitoring; surgery is a long-term commitment, not a one-off cure.

obesity-management-bariatric-surgery.stem: Regarding how bariatric surgery improves diabetes — which is correct?

options.text: Bariatric surgery improves type 2 diabetes only after substantial weight loss, purely by restricting intake

Bariatric ("metabolic") surgery often improves or remits type 2 diabetes RAPIDLY — sometimes before much weight is lost — because it alters GUT HORMONES (↑GLP-1/PYY, ↓ghrelin), not merely by restricting food intake
Most effective, durable treatment for severe obesity

obesity-management-bariatric-surgery.explanation: Attributing the diabetes benefit solely to weight loss misses the hormonal/metabolic mechanism that explains its speed and magnitude, which is why it is called metabolic surgery.

obesity-management-bariatric-surgery.stem: What best explains the finding: “Lifestyle modification as the foundation of all obesity treatment”?

options.text: Most effective, durable treatment for severe obesity

obesity-management-bariatric-surgery.explanation: Lifestyle modification as the foundation of all obesity treatment → Sustained energy deficit (first-line for everyone).

obesity-management-bariatric-surgery.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bariatric surgery offered at BMI ≥40 (or ≥35 with comorbidity)”?

options.text: Most effective, durable treatment for severe obesity

obesity-management-bariatric-surgery.explanation: Bariatric surgery offered at BMI ≥40 (or ≥35 with comorbidity) → Most effective, durable treatment for severe obesity.

obesity-management-bariatric-surgery.stem: Which should you review before “Obesity Management & Bariatric Surgery”?
obesity-management-bariatric-surgery.explanation: Understanding liver complications can be relevant in obesity management.

gut-hormones-appetite-regulation.stem: Which gut hormone is the principal driver of hunger (orexigenic), rising before meals?
gut-hormones-appetite-regulation.explanation: Ghrelin, secreted by the stomach when empty and rising before meals, is the main orexigenic (hunger) hormone; GLP-1, PYY and CCK are released after eating and signal satiety.

gut-hormones-appetite-regulation.stem: The greater insulin release seen after oral glucose compared with the same amount given intravenously is explained by:
gut-hormones-appetite-regulation.explanation: Oral glucose stimulates intestinal L and K cells to release the incretins GLP-1 and GIP, which augment glucose-dependent insulin secretion — the incretin effect. GLP-1 also promotes satiety and slows gastric emptying, exploited by GLP-1 analogues.

gut-hormones-appetite-regulation.stem: Regarding which gut hormone drives hunger — which is correct?

options.text: The gut hormones released after eating (GLP-1, PYY) increase appetite

Post-meal gut hormones (GLP-1, PYY, CCK) signal SATIETY (reduce appetite); GHRELIN — released from the stomach when empty, before meals — is the main hormone that drives HUNGER (essentially the only orexigenic gut hormone)

gut-hormones-appetite-regulation.explanation: Reversing the direction of these signals misunderstands appetite control; the meal-associated hormones suppress hunger (and are exploited by GLP-1 drugs), whereas fasting ghrelin promotes it.

gut-hormones-appetite-regulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rising hunger signal before meals”?
gut-hormones-appetite-regulation.explanation: Rising hunger signal before meals → Ghrelin (the main orexigenic gut hormone).

gut-hormones-appetite-regulation.stem: What best explains the finding: “Greater insulin release from oral than IV glucose”?
gut-hormones-appetite-regulation.explanation: Greater insulin release from oral than IV glucose → The incretin effect (GLP-1, GIP).

gut-hormones-appetite-regulation.stem: Which should you review before “Gut Hormones & Appetite Regulation”?

options.text: Inhibiting pancreatic and gastric lipase to block dietary fat absorption

obesity-pharmacotherapy.explanation: Orlistat inhibits lipases, preventing absorption of about a third of dietary fat; the unabsorbed fat causes steatorrhoea and can lead to deficiency of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), which should be supplemented.

obesity-pharmacotherapy.stem: GLP-1 receptor agonists such as semaglutide produce weight loss mainly by:

options.text: Blocking fat absorption in the gut
Enhancing satiety and slowing gastric emptying (with improved glycaemic control)

obesity-pharmacotherapy.explanation: GLP-1 receptor agonists are incretin mimetics that increase satiety via central appetite centres, slow gastric emptying and improve glycaemic control, producing substantial weight loss; nausea is the common side effect.

obesity-pharmacotherapy.stem: Regarding role of anti-obesity drugs — which is correct?

options.text: Anti-obesity medications replace the need for diet and exercise

Anti-obesity drugs are ADJUNCTS to lifestyle modification (diet + activity), used when lifestyle alone is insufficient and BMI thresholds are met — they augment, not replace, a sustained energy deficit

obesity-pharmacotherapy.explanation: Framing drugs as a substitute for lifestyle change ignores that they work best (and are indicated) alongside diet and exercise; stopping them without lifestyle change leads to weight regain.

obesity-pharmacotherapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Substantial weight loss + improved glycaemia + nausea”?
obesity-pharmacotherapy.explanation: Substantial weight loss + improved glycaemia + nausea → GLP-1 receptor agonist (semaglutide/liraglutide).

obesity-pharmacotherapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Oily stools, flatulence and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency”?
obesity-pharmacotherapy.explanation: Oily stools, flatulence and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency → Orlistat (lipase inhibition blocks fat absorption).

obesity-pharmacotherapy.stem: Which should you review before “Drugs for Obesity”?
obesity-pharmacotherapy.explanation: Knowledge of obesity mechanisms is critical for understanding drug actions.

pharmacology-in-liver-disease.stem: The first-line diuretic for the ascites of cirrhosis is spironolactone because it:

options.text: Is a loop diuretic with the strongest effect
Antagonises aldosterone, countering the secondary hyperaldosteronism that drives sodium and water retention

pharmacology-in-liver-disease.explanation: Cirrhotic ascites involves secondary hyperaldosteronism; spironolactone (an aldosterone antagonist) is first-line, often combined with furosemide, alongside salt restriction. Large-volume paracentesis with albumin is used for tense ascites.

pharmacology-in-liver-disease.stem: Lactulose improves hepatic encephalopathy mainly by:

options.text: Trapping ammonia in the gut (as ammonium) and speeding its excretion

pharmacology-in-liver-disease.explanation: Lactulose acidifies the colon, converting ammonia (NH₃) to poorly absorbed ammonium (NH₄⁺) and acting as an osmotic laxative to remove it; rifaximin adds benefit by reducing ammonia-producing gut bacteria. Sedatives must be avoided.

pharmacology-in-liver-disease.stem: Regarding sedatives in hepatic encephalopathy — which is correct?

options.text: A cirrhotic patient who is agitated from encephalopathy should be calmed with a benzodiazepine

AVOID sedatives (benzodiazepines, opioids) in hepatic encephalopathy — the failing liver cannot clear them and they PRECIPITATE/worsen encephalopathy; treat the precipitant and give lactulose/rifaximin instead
Splanchnic vasoconstriction + SBP prophylaxis + definitive haemostasis

pharmacology-in-liver-disease.explanation: Sedatives potentiate the same CNS depression that encephalopathy causes and accumulate due to poor hepatic clearance, deepening coma; the correct approach targets ammonia and precipitants, not sedation.

pharmacology-in-liver-disease.stem: What best explains the finding: “Non-selective β-blocker to prevent variceal bleeding”?

options.text: Splanchnic vasoconstriction + SBP prophylaxis + definitive haemostasis

pharmacology-in-liver-disease.explanation: Non-selective β-blocker to prevent variceal bleeding → Reduces portal pressure.

pharmacology-in-liver-disease.stem: What best explains the finding: “Terlipressin/octreotide + ceftriaxone + band ligation in acute variceal bleed”?

options.text: Splanchnic vasoconstriction + SBP prophylaxis + definitive haemostasis

pharmacology-in-liver-disease.explanation: Terlipressin/octreotide + ceftriaxone + band ligation in acute variceal bleed → Splanchnic vasoconstriction + SBP prophylaxis + definitive haemostasis.

pharmacology-in-liver-disease.stem: Which should you review before “Pharmacology in Liver Disease”?
pharmacology-in-liver-disease.explanation: Cirrhosis management is directly related to understanding its complications.

hepatitis-a-e-acute.stem: Which pair of hepatitis viruses is transmitted by the faecal–oral route and causes acute, self-limited infection without a chronic carrier state?
hepatitis-a-e-acute.explanation: Hepatitis A and E are enterically (faecal–oral) transmitted and cause acute, self-limited hepatitis without chronicity (except HEV in the immunocompromised). Hepatitis B, C and D are blood-borne and can become chronic.

hepatitis-a-e-acute.stem: Hepatitis E infection is particularly dangerous in which group?

options.text: Pregnant women (high risk of fulminant hepatitis)

hepatitis-a-e-acute.explanation: Hepatitis E, although usually self-limited, carries a high risk of fulminant hepatic failure and mortality in pregnant women — a classic exam point distinguishing it from hepatitis A.

hepatitis-a-e-acute.stem: Regarding chronicity of hepatitis a and e — which is correct?

options.text: All viral hepatitides can progress to chronic infection and cirrhosis

Hepatitis A and E are enterically transmitted and ACUTE/self-limited — they do NOT cause chronic infection or cirrhosis (the sole exception is chronic HEV in immunocompromised patients); chronicity is a feature of the blood-borne B, C and D

hepatitis-a-e-acute.explanation: Assuming HAV/HEV can chronically damage the liver misclassifies them; their acute-only nature (and HEV's pregnancy risk) is exactly what distinguishes them from the cirrhosis-causing blood-borne viruses.

hepatitis-a-e-acute.stem: What best explains the finding: “Acute hepatitis after travel/contaminated food, then full recovery”?
hepatitis-a-e-acute.explanation: Acute hepatitis after travel/contaminated food, then full recovery → Hepatitis A (faecal-oral, self-limited).

hepatitis-a-e-acute.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fulminant hepatitis in a pregnant woman”?
hepatitis-a-e-acute.explanation: Fulminant hepatitis in a pregnant woman → Hepatitis E (high mortality in pregnancy).

hepatitis-a-e-acute.stem: Which should you review before “Hepatitis A & E (Enterically Transmitted)”?
hepatitis-a-e-acute.explanation: Understanding patterns of hepatic injury is essential for grasping hepatitis mechanisms.

hepatitis-b-c-d-chronic.stem: A healthy person's hepatitis B panel shows anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc negative and HBsAg negative. This indicates:
hepatitis-b-c-d-chronic.explanation: Anti-HBs indicates immunity; the negative anti-HBc shows no exposure to viral core antigen, so this is vaccine-induced immunity. Recovery from natural infection would be anti-HBs AND anti-HBc positive.

hepatitis-b-c-d-chronic.stem: The risk that hepatitis B infection becomes chronic is:

options.text: Highest when infection is acquired at birth (~90%) and lowest in adults (<5%)
Highest in adults and lowest in neonates

hepatitis-b-c-d-chronic.explanation: Chronicity of HBV is inversely related to age at infection: about 90% of perinatally infected neonates develop chronic infection versus under 5% of infected adults — the rationale for birth-dose vaccination.

hepatitis-b-c-d-chronic.stem: Regarding distinguishing vaccination from natural infection (hbv serology) — which is correct?

options.text: A positive anti-HBs simply means the person had hepatitis B in the past

Anti-HBs indicates immunity from EITHER recovery OR vaccination — the discriminator is anti-HBc: a VACCINATED person is anti-HBs positive but anti-HBc NEGATIVE, whereas someone who cleared a natural infection is positive for BOTH

hepatitis-b-c-d-chronic.explanation: Anti-HBc marks exposure to the actual virus (core antigen is not in the vaccine); using it alongside anti-HBs separates vaccine-induced immunity from resolved infection — a very common exam distinction.

hepatitis-b-c-d-chronic.stem: What best explains the finding: “HBsAg positive for more than 6 months”?
hepatitis-b-c-d-chronic.explanation: HBsAg positive for more than 6 months → Chronic hepatitis B infection.

hepatitis-b-c-d-chronic.stem: What best explains the finding: “Anti-HBs positive but anti-HBc negative”?
hepatitis-b-c-d-chronic.explanation: Anti-HBs positive but anti-HBc negative → Vaccine-induced immunity (no core exposure).

hepatitis-b-c-d-chronic.stem: Which should you review before “Hepatitis B, C & D (Blood-Borne, Chronic)”?

options.text: DNA Viruses II: Hepatitis B, HPV, Pox & Others

hepatitis-b-c-d-chronic.explanation: Hepatitis B is a DNA virus, linking to broader viral pathology.

viral-hepatitis-prevention-immunization.stem: Vaccination against hepatitis B also prevents hepatitis D infection because:

options.text: The vaccine contains hepatitis D antigen
Hepatitis D requires HBsAg (hepatitis B) to replicate

viral-hepatitis-prevention-immunization.explanation: Hepatitis D is a defective virus that can only replicate using hepatitis B surface antigen; preventing HBV infection with the hepatitis B vaccine therefore also prevents hepatitis D.

viral-hepatitis-prevention-immunization.stem: Which statement about hepatitis prevention is correct?

options.text: There is an effective hepatitis C vaccine
Hepatitis B is vaccine-preventable, and infants of HBsAg-positive mothers receive HBIG plus vaccine at birth
Hepatitis A is prevented only by blood precautions
Vaccination has no role in preventing liver cancer

viral-hepatitis-prevention-immunization.explanation: Hepatitis B is vaccine-preventable; perinatal transmission (high chronicity) is prevented by a birth-dose vaccine plus hepatitis B immunoglobulin for infants of HBsAg-positive mothers. There is no hepatitis C vaccine, and preventing HBV reduces hepatocellular carcinoma.

viral-hepatitis-prevention-immunization.stem: Regarding preventing hepatitis d — which is correct?

options.text: A separate vaccine is needed to prevent hepatitis D
There is NO separate hepatitis D vaccine — because HDV can only replicate in the presence of HBsAg, the HEPATITIS B vaccine also prevents hepatitis D by preventing HBV infection

viral-hepatitis-prevention-immunization.explanation: HDV's dependence on HBV means blocking HBV blocks HDV; looking for a dedicated HDV vaccine misunderstands its defective, HBV-dependent biology.

viral-hepatitis-prevention-immunization.stem: What best explains the finding: “Anti-HBs positive with anti-HBc negative”?
viral-hepatitis-prevention-immunization.explanation: Anti-HBs positive with anti-HBc negative → Successful hepatitis B vaccination.

viral-hepatitis-prevention-immunization.stem: What best explains the finding: “HBIG + hepatitis B vaccine given to a newborn of an HBsAg+ mother”?
viral-hepatitis-prevention-immunization.explanation: HBIG + hepatitis B vaccine given to a newborn of an HBsAg+ mother → Perinatal HBV post-exposure prophylaxis.

viral-hepatitis-prevention-immunization.stem: Which should you review before “Viral Hepatitis: Prevention & Immunisation”?
viral-hepatitis-prevention-immunization.explanation: Understanding vaccines is crucial for hepatitis B prevention.

viral-gastroenteritis.stem: The leading cause of severe, dehydrating gastroenteritis in infants and young children, now preventable by a live oral vaccine, is:
viral-gastroenteritis.explanation: Rotavirus is the leading cause of severe dehydrating diarrhoea in infants; its NSP4 acts as a viral enterotoxin, and a live oral vaccine has substantially reduced childhood diarrhoeal deaths.

options.text: Bloody, mucoid diarrhoea with fever and faecal leukocytes
Watery, non-inflammatory diarrhoea with vomiting and risk of dehydration

viral-gastroenteritis.explanation: Viruses damage small-bowel villous enterocytes, producing watery, non-inflammatory diarrhoea (no blood or faecal leukocytes) with vomiting; the main hazard is dehydration, treated with rehydration.

viral-gastroenteritis.stem: Regarding treating viral gastroenteritis — which is correct?

options.text: Acute watery diarrhoea should be treated with antibiotics to be safe

Viral gastroenteritis (watery, non-inflammatory diarrhoea) is treated with REHYDRATION, not antibiotics — antibiotics are ineffective against viruses and unnecessary; the priority is preventing dehydration

viral-gastroenteritis.explanation: Reaching for antibiotics in viral diarrhoea offers no benefit and promotes resistance/adverse effects; recognising the non-inflammatory watery pattern directs you to rehydration instead.

viral-gastroenteritis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Severe watery diarrhoea + dehydration in an infant”?
viral-gastroenteritis.explanation: Severe watery diarrhoea + dehydration in an infant → Rotavirus gastroenteritis.

viral-gastroenteritis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Outbreak of acute vomiting/diarrhoea on a cruise ship”?
viral-gastroenteritis.explanation: Outbreak of acute vomiting/diarrhoea on a cruise ship → Norovirus (highly contagious, low dose).

viral-gastroenteritis.stem: Which should you review before “Viral Gastroenteritis”?
viral-gastroenteritis.explanation: Understanding rehydration management is crucial for viral gastroenteritis.

secretory-toxigenic-enteritis.stem: Cholera toxin produces profuse watery ("rice-water") diarrhoea by:

options.text: ADP-ribosylating Gs to persistently activate adenylate cyclase, raising cAMP and driving chloride/water secretion

secretory-toxigenic-enteritis.explanation: The cholera AB5 toxin binds GM1 ganglioside and ADP-ribosylates Gs, locking adenylate cyclase on; the resulting rise in cAMP drives massive chloride and water secretion — a non-invasive, secretory mechanism treated with rehydration.

secretory-toxigenic-enteritis.stem: Rapid-onset vomiting (1–6 hours) after eating reheated fried rice is most characteristic of:
secretory-toxigenic-enteritis.explanation: Bacillus cereus produces a heat-stable preformed emetic toxin classically associated with reheated fried rice, causing vomiting within a few hours; the short incubation reflects toxin already present in the food.

secretory-toxigenic-enteritis.stem: Regarding treating cholera — which is correct?

options.text: Massive cholera fluid loss means the gut can no longer absorb, so only IV fluids will work

Even in profuse cholera, the intestinal Na⁺–GLUCOSE cotransporter keeps working, so ORAL REHYDRATION SOLUTION (glucose + salt) effectively replaces losses — it is the mainstay and is life-saving (IV is reserved for severe shock/inability to drink)

secretory-toxigenic-enteritis.explanation: Cholera toxin drives secretion but does not disable glucose-coupled sodium absorption; understanding this is why cheap oral ORS, not just IV fluids, has saved millions of lives.

secretory-toxigenic-enteritis.stem: What best explains the finding: “"Rice-water" stool with profound dehydration”?
secretory-toxigenic-enteritis.explanation: "Rice-water" stool with profound dehydration → Cholera toxin (↑cAMP secretory diarrhoea).

secretory-toxigenic-enteritis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Watery diarrhoea in a traveller”?
secretory-toxigenic-enteritis.explanation: Watery diarrhoea in a traveller → Enterotoxigenic E. coli (LT/ST toxins).

secretory-toxigenic-enteritis.stem: Which should you review before “Secretory (Toxigenic) Bacterial Diarrhoea”?
secretory-toxigenic-enteritis.explanation: Understanding ORS is crucial for managing secretory diarrhoea.

inflammatory-invasive-enteritis.stem: A child develops bloody diarrhoea after eating undercooked beef, then microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury. The organism and the key management point are:

options.text: EHEC O157:H7 — avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents

inflammatory-invasive-enteritis.explanation: This is haemolytic-uraemic syndrome from enterohaemorrhagic E. coli O157:H7 (Shiga-like toxin). Antibiotics and antimotility agents increase toxin release and HUS risk, so management is supportive.

inflammatory-invasive-enteritis.stem: Which feature indicates an invasive (inflammatory) rather than a secretory bacterial diarrhoea?

options.text: Large-volume watery stool with no blood or fever
Bloody, mucoid stool with fever and faecal leukocytes

inflammatory-invasive-enteritis.explanation: Invasive organisms damage the colonic mucosa, producing bloody/mucoid diarrhoea with fever and faecal leukocytes (dysentery). Watery, non-bloody, afebrile diarrhoea indicates a secretory/toxigenic mechanism.

inflammatory-invasive-enteritis.stem: Regarding antibiotics in ehec (o157:h7) infection — which is correct?

options.text: Bloody diarrhoea from E. coli should be treated promptly with antibiotics

In enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (O157:H7), antibiotics and antimotility agents are CONTRAINDICATED — they increase Shiga-like toxin release and the risk of haemolytic-uraemic syndrome; management is supportive

inflammatory-invasive-enteritis.explanation: Killing EHEC or slowing transit raises toxin exposure, precipitating HUS (haemolysis, thrombocytopenia, kidney failure); the reflex to "treat bloody diarrhoea with antibiotics" is exactly wrong here.

inflammatory-invasive-enteritis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bloody, mucoid diarrhoea with fever and faecal leukocytes”?
inflammatory-invasive-enteritis.explanation: Bloody, mucoid diarrhoea with fever and faecal leukocytes → Invasive bacterial dysentery.

inflammatory-invasive-enteritis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bloody diarrhoea + HUS after undercooked beef”?
inflammatory-invasive-enteritis.explanation: Bloody diarrhoea + HUS after undercooked beef → EHEC O157:H7 (Shiga-like toxin) — avoid antibiotics.

inflammatory-invasive-enteritis.stem: Which should you review before “Inflammatory (Invasive) Bacterial Diarrhoea”?
inflammatory-invasive-enteritis.explanation: E. coli is a key organism in bacterial diarrhoea.

food-poisoning-post-infectious.stem: Several people vomit within 3 hours of eating a cream-filled pastry left unrefrigerated. The most likely cause is:
food-poisoning-post-infectious.explanation: Rapid-onset vomiting (1–6 h) after dairy/cream foods indicates a preformed Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin; the very short incubation reflects toxin already present in the food, and the illness is self-limited.

food-poisoning-post-infectious.stem: Guillain–Barré syndrome occurring a couple of weeks after a diarrhoeal illness is most classically a sequela of infection with:
food-poisoning-post-infectious.explanation: Campylobacter jejuni is the classic antecedent infection for Guillain–Barré syndrome (an immune-mediated ascending demyelinating polyneuropathy), and it is also linked to reactive arthritis and post-infectious IBS.

food-poisoning-post-infectious.stem: Regarding using incubation time to identify food poisoning — which is correct?

options.text: The specific food eaten is the best clue to the cause of food poisoning

The INCUBATION PERIOD (and whether vomiting or diarrhoea predominates) is the most useful discriminator: very short (1–6 h) vomiting = preformed toxin (S. aureus/B. cereus), ~8–16 h diarrhoea = in-vivo toxin (C. perfringens), longer/bloody = invasive organisms
Preformed toxin (S. aureus or B. cereus emetic)

food-poisoning-post-infectious.explanation: Foods overlap between organisms, but the timeline reliably separates preformed-toxin (rapid) from in-vivo-toxin and invasive (slower) causes — the framework that guides diagnosis and reassures that most are self-limited.

food-poisoning-post-infectious.stem: What best explains the finding: “Vomiting within 1–6 h of a meal”?

options.text: Preformed toxin (S. aureus or B. cereus emetic)

food-poisoning-post-infectious.explanation: Vomiting within 1–6 h of a meal → Preformed toxin (S. aureus or B. cereus emetic).

food-poisoning-post-infectious.stem: What best explains the finding: “Watery diarrhoea ~8–16 h after reheated meat”?

options.text: Preformed toxin (S. aureus or B. cereus emetic)

food-poisoning-post-infectious.explanation: Watery diarrhoea ~8–16 h after reheated meat → Clostridium perfringens (in-vivo toxin).

food-poisoning-post-infectious.stem: Which should you review before “Food Poisoning & Post-Infectious Sequelae”?
food-poisoning-post-infectious.explanation: Understanding invasive bacterial diarrhoea is crucial for differentiating from food poisoning.

intestinal-roundworms-phasmid.stem: Chronic iron-deficiency anaemia in a barefoot agricultural worker from an endemic region is most likely caused by which intestinal nematode?
intestinal-roundworms-phasmid.explanation: Hookworm larvae penetrate the skin (bare feet), migrate through the lungs and attach to the small-bowel mucosa where they suck blood, causing chronic iron-deficiency anaemia and hypoproteinaemia.

intestinal-roundworms-phasmid.stem: Which nematode can autoinfect the host and cause a disseminated hyperinfection syndrome in immunosuppressed patients?
intestinal-roundworms-phasmid.explanation: Strongyloides stercoralis can complete its life cycle within the host (autoinfection), persisting for years; immunosuppression (e.g. steroids) allows massive dissemination — hyperinfection — so it should be screened for and treated (ivermectin) beforehand.

intestinal-roundworms-phasmid.stem: Regarding diagnosing pinworm (enterobius) — which is correct?

options.text: Pinworm infection is diagnosed by finding eggs on routine stool microscopy
Enterobius (pinworm) is diagnosed by the adhesive "Scotch-tape" test applied to the PERIANAL skin in the morning — the female lays eggs there at night, so they are usually absent from the stool

intestinal-roundworms-phasmid.explanation: Because the worm deposits eggs on perianal skin rather than in the faeces, stool exams miss it; the tape test targets the correct site, and treating the whole household prevents reinfection.

intestinal-roundworms-phasmid.stem: What best explains the finding: “Intestinal or biliary obstruction by a bolus of worms”?
intestinal-roundworms-phasmid.explanation: Intestinal or biliary obstruction by a bolus of worms → Heavy Ascaris lumbricoides infection.

intestinal-roundworms-phasmid.stem: What best explains the finding: “Chronic iron-deficiency anaemia in an endemic area”?
intestinal-roundworms-phasmid.explanation: Chronic iron-deficiency anaemia in an endemic area → Hookworm intestinal blood loss.

intestinal-roundworms-phasmid.stem: Which should you review before “Intestinal Roundworms (Soil-Transmitted Nematodes)”?
intestinal-roundworms-phasmid.explanation: Understanding helminth classification is essential for grasping intestinal roundworm characteristics.

aphasmid-nematodes.stem: A patient develops fever, periorbital oedema, severe muscle pain and marked eosinophilia a week after eating undercooked pork. The likely organism is:
aphasmid-nematodes.explanation: Trichinellosis follows ingestion of undercooked pork with encysted larvae; the larvae migrate to striated muscle, producing the classic tetrad of fever, periorbital oedema, myalgia and eosinophilia.

aphasmid-nematodes.stem: Heavy infection with which nematode classically causes rectal prolapse in children?
aphasmid-nematodes.explanation: The whipworm Trichuris trichiura threads its thin anterior end into the colonic mucosa; heavy infection in children causes chronic diarrhoea and rectal prolapse, sometimes with worms visible on the prolapsed mucosa.

aphasmid-nematodes.stem: Regarding source of trichinella infection — which is correct?

options.text: Trichinellosis is acquired from contaminated soil like most intestinal worms

Trichinella spiralis is acquired by eating UNDERCOOKED PORK (or game) containing encysted larvae — not from soil; the larvae then migrate to and encyst in striated muscle, causing myalgia, periorbital oedema and eosinophilia

aphasmid-nematodes.explanation: Its meat-borne route (and muscle-encysting biology) is what makes cooking pork the key prevention; treating it like a soil-transmitted helminth misses both the source and the characteristic muscle disease.

aphasmid-nematodes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rectal prolapse in a child with chronic diarrhoea”?
aphasmid-nematodes.explanation: Rectal prolapse in a child with chronic diarrhoea → Heavy Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) infection.

aphasmid-nematodes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fever, periorbital oedema, myalgia and eosinophilia after undercooked pork”?
aphasmid-nematodes.explanation: Fever, periorbital oedema, myalgia and eosinophilia after undercooked pork → Trichinellosis (Trichinella spiralis).

aphasmid-nematodes.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Aphasmid Nematodes (Trichuris, Trichinella, Capillaria)”?
aphasmid-nematodes.explanation: Infections like Trichuris and Capillaria can lead to malnutrition.

aphasmid-nematodes.stem: Which should you review before “Aphasmid Nematodes (Trichuris, Trichinella, Capillaria)”?
aphasmid-nematodes.explanation: Understanding phasmid nematodes is essential for grasping the differences with aphasmids.

liver-flukes-cholangiocarcinoma.stem: In Northeast Thailand, chronic infection with which parasite is a leading, preventable cause of cholangiocarcinoma?
liver-flukes-cholangiocarcinoma.explanation: Opisthorchis viverrini, acquired by eating raw freshwater fish, lives in the bile ducts; chronic infection causes periductal inflammation and fibrosis that predispose to cholangiocarcinoma — a WHO group 1 carcinogen and a major regional problem.

liver-flukes-cholangiocarcinoma.stem: The definitive way to prevent Opisthorchis (and Clonorchis) liver-fluke infection is to:

options.text: Wear shoes to avoid skin penetration
Thoroughly cook freshwater fish before eating

liver-flukes-cholangiocarcinoma.explanation: Humans acquire these liver flukes by eating raw or undercooked freshwater fish containing metacercariae; thorough cooking of the fish interrupts transmission and prevents both the infection and its cancer risk.

liver-flukes-cholangiocarcinoma.stem: Regarding cause of cholangiocarcinoma in endemic areas — which is correct?

options.text: Cholangiocarcinoma is essentially always sporadic with no identifiable cause

In endemic regions (e.g. Northeast Thailand), chronic Opisthorchis viverrini liver-fluke infection from eating raw freshwater fish is a MAJOR, PREVENTABLE cause of cholangiocarcinoma (a WHO group 1 carcinogen)

liver-flukes-cholangiocarcinoma.explanation: Missing the fluke link overlooks both a diagnostic clue (dietary/egg findings) and a powerful prevention message (cooking fish, deworming) that can reduce a regionally devastating cancer.

liver-flukes-cholangiocarcinoma.stem: What best explains the finding: “RUQ discomfort + hepatomegaly with a raw-freshwater-fish diet”?
liver-flukes-cholangiocarcinoma.explanation: RUQ discomfort + hepatomegaly with a raw-freshwater-fish diet → Opisthorchis viverrini liver-fluke infection.

liver-flukes-cholangiocarcinoma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cholangiocarcinoma in an endemic (NE Thailand) patient”?
liver-flukes-cholangiocarcinoma.explanation: Cholangiocarcinoma in an endemic (NE Thailand) patient → Chronic Opisthorchis infection (group 1 carcinogen).

liver-flukes-cholangiocarcinoma.stem: Which should you review before “Liver Flukes & Cholangiocarcinoma”?
liver-flukes-cholangiocarcinoma.explanation: Understanding tapeworms provides context for fluke-related diseases.

intestinal-flukes-tapeworms.stem: Infection with which tapeworm classically causes vitamin B12 deficiency and megaloblastic anaemia?
intestinal-flukes-tapeworms.explanation: Diphyllobothrium latum, acquired from raw freshwater fish, competes with the host for vitamin B12, and heavy infection can cause megaloblastic (B12-deficiency) anaemia — the classic tapeworm-B12 association.

intestinal-flukes-tapeworms.stem: Neurocysticercosis (a leading cause of adult-onset seizures in endemic areas) results from:

options.text: Ingesting Taenia solium eggs (faecal–oral), making humans the intermediate host

intestinal-flukes-tapeworms.explanation: Ingesting Taenia solium eggs (faecal–oral) leads to larval cysts in tissues (cysticercosis); CNS involvement (neurocysticercosis) is a major cause of seizures. Eating larvae in pork instead produces an intestinal adult tapeworm.

intestinal-flukes-tapeworms.stem: Regarding how taenia solium causes neurocysticercosis — which is correct?

options.text: Eating undercooked pork with Taenia solium directly causes brain cysts (neurocysticercosis)

Eating undercooked pork with larvae gives an intestinal ADULT tapeworm; NEUROCYSTICERCOSIS arises when humans ingest the EGGS (faecal–oral) and become the intermediate host, so larval cysts form in tissues including the brain

intestinal-flukes-tapeworms.explanation: The route determines the disease: meat with larvae → gut tapeworm, but faecal–oral eggs → tissue cysticercosis; conflating them misses that hygiene/faecal–oral spread (not just cooking meat) drives the dangerous CNS disease.

intestinal-flukes-tapeworms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Adult-onset seizures with brain cysts in an endemic patient”?
intestinal-flukes-tapeworms.explanation: Adult-onset seizures with brain cysts in an endemic patient → Neurocysticercosis (Taenia solium eggs).

intestinal-flukes-tapeworms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Megaloblastic (B12-deficiency) anaemia + raw freshwater fish”?
intestinal-flukes-tapeworms.explanation: Megaloblastic (B12-deficiency) anaemia + raw freshwater fish → Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm).

intestinal-flukes-tapeworms.stem: Which should you review before “Intestinal Flukes & Tapeworms”?

fat-soluble-vitamins.stem: A patient with chronic cholestasis develops easy bruising and a prolonged prothrombin time that corrects with vitamin supplementation. The deficient vitamin is:
fat-soluble-vitamins.explanation: Vitamin K is required for γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X; fat malabsorption from cholestasis reduces its absorption, causing bleeding and a prolonged prothrombin time that responds to vitamin K.

fat-soluble-vitamins.stem: Why does fat malabsorption tend to cause deficiency of vitamins A, D, E and K together?

options.text: They share the same transport protein in blood
They are all absorbed together with dietary fat
They are all synthesised in the colon

fat-soluble-vitamins.explanation: A, D, E and K are fat-soluble and absorbed with dietary lipids; conditions that impair fat absorption (cholestasis, pancreatic insufficiency, coeliac disease, orlistat) therefore reduce absorption of all four simultaneously.

fat-soluble-vitamins.stem: Regarding toxicity potential of vitamins — which is correct?

options.text: Taking large doses of any vitamin is harmless because excess is simply excreted

FAT-SOLUBLE vitamins (A, D, E, K) are STORED, so excess — especially vitamin A (teratogenic, raised ICP, hepatotoxic) and vitamin D (hypercalcaemia) — can cause TOXICITY, unlike most water-soluble vitamins that are excreted

fat-soluble-vitamins.explanation: The storage that protects against short-term deficiency also allows accumulation to toxic levels; assuming all vitamins are harmless in excess ignores the real risks of hypervitaminosis A and D.

fat-soluble-vitamins.stem: What best explains the finding: “Night blindness progressing to xerophthalmia”?

options.text: Vitamin K deficiency (factors II, VII, IX, X)

fat-soluble-vitamins.explanation: Night blindness progressing to xerophthalmia → Vitamin A deficiency.

fat-soluble-vitamins.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rickets (children) / osteomalacia (adults)”?

options.text: Vitamin K deficiency (factors II, VII, IX, X)

fat-soluble-vitamins.explanation: Rickets (children) / osteomalacia (adults) → Vitamin D deficiency (impaired bone mineralisation).

fat-soluble-vitamins.stem: Which should you review before “Fat-Soluble Vitamins (A, D, E, K)”?

options.text: Ascending Cholangitis, Bile Flow & Fat-Soluble Vitamins

fat-soluble-vitamins.explanation: Understanding bile flow is crucial for fat-soluble vitamin absorption.

water-soluble-vitamins-trace-elements.stem: A patient has megaloblastic anaemia together with impaired proprioception and a spastic gait (subacute combined degeneration). The deficiency is:
water-soluble-vitamins-trace-elements.explanation: Both folate and B12 deficiency cause megaloblastic anaemia, but only vitamin B12 deficiency produces neurological disease (subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts). Folate alone would not explain the neurology and could mask it.

water-soluble-vitamins-trace-elements.stem: Deficiency of niacin (vitamin B3) classically produces the triad of:

options.text: Bowing of the legs and bone pain

water-soluble-vitamins-trace-elements.explanation: Niacin deficiency causes pellagra, remembered as the three D's — dermatitis (photosensitive), diarrhoea and dementia. Ophthalmoplegia/ataxia/confusion is thiamine-deficiency Wernicke encephalopathy.

water-soluble-vitamins-trace-elements.stem: Regarding treating megaloblastic anaemia — which is correct?

options.text: Any megaloblastic anaemia can safely be treated with folate
Giving FOLATE alone to a B12-deficient patient corrects the anaemia but allows the NEUROLOGICAL damage (subacute combined degeneration) to progress unchecked — you must confirm/replace B12 too

water-soluble-vitamins-trace-elements.explanation: Both folate and B12 deficiency cause megaloblastic anaemia, but only B12 deficiency damages the cord; masking the anaemia with folate removes the warning sign while the neuropathy worsens irreversibly.
