water-soluble-vitamins-trace-elements.stem: What best explains the finding: “Megaloblastic anaemia with neurological signs (SCD)”?
water-soluble-vitamins-trace-elements.explanation: Megaloblastic anaemia with neurological signs (SCD) → Vitamin B12 deficiency.

water-soluble-vitamins-trace-elements.stem: What best explains the finding: “Confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia in an alcoholic”?
water-soluble-vitamins-trace-elements.explanation: Confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia in an alcoholic → Thiamine (B1) deficiency — Wernicke encephalopathy.

water-soluble-vitamins-trace-elements.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Water-Soluble Vitamins & Trace Elements”?
water-soluble-vitamins-trace-elements.explanation: Folate is crucial in neural tube development.

water-soluble-vitamins-trace-elements.stem: Which should you review before “Water-Soluble Vitamins & Trace Elements”?

options.text: Ascending Cholangitis, Bile Flow & Fat-Soluble Vitamins

water-soluble-vitamins-trace-elements.explanation: Bile flow issues can impact fat-soluble vitamin absorption.

eating-disorders.stem: A normal-weight young woman has dental enamel erosion, parotid swelling, calluses on the knuckles (Russell sign) and hypokalaemia. The most likely diagnosis is:
eating-disorders.explanation: Recurrent self-induced vomiting at a normal body weight, with dental erosion, parotid enlargement, Russell sign and hypokalaemia, is characteristic of bulimia nervosa. Anorexia nervosa instead features markedly low body weight.

eating-disorders.stem: Which is the most immediately life-threatening medical concern in a purging eating disorder?
eating-disorders.explanation: Repeated vomiting/laxative use causes potassium loss; hypokalaemia (with metabolic alkalosis) can precipitate fatal cardiac arrhythmias — the most urgent danger. Refeeding must also be cautious to avoid refeeding syndrome.

eating-disorders.stem: Regarding recognising bulimia at a normal weight — which is correct?

options.text: A patient with a normal body weight cannot have a serious eating disorder

BULIMIA nervosa typically occurs at a NORMAL or near-normal body weight, yet carries serious risks (hypokalaemia and arrhythmia from purging); normal weight does NOT exclude a dangerous eating disorder

eating-disorders.explanation: Because bulimic patients often look well and maintain normal weight, the diagnosis is missed if you rely on low weight alone — the purging complications (electrolytes, dental erosion, Russell sign) are the clues.

eating-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Very low body weight + amenorrhoea + bradycardia + lanugo”?
eating-disorders.explanation: Very low body weight + amenorrhoea + bradycardia + lanugo → Anorexia nervosa (starvation).

eating-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Normal weight + dental erosion + parotid swelling + knuckle calluses”?
eating-disorders.explanation: Normal weight + dental erosion + parotid swelling + knuckle calluses → Bulimia nervosa (self-induced vomiting; Russell sign).

eating-disorders.stem: Which should you review before “Eating Disorders”?
eating-disorders.explanation: Understanding malnutrition is crucial for managing eating disorders.

parasitology-host-relationships.stem: The definitive host of a parasite is the host that harbours the:
parasitology-host-relationships.explanation: By definition the definitive host harbours the adult or sexually reproducing stage of the parasite; the intermediate host harbours larval or asexual stages. For malaria the mosquito is the definitive host.

parasitology-host-relationships.stem: In the malaria life cycle, the human is best described as the:
parasitology-host-relationships.explanation: The sexual cycle of Plasmodium occurs in the Anopheles mosquito, making it the definitive host (and vector); the asexual cycle occurs in humans, so the human is the intermediate host.

parasitology-host-relationships.stem: Regarding which host is definitive in malaria — which is correct?

options.text: Humans are always the definitive host of a parasite
The definitive host is defined by the SEXUAL/ADULT stage, not by being human — in malaria the MOSQUITO is the definitive host (the sexual cycle occurs in it) and the human is the intermediate host

parasitology-host-relationships.explanation: Assuming humans are always the definitive host misclassifies several important parasites (malaria, echinococcosis); the stage of the parasite present, not the species of host, determines the label.

parasitology-host-relationships.stem: What best explains the finding: “The host harbouring the adult/sexual stage”?

options.text: Sexual cycle occurs in the mosquito (human = intermediate)

parasitology-host-relationships.explanation: The host harbouring the adult/sexual stage → Definitive host.

parasitology-host-relationships.stem: What best explains the finding: “The host harbouring larval/asexual stages”?

options.text: Sexual cycle occurs in the mosquito (human = intermediate)

parasitology-host-relationships.explanation: The host harbouring larval/asexual stages → Intermediate host.

parasitology-host-relationships.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Host Types & Parasite Relationships”?

options.text: Host Defenses of the Urinary Tract

parasitology-host-relationships.explanation: Understanding host defenses can relate to parasitic infections.

parasite-transmission-diagnosis.stem: The Anopheles mosquito transmitting malaria is an example of a:

options.text: Biological vector (the parasite develops within it)

parasite-transmission-diagnosis.explanation: Plasmodium completes part of its life cycle (the sexual cycle) within the Anopheles mosquito, making it a biological vector. A mechanical vector, like a housefly, merely carries organisms on its body without any parasite development.

parasite-transmission-diagnosis.stem: The first-line laboratory investigation for a suspected intestinal parasitic infection is:

options.text: Stool examination for ova and parasites (O&P)

parasite-transmission-diagnosis.explanation: Stool O&P microscopy (often with concentration techniques) is the workhorse for detecting intestinal protozoan cysts/trophozoites and helminth eggs; blood films are for malaria and microfilariae.

parasite-transmission-diagnosis.stem: Regarding biological vs mechanical vector — which is correct?

options.text: Any arthropod that transmits a parasite is a biological vector

A BIOLOGICAL vector is one in which the parasite DEVELOPS or multiplies (a required part of the life cycle, e.g. Anopheles for malaria); a MECHANICAL vector merely carries the organism externally (e.g. a housefly) without any development

parasite-transmission-diagnosis.explanation: The distinction matters for control and specificity: biological vectors are essential, specific hosts (targeting them interrupts the cycle), whereas mechanical transmission is incidental and non-specific.

parasite-transmission-diagnosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “A parasite that multiplies within its arthropod host”?
parasite-transmission-diagnosis.explanation: A parasite that multiplies within its arthropod host → Biological vector (e.g. Anopheles/malaria).

parasite-transmission-diagnosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “A housefly carrying enteric pathogens on its body”?
parasite-transmission-diagnosis.explanation: A housefly carrying enteric pathogens on its body → Mechanical vector.

protozoa-classification-biology.stem: The four groups of medically important protozoa are classified primarily by their:

options.text: Means of locomotion (pseudopods, flagella, cilia, or apical complex)

protozoa-classification-biology.explanation: Medical protozoa are grouped by their locomotory apparatus: amoebae (pseudopods), flagellates (flagella), ciliates (cilia) and apicomplexa (no locomotory organelle, with an apical complex for cell invasion).

protozoa-classification-biology.stem: The resistant, environmentally stable stage responsible for transmitting many intestinal protozoa is the:
protozoa-classification-biology.explanation: The cyst (or oocyst in apicomplexa) is the resistant, infective transmission stage that survives outside the host; the trophozoite is the active, feeding stage that causes disease but does not survive well in the environment.

protozoa-classification-biology.stem: Regarding trophozoite vs cyst — which is correct?

options.text: The trophozoite is the stage that spreads the infection between people

The CYST (or oocyst) is the resistant, environmentally stable INFECTIVE/transmission stage that spreads infection; the TROPHOZOITE is the active, fragile, feeding stage that causes disease but is destroyed outside the host

protozoa-classification-biology.explanation: Reversing these misreads both transmission (cysts in contaminated food/water) and diagnosis (which stage to look for in which specimen), and explains why trophozoites are seen in fresh dysenteric stool but cysts in formed stool.

protozoa-classification-biology.stem: What best explains the finding: “A protozoan moving by pseudopods”?
protozoa-classification-biology.explanation: A protozoan moving by pseudopods → Amoeba (Sarcodina).

protozoa-classification-biology.stem: What best explains the finding: “The active, feeding, motile disease-causing stage”?
protozoa-classification-biology.explanation: The active, feeding, motile disease-causing stage → Trophozoite.

protozoa-classification-biology.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Protozoa: Classification & Biology”?
protozoa-classification-biology.explanation: Clinical implications of protozoan infections may relate to pulmonary complications.

protozoa-classification-biology.stem: Which should you review before “Protozoa: Classification & Biology”?
protozoa-classification-biology.explanation: Understanding transmission and diagnosis is essential for protozoan classification.

entamoeba-histolytica-amoebiasis.stem: A traveller returns with several weeks of right upper quadrant pain and fever; imaging shows a right-lobe liver abscess with "anchovy-paste" contents and serology is positive. The organism is:
entamoeba-histolytica-amoebiasis.explanation: Amoebic liver abscess from Entamoeba histolytica classically affects the right lobe with "anchovy-paste" material and is diagnosed serologically; trophozoites reach the liver via the portal vein. Treatment is metronidazole plus a luminal agent.

entamoeba-histolytica-amoebiasis.stem: Which microscopic finding indicates invasive Entamoeba histolytica rather than the non-pathogenic E. dispar?

options.text: Trophozoites containing ingested red blood cells

entamoeba-histolytica-amoebiasis.explanation: Erythrophagocytosis — trophozoites with ingested red blood cells — is a marker of invasive E. histolytica; the two species are otherwise morphologically identical and are distinguished by antigen detection or PCR.

entamoeba-histolytica-amoebiasis.stem: Regarding completing treatment of amoebiasis — which is correct?

options.text: Metronidazole alone fully cures intestinal amoebiasis

Metronidazole treats the INVASIVE (tissue) trophozoites but does not reliably clear intraluminal CYSTS — a LUMINAL agent (paromomycin/diloxanide) must be added to eradicate cysts and prevent relapse and ongoing transmission

entamoeba-histolytica-amoebiasis.explanation: Cysts in the gut lumen survive tissue amoebicides; failing to add a luminal agent leaves the patient a cyst-passer who can relapse and infect others.

entamoeba-histolytica-amoebiasis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bloody, mucoid diarrhoea (dysentery) with flask-shaped ulcers”?
entamoeba-histolytica-amoebiasis.explanation: Bloody, mucoid diarrhoea (dysentery) with flask-shaped ulcers → Invasive intestinal amoebiasis.

entamoeba-histolytica-amoebiasis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Trophozoites containing ingested red blood cells”?
entamoeba-histolytica-amoebiasis.explanation: Trophozoites containing ingested red blood cells → Invasive E. histolytica (erythrophagocytosis).

entamoeba-histolytica-amoebiasis.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Entamoeba histolytica & Amoebiasis”?
entamoeba-histolytica-amoebiasis.explanation: Amoebiasis can present similarly to other invasive enteric infections.

entamoeba-histolytica-amoebiasis.stem: Which should you review before “Entamoeba histolytica & Amoebiasis”?
entamoeba-histolytica-amoebiasis.explanation: Understanding protozoa classification is essential for identifying E. histolytica.

free-living-nonpathogenic-amoebae.stem: A previously healthy teenager develops fulminant, rapidly fatal meningoencephalitis days after swimming in a warm freshwater lake. The most likely organism is:
free-living-nonpathogenic-amoebae.explanation: Naegleria fowleri, the "brain-eating amoeba", lives in warm fresh water and enters via the nose, travelling through the cribriform plate to cause acute, almost uniformly fatal primary amoebic meningoencephalitis in otherwise healthy people.

free-living-nonpathogenic-amoebae.stem: Acanthamoeba is an important cause of keratitis particularly in:
free-living-nonpathogenic-amoebae.explanation: Acanthamoeba keratitis is classically associated with contact-lens wear (poor hygiene or exposure to water); Acanthamoeba and Balamuthia also cause chronic granulomatous amoebic encephalitis in the immunocompromised.

free-living-nonpathogenic-amoebae.stem: Regarding distinguishing the free-living amoebic cns diseases — which is correct?

options.text: All free-living amoebae cause the same rapidly fatal brain infection in healthy people

They differ: NAEGLERIA causes ACUTE PAM in HEALTHY freshwater swimmers (via the nose), whereas ACANTHAMOEBA/Balamuthia cause CHRONIC granulomatous encephalitis (GAE) in the IMMUNOCOMPROMISED (and Acanthamoeba also causes contact-lens keratitis)

free-living-nonpathogenic-amoebae.explanation: The host (healthy vs immunocompromised), tempo (acute vs chronic) and route (nasal vs haematogenous) differ, so lumping them together loses the exposure clues that lead to the right diagnosis.

free-living-nonpathogenic-amoebae.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fatal acute meningoencephalitis in a healthy freshwater swimmer”?
free-living-nonpathogenic-amoebae.explanation: Fatal acute meningoencephalitis in a healthy freshwater swimmer → Naegleria fowleri (PAM, nasal route).

free-living-nonpathogenic-amoebae.stem: What best explains the finding: “Painful, sight-threatening keratitis in a contact-lens wearer”?
free-living-nonpathogenic-amoebae.explanation: Painful, sight-threatening keratitis in a contact-lens wearer → Acanthamoeba keratitis.

free-living-nonpathogenic-amoebae.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Free-Living & Non-Pathogenic Amoebae”?
free-living-nonpathogenic-amoebae.explanation: Both modules involve infectious agents but are not directly related in pathology.

free-living-nonpathogenic-amoebae.stem: Which should you review before “Free-Living & Non-Pathogenic Amoebae”?
free-living-nonpathogenic-amoebae.explanation: Understanding protozoa classification is essential for grasping amoebae characteristics.

giardia-intestinal-flagellates.stem: A hiker develops greasy, foul-smelling, non-bloody diarrhoea with bloating and weight loss after drinking from a mountain stream. The most likely organism is:
giardia-intestinal-flagellates.explanation: Giardiasis causes malabsorptive, fatty, non-bloody diarrhoea after ingesting cysts from untreated water; the trophozoite attaches to (but does not invade) the duodenal mucosa. Treatment is metronidazole.

giardia-intestinal-flagellates.stem: Giardia lamblia causes malabsorption because the trophozoite:

options.text: Attaches to and coats the duodenal/jejunal absorptive surface without invading

giardia-intestinal-flagellates.explanation: Giardia trophozoites attach via a ventral sucking disc to the small-intestinal mucosa, impairing absorption without tissue invasion — hence a non-bloody, fatty, malabsorptive diarrhoea rather than dysentery.

giardia-intestinal-flagellates.stem: Regarding excluding giardiasis with a single stool test — which is correct?

options.text: A single negative stool ova-and-parasite test rules out giardiasis
Giardia cysts are shed INTERMITTENTLY, so a single negative stool O&P does NOT exclude it — repeat testing or (better) a stool ANTIGEN test/PCR is used when clinical suspicion is high

giardia-intestinal-flagellates.explanation: Intermittent shedding lowers the sensitivity of a single microscopy; relying on one negative result misses cases, whereas antigen/PCR testing is far more sensitive.

giardia-intestinal-flagellates.stem: What best explains the finding: “Greasy, foul, non-bloody diarrhoea + bloating after untreated water”?

options.text: Intermittent cyst shedding — use stool antigen/PCR

giardia-intestinal-flagellates.explanation: Greasy, foul, non-bloody diarrhoea + bloating after untreated water → Giardiasis (malabsorption).

giardia-intestinal-flagellates.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pear-shaped trophozoite with two nuclei ("owl face")”?

options.text: Intermittent cyst shedding — use stool antigen/PCR

giardia-intestinal-flagellates.explanation: Pear-shaped trophozoite with two nuclei ("owl face") → Giardia lamblia.

giardia-intestinal-flagellates.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Giardia & Intestinal Flagellates”?
giardia-intestinal-flagellates.explanation: Understanding transmission and diagnosis is crucial for managing Giardia infections.

giardia-intestinal-flagellates.stem: Which should you review before “Giardia & Intestinal Flagellates”?
giardia-intestinal-flagellates.explanation: Giardia causes malabsorption, linking to clinical patterns of maldigestion.

trichomonas-balantidium.stem: A woman has a frothy, malodorous yellow-green vaginal discharge with a "strawberry cervix" and vaginal pH above 4.5. Motile pear-shaped flagellates are seen on wet mount. The correct management includes:

options.text: Metronidazole for the patient and her sexual partner

trichomonas-balantidium.explanation: This is trichomoniasis, a sexually transmitted flagellate infection with no cyst stage. Treatment is metronidazole (or tinidazole) for the patient and the sexual partner to prevent reinfection.

trichomonas-balantidium.stem: Balantidium coli is notable as the:

options.text: Only pathogenic ciliate and largest human protozoan, acquired from pigs

trichomonas-balantidium.explanation: Balantidium coli is the only pathogenic ciliate and the largest human protozoan; it is acquired faecal–orally, often zoonotically from pigs, and invades the colon to cause a dysentery that can resemble amoebiasis.

trichomonas-balantidium.stem: Regarding how trichomonas is transmitted and treated — which is correct?

options.text: Trichomonas vaginalis is spread faecal–orally by cysts like other intestinal protozoa

Trichomonas vaginalis is a SEXUALLY transmitted flagellate with NO cyst stage — it spreads directly as the trophozoite, so prevention is safe sex (not sanitation) and BOTH partners must be treated to prevent reinfection

trichomonas-balantidium.explanation: Treating it like a faecal–oral cyst-forming protozoan misses that it is an STI: cure requires partner treatment and the absence of a cyst stage means environmental measures are irrelevant.

trichomonas-balantidium.stem: What best explains the finding: “Frothy yellow-green vaginal discharge + strawberry cervix”?
trichomonas-balantidium.explanation: Frothy yellow-green vaginal discharge + strawberry cervix → Trichomonas vaginalis vaginitis.

trichomonas-balantidium.stem: What best explains the finding: “Motile pear-shaped flagellate on a vaginal wet mount”?
trichomonas-balantidium.explanation: Motile pear-shaped flagellate on a vaginal wet mount → Trichomonas trophozoite (no cyst stage).

trichomonas-balantidium.stem: Which should you review before “Trichomonas & Balantidium”?
trichomonas-balantidium.explanation: Classification knowledge is essential for distinguishing between Trichomonas and Balantidium.

helminth-classification-overview.stem: A flat, segmented worm with a scolex (attachment head) and no digestive tract belongs to which helminth group?
helminth-classification-overview.explanation: Cestodes (tapeworms) are flat, segmented worms with a scolex for attachment and no gut, absorbing nutrients through the body wall. Nematodes are round with a gut; trematodes are flat but leaf-shaped and unsegmented.

helminth-classification-overview.stem: Which statement about helminth reproduction is correct?

options.text: Nematodes have separate sexes, and most trematodes are hermaphroditic (except Schistosoma)

helminth-classification-overview.explanation: Nematodes have separate male and female worms; most trematodes are hermaphroditic, with the blood flukes (Schistosoma) being the notable exception with separate sexes.

helminth-classification-overview.stem: Regarding sexes in nematodes vs flukes — which is correct?

options.text: NEMATODES have SEPARATE sexes (male and female worms), and most TREMATODES are HERMAPHRODITE — with the important exception of Schistosoma (the blood flukes), which have separate sexes

helminth-classification-overview.explanation: The reproductive pattern is a defining group feature; assuming all worms are hermaphroditic misclassifies nematodes and forgets the Schistosoma exception among the flukes.

helminth-classification-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Round, unsegmented worm with separate sexes”?
helminth-classification-overview.explanation: Round, unsegmented worm with separate sexes → Nematode (roundworm).

helminth-classification-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Flat, leaf-shaped hermaphroditic worm needing a snail host”?
helminth-classification-overview.explanation: Flat, leaf-shaped hermaphroditic worm needing a snail host → Trematode (fluke).

helminth-classification-overview.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Helminths: Classification Overview”?
helminth-classification-overview.explanation: Focus on intestinal roundworms ties directly to nematodes discussed.

ascariasis-large-roundworm.stem: A child from an area with poor sanitation develops a transient cough with eosinophilia and migratory lung infiltrates, followed weeks later by abdominal symptoms. This pulmonary phase reflects:

options.text: Direct lung infection by adult worms
Larval migration of Ascaris through the lungs (Löffler syndrome)

ascariasis-large-roundworm.explanation: Ascaris larvae migrate from the gut through the bloodstream to the lungs, causing a transient eosinophilic pneumonia (Löffler syndrome) before being coughed up, swallowed and maturing into adults in the small intestine.

ascariasis-large-roundworm.stem: A heavy Ascaris lumbricoides burden in a child most characteristically causes:

options.text: Intestinal (or biliary) obstruction by a mass of worms

ascariasis-large-roundworm.explanation: Because the adult worms are large, a heavy burden can form a bolus that causes intestinal obstruction, or a worm may migrate into the bile duct causing biliary obstruction. Blood-sucking anaemia is hookworm; rectal prolapse is Trichuris; perianal itch is Enterobius.

ascariasis-large-roundworm.stem: Regarding the ascaris life cycle — which is correct?

options.text: Ascaris larvae stay in the gut after the eggs are swallowed

Ascaris larvae undergo a LUNG MIGRATION — they penetrate the gut wall, travel via the blood to the lungs, are coughed up and re-swallowed, and only then mature into adults in the small intestine (causing Löffler syndrome during the lung phase)

ascariasis-large-roundworm.explanation: Missing the transpulmonary migration overlooks why ascariasis can present with a cough/eosinophilia and pulmonary infiltrates before any GI symptoms — a classic exam point shared with hookworm and Strongyloides.

ascariasis-large-roundworm.stem: What best explains the finding: “Transient cough + eosinophilia + migratory lung infiltrates”?
ascariasis-large-roundworm.explanation: Transient cough + eosinophilia + migratory lung infiltrates → Larval lung migration (Löffler syndrome).

ascariasis-large-roundworm.stem: What best explains the finding: “Intestinal obstruction by a bolus of worms in a child”?
ascariasis-large-roundworm.explanation: Intestinal obstruction by a bolus of worms in a child → Heavy Ascaris burden.

ascariasis-large-roundworm.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Ascariasis (Ascaris lumbricoides)”?
ascariasis-large-roundworm.explanation: Löffler syndrome links the pulmonary phase of Ascaris to clinical presentations of lung infections.

ascariasis-large-roundworm.stem: Which should you review before “Ascariasis (Ascaris lumbricoides)”?
ascariasis-large-roundworm.explanation: Basic embryological concepts may provide context for developmental aspects.

toxocariasis-larva-migrans.stem: A young child with a habit of eating soil presents with fever, hepatomegaly, wheeze and marked eosinophilia; stool examination is negative but Toxocara serology is positive. The diagnosis is:
toxocariasis-larva-migrans.explanation: Ingested Toxocara eggs (from pet-faeces-contaminated soil) release larvae that migrate through viscera in this dead-end human host, causing visceral larva migrans — fever, hepatomegaly, wheeze and eosinophilia — diagnosed serologically since no eggs are passed in stool.

toxocariasis-larva-migrans.stem: Ocular larva migrans due to Toxocara is an important differential diagnosis of which paediatric eye condition?
toxocariasis-larva-migrans.explanation: A Toxocara larva in the eye can form a retinal granuloma that mimics retinoblastoma (e.g. presenting with leukocoria or an eye mass) — a critical distinction, as the management is completely different.

toxocariasis-larva-migrans.stem: Regarding diagnosing toxocariasis — which is correct?

options.text: Toxocariasis is diagnosed by finding Toxocara eggs in the stool

In humans, Toxocara larvae are trapped in TISSUE and never mature into egg-laying adults, so there are NO eggs in the stool — diagnosis is SEROLOGICAL (Toxocara ELISA) supported by eosinophilia and the clinical picture

toxocariasis-larva-migrans.explanation: Because humans are a dead-end host, stool microscopy is negative; expecting eggs in stool misses the diagnosis, which relies on serology and recognising the larva-migrans syndrome.

toxocariasis-larva-migrans.stem: What best explains the finding: “Child with pica, hepatomegaly, wheeze and marked eosinophilia”?

options.text: Larvae are in tissue, not the gut (no eggs in stool)

toxocariasis-larva-migrans.explanation: Child with pica, hepatomegaly, wheeze and marked eosinophilia → Visceral larva migrans (Toxocara).

toxocariasis-larva-migrans.stem: What best explains the finding: “Retinal granuloma/leukocoria mimicking retinoblastoma”?

options.text: Larvae are in tissue, not the gut (no eggs in stool)

toxocariasis-larva-migrans.explanation: Retinal granuloma/leukocoria mimicking retinoblastoma → Ocular larva migrans (Toxocara).

toxocariasis-larva-migrans.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Toxocariasis & Larva Migrans”?
toxocariasis-larva-migrans.explanation: Ocular larva migrans may involve extraocular muscle pathology.

toxocariasis-larva-migrans.stem: Which should you review before “Toxocariasis & Larva Migrans”?
toxocariasis-larva-migrans.explanation: Understanding helminth classification is essential for grasping Toxocara and related infections.

anisakiasis.stem: A patient develops acute severe epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting a few hours after eating raw marine fish (sashimi); endoscopy shows a worm larva burrowing into the gastric mucosa. The organism is:
anisakiasis.explanation: Anisakiasis follows ingestion of raw/undercooked saltwater fish; the larva penetrates the gastric wall causing acute epigastric pain, and endoscopy both diagnoses and treats it by removing the larva.

anisakiasis.stem: Beyond causing gastric pain, Anisakis is also an important cause of:

options.text: IgE-mediated food allergy (urticaria/anaphylaxis), sometimes even to cooked fish

anisakiasis.explanation: Anisakis allergens can trigger IgE-mediated reactions ranging from urticaria to anaphylaxis after eating fish, and because some allergens are heat-stable, reactions can occur even when the fish is cooked.

anisakiasis.stem: Regarding source of anisakis vs freshwater-fish parasites — which is correct?

options.text: Anisakis is acquired from raw freshwater fish like the other fish-borne parasites

Anisakis is acquired from raw/undercooked SALTWATER (MARINE) fish and squid (sushi/sashimi), unlike Gnathostoma and Opisthorchis which come from raw FRESHWATER fish — the type of fish is the key distinguishing exposure

anisakiasis.explanation: Grouping all raw-fish parasites together loses the marine-vs-freshwater distinction that points to the right organism and the right dietary history.

anisakiasis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Acute severe epigastric pain hours after raw marine fish”?
anisakiasis.explanation: Acute severe epigastric pain hours after raw marine fish → Gastric anisakiasis (larva penetrating the wall).

anisakiasis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Lower abdominal pain mimicking appendicitis after sushi”?
anisakiasis.explanation: Lower abdominal pain mimicking appendicitis after sushi → Intestinal anisakiasis.

gnathostomiasis.stem: A patient in Thailand who eats raw freshwater fish develops recurrent, migrating subcutaneous swellings with marked eosinophilia. The most likely organism is:
gnathostomiasis.explanation: Gnathostomiasis, endemic in Thailand and acquired from raw freshwater fish/eel/frog, causes intermittent migratory subcutaneous swellings with eosinophilia as the dead-end larva wanders; it can also invade the CNS.

gnathostomiasis.stem: A serious complication of gnathostomiasis is:
gnathostomiasis.explanation: The migrating Gnathostoma larva can enter the central nervous system, causing eosinophilic meningitis or a painful radiculomyelitis that may be haemorrhagic — a serious, potentially fatal complication.

gnathostomiasis.stem: Regarding diagnosing gnathostomiasis — which is correct?

options.text: Gnathostomiasis is diagnosed by finding eggs on stool microscopy

The larva is trapped in TISSUE and never matures in humans, so stool microscopy is negative — diagnosis is CLINICAL (migratory swellings + eosinophilia + raw-freshwater-food history in an endemic area) supported by SEROLOGY

gnathostomiasis.explanation: Because humans are a dead-end host, no eggs are produced; expecting stool eggs misses the diagnosis, which depends on the migratory swellings, eosinophilia, exposure history and serology.

gnathostomiasis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Intermittent migratory subcutaneous swellings + eosinophilia”?

options.text: Larva in tissue, not gut (no eggs passed)

gnathostomiasis.explanation: Intermittent migratory subcutaneous swellings + eosinophilia → Gnathostomiasis (wandering larva).

gnathostomiasis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Raw freshwater fish/eel/frog consumption in Thailand/SE Asia”?

options.text: Larva in tissue, not gut (no eggs passed)

gnathostomiasis.explanation: Raw freshwater fish/eel/frog consumption in Thailand/SE Asia → Typical Gnathostoma exposure.
Both involve larva migrans and eosinophilia.

angiostrongyliasis-eosinophilic-meningit.stem: A patient in Southeast Asia develops headache and neck stiffness after eating raw snails; lumbar puncture shows eosinophils in the CSF. The most likely cause is:
angiostrongyliasis-eosinophilic-meningit.explanation: Angiostrongylus cantonensis, acquired from raw snails/slugs, is the leading cause of eosinophilic meningitis; larvae migrate to the CNS and die, provoking an eosinophilic inflammatory response with eosinophils in the CSF.

angiostrongyliasis-eosinophilic-meningit.stem: The characteristic cerebrospinal fluid finding in Angiostrongylus meningitis is:
angiostrongyliasis-eosinophilic-meningit.explanation: Eosinophilic meningitis is defined by eosinophils in the CSF; together with peripheral eosinophilia and an exposure history (snails/slugs), it points to Angiostrongylus cantonensis (Gnathostoma is the other major cause).

angiostrongyliasis-eosinophilic-meningit.stem: Regarding treating eosinophilic meningitis from angiostrongylus — which is correct?

options.text: Aggressive anti-helminthic (larvicidal) drugs should always be given to kill the worms in the CNS

Angiostrongylus meningitis is largely managed SUPPORTIVELY (analgesia, careful corticosteroids, repeated LP for headache) — aggressively killing larvae in the CNS can WORSEN the inflammatory reaction; the disease is usually self-limiting

angiostrongyliasis-eosinophilic-meningit.explanation: The damage is from the eosinophilic inflammatory response to dying larvae, so provoking more larval death can intensify CNS inflammation; supportive care and cautious anti-inflammatory treatment are preferred.

angiostrongyliasis-eosinophilic-meningit.stem: What best explains the finding: “Headache, neck stiffness with eosinophils in the CSF after eating snails”?
angiostrongyliasis-eosinophilic-meningit.explanation: Headache, neck stiffness with eosinophils in the CSF after eating snails → Angiostrongylus cantonensis eosinophilic meningitis.

angiostrongyliasis-eosinophilic-meningit.stem: What best explains the finding: “CSF eosinophilic pleocytosis + peripheral eosinophilia”?
angiostrongyliasis-eosinophilic-meningit.explanation: CSF eosinophilic pleocytosis + peripheral eosinophilia → Eosinophilic meningitis (parasitic).

angiostrongyliasis-eosinophilic-meningit.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Angiostrongyliasis & Eosinophilic Meningitis”?
angiostrongyliasis-eosinophilic-meningit.explanation: Eosinophilic meningitis is a differential diagnosis in chronic meningitis cases.

angiostrongyliasis-eosinophilic-meningit.stem: Which should you review before “Angiostrongyliasis & Eosinophilic Meningitis”?
angiostrongyliasis-eosinophilic-meningit.explanation: Both involve eosinophilic responses to parasitic infections.

trematodes-flukes-overview.stem: Which feature is shared by ALL trematodes (flukes)?

options.text: They require a snail as an intermediate host
They are acquired only by skin penetration
They live only in the intestine

trematodes-flukes-overview.explanation: All trematodes require a snail as the first intermediate host. They are otherwise diverse (liver, intestinal, lung and blood flukes); most are hermaphroditic except the schistosomes, which have separate sexes and are acquired by skin-penetrating cercariae.

trematodes-flukes-overview.stem: The treatment effective against most flukes (e.g. Opisthorchis, Paragonimus, Schistosoma) is:
trematodes-flukes-overview.explanation: Praziquantel is the treatment for most flukes, including the liver fluke Opisthorchis, the lung fluke Paragonimus and the blood fluke Schistosoma. Fasciola is the notable exception, treated with triclabendazole.

trematodes-flukes-overview.stem: Regarding how schistosomes are acquired vs other flukes — which is correct?

options.text: All flukes are acquired by eating undercooked food
Most flukes are FOOD-BORNE (raw fish, crab or plants), but the BLOOD flukes (Schistosoma) are acquired when CERCARIAE PENETRATE THE SKIN during freshwater contact — not by eating

trematodes-flukes-overview.explanation: The route determines prevention: cooking food prevents the food-borne flukes, but avoiding freshwater skin exposure prevents schistosomiasis; conflating them misdirects prevention and the exposure history.

trematodes-flukes-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cholangiocarcinoma after eating raw freshwater fish (NE Thailand)”?
trematodes-flukes-overview.explanation: Cholangiocarcinoma after eating raw freshwater fish (NE Thailand) → Opisthorchis viverrini (liver fluke).

trematodes-flukes-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Chronic cough + haemoptysis mimicking TB after raw crab”?
trematodes-flukes-overview.explanation: Chronic cough + haemoptysis mimicking TB after raw crab → Paragonimus westermani (lung fluke).

trematodes-flukes-overview.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Trematodes (Flukes) Overview”?
trematodes-flukes-overview.explanation: Clinical relevance of intestinal flukes and their symptoms.

cestodes-tapeworms-overview.stem: Which tapeworm infection is acquired by eating raw freshwater fish and can cause vitamin B12 deficiency?
cestodes-tapeworms-overview.explanation: Diphyllobothrium latum (the fish tapeworm, the largest human tapeworm) is acquired from raw freshwater fish and competes for vitamin B12, potentially causing megaloblastic anaemia.

cestodes-tapeworms-overview.stem: Neurocysticercosis, a leading cause of adult-onset seizures in endemic areas, results from:

options.text: Ingesting Taenia solium eggs (faecal–oral), with humans as the intermediate host

cestodes-tapeworms-overview.explanation: Ingesting Taenia solium eggs (faecal–oral) leads to larval cysts in tissues (cysticercosis); CNS involvement (neurocysticercosis) is a major cause of seizures. Eating larvae in pork instead produces an adult intestinal tapeworm.

cestodes-tapeworms-overview.stem: Regarding taenia solium: adult tapeworm vs cysticercosis — which is correct?

options.text: Eating undercooked pork with Taenia solium directly causes brain cysts (neurocysticercosis)

Eating undercooked pork with larvae gives an intestinal ADULT tapeworm; NEUROCYSTICERCOSIS occurs when humans ingest the EGGS (faecal–oral) and become the intermediate host, forming larval cysts in tissues including the brain

cestodes-tapeworms-overview.explanation: The route determines the disease: meat with larvae → mild gut tapeworm, but faecal–oral eggs → dangerous tissue cysticercosis; conflating them misses that hygiene (not just cooking meat) drives the CNS disease.

cestodes-tapeworms-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Adult-onset seizures with brain cysts in an endemic patient”?
cestodes-tapeworms-overview.explanation: Adult-onset seizures with brain cysts in an endemic patient → Neurocysticercosis (Taenia solium eggs).

cestodes-tapeworms-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Megaloblastic (B12-deficiency) anaemia + raw freshwater fish”?
cestodes-tapeworms-overview.explanation: Megaloblastic (B12-deficiency) anaemia + raw freshwater fish → Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm).

cestodes-tapeworms-overview.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Cestodes (Tapeworms) Overview”?
cestodes-tapeworms-overview.explanation: Clinical relevance of tapeworms in gastrointestinal diseases.

intestinal-coccidia-cryptosporidium.stem: A patient with advanced HIV (low CD4) has chronic, profuse watery diarrhoea; stool shows acid-fast oocysts. The most likely organism is:
intestinal-coccidia-cryptosporidium.explanation: Cryptosporidium causes chronic, severe watery diarrhoea in the immunocompromised (advanced HIV); its acid-fast oocysts are seen on modified acid-fast staining. It resists chlorine and there is no reliably effective drug, so immune reconstitution is key.

intestinal-coccidia-cryptosporidium.stem: The intestinal coccidia (Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Cystoisospora) are best detected in stool using:
intestinal-coccidia-cryptosporidium.explanation: The oocysts of intestinal coccidia are acid-fast and are demonstrated with a modified acid-fast (Kinyoun/Ziehl–Neelsen) stain; routine ova-and-parasite microscopy often misses them.

intestinal-coccidia-cryptosporidium.stem: Regarding detecting intestinal coccidia — which is correct?

options.text: A routine stool ova-and-parasite examination reliably detects Cryptosporidium

Coccidian OOCYSTS are easily missed on routine O&P — they require a MODIFIED ACID-FAST stain (or specific antigen/PCR for Cryptosporidium) to be seen; you must specifically request these tests when coccidia are suspected

intestinal-coccidia-cryptosporidium.explanation: Because the oocysts are small and not highlighted by standard stains, relying on routine O&P gives false negatives; suspecting coccidia (watery diarrhoea, HIV, water/produce exposure) prompts the correct acid-fast stain.

intestinal-coccidia-cryptosporidium.stem: What best explains the finding: “Chronic severe watery diarrhoea in advanced HIV”?
intestinal-coccidia-cryptosporidium.explanation: Chronic severe watery diarrhoea in advanced HIV → Cryptosporidium (immunocompromised).

intestinal-coccidia-cryptosporidium.stem: What best explains the finding: “Waterborne diarrhoea outbreak (chlorine-resistant)”?
Which should you review before “Intestinal Coccidia (Cryptosporidium & Cyclospora)”?
intestinal-coccidia-cryptosporidium.explanation: Understanding protozoa classification is essential for grasping intestinal coccidia.

toxoplasmosis.stem: A neonate has chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcifications. The most likely congenital infection is:
toxoplasmosis.explanation: The classic triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcifications indicates congenital toxoplasmosis, following primary maternal infection in pregnancy with transplacental spread of Toxoplasma gondii.

toxoplasmosis.stem: In a patient with advanced HIV, multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions are most classically caused by reactivation of:
toxoplasmosis.explanation: Reactivation of latent Toxoplasma tissue cysts in advanced HIV causes toxoplasma encephalitis with multiple ring-enhancing lesions — the classic differential of a ring-enhancing brain lesion in AIDS (versus CNS lymphoma).

toxoplasmosis.stem: Regarding routes of toxoplasma infection — which is correct?

options.text: Toxoplasmosis is acquired only from contact with cats

Humans acquire Toxoplasma from cat-faeces OOCYSTS (soil, litter) AND, importantly, from TISSUE CYSTS in UNDERCOOKED MEAT — so avoiding infection in pregnancy means both cat-litter precautions AND cooking meat thoroughly

toxoplasmosis.explanation: Focusing only on cats misses the major meat-borne route; both must be addressed for prevention (especially in pregnancy), and the meat route explains cases in people without cats.

toxoplasmosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Chorioretinitis + hydrocephalus + intracranial calcifications in a neonate”?
toxoplasmosis.explanation: Chorioretinitis + hydrocephalus + intracranial calcifications in a neonate → Congenital toxoplasmosis.

toxoplasmosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions in advanced HIV”?
toxoplasmosis.explanation: Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions in advanced HIV → Reactivation Toxoplasma encephalitis.

blood-apicomplexa-malaria-babesia.stem: Which Plasmodium species is responsible for severe, potentially fatal (cerebral) malaria with high parasitaemia?
blood-apicomplexa-malaria-babesia.explanation: Plasmodium falciparum causes severe malaria (cerebral malaria, severe anaemia, blackwater fever) because infected red cells sequester in capillaries and parasitaemia can be very high; it is the main killer and needs IV artesunate when severe.

blood-apicomplexa-malaria-babesia.stem: Why is primaquine added to treat Plasmodium vivax or ovale malaria (after checking G6PD status)?

options.text: To eradicate dormant liver hypnozoites and prevent relapse

blood-apicomplexa-malaria-babesia.explanation: P. vivax and P. ovale form dormant liver hypnozoites that cause relapses; primaquine is a hypnozoiticide that eradicates them (radical cure). G6PD deficiency must be excluded first because primaquine causes haemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients.

blood-apicomplexa-malaria-babesia.stem: Regarding preventing malaria relapse — which is correct?

options.text: Standard blood-stage antimalarials (e.g. an ACT) cure all forms of malaria completely

Blood-stage drugs clear the RBC infection but do NOT kill the dormant liver HYPNOZOITES of P. VIVAX and P. OVALE — PRIMAQUINE (a hypnozoiticide, given after checking G6PD status) is required to prevent relapse

blood-apicomplexa-malaria-babesia.explanation: Missing the hypnozoite stage leads to relapses weeks to months later; radical cure of vivax/ovale requires primaquine, and G6PD deficiency must be excluded first because primaquine causes haemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients.

blood-apicomplexa-malaria-babesia.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cyclical fever, haemolytic anaemia and splenomegaly after travel”?
blood-apicomplexa-malaria-babesia.explanation: Cyclical fever, haemolytic anaemia and splenomegaly after travel → Malaria (RBC cycle).

blood-apicomplexa-malaria-babesia.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cerebral malaria / high parasitaemia / blackwater fever”?
blood-apicomplexa-malaria-babesia.explanation: Cerebral malaria / high parasitaemia / blackwater fever → Plasmodium falciparum (severe malaria).

blood-apicomplexa-malaria-babesia.stem: Which should you review before “Blood Apicomplexa: Malaria & Babesia”?
blood-apicomplexa-malaria-babesia.explanation: Understanding host-parasite interactions is crucial for grasping malaria transmission.

medical-mites-acarology.stem: A patient has intense nocturnal itching with small burrows in the finger web spaces and wrists. The cause and treatment are:
medical-mites-acarology.explanation: Burrows with intense nocturnal itch, classically in the web spaces and wrists, indicate scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei); treatment is topical permethrin (or oral ivermectin) with treatment of close contacts.

medical-mites-acarology.stem: In Asia, the larvae of trombiculid mites ("chiggers") are the vector for which disease, classically producing an eschar at the bite site?
medical-mites-acarology.explanation: Chigger (trombiculid mite) larvae transmit scrub typhus, caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi, which characteristically produces an eschar at the bite site with fever, rash and lymphadenopathy; it is treated with doxycycline.

medical-mites-acarology.stem: Regarding recognising crusted (norwegian) scabies — which is correct?

options.text: Scabies is always intensely itchy, so a poorly-itchy crusted rash is not scabies

CRUSTED (Norwegian) scabies — a hyperinfestation with thousands of mites in the IMMUNOCOMPROMISED — can be only mildly itchy yet is EXTREMELY contagious (an outbreak source in hospitals/care homes); it must not be missed despite the atypical presentation

medical-mites-acarology.explanation: The impaired immune response means the usual intense itch may be blunted while the mite burden is enormous; underestimating it (because it itches less) allows major outbreaks.

medical-mites-acarology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Intense nocturnal itch with burrows in web spaces/wrists”?
medical-mites-acarology.explanation: Intense nocturnal itch with burrows in web spaces/wrists → Scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei).

medical-mites-acarology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thick, crusted, hyperinfested skin in an immunocompromised patient”?
medical-mites-acarology.explanation: Thick, crusted, hyperinfested skin in an immunocompromised patient → Crusted (Norwegian) scabies — highly contagious.

medical-mites-acarology.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Medical Acarology: Mites”?
medical-mites-acarology.explanation: Skin infestations are clinically relevant to mite infections.

medical-mites-acarology.stem: Which should you review before “Medical Acarology: Mites”?
medical-mites-acarology.explanation: Understanding vectors is essential for grasping mite-related diseases.

sparganosis-spirometra.stem: A patient develops a slowly migrating, painful subcutaneous nodule after eating undercooked frog; surgical removal reveals a ribbon-like larva. The diagnosis is:
sparganosis-spirometra.explanation: Sparganosis is caused by the plerocercoid larva (sparganum) of Spirometra, acquired from infected copepods in water, raw frog/snake, or a frog-flesh poultice; the migrating larva is removed and identified surgically.

sparganosis-spirometra.stem: Why is stool examination negative in sparganosis?

options.text: The larva never matures into an egg-laying adult in the human (accidental) host
The eggs are too small to see
The parasite lives only in the blood
The stool is not the right specimen for any tapeworm

sparganosis-spirometra.explanation: Humans are an accidental host for Spirometra; the sparganum larva migrates in the tissues but never develops into an adult tapeworm, so no eggs are produced or passed in stool. Diagnosis relies on removing and identifying the larva.

sparganosis-spirometra.stem: Regarding diagnosing and treating sparganosis — which is correct?

options.text: Sparganosis is diagnosed by stool eggs and cured with praziquantel like an intestinal tapeworm

The sparganum is a TISSUE LARVA that never matures, so there are NO eggs in stool — diagnosis and treatment are by SURGICAL REMOVAL of the migrating larva (praziquantel is unreliable against the tissue larva)

sparganosis-spirometra.explanation: Treating it like an adult intestinal tapeworm (stool eggs, praziquantel) fails; the larva is in tissue, so surgical excision is both the diagnostic and therapeutic step.

sparganosis-spirometra.stem: What best explains the finding: “Slowly migrating subcutaneous nodule after eating raw frog/snake”?
sparganosis-spirometra.explanation: Slowly migrating subcutaneous nodule after eating raw frog/snake → Sparganosis (Spirometra plerocercoid).

sparganosis-spirometra.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ocular/periorbital swelling after a frog-flesh poultice”?
sparganosis-spirometra.explanation: Ocular/periorbital swelling after a frog-flesh poultice → Ocular sparganosis (traditional poultice route).

sparganosis-spirometra.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Sparganosis (Spirometra)”?
sparganosis-spirometra.explanation: Sparganosis can present with skin infestations.
Understanding cestodes is essential for grasping sparganosis.

echinococcosis-hydatid.stem: A shepherd with dog contact has a slowly enlarging, well-defined liver cyst containing daughter cysts. The most important management principle is to:

options.text: Aspirate the cyst immediately for diagnosis
Avoid rupture/spillage (risk of anaphylaxis and dissemination) and treat with surgery/PAIR plus albendazole

echinococcosis-hydatid.explanation: This is cystic echinococcosis (hydatid disease). Careless aspiration/rupture can cause anaphylaxis and seed daughter cysts, so management is careful surgery or the PAIR technique under albendazole cover, with diagnosis supported by imaging and serology.

echinococcosis-hydatid.stem: Humans acquire cystic echinococcosis (hydatid disease) by:

options.text: Ingesting Echinococcus eggs shed in dog faeces

echinococcosis-hydatid.explanation: The dog is the definitive host; humans become accidental intermediate hosts by ingesting Echinococcus eggs from dog faeces, and larval hydatid cysts then develop, most often in the liver.

echinococcosis-hydatid.stem: Regarding managing a suspected hydatid cyst — which is correct?

options.text: A liver cyst should be diagnostically aspirated to obtain fluid for analysis

Do NOT carelessly aspirate a suspected HYDATID cyst — spillage of antigenic fluid can cause ANAPHYLAXIS and seed daughter cysts; diagnosis uses imaging + SEROLOGY, and treatment is careful surgery or PAIR under albendazole cover

echinococcosis-hydatid.explanation: Routine aspiration of a hydatid cyst is dangerous (anaphylaxis, dissemination); recognising the cyst as possibly hydatid before aspirating and using serology/imaging avoids a catastrophic complication.

echinococcosis-hydatid.stem: What best explains the finding: “Slowly growing liver cyst with daughter cysts in a person with dog contact”?
echinococcosis-hydatid.explanation: Slowly growing liver cyst with daughter cysts in a person with dog contact → Cystic echinococcosis (E. granulosus).

echinococcosis-hydatid.stem: What best explains the finding: “Anaphylaxis after cyst rupture/aspiration”?
echinococcosis-hydatid.explanation: Anaphylaxis after cyst rupture/aspiration → Release of antigenic hydatid fluid.

echinococcosis-hydatid.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Echinococcosis (Hydatid Disease)”?
echinococcosis-hydatid.explanation: Potential overlap in clinical presentations related to liver lesions.

echinococcosis-hydatid.stem: Which should you review before “Echinococcosis (Hydatid Disease)”?
echinococcosis-hydatid.explanation: Understanding tapeworms is essential for grasping hydatid disease.

medical-entomology-vectors.stem: Which is an example of a MECHANICAL (rather than biological) vector?

options.text: A housefly carrying enteric bacteria from faeces to food

medical-entomology-vectors.explanation: A housefly is a mechanical vector — it merely carries pathogens on its body surface from faeces to food, with no development of the organism. Anopheles, sandflies and tsetse flies are biological vectors in which the parasite develops.

medical-entomology-vectors.stem: The mainstay of preventing most vector-borne parasitic diseases is:

options.text: Vector control (bed nets, insecticide spraying, larval-source management, repellents)

medical-entomology-vectors.explanation: Because transmission depends on the arthropod vector, vector control — insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying, larval-source management and personal protection (repellents, clothing) — is the central strategy for preventing vector-borne disease.

medical-entomology-vectors.stem: Regarding biological vs mechanical transmission — which is correct?

options.text: Any insect that lands on food and then on a wound is a biological vector of whatever it carries

That is MECHANICAL transmission (the housefly merely carries organisms on its body); a BIOLOGICAL vector is one in which the pathogen DEVELOPS or multiplies as a required step in its life cycle (e.g. malaria in Anopheles)
Biological vector (essential to the life cycle)

medical-entomology-vectors.explanation: The distinction determines specificity and control: biological vectors are essential, specific hosts (targeting them interrupts the cycle), whereas mechanical transmission is non-specific and incidental.

medical-entomology-vectors.stem: What best explains the finding: “A pathogen that multiplies within its arthropod vector”?

options.text: Biological vector (essential to the life cycle)

medical-entomology-vectors.explanation: A pathogen that multiplies within its arthropod vector → Biological vector (essential to the life cycle).

medical-entomology-vectors.stem: What best explains the finding: “A housefly carrying enteric pathogens on its body”?

options.text: Biological vector (essential to the life cycle)

medical-entomology-vectors.explanation: A housefly carrying enteric pathogens on its body → Mechanical vector.

medical-entomology-vectors.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Medical Entomology & Vectors”?
medical-entomology-vectors.explanation: Minimal direct clinical application related to entomology.

medical-entomology-vectors.stem: Which should you review before “Medical Entomology & Vectors”?
medical-entomology-vectors.explanation: Mites are a key group of arthropods studied in medical entomology.

mosquito-borne-diseases.stem: Dengue, Zika and chikungunya viruses are transmitted primarily by which day-biting mosquito genus?
mosquito-borne-diseases.explanation: Aedes mosquitoes (A. aegypti/albopictus), which bite during the day and breed in small containers of clean water, are the main vectors of dengue, Zika, chikungunya and yellow fever, driving urban arbovirus outbreaks.

mosquito-borne-diseases.stem: Lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti) causing lymphoedema is diagnosed by finding microfilariae on a blood film taken:
mosquito-borne-diseases.explanation: Wuchereria bancrofti microfilariae show nocturnal periodicity, appearing in peripheral blood at night (matching the biting time of the Culex/Anopheles vectors), so blood films for diagnosis are taken at night.

mosquito-borne-diseases.stem: Regarding matching mosquito genus to disease — which is correct?

options.text: Only ANOPHELES transmits malaria; AEDES transmits the arboviruses (dengue, Zika, chikungunya, yellow fever — and it is a DAY-biter), and CULEX transmits lymphatic filariasis and Japanese encephalitis — the genus determines the disease

mosquito-borne-diseases.explanation: The genera differ in the pathogens they carry and their biting behaviour (Aedes bites by day, Anopheles at night), which changes both the differential for a febrile patient and the control strategy.

mosquito-borne-diseases.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cyclical fever after travel to a malarious area”?
mosquito-borne-diseases.explanation: Cyclical fever after travel to a malarious area → Malaria (Anopheles-transmitted).

mosquito-borne-diseases.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dengue/Zika/chikungunya outbreak in an urban area”?
mosquito-borne-diseases.explanation: Dengue/Zika/chikungunya outbreak in an urban area → Aedes (day-biting, container-breeding) vector.

mosquito-borne-diseases.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Mosquito Vectors & Their Diseases”?
mosquito-borne-diseases.explanation: Limited clinical relevance but may touch on treatment aspects in broader contexts.

mosquito-borne-diseases.stem: Which should you review before “Mosquito Vectors & Their Diseases”?
mosquito-borne-diseases.explanation: Malaria is directly linked to Anopheles mosquitoes.

myiasis-and-fly-vectors.stem: The housefly (Musca domestica) contributes to the spread of diarrhoeal disease and typhoid primarily as a:

options.text: Biological vector in which the pathogen multiplies
Mechanical vector carrying pathogens on its body from faeces to food

myiasis-and-fly-vectors.explanation: The housefly is a mechanical vector: it transfers enteric pathogens on its body and mouthparts between faeces and food, without the organism developing inside it. Control relies on sanitation and food hygiene.

options.text: A boil-like nodule with a central pore through which the larva breathes
A migrating subcutaneous swelling with eosinophilia

myiasis-and-fly-vectors.explanation: Furuncular myiasis is a boil-like nodule containing a fly larva, with a central pore through which the larva breathes; treatment is to occlude the pore or extract the larva.

myiasis-and-fly-vectors.stem: Regarding the housefly as a vector — which is correct?

options.text: The housefly is a biological vector because it spreads so many diseases

The housefly is a MECHANICAL vector — it carries pathogens on its body/mouthparts from faeces to food without any parasite development inside it; that is why sanitation and food hygiene (not a specific life-cycle target) control it
Mechanical vector (carries pathogens on the body)

myiasis-and-fly-vectors.explanation: Mislabelling it biological misunderstands the transmission: there is no development stage in the fly, so control targets contamination and hygiene rather than the vector's life cycle.

myiasis-and-fly-vectors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Houseflies spreading diarrhoeal disease/typhoid”?

options.text: Mechanical vector (carries pathogens on the body)

myiasis-and-fly-vectors.explanation: Houseflies spreading diarrhoeal disease/typhoid → Mechanical vector (carries pathogens on the body).

myiasis-and-fly-vectors.stem: What best explains the finding: “A boil-like nodule with a central pore and a moving larva”?

options.text: Mechanical vector (carries pathogens on the body)

myiasis-and-fly-vectors.explanation: A boil-like nodule with a central pore and a moving larva → Cutaneous (furuncular) myiasis.

myiasis-and-fly-vectors.stem: Which should you review before “Flies & Myiasis”?
myiasis-and-fly-vectors.explanation: Understanding medical entomology is essential for grasping the role of flies as vectors.

bloodsucking-fly-vectors.stem: Onchocerciasis ("river blindness"), caused by Onchocerca volvulus, is transmitted by which fly that breeds in fast-flowing rivers?
bloodsucking-fly-vectors.explanation: Blackflies (Simulium), which breed in fast-flowing rivers, transmit Onchocerca volvulus, causing onchocerciasis with itchy dermatitis, subcutaneous nodules and progressive blindness — "river blindness", controlled with ivermectin.

bloodsucking-fly-vectors.stem: A patient has a chronic skin ulcer ("oriental sore") after a sandfly bite. The causative organism is:
bloodsucking-fly-vectors.explanation: Sandflies (Phlebotomus) transmit Leishmania; cutaneous leishmaniasis produces a chronic skin ulcer ("oriental sore"), while visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) causes fever, massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia.

bloodsucking-fly-vectors.stem: Regarding matching the fly to its disease — which is correct?

options.text: All biting flies transmit the same kinds of infection

Each blood-sucking fly is a SPECIFIC biological vector: SANDFLY → leishmaniasis, TSETSE → African trypanosomiasis, BLACKFLY → onchocerciasis (river blindness) — the fly identifies the disease and vice versa

bloodsucking-fly-vectors.explanation: Because these are biological vectors with specific parasite–vector pairings, the fly (and its habitat, e.g. blackflies near fast rivers) is a strong clue to the disease and to control strategy.

bloodsucking-fly-vectors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Chronic skin ulcer ("oriental sore") after a sandfly bite”?
bloodsucking-fly-vectors.explanation: Chronic skin ulcer ("oriental sore") after a sandfly bite → Cutaneous leishmaniasis.

bloodsucking-fly-vectors.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fever + massive splenomegaly + pancytopenia (kala-azar)”?
bloodsucking-fly-vectors.explanation: Fever + massive splenomegaly + pancytopenia (kala-azar) → Visceral leishmaniasis (Leishmania donovani).

bloodsucking-fly-vectors.stem: Which should you review before “Blood-Sucking Fly Vectors”?
bloodsucking-fly-vectors.explanation: Essential for understanding the role of various vectors in disease transmission.

spinal-cord-anatomy-organization.stem: In the spinal cord, the lower motor neurons that innervate skeletal muscle are located in the:
spinal-cord-anatomy-organization.explanation: The ventral (anterior) horn, derived from the basal plate, contains the lower motor neurons — the final common pathway to skeletal muscle. The dorsal horn is sensory, the lateral horn (T1–L2) is sympathetic, and the dorsal root ganglion holds sensory cell bodies outside the cord.

spinal-cord-anatomy-organization.stem: In the adult, the spinal cord typically terminates (as the conus medullaris) at approximately which vertebral level?
spinal-cord-anatomy-organization.explanation: The cord grows less than the vertebral column, so in the adult it ends as the conus medullaris at about L1–L2; below this the lumbosacral roots continue as the cauda equina. This is why a lumbar puncture is performed at L3/4 or below, avoiding the cord.

spinal-cord-anatomy-organization.stem: Regarding conus medullaris vs cauda equina syndrome — which is correct?

options.text: A lesion low in the spinal canal must be a pure lower-motor-neuron (cauda equina) problem

The CONUS MEDULLARIS (cord tip, ~L1) still contains cord, so its syndrome is MIXED UMN+LMN with EARLY, SYMMETRIC saddle anaesthesia and bladder/bowel loss; the CAUDA EQUINA (roots below the conus) is pure LMN with ASYMMETRIC radicular pain and later, variable sphincter involvement — location relative to the conus decides the picture
Conus medullaris (cord terminates above the vertebral end)
Anterior horn (basal plate) — final common pathway to muscle

spinal-cord-anatomy-organization.explanation: Distinguishing conus from cauda equina changes the expected signs and urgency; both threaten sphincter function, but the level (cord tip vs roots) determines whether UMN signs and early symmetric sphincter loss appear.

spinal-cord-anatomy-organization.stem: What best explains the finding: “Cord tapering to a tip at ~L1”?

options.text: Anterior horn (basal plate) — final common pathway to muscle
Conus medullaris (cord terminates above the vertebral end)

spinal-cord-anatomy-organization.explanation: Cord tapering to a tip at ~L1 → Conus medullaris (cord terminates above the vertebral end).

spinal-cord-anatomy-organization.stem: What best explains the finding: “Lower motor neurons of the ventral horn”?

options.text: Conus medullaris (cord terminates above the vertebral end)
Anterior horn (basal plate) — final common pathway to muscle

spinal-cord-anatomy-organization.explanation: Lower motor neurons of the ventral horn → Anterior horn (basal plate) — final common pathway to muscle.

spinal-cord-anatomy-organization.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Spinal Cord Anatomy & Organisation”?
spinal-cord-anatomy-organization.explanation: Reflexes involve spinal cord pathways and proprioceptive input.

spinal-cord-anatomy-organization.stem: Which should you review before “Spinal Cord Anatomy & Organisation”?
spinal-cord-anatomy-organization.explanation: Understanding spinal cord anatomy aids in grasping brachial plexus organization.

dermatomes-spinal-nerves.stem: A sensory level detected at the umbilicus corresponds to which dermatome?
dermatomes-spinal-nerves.explanation: The umbilicus is the T10 dermatome (the nipple is T4, the groin ~L1). Landmark dermatomes let you map a sensory level to a spinal cord/root segment — a key part of localising a spinal lesion.

dermatomes-spinal-nerves.stem: Compared with a single dermatome, the sensory loss from a single spinal nerve root lesion is often only partial because:

options.text: Adjacent dermatomes overlap, so neighbouring roots still supply the area
Dermatomes are supplied by peripheral nerves, not roots

dermatomes-spinal-nerves.explanation: Adjacent dermatomes overlap considerably, so a single-root lesion leaves the area partly innervated by neighbouring roots and produces only partial sensory loss. This overlap (absent in peripheral-nerve territories) helps distinguish a radiculopathy from a peripheral neuropathy.

dermatomes-spinal-nerves.stem: Regarding radiculopathy vs peripheral neuropathy pattern — which is correct?

options.text: A single nerve-root lesion should cause complete numbness in its dermatome

Because adjacent DERMATOMES OVERLAP, a single-root lesion causes only PARTIAL (often subtle) sensory loss in that dermatome, whereas a PERIPHERAL NERVE lesion causes a SHARPLY demarcated deficit in the nerve's territory — the pattern (dermatomal + overlapping vs nerve-territory + sharp) tells root from nerve
Peripheral nerve lesion (not dermatomal — no overlap)

dermatomes-spinal-nerves.explanation: The overlap explains why radiculopathies present with pain/weakness more than dense numbness, and distinguishing dermatomal from peripheral-nerve patterns is central to localising the lesion (disc/root vs nerve).

dermatomes-spinal-nerves.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sensory loss in a dermatomal strip with myotomal weakness”?

options.text: Peripheral nerve lesion (not dermatomal — no overlap)

dermatomes-spinal-nerves.explanation: Sensory loss in a dermatomal strip with myotomal weakness → Radiculopathy (single nerve-root compression, e.g. disc).

dermatomes-spinal-nerves.stem: What best explains the finding: “A sharply demarcated sensory deficit in a nerve territory”?

options.text: Peripheral nerve lesion (not dermatomal — no overlap)

dermatomes-spinal-nerves.explanation: A sharply demarcated sensory deficit in a nerve territory → Peripheral nerve lesion (not dermatomal — no overlap).

dermatomes-spinal-nerves.stem: Which should you review before “Spinal Nerves & Dermatomes”?
dermatomes-spinal-nerves.explanation: Understanding abdominal wall anatomy is crucial for recognizing dermatomes in the abdominal region.

brainstem-anatomy-organization.stem: The nuclei of which cranial nerves are located in the medulla?
brainstem-anatomy-organization.explanation: By the "rule of 4": the midbrain houses CN III–IV, the pons CN V–VIII, and the medulla CN IX–XII. (CN I and II are not true brainstem nerves.) Motor nuclei lie medially and sensory nuclei laterally.

brainstem-anatomy-organization.stem: A patient has a right-sided cranial nerve palsy with left-sided limb weakness ("crossed signs"). This pattern localises the lesion to the:
brainstem-anatomy-organization.explanation: Crossed signs — an ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy with contralateral limb weakness — are the hallmark of a brainstem lesion: the cranial nerve nucleus is affected on the same side, while the long motor tract (which crosses lower in the medulla) produces weakness on the opposite side.

brainstem-anatomy-organization.stem: Regarding crossed brainstem signs — which is correct?

options.text: A lesion causing a facial (cranial nerve) palsy and limb weakness on OPPOSITE sides means there are two separate lesions

A single unilateral BRAINSTEM lesion classically produces CROSSED signs — an IPSILATERAL cranial nerve palsy (its nucleus/nerve at that level) with CONTRALATERAL limb weakness/sensory loss (long tracts that decussate lower) — one lesion, localised to the brainstem level of the affected cranial nerve
Brainstem lesion (crossed signs) — CN nucleus + uncrossed long tract

brainstem-anatomy-organization.explanation: Recognising crossed signs as one brainstem lesion (not two) both localises to the brainstem and identifies the level from the cranial nerve involved — a core neuro-localisation skill.

brainstem-anatomy-organization.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy + contralateral hemiparesis”?

options.text: Brainstem lesion (crossed signs) — CN nucleus + uncrossed long tract

brainstem-anatomy-organization.explanation: Ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy + contralateral hemiparesis → Brainstem lesion (crossed signs) — CN nucleus + uncrossed long tract.

brainstem-anatomy-organization.stem: What best explains the finding: “CN III–IV signs localising a lesion”?

options.text: Brainstem lesion (crossed signs) — CN nucleus + uncrossed long tract

brainstem-anatomy-organization.explanation: CN III–IV signs localising a lesion → Midbrain level.

brainstem-anatomy-organization.stem: Which should you review before “Brainstem Anatomy & Organisation”?
brainstem-anatomy-organization.explanation: Understanding cranial fossae is essential for localizing cranial nerve nuclei.

cranial-nerves-overview.stem: A patient with a right hemispheric stroke has drooping of the right lower face but can still wrinkle the right forehead normally. This pattern indicates:

options.text: A lower motor neuron (CN VII) lesion
An upper motor neuron (corticobulbar) lesion, because the forehead is bilaterally innervated

cranial-nerves-overview.explanation: The forehead receives bilateral upper motor neuron (corticobulbar) input, so a UMN lesion spares the forehead and causes only contralateral lower-face weakness. A lower motor neuron (CN VII) lesion, such as Bell's palsy, would paralyse the whole half-face including the forehead.

cranial-nerves-overview.stem: Which set of cranial nerves carries parasympathetic fibres?
cranial-nerves-overview.explanation: Four cranial nerves carry parasympathetic fibres: III (pupillary constriction/accommodation), VII (lacrimal and salivary glands), IX (parotid gland) and X (thoracic and abdominal viscera). The others are purely somatic motor, sensory, or mixed without a parasympathetic component.

cranial-nerves-overview.stem: Regarding umn vs lmn facial palsy — which is correct?

options.text: Any facial droop means a facial nerve (Bell's palsy) problem

The FOREHEAD receives BILATERAL corticobulbar (UMN) input, so a cortical/internal-capsule stroke (UMN) causes CONTRALATERAL LOWER-face weakness with the FOREHEAD SPARED, whereas a CN VII nucleus/nerve lesion (LMN, e.g. Bell's palsy) weakens the ENTIRE ipsilateral half-face including the forehead — the forehead is the discriminator
LMN facial (CN VII) lesion — e.g. Bell's palsy

cranial-nerves-overview.explanation: Whether the forehead is involved instantly separates a central (stroke, forehead spared) from a peripheral (Bell's palsy, whole face) facial weakness — different causes, urgency and management.

cranial-nerves-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Whole half-face weakness including the forehead”?

options.text: LMN facial (CN VII) lesion — e.g. Bell's palsy

cranial-nerves-overview.explanation: Whole half-face weakness including the forehead → LMN facial (CN VII) lesion — e.g. Bell's palsy.

cranial-nerves-overview.stem: What best explains the finding: “Lower-face droop with forehead spared”?

options.text: LMN facial (CN VII) lesion — e.g. Bell's palsy

cranial-nerves-overview.explanation: Lower-face droop with forehead spared → UMN (corticobulbar) lesion — forehead bilaterally innervated.

cranial-nerves-overview.stem: Which should you review before “Cranial Nerves (I–XII) Overview”?
cranial-nerves-overview.explanation: Understanding facial muscle innervation is crucial for grasping cranial nerve functions.

cerebral-cortex-organization.stem: The primary somatosensory cortex, which contains the sensory homunculus, is located in the:
cerebral-cortex-organization.explanation: The primary somatosensory cortex lies in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe and carries the sensory homunculus; the primary motor cortex is in the precentral gyrus (frontal), primary visual in the occipital calcarine cortex, and primary auditory in the superior temporal gyrus.

cerebral-cortex-organization.stem: The principal excitatory projection neuron of the cerebral cortex is the:
cerebral-cortex-organization.explanation: Pyramidal cells (glutamatergic, ~80% of cortical neurons) are the main excitatory output neurons — layer V pyramidal cells give rise to the corticospinal tract, for example. The remaining ~20% are mostly inhibitory GABAergic interneurons. Purkinje cells belong to the cerebellum.

cerebral-cortex-organization.stem: Regarding why the homunculus is distorted — which is correct?

options.text: The size of a body part in the cortex reflects the physical size of that body part

Cortical representation is proportional to the DENSITY of innervation and the FINENESS of control, NOT to physical size — so the hands, lips and face occupy huge territories while the trunk and legs occupy little; this cortical magnification is why the homunculus looks grotesquely distorted

cerebral-cortex-organization.explanation: The distortion reflects functional importance (dexterity and sensory acuity), which is why hand and face lesions cause prominent deficits and why fine-movement regions dominate the map.

cerebral-cortex-organization.stem: What best explains the finding: “Voluntary movement map on the precentral gyrus”?

options.text: Distorted homunculus (cortical magnification of fine-control regions)

cerebral-cortex-organization.explanation: Voluntary movement map on the precentral gyrus → Primary motor cortex (with motor homunculus).

cerebral-cortex-organization.stem: What best explains the finding: “Body sensation map on the postcentral gyrus”?

options.text: Distorted homunculus (cortical magnification of fine-control regions)

cerebral-cortex-organization.explanation: Body sensation map on the postcentral gyrus → Primary somatosensory cortex (sensory homunculus).

cerebral-cortex-organization.stem: Which should you review before “Cerebral Cortex: Organisation”?
cerebral-cortex-organization.explanation: Basic understanding of anatomical variations may aid in grasping cortical organization.

cortical-areas-language.stem: A patient produces fluent but meaningless speech full of neologisms and cannot understand spoken commands. This is:
cortical-areas-language.explanation: Fluent, nonsensical ("word salad") speech with impaired comprehension is Wernicke (receptive) aphasia, from a lesion of the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. Broca aphasia is non-fluent with preserved comprehension; dysarthria is a motor articulation problem, not a language disorder.

cortical-areas-language.stem: Fluent speech with intact comprehension but a selective inability to repeat phrases suggests damage to the:
cortical-areas-language.explanation: Conduction aphasia results from damage to the arcuate fasciculus connecting Wernicke's and Broca's areas: comprehension and fluency are preserved, but repetition is disproportionately impaired because the comprehension–production link is disconnected.

cortical-areas-language.stem: Regarding broca vs wernicke aphasia — which is correct?

options.text: A patient who speaks fluently cannot have significant aphasia

WERNICKE (receptive) aphasia is FLUENT — speech flows effortlessly but is full of neologisms/"word salad" and comprehension is impaired, and the patient is often unaware; fluency does NOT equal normal language. BROCA (expressive) aphasia is the non-fluent one, with preserved comprehension

cortical-areas-language.explanation: Judging language by fluency alone misses Wernicke aphasia entirely; comprehension and repetition must be tested, because fluent speech can be meaningless while non-fluent speech can carry intact understanding.

cortical-areas-language.stem: What best explains the finding: “Non-fluent, effortful speech with intact comprehension”?

options.text: Broca lesion adjacent to motor cortex (dominant MCA)

cortical-areas-language.explanation: Non-fluent, effortful speech with intact comprehension → Broca (expressive) aphasia — inferior frontal gyrus.

cortical-areas-language.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension”?

options.text: Broca lesion adjacent to motor cortex (dominant MCA)

cortical-areas-language.explanation: Fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension → Wernicke (receptive) aphasia — superior temporal gyrus.

cortical-areas-language.stem: Which should you review before “Language Areas & Aphasia”?
cortical-areas-language.explanation: Wernicke's area is directly related to Wernicke's encephalopathy.

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: Fibres of the corpus callosum are an example of which type of cerebral white matter?
cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: Commissural fibres connect the two hemispheres — the corpus callosum is the largest. Association fibres connect areas within one hemisphere (e.g. the arcuate fasciculus), and projection fibres connect the cortex with lower structures (e.g. the internal capsule).

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: A small lacunar infarct in the posterior limb of the internal capsule characteristically produces:

options.text: A mild transient sensory tingle only
A dense contralateral hemiparesis out of proportion to the lesion size

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: The internal capsule concentrates the corticospinal and thalamocortical fibres into a small area, so even a tiny (lacunar) lesion interrupts a large volume of traffic and causes a dense contralateral hemiparesis (pure motor stroke) — a deficit disproportionate to the lesion size.

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.stem: Regarding why an internal capsule lacune is so disabling — which is correct?

options.text: A very small deep stroke should cause only a minor deficit

The INTERNAL CAPSULE packs the entire corticospinal, corticobulbar and thalamocortical projection into a tiny cross-section, so a small (lacunar) lesion there can produce a DENSE contralateral hemiparesis and/or hemisensory loss — the deficit is out of all proportion to the lesion size

cerebrum-lobes-white-matter.explanation: Because projection fibres are concentrated in the capsule (unlike the spread-out cortex), a minute lesion interrupts a huge fraction of descending/ascending traffic — hence classic pure motor/sensory lacunar syndromes.
