drug-development-bioequivalence.explanation: A generic contains the same active ingredient and is approved by proving bioequivalence — comparable rate and extent of absorption (AUC and Cmax, typically 90% CI within 80–125%) — which lets it inherit the reference drug's indications without repeating efficacy trials.

drug-development-bioequivalence.stem: Regarding generic vs biosimilar — which is correct?

options.text: A biosimilar is just the "generic version" of a biologic drug

A GENERIC (small molecule) is chemically IDENTICAL to the reference and approved by simple BIOEQUIVALENCE; a BIOSIMILAR is a large, complex BIOLOGIC that can only be made "highly SIMILAR" (not identical), so it requires extensive comparative analytical, PK/PD and often clinical/immunogenicity data — it is not a generic

drug-development-bioequivalence.explanation: The molecular complexity of biologics means exact copies are impossible, so biosimilars carry a higher evidentiary bar (and immunogenicity concerns) than generics — a distinction with real prescribing and substitution implications.

drug-development-bioequivalence.stem: What best explains the finding: “A first-in-human study in healthy volunteers testing safety/PK”?
drug-development-bioequivalence.explanation: A first-in-human study in healthy volunteers testing safety/PK → Phase I trial (single/multiple ascending dose).

drug-development-bioequivalence.stem: What best explains the finding: “A large randomised controlled trial vs standard therapy before licensing”?
drug-development-bioequivalence.explanation: A large randomised controlled trial vs standard therapy before licensing → Phase III trial.

drug-development-bioequivalence.stem: Which should you review before “Drug Development, Bioequivalence & Biosimilars”?
drug-development-bioequivalence.explanation: Understanding drug development requires knowledge of preclinical processes.

pharmacokinetics-adme.stem: Which parameter is used to calculate the maintenance dose rate of a drug at steady state?
pharmacokinetics-adme.explanation: At steady state, rate in = rate out, so the maintenance dosing rate = clearance × target concentration (adjusted for bioavailability). Volume of distribution determines the loading dose (Vd × C), while half-life (0.693·Vd/CL) sets the dosing interval and time to steady state.

pharmacokinetics-adme.stem: An intravenous drug by definition has a bioavailability (F) of:
pharmacokinetics-adme.explanation: Bioavailability is the fraction of an administered dose reaching the systemic circulation unchanged. An intravenous dose enters the circulation directly, so F = 100% by definition; oral bioavailability is reduced by incomplete absorption and first-pass (gut/hepatic) metabolism.

pharmacokinetics-adme.stem: Regarding first-order vs zero-order kinetics — which is correct?

options.text: All drugs are eliminated at a rate proportional to their concentration

MOST drugs are FIRST-ORDER (a constant FRACTION per unit time, so rate rises with concentration and t½ is constant), but a few with saturable elimination are ZERO-ORDER (a constant AMOUNT per unit time regardless of concentration) — e.g. ethanol, phenytoin and high-dose aspirin — where small dose increases cause large, potentially toxic concentration jumps
Lipophilic, tissue-bound drug (little stays in plasma)

pharmacokinetics-adme.explanation: Zero-order (saturable) kinetics means no constant half-life and a narrow margin for dose changes, explaining why phenytoin and ethanol levels can rise disproportionately — a key safety distinction.

pharmacokinetics-adme.stem: What best explains the finding: “Low oral bioavailability despite good absorption”?

options.text: Lipophilic, tissue-bound drug (little stays in plasma)

pharmacokinetics-adme.explanation: Low oral bioavailability despite good absorption → Extensive first-pass (gut/hepatic) metabolism.

pharmacokinetics-adme.stem: What best explains the finding: “A very large volume of distribution (> body water)”?

options.text: Lipophilic, tissue-bound drug (little stays in plasma)

pharmacokinetics-adme.explanation: A very large volume of distribution (> body water) → Lipophilic, tissue-bound drug (little stays in plasma).

pharmacokinetics-adme.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Pharmacokinetics: ADME & Dosing”?
pharmacokinetics-adme.explanation: Renal impairment affects drug clearance and dosing strategies.

pharmacokinetics-adme.stem: Which should you review before “Pharmacokinetics: ADME & Dosing”?
pharmacokinetics-adme.explanation: Understanding bioequivalence is essential for grasping pharmacokinetics.

pharmacodynamics-receptors-dose-response.stem: A competitive (reversible) antagonist added to an agonist will:

options.text: Lower the maximal response (Emax) that cannot be overcome
Shift the agonist dose–response curve to the right in parallel, with Emax preserved if enough agonist is given
Have no effect on the agonist

pharmacodynamics-receptors-dose-response.explanation: A competitive antagonist binds reversibly at the same site, so adding more agonist can outcompete it (surmountable): the curve shifts right in parallel with a reduced apparent potency but a preserved maximum. A non-competitive/irreversible antagonist instead lowers Emax and cannot be overcome by more agonist.

pharmacodynamics-receptors-dose-response.stem: A narrow therapeutic index (e.g. warfarin, digoxin, lithium) means:

options.text: The drug is very safe with a wide margin
The toxic and effective doses are close, so small changes risk toxicity (monitoring needed)

pharmacodynamics-receptors-dose-response.explanation: The therapeutic index (TD50/ED50) measures the safety margin. A narrow (low) TI means the toxic and therapeutic doses are close together, so small dosing or pharmacokinetic changes can cause toxicity — hence drugs like warfarin, digoxin, lithium and phenytoin require plasma-level monitoring.

pharmacodynamics-receptors-dose-response.stem: Regarding potency vs efficacy — which is correct?

options.text: A more potent drug is always the better/stronger drug

POTENCY (position on the dose axis, EC50) only tells you the DOSE needed — a more potent drug works at a lower dose but may have the SAME or LOWER maximal effect; EFFICACY (Emax, the ceiling) is what determines the greatest achievable response. A low-potency, high-efficacy drug can outperform a high-potency, low-efficacy one

pharmacodynamics-receptors-dose-response.explanation: Confusing potency with efficacy misjudges drugs: potency is just a dose scaling (adjustable by giving more), whereas efficacy sets the maximum benefit — clinically, efficacy usually matters more than potency.

pharmacodynamics-receptors-dose-response.stem: What best explains the finding: “A drug that binds receptors but produces no response”?
pharmacodynamics-receptors-dose-response.explanation: A drug that binds receptors but produces no response → Antagonist (affinity without efficacy).

pharmacodynamics-receptors-dose-response.stem: What best explains the finding: “Agonist curve shifted right in parallel, same maximum”?
pharmacodynamics-receptors-dose-response.explanation: Agonist curve shifted right in parallel, same maximum → Competitive (reversible) antagonism (surmountable).

pharmacodynamics-receptors-dose-response.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Pharmacodynamics: Receptors & Dose–Response”?
pharmacodynamics-receptors-dose-response.explanation: Clinical applications of pharmacodynamics in the context of anxiolytics.

pharmacodynamics-receptors-dose-response.stem: Which should you review before “Pharmacodynamics: Receptors & Dose–Response”?
pharmacodynamics-receptors-dose-response.explanation: Understanding drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion is essential for pharmacodynamics.

antifungal-agents.stem: Amphotericin B exerts its antifungal effect by:

options.text: Binding ergosterol in the fungal membrane to form pores

antifungal-agents.explanation: Amphotericin B is a polyene that binds ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane, forming pores that cause leakage of ions and cell death (fungicidal). Azoles instead inhibit ergosterol synthesis (14-α-demethylase), and echinocandins block β-(1,3)-glucan cell-wall synthesis.

antifungal-agents.stem: A patient on IV amphotericin B for systemic mycosis is at greatest risk of which toxicity?
antifungal-agents.explanation: Amphotericin B is classically nephrotoxic (dose-dependent), causing renal impairment with potassium and magnesium wasting (hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia), along with infusion-related fever/rigors. Liposomal formulations reduce this toxicity.

antifungal-agents.stem: Regarding azole drug interactions — which is correct?

options.text: Azole antifungals only affect the fungus, so they are free of systemic drug interactions

Azoles inhibit the fungal CYP450 (14-α-demethylase) but ALSO inhibit HUMAN CYP450 enzymes, so they raise levels of many co-administered drugs (statins, warfarin, calcineurin inhibitors, etc.) and cause interactions and hepatotoxicity — a major clinical caution, especially with ketoconazole/itraconazole/voriconazole

antifungal-agents.explanation: The shared CYP450 chemistry means azoles are potent human enzyme inhibitors, so their interaction profile — not just antifungal spectrum — governs safe prescribing.

antifungal-agents.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rising creatinine + hypokalaemia during antifungal therapy”?
antifungal-agents.explanation: Rising creatinine + hypokalaemia during antifungal therapy → Amphotericin B nephrotoxicity.

antifungal-agents.stem: What best explains the finding: “Multiple drug interactions + hepatotoxicity with an oral antifungal”?
antifungal-agents.explanation: Multiple drug interactions + hepatotoxicity with an oral antifungal → Azole inhibition of human CYP450.

antifungal-agents.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Antifungal Agents”?
antifungal-agents.explanation: Clinical application of antifungals in treating skin infections.

anthelmintic-agents.stem: The drug of choice for schistosomiasis and for most tapeworm (cestode) infections is:
anthelmintic-agents.explanation: Praziquantel increases calcium permeability in the worm, causing tetanic paralysis and tegumental damage; it is the drug of choice for trematodes (schistosomes, liver/lung flukes) and most cestodes (tapeworms). Benzimidazoles cover intestinal nematodes, and ivermectin covers Strongyloides/onchocerciasis.

anthelmintic-agents.stem: Albendazole and mebendazole kill nematodes primarily by:

options.text: Binding β-tubulin to block microtubule assembly and glucose uptake (starving the worm)

anthelmintic-agents.explanation: Benzimidazoles bind parasite β-tubulin, inhibiting microtubule polymerisation and glucose uptake, effectively starving the worm of energy. Ivermectin acts on glutamate-gated chloride channels, and praziquantel increases calcium permeability.

anthelmintic-agents.stem: Regarding matching anthelmintic to worm class — which is correct?

options.text: One anthelmintic (e.g. albendazole) treats all worms equally well

Drug choice depends on worm CLASS: benzimidazoles (albendazole/mebendazole) are the broad NEMATODE (roundworm) drugs, but PRAZIQUANTEL is required for TREMATODES (flukes) and most CESTODES (tapeworms), and IVERMECTIN is specific for Strongyloides and onchocerciasis — using the wrong class fails

anthelmintic-agents.explanation: Helminths differ in the drug targets they express, so the nematode/trematode/cestode classification (from parasitology) dictates the correct agent — a frequent exam and clinical decision point.

anthelmintic-agents.stem: What best explains the finding: “Broad-spectrum oral drug for intestinal roundworms”?
anthelmintic-agents.explanation: Broad-spectrum oral drug for intestinal roundworms → Albendazole/mebendazole (benzimidazole, β-tubulin).

anthelmintic-agents.stem: What best explains the finding: “Drug of choice for schistosomiasis and tapeworms”?
anthelmintic-agents.explanation: Drug of choice for schistosomiasis and tapeworms → Praziquantel (↑Ca²⁺ permeability).

anthelmintic-agents.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Anthelmintic Agents”?
anthelmintic-agents.explanation: Ivermectin is used in clinical settings for scabies treatment.

anthelmintic-agents.stem: Which should you review before “Anthelmintic Agents”?
anthelmintic-agents.explanation: Understanding helminth classification is essential for selecting appropriate anthelmintic agents.

antiviral-antiretroviral-agents.stem: Aciclovir is selectively active against herpes-infected cells because it is first phosphorylated by:

options.text: Host thymidine kinase in all cells
Viral thymidine kinase, present only in infected cells

antiviral-antiretroviral-agents.explanation: Aciclovir requires initial monophosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase, which is present only in HSV/VZV-infected cells; host enzymes then complete activation. The active triphosphate chain-terminates viral DNA polymerase. This viral-activation step gives aciclovir its selectivity and safety.

antiviral-antiretroviral-agents.stem: Standard treatment of HIV infection (HAART) uses:

options.text: A combination of at least three drugs from at least two classes

antiviral-antiretroviral-agents.explanation: HIV is treated with combination antiretroviral therapy — at least three drugs from at least two classes (e.g. two NRTIs plus an integrase inhibitor) — to maximally suppress viral replication and prevent the emergence of resistance. Monotherapy rapidly selects resistant virus.

antiviral-antiretroviral-agents.stem: Regarding why aciclovir is selectively toxic to virus — which is correct?

options.text: Aciclovir directly inhibits DNA polymerase in all cells, so it is broadly cytotoxic

Aciclovir is a PRODRUG that must be MONOPHOSPHORYLATED by VIRAL thymidine kinase (present only in HSV/VZV-infected cells) before host kinases finish activating it — so it is concentrated and active almost exclusively in infected cells, giving its selectivity and low toxicity; thymidine-kinase-deficient mutants are resistant

antiviral-antiretroviral-agents.explanation: The viral-enzyme activation step is what makes aciclovir safe and selective, and explains why TK-negative resistant strains need foscarnet (which acts directly on the polymerase, no activation needed).

antiviral-antiretroviral-agents.stem: What best explains the finding: “Selective anti-HSV drug requiring viral thymidine kinase for activation”?
antiviral-antiretroviral-agents.explanation: Selective anti-HSV drug requiring viral thymidine kinase for activation → Aciclovir (chain-terminates viral DNA polymerase).

antiviral-antiretroviral-agents.stem: What best explains the finding: “Influenza drug most effective within 48 h of symptom onset”?
antiviral-antiretroviral-agents.explanation: Influenza drug most effective within 48 h of symptom onset → Oseltamivir (neuraminidase inhibitor).

antiviral-antiretroviral-agents.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Antiviral & Antiretroviral Agents”?
antiviral-antiretroviral-agents.explanation: Focuses on antiviral drugs used in respiratory infections.

antibacterial-cell-wall-agents.stem: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) resists β-lactams through:

options.text: An altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a, encoded by mecA)

antibacterial-cell-wall-agents.explanation: MRSA carries the mecA gene encoding PBP2a, an altered penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for β-lactams, making it resistant to all standard β-lactam antibiotics (so vancomycin or newer anti-MRSA agents are needed). β-lactamase production is a separate mechanism defeated by inhibitors.

antibacterial-cell-wall-agents.stem: Oral vancomycin is used specifically to treat:

options.text: Clostridioides difficile colitis (because it is not absorbed and acts in the gut lumen)

antibacterial-cell-wall-agents.explanation: Vancomycin is not absorbed from the gut, so oral vancomycin stays in the lumen and is used for C. difficile colitis. Systemic Gram-positive/MRSA infections require intravenous vancomycin, where nephrotoxicity and red-man syndrome are the key concerns.

antibacterial-cell-wall-agents.stem: Regarding red-man syndrome vs true allergy — which is correct?

options.text: Flushing during a vancomycin infusion means the patient is allergic and must never receive it again

"Red-man syndrome" is a rate-related, non-immune HISTAMINE release reaction (flushing/erythema of the upper body) — NOT an IgE allergy; it is managed by SLOWING the infusion (± antihistamine), and vancomycin can still be used, unlike a true anaphylactic allergy

antibacterial-cell-wall-agents.explanation: Mislabelling red-man syndrome as allergy needlessly removes a key anti-MRSA drug; recognising it as an infusion-rate phenomenon allows safe continued use.

antibacterial-cell-wall-agents.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bactericidal drug blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking”?
antibacterial-cell-wall-agents.explanation: Bactericidal drug blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking → β-lactam binding penicillin-binding proteins.

antibacterial-cell-wall-agents.stem: What best explains the finding: “MRSA resistant to all standard β-lactams”?
antibacterial-cell-wall-agents.explanation: MRSA resistant to all standard β-lactams → Altered PBP2a (mecA gene).

antibacterial-cell-wall-agents.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Antibacterials I: Cell-Wall Agents”?
antibacterial-cell-wall-agents.explanation: Knowledge of cell-wall agents is relevant for selecting antibiotics for respiratory infections.

antibacterial-cell-wall-agents.stem: Which should you review before “Antibacterials I: Cell-Wall Agents”?
antibacterial-cell-wall-agents.explanation: Understanding bacterial cell wall structure is essential for grasping how cell-wall agents function.

antibacterial-protein-synthesis-inhibito.stem: A patient on ciprofloxacin develops posterior ankle pain and is warned about tendon rupture. Fluoroquinolones act by inhibiting:

options.text: DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV

antibacterial-protein-synthesis-inhibito.explanation: Fluoroquinolones inhibit bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, blocking DNA supercoiling/replication (bactericidal). Class toxicities include tendonitis/rupture, QT prolongation, CNS effects and dysglycaemia, and they are generally avoided in children and pregnancy.

options.text: Sequentially blocking two steps of bacterial folate synthesis (dihydropteroate synthase and dihydrofolate reductase)
Inhibiting DNA gyrase and RNA polymerase

antibacterial-protein-synthesis-inhibito.explanation: Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase and trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase — sequential steps in the bacterial folate pathway — giving synergistic, often bactericidal, blockade. Humans obtain folate from the diet, providing selectivity.

antibacterial-protein-synthesis-inhibito.stem: Regarding rifampin: inducer vs inhibitor — which is correct?

options.text: Antibiotics that affect CYP450 all raise the levels of co-administered drugs

RIFAMPIN is a potent CYP450 INDUCER — it LOWERS levels of many drugs (warfarin, oral contraceptives, protease inhibitors, etc.), risking therapeutic failure — whereas MACROLIDES (e.g. clarithromycin/erythromycin) are CYP INHIBITORS that RAISE drug levels; direction of the interaction is opposite

antibacterial-protein-synthesis-inhibito.explanation: Confusing induction with inhibition inverts the clinical consequence (failure vs toxicity) — rifampin can cause contraceptive failure or subtherapeutic anticoagulation, while macrolides cause accumulation/toxicity.

antibacterial-protein-synthesis-inhibito.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity with a bactericidal Gram-negative agent”?
antibacterial-protein-synthesis-inhibito.explanation: Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity with a bactericidal Gram-negative agent → Aminoglycoside (30S, concentration-dependent).

antibacterial-protein-synthesis-inhibito.stem: What best explains the finding: “Tooth discolouration if given to a child/pregnant patient”?
antibacterial-protein-synthesis-inhibito.explanation: Tooth discolouration if given to a child/pregnant patient → Tetracycline (chelates calcium in bone/teeth).

antibacterial-protein-synthesis-inhibito.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Antibacterials II: Protein, DNA & Folate Inhibitors”?

options.text: Nephrotoxic Drugs & Prescribing in Renal Impairment

antibacterial-protein-synthesis-inhibito.explanation: Awareness of nephrotoxic effects of aminoglycosides is critical in prescribing.

antibacterial-protein-synthesis-inhibito.stem: Which should you review before “Antibacterials II: Protein, DNA & Folate Inhibitors”?
antibacterial-protein-synthesis-inhibito.explanation: Understanding protein synthesis is essential for grasping antibacterial mechanisms.

cholinergic-drugs.stem: A farmer presents with pinpoint pupils, profuse salivation, bronchorrhoea, bradycardia and muscle fasciculations after pesticide exposure. The best initial pharmacologic management is:
cholinergic-drugs.explanation: This is a cholinergic crisis from organophosphate (AChE inhibitor) poisoning. Atropine blocks the muscarinic effects, and pralidoxime reactivates acetylcholinesterase (given early, before ageing) to address the nicotinic neuromuscular effects. Giving more cholinergic drug (pyridostigmine/neostigmine/bethanechol) would worsen it.

cholinergic-drugs.stem: Which drug is an antimuscarinic used as an inhaled bronchodilator in COPD?
cholinergic-drugs.explanation: Ipratropium (and tiotropium) are inhaled antimuscarinic agents that block muscarinic-mediated bronchoconstriction, producing bronchodilation with limited systemic absorption. Pilocarpine and bethanechol are muscarinic agonists, and pyridostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor.

cholinergic-drugs.stem: Regarding what atropine does and does not treat in op poisoning — which is correct?

options.text: Atropine alone fully reverses organophosphate poisoning

Atropine only blocks the MUSCARINIC effects (secretions, bradycardia, bronchoconstriction) — it does NOT relieve the NICOTINIC effects (muscle weakness, fasciculations, paralysis, respiratory muscle failure); those require PRALIDOXIME (to reactivate acetylcholinesterase before "ageing") plus airway/ventilatory support

cholinergic-drugs.explanation: Relying on atropine alone leaves the life-threatening nicotinic neuromuscular failure untreated; pralidoxime and ventilation are essential, and pralidoxime must be given early before the enzyme–OP bond "ages" irreversibly.

cholinergic-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “SLUDGE, miosis, bradycardia, bronchorrhoea, fasciculations after insecticide exposure”?
cholinergic-drugs.explanation: SLUDGE, miosis, bradycardia, bronchorrhoea, fasciculations after insecticide exposure → Organophosphate (irreversible AChE inhibition) — cholinergic crisis.

cholinergic-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Improved strength in myasthenia gravis with an oral drug”?
cholinergic-drugs.explanation: Improved strength in myasthenia gravis with an oral drug → Pyridostigmine (AChE inhibitor).

cholinergic-drugs.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Cholinergic (Parasympathetic) Drugs”?
cholinergic-drugs.explanation: Cholinergic drugs act on the autonomic nervous system.

cholinergic-drugs.stem: Which should you review before “Cholinergic (Parasympathetic) Drugs”?
cholinergic-drugs.explanation: Basic metabolic pathways may relate to drug metabolism.

adrenergic-drugs.stem: The drug of choice for anaphylaxis is adrenaline because it simultaneously:

options.text: Causes α1 vasoconstriction, β2 bronchodilation and β1 cardiac support

adrenergic-drugs.explanation: Adrenaline activates α1 (reversing vasodilation/hypotension and mucosal oedema), β2 (bronchodilation) and β1 (cardiac support) receptors — addressing all the life-threatening features of anaphylaxis at once, which is why it is first-line and given intramuscularly without delay.

adrenergic-drugs.stem: A cardioselective β-blocker (e.g. metoprolol, bisoprolol) is preferred over a non-selective one in a patient with asthma because it:

options.text: Preferentially blocks β1 and spares β2, reducing the risk of bronchospasm

adrenergic-drugs.explanation: Cardioselective β-blockers preferentially antagonise β1 (cardiac) receptors and largely spare β2 (bronchial) receptors, lowering the risk of bronchospasm in asthma/COPD — though selectivity is relative and lost at higher doses, so caution remains.

adrenergic-drugs.stem: Regarding β-blockade in phaeochromocytoma — which is correct?

options.text: A hypertensive, tachycardic phaeochromocytoma patient should be given a β-blocker first to control heart rate

Giving a β-blocker FIRST is dangerous: blocking β2-mediated vasodilation leaves α1 vasoconstriction UNOPPOSED, precipitating a hypertensive crisis — α-blockade (e.g. phenoxybenzamine) must be established BEFORE any β-blocker in phaeochromocytoma
Adrenaline (α1 vasoconstriction + β2 bronchodilation + β1 support)

adrenergic-drugs.explanation: The catecholamine excess acts on both α and β; removing the β vasodilatory brake before controlling α causes severe vasoconstriction — hence the strict "α before β" sequence.

adrenergic-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “First-line drug for anaphylaxis”?

options.text: β-blocker adverse effects (use cardioselective in asthma/diabetes)
Adrenaline (α1 vasoconstriction + β2 bronchodilation + β1 support)

adrenergic-drugs.explanation: First-line drug for anaphylaxis → Adrenaline (α1 vasoconstriction + β2 bronchodilation + β1 support).

adrenergic-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rescue bronchodilation in acute asthma”?

options.text: Adrenaline (α1 vasoconstriction + β2 bronchodilation + β1 support)
β-blocker adverse effects (use cardioselective in asthma/diabetes)

adrenergic-drugs.explanation: Rescue bronchodilation in acute asthma → Short-acting β2-agonist (salbutamol).

adrenergic-drugs.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Adrenergic (Sympathetic) Drugs”?
adrenergic-drugs.explanation: Adrenergic drugs are a key component of the autonomic nervous system.

adrenergic-drugs.stem: Which should you review before “Adrenergic (Sympathetic) Drugs”?
adrenergic-drugs.explanation: Understanding adrenergic drugs requires knowledge of the opposing cholinergic system.

antineoplastic-principles.stem: High-dose methotrexate toxicity is limited by "rescuing" normal cells with:
antineoplastic-principles.explanation: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking folate regeneration. Leucovorin (folinic acid) is a reduced folate that bypasses the block and rescues normal cells. (Mesna prevents cyclophosphamide cystitis; dexrazoxane protects against anthracycline cardiotoxicity.)

antineoplastic-principles.stem: Which agent causes cumulative, dose-dependent cardiotoxicity?
antineoplastic-principles.explanation: Anthracyclines such as doxorubicin cause cumulative dose-dependent cardiotoxicity (dilated cardiomyopathy/heart failure), monitored by cumulative dose and cardiac function. Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis, vincristine neuropathy, and cisplatin nephro/ototoxicity.

antineoplastic-principles.stem: Regarding why chemotherapy causes its shared toxicities — which is correct?

options.text: Chemotherapy toxicity means the drug is attacking the wrong (non-cancer) organs by mistake

Classic cytotoxic chemotherapy targets RAPIDLY DIVIDING cells, so it predictably harms the fastest-dividing NORMAL tissues — bone marrow (myelosuppression), GI mucosa (mucositis), hair follicles (alopecia) — because they share the proliferative feature being attacked, not because of off-target error; this is why the therapeutic index is narrow
Toxicity to rapidly dividing normal cells (myelosuppression)

antineoplastic-principles.explanation: Understanding that toxicity follows proliferation rate (not random off-target effects) explains the predictable side-effect profile, the use of growth-factor/mucosal support, and why targeted agents (which exploit tumour-specific molecules) spare these tissues better.

antineoplastic-principles.stem: What best explains the finding: “Neutropenia, mucositis and alopecia during chemotherapy”?

options.text: Toxicity to rapidly dividing normal cells (myelosuppression)

antineoplastic-principles.explanation: Neutropenia, mucositis and alopecia during chemotherapy → Toxicity to rapidly dividing normal cells (myelosuppression).

antineoplastic-principles.stem: What best explains the finding: “Haemorrhagic cystitis prevented by mesna”?

options.text: Toxicity to rapidly dividing normal cells (myelosuppression)

antineoplastic-principles.explanation: Haemorrhagic cystitis prevented by mesna → Cyclophosphamide (acrolein metabolite).

antineoplastic-principles.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Principles of Antineoplastic Agents”?
antineoplastic-principles.explanation: Understanding chemotherapy principles is essential for treating urinary system neoplasms.

antineoplastic-principles.stem: Which should you review before “Principles of Antineoplastic Agents”?
antineoplastic-principles.explanation: Antimetabolites and their mechanisms are foundational for understanding chemotherapy.

drug-interactions-mechanisms.stem: Adding clarithromycin (a CYP3A4 inhibitor) to a patient on simvastatin most likely causes:

options.text: Reduced statin effect and higher cholesterol
Increased statin levels and risk of myopathy/rhabdomyolysis

drug-interactions-mechanisms.explanation: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4, which metabolises simvastatin, so statin levels rise and the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis increases. CYP inhibitors raise substrate concentrations (toxicity), whereas inducers like rifampin lower them (failure).

drug-interactions-mechanisms.stem: Rifampin reduces the effectiveness of many drugs (e.g. oral contraceptives, warfarin) because it:

options.text: Induces CYP450, accelerating their metabolism and lowering their levels

drug-interactions-mechanisms.explanation: Rifampin is a potent CYP450 inducer: it increases enzyme synthesis over days, accelerating metabolism of many substrates and lowering their levels — causing therapeutic failure such as contraceptive failure or subtherapeutic anticoagulation. Its effect is delayed in both onset and offset.

drug-interactions-mechanisms.stem: Regarding time course of inducers vs inhibitors — which is correct?

options.text: CYP inducers and inhibitors both change drug levels immediately

CYP INHIBITION is usually FAST (competitive, within a dose or two → rapid rise and toxicity), whereas CYP INDUCTION is SLOW in onset AND offset (it requires synthesis of new enzyme over days–weeks, and levels take days to fall when the inducer is added and to recover when it is stopped) — so induction interactions are easy to miss and persist after stopping the inducer

drug-interactions-mechanisms.explanation: The delayed, prolonged course of enzyme induction means a substrate can fail days after adding rifampin and become toxic days after stopping it — a timing trap that immediate-effect thinking misses.

drug-interactions-mechanisms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Warfarin over-anticoagulation after starting an azole/macrolide”?
drug-interactions-mechanisms.explanation: Warfarin over-anticoagulation after starting an azole/macrolide → CYP inhibition raising warfarin level.

drug-interactions-mechanisms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Subtherapeutic drug levels / contraceptive failure on rifampin”?
drug-interactions-mechanisms.explanation: Subtherapeutic drug levels / contraceptive failure on rifampin → CYP induction lowering substrate levels.

drug-interactions-mechanisms.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Drug Interactions”?
Which should you review before “Drug Interactions”?
drug-interactions-mechanisms.explanation: Understanding ADME is essential for grasping drug interactions.

antidotes-principles.stem: The antidote for paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose works by:
antidotes-principles.explanation: Paracetamol overdose depletes glutathione, allowing the toxic metabolite NAPQI to accumulate and injure the liver. N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione (and provides substrate), detoxifying NAPQI — most effective when given early and guided by the timed-level nomogram.

antidotes-principles.stem: Which poison is correctly paired with its antidote?
antidotes-principles.explanation: Organophosphate (cholinergic crisis) is treated with atropine (muscarinic blockade) plus pralidoxime (reactivates acetylcholinesterase). Iron→deferoxamine, warfarin→vitamin K (protamine reverses heparin), and opioids→naloxone (flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines).

antidotes-principles.stem: Regarding role of specific antidotes — which is correct?

options.text: Every poisoning has a specific antidote that is the main treatment

Only a MINORITY of poisons have a specific antidote; the mainstay for most overdoses is SUPPORTIVE care (airway, breathing, circulation) plus decontamination/enhanced elimination — and even when an antidote exists, timing and correct use (e.g. NAC within the effective window, pralidoxime before ageing, avoiding flumazenil in seizure-prone patients) are critical

antidotes-principles.explanation: Over-focusing on antidotes neglects the supportive care that actually saves most poisoned patients, and misusing an antidote (wrong timing/indication) can be ineffective or harmful.

antidotes-principles.stem: What best explains the finding: “Opioid triad (coma, respiratory depression, pinpoint pupils) reversed by an antagonist”?
antidotes-principles.explanation: Opioid triad (coma, respiratory depression, pinpoint pupils) reversed by an antagonist → Naloxone (opioid receptor blockade).

antidotes-principles.stem: What best explains the finding: “Paracetamol overdose treated by replenishing glutathione”?
antidotes-principles.explanation: Paracetamol overdose treated by replenishing glutathione → N-acetylcysteine (early, nomogram-guided).

antidotes-principles.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Principles of Antidotes”?
antidotes-principles.explanation: Understanding acid-base balance is crucial in managing certain poisonings.

antidotes-principles.stem: Which should you review before “Principles of Antidotes”?
antidotes-principles.explanation: Understanding antidotes for cholinergic toxicity requires knowledge of cholinergic drugs.

immunomodulating-agents.stem: Ciclosporin and tacrolimus suppress the immune system by ultimately reducing production of:

options.text: Interleukin-2 (via calcineurin inhibition), reducing T-cell activation

immunomodulating-agents.explanation: Ciclosporin (via cyclophilin) and tacrolimus (via FKBP) inhibit calcineurin, preventing dephosphorylation of NFAT and thus transcription of IL-2. Reduced IL-2 curtails T-cell activation/proliferation. Their key toxicity is nephrotoxicity, and they need level monitoring.

immunomodulating-agents.stem: Before starting anti-TNF-α biologic therapy, it is essential to screen for:
immunomodulating-agents.explanation: TNF-α maintains granulomas that contain Mycobacterium tuberculosis, so anti-TNF agents can reactivate latent TB (and hepatitis B). Screening and treating latent infection before starting therapy is mandatory. Immunosuppression also contraindicates live vaccines.

immunomodulating-agents.stem: Regarding biologics and latent infection — which is correct?

options.text: Targeted biologics like anti-TNF agents are precise, so they carry little infection risk

Anti-TNF-α agents specifically neutralise a cytokine ESSENTIAL for granuloma maintenance, so they characteristically REACTIVATE latent tuberculosis (and hepatitis B) — patients must be SCREENED and treated for latent TB before starting; targeted does not mean low-risk for infection

immunomodulating-agents.explanation: TNF-α is central to containing intracellular pathogens in granulomas, so blocking it unmasks latent TB — a mandatory pre-treatment screen that a "precise = safe" assumption would miss.

immunomodulating-agents.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nephrotoxicity, hypertension and tremor in a transplant patient”?
immunomodulating-agents.explanation: Nephrotoxicity, hypertension and tremor in a transplant patient → Calcineurin inhibitor (ciclosporin/tacrolimus) toxicity.

immunomodulating-agents.stem: What best explains the finding: “Reactivation of latent tuberculosis after starting a biologic”?
immunomodulating-agents.explanation: Reactivation of latent tuberculosis after starting a biologic → Anti-TNF-α therapy (screen TB before starting).

immunomodulating-agents.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Immunomodulating Agents”?
immunomodulating-agents.explanation: Some immunomodulating agents are used in dermatologic conditions.

immunomodulating-agents.stem: Which should you review before “Immunomodulating Agents”?
immunomodulating-agents.explanation: Understanding drug interactions is crucial for managing immunomodulating agents.

pharmacogenomics.stem: Why can codeine cause dangerous opioid toxicity in a CYP2D6 "ultrarapid metaboliser"?

options.text: Codeine is a prodrug converted by CYP2D6 to morphine, so ultrarapid metabolism produces excess morphine

pharmacogenomics.explanation: Codeine is a prodrug activated by CYP2D6 to morphine. Ultrarapid metabolisers convert more codeine to morphine, risking respiratory depression (notably in children and breastfed infants), whereas poor metabolisers get little analgesia. The prodrug relationship reverses the usual metaboliser–risk logic.

pharmacogenomics.stem: Screening for HLA-B*15:02 before prescribing carbamazepine (especially in Southeast Asian patients) reduces the risk of:
pharmacogenomics.explanation: HLA-B*15:02 strongly predisposes to carbamazepine-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis, particularly in Southeast Asian populations, so genotyping before prescribing prevents these life-threatening severe cutaneous adverse reactions. (HLA-B*57:01→abacavir, HLA-B*58:01→allopurinol are analogous.)

pharmacogenomics.stem: Regarding poor vs ultrarapid metaboliser with a prodrug — which is correct?

options.text: A "poor metaboliser" is always at higher risk of drug toxicity

It depends on whether the drug is ACTIVE or a PRODRUG: for an ACTIVE drug, a poor metaboliser accumulates it (toxicity); but for a PRODRUG (e.g. codeine → morphine, clopidogrel → active metabolite), the poor metaboliser UNDER-activates it (treatment failure), while the ULTRARAPID metaboliser over-activates it (toxicity — e.g. codeine-induced respiratory depression)
CYP2D6 ultrarapid metaboliser (excess morphine from prodrug)

pharmacogenomics.explanation: The prodrug/active-drug distinction inverts the risk of each metaboliser phenotype, so predicting toxicity vs failure requires knowing whether metabolism activates or inactivates the drug.

pharmacogenomics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Opioid toxicity in a child given codeine”?

options.text: CYP2D6 ultrarapid metaboliser (excess morphine from prodrug)

pharmacogenomics.explanation: Opioid toxicity in a child given codeine → CYP2D6 ultrarapid metaboliser (excess morphine from prodrug).

pharmacogenomics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Reduced antiplatelet effect of clopidogrel”?

options.text: CYP2D6 ultrarapid metaboliser (excess morphine from prodrug)

pharmacogenomics.explanation: Reduced antiplatelet effect of clopidogrel → CYP2C19 poor metaboliser (prodrug under-activated).

pharmacogenomics.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Pharmacogenomics”?
pharmacogenomics.explanation: Pharmacogenomics is linked to the risk of cutaneous drug reactions.
Understanding drug interactions is essential for pharmacogenomics.

adverse-drug-reactions-allergy.stem: A dose-dependent, predictable adverse reaction that is an extension of a drug's known pharmacology (e.g. hypoglycaemia from insulin) is classified as:
adverse-drug-reactions-allergy.explanation: Type A ("augmented") ADRs are dose-dependent, predictable extensions of the drug's pharmacological action (e.g. bleeding on warfarin, hypoglycaemia on insulin, bradycardia on β-blockers) and are common. Type B reactions are unpredictable, host-dependent (allergy/idiosyncrasy) and dose-independent.

adverse-drug-reactions-allergy.stem: The immediate first-line treatment for drug-induced anaphylaxis is:
adverse-drug-reactions-allergy.explanation: Anaphylaxis (Type I, IgE-mediated) is treated first with intramuscular adrenaline, which reverses vasodilation/hypotension (α1), bronchospasm (β2) and supports the heart (β1). Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts, not substitutes, and must not delay adrenaline.

adverse-drug-reactions-allergy.stem: Regarding true allergy vs side-effect vs pseudo-allergy — which is correct?

options.text: Any unpleasant reaction to a drug is a drug "allergy" that permanently contraindicates it

Only IMMUNE-mediated (Gell-Coombs) reactions are true allergy; predictable pharmacologic SIDE-EFFECTS (e.g. nausea, dose-related effects) and PSEUDO-ALLERGY (direct mast-cell release — vancomycin red-man, contrast, opioids; not IgE) are NOT true allergies — mislabelling them wrongly removes useful drugs, though genuine anaphylaxis and SCARs (SJS/TEN/DRESS) do mandate strict avoidance

adverse-drug-reactions-allergy.explanation: Over-labelling side-effects/pseudo-allergy as allergy (e.g. "penicillin allergy") drives use of inferior, broader antibiotics; accurate classification preserves options while still protecting against genuine IgE anaphylaxis and life-threatening SCARs.

adverse-drug-reactions-allergy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Predictable, dose-related bleeding on warfarin”?

options.text: SJS/TEN (Type IV SCAR) — stop the drug

adverse-drug-reactions-allergy.explanation: Predictable, dose-related bleeding on warfarin → Type A (augmented) ADR.

adverse-drug-reactions-allergy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm and hypotension minutes after a drug”?

options.text: SJS/TEN (Type IV SCAR) — stop the drug

adverse-drug-reactions-allergy.explanation: Urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm and hypotension minutes after a drug → Type I (IgE) anaphylaxis → IM adrenaline.

adverse-drug-reactions-allergy.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Adverse Drug Reactions & Drug Allergy”?
adverse-drug-reactions-allergy.explanation: This module covers reactions relevant to drug allergies.

adverse-drug-reactions-allergy.stem: Which should you review before “Adverse Drug Reactions & Drug Allergy”?
adverse-drug-reactions-allergy.explanation: Understanding ADR types is crucial for drug allergy classification.

preclinical-drug-discovery.stem: The primary purpose of preclinical toxicology studies before first-in-human trials is to:

options.text: Prove the drug is effective in patients
Characterise toxicity and define a safe starting dose

preclinical-drug-discovery.explanation: Preclinical (in-vitro and animal) toxicology characterises acute/chronic toxicity, genotoxicity, carcinogenicity and reproductive effects, defining the therapeutic window and a safe first-in-human starting dose. Efficacy in humans is established later in Phase II/III trials.

preclinical-drug-discovery.stem: The regulatory application that must be approved before a candidate drug can first be given to humans is the:
preclinical-drug-discovery.explanation: The Investigational New Drug (IND) application, supported by preclinical data, permits the start of human clinical trials. After successful Phase I–III trials, a New Drug Application (NDA)/marketing authorisation is submitted to market the drug.

preclinical-drug-discovery.stem: Regarding role of preclinical testing — which is correct?

options.text: Preclinical animal studies mainly prove that a drug works

Preclinical studies primarily establish SAFETY (toxicology) and PK/mechanism to justify first-in-human dosing and set a safe STARTING DOSE — efficacy in humans is only established later in Phase II/III; animal efficacy is supportive but does not reliably predict clinical benefit

preclinical-drug-discovery.explanation: Over-reading preclinical efficacy leads to over-confidence; the essential output of preclinical work is a safety/PK package (and starting dose), with human efficacy still to be proven in trials.

preclinical-drug-discovery.stem: What best explains the finding: “Animal/in-vitro studies defining toxicity and a safe first dose”?
preclinical-drug-discovery.explanation: Animal/in-vitro studies defining toxicity and a safe first dose → Preclinical development.

preclinical-drug-discovery.stem: What best explains the finding: “The regulatory step permitting first-in-human trials”?
preclinical-drug-discovery.explanation: The regulatory step permitting first-in-human trials → Investigational New Drug (IND) application.

preclinical-drug-discovery.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Drug Discovery & Preclinical Development”?
preclinical-drug-discovery.explanation: Understanding drug effects in clinical scenarios like STEMI.

preclinical-drug-discovery.stem: Which should you review before “Drug Discovery & Preclinical Development”?

options.text: Germ Theory → Modern Medicine: Vaccines, Antisepsis, Antibiotics & EBM

preclinical-drug-discovery.explanation: Understanding germ theory is foundational for drug discovery and development.

drug-absorption-routes.stem: Glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) is given sublingually rather than swallowed because the sublingual route:

options.text: Bypasses hepatic first-pass metabolism, giving rapid systemic levels
Slows absorption for a depot effect

drug-absorption-routes.explanation: Sublingual absorption drains into the systemic venous circulation, largely bypassing the hepatic portal system and first-pass metabolism, so GTN reaches the circulation rapidly and effectively — important for a drug otherwise heavily metabolised on first pass.

drug-absorption-routes.stem: A weak acid such as aspirin is best absorbed in the stomach because in the acidic gastric environment it is largely:
drug-absorption-routes.explanation: In an acidic environment a weak acid stays largely un-ionised (protonated), which is lipid-soluble and diffuses across membranes readily. Ionised drug is "trapped" and poorly absorbed — the principle of pH partitioning/ion trapping.

drug-absorption-routes.stem: Regarding first-pass metabolism and route choice — which is correct?

options.text: If a drug is well absorbed from the gut, its oral bioavailability must be high

Good gut ABSORPTION does not guarantee high BIOAVAILABILITY — a well-absorbed drug can still have low oral F if it undergoes extensive FIRST-PASS metabolism in the gut wall and liver before reaching the systemic circulation, which is why some drugs are given IV, sublingually or rectally to bypass the liver

drug-absorption-routes.explanation: Bioavailability reflects absorption MINUS first-pass loss; ignoring first-pass overestimates oral F and misjudges route/dose choices (e.g. GTN, propranolol).

drug-absorption-routes.stem: What best explains the finding: “A large oral-to-IV dose difference for the same effect”?

options.text: Weak acid un-ionised in acidic gastric pH (ion trapping)

drug-absorption-routes.explanation: A large oral-to-IV dose difference for the same effect → Extensive first-pass metabolism (low oral F).

drug-absorption-routes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sublingual GTN acting faster than swallowed GTN”?

options.text: Weak acid un-ionised in acidic gastric pH (ion trapping)

drug-absorption-routes.explanation: Sublingual GTN acting faster than swallowed GTN → Sublingual route bypasses hepatic first-pass.

drug-absorption-routes.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Drug Absorption & Routes of Administration”?
drug-absorption-routes.explanation: Understanding hormone absorption may relate to drug absorption.

drug-absorption-routes.stem: Which should you review before “Drug Absorption & Routes of Administration”?
drug-absorption-routes.explanation: Understanding bioavailability is crucial for drug development.

drug-metabolism-cyp450.stem: Phase I drug metabolism reactions are predominantly carried out by:
drug-metabolism-cyp450.explanation: Phase I reactions (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) are dominated by the cytochrome P450 enzyme family, which introduces or exposes functional groups. Phase II conjugation (e.g. glucuronidation by UGTs) then adds polar groups to make metabolites water-soluble for excretion.

drug-metabolism-cyp450.stem: A CYP inducer such as rifampin will, over several days, cause the plasma level of a CYP-metabolised substrate to:
drug-metabolism-cyp450.explanation: CYP inducers increase enzyme synthesis over days, accelerating metabolism of substrates and lowering their plasma levels — risking therapeutic failure (e.g. contraceptive failure). The effect is delayed in onset and offset, unlike the rapid rise caused by CYP inhibitors.

drug-metabolism-cyp450.stem: Regarding prodrug response to enzyme inhibition — which is correct?

options.text: A CYP inhibitor always increases a drug's effect by raising its level

For an ordinary ACTIVE drug a CYP inhibitor raises levels and effect/toxicity, but for a PRODRUG that CYP ACTIVATES (e.g. codeine→morphine, clopidogrel), inhibiting the enzyme REDUCES formation of the active metabolite and DECREASES the effect — the prodrug relationship reverses the expected direction

drug-metabolism-cyp450.explanation: Whether metabolism activates or inactivates a drug flips the consequence of enzyme inhibition/induction (and of metaboliser genotype), so knowing prodrug status is essential to predict the interaction.

drug-metabolism-cyp450.stem: What best explains the finding: “A drug with no activity until metabolised (e.g. codeine → morphine)”?
drug-metabolism-cyp450.explanation: A drug with no activity until metabolised (e.g. codeine → morphine) → Prodrug requiring CYP activation.

drug-metabolism-cyp450.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hepatotoxicity in paracetamol overdose once glutathione is depleted”?
drug-metabolism-cyp450.explanation: Hepatotoxicity in paracetamol overdose once glutathione is depleted → Toxic metabolite NAPQI accumulation.

drug-metabolism-cyp450.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Drug Metabolism & the Cytochrome P450 System”?

options.text: Development of the Kidney & Urinary Tract

drug-metabolism-cyp450.explanation: Understanding kidney development may provide insights into drug excretion.

drug-metabolism-cyp450.stem: Which should you review before “Drug Metabolism & the Cytochrome P450 System”?
drug-metabolism-cyp450.explanation: Basic understanding of developmental biology may aid in grasping drug metabolism concepts.

agonists-antagonists-pharmacology.stem: A partial agonist administered together with a full agonist at the same receptor will:

options.text: Increase the maximal response above that of the full agonist
Reduce the response toward the partial agonist's lower ceiling (acting as a partial antagonist)
Convert the full agonist into an antagonist

agonists-antagonists-pharmacology.explanation: A partial agonist has lower intrinsic efficacy (a sub-maximal ceiling). In the presence of a full agonist it competes for receptors and lowers the overall response toward its own maximum — effectively acting as a partial antagonist (e.g. buprenorphine precipitating opioid withdrawal).

options.text: Affinity with zero efficacy (binds without activating)

agonists-antagonists-pharmacology.explanation: An antagonist binds the receptor (has affinity) but produces no activation (zero efficacy), thereby blocking agonist access. A drug reducing baseline constitutive activity is an inverse agonist, and one with affinity and efficacy is an agonist.

agonists-antagonists-pharmacology.stem: Regarding partial agonist in the presence of a full agonist — which is correct?

options.text: A partial agonist always increases receptor activity, so adding it to a full agonist boosts the response

A PARTIAL agonist has a LOWER maximal effect, so when a FULL agonist is already present, the partial agonist COMPETES for receptors and pulls the response DOWN toward its own lower ceiling — behaving as a PARTIAL ANTAGONIST (e.g. buprenorphine can precipitate opioid withdrawal by displacing a full agonist)

agonists-antagonists-pharmacology.explanation: The net effect of a partial agonist depends on context: alone it stimulates, but against a full agonist it reduces the response — a clinically critical point for drugs like buprenorphine and β-blockers with partial agonism.

agonists-antagonists-pharmacology.stem: What best explains the finding: “A drug giving a sub-maximal response and blunting a full agonist”?
agonists-antagonists-pharmacology.explanation: A drug giving a sub-maximal response and blunting a full agonist → Partial agonist (acts as partial antagonist).

agonists-antagonists-pharmacology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Agonist curve shifted right, same maximum with more agonist”?
agonists-antagonists-pharmacology.explanation: Agonist curve shifted right, same maximum with more agonist → Competitive (reversible) antagonism (surmountable).

agonists-antagonists-pharmacology.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Agonists, Antagonists & Efficacy”?
agonists-antagonists-pharmacology.explanation: Understanding pharmacodynamics can aid in comprehending drug effects on gas exchange.

agonists-antagonists-pharmacology.stem: Which should you review before “Agonists, Antagonists & Efficacy”?
agonists-antagonists-pharmacology.explanation: Basic genetic concepts may provide context for pharmacogenomics.

drug-receptor-signal-transduction.stem: A β-adrenoceptor agonist produces its effect largely by a Gs-coupled pathway that:

options.text: Activates adenylyl cyclase to increase cAMP
Directly alters gene transcription in minutes

drug-receptor-signal-transduction.explanation: β-adrenoceptors couple to Gs, which activates adenylyl cyclase to raise cAMP and activate protein kinase A. Gi-coupled receptors lower cAMP, and Gq-coupled receptors act via phospholipase C (IP3/DAG, calcium).

drug-receptor-signal-transduction.stem: Why should a chronically administered β-blocker be tapered rather than stopped abruptly?

options.text: It causes receptor down-regulation, so stopping does nothing
Chronic blockade up-regulates β-receptors, so abrupt cessation causes rebound tachycardia/hypertension
The drug has a very short half-life
It becomes an agonist when stopped

drug-receptor-signal-transduction.explanation: Chronic antagonism causes compensatory up-regulation and supersensitivity of β-receptors. Stopping abruptly unmasks this with rebound tachycardia, hypertension and ischaemia risk, so β-blockers (and clonidine) are tapered gradually.

drug-receptor-signal-transduction.stem: Regarding rebound after chronic receptor antagonism — which is correct?

options.text: A receptor antagonist can be stopped abruptly at any time without consequence

Chronic ANTAGONISM causes compensatory UP-REGULATION/supersensitivity of the receptor, so ABRUPT withdrawal unmasks an exaggerated response (REBOUND) — e.g. rebound hypertension/tachycardia on stopping β-blockers or clonidine suddenly; these should be TAPERED, not stopped abruptly

drug-receptor-signal-transduction.explanation: Receptor up-regulation during blockade means sudden cessation produces a dangerous rebound; recognising this changes practice (gradual tapering) for β-blockers, clonidine and similar agents.

drug-receptor-signal-transduction.stem: What best explains the finding: “β-agonist raising intracellular cAMP”?
drug-receptor-signal-transduction.explanation: β-agonist raising intracellular cAMP → Gs-coupled GPCR → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP.

drug-receptor-signal-transduction.stem: What best explains the finding: “α1-agonist raising intracellular calcium”?
drug-receptor-signal-transduction.explanation: α1-agonist raising intracellular calcium → Gq → phospholipase C → IP3 (Ca²⁺ release).

drug-receptor-signal-transduction.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Receptor Signal Transduction & Regulation”?
drug-receptor-signal-transduction.explanation: Sensory receptors also involve signal transduction mechanisms.

drug-receptor-signal-transduction.stem: Which should you review before “Receptor Signal Transduction & Regulation”?
drug-receptor-signal-transduction.explanation: Understanding receptor types is essential for grasping signal transduction.

superficial-antifungals-clinical.stem: The oral drug of choice for dermatophyte onychomycosis (fungal nail infection) is:
superficial-antifungals-clinical.explanation: Oral terbinafine (a squalene epoxidase inhibitor that concentrates in keratin) is first-line for dermatophyte onychomycosis; topical agents fail to penetrate the nail plate. Griseofulvin is a classic option for tinea capitis, and nystatin is a topical anti-Candida polyene.

superficial-antifungals-clinical.stem: Nystatin is used only topically or within the gut lumen because it:

options.text: Is too toxic for any use
Is not absorbed from the gut (so it acts locally on Candida)

superficial-antifungals-clinical.explanation: Nystatin is a polyene that is not absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, so it is used topically (skin, mouth, vagina) or in the gut lumen to treat local Candida infections rather than systemically.

superficial-antifungals-clinical.stem: Regarding topical vs oral for nail/scalp fungal infection — which is correct?

options.text: Onychomycosis and tinea capitis can be cleared with topical antifungal creams

NAIL (onychomycosis) and SCALP (tinea capitis) infections generally REQUIRE ORAL antifungals (terbinafine, griseofulvin/itraconazole) because topical agents do NOT penetrate the keratinised nail plate or hair follicle adequately — topical monotherapy typically fails at these sites

superficial-antifungals-clinical.explanation: Poor keratin penetration means topicals cannot eradicate nail/scalp infection, so recognising the need for systemic therapy (with its monitoring) avoids repeated treatment failure.

superficial-antifungals-clinical.stem: What best explains the finding: “Oral drug of choice for dermatophyte nail infection”?
superficial-antifungals-clinical.explanation: Oral drug of choice for dermatophyte nail infection → Terbinafine (squalene epoxidase inhibitor).

superficial-antifungals-clinical.stem: What best explains the finding: “Oral agent for childhood tinea capitis”?
superficial-antifungals-clinical.explanation: Oral agent for childhood tinea capitis → Griseofulvin (± terbinafine).

superficial-antifungals-clinical.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Antifungals for Superficial Infections”?
superficial-antifungals-clinical.explanation: Clinical application of antifungal treatment in skin infections.

anthelmintic-drug-classes.stem: Treatment of a tissue helminth infection such as hydatid disease or neurocysticercosis differs from intestinal deworming in that it requires:

options.text: A single low dose of a non-absorbed drug
Prolonged, higher-dose well-absorbed albendazole (often with corticosteroid cover)

anthelmintic-drug-classes.explanation: Tissue helminth infections need systemically absorbed drug at the site of infection, so prolonged, higher-dose albendazole (taken with fatty food to improve absorption) is used, frequently with corticosteroids to blunt inflammation from dying larvae (e.g. in neurocysticercosis).

anthelmintic-drug-classes.stem: Ivermectin paralyses susceptible worms by acting on:
anthelmintic-drug-classes.explanation: Ivermectin opens invertebrate glutamate-gated chloride channels, hyperpolarising and paralysing the worm; it is used for Strongyloides, onchocerciasis and scabies. Benzimidazoles act on β-tubulin, and praziquantel increases tegumental calcium permeability.

anthelmintic-drug-classes.stem: Regarding intestinal vs tissue helminth dosing — which is correct?

options.text: A single dose of albendazole treats all worm infections

INTESTINAL (luminal) worm infections often clear with a SINGLE or short course, but TISSUE infections (hydatid cyst, neurocysticercosis, disseminated strongyloidiasis) require PROLONGED, higher-dose, well-absorbed therapy (albendazole with fatty food) — and often corticosteroid cover for inflammatory reactions; a single dose is inadequate for tissue disease

anthelmintic-drug-classes.explanation: The site of infection (lumen vs tissue) dictates dose, duration and the need for systemic absorption and anti-inflammatory cover, so applying intestinal-worm dosing to tissue disease fails.

anthelmintic-drug-classes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Broad-spectrum single/short course for intestinal roundworms”?

options.text: Prevent inflammatory reaction to dying larvae

anthelmintic-drug-classes.explanation: Broad-spectrum single/short course for intestinal roundworms → Benzimidazole (albendazole/mebendazole).

anthelmintic-drug-classes.stem: What best explains the finding: “Prolonged high-dose albendazole with fatty food for hydatid disease”?

options.text: Prevent inflammatory reaction to dying larvae

anthelmintic-drug-classes.explanation: Prolonged high-dose albendazole with fatty food for hydatid disease → Tissue infection needs systemic absorption.

anthelmintic-drug-classes.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Anthelmintic Drug Classes & Clinical Use”?
anthelmintic-drug-classes.explanation: This module discusses clinical manifestations of helminthic infections, linking basic science to clinical practice.

anthelmintic-drug-classes.stem: Which should you review before “Anthelmintic Drug Classes & Clinical Use”?
anthelmintic-drug-classes.explanation: Understanding helminth classification is essential for selecting appropriate anthelmintic therapy.

herpesvirus-cmv-antivirals.stem: The dose-limiting toxicity of ganciclovir (used for CMV) is:
herpesvirus-cmv-antivirals.explanation: Ganciclovir/valganciclovir treats CMV disease (e.g. retinitis in the immunosuppressed) but characteristically causes dose-limiting bone-marrow suppression (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia). Aciclovir's key caution is crystalline nephrotoxicity, and foscarnet/cidofovir are nephrotoxic.

herpesvirus-cmv-antivirals.stem: Aciclovir-resistant HSV (from a thymidine-kinase mutation) is best treated with:
herpesvirus-cmv-antivirals.explanation: Thymidine-kinase-deficient resistant HSV cannot phosphorylate/activate aciclovir, so dose escalation fails. Foscarnet (and cidofovir) inhibit the viral DNA polymerase directly without needing viral kinase activation, at the cost of nephrotoxicity.

herpesvirus-cmv-antivirals.stem: Regarding managing aciclovir-resistant herpesvirus — which is correct?

options.text: If aciclovir fails, simply increase the aciclovir dose

Aciclovir resistance is usually from a viral THYMIDINE-KINASE mutation, so the virus can no longer activate aciclovir (or ganciclovir) — raising the dose does not help; you switch to FOSCARNET or CIDOFOVIR, which inhibit the viral DNA polymerase DIRECTLY without needing viral kinase activation (accepting their nephrotoxicity)

herpesvirus-cmv-antivirals.explanation: Because resistance abolishes the activation step, escalating aciclovir is futile; understanding that foscarnet/cidofovir bypass activation explains the correct switch for resistant disease.

herpesvirus-cmv-antivirals.stem: What best explains the finding: “Selective anti-HSV agent needing viral thymidine kinase”?
herpesvirus-cmv-antivirals.explanation: Selective anti-HSV agent needing viral thymidine kinase → Aciclovir.

herpesvirus-cmv-antivirals.stem: What best explains the finding: “Empiric IV therapy for suspected HSV encephalitis”?
herpesvirus-cmv-antivirals.explanation: Empiric IV therapy for suspected HSV encephalitis → Aciclovir given early (neurological emergency).

herpesvirus-cmv-antivirals.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Antivirals for Herpesviruses & CMV”?
herpesvirus-cmv-antivirals.explanation: Clinical manifestations of herpesvirus infections are relevant to antiviral treatment.

herpesvirus-cmv-antivirals.stem: Which should you review before “Antivirals for Herpesviruses & CMV”?
herpesvirus-cmv-antivirals.explanation: Understanding transcription is essential for grasping how antivirals target viral DNA synthesis.

hiv-antiretroviral-therapy.stem: Before prescribing abacavir, testing is recommended for which allele to avoid a severe hypersensitivity reaction?
hiv-antiretroviral-therapy.explanation: Abacavir hypersensitivity is strongly associated with HLA-B*57:01, so patients are screened before starting it (a pharmacogenomic safeguard). HLA-B*15:02 relates to carbamazepine and HLA-B*58:01 to allopurinol SCARs.

hiv-antiretroviral-therapy.stem: The rationale for using at least three antiretroviral drugs from two classes in HIV is to:

options.text: Achieve full viral suppression and prevent the emergence of resistance

hiv-antiretroviral-therapy.explanation: HIV mutates rapidly, so single-drug therapy quickly selects resistance. Combining ≥3 drugs from ≥2 classes that block different steps of the life cycle achieves durable viral suppression and prevents resistance — the basis of HAART.

hiv-antiretroviral-therapy.stem: Regarding why hiv is never treated with one drug — which is correct?

options.text: A single potent antiretroviral should suppress HIV if the drug is strong enough

HIV replicates rapidly with an error-prone reverse transcriptase, so under SINGLE-drug pressure it quickly selects RESISTANT mutants — therefore treatment always uses a COMBINATION of ≥3 drugs from ≥2 classes (attacking different steps) to suppress replication fully and prevent resistance; monotherapy predictably fails

hiv-antiretroviral-therapy.explanation: The high mutation rate means monotherapy selects resistance within weeks; combination therapy is the defining principle of successful HIV treatment (and of PrEP/PEP regimens).

hiv-antiretroviral-therapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Life-threatening hypersensitivity to an NRTI”?

options.text: HIV mutation under monotherapy (hence combination ART)

hiv-antiretroviral-therapy.explanation: Life-threatening hypersensitivity to an NRTI → Abacavir — HLA-B*57:01 (screen first).

hiv-antiretroviral-therapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Many drug interactions and lipodystrophy on ART”?

options.text: HIV mutation under monotherapy (hence combination ART)

hiv-antiretroviral-therapy.explanation: Many drug interactions and lipodystrophy on ART → Protease inhibitor CYP3A4 effects.

hiv-antiretroviral-therapy.stem: Which should you review before “HIV Antiretroviral Therapy”?
hiv-antiretroviral-therapy.explanation: Screening for HLA-B*57:01 is critical before using abacavir.

antibacterial-resistance-mechanisms.stem: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus resists β-lactams primarily by which mechanism?

options.text: Target alteration (an altered penicillin-binding protein, PBP2a)

antibacterial-resistance-mechanisms.explanation: MRSA carries mecA encoding PBP2a, an altered penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for β-lactams — a target-alteration mechanism making it resistant to all standard β-lactams. β-lactamase production is a separate (enzymatic) mechanism.

antibacterial-resistance-mechanisms.stem: A core principle of antimicrobial stewardship is to:

options.text: Always use the broadest antibiotic available
Use the narrowest effective agent for an adequate dose/duration and de-escalate on culture results
Stop antibiotics as soon as the patient feels slightly better regardless of course

antibacterial-resistance-mechanisms.explanation: Stewardship aims to preserve antibiotic effectiveness by prescribing only when indicated, selecting the narrowest effective agent at an adequate dose and duration, and de-escalating once cultures identify the organism — reducing the selection pressure that drives resistance.

antibacterial-resistance-mechanisms.stem: Regarding how resistance spreads — which is correct?

options.text: Antibiotic resistance only arises by spontaneous mutation within each bacterium

While mutation contributes, much resistance spreads by HORIZONTAL GENE TRANSFER — bacteria share resistance genes on PLASMIDS/transposons via conjugation, transformation and transduction, transferring resistance even BETWEEN species — which is why resistance can appear and disseminate rapidly and why stewardship/infection control matter beyond any single patient

antibacterial-resistance-mechanisms.explanation: Horizontal transfer means resistance is a communicable, community-level problem (not just per-organism mutation), underpinning the rationale for stewardship and isolation of resistant organisms.

antibacterial-resistance-mechanisms.stem: What best explains the finding: “β-lactam inactivated by a bacterial enzyme”?
antibacterial-resistance-mechanisms.explanation: β-lactam inactivated by a bacterial enzyme → β-lactamase (enzymatic inactivation).

antibacterial-resistance-mechanisms.stem: What best explains the finding: “S. aureus resistant to all standard β-lactams”?
antibacterial-resistance-mechanisms.explanation: S. aureus resistant to all standard β-lactams → Altered PBP2a (mecA) — target alteration (MRSA).

antibacterial-resistance-mechanisms.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Antibacterial Resistance & Stewardship”?

options.text: Protein & Nucleic Acid Digestion and Absorption

antibacterial-resistance-mechanisms.explanation: Understanding digestion may help in grasping the absorption of antibiotics.

antimycobacterial-drugs.stem: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is co-administered with which anti-TB drug to prevent peripheral neuropathy?
antimycobacterial-drugs.explanation: Isoniazid can cause peripheral neuropathy (via pyridoxine depletion), so vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is given alongside it, especially in at-risk patients. Isoniazid also causes hepatotoxicity; ethambutol causes optic neuritis and rifampin induces CYP450.

antimycobacterial-drugs.stem: Which anti-TB drug is a potent CYP450 inducer that lowers the levels of many co-administered drugs?
antimycobacterial-drugs.explanation: Rifampin (which inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase) is a potent inducer of hepatic CYP450 enzymes, accelerating metabolism of many drugs (e.g. oral contraceptives, warfarin, protease inhibitors) and causing therapeutic failure; it also colours secretions orange.

antimycobacterial-drugs.stem: Regarding why tb needs combination therapy — which is correct?

options.text: A single potent anti-TB drug for a short course should cure tuberculosis

TB requires PROLONGED, MULTI-DRUG therapy (RIPE for months) because the slow-growing, partly intracellular/dormant bacilli and the rapid selection of resistance under single-drug pressure mean monotherapy fails and breeds resistance — combination therapy and adherence (DOT) are essential to cure and to prevent MDR-TB

antimycobacterial-drugs.explanation: The organism's biology (slow growth, persistence) and resistance risk make short single-drug courses ineffective; understanding this justifies the lengthy combination regimen and adherence support.

antimycobacterial-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Peripheral neuropathy prevented by pyridoxine during TB therapy”?
antimycobacterial-drugs.explanation: Peripheral neuropathy prevented by pyridoxine during TB therapy → Isoniazid (give vitamin B6).

antimycobacterial-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Orange tears/urine and many drug interactions on TB therapy”?
antimycobacterial-drugs.explanation: Orange tears/urine and many drug interactions on TB therapy → Rifampin (CYP450 inducer).

antimycobacterial-drugs.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Antimycobacterial (TB) Drugs”?
antimycobacterial-drugs.explanation: Rifampin's role as a CYP450 inducer is critical for drug interactions.

antimuscarinic-anticholinergic-drugs.stem: A patient who overdosed on an antimuscarinic drug is likely to be:

options.text: Bradycardic, sweaty and with pinpoint pupils
Hyperthermic, dry, flushed, with dilated pupils and delirium

antimuscarinic-anticholinergic-drugs.explanation: The anticholinergic toxidrome is "hot as a hare (hyperthermia from no sweating), dry as a bone, red as a beet, blind as a bat (mydriasis/blurred vision), mad as a hatter (delirium)", with tachycardia and urinary retention. This is the opposite of the cholinergic (SLUDGE) picture.

antimuscarinic-anticholinergic-drugs.stem: Antimuscarinic drugs should be used with particular caution or avoided in a patient with:

options.text: Narrow-angle glaucoma or bladder outlet obstruction

antimuscarinic-anticholinergic-drugs.explanation: Antimuscarinics cause mydriasis (which can precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma) and reduce detrusor contraction (precipitating urinary retention in outlet obstruction/BPH); they also cause confusion in the frail elderly. These are key contraindications/cautions.

antimuscarinic-anticholinergic-drugs.stem: Regarding antimuscarinics in the elderly and obstruction — which is correct?

options.text: Antimuscarinics are benign symptomatic drugs suitable for any patient

Antimuscarinics carry real hazards: they precipitate ACUTE ANGLE-CLOSURE GLAUCOMA (mydriasis) and URINARY RETENTION (outlet obstruction/BPH), and cause CONFUSION/falls in the frail ELDERLY — where cumulative "anticholinergic burden" from combined drugs (antihistamines, TCAs, bladder agents) is a recognised cause of delirium; they should be used cautiously and avoided in these groups

antimuscarinic-anticholinergic-drugs.explanation: Underestimating antimuscarinic risks leads to preventable glaucoma crises, retention and delirium, especially with polypharmacy in older patients — recognising the burden changes prescribing.

antimuscarinic-anticholinergic-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hot, dry, flushed, dilated pupils, delirious with tachycardia and retention”?
antimuscarinic-anticholinergic-drugs.explanation: Hot, dry, flushed, dilated pupils, delirious with tachycardia and retention → Anticholinergic toxidrome.

antimuscarinic-anticholinergic-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bronchodilation in COPD with minimal systemic effect”?
antimuscarinic-anticholinergic-drugs.explanation: Bronchodilation in COPD with minimal systemic effect → Inhaled antimuscarinic (ipratropium/tiotropium).

antimuscarinic-anticholinergic-drugs.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Antimuscarinic & Anticholinergic Drugs”?

options.text: Drugs for Urinary Frequency, Incontinence & Enuresis

antimuscarinic-anticholinergic-drugs.explanation: Antimuscarinics are used to treat urinary retention and incontinence.

adrenergic-antagonists-blockers.stem: A cardioselective β-blocker is preferred over a non-selective one in a patient with asthma because it:

options.text: Has no effect on the heart
Preferentially blocks β1 and largely spares β2, reducing bronchospasm risk

adrenergic-antagonists-blockers.explanation: Cardioselective β-blockers preferentially antagonise β1 (cardiac) receptors and largely spare β2 (bronchial) receptors, lowering bronchospasm risk in asthma/COPD — though selectivity is relative and reduced at higher doses.

adrenergic-antagonists-blockers.stem: In a patient with a phaeochromocytoma, the correct order of adrenergic blockade is:
adrenergic-antagonists-blockers.explanation: α-blockade must be established before β-blockade in phaeochromocytoma. Giving a β-blocker first removes β2-mediated vasodilation, leaving α1 vasoconstriction unopposed and precipitating a hypertensive crisis. "α before β" is the rule.

adrenergic-antagonists-blockers.stem: Regarding β-blocker starting in heart failure — which is correct?

options.text: β-blockers reduce cardiac output, so they must never be used in heart failure

β-blockers (bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol succinate) IMPROVE survival in CHRONIC stable heart failure and are guideline therapy — but they are started at LOW dose and UP-TITRATED slowly, and are AVOIDED in ACUTE DECOMPENSATED heart failure (where negative inotropy is harmful); the distinction is chronic-stable (use, up-titrate) vs acute-decompensated (avoid)

adrenergic-antagonists-blockers.explanation: Blanket avoidance denies a survival benefit in chronic HF, while starting/uptitrating during acute decompensation is dangerous — the timing (stable vs decompensated) determines correct use.

adrenergic-antagonists-blockers.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bradycardia, fatigue and bronchospasm on a cardiac drug”?
adrenergic-antagonists-blockers.explanation: Bradycardia, fatigue and bronchospasm on a cardiac drug → β-blocker adverse effects.

adrenergic-antagonists-blockers.stem: What best explains the finding: “Masked hypoglycaemia warning signs in a diabetic”?
adrenergic-antagonists-blockers.explanation: Masked hypoglycaemia warning signs in a diabetic → Non-selective β-blockade (use cardioselective).

adrenergic-antagonists-blockers.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Adrenergic Antagonists (α- & β-Blockers)”?
adrenergic-antagonists-blockers.explanation: Adrenergic antagonists are part of the autonomic nervous system pharmacology.

adrenergic-antagonists-blockers.stem: Which should you review before “Adrenergic Antagonists (α- & β-Blockers)”?
adrenergic-antagonists-blockers.explanation: Understanding receptor signaling is essential for grasping adrenergic antagonist mechanisms.

cytotoxic-chemotherapy-agents.stem: Mesna is co-administered with cyclophosphamide to prevent:
cytotoxic-chemotherapy-agents.explanation: Cyclophosphamide produces acrolein, which is toxic to the bladder urothelium and causes haemorrhagic cystitis. Mesna binds and detoxifies acrolein in the urine, preventing this. (Dexrazoxane protects against anthracycline cardiotoxicity; leucovorin rescues from methotrexate.)

cytotoxic-chemotherapy-agents.stem: Which agent is correctly paired with its characteristic toxicity?
cytotoxic-chemotherapy-agents.explanation: Vincristine characteristically causes peripheral neuropathy. Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis, cisplatin causes nephro/ototoxicity, and doxorubicin (an anthracycline) causes cumulative cardiotoxicity.

cytotoxic-chemotherapy-agents.stem: Regarding why combination chemotherapy is used — which is correct?

options.text: Using one maximally-dosed drug is the best way to kill a tumour

Chemotherapy is usually given as COMBINATIONS of drugs with DIFFERENT mechanisms and NON-OVERLAPPING toxicities — this maximises tumour cell kill (log-kill from multiple mechanisms), limits the dose-limiting toxicity of any single agent, and reduces the emergence of resistance; single-agent maximal dosing is more toxic and more prone to resistance

cytotoxic-chemotherapy-agents.explanation: Combination regimens achieve greater kill with tolerable toxicity and less resistance than escalating one drug — the rationale behind standard multi-agent protocols.

cytotoxic-chemotherapy-agents.stem: What best explains the finding: “Haemorrhagic cystitis prevented by mesna”?
cytotoxic-chemotherapy-agents.explanation: Haemorrhagic cystitis prevented by mesna → Cyclophosphamide (acrolein).

cytotoxic-chemotherapy-agents.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity and severe emesis from chemotherapy”?
cytotoxic-chemotherapy-agents.explanation: Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity and severe emesis from chemotherapy → Cisplatin.

cytotoxic-chemotherapy-agents.stem: Which should you review before “Cytotoxic Chemotherapy Agents”?
cytotoxic-chemotherapy-agents.explanation: Understanding nucleotide metabolism is crucial for grasping antimetabolite mechanisms.
