Melanocytes SYNTHESISE melanin (in melanosomes) but TRANSFER it to surrounding KERATINOCYTES, where it forms a supranuclear "cap" shielding keratinocyte DNA from UV — so most epidermal pigment resides in keratinocytes, not melanocytes; skin-colour differences reflect melanin amount/type and distribution, not melanocyte number

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: Understanding melanin transfer explains why pigment protects keratinocyte DNA (and why melanocyte number is similar across skin colours), underpinning pigmentary disorders and photoprotection.

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Retained nuclei in the stratum corneum (parakeratosis)”?
epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: Retained nuclei in the stratum corneum (parakeratosis) → Accelerated keratinocyte turnover (psoriasis).

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: What best explains the finding: “The proliferating basal layer on the basement membrane”?
epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: The proliferating basal layer on the basement membrane → Stratum basale (epidermal stem cells).

epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.stem: Which should you review before “Epidermis & Keratinocyte Biology”?
epidermis-keratinocyte-biology.explanation: Understanding body membranes is essential for grasping epidermal structure.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: Sebaceous glands of the pilosebaceous unit secrete sebum by which mechanism?

options.text: Holocrine (disintegration of the whole secretory cell)

dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Sebaceous glands are holocrine — the entire secretory cell disintegrates to release sebum. They are androgen-driven and central to acne. Eccrine sweat glands are merocrine, and apocrine glands release by decapitation/apocrine secretion.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: Thermoregulatory sweating is provided by which gland, under which unusual autonomic control?
dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Eccrine glands provide thermoregulatory sweating and are the classic "sympathetic cholinergic" exception — sympathetically innervated but using acetylcholine (muscarinic), which is why antimuscarinic drugs reduce sweating.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: Regarding eccrine vs apocrine glands — which is correct?

options.text: All sweat glands are the same and produce body odour

ECCRINE glands are distributed over the whole body, open directly onto the skin and produce watery THERMOREGULATORY sweat (sympathetic-cholinergic), whereas APOCRINE glands are limited to the axilla/groin/areola, open into HAIR FOLLICLES and produce a secretion that bacteria break down into ODOUR (and can occlude → hidradenitis suppurativa) — different distribution, function and clinical disease

dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Distinguishing thermoregulatory eccrine from odour-producing apocrine glands explains hyperhidrosis vs body odour vs hidradenitis, which have different treatments.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sebaceous gland secreting by disintegration of its whole cells”?
dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Sebaceous gland secreting by disintegration of its whole cells → Holocrine secretion (pilosebaceous unit).

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: What best explains the finding: “Thermoregulatory sweating blocked by antimuscarinics”?
dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Thermoregulatory sweating blocked by antimuscarinics → Eccrine glands are sympathetic-cholinergic.

dermis-appendages-glands.stem: Which should you review before “Dermis, Appendages & Skin Glands”?
dermis-appendages-glands.explanation: Understanding skin appendages is crucial for grasping dermal functions.

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: The sun protection factor (SPF) of a sunscreen primarily quantifies protection against:
photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: SPF measures protection against UVB (the sunburn/DNA-damaging band). Because UVA drives dermal ageing and contributes to carcinogenesis, a "broad-spectrum" sunscreen covering both UVA and UVB is needed, applied generously with reapplication.

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: Which patient has the highest risk of sunburn and skin cancer and needs the most emphatic photoprotection advice?

options.text: A Fitzpatrick type VI patient who never burns
A Fitzpatrick type I–II patient who always burns and rarely tans
Anyone regardless of skin type equally
A patient who already uses sunscreen

photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: Fitzpatrick types I–II (fair skin that always burns, rarely tans) have the least melanin protection and the highest risk of sunburn and skin cancer, so they warrant the strongest photoprotection counselling — though all skin types benefit from protection.

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: Regarding what spf covers — which is correct?

options.text: A high SPF alone gives complete protection against all UV-related damage

SPF measures protection against UVB (sunburn) only — a high SPF that is NOT broad-spectrum leaves UVA (dermal ageing, some carcinogenesis) largely uncovered; effective photoprotection needs a BROAD-SPECTRUM product (UVA+UVB), applied generously and reapplied, PLUS clothing/shade/avoidance

photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: Relying on SPF number alone (UVB) misses UVA damage; broad-spectrum coverage and behaviour are essential for genuine protection against ageing and cancer.

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: What best explains the finding: “Deep dermal collagen/elastin damage from long-wavelength UV”?
photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: Deep dermal collagen/elastin damage from long-wavelength UV → UVA (aging).

photoaging-photoprotection.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sunburn and epidermal DNA damage from shorter-wavelength UV”?
photoaging-photoprotection.explanation: Sunburn and epidermal DNA damage from shorter-wavelength UV → UVB (burning/carcinogenesis).

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: The principal antigen-presenting (dendritic) cell of the epidermis, central to sensitisation in allergic contact dermatitis, is the:
skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: Langerhans cells are the epidermal dendritic antigen-presenting cells; they capture antigen and migrate to lymph nodes to prime T cells, a key step in allergic contact dermatitis (Type IV) and immune surveillance.

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: Psoriasis is predominantly driven by which T-helper pathway, targeted by modern biologics?
skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: Psoriasis is driven largely by the Th17 (IL-17/IL-23) axis (with Th1), which is why anti-IL-17 and anti-IL-23 biologics are effective. Atopic dermatitis is Th2-driven (IL-4/IL-13), targeted by dupilumab.

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: Regarding keratinocytes as immune cells — which is correct?

options.text: Keratinocytes are just passive structural/barrier cells with no immune role

Keratinocytes are ACTIVE participants in cutaneous immunity — they express pattern-recognition receptors (Toll-like receptors), sense danger, and secrete CYTOKINES (IL-1, TNF, chemokines) and antimicrobial peptides that recruit and instruct immune cells, initiating and amplifying inflammatory responses (as in psoriasis)

skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: Recognising keratinocytes as immune effectors (not just bricks) explains how skin initiates inflammation and why cytokine-targeted biologics are effective.

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: What best explains the finding: “The epidermal antigen-presenting dendritic cell”?
skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: The epidermal antigen-presenting dendritic cell → Langerhans cell.

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: What best explains the finding: “Keratinocytes releasing cytokines in response to a pathogen”?
skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: Keratinocytes releasing cytokines in response to a pathogen → Innate immune sensing (TLRs).

skin-immune-system-cells.stem: Which should you review before “The Skin Immune System”?
skin-immune-system-cells.explanation: Knowledge of innate barriers and pattern recognition is crucial for understanding skin immunity.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: A patient develops itchy dermatitis 2–3 days after their skin contacts a nickel belt buckle, with a positive patch test. This is which hypersensitivity type?
cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: Allergic contact dermatitis is a Type IV delayed (T-cell-mediated) hypersensitivity, appearing 48–72 h after re-exposure in a sensitised person and diagnosed by patch testing. Type I (IgE) reactions such as urticaria are immediate.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: Transient itchy wheals that each resolve within 24 hours (urticaria) are typically mediated by:

options.text: IgE and mast-cell histamine release (Type I)

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: Urticaria is usually a Type I, IgE/mast-cell-mediated reaction releasing histamine, with transient individual wheals (<24 h). It is treated with antihistamines, reserving adrenaline for anaphylaxis/airway angioedema.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: Regarding urticaria vs contact dermatitis timing — which is correct?

options.text: All allergic skin reactions appear immediately after exposure

Timing separates the mechanisms: TYPE I urticaria is IMMEDIATE (minutes, IgE/mast-cell, transient wheals), whereas TYPE IV allergic contact dermatitis is DELAYED (48–72 hours, T-cell) — so a rash appearing days after contact points to a delayed T-cell reaction (patch-test positive), not an immediate IgE allergy

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: The immediate-vs-delayed distinction changes the mechanism, diagnostic test (prick vs patch) and treatment; assuming all reactions are immediate misclassifies delayed contact dermatitis.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Transient itchy wheals resolving within 24 h”?
cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: Transient itchy wheals resolving within 24 h → Type I urticaria (IgE/mast-cell).

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Itchy dermatitis at a nickel-contact site, patch-test positive”?
cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: Itchy dermatitis at a nickel-contact site, patch-test positive → Type IV allergic contact dermatitis.

cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.stem: Which should you review before “Cutaneous Hypersensitivity Reactions”?
cutaneous-hypersensitivity-reactions.explanation: Understanding drug allergies is essential for managing cutaneous hypersensitivity.

skin-barrier-function.stem: Loss-of-function mutations in which protein impair the skin barrier and predispose to ichthyosis vulgaris and atopic dermatitis?
skin-barrier-function.explanation: Filaggrin aggregates keratin and yields natural moisturising factor; loss-of-function mutations produce a dry, defective barrier causing ichthyosis vulgaris and strongly predisposing to atopic dermatitis (and the atopic march). Emollient barrier repair is foundational.

skin-barrier-function.stem: The permeability barrier of the skin is provided mainly by:

options.text: The stratum corneum (corneocytes in intercellular lipid lamellae)

skin-barrier-function.explanation: The stratum corneum forms the permeability barrier as a "brick and mortar" structure — corneocytes (bricks) embedded in ceramide-rich intercellular lipid lamellae (mortar) — limiting transepidermal water loss and excluding microbes/allergens.

skin-barrier-function.stem: Regarding barrier defect as cause vs consequence in eczema — which is correct?

options.text: Dry, cracked skin in eczema is only a result of the inflammation, so treating inflammation alone is enough

A BARRIER DEFECT (e.g. filaggrin loss) is a PRIMARY driver of atopic dermatitis — the leaky barrier lets in allergens/microbes that trigger inflammation and itch — so EMOLLIENT-based barrier repair is FOUNDATIONAL, used continuously alongside anti-inflammatory therapy (not just steroids for flares); ignoring the barrier leads to relapse

skin-barrier-function.explanation: Because the barrier defect both causes and perpetuates eczema, continuous emollient use (not just treating inflammation during flares) is essential to control disease and reduce steroid need.

skin-barrier-function.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dry skin with increased transepidermal water loss”?
skin-barrier-function.explanation: Dry skin with increased transepidermal water loss → Barrier (stratum corneum) dysfunction.

skin-barrier-function.stem: What best explains the finding: “Ichthyosis vulgaris and atopic dermatitis in the same patient”?
skin-barrier-function.explanation: Ichthyosis vulgaris and atopic dermatitis in the same patient → Filaggrin loss-of-function mutation.

skin-barrier-function.stem: Which should you review before “The Skin Barrier”?
skin-barrier-function.explanation: Understanding skin immune cells is essential for grasping the immunological aspect of the skin barrier.

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: Before applying compression bandaging to a leg ulcer thought to be venous, it is essential to:

options.text: Exclude significant arterial disease (check the ankle-brachial pressure index)

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Compression treats venous ulcers but worsens arterial (ischaemic) ulcers, so the ankle-brachial pressure index must confirm adequate arterial supply before compression is applied. Arterial ulcers (painful, punched-out, low ABPI) need revascularisation, not compression.

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: A painless ulcer under a callus at a metatarsal head in a person with long-standing diabetes is best explained by:

options.text: Peripheral neuropathy with pressure/repetitive trauma (diabetic foot ulcer)

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Diabetic (neuropathic) foot ulcers are painless because of peripheral neuropathy and occur at pressure points (e.g. metatarsal heads) with callus, often complicated by ischaemia and infection. Management includes offloading, glycaemic control, debridement and infection treatment.

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: Regarding compression in leg ulcers — which is correct?

options.text: All leg ulcers benefit from compression bandaging

Compression is the treatment for VENOUS ulcers but is DANGEROUS in ARTERIAL disease — so you must EXCLUDE significant arterial insufficiency (check the ANKLE-BRACHIAL PRESSURE INDEX) BEFORE applying compression; compressing an ischaemic (arterial) leg can worsen ischaemia and cause tissue loss
Arterial ulcer (low ABPI — do not compress)

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Applying compression to an arterial ulcer worsens ischaemia and can lead to amputation, so ABPI must confirm adequate arterial supply before compression — a critical safety step.

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: What best explains the finding: “Shallow ulcer over the medial malleolus with oedema and haemosiderin staining”?

options.text: Arterial ulcer (low ABPI — do not compress)

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Shallow ulcer over the medial malleolus with oedema and haemosiderin staining → Venous ulcer (compression, normal ABPI).

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: What best explains the finding: “Painful punched-out ulcer on the toes with a cold, pulseless foot”?

options.text: Arterial ulcer (low ABPI — do not compress)

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Painful punched-out ulcer on the toes with a cold, pulseless foot → Arterial ulcer (low ABPI — do not compress).

chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.stem: Which should you review before “Chronic Wounds & Leg Ulcers”?
chronic-wounds-leg-ulcers.explanation: Understanding venous pressure can aid in assessing venous ulcers.

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: Erysipelas differs from cellulitis in that erysipelas:

options.text: Is superficial (upper dermis) with sharply demarcated, raised borders (usually streptococcal)

bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Erysipelas involves the superficial dermis and lymphatics, producing a sharply demarcated, raised, bright-red plaque (usually streptococcal, often facial or on the shins), whereas cellulitis extends deeper with ill-defined borders (staph or strep).

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: Which feature most strongly suggests necrotising fasciitis rather than simple cellulitis?

options.text: Pain out of proportion to the skin findings with systemic toxicity
A slowly enlarging patch over weeks

bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Necrotising fasciitis classically causes severe pain out of proportion to the (initially modest) skin findings, with rapid progression and systemic toxicity (± crepitus/necrosis). It is a surgical emergency needing urgent debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics.

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: Regarding necrotising fasciitis vs cellulitis — which is correct?

options.text: Severe leg pain with only mild redness is just cellulitis that antibiotics will fix

PAIN OUT OF PROPORTION to modest skin findings, with rapid progression, systemic toxicity, crepitus, bullae or skin necrosis, signals NECROTISING FASCIITIS — a SURGICAL EMERGENCY requiring urgent DEBRIDEMENT plus broad-spectrum antibiotics, NOT antibiotics alone; early skin signs can look deceptively mild

bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Necrotising fasciitis is rapidly fatal and its surface appearance underplays the deep destruction, so recognising disproportionate pain/toxicity and acting surgically (not just medically) is life-saving.

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: What best explains the finding: “Honey-coloured crusts on a child's face”?
bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Honey-coloured crusts on a child's face → Impetigo (S. aureus/S. pyogenes).

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: What best explains the finding: “Sharply demarcated, raised, bright-red facial plaque with fever”?
bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Sharply demarcated, raised, bright-red facial plaque with fever → Erysipelas (streptococcal, superficial).

bacterial-skin-infections.stem: Which should you review before “Bacterial Skin Infections”?
bacterial-skin-infections.explanation: Understanding antibiotics is crucial for treating bacterial skin infections.

viral-skin-infections.stem: A child with atopic eczema develops widespread painful, punched-out vesicles/erosions and fever. The most likely diagnosis is:

options.text: Eczema herpeticum (disseminated HSV) — needs systemic aciclovir

viral-skin-infections.explanation: Disseminated HSV over eczematous skin (eczema herpeticum) produces painful, monomorphic punched-out erosions with fever/malaise — a dermatological emergency requiring systemic aciclovir. It should not be mistaken for a simple eczema flare or impetigo.

viral-skin-infections.stem: Extensive or persistent molluscum contagiosum in an adult should prompt consideration of:
viral-skin-infections.explanation: Molluscum contagiosum (a poxvirus) causes umbilicated papules, usually self-limiting in children; extensive or persistent disease in an adult suggests immunosuppression such as HIV, warranting evaluation.

viral-skin-infections.stem: Regarding eczema herpeticum recognition — which is correct?

options.text: Rapidly worsening, painful eczema just needs stronger topical steroids

Painful, monomorphic PUNCHED-OUT erosions/vesicles with fever over eczematous skin suggest ECZEMA HERPETICUM (disseminated herpes simplex) — a dermatological EMERGENCY needing systemic ACICLOVIR; escalating topical steroids alone can worsen it and allow HSV to disseminate

viral-skin-infections.explanation: Missing eczema herpeticum and treating it as a steroid-responsive flare risks widespread HSV dissemination and serious complications; the painful punched-out lesions and systemic upset are the clues to give antivirals urgently.

viral-skin-infections.stem: What best explains the finding: “Recurrent grouped vesicles on the lip”?
viral-skin-infections.explanation: Recurrent grouped vesicles on the lip → HSV reactivation (cold sore).

viral-skin-infections.stem: What best explains the finding: “Painful punched-out erosions + fever over eczema”?
viral-skin-infections.explanation: Painful punched-out erosions + fever over eczema → Eczema herpeticum (disseminated HSV) — emergency.

viral-skin-infections.stem: Which should you review before “Viral Skin Infections”?
viral-skin-infections.explanation: Understanding antiviral treatments is crucial for managing viral skin infections.

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: When treating a patient for scabies, it is essential to also:

options.text: Treat only the patient and observe others
Treat all close/household contacts simultaneously and launder bedding/clothing

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: All close/household contacts (even asymptomatic) must be treated simultaneously and bedding/clothing laundered, because the itch lags infestation and untreated contacts cause re-infestation ("ping-pong"). Post-scabetic itch afterward is managed with emollients/steroids, not more scabicide.

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: Thick hyperkeratotic crusts containing thousands of mites, highly contagious, in an elderly immunosuppressed patient describe:
scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: Crusted (Norwegian) scabies is a hyperinfestation with thousands of mites forming thick crusts (often less itchy) in the immunosuppressed/elderly; it is extremely contagious (care-home outbreaks) and requires combined topical plus repeated oral ivermectin and strict infection control.

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: Regarding persistent itch after scabies treatment — which is correct?

options.text: If itching continues after scabies treatment, the treatment failed and needs immediate repeating

Scabies itch is a DELAYED HYPERSENSITIVITY reaction, so it commonly PERSISTS for 2–4 WEEKS AFTER successful eradication — this is POST-SCABETIC itch, treated with emollients/topical steroids/antihistamines, NOT automatically more scabicide (over-treatment causes irritant dermatitis); re-treat only if there is evidence of ongoing/reinfestation

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: Because the itch lags the infestation and outlasts cure, assuming persistent itch means failure leads to unnecessary repeated scabicide and irritant dermatitis — the hypersensitivity nature must be recognised.

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nocturnal itch with grey burrows in finger web spaces”?
scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: Nocturnal itch with grey burrows in finger web spaces → Scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei).

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: What best explains the finding: “Itch persisting weeks after correct scabies treatment”?
scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: Itch persisting weeks after correct scabies treatment → Post-scabetic hypersensitivity (not treatment failure).

scabies-pediculosis-clinical.stem: Which should you review before “Scabies & Pediculosis (Clinical)”?
scabies-pediculosis-clinical.explanation: Understanding scabicides like permethrin and ivermectin.

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: A young patient develops crops of small, drop-like scaly papules over the trunk about two weeks after a sore throat. This is:
psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Guttate psoriasis presents as small "drop-like" papules, classically after a streptococcal throat infection in a young person. It may resolve or evolve into chronic plaque psoriasis, and treatment includes topical therapy/phototherapy.

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: Which systemic complication should be actively screened for in patients with psoriasis?
psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Up to about 30% of psoriasis patients develop psoriatic arthritis, which can be destructive if untreated, so joint symptoms should be screened for. Psoriasis is also associated with metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disease, warranting cardiometabolic risk assessment.

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: Regarding psoriasis as systemic disease — which is correct?

options.text: Psoriasis is purely a skin problem treatable with creams

Psoriasis is a SYSTEMIC inflammatory disease: up to ~30% develop PSORIATIC ARTHRITIS (potentially destructive — screen for joint symptoms), and it carries increased cardiometabolic and psychological morbidity — so management includes comorbidity screening and, for moderate-severe disease, systemic/biologic therapy, not just topical creams

psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Treating psoriasis as skin-only misses joint destruction and cardiovascular risk; recognising it as systemic changes screening and escalates therapy appropriately.

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “Silvery-scaled extensor plaques with pinpoint bleeding on scale removal”?
psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Silvery-scaled extensor plaques with pinpoint bleeding on scale removal → Plaque psoriasis (Auspitz sign).

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “Small drop-like papules after a sore throat in a young person”?
psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Small drop-like papules after a sore throat in a young person → Guttate psoriasis (post-streptococcal).

psoriasis-clinical-management.stem: Which should you review before “Psoriasis: Clinical Types & Management”?
psoriasis-clinical-management.explanation: Understanding cell adhesion is relevant to psoriasis pathology.

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: A child presents with palpable purpura over the buttocks and legs, joint pain, abdominal pain and haematuria. The diagnosis is:
cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura), the commonest childhood vasculitis, presents with palpable purpura (buttocks/legs), arthralgia, abdominal pain and nephritis, with IgA immune-complex deposition. Renal involvement should be monitored with urinalysis.

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: Palpable (raised, non-blanching) purpura is the hallmark of:
cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: Palpable purpura (you can feel the raised lesion) indicates inflammation of vessel walls — small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis (immune-complex/Type III). Flat, non-palpable purpura instead suggests a platelet or coagulation disorder.

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: Regarding assessing systemic involvement in cutaneous vasculitis — which is correct?

options.text: Skin vasculitis (palpable purpura) is just a skin problem that will settle on its own

Cutaneous vasculitis can be the visible sign of SYSTEMIC vasculitis, so palpable purpura mandates evaluation for a TRIGGER and for ORGAN involvement — especially RENAL disease (URINALYSIS for blood/protein) — because renal or other systemic involvement changes prognosis and requires immunosuppression, not just observation

cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: Missing renal or systemic involvement behind skin vasculitis risks progressive organ damage; urinalysis and a systemic assessment are essential even when the skin looks isolated.

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Raised, non-blanching purpuric papules on the lower legs”?
cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: Raised, non-blanching purpuric papules on the lower legs → Small-vessel (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis.

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Purpura + arthralgia + abdominal pain + haematuria in a child”?
cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: Purpura + arthralgia + abdominal pain + haematuria in a child → IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein).

cutaneous-vasculitis.stem: Which should you review before “Cutaneous Vasculitis”?

options.text: Blood Vessel Histology: Wall Layers & Vessel Types

cutaneous-vasculitis.explanation: Knowledge of blood vessel histology is essential for understanding the pathology of vasculitis.

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: The heliotrope rash and Gottron papules with proximal muscle weakness are pathognomonic of:

options.text: Dermatomyositis (with a need to screen for malignancy in adults)

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: The heliotrope (violaceous eyelid) rash and Gottron papules (over the knuckles) with proximal weakness and raised CK are pathognomonic of dermatomyositis; in adults it is associated with underlying malignancy, so cancer screening is required.

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: The malar (butterfly) rash of acute cutaneous lupus characteristically:
cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: The lupus malar rash is a photosensitive erythema over the cheeks and nose that spares the nasolabial folds — a helpful feature distinguishing it from rosacea and seborrhoeic dermatitis, which typically involve those folds.

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: Regarding malar rash location — which is correct?

options.text: The lupus malar rash covers the whole face including the folds beside the nose

The lupus "butterfly" malar rash characteristically SPARES the NASOLABIAL FOLDS (the creases from nose to mouth) — a feature that helps distinguish it from rosacea and seborrhoeic dermatitis, which typically INVOLVE the nasolabial folds; the sparing reflects the photosensitive, sun-exposed distribution

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: Nasolabial-fold sparing is a specific clue separating acute cutaneous lupus from common facial rashes (rosacea, seborrhoeic dermatitis) that involve those folds, refining the differential.

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds”?
cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: Photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds → Acute cutaneous lupus (SLE).

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: What best explains the finding: “Scarring, atrophic disc plaques with follicular plugging”?
cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: Scarring, atrophic disc plaques with follicular plugging → Discoid lupus erythematosus.

cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.stem: Which should you review before “Cutaneous Lupus & Dermatomyositis”?
cutaneous-lupus-dermatomyositis.explanation: Understanding photoprotection is crucial for managing cutaneous lupus and dermatomyositis.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: Fever, painful skin, mucosal erosions and epidermal detachment with a positive Nikolsky sign after starting allopurinol indicates:
severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Painful skin with mucosal erosions and epidermal detachment (Nikolsky positive) is SJS/TEN — a severe cutaneous adverse reaction (allopurinol is a classic culprit, HLA-B*58:01-linked). Management is immediate drug cessation and burns-unit supportive care, with urgent ophthalmology for eye involvement.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: DRESS syndrome is distinguished from a simple drug rash by:

options.text: Appearing within minutes of the drug
A delayed (2–8 week) onset with fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia and internal organ involvement

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: DRESS is a delayed (2–8 week) severe reaction with rash, fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia and internal organ involvement (commonly hepatitis), classically to anticonvulsants, allopurinol or sulfonamides — requiring prompt drug withdrawal and organ monitoring.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: Regarding benign drug rash vs early scar — which is correct?

options.text: A drug rash can be watched while the drug is continued, since most are harmless

Although most drug rashes are benign morbilliform eruptions, you MUST screen for RED FLAGS of a SCAR — mucosal erosions, skin PAIN/blistering/detachment (Nikolsky+), facial oedema, fever, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia or deranged LFTs — because SJS/TEN and DRESS are life-threatening and require IMMEDIATE drug cessation; continuing the drug in an evolving SCAR can be fatal
SJS/TEN — stop the drug, burns-unit care

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Early SJS/TEN or DRESS can resemble an ordinary rash, so the presence of any red flag (not the rash alone) determines urgency; continuing the culprit in a developing SCAR risks death.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Painful skin, mucosal erosions and epidermal detachment”?

options.text: SJS/TEN — stop the drug, burns-unit care

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Painful skin, mucosal erosions and epidermal detachment → SJS/TEN — stop the drug, burns-unit care.

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Mucocutaneous blistering weeks after allopurinol/carbamazepine”?

options.text: SJS/TEN — stop the drug, burns-unit care

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Mucocutaneous blistering weeks after allopurinol/carbamazepine → SJS/TEN (HLA-linked culprits).

severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.stem: Which should you review before “Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions (SCARs)”?
severe-cutaneous-drug-reactions.explanation: Foundational knowledge for recognizing drug allergies.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: A well 3-day-old newborn has blotchy erythema with scattered pustules on a red base; a smear shows eosinophils. The most likely diagnosis is:
neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Erythema toxicum neonatorum is a common benign self-limiting rash of the first days of life in a well baby — blotchy erythema with pustules containing eosinophils — needing only reassurance. Vesicles/erosions in an unwell neonate would instead raise concern for HSV.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: A nappy rash that involves the skin folds and shows satellite pustules is most likely due to:
neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Irritant nappy dermatitis typically spares the folds, whereas candidal nappy rash involves the folds with satellite pustules and requires a topical antifungal. Recognising the pattern directs correct treatment.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: Regarding irritant vs candidal nappy rash — which is correct?

options.text: All nappy rashes are the same and treated with barrier cream alone

The pattern distinguishes them: IRRITANT nappy dermatitis SPARES the skin FOLDS (the convex surfaces in contact with the nappy are affected) and responds to barrier care, whereas CANDIDAL nappy rash INVOLVES the FOLDS with SATELLITE pustules and needs a TOPICAL ANTIFUNGAL — treating candida as simple irritant dermatitis fails

neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Fold involvement with satellites signals candida, which requires antifungal therapy; the sparing-vs-involvement pattern directs correct treatment.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Blotchy erythema with pustules in a well newborn, first days”?
neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Blotchy erythema with pustules in a well newborn, first days → Erythema toxicum neonatorum (benign).

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nappy rash sparing the skin folds”?
neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Nappy rash sparing the skin folds → Irritant nappy dermatitis.

neonatal-skin-conditions.stem: Which should you review before “Neonatal & Infantile Skin Conditions”?
neonatal-skin-conditions.explanation: Understanding metabolic conditions can aid in recognizing skin manifestations.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: Six or more large café-au-lait macules, especially with axillary freckling, suggest which genodermatosis?
vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: Multiple (≥6) large café-au-lait macules with axillary/inguinal freckling are diagnostic features of neurofibromatosis type 1 (also neurofibromas, Lisch nodules). Tuberous sclerosis features ash-leaf macules, shagreen patches and angiofibromas.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: A persistent flat vascular birthmark present at birth in the ophthalmic (V1) trigeminal distribution should prompt evaluation for:
vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: A port-wine stain (capillary malformation) in the V1 distribution can be associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome (leptomeningeal angioma, seizures, glaucoma), so it warrants neuroimaging and ophthalmological evaluation. Unlike haemangiomas, port-wine stains persist.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: Regarding haemangioma vs port-wine stain behaviour — which is correct?

options.text: All vascular birthmarks are permanent and require the same treatment

They behave oppositely: an INFANTILE HAEMANGIOMA (vascular TUMOUR) appears AFTER birth, proliferates then spontaneously INVOLUTES (treat only if function-threatening/ulcerating — propranolol), whereas a PORT-WINE STAIN (capillary MALFORMATION) is present at birth, PERSISTS and grows with the child (laser), and if in the V1 distribution warrants evaluation for Sturge-Weber syndrome

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: Tumour (involutes) vs malformation (persists) determines whether to observe/treat and whether to screen for an associated syndrome — distinguishing them avoids both over- and under-treatment.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: What best explains the finding: “A red vascular lesion appearing after birth that later involutes”?
vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: A red vascular lesion appearing after birth that later involutes → Infantile haemangioma (propranolol if problematic).

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: What best explains the finding: “A persistent flat port-wine stain in the V1 trigeminal area”?
vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: A persistent flat port-wine stain in the V1 trigeminal area → Consider Sturge-Weber syndrome.

vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.stem: Which should you review before “Birthmarks & Genodermatoses”?
vascular-birthmarks-genodermatoses.explanation: Understanding congenital anomalies is essential for recognizing birthmarks and their implications.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: The single most important initial distinction when assessing hair loss is whether it is:
alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: Scarring alopecia destroys follicles permanently (loss of follicular openings) and needs prompt biopsy/treatment to save remaining hair, whereas non-scarring alopecia is potentially reversible. This distinction drives urgency and management, before considering pattern.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: Diffuse hair shedding beginning about 2–3 months after childbirth, with a positive hair-pull test and full recovery expected, is:
alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: Telogen effluvium is a reversible, diffuse shedding occurring 2–3 months after a stressor (e.g. childbirth, illness, weight loss), as hairs pushed into telogen are shed. The hair-pull test is positive, and regrowth follows once the trigger resolves.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: Regarding telogen effluvium timing — which is correct?

options.text: Diffuse hair shedding must be from something happening right now

TELOGEN EFFLUVIUM is a DELAYED diffuse shedding that typically occurs 2–3 MONTHS AFTER a triggering stressor (severe illness, childbirth, surgery, rapid weight loss, certain drugs) — because the trigger pushed hairs into telogen (rest) which then shed months later — so the cause must be sought in the RECENT PAST, not only the present; it is reversible

alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: The 2–3 month lag means the causative stressor is historical; looking only at current events misses the trigger, and understanding the delay reassures patients that regrowth follows.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: What best explains the finding: “Smooth scarred patch with loss of follicular openings”?
alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: Smooth scarred patch with loss of follicular openings → Cicatricial (scarring) alopecia — permanent, biopsy.

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: What best explains the finding: “Diffuse shedding 2–3 months after childbirth/illness, positive hair-pull”?
alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: Diffuse shedding 2–3 months after childbirth/illness, positive hair-pull → Telogen effluvium (reversible).

alopecia-clinical-approach.stem: Which should you review before “Clinical Approach to Alopecia”?
alopecia-clinical-approach.explanation: Understanding scarring alopecia requires knowledge of discoid lupus.

hyperpigmentation-melasma.stem: Symmetric brown patches on the cheeks and forehead of a pregnant woman, worsened by sun exposure, are characteristic of:
hyperpigmentation-melasma.explanation: Melasma is driven by UV and hormones (pregnancy, oral contraceptives), producing symmetric brown facial patches, more common in women and darker skin. Management centres on strict photoprotection plus topical lightening agents (hydroquinone, retinoids).

hyperpigmentation-melasma.stem: The single most important foundation of treatment for melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation is:
hyperpigmentation-melasma.explanation: Because UV drives and worsens both melasma and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, photoprotection is the essential foundation; topical lightening agents relapse without it, and procedures can worsen pigmentation (especially in darker skin) if sun exposure continues.

hyperpigmentation-melasma.stem: Regarding photoprotection in hyperpigmentation — which is correct?

options.text: Treating melasma/PIH is all about bleaching creams; sun exposure does not matter much

UV is a PRIMARY driver of melasma and worsens post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, so PHOTOPROTECTION (broad-spectrum sunscreen, avoidance) is the ESSENTIAL foundation — topical lightening agents fail or relapse without it; conversely, aggressive procedures without sun protection can worsen pigmentation, especially in darker skin

hyperpigmentation-melasma.explanation: Because UV both causes and perpetuates these disorders, omitting photoprotection undermines every other treatment and can worsen pigmentation — it is the cornerstone, not an optional add-on.

hyperpigmentation-melasma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Symmetric brown facial patches, worse with sun/pregnancy”?
hyperpigmentation-melasma.explanation: Symmetric brown facial patches, worse with sun/pregnancy → Melasma (UV + hormones).

hyperpigmentation-melasma.stem: What best explains the finding: “Brown discolouration at sites of resolved acne in darker skin”?
hyperpigmentation-melasma.explanation: Brown discolouration at sites of resolved acne in darker skin → Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

hyperpigmentation-melasma.stem: Which should you review before “Hyperpigmentation & Melasma”?
hyperpigmentation-melasma.explanation: Photoprotection is essential in managing hyperpigmentation.

atopic-dermatitis-clinical.stem: In an infant, atopic dermatitis characteristically involves the:
atopic-dermatitis-clinical.explanation: Infantile atopic dermatitis favours the face and extensor surfaces (and scalp), whereas in older children and adults it becomes flexural (antecubital/popliteal fossae). It reflects a barrier (filaggrin) defect and Th2 inflammation within the atopic march.

atopic-dermatitis-clinical.stem: The foundation (used continuously) of atopic dermatitis management is:

options.text: Liberal emollients plus trigger/irritant avoidance (barrier repair)

atopic-dermatitis-clinical.explanation: Because atopic dermatitis is driven by a skin-barrier defect, continuous liberal emollient use with trigger avoidance is foundational, reducing flares and steroid requirement. Topical corticosteroids/calcineurin inhibitors treat flares, with phototherapy and biologics (dupilumab) for severe disease.

atopic-dermatitis-clinical.stem: Regarding emollients as continuous therapy — which is correct?

options.text: Emollients are just a soothing extra; the real treatment is intermittent steroid cream during flares

EMOLLIENTS are the FOUNDATION and are used CONTINUOUSLY (not just during flares) because atopic dermatitis is driven by a barrier defect — regular emollient use repairs the barrier, reduces water loss, and lowers flare frequency and STEROID requirement; relying on intermittent steroids alone leads to more flares

atopic-dermatitis-clinical.explanation: Because the barrier defect is central and ongoing, daily emollient use (between and during flares) is disease-modifying, whereas treating only flares with steroids misses the underlying driver.

atopic-dermatitis-clinical.stem: What best explains the finding: “Itchy, lichenified flexural dermatitis in a child with asthma/hay fever”?
atopic-dermatitis-clinical.explanation: Itchy, lichenified flexural dermatitis in a child with asthma/hay fever → Atopic dermatitis (atopic march).

atopic-dermatitis-clinical.stem: What best explains the finding: “Face and extensor involvement in an infant”?
atopic-dermatitis-clinical.explanation: Face and extensor involvement in an infant → Infantile atopic dermatitis distribution.

atopic-dermatitis-clinical.stem: Which should you review before “Atopic Dermatitis: Clinical & Management”?
atopic-dermatitis-clinical.explanation: Understanding skin barrier function is essential for grasping the pathophysiology of atopic dermatitis.

contact-dermatitis-clinical.stem: A well-demarcated itchy dermatitis appears under a patient's nickel watch strap and is patch-test positive to nickel. This is:
contact-dermatitis-clinical.explanation: A dermatitis localised to a nickel-contact site with a positive patch test is allergic contact dermatitis — a Type IV delayed hypersensitivity requiring prior sensitisation. Distribution (where the agent contacts skin) is a key diagnostic clue.

contact-dermatitis-clinical.stem: Which statement about irritant contact dermatitis is correct?

options.text: It requires prior sensitisation and is patch-test positive
It is a non-immune reaction that can affect anyone with sufficient exposure
It is a Type I IgE reaction
It only occurs in atopic individuals

contact-dermatitis-clinical.explanation: Irritant contact dermatitis is a non-immune, direct chemical/physical injury to the skin that can affect anyone given enough cumulative exposure (e.g. wet-work hand dermatitis); it does not require sensitisation and is patch-test negative, unlike Type IV allergic contact dermatitis.

contact-dermatitis-clinical.stem: Regarding irritant vs allergic contact dermatitis — which is correct?

options.text: A dermatitis from touching a substance is always an allergy to it

Most contact dermatitis is IRRITANT — a NON-immune, direct chemical/physical injury that can affect ANYONE with enough exposure (no sensitisation, patch-test negative) — whereas ALLERGIC contact dermatitis is a Type IV reaction requiring prior SENSITISATION and confirmed by PATCH testing; distinguishing them changes management (reduce irritant exposure/barrier vs identify and avoid the specific allergen)

contact-dermatitis-clinical.explanation: Labelling irritant dermatitis as allergy leads to unnecessary allergy testing and misses the real fix (reducing irritant exposure); only allergic contact dermatitis is immune-mediated and patch-test positive.

contact-dermatitis-clinical.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hand dermatitis in a cleaner with cumulative exposure, no sensitisation”?
contact-dermatitis-clinical.explanation: Hand dermatitis in a cleaner with cumulative exposure, no sensitisation → Irritant contact dermatitis (non-immune).

contact-dermatitis-clinical.stem: What best explains the finding: “Itchy dermatitis under a nickel belt buckle, patch-test positive”?
contact-dermatitis-clinical.explanation: Itchy dermatitis under a nickel belt buckle, patch-test positive → Allergic contact dermatitis (Type IV).

contact-dermatitis-clinical.stem: Which should you review before “Contact Dermatitis: Irritant vs Allergic”?
contact-dermatitis-clinical.explanation: Understanding hypersensitivity mechanisms is crucial for differentiating contact dermatitis types.

acne-management.stem: To limit Cutibacterium acnes resistance, antibiotics in acne should be:

options.text: Combined with benzoyl peroxide and used for a limited course (not as monotherapy)

acne-management.explanation: Antibiotics for acne should be combined with benzoyl peroxide (which reduces resistance) and a topical retinoid, and used for a limited duration rather than as long-term monotherapy. First-line therapy centres on topical retinoids plus benzoyl peroxide, escalating by severity.

acne-management.stem: Severe nodulocystic or scarring acne unresponsive to other treatments is best managed with:
acne-management.explanation: Severe nodulocystic or scarring/treatment-resistant acne is treated with oral isotretinoin, which is highly effective but teratogenic — requiring a strict pregnancy-prevention programme and monitoring of lipids/liver function.

acne-management.stem: Regarding antibiotic use in acne — which is correct?

options.text: Long-term antibiotics alone are a good way to keep acne under control

Antibiotics (topical or oral) should NOT be used as MONOTHERAPY or long-term alone in acne — this drives C. acnes RESISTANCE; they are combined with BENZOYL PEROXIDE (± a topical retinoid), used for a LIMITED course, with a topical retinoid continued for maintenance; persistent/severe acne is better served by isotretinoin or hormonal therapy

acne-management.explanation: Antibiotic monotherapy breeds resistance and gives poorer long-term control; combining with benzoyl peroxide/retinoids and limiting duration is the resistance-conscious, more effective approach.

acne-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “First-line comedolytic topical agent for acne”?
acne-management.explanation: First-line comedolytic topical agent for acne → Topical retinoid (adapalene/tretinoin).

acne-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “Topical/oral antibiotic combined with benzoyl peroxide”?
acne-management.explanation: Topical/oral antibiotic combined with benzoyl peroxide → Limiting C. acnes antibiotic resistance.

melanoma-clinical.stem: The single most important prognostic factor for a primary cutaneous melanoma is:
melanoma-clinical.explanation: Breslow thickness — the depth of tumour invasion measured histologically — is the strongest prognostic factor and guides excision margins and staging, so a suspected melanoma is removed by excisional (full-thickness) biopsy to measure it accurately.

melanoma-clinical.stem: The commonest subtype of melanoma in darker-skinned and Asian patients, occurring on palms/soles/nail beds and unrelated to sun exposure, is:
melanoma-clinical.explanation: Acral lentiginous melanoma arises on palms, soles and nail beds, is not sun-related, and is the commonest melanoma subtype in darker-skinned and Asian populations; it is often diagnosed late, so pigmented acral/subungual lesions warrant careful evaluation.

melanoma-clinical.stem: Regarding melanoma in darker skin — which is correct?

options.text: People with darker skin do not really get melanoma, so acral lesions can be ignored

Although melanoma is less common in darker skin, ACRAL LENTIGINOUS melanoma (palms, soles, nail beds — NOT sun-related) is the COMMONEST subtype in darker-skinned and Asian patients and is often diagnosed LATE (worse prognosis) — so pigmented acral/subungual lesions (a nail streak, a sole lesion) must be examined and biopsied, not dismissed

melanoma-clinical.explanation: Assuming darker skin is protected leads to missed, late-stage acral melanoma; awareness that acral lentiginous melanoma predominates in these groups prompts timely evaluation.

melanoma-clinical.stem: What best explains the finding: “A pigmented lesion that is asymmetric, irregular, multicoloured and changing”?
melanoma-clinical.explanation: A pigmented lesion that is asymmetric, irregular, multicoloured and changing → Melanoma (ABCDE).

melanoma-clinical.stem: What best explains the finding: “A mole that looks different from all the others”?
melanoma-clinical.explanation: A mole that looks different from all the others → "Ugly duckling" sign of melanoma.

melanoma-clinical.stem: Which should you review before “Melanoma: Diagnosis & Staging”?
melanoma-clinical.explanation: Understanding photoprotection is crucial for melanoma prevention.

keratinocyte-carcinomas.stem: A slow-growing pearly papule with a rolled border, telangiectasia and central ulceration on the face is most likely:
keratinocyte-carcinomas.explanation: A pearly, translucent papule with rolled edges, surface telangiectasia and central ulceration ("rodent ulcer") on sun-exposed skin is a basal cell carcinoma — the commonest skin cancer, locally invasive but almost never metastasising, treated by excision.

keratinocyte-carcinomas.stem: Compared with basal cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma:

options.text: Can metastasise, especially on the lip/ear, in scars or in immunosuppressed patients

keratinocyte-carcinomas.explanation: Unlike BCC (which rarely metastasises), squamous cell carcinoma can metastasise — the risk is higher on the lip/ear, in scars/chronic wounds (Marjolin ulcer) and in immunosuppressed (transplant) patients — so SCC warrants prompt excision and follow-up. It arises from actinic keratosis/Bowen disease.

keratinocyte-carcinomas.stem: Regarding metastatic potential of bcc vs scc — which is correct?

options.text: Basal cell and squamous cell carcinomas behave similarly and carry the same metastatic risk

They differ importantly: BASAL cell carcinoma is locally invasive but almost NEVER metastasises (excellent prognosis with excision), whereas SQUAMOUS cell carcinoma CAN metastasise — especially on the lip/ear, in scars/chronic wounds, and in IMMUNOSUPPRESSED patients — so SCC needs more vigilant treatment and follow-up

keratinocyte-carcinomas.explanation: Triaging by metastatic potential (BCC low, SCC moderate/higher in high-risk sites and immunosuppression) focuses follow-up and urgency appropriately rather than treating both identically.

keratinocyte-carcinomas.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pearly papule with rolled edge, telangiectasia and central ulcer on the face”?
keratinocyte-carcinomas.explanation: Pearly papule with rolled edge, telangiectasia and central ulcer on the face → Basal cell carcinoma (rarely metastasises).

keratinocyte-carcinomas.stem: What best explains the finding: “Firm scaly/ulcerated nodule on the lip or ear”?
keratinocyte-carcinomas.explanation: Firm scaly/ulcerated nodule on the lip or ear → Squamous cell carcinoma (can metastasise).

keratinocyte-carcinomas.stem: Which should you review before “Keratinocyte Carcinomas (BCC & SCC)”?
keratinocyte-carcinomas.explanation: Understanding UV damage is crucial for grasping keratinocyte carcinomas.

topical-dermatologic-therapy.stem: Which topical corticosteroid potency is most appropriate for an inflammatory rash on the face?
topical-dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Facial skin is thin and highly absorptive, so only mild topical steroids should be used there to avoid atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, perioral dermatitis and systemic absorption. Potent steroids are reserved for thick skin (e.g. palms/soles) or resistant plaques, for the shortest effective time.

topical-dermatologic-therapy.stem: For a dry, thickened (lichenified) chronic plaque, the most suitable and potent topical vehicle is generally a(n):
topical-dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Following "if it's dry, wet it", greasy occlusive ointments are the most hydrating and potent vehicle for dry, lichenified lesions, increasing drug penetration. Lotions, gels and solutions suit weepy or hairy areas ("if it's wet, dry it").

topical-dermatologic-therapy.stem: Regarding matching steroid potency to site — which is correct?

options.text: A potent topical steroid is fine anywhere, including the face, if it clears the rash

Steroid potency must be MATCHED to the SITE: the FACE, flexures and genitals have THIN, highly absorptive skin, so only MILD steroids should be used there (potent ones cause atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, perioral dermatitis, and possible systemic absorption), whereas thick skin (palms/soles) tolerates and needs POTENT steroids

topical-dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Because absorption and atrophy risk depend on skin thickness, using a potent steroid on the face/flexures causes disfiguring local side-effects and possible HPA suppression — site-appropriate potency is essential.

topical-dermatologic-therapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Skin thinning, striae and telangiectasia after prolonged potent steroid use”?

options.text: Thin facial skin → high absorption → lower potency

topical-dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Skin thinning, striae and telangiectasia after prolonged potent steroid use → Topical corticosteroid atrophy.

topical-dermatologic-therapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “A greasy ointment chosen for a dry, lichenified plaque”?

options.text: Thin facial skin → high absorption → lower potency

topical-dermatologic-therapy.explanation: A greasy ointment chosen for a dry, lichenified plaque → Vehicle selection ("dry → wet"; occlusion ↑ potency).

systemic-dermatologic-therapy.stem: Before starting an anti-TNF biologic for severe psoriasis, it is essential to screen for:
systemic-dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Anti-TNF biologics can reactivate latent tuberculosis (and hepatitis B), so screening and treating latent infection before starting is mandatory; live vaccines are also contraindicated during biologic/immunosuppressive therapy.

systemic-dermatologic-therapy.stem: A patient on methotrexate for psoriasis should also receive which supplement, with monitoring of which parameters?

options.text: Folic acid; full blood count and liver function

systemic-dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Methotrexate is a folate antagonist, so folic acid is co-prescribed to reduce toxicity, and full blood count and liver function are monitored (risk of myelosuppression and hepatotoxicity). It is also teratogenic, requiring contraception.

systemic-dermatologic-therapy.stem: Regarding safety before systemic dermatology drugs — which is correct?

options.text: Systemic dermatology drugs can be started for severe skin disease without special screening

Each systemic agent carries mandatory safety steps: TERATOGENIC drugs (methotrexate, isotretinoin, acitretin) require pregnancy prevention/testing; METHOTREXATE needs folate + FBC/LFT monitoring; CICLOSPORIN needs renal/BP monitoring; and BIOLOGICS require infection SCREENING (latent TB, hepatitis) and avoidance of LIVE VACCINES — starting them without these precautions risks serious harm

systemic-dermatologic-therapy.explanation: These drugs are effective but hazardous, so the pre-treatment screening and monitoring (pregnancy, organ function, infection) are integral to safe use — omitting them causes preventable harm.

systemic-dermatologic-therapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Narrowband UVB for extensive psoriasis/vitiligo”?
systemic-dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Narrowband UVB for extensive psoriasis/vitiligo → Phototherapy (steroid-sparing).

systemic-dermatologic-therapy.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hepatotoxicity/myelosuppression on a folate-antagonist for psoriasis”?
systemic-dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Hepatotoxicity/myelosuppression on a folate-antagonist for psoriasis → Methotrexate (give folic acid, monitor FBC/LFTs).

systemic-dermatologic-therapy.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Phototherapy & Systemic Dermatologic Therapy”?
systemic-dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Basic pharmacology knowledge may support understanding of drug mechanisms.

systemic-dermatologic-therapy.stem: Which should you review before “Phototherapy & Systemic Dermatologic Therapy”?
systemic-dermatologic-therapy.explanation: Understanding systemic agents is crucial for therapy.

renal-defense-mechanisms.stem: The most important mechanism keeping the upper urinary tract sterile is:

options.text: The flushing action of urine flow with complete bladder emptying

renal-defense-mechanisms.explanation: Regular, unidirectional urine flow and complete bladder emptying physically wash out organisms before they can adhere and ascend — the principal defence. This is why stasis from obstruction, incomplete emptying, catheters or reflux is the dominant risk factor for urinary tract infection.

renal-defense-mechanisms.stem: Vesicoureteric reflux predisposes to pyelonephritis and renal scarring because it:

options.text: Allows bladder urine (and bacteria) to flow back up toward the kidney

renal-defense-mechanisms.explanation: The vesicoureteric junction normally acts as a one-way valve. In vesicoureteric reflux this valve fails, allowing bladder urine and bacteria to reflux up the ureter to the renal pelvis, predisposing to pyelonephritis and, in children, renal scarring.

renal-defense-mechanisms.stem: Regarding the main urinary tract defence — which is correct?

options.text: Urine is sterile mainly because of antibodies and immune cells in the bladder

While chemical (low pH, urea, Tamm-Horsfall/IgA) and mucosal/innate defences contribute, the PRINCIPAL defence is the MECHANICAL flushing of URINE FLOW with complete bladder emptying — which is why STASIS (obstruction, incomplete voiding, catheters, reflux) is the dominant risk factor for UTI, more than any immune deficiency

renal-defense-mechanisms.explanation: Recognising flow/emptying as the key defence explains why relieving obstruction, treating incomplete emptying and hydration prevent recurrent UTI, and why stasis (not immune failure) underlies most infections.

renal-defense-mechanisms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Recurrent UTI with incomplete bladder emptying or obstruction”?
renal-defense-mechanisms.explanation: Recurrent UTI with incomplete bladder emptying or obstruction → Loss of the urine-flushing defence (stasis).

renal-defense-mechanisms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Childhood pyelonephritis with renal scarring”?
renal-defense-mechanisms.explanation: Childhood pyelonephritis with renal scarring → Vesicoureteric reflux (failed one-way valve).

renal-defense-mechanisms.stem: Which should you review before “Renal & Urinary Tract Defense Mechanisms”?
renal-defense-mechanisms.explanation: Understanding innate immunity is crucial for grasping urinary tract defenses.

uti-pathogenesis-microbiology.stem: A patient with recurrent UTIs has persistently alkaline urine and a large staghorn calculus. The most likely organism is:
uti-pathogenesis-microbiology.explanation: Proteus produces urease, which splits urea to ammonia, alkalinising the urine and precipitating struvite (magnesium-ammonium-phosphate) stones that can form staghorn calculi. E. coli is the commonest overall uropathogen but does not typically cause struvite stones.

uti-pathogenesis-microbiology.stem: Asymptomatic bacteriuria should be treated with antibiotics in which situation?
uti-pathogenesis-microbiology.explanation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is generally not treated, because treatment does not benefit patients and promotes resistance. The important exceptions are pregnancy (to prevent pyelonephritis and preterm birth) and before invasive urological procedures.

uti-pathogenesis-microbiology.stem: Regarding treating asymptomatic bacteriuria — which is correct?

options.text: Any positive urine culture should be treated with antibiotics

ASYMPTOMATIC bacteriuria (positive culture, NO symptoms) should generally NOT be treated — treatment does not help and drives resistance — with two key EXCEPTIONS: PREGNANCY (untreated ASB risks pyelonephritis and preterm birth) and before an invasive UROLOGICAL procedure; elsewhere, treat only symptomatic UTI

uti-pathogenesis-microbiology.explanation: Reflexively treating every positive culture causes unnecessary antibiotic use and resistance; the evidence-based exceptions (pregnancy, pre-procedure) are the high-yield points, while symptoms otherwise define the need to treat.

uti-pathogenesis-microbiology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Commonest organism cultured from an uncomplicated UTI”?

options.text: Sterile pyuria (TB, chlamydia/GC, stones, treated UTI)

uti-pathogenesis-microbiology.explanation: Commonest organism cultured from an uncomplicated UTI → Uropathogenic E. coli.

uti-pathogenesis-microbiology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Alkaline urine with struvite staghorn calculi”?

options.text: Sterile pyuria (TB, chlamydia/GC, stones, treated UTI)

uti-pathogenesis-microbiology.explanation: Alkaline urine with struvite staghorn calculi → Proteus (urease-producing).

uti-pathogenesis-microbiology.stem: Which should you review before “UTI: Pathogenesis & Microbiology”?
uti-pathogenesis-microbiology.explanation: Knowledge of E. coli and Klebsiella is essential for understanding uropathogens.

urinalysis-urine-examination.stem: Red-cell casts in the urine sediment localise the source of bleeding/inflammation to the:
urinalysis-urine-examination.explanation: Casts form in the renal tubules, so their presence indicates a renal parenchymal source. Red-cell casts specifically indicate glomerular bleeding (glomerulonephritis/nephritic syndrome). White-cell casts indicate pyelonephritis/interstitial nephritis, and muddy-brown granular casts indicate acute tubular necrosis.

urinalysis-urine-examination.stem: Muddy-brown granular casts in a patient with acute kidney injury are characteristic of:
urinalysis-urine-examination.explanation: Muddy-brown granular ("dirty brown") casts are the classic urinary finding of acute tubular necrosis, reflecting sloughed tubular epithelial debris. Nephrotic syndrome shows fatty casts/oval fat bodies, and pure prerenal azotaemia typically has a bland sediment with hyaline casts.

urinalysis-urine-examination.stem: Regarding glomerular vs urologic haematuria — which is correct?

options.text: Blood on urine dipstick always means a stone or bladder problem

The SOURCE of haematuria is distinguished by the microscopy: DYSMORPHIC red cells and RED-CELL CASTS (± proteinuria) indicate a GLOMERULAR source (glomerulonephritis) needing a nephrology/renal work-up, whereas ISOMORPHIC (normal-shaped) red cells without casts suggest a LOWER-tract/urologic source (stone, tumour, infection) needing urologic imaging/cystoscopy

urinalysis-urine-examination.explanation: RBC casts and dysmorphic cells reroute the work-up entirely (glomerular vs urologic), so treating all haematuria as urologic would miss glomerulonephritis — and vice versa.

urinalysis-urine-examination.stem: What best explains the finding: “Red-cell casts and dysmorphic red cells”?
urinalysis-urine-examination.explanation: Red-cell casts and dysmorphic red cells → Glomerulonephritis (nephritic — glomerular bleeding).

urinalysis-urine-examination.stem: What best explains the finding: “White-cell casts”?
urinalysis-urine-examination.explanation: White-cell casts → Pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis.

urinalysis-urine-examination.stem: Which should you review before “Urine Collection & Examination”?
urinalysis-urine-examination.explanation: Physical and chemical examination is foundational for understanding urinalysis.

urinary-tract-pathology.stem: Which urinary stone type is typically radiolucent and forms in acidic urine, classically in patients with gout or high purine turnover?
urinary-tract-pathology.explanation: Uric acid stones are radiolucent (not seen on plain X-ray), form in acidic urine, and are associated with gout/hyperuricosuria; they may be dissolved by urinary alkalinisation. Calcium stones are radio-opaque and commonest, and struvite stones form in alkaline urine from urease-producing organisms.

urinary-tract-pathology.stem: Prolonged urinary tract obstruction leads to:

options.text: Hydronephrosis with progressive renal parenchymal atrophy
No effect if urine is sterile

urinary-tract-pathology.explanation: Obstruction raises pressure upstream, dilating the pelvicalyceal system (hydronephrosis) and, over time, compressing and atrophying the renal parenchyma — potentially causing renal failure if bilateral or prolonged. Prompt relief of obstruction can reverse early damage.

urinary-tract-pathology.stem: Regarding obstructed infected kidney — which is correct?

options.text: A kidney stone with fever just needs antibiotics and analgesia

An OBSTRUCTING stone WITH INFECTION (fever, systemic upset) is a urological EMERGENCY — antibiotics alone cannot sterilise an obstructed, pus-filled system; it requires URGENT DECOMPRESSION/DRAINAGE (nephrostomy or ureteric stent) to prevent pyonephrosis, sepsis and kidney loss

urinary-tract-pathology.explanation: Infection behind an obstruction cannot drain or be cleared by antibiotics alone, so prompt drainage — not just medical therapy — is life- and kidney-saving; missing this leads to sepsis.

urinary-tract-pathology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dilated pelvicalyceal system on imaging”?
urinary-tract-pathology.explanation: Dilated pelvicalyceal system on imaging → Hydronephrosis from obstruction.

urinary-tract-pathology.stem: What best explains the finding: “Severe colicky loin-to-groin pain with haematuria”?
urinary-tract-pathology.explanation: Severe colicky loin-to-groin pain with haematuria → Ureteric stone (renal colic).

urinary-tract-pathology.stem: Which should you review before “Urinary Tract Pathology & Stones”?
urinary-tract-pathology.explanation: Anatomical knowledge is fundamental for understanding urinary tract pathology.

uti-clinical-management.stem: Fever, rigors and costovertebral-angle (loin) tenderness in a patient with a UTI indicate:
uti-clinical-management.explanation: Fever, rigors and loin/costovertebral-angle tenderness signify renal parenchymal infection — acute pyelonephritis (upper UTI) — which needs a longer, often initially broader or intravenous antibiotic course with urine culture, unlike afebrile lower-tract cystitis.

uti-clinical-management.stem: Which patient has, by definition, a "complicated" UTI?

options.text: A healthy non-pregnant woman with dysuria
A pregnant woman with a UTI
A woman with a first episode of cystitis
A woman with a normal urinary tract

uti-clinical-management.explanation: Complicated UTI occurs with a factor increasing the risk of failure or harm — pregnancy, male sex, catheterisation, obstruction/stones, immunosuppression, diabetes or structural/functional abnormality. These require urine culture, longer therapy and often imaging, unlike uncomplicated cystitis in a healthy non-pregnant woman.

uti-clinical-management.stem: Regarding uti in men and pregnancy — which is correct?

options.text: A UTI in a man can be treated with the same short course as uncomplicated cystitis in a woman

Any UTI in a MAN (and in PREGNANCY) is by definition COMPLICATED — it warrants a urine CULTURE, a LONGER antibiotic course, and evaluation for an underlying cause (prostatitis, obstruction, structural abnormality) — the short single-agent course used for uncomplicated female cystitis is inappropriate

uti-clinical-management.explanation: Male and pregnancy-associated UTIs carry higher risk and often an underlying abnormality, so treating them like simple female cystitis risks failure, relapse and missed pathology.

uti-clinical-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “Dysuria, frequency and urgency without fever”?
uti-clinical-management.explanation: Dysuria, frequency and urgency without fever → Cystitis (lower UTI).

uti-clinical-management.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fever, rigors and costovertebral-angle tenderness”?
uti-clinical-management.explanation: Fever, rigors and costovertebral-angle tenderness → Acute pyelonephritis (upper UTI).

uti-clinical-management.stem: Which should you review before “UTI: Clinical Syndromes & Management”?

options.text: Antibacterials II: Protein, DNA & Folate Inhibitors

uti-clinical-management.explanation: Understanding antibiotic classes is crucial for UTI management.

nephrotic-syndrome.stem: A 4-year-old presents with periorbital oedema, heavy proteinuria and hypoalbuminaemia; light microscopy is normal and the condition responds to steroids. The diagnosis is:
nephrotic-syndrome.explanation: Minimal change disease is the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in children: normal light microscopy with foot-process (podocyte) effacement on electron microscopy, and typically steroid-responsive. It is treated empirically with steroids without biopsy in the typical paediatric case.

nephrotic-syndrome.stem: The hypercoagulable state (e.g. renal vein thrombosis) in nephrotic syndrome is largely due to urinary loss of:
nephrotic-syndrome.explanation: Nephrotic-range proteinuria causes urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins, notably antithrombin III, producing a hypercoagulable state with increased risk of renal vein thrombosis and venous thromboembolism. Loss of immunoglobulins similarly predisposes to infection.

nephrotic-syndrome.stem: Regarding nephrotic vs nephritic — which is correct?

options.text: Heavy proteinuria and haematuria with red-cell casts are the same glomerular syndrome

NEPHROTIC syndrome is PODOCYTE injury with HEAVY proteinuria (>3.5 g) and a relatively BLAND urine (little blood/inflammation), producing hypoalbuminaemia/oedema/hyperlipidaemia/hypercoagulability; NEPHRITIC syndrome is INFLAMMATORY glomerular injury with HAEMATURIA, RED-CELL CASTS, hypertension and often renal impairment with only sub-nephrotic proteinuria — the urinary picture (bland/heavy-protein vs active/blood) separates them

nephrotic-syndrome.explanation: The two syndromes have different mechanisms, differentials and treatments, so distinguishing bland heavy proteinuria (nephrotic) from an active sediment with RBC casts (nephritic) directs the entire work-up.

nephrotic-syndrome.stem: What best explains the finding: “Proteinuria >3.5 g/day with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema”?
nephrotic-syndrome.explanation: Proteinuria >3.5 g/day with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema → Nephrotic syndrome (podocyte injury).

nephrotic-syndrome.stem: What best explains the finding: “Nephrotic syndrome in a child, steroid-responsive”?
nephrotic-syndrome.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome in a child, steroid-responsive → Minimal change disease.

nephrotic-syndrome.stem: Which should you review before “Nephrotic Syndrome”?
nephrotic-syndrome.explanation: Understanding proteinuria evaluation is essential for diagnosing nephrotic syndrome.

nephritic-syndrome.stem: A young adult develops visible haematuria within 1–2 days of an upper respiratory tract infection, with a normal complement level. The most likely diagnosis is:
nephritic-syndrome.explanation: IgA nephropathy classically causes "synpharyngitic" haematuria concurrent with or 1–2 days after a mucosal (respiratory) infection, with normal complement and mesangial IgA deposits. Post-streptococcal GN instead follows 1–3 weeks after streptococcal infection with a low C3.

nephritic-syndrome.stem: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) is characterised histologically by:
nephritic-syndrome.explanation: RPGN shows crescents (proliferating cells and fibrin in Bowman's space) and causes rapid renal decline over days to weeks — a nephrological emergency. Its immunofluorescence patterns (linear anti-GBM, granular immune-complex, pauci-immune ANCA) guide urgent immunosuppression ± plasma exchange.

nephritic-syndrome.stem: Regarding iga nephropathy vs post-streptococcal gn timing — which is correct?

options.text: Haematuria after a throat infection is always post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

TIMING distinguishes them: IgA NEPHROPATHY causes haematuria CONCURRENT with or 1–2 DAYS after an upper-respiratory infection ("synpharyngitic", normal complement), whereas POST-STREPTOCOCCAL GN follows 1–3 WEEKS after a streptococcal throat/skin infection (with LOW C3 and positive strep serology) — same trigger organ, very different latency and complement

nephritic-syndrome.explanation: The interval (days vs weeks) and complement level separate two common post-infectious nephritides with different courses (IgA is chronic/relapsing; post-strep is usually self-limiting), so timing changes the diagnosis and prognosis.

nephritic-syndrome.stem: What best explains the finding: “Haematuria with red-cell casts, hypertension and rising creatinine”?
nephritic-syndrome.explanation: Haematuria with red-cell casts, hypertension and rising creatinine → Nephritic syndrome (glomerulonephritis).

nephritic-syndrome.stem: What best explains the finding: “Visible haematuria 1–2 days after a sore throat”?
nephritic-syndrome.explanation: Visible haematuria 1–2 days after a sore throat → IgA nephropathy (synpharyngitic).

nephritic-syndrome.stem: Which should you review before “Nephritic Syndrome & Glomerulonephritis”?
nephritic-syndrome.explanation: Evaluating proteinuria is essential in differentiating nephritic from nephrotic syndromes.

interstitial-nephritis-obstruction.stem: A patient develops acute kidney injury with fever, a rash, eosinophilia and white-cell casts one week after starting an antibiotic. The most likely diagnosis and management are:

options.text: Acute tubular necrosis — give more of the drug
Acute interstitial nephritis — stop the offending drug (± steroids)

interstitial-nephritis-obstruction.explanation: Drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis is a hypersensitivity reaction causing AKI with fever, rash, eosinophilia and eosinophiluria/white-cell casts. The mainstay is prompt withdrawal of the culprit drug (antibiotics, NSAIDs, PPIs), sometimes with corticosteroids, and it is usually reversible.

interstitial-nephritis-obstruction.stem: Why must obstruction be excluded in every case of acute kidney injury?

options.text: Post-renal (obstructive) AKI is reversible if the obstruction is relieved promptly

interstitial-nephritis-obstruction.explanation: Obstruction is a readily reversible cause of AKI — relief (catheter, stent or nephrostomy) can restore function if done before permanent damage. Evaluation includes a bladder scan (for retention) and ultrasound (for hydronephrosis); recovery may be followed by a post-obstructive diuresis.

interstitial-nephritis-obstruction.stem: Regarding obstruction as a reversible cause of aki — which is correct?

options.text: Acute kidney injury is a parenchymal (intrinsic) problem, so imaging for obstruction is unnecessary

Every AKI work-up must EXCLUDE post-renal OBSTRUCTION (bladder scan for retention, ultrasound for hydronephrosis), because obstructive AKI is REVERSIBLE if relieved promptly — and although each kidney can compensate, obstruction causing significant AKI usually means BILATERAL (or single-functioning-kidney) blockage; missing it risks permanent loss

interstitial-nephritis-obstruction.explanation: Obstruction is a readily reversible cause of AKI that is easy to overlook and simple to treat (catheter/nephrostomy), so ruling it out early prevents avoidable permanent kidney damage.

interstitial-nephritis-obstruction.stem: What best explains the finding: “AKI with fever, rash, eosinophilia and eosinophiluria after a new drug”?
interstitial-nephritis-obstruction.explanation: AKI with fever, rash, eosinophilia and eosinophiluria after a new drug → Acute interstitial nephritis (drug hypersensitivity).

interstitial-nephritis-obstruction.stem: What best explains the finding: “AKI with a palpable bladder / bilateral hydronephrosis”?
interstitial-nephritis-obstruction.explanation: AKI with a palpable bladder / bilateral hydronephrosis → Obstructive (post-renal) AKI — reversible.

interstitial-nephritis-obstruction.stem: Which should you review before “Interstitial Nephritis & Obstructive Uropathy”?
interstitial-nephritis-obstruction.explanation: Drug hypersensitivity in acute interstitial nephritis often involves antibiotics.

cystic-kidney-diseases.stem: An adult with bilaterally enlarged kidneys full of cysts, hypertension and a family history of kidney failure is at increased risk of which extrarenal complication?
