renal-replacement-therapy.stem: Which should you review before “Renal Replacement Therapy: Dialysis & Transplant”?
renal-replacement-therapy.explanation: Understanding immunosuppressants is crucial for managing transplant patients.

loop-thiazide-diuretics.stem: A thiazide diuretic and a loop diuretic differ in their effect on urinary calcium in that:

options.text: Loops increase calcium excretion; thiazides decrease it

loop-thiazide-diuretics.explanation: Loop diuretics increase urinary calcium (helpful in hypercalcaemia) by abolishing the gradient driving calcium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, whereas thiazides decrease urinary calcium (helpful in calcium stones/osteoporosis) — "loops lose, thiazides retain" calcium.

loop-thiazide-diuretics.stem: Why do both loop and thiazide diuretics tend to cause hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis?

options.text: They directly block potassium channels in muscle
They increase sodium delivery to the distal nephron, enhancing potassium and hydrogen secretion

loop-thiazide-diuretics.explanation: By blocking sodium reabsorption upstream, both classes increase sodium delivery to the distal nephron/collecting duct, where enhanced sodium reabsorption drives potassium and hydrogen secretion — producing hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis.

loop-thiazide-diuretics.stem: Regarding calcium handling of loops vs thiazides — which is correct?

options.text: Loop and thiazide diuretics have the same effect on calcium excretion

They are OPPOSITE: LOOP diuretics INCREASE urinary calcium (by abolishing the lumen-positive potential in the thick ascending limb that drives calcium reabsorption) — useful in hypercalcaemia — whereas THIAZIDES DECREASE urinary calcium — useful in recurrent calcium stones and osteoporosis; "loops lose calcium, thiazides retain calcium"
Increased distal Na delivery → K+/H+ secretion

loop-thiazide-diuretics.explanation: This opposite calcium handling determines drug choice — a loop for hypercalcaemia, a thiazide for calcium-stone prevention — so confusing them leads to the wrong prescription.

loop-thiazide-diuretics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Rapid diuresis in acute pulmonary oedema”?

options.text: Increased distal Na delivery → K+/H+ secretion

loop-thiazide-diuretics.explanation: Rapid diuresis in acute pulmonary oedema → Loop diuretic (NKCC2 blockade).

loop-thiazide-diuretics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hypokalaemia with metabolic alkalosis on a diuretic”?

options.text: Increased distal Na delivery → K+/H+ secretion

loop-thiazide-diuretics.explanation: Hypokalaemia with metabolic alkalosis on a diuretic → Increased distal Na delivery → K+/H+ secretion.

potassium-sparing-osmotic-diuretics.stem: Which diuretic acts on the collecting-duct mineralocorticoid receptor, improves survival in heart failure, and can cause hyperkalaemia and gynaecomastia?
potassium-sparing-osmotic-diuretics.explanation: Spironolactone is an aldosterone (mineralocorticoid-receptor) antagonist acting in the collecting duct; it retains potassium (hyperkalaemia risk), improves heart-failure survival, treats Conn syndrome and cirrhotic ascites, and its anti-androgen action causes gynaecomastia (eplerenone is more selective).

potassium-sparing-osmotic-diuretics.stem: Acetazolamide, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor acting in the proximal tubule, characteristically causes:
potassium-sparing-osmotic-diuretics.explanation: By inhibiting proximal tubule carbonic anhydrase, acetazolamide causes urinary bicarbonate loss and a metabolic acidosis; this is used therapeutically (glaucoma, altitude sickness, urinary alkalinisation), unlike loops/thiazides which cause metabolic alkalosis.

potassium-sparing-osmotic-diuretics.stem: Regarding hyperkalaemia risk of potassium-sparing diuretics — which is correct?

options.text: Adding spironolactone to an ACE inhibitor is always safe because they treat the same conditions

Potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, eplerenone, amiloride) RETAIN potassium, so combining them with ACE inhibitors/ARBs (which also raise potassium), potassium supplements, or using them in renal impairment can cause dangerous HYPERKALAEMIA — the combination is used deliberately in heart failure but demands monitoring of potassium and renal function, not casual co-prescription

potassium-sparing-osmotic-diuretics.explanation: Both drug classes raise serum potassium, so their combination (common in heart failure) can precipitate life-threatening hyperkalaemia without monitoring — the opposite electrolyte risk to loops/thiazides.

potassium-sparing-osmotic-diuretics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Survival benefit and potassium retention in heart failure”?
potassium-sparing-osmotic-diuretics.explanation: Survival benefit and potassium retention in heart failure → Aldosterone antagonist (spironolactone/eplerenone).

potassium-sparing-osmotic-diuretics.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hyperkalaemia when spironolactone is combined with an ACE inhibitor”?
potassium-sparing-osmotic-diuretics.explanation: Hyperkalaemia when spironolactone is combined with an ACE inhibitor → Additive potassium retention.

potassium-sparing-osmotic-diuretics.stem: Which should you review before “Potassium-Sparing, Osmotic & CA-Inhibitor Diuretics”?
potassium-sparing-osmotic-diuretics.explanation: Essential for understanding potassium handling in diuretics.

nephrotoxic-drugs.stem: The "triple whammy" combination most likely to precipitate acute kidney injury is:
nephrotoxic-drugs.explanation: NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole, ACEi/ARBs dilate the efferent, and diuretics deplete volume; together this "triple whammy" undermines the autoregulation maintaining GFR and commonly precipitates prerenal/haemodynamic AKI, especially in volume-depleted or elderly patients.

nephrotoxic-drugs.stem: Which drug should generally be withheld at low GFR because of the risk of lactic acidosis?
nephrotoxic-drugs.explanation: Metformin is renally cleared and accumulates in renal impairment, risking lactic acidosis, so it is dose-reduced or withheld at low GFR and during acute illness ("sick-day rules"). Nitrofurantoin (ineffective/toxic) and gadolinium (nephrogenic systemic fibrosis) are also avoided at low GFR.

nephrotoxic-drugs.stem: Regarding creatinine rise without true kidney injury — which is correct?

options.text: Any rise in serum creatinine after starting a drug means the drug has damaged the kidney

Some drugs — notably TRIMETHOPRIM and CIMETIDINE — inhibit tubular SECRETION of creatinine, RAISING serum creatinine WITHOUT reducing the true GFR (a "pseudo-AKI"); the urea and actual filtration are unchanged, so this is a benign, reversible effect and should be distinguished from genuine nephrotoxicity to avoid stopping a needed drug unnecessarily

nephrotoxic-drugs.explanation: Misreading the creatinine bump from blocked tubular secretion as real AKI leads to needless drug discontinuation and investigation; recognising the mechanism (unchanged GFR/urea) avoids that error.

nephrotoxic-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “AKI after NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic in a dehydrated patient”?
nephrotoxic-drugs.explanation: AKI after NSAID + ACE inhibitor + diuretic in a dehydrated patient → Haemodynamic "triple whammy".

nephrotoxic-drugs.stem: What best explains the finding: “Non-oliguric AKI with tubular injury after aminoglycosides”?
nephrotoxic-drugs.explanation: Non-oliguric AKI with tubular injury after aminoglycosides → Direct tubular nephrotoxicity.

nephrotoxic-drugs.stem: Which should you review before “Nephrotoxic Drugs & Prescribing in Renal Impairment”?
nephrotoxic-drugs.explanation: AIN is a key pattern of nephrotoxic injury.

glomerular-disease-immune-mechanisms.stem: Linear IgG deposition along the glomerular basement membrane on immunofluorescence, with pulmonary haemorrhage, indicates:
glomerular-disease-immune-mechanisms.explanation: Linear IgG along the GBM reflects antibodies to type IV collagen (anti-GBM disease); when it affects both lung and kidney it is Goodpasture syndrome. Granular deposits indicate immune-complex disease, and scant/absent staining indicates pauci-immune (ANCA) vasculitis.

glomerular-disease-immune-mechanisms.stem: A low serum complement in a nephritic patient narrows the differential toward:

options.text: IgA nephropathy, anti-GBM disease and ANCA vasculitis
Post-streptococcal GN, lupus nephritis and MPGN/C3 glomerulopathy

glomerular-disease-immune-mechanisms.explanation: Low-complement nephritic diseases include post-streptococcal GN, lupus nephritis, and MPGN/C3 glomerulopathy (and cryoglobulinaemia), whereas IgA nephropathy, anti-GBM disease and ANCA vasculitis typically have normal complement — so complement helps triage the causes.

glomerular-disease-immune-mechanisms.stem: Regarding recognising rapidly progressive gn — which is correct?

options.text: Nephritic syndrome can always be worked up slowly as an outpatient

A nephritic picture with RAPIDLY rising creatinine over days–weeks is RAPIDLY PROGRESSIVE GN (crescentic GN) — a nephrological EMERGENCY: it can arise from any immune mechanism (immune-complex, anti-GBM, or pauci-immune ANCA), and delayed diagnosis/immunosuppression (± plasma exchange for anti-GBM/severe ANCA) leads to irreversible renal failure, so it needs urgent serology and biopsy, not a leisurely work-up

glomerular-disease-immune-mechanisms.explanation: Crescentic GN destroys nephrons within weeks, so treating it as routine nephritis loses the narrow window in which urgent immunosuppression can preserve kidney function.

glomerular-disease-immune-mechanisms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Heavy proteinuria with a bland urinary sediment”?
glomerular-disease-immune-mechanisms.explanation: Heavy proteinuria with a bland urinary sediment → Nephrotic (podocyte/barrier injury).

glomerular-disease-immune-mechanisms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Haematuria with RBC casts, hypertension and reduced GFR”?
glomerular-disease-immune-mechanisms.explanation: Haematuria with RBC casts, hypertension and reduced GFR → Nephritic (proliferative injury).

glomerular-disease-immune-mechanisms.stem: Which should you review before “Immune Mechanisms of Glomerular Injury”?
glomerular-disease-immune-mechanisms.explanation: Understanding podocytopathies is essential for nephrotic syndrome.

sodium-water-disorders.stem: A patient with euvolaemic hyponatraemia, low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine and urine sodium >30 mmol/L most likely has:
sodium-water-disorders.explanation: SIADH causes euvolaemic hyponatraemia: excess ADH concentrates the urine inappropriately despite low serum osmolality, with urine sodium typically >30 mmol/L. It is managed by fluid restriction and treating the cause, after excluding hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency.

sodium-water-disorders.stem: Correcting chronic hyponatraemia too rapidly risks which complication?
sodium-water-disorders.explanation: Brain cells adapt to chronic hyponatraemia by losing osmoles; raising serum sodium too fast causes them to shrink, producing osmotic demyelination (central pontine myelinolysis). Chronic hyponatraemia is therefore corrected slowly, with limits on the sodium rise per 24 hours.

sodium-water-disorders.stem: Regarding rate of hyponatraemia correction — which is correct?

options.text: Severe hyponatraemia should be corrected back to normal as quickly as possible

CHRONIC hyponatraemia must be corrected SLOWLY (limiting the rise in sodium per 24 hours) because over-rapid correction causes OSMOTIC DEMYELINATION SYNDROME (central pontine myelinolysis) — brain cells that adapted to low osmolality shrink when it rises too fast; only ACUTE, symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma) warrants urgent hypertonic saline, and even then correction is limited

sodium-water-disorders.explanation: Aggressive correction of chronic hyponatraemia trades a treatable electrolyte problem for irreversible neurological injury; the safe rate of correction is as important as the direction.

sodium-water-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and urine Na >30”?
sodium-water-disorders.explanation: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and urine Na >30 → SIADH.

sodium-water-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hyponatraemia with oedema in heart failure or cirrhosis”?
sodium-water-disorders.explanation: Hyponatraemia with oedema in heart failure or cirrhosis → Hypervolaemic (low effective circulating volume → ADH).

sodium-water-disorders.stem: Which should you review before “Sodium & Water Disorders (Hypo/Hypernatraemia)”?
sodium-water-disorders.explanation: Essential for understanding sodium and water regulation.

potassium-disorders.stem: In a patient with severe hyperkalaemia and peaked T-waves, what is the role of intravenous calcium gluconate?

options.text: It rapidly lowers the serum potassium
It stabilises the cardiac membrane to prevent arrhythmia (without lowering potassium)
It removes potassium via the gut

potassium-disorders.explanation: Calcium stabilises the myocardium (raising the threshold potential) to prevent lethal arrhythmia but does not lower potassium; the level is reduced by shifting potassium into cells (insulin/glucose, salbutamol) and removing it (diuretics, binders, dialysis).

potassium-disorders.stem: A patient on a thiazide has persistent hypokalaemia despite potassium replacement. What should also be checked and corrected?
potassium-disorders.explanation: Hypomagnesaemia promotes renal potassium wasting and makes hypokalaemia refractory to replacement; correcting magnesium is often necessary before potassium will normalise, so magnesium should be checked and replaced alongside potassium.

potassium-disorders.stem: Regarding role of calcium in hyperkalaemia — which is correct?

options.text: IV calcium is given in hyperkalaemia to lower the serum potassium level

IV CALCIUM does NOT lower serum potassium — it STABILISES the cardiac membrane (raising the threshold potential) to prevent arrhythmia, buying time; the potassium is actually LOWERED by SHIFTING it into cells (insulin/glucose, salbutamol) and then REMOVING it from the body (diuretics, binders, dialysis), so calcium is the first protective step but must be followed by shifting and removal

potassium-disorders.explanation: Believing calcium "treats" the potassium leads to stopping after giving it, leaving a dangerously high potassium that will re-manifest; calcium only protects the heart while the shifting/removal steps actually correct the level.

potassium-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Peaked T-waves progressing to a widened QRS”?
potassium-disorders.explanation: Peaked T-waves progressing to a widened QRS → Hyperkalaemia (cardiac emergency).

potassium-disorders.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hyperkalaemia after ACE inhibitor + spironolactone in CKD”?
potassium-disorders.explanation: Hyperkalaemia after ACE inhibitor + spironolactone in CKD → Reduced renal potassium excretion.

potassium-disorders.stem: Which should you review before “Potassium Disorders (Hypo/Hyperkalaemia)”?
potassium-disorders.explanation: Diuretics are a major cause of hypokalaemia.

high-anion-gap-metabolic-acidosis.stem: A metabolic acidosis with a HIGH anion gap indicates:

options.text: Loss of bicarbonate replaced by chloride
Addition of an unmeasured acid consuming bicarbonate

high-anion-gap-metabolic-acidosis.explanation: A high anion gap means an unmeasured acid has been added (e.g. lactate, ketoacids, uraemic acids, toxic-alcohol metabolites, salicylate), consuming bicarbonate; a normal (hyperchloraemic) gap instead reflects bicarbonate loss (diarrhoea, RTA) replaced by chloride.

high-anion-gap-metabolic-acidosis.stem: A high anion gap metabolic acidosis accompanied by a raised osmolar gap should prompt urgent consideration of:

options.text: Toxic alcohol (methanol or ethylene glycol) poisoning

high-anion-gap-metabolic-acidosis.explanation: A raised osmolar gap with a high anion gap acidosis suggests ingestion of toxic alcohols (methanol, ethylene glycol), whose osmotically active parent molecules widen the osmolar gap before metabolism to acids — a time-critical poisoning needing specific antidotes (fomepizole/ethanol) and often dialysis.

high-anion-gap-metabolic-acidosis.stem: Regarding using the anion gap — which is correct?

options.text: All metabolic acidoses are basically the same and the anion gap is just a formality

The ANION GAP separates two mechanistically distinct groups with different causes and treatments: a HIGH gap indicates an ADDED unmeasured ACID (lactate, ketoacids, uraemia, toxic alcohols, salicylate — some needing antidotes or dialysis), whereas a NORMAL (hyperchloraemic) gap indicates BICARBONATE LOSS (diarrhoea or renal tubular acidosis, separated by the urine anion gap) — so calculating the gap (and the osmolar/delta gaps) is essential to find the cause and give the right, sometimes urgent, treatment

high-anion-gap-metabolic-acidosis.explanation: Skipping the anion gap merges unrelated conditions (e.g. life-threatening methanol poisoning vs diarrhoeal bicarbonate loss) that demand completely different management; the gap is the key branch point in the diagnostic algorithm.

high-anion-gap-metabolic-acidosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “High anion gap acidosis with a raised lactate in a septic/shocked patient”?

options.text: GI bicarbonate loss (negative urine anion gap)

high-anion-gap-metabolic-acidosis.explanation: High anion gap acidosis with a raised lactate in a septic/shocked patient → Lactic acidosis (commonest high-gap cause).

high-anion-gap-metabolic-acidosis.stem: What best explains the finding: “High anion gap acidosis with ketones in a diabetic”?

options.text: GI bicarbonate loss (negative urine anion gap)

high-anion-gap-metabolic-acidosis.explanation: High anion gap acidosis with ketones in a diabetic → Diabetic ketoacidosis.

high-anion-gap-metabolic-acidosis.stem: Which should you review before “High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis”?
high-anion-gap-metabolic-acidosis.explanation: Fundamental understanding of acid-base balance is essential.

options.text: Fragile and spread mainly by blood or sexual contact
Hardy — resistant to acid, bile and drying — and often spread faecal-orally
Unable to survive outside the body

virology-principles-classification.explanation: Naked viruses lack a fragile lipid envelope, so they resist acid, bile, detergents and drying and survive on fomites and through the gut — favouring faecal-oral transmission (e.g. enteroviruses, rotavirus, norovirus, hepatitis A). Enveloped viruses are fragile and spread by close contact/blood/sexual routes.

virology-principles-classification.stem: Which step of the viral replication cycle principally determines a virus's tissue tropism?

options.text: Attachment to a specific host cell receptor

virology-principles-classification.explanation: Attachment depends on the interaction between viral surface proteins and specific host cell receptors, so it determines which cells/tissues a virus can infect (tropism) — e.g. HIV gp120 binding CD4. Subsequent steps (penetration, uncoating, replication, assembly, release) follow.

virology-principles-classification.stem: Regarding enveloped vs naked virus stability — which is correct?

options.text: Having an envelope makes a virus more robust and harder to kill

The opposite: the lipid ENVELOPE is FRAGILE — easily disrupted by drying, heat, acid, bile, detergents and alcohol — so ENVELOPED viruses are LESS stable in the environment and spread by close contact/droplet/blood/sexual routes, whereas NAKED (non-enveloped) viruses are HARDY and survive fomites and the gastrointestinal tract for faecal-oral transmission

virology-principles-classification.explanation: The envelope's lipid nature makes enveloped viruses easy to inactivate (hand hygiene, alcohol), while naked viruses persist on surfaces and through the gut — a distinction that drives transmission routes and infection control.

virology-principles-classification.stem: What best explains the finding: “A virus that survives the gut and spreads faecal-orally”?

options.text: Attachment to a specific host receptor

virology-principles-classification.explanation: A virus that survives the gut and spreads faecal-orally → Naked (non-enveloped) virus — hardy.

virology-principles-classification.stem: What best explains the finding: “A virus inactivated by alcohol/detergent and spread by close contact”?

options.text: Attachment to a specific host receptor

virology-principles-classification.explanation: A virus inactivated by alcohol/detergent and spread by close contact → Enveloped virus — fragile lipid envelope.

nonenveloped-rna-viruses.stem: The leading cause of severe dehydrating diarrhoea in infants worldwide, preventable by a live oral vaccine, is:
nonenveloped-rna-viruses.explanation: Rotavirus (a naked dsRNA reovirus) is the leading cause of severe infantile gastroenteritis and dehydration, and is prevented by a live oral vaccine. Norovirus causes adult epidemic gastroenteritis; poliovirus causes paralysis.

nonenveloped-rna-viruses.stem: Which hepatitis virus is enterically (faecal-orally) transmitted and notable for high mortality in pregnant women?
nonenveloped-rna-viruses.explanation: Hepatitis E is a naked RNA virus transmitted faecal-orally (often waterborne), causing acute self-limiting hepatitis but with notably high mortality in pregnancy. Hepatitis B, C and D are blood-borne and can become chronic.

nonenveloped-rna-viruses.stem: Regarding hepatitis a/e chronicity — which is correct?

options.text: All hepatitis viruses can become chronic

The ENTERICALLY-transmitted, naked hepatitis viruses — hepatitis A and hepatitis E — cause ACUTE, self-limiting hepatitis and do NOT become chronic (unlike the blood-borne enveloped hepatitis B and C); hepatitis E is notable for high mortality in PREGNANCY

nonenveloped-rna-viruses.explanation: The route and chronicity differ: faecal-oral hep A/E are acute-only, while blood-borne hep B/C cause chronic disease/cirrhosis/cancer — a key distinction for prognosis and screening.

nonenveloped-rna-viruses.stem: What best explains the finding: “Acute flaccid paralysis in an unvaccinated child”?
nonenveloped-rna-viruses.explanation: Acute flaccid paralysis in an unvaccinated child → Poliovirus (enterovirus/picornavirus).

nonenveloped-rna-viruses.stem: What best explains the finding: “Explosive vomiting/diarrhoea outbreak on a cruise ship”?
nonenveloped-rna-viruses.explanation: Explosive vomiting/diarrhoea outbreak on a cruise ship → Norovirus (calicivirus).

nonenveloped-rna-viruses.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Non-enveloped RNA Viruses”?
nonenveloped-rna-viruses.explanation: Non-enveloped RNA viruses like norovirus are key causes of viral gastroenteritis.

nonenveloped-rna-viruses.stem: Which should you review before “Non-enveloped RNA Viruses”?
nonenveloped-rna-viruses.explanation: Understanding virology principles is essential for grasping non-enveloped RNA viruses.

enveloped-rna-viruses-orthomyxo-paramyxo.stem: Influenza pandemics arise mainly through antigenic shift, which is:

options.text: Reassortment of genome segments producing a novel haemagglutinin/neuraminidase

enveloped-rna-viruses-orthomyxo-paramyxo.explanation: Antigenic shift is the reassortment of segments between influenza strains, producing a virus with a novel HA/NA to which the population lacks immunity — causing pandemics. Antigenic drift (gradual point mutations) causes seasonal epidemics and the annual need to update the vaccine.

enveloped-rna-viruses-orthomyxo-paramyxo.stem: The leading cause of bronchiolitis and viral pneumonia in infants, forming multinucleate syncytia, is:
enveloped-rna-viruses-orthomyxo-paramyxo.explanation: RSV is the leading cause of infant bronchiolitis and pneumonia; it induces multinucleate syncytia (giant cells). Management is supportive, with palivizumab (monoclonal) prophylaxis for high-risk infants. Parainfluenza causes croup.

enveloped-rna-viruses-orthomyxo-paramyxo.stem: Regarding antigenic drift vs shift — which is correct?

options.text: Antigenic drift and shift are just two names for the same influenza mutation process

DRIFT is gradual accumulation of POINT mutations in HA/NA (causing SEASONAL epidemics and the need to update the vaccine yearly), whereas SHIFT is an abrupt REASSORTMENT of whole genome SEGMENTS between different influenza strains, generating a novel HA/NA to which the population has no immunity — the mechanism of PANDEMICS; only segmented viruses can undergo shift

enveloped-rna-viruses-orthomyxo-paramyxo.explanation: Drift (minor, epidemic) and shift (major, pandemic) have different mechanisms and public-health impact; recognising that shift requires the segmented genome explains why influenza — but not most viruses — causes pandemics.

enveloped-rna-viruses-orthomyxo-paramyxo.stem: What best explains the finding: “A novel pandemic influenza strain from genome reassortment”?
enveloped-rna-viruses-orthomyxo-paramyxo.explanation: A novel pandemic influenza strain from genome reassortment → Antigenic shift (segmented genome).

enveloped-rna-viruses-orthomyxo-paramyxo.stem: What best explains the finding: “Secondary bacterial pneumonia after influenza”?
enveloped-rna-viruses-orthomyxo-paramyxo.explanation: Secondary bacterial pneumonia after influenza → S. aureus/pneumococcus superinfection.

enveloped-rna-viruses-orthomyxo-paramyxo.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Influenza & Paramyxoviruses”?
enveloped-rna-viruses-orthomyxo-paramyxo.explanation: Clinical management of influenza is relevant to understanding COVID-19 pneumonia.

enveloped-rna-viruses-orthomyxo-paramyxo.stem: Which should you review before “Influenza & Paramyxoviruses”?
enveloped-rna-viruses-orthomyxo-paramyxo.explanation: Understanding virology principles is essential for grasping influenza and paramyxovirus mechanisms.

other-enveloped-rna-viruses.stem: Rabies virus reaches the central nervous system by:

options.text: Retrograde transport up peripheral nerves from the bite site

other-enveloped-rna-viruses.explanation: Rabies virus travels retrograde along peripheral nerve axons from the inoculation (bite) site to the CNS, causing fatal encephalitis (hydrophobia; Negri bodies). The slow nerve transit gives a long incubation, allowing effective post-exposure prophylaxis before symptoms.

other-enveloped-rna-viruses.stem: Maternal infection in early pregnancy causing cataracts, sensorineural deafness and cardiac defects in the neonate is due to:
other-enveloped-rna-viruses.explanation: Rubella infection in early pregnancy causes congenital rubella syndrome — classically cataracts, sensorineural deafness and cardiac defects (e.g. PDA). It is prevented by MMR vaccination, and rubella is otherwise a mild rash illness.

other-enveloped-rna-viruses.stem: Regarding rabies post-exposure prophylaxis — which is correct?

options.text: Because rabies is almost always fatal, nothing can be done after a bite

Rabies has a LONG, variable INCUBATION period as the virus travels slowly up peripheral nerves, so prompt POST-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS after a bite — thorough wound washing PLUS rabies IMMUNOGLOBULIN and VACCINE — reliably PREVENTS disease; it is only untreatable ONCE symptomatic (encephalitis) — so post-exposure prophylaxis is urgent and effective

other-enveloped-rna-viruses.explanation: The window before the virus reaches the CNS is what makes rabies preventable after exposure; assuming futility misses a life-saving, time-critical intervention.

other-enveloped-rna-viruses.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pneumonia/ARDS from a spike-protein virus binding ACE2”?
other-enveloped-rna-viruses.explanation: Pneumonia/ARDS from a spike-protein virus binding ACE2 → SARS-CoV-2 (coronavirus).

other-enveloped-rna-viruses.stem: What best explains the finding: “Hydrophobia and fatal encephalitis after a dog bite”?
other-enveloped-rna-viruses.explanation: Hydrophobia and fatal encephalitis after a dog bite → Rabies (rhabdovirus) — retrograde nerve spread.

other-enveloped-rna-viruses.stem: Which should you review before “Coronaviruses, Rabies & Haemorrhagic Fever Viruses”?
other-enveloped-rna-viruses.explanation: Understanding virology principles is essential for grasping the mechanisms of these viruses.

retroviruses-hiv.stem: HIV establishes lifelong infection because reverse transcriptase and integrase allow it to:

options.text: Convert its RNA to DNA and integrate a provirus into the host genome
Replicate only in the cytoplasm without a DNA stage

retroviruses-hiv.explanation: Retroviruses use reverse transcriptase to make DNA from their RNA genome, which integrase inserts into host DNA as a provirus. This integrated, latent reservoir persists for life and cannot be eradicated by current therapy, so ART suppresses but does not cure HIV.

retroviruses-hiv.stem: A CD4 count below 200 cells/µL in an HIV-positive patient is associated with:

options.text: AIDS-level immunodeficiency with risk of opportunistic infections (e.g. PJP)

retroviruses-hiv.explanation: As HIV depletes CD4⁺ T-helper cells, a count below 200 cells/µL marks severe immunodeficiency (AIDS), with susceptibility to opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis pneumonia, cryptococcal meningitis, TB and CMV, and AIDS-defining malignancies. ART restores CD4 counts.

retroviruses-hiv.stem: Regarding why hiv persists lifelong — which is correct?

options.text: A strong immune response or effective drugs should be able to clear HIV completely

HIV reverse-transcribes its RNA into DNA that INTEGRATES into the host genome as a latent PROVIRUS in long-lived cells — a reservoir that current therapy cannot eradicate — so ART SUPPRESSES but does not CURE the infection; stopping treatment allows rebound, which is why lifelong adherence is required

retroviruses-hiv.explanation: The integrated proviral reservoir explains why HIV is a lifelong infection controlled (not cured) by continuous ART — a fundamental point for counselling and adherence.

retroviruses-hiv.stem: What best explains the finding: “Progressive CD4⁺ T-cell depletion and opportunistic infections”?
retroviruses-hiv.explanation: Progressive CD4⁺ T-cell depletion and opportunistic infections → HIV (gp120→CD4).

retroviruses-hiv.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pneumocystis pneumonia / cryptococcal meningitis with CD4 <200”?
retroviruses-hiv.explanation: Pneumocystis pneumonia / cryptococcal meningitis with CD4 <200 → AIDS-defining opportunistic infection.

retroviruses-hiv.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Retroviruses & HIV”?
retroviruses-hiv.explanation: Understanding opportunistic infections in HIV may relate to metabolic derangements.

retroviruses-hiv.stem: Which should you review before “Retroviruses & HIV”?
retroviruses-hiv.explanation: Understanding retroviruses requires foundational virology knowledge.

arboviruses-mosquito-borne.stem: Severe dengue (haemorrhagic fever/shock) is most associated with:

options.text: A first infection with any serotype
Secondary infection with a different serotype (antibody-dependent enhancement)

arboviruses-mosquito-borne.explanation: Severe dengue characteristically occurs with a secondary infection by a different serotype: pre-existing non-neutralising antibodies enhance viral entry (antibody-dependent enhancement), driving plasma leakage, bleeding and shock. Management is careful fluid balance, avoiding NSAIDs/aspirin.

arboviruses-mosquito-borne.stem: Which arbovirus, transmitted by day-biting Aedes mosquitoes, causes congenital microcephaly?
arboviruses-mosquito-borne.explanation: Zika virus (Aedes-borne, also sexually and vertically transmitted) is usually mild but causes congenital Zika syndrome including microcephaly, and can trigger Guillain-Barré syndrome. Japanese encephalitis (Culex) causes encephalitis; chikungunya causes prolonged arthralgia.

arboviruses-mosquito-borne.stem: Regarding severe dengue and prior immunity — which is correct?

options.text: Having had dengue once makes future dengue infections milder because of immunity

Prior dengue gives lifelong immunity only to that SEROTYPE; infection with a DIFFERENT serotype can be MORE severe because non-neutralising cross-reactive antibodies enhance viral uptake (ANTIBODY-DEPENDENT ENHANCEMENT), causing plasma leakage, haemorrhage and shock (severe dengue) — so a second, heterotypic infection is the high-risk scenario

arboviruses-mosquito-borne.explanation: Counter-intuitively, previous exposure increases the risk of severe disease on heterotypic re-infection, which shapes clinical vigilance and vaccine strategy in dengue-endemic areas.

arboviruses-mosquito-borne.stem: What best explains the finding: “High fever, severe myalgia, rash and thrombocytopenia in the tropics”?
arboviruses-mosquito-borne.explanation: High fever, severe myalgia, rash and thrombocytopenia in the tropics → Dengue (flavivirus).

arboviruses-mosquito-borne.stem: What best explains the finding: “Plasma leakage, bleeding and shock in a second dengue infection”?
arboviruses-mosquito-borne.explanation: Plasma leakage, bleeding and shock in a second dengue infection → Severe dengue (antibody-dependent enhancement).

arboviruses-mosquito-borne.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Arboviruses (Mosquito-borne)”?

arboviruses-mosquito-borne.explanation: Understanding arboviruses requires knowledge of virology principles.

dna-viruses-herpesviruses.stem: The defining biological feature shared by all human herpesviruses is:

options.text: Establishment of lifelong latency with the potential to reactivate

dna-viruses-herpesviruses.explanation: Herpesviruses (large enveloped dsDNA viruses) characteristically establish lifelong latency (in sensory ganglia or lymphocytes) after primary infection and can reactivate, particularly during immunosuppression — explaining recurrent and reactivation disease.

dna-viruses-herpesviruses.stem: The most common congenital viral infection, a cause of sensorineural deafness and a serious pathogen in transplant/HIV patients (with "owl's eye" inclusions), is:
dna-viruses-herpesviruses.explanation: CMV (HHV-5) is the commonest congenital viral infection (causing deafness, microcephaly) and a major opportunistic pathogen in the immunosuppressed (retinitis, colitis, pneumonitis), with characteristic "owl's eye" intranuclear inclusions; it is treated with ganciclovir.

dna-viruses-herpesviruses.stem: Regarding herpesvirus persistence — which is correct?

options.text: Once herpes lesions heal and the immune response develops, the virus is cleared

Herpesviruses are NEVER cleared — after primary infection they establish LIFELONG LATENCY (e.g. HSV/VZV in sensory ganglia, EBV/CMV in lymphocytes) and can REACTIVATE, especially with immunosuppression or stress; antivirals suppress replication but do not eradicate latent virus

dna-viruses-herpesviruses.explanation: Understanding lifelong latency explains recurrent cold sores/shingles, reactivation disease in the immunosuppressed, and why antivirals control but never cure herpesvirus infection.

dna-viruses-herpesviruses.stem: What best explains the finding: “Temporal-lobe encephalitis”?
dna-viruses-herpesviruses.explanation: Temporal-lobe encephalitis → HSV encephalitis (empiric IV aciclovir).

dna-viruses-herpesviruses.stem: What best explains the finding: “Painful dermatomal vesicles not crossing the midline”?
dna-viruses-herpesviruses.explanation: Painful dermatomal vesicles not crossing the midline → Herpes zoster (VZV reactivation).

dna-viruses-herpesviruses.stem: Which is a clinical application of “DNA Viruses I: Herpesviruses”?

options.text: Normal Puberty, HPG Reactivation & Tanner Staging

dna-viruses-herpesviruses.explanation: Understanding puberty and HPG reactivation may provide context for immune responses.

dna-viruses-herpesviruses.stem: Which should you review before “DNA Viruses I: Herpesviruses”?
dna-viruses-herpesviruses.explanation: Understanding virology principles is essential for grasping herpesvirus characteristics.

dna-viruses-other.stem: High-risk human papillomavirus types (16, 18) drive cervical cancer mainly because their oncoproteins:

options.text: Inactivate the tumour suppressors p53 (E6) and Rb (E7)

dna-viruses-other.explanation: High-risk HPV E6 targets p53 for degradation and E7 inactivates Rb, disabling two key tumour-suppressor pathways and driving malignant transformation (cervical, anogenital and oropharyngeal cancers). HPV vaccination and cervical screening are preventive.

dna-viruses-other.stem: In hepatitis B serology, a positive HBsAg indicates:
dna-viruses-other.explanation: HBsAg (hepatitis B surface antigen) indicates current, active infection (the patient is infectious). Anti-HBs indicates immunity (vaccination or resolved infection), and anti-HBc distinguishes natural infection from vaccination.

dna-viruses-other.stem: Regarding hbsag vs anti-hbs — which is correct?

options.text: Any positive hepatitis B test means active, infectious disease

The specific marker matters: HBsAg (surface ANTIGEN) positive = current INFECTION (infectious), whereas anti-HBs (surface ANTIBODY) positive = IMMUNITY (from vaccination or resolved infection, not active disease) — so "hepatitis B positive" must be interpreted by which marker is present (antigen vs antibody), with anti-HBc distinguishing natural infection from vaccination

dna-viruses-other.explanation: Confusing HBsAg (active infection) with anti-HBs (immunity) inverts the clinical meaning — one needs treatment/isolation counselling, the other indicates protection; the serologic panel must be read carefully.

dna-viruses-other.stem: What best explains the finding: “Chronic hepatitis progressing to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma”?
dna-viruses-other.explanation: Chronic hepatitis progressing to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma → Hepatitis B (hepadnavirus).

dna-viruses-other.stem: What best explains the finding: “HBsAg positive with anti-HBc IgG (no anti-HBs)”?
dna-viruses-other.explanation: HBsAg positive with anti-HBc IgG (no anti-HBs) → Chronic HBV infection.

dna-viruses-other.stem: Which is a clinical application of “DNA Viruses II: Hepatitis B, HPV, Pox & Others”?
dna-viruses-other.explanation: Clinical implications of HBV include chronic hepatitis and liver cancer.

dna-viruses-other.stem: Which should you review before “DNA Viruses II: Hepatitis B, HPV, Pox & Others”?
dna-viruses-other.explanation: Herpesviruses are part of the broader DNA virus classification.

bacterial-structure-cell-wall.stem: The component of Gram-negative lipopolysaccharide responsible for fever, hypotension and DIC in sepsis is:
bacterial-structure-cell-wall.explanation: Lipid A is the toxic moiety of LPS (endotoxin) in the Gram-negative outer membrane; it triggers cytokine release causing fever, hypotension, and disseminated intravascular coagulation in Gram-negative sepsis. The O-antigen is used for serotyping, not toxicity.

bacterial-structure-cell-wall.stem: Why are Mycoplasma species intrinsically resistant to β-lactam antibiotics?

options.text: They lack a cell wall (no peptidoglycan target)

bacterial-structure-cell-wall.explanation: β-Lactams act by inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking in the cell wall; Mycoplasma (and L-forms) have no cell wall, so there is no target and they are intrinsically β-lactam resistant — treated instead with agents like macrolides or tetracyclines.

bacterial-structure-cell-wall.stem: Regarding gram stain colour and wall structure — which is correct?

options.text: Gram-positive and Gram-negative differ mainly in the thickness of the outer membrane

Gram-POSITIVE bacteria have a THICK PEPTIDOGLYCAN layer with teichoic acids and NO outer membrane (they retain crystal violet → purple), whereas Gram-NEGATIVE bacteria have a THIN peptidoglycan layer PLUS an OUTER MEMBRANE containing LPS/endotoxin (crystal violet washes out, so they take safranin → pink); it is the outer membrane and LPS that are unique to Gram-negatives and drive endotoxic sepsis

bacterial-structure-cell-wall.explanation: The purple/pink result reflects peptidoglycan thickness and the presence of an outer membrane, which in turn predicts endotoxin-mediated sepsis (Gram-negative) and guides antibiotic choice — so the structural basis, not just the colour, matters.

bacterial-structure-cell-wall.stem: What best explains the finding: “Purple cocci in clusters retaining crystal violet”?
bacterial-structure-cell-wall.explanation: Purple cocci in clusters retaining crystal violet → Gram-positive (thick peptidoglycan).

bacterial-structure-cell-wall.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pink rods taking the safranin counterstain”?
bacterial-structure-cell-wall.explanation: Pink rods taking the safranin counterstain → Gram-negative (thin peptidoglycan + outer membrane).

bacterial-physiology-growth-identificati.stem: On MacConkey agar, a lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod such as E. coli produces:
bacterial-physiology-growth-identificati.explanation: MacConkey agar contains lactose and a pH indicator; lactose fermenters (E. coli, Klebsiella) acidify the medium and form pink colonies, whereas non-fermenters (Salmonella, Shigella) remain colourless. Bile salts/crystal violet also make it selective for Gram-negatives.

bacterial-physiology-growth-identificati.stem: An obligate anaerobe is killed by oxygen mainly because it lacks:

options.text: Detoxifying enzymes such as catalase and superoxide dismutase

bacterial-physiology-growth-identificati.explanation: Obligate anaerobes lack (or have insufficient) catalase and superoxide dismutase, so they cannot detoxify the reactive oxygen species (superoxide, hydrogen peroxide) generated in the presence of oxygen, and are killed by it — hence the need for anaerobic culture.

bacterial-physiology-growth-identificati.stem: Regarding selective vs differential media — which is correct?

options.text: Selective and differential media mean the same thing

A SELECTIVE medium contains inhibitors that SUPPRESS unwanted organisms so only the target grows, whereas a DIFFERENTIAL medium lets organisms be DISTINGUISHED by their appearance/reaction (e.g. colour, haemolysis); MacConkey agar is BOTH — bile salts/crystal violet select for Gram-negatives while the lactose/pH indicator differentiates pink fermenters from colourless non-fermenters

bacterial-physiology-growth-identificati.explanation: Confusing the two misreads what a plate is doing; recognising MacConkey as selective (Gram-negatives only) AND differential (lactose fermentation) explains how a single plate both isolates and begins to identify enteric pathogens.

bacterial-physiology-growth-identificati.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pink colonies on MacConkey agar”?
bacterial-physiology-growth-identificati.explanation: Pink colonies on MacConkey agar → Lactose fermenter (e.g. E. coli/Klebsiella).

bacterial-physiology-growth-identificati.stem: What best explains the finding: “Colourless colonies on MacConkey agar”?
bacterial-physiology-growth-identificati.explanation: Colourless colonies on MacConkey agar → Non-lactose fermenter (e.g. Salmonella/Shigella).

bacterial-physiology-growth-identificati.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Bacterial Physiology, Growth & Identification”?
bacterial-physiology-growth-identificati.explanation: Understanding oxygen transport is relevant for clinical implications of bacterial oxygen requirements.

bacterial-physiology-growth-identificati.stem: Which should you review before “Bacterial Physiology, Growth & Identification”?
bacterial-physiology-growth-identificati.explanation: Basic understanding of metabolic disorders may aid in grasping bacterial metabolism.

bacterial-gene-transfer.stem: Transfer of a multidrug-resistance plasmid from one bacterium to another through a sex pilus, requiring cell-to-cell contact, is called:
bacterial-gene-transfer.explanation: Conjugation is direct plasmid transfer between bacteria through a sex pilus, requiring cell-to-cell contact; conjugative R-plasmids are the main vehicle for spreading multidrug resistance among Gram-negative bacteria. Transformation uses naked DNA and transduction uses a bacteriophage.

bacterial-gene-transfer.stem: A bacteriophage transfers a resistance or toxin gene from one bacterium to another. This mechanism is:
bacterial-gene-transfer.explanation: Transduction is the transfer of bacterial DNA between cells by a bacteriophage (generalised or specialised); it can move virulence (toxin) and resistance genes. Transformation involves uptake of naked DNA, and conjugation involves plasmid transfer through a pilus.

bacterial-gene-transfer.stem: Regarding distinguishing the gene-transfer mechanisms — which is correct?

options.text: All horizontal gene transfer is basically bacteria swapping DNA the same way

The three mechanisms differ by the VEHICLE and requirements: TRANSFORMATION is uptake of NAKED environmental DNA (no vector, needs competence), TRANSDUCTION uses a BACTERIOPHAGE to carry DNA, and CONJUGATION transfers a PLASMID directly through a SEX PILUS requiring CELL-TO-CELL CONTACT — conjugation is the principal route for spreading multidrug-resistance plasmids

bacterial-gene-transfer.explanation: Exam questions hinge on the carrier: naked DNA (transformation) vs phage (transduction) vs pilus/plasmid contact (conjugation); conflating them misses that conjugation is what disseminates resistance plasmids across Gram-negatives.

bacterial-gene-transfer.stem: What best explains the finding: “Transfer of a resistance plasmid through a sex pilus between two bacteria”?
bacterial-gene-transfer.explanation: Transfer of a resistance plasmid through a sex pilus between two bacteria → Conjugation.

bacterial-gene-transfer.stem: What best explains the finding: “A bacterium taking up free DNA from a lysed neighbour”?
bacterial-gene-transfer.explanation: A bacterium taking up free DNA from a lysed neighbour → Transformation (competent cells).

bacterial-gene-transfer.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Bacterial Genetics & Gene Transfer”?
bacterial-gene-transfer.explanation: Histological understanding may relate to infections influenced by gene transfer.

bacterial-gene-transfer.stem: Which should you review before “Bacterial Genetics & Gene Transfer”?
bacterial-gene-transfer.explanation: Understanding bacterial structure is essential for grasping gene transfer mechanisms.

antibiotic-resistance-mechanisms.stem: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) resists β-lactams principally through:

options.text: An altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a) encoded by mecA

antibiotic-resistance-mechanisms.explanation: MRSA carries mecA, which encodes PBP2a — a penicillin-binding protein with low affinity for β-lactams — so target modification (not just β-lactamase) confers resistance to essentially all standard β-lactams, requiring agents such as vancomycin or linezolid.

antibiotic-resistance-mechanisms.stem: Vancomycin resistance in enterococci (VRE) arises because the drug target changes from:
antibiotic-resistance-mechanisms.explanation: Vancomycin binds the terminal D-Ala-D-Ala of peptidoglycan precursors; VRE remodels this to D-Ala-D-Lac, which vancomycin cannot bind, abolishing its activity — a target-modification mechanism spread on mobile genetic elements.

antibiotic-resistance-mechanisms.stem: Regarding mechanism of mrsa resistance — which is correct?

options.text: MRSA is resistant to methicillin because it produces more β-lactamase (penicillinase)

MRSA resistance is NOT primarily due to β-lactamase — it is a TARGET modification: the mecA gene encodes an altered penicillin-binding protein, PBP2a, with LOW AFFINITY for β-lactams, so essentially ALL standard β-lactams (including anti-staphylococcal penicillins and most cephalosporins) fail; this is why β-lactamase inhibitors do not restore activity and alternative agents (vancomycin, linezolid) are needed

antibiotic-resistance-mechanisms.explanation: Because MRSA changes the drug target rather than merely destroying the drug, adding a β-lactamase inhibitor does not help; recognising the mecA/PBP2a mechanism explains the need for non-β-lactam therapy.

antibiotic-resistance-mechanisms.stem: What best explains the finding: “A Gram-negative resistant to most cephalosporins via a plasmid enzyme”?
antibiotic-resistance-mechanisms.explanation: A Gram-negative resistant to most cephalosporins via a plasmid enzyme → Extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL).

antibiotic-resistance-mechanisms.stem: What best explains the finding: “Staph. aureus resistant to all standard β-lactams”?
antibiotic-resistance-mechanisms.explanation: Staph. aureus resistant to all standard β-lactams → MRSA (mecA → PBP2a target change).

antibiotic-resistance-mechanisms.stem: Which should you review before “Antibiotic Resistance Mechanisms”?
antibiotic-resistance-mechanisms.explanation: Understanding genetic code is essential for grasping antibiotic resistance mechanisms.

staphylococcus-aureus.stem: Which pair of tests identifies Staphylococcus aureus and separates it from streptococci and other staphylococci?

options.text: Catalase positive (vs strep) and coagulase positive (vs other staph)

staphylococcus-aureus.explanation: Staphylococci are catalase-positive (streptococci are catalase-negative), and S. aureus is coagulase-positive, distinguishing it from the coagulase-negative staphylococci (e.g. S. epidermidis, S. saprophyticus).

staphylococcus-aureus.stem: Toxic shock syndrome caused by S. aureus TSST-1 occurs because the toxin acts as a:

options.text: Superantigen causing massive nonspecific T-cell activation and cytokine release

staphylococcus-aureus.explanation: TSST-1 is a superantigen that cross-links MHC II and T-cell receptors nonspecifically, triggering massive cytokine release (fever, rash, hypotension, multi-organ involvement) — the mechanism of staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome.

staphylococcus-aureus.stem: Regarding staphylococcal food poisoning timing — which is correct?

options.text: Staphylococcal food poisoning takes a day or two because the bacteria must grow in the gut

Staphylococcal food poisoning is caused by a PRE-FORMED, HEAT-STABLE ENTEROTOXIN already in the food, so symptoms (prominent VOMITING) begin RAPIDLY — typically 1–6 HOURS after eating — without needing the organism to colonise the gut; this rapid, toxin-mediated onset distinguishes it from infectious enteritis (which takes longer)

staphylococcus-aureus.explanation: Because the toxin is pre-formed and heat-stable (survives reheating), the illness is fast and vomiting-predominant; expecting a delayed, infection-type course misidentifies the mechanism and source.

staphylococcus-aureus.stem: What best explains the finding: “Gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase- and coagulase-positive”?
staphylococcus-aureus.explanation: Gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase- and coagulase-positive → Staphylococcus aureus.

staphylococcus-aureus.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fever, diffuse rash, hypotension and desquamation with tampon use”?
staphylococcus-aureus.explanation: Fever, diffuse rash, hypotension and desquamation with tampon use → TSST-1 toxic shock syndrome (superantigen).

staphylococcus-aureus.stem: Which should you review before “Staphylococcus aureus”?
staphylococcus-aureus.explanation: Understanding antibiotic resistance is crucial for managing MRSA infections.

coagulase-negative-staphylococci.stem: A young, sexually active woman has dysuria and frequency; urine grows a coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant staphylococcus. The organism is:
coagulase-negative-staphylococci.explanation: S. saprophyticus (coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant) is a leading cause of uncomplicated cystitis in young, sexually active women, second only to E. coli — a genuine uropathogen in this setting.

coagulase-negative-staphylococci.stem: Staphylococcus epidermidis causes prosthetic-device and catheter infections mainly because it:

options.text: Forms a polysaccharide biofilm ("slime") that adheres to devices and resists clearance

coagulase-negative-staphylococci.explanation: S. epidermidis produces a polysaccharide biofilm that lets it adhere to prosthetic valves, catheters, shunts and joints and evade host defences and antibiotics, so device-related infections typically require removal of the hardware plus antibiotics (often vancomycin).

coagulase-negative-staphylococci.stem: Regarding positive blood culture for s. epidermidis — which is correct?

options.text: Any blood culture growing Staphylococcus epidermidis must be treated as a true bloodstream infection

Because S. epidermidis is a normal SKIN commensal, a single positive blood culture in a well patient is frequently a CONTAMINANT, not a true infection; genuine infection is suggested by MULTIPLE positive cultures, the presence of a PROSTHETIC DEVICE/line, and clinical signs — so interpretation requires clinical context, and true device infections often need the device REMOVED as well as antibiotics

coagulase-negative-staphylococci.explanation: Treating every S. epidermidis culture as real infection leads to unnecessary vancomycin, while the true device infections need hardware removal; distinguishing contamination from infection by context is the key judgement.

coagulase-negative-staphylococci.stem: What best explains the finding: “Prosthetic valve or IV-line infection with a biofilm-forming CoNS”?
coagulase-negative-staphylococci.explanation: Prosthetic valve or IV-line infection with a biofilm-forming CoNS → S. epidermidis (device biofilm).

coagulase-negative-staphylococci.stem: What best explains the finding: “A single blood culture growing S. epidermidis in a well patient”?
coagulase-negative-staphylococci.explanation: A single blood culture growing S. epidermidis in a well patient → Likely skin contamination.

coagulase-negative-staphylococci.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Coagulase-Negative Staphylococci”?
coagulase-negative-staphylococci.explanation: S. epidermidis is associated with device-related infections, relevant to catheter-associated UTIs.

streptococcus-pyogenes-agalactiae.stem: Which post-streptococcal complication follows ONLY pharyngitis (not skin infection) and is prevented by treating strep throat?
streptococcus-pyogenes-agalactiae.explanation: Rheumatic fever follows Group A streptococcal pharyngitis (via molecular mimicry) and is prevented by promptly treating strep throat; post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, by contrast, can follow throat or skin infection and is not antibiotic-preventable.

streptococcus-pyogenes-agalactiae.stem: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B strep) is clinically most important as a cause of:

options.text: Neonatal sepsis and meningitis (prevented by intrapartum prophylaxis)

streptococcus-pyogenes-agalactiae.explanation: Group B strep colonises the maternal genital/GI tract and is a leading cause of early- and late-onset neonatal sepsis, pneumonia and meningitis, so pregnant women are screened and given intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis. It is CAMP-test and hippurate positive.

streptococcus-pyogenes-agalactiae.stem: Regarding rheumatic fever vs psgn precipitant — which is correct?

options.text: Both rheumatic fever and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis follow either strep throat or skin infection equally

The precipitants differ: RHEUMATIC FEVER follows only streptococcal PHARYNGITIS (not skin infection) and is PREVENTED by treating strep throat, whereas POST-STREPTOCOCCAL GLOMERULONEPHRITIS can follow EITHER pharyngitis OR a SKIN infection (impetigo) and is NOT prevented by antibiotic treatment of the infection

streptococcus-pyogenes-agalactiae.explanation: This distinction (throat-only rheumatic fever vs throat-or-skin PSGN, and only rheumatic fever being antibiotic-preventable) is a classic exam point and shapes why we treat strep throat but cannot avert PSGN.

streptococcus-pyogenes-agalactiae.stem: What best explains the finding: “β-haemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive Gram-positive cocci in chains”?
streptococcus-pyogenes-agalactiae.explanation: β-haemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive Gram-positive cocci in chains → Group A strep (S. pyogenes).

streptococcus-pyogenes-agalactiae.stem: What best explains the finding: “Migratory arthritis, carditis and chorea weeks after strep throat”?
streptococcus-pyogenes-agalactiae.explanation: Migratory arthritis, carditis and chorea weeks after strep throat → Rheumatic fever (molecular mimicry).

streptococcus-pyogenes-agalactiae.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Streptococcus pyogenes & agalactiae (GAS/GBS)”?
streptococcus-pyogenes-agalactiae.explanation: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a clinical manifestation of S. pyogenes infection.

streptococcus-pneumoniae-enterococci.stem: An α-haemolytic, lancet-shaped diplococcus that is optochin-sensitive and bile-soluble is:
streptococcus-pneumoniae-enterococci.explanation: Optochin sensitivity and bile solubility identify Streptococcus pneumoniae, an encapsulated α-haemolytic diplococcus causing pneumonia, meningitis and otitis; viridans streptococci are optochin-resistant and bile-insoluble.

streptococcus-pneumoniae-enterococci.stem: Which feature helps identify enterococci in the laboratory?
streptococcus-pneumoniae-enterococci.explanation: Enterococci (group D) are hardy organisms that grow in bile and in 6.5% NaCl, distinguishing them from other streptococci; they cause UTIs, biliary/intra-abdominal infection and endocarditis, and include vancomycin-resistant enterococcus (VRE).

streptococcus-pneumoniae-enterococci.stem: Regarding separating pneumococcus from viridans streptococci — which is correct?

options.text: All α-haemolytic streptococci are essentially the same organism

α-haemolytic streptococci must be split: S. PNEUMONIAE is OPTOCHIN-SENSITIVE and BILE-SOLUBLE (encapsulated, lancet-shaped diplococcus → pneumonia/meningitis/otitis), whereas VIRIDANS streptococci are OPTOCHIN-RESISTANT and bile-INSOLUBLE (mouth flora → dental caries and subacute endocarditis) — the optochin and bile-solubility tests distinguish two clinically very different groups
Loss of splenic clearance of encapsulated bacteria

streptococcus-pneumoniae-enterococci.explanation: Lumping α-haemolytic strep together confuses a vaccine-preventable, capsule-dependent invasive pathogen (pneumococcus) with low-virulence oral flora (viridans); the optochin/bile tests and clinical syndromes separate them.

streptococcus-pneumoniae-enterococci.stem: What best explains the finding: “α-haemolytic, optochin-sensitive, bile-soluble diplococci in CAP”?

options.text: Loss of splenic clearance of encapsulated bacteria

streptococcus-pneumoniae-enterococci.explanation: α-haemolytic, optochin-sensitive, bile-soluble diplococci in CAP → Streptococcus pneumoniae.

streptococcus-pneumoniae-enterococci.stem: What best explains the finding: “Fulminant sepsis after pneumococcus in an asplenic patient”?

options.text: Loss of splenic clearance of encapsulated bacteria

streptococcus-pneumoniae-enterococci.explanation: Fulminant sepsis after pneumococcus in an asplenic patient → Loss of splenic clearance of encapsulated bacteria.

streptococcus-pneumoniae-enterococci.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Pneumococcus, Viridans Strep & Enterococci”?
streptococcus-pneumoniae-enterococci.explanation: Viridans streptococci are a common cause of subacute endocarditis.

streptococcus-pneumoniae-enterococci.stem: Which should you review before “Pneumococcus, Viridans Strep & Enterococci”?
streptococcus-pneumoniae-enterococci.explanation: Understanding VRE and antibiotic resistance is crucial for managing enterococci infections.

bacillus-anthracis-cereus.stem: A painless black necrotic eschar with marked surrounding oedema develops on the hand of an animal-hide worker. The most likely organism is:
bacillus-anthracis-cereus.explanation: Cutaneous anthrax (B. anthracis) produces a characteristically painless black eschar with prominent oedema after spore inoculation through skin; B. anthracis is distinctive for its protein capsule and the tripartite anthrax toxin.

bacillus-anthracis-cereus.stem: Vomiting beginning 1–6 hours after eating reheated fried rice is caused by which organism and mechanism?

options.text: Bacillus cereus, via a pre-formed heat-stable emetic toxin
Salmonella, via invasion of the gut

bacillus-anthracis-cereus.explanation: The emetic form of Bacillus cereus food poisoning results from a pre-formed, heat-stable toxin (classically in reheated rice), causing rapid vomiting within 1–6 hours; a separate heat-labile enterotoxin causes a later diarrhoeal syndrome.

bacillus-anthracis-cereus.stem: Regarding the anthrax eschar — which is correct?

options.text: A necrotic black skin ulcer from anthrax would be intensely painful

The cutaneous anthrax lesion is a PAINLESS black necrotic ESCHAR (with striking surrounding non-pitting OEDEMA) — the lack of pain despite the alarming necrotic appearance is characteristic and helps distinguish it from painful ulcers/spider bites; it follows inoculation of spores through skin (e.g. handling animal hides/wool)

bacillus-anthracis-cereus.explanation: The painlessness of the eschar is a classic clue; expecting pain could lead to misdiagnosis, whereas a painless black eschar with oedema in someone exposed to animal products should raise anthrax.

bacillus-anthracis-cereus.stem: What best explains the finding: “Painless black necrotic eschar with surrounding oedema after skin contact with animal hides”?
bacillus-anthracis-cereus.explanation: Painless black necrotic eschar with surrounding oedema after skin contact with animal hides → Cutaneous anthrax (B. anthracis).

bacillus-anthracis-cereus.stem: What best explains the finding: “Widened mediastinum and haemorrhagic mediastinitis after spore inhalation”?
bacillus-anthracis-cereus.explanation: Widened mediastinum and haemorrhagic mediastinitis after spore inhalation → Inhalational anthrax.

options.text: ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor EF-2, halting protein synthesis

corynebacterium-listeria.explanation: The phage-encoded diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates elongation factor EF-2, arresting host protein synthesis; locally this produces the pharyngeal pseudomembrane and systemically causes myocarditis and neuropathy. Early antitoxin neutralises circulating toxin.

corynebacterium-listeria.stem: Empiric antibiotics for meningitis in a neonate or an elderly patient should include ampicillin because cephalosporins do not cover:
corynebacterium-listeria.explanation: Listeria monocytogenes is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins and is a leading cause of meningitis in neonates, the elderly and the immunocompromised, so ampicillin (± gentamicin) is added to empiric regimens at the extremes of age.

corynebacterium-listeria.stem: Regarding empiric meningitis cover for listeria — which is correct?

options.text: A third-generation cephalosporin alone adequately covers bacterial meningitis in all age groups

LISTERIA MONOCYTOGENES is NOT covered by cephalosporins, so empiric meningitis therapy in NEONATES, the ELDERLY and the IMMUNOCOMPROMISED must ADD AMPICILLIN (± gentamicin) to the cephalosporin; relying on a cephalosporin alone at the extremes of age risks missing Listeria, a leading cause of meningitis in exactly those groups

corynebacterium-listeria.explanation: Cephalosporins have a well-known gap against Listeria, so omitting ampicillin in at-risk age groups leaves a treatable, dangerous cause of meningitis uncovered — a classic exam and clinical safety point.

corynebacterium-listeria.stem: What best explains the finding: “Grey adherent pharyngeal pseudomembrane that bleeds when scraped”?
corynebacterium-listeria.explanation: Grey adherent pharyngeal pseudomembrane that bleeds when scraped → Diphtheria toxin (C. diphtheriae).

corynebacterium-listeria.stem: What best explains the finding: “Myocarditis and neuropathy complicating a throat infection”?
corynebacterium-listeria.explanation: Myocarditis and neuropathy complicating a throat infection → Systemic diphtheria toxin.

corynebacterium-listeria.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Corynebacterium & Listeria”?
corynebacterium-listeria.explanation: Diphtheria's clinical presentation is crucial for diagnosis and management.

enterobacterales-ecoli-klebsiella.stem: A child develops bloody diarrhoea followed by acute kidney injury, anaemia and thrombocytopenia after eating undercooked beef. The organism and the key management point are:

options.text: EHEC O157:H7; avoid antibiotics (they increase HUS risk)

enterobacterales-ecoli-klebsiella.explanation: Enterohaemorrhagic E. coli O157:H7 produces Shiga-like toxin causing bloody diarrhoea and haemolytic-uraemic syndrome; antibiotics can increase toxin release and HUS risk, so management is supportive with monitoring for HUS.

enterobacterales-ecoli-klebsiella.stem: On MacConkey agar, E. coli and Klebsiella appear pink because they:
enterobacterales-ecoli-klebsiella.explanation: E. coli, Klebsiella and Enterobacter are lactose fermenters, acidifying MacConkey agar and forming pink colonies, distinguishing them from non-lactose fermenters (Salmonella, Shigella) that remain colourless. (Serratia produces a red pigment but is a weak/late lactose fermenter.)

enterobacterales-ecoli-klebsiella.stem: Regarding antibiotics in ehec o157 infection — which is correct?

options.text: Bloody diarrhoea from E. coli O157:H7 should be treated promptly with antibiotics like any bacterial dysentery

In EHEC/STEC (O157:H7) infection, ANTIBIOTICS are generally AVOIDED because they can INCREASE Shiga-toxin release and raise the risk of HAEMOLYTIC-URAEMIC SYNDROME; management is supportive (fluids, monitoring for HUS), unlike other bacterial dysenteries — so recognising bloody diarrhoea + potential HUS as EHEC changes the treatment decision

enterobacterales-ecoli-klebsiella.explanation: Treating EHEC like ordinary bacterial dysentery can precipitate HUS via increased toxin release; withholding antibiotics and giving supportive care is the correct, counter-intuitive management.

enterobacterales-ecoli-klebsiella.stem: What best explains the finding: “Pink (lactose-fermenting) Gram-negative rods on MacConkey”?
enterobacterales-ecoli-klebsiella.explanation: Pink (lactose-fermenting) Gram-negative rods on MacConkey → E. coli / Klebsiella / Enterobacter.

enterobacterales-ecoli-klebsiella.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bloody diarrhoea and haemolytic-uraemic syndrome after undercooked beef”?
enterobacterales-ecoli-klebsiella.explanation: Bloody diarrhoea and haemolytic-uraemic syndrome after undercooked beef → EHEC O157:H7 (Shiga toxin).

enterobacterales-ecoli-klebsiella.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Enterobacterales: E. coli & Klebsiella”?
enterobacterales-ecoli-klebsiella.explanation: Directly relates to E. coli's role in UTIs and its microbiological aspects.

enterobacterales-ecoli-klebsiella.stem: Which should you review before “Enterobacterales: E. coli & Klebsiella”?
enterobacterales-ecoli-klebsiella.explanation: Understanding resistance mechanisms is crucial for grasping Klebsiella's ESBL and CRE roles.

salmonella-shigella-yersinia.stem: A returning traveller has a week of stepwise rising fever, relative bradycardia, abdominal pain and faint rose-coloured spots on the trunk. The likely diagnosis is:
salmonella-shigella-yersinia.explanation: Stepwise fever, relative bradycardia and rose spots after travel are classic for enteric (typhoid) fever caused by Salmonella Typhi, which invades through Peyer's patches; humans are the only reservoir and chronic gallbladder carriage can occur. It requires antibiotics.

salmonella-shigella-yersinia.stem: Non-typhoidal Salmonella is a characteristic cause of osteomyelitis in patients with:
salmonella-shigella-yersinia.explanation: While S. aureus is the commonest overall cause of osteomyelitis, non-typhoidal Salmonella has a well-known predilection for causing osteomyelitis in patients with sickle-cell disease — a classic association.

salmonella-shigella-yersinia.stem: Regarding antibiotics: shigella vs non-typhoidal salmonella — which is correct?

options.text: All bacterial gastroenteritis should either always or never be given antibiotics

It depends on the organism: SHIGELLA dysentery IS treated with antibiotics (very low infective dose, invasive, reduces spread/duration), whereas uncomplicated NON-TYPHOIDAL SALMONELLA gastroenteritis is usually NOT (antibiotics can prolong carriage and are reserved for severe disease or high-risk hosts); enteric fever (S. Typhi) always needs antibiotics, and EHEC should NOT get antibiotics — so the decision is organism-specific

salmonella-shigella-yersinia.explanation: Blanket rules fail: treating non-typhoidal Salmonella can prolong carriage, while withholding antibiotics in Shigella or typhoid is wrong — matching the antibiotic decision to the specific pathogen is the key skill.

salmonella-shigella-yersinia.stem: What best explains the finding: “Stepwise fever, relative bradycardia and rose spots after travel”?
salmonella-shigella-yersinia.explanation: Stepwise fever, relative bradycardia and rose spots after travel → Enteric (typhoid) fever — S. Typhi.

salmonella-shigella-yersinia.stem: What best explains the finding: “Osteomyelitis caused by Salmonella in a sickle-cell patient”?
salmonella-shigella-yersinia.explanation: Osteomyelitis caused by Salmonella in a sickle-cell patient → Non-typhoidal Salmonella predilection.

salmonella-shigella-yersinia.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Salmonella, Shigella & Yersinia”?

options.text: Enteric Nervous System, Autonomics & GI Reflexes

salmonella-shigella-yersinia.explanation: Understanding the enteric nervous system is crucial for grasping gastrointestinal infections.

salmonella-shigella-yersinia.stem: Which should you review before “Salmonella, Shigella & Yersinia”?

vibrio-campylobacter-helicobacter.stem: Cholera toxin causes profuse "rice-water" diarrhoea by:

options.text: ADP-ribosylating Gs, raising cAMP and driving chloride/water secretion
Invading and destroying the colonic mucosa

vibrio-campylobacter-helicobacter.explanation: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the Gs protein, locking adenylate cyclase on; the resulting sustained rise in cAMP drives massive chloride and water secretion into the gut lumen, producing painless "rice-water" stools and dehydration. Treatment is rehydration.

vibrio-campylobacter-helicobacter.stem: Which organism, a common cause of bloody diarrhoea from poultry, is the classic antecedent of Guillain-Barré syndrome?
vibrio-campylobacter-helicobacter.explanation: Campylobacter jejuni, a microaerophilic curved rod growing at 42°C, causes inflammatory/bloody diarrhoea and is the commonest infectious trigger of Guillain-Barré syndrome through molecular mimicry between its lipo-oligosaccharide and nerve gangliosides.

vibrio-campylobacter-helicobacter.stem: Regarding priority treatment in cholera — which is correct?

options.text: The most important treatment for cholera is prompt antibiotics to kill Vibrio cholerae

The life-saving priority in cholera is aggressive REHYDRATION (oral rehydration solution or IV fluids) to replace the massive cAMP-driven fluid losses — this is what prevents death from hypovolaemic shock; ANTIBIOTICS are an ADJUNCT that shorten the illness and reduce shedding but are secondary to fluid replacement

vibrio-campylobacter-helicobacter.explanation: Cholera kills by dehydration, not by tissue invasion, so fluid replacement (not antibiotics) is the primary, life-saving intervention — a core public-health teaching point.

vibrio-campylobacter-helicobacter.stem: What best explains the finding: “Profuse painless "rice-water" watery diarrhoea with severe dehydration”?
vibrio-campylobacter-helicobacter.explanation: Profuse painless "rice-water" watery diarrhoea with severe dehydration → Cholera toxin (↑cAMP secretion).

vibrio-campylobacter-helicobacter.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bloody, inflammatory diarrhoea after undercooked poultry”?
vibrio-campylobacter-helicobacter.explanation: Bloody, inflammatory diarrhoea after undercooked poultry → Campylobacter jejuni.

vibrio-campylobacter-helicobacter.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Vibrio, Campylobacter & Helicobacter”?
vibrio-campylobacter-helicobacter.explanation: Both modules involve mechanisms but in different systems.

vibrio-campylobacter-helicobacter.stem: Which should you review before “Vibrio, Campylobacter & Helicobacter”?
vibrio-campylobacter-helicobacter.explanation: Understanding Enterobacterales is essential for grasping Gram-negative bacilli.

pseudomonas-burkholderia-nonfermenters.stem: A diabetic rice farmer in northeast Thailand presents with pneumonia, splenic abscesses and sepsis. Which organism and treatment approach fit best?

options.text: Burkholderia pseudomallei; IV ceftazidime/carbapenem then months of oral co-trimoxazole

pseudomonas-burkholderia-nonfermenters.explanation: Melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei) is endemic in northeast Thailand, acquired from soil/water especially by diabetics, causing pneumonia, abscesses and sepsis. It requires an intensive IV phase (ceftazidime or a carbapenem) followed by months of oral eradication (co-trimoxazole) because relapse is common.

pseudomonas-burkholderia-nonfermenters.stem: Which feature is characteristic of Pseudomonas aeruginosa?

options.text: A blue-green pigment (pyocyanin) and preference for moist environments

pseudomonas-burkholderia-nonfermenters.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an aerobic, oxidase-positive non-fermenter that produces blue-green pyocyanin (and pyoverdin) with a fruity odour and thrives in moisture, causing infections in burns, ventilated patients, cystic fibrosis and diabetic wounds; it is intrinsically multidrug-resistant.

pseudomonas-burkholderia-nonfermenters.stem: Regarding melioidosis in the endemic setting — which is correct?

options.text: A febrile diabetic rice farmer in northeast Thailand with abscesses and sepsis just has ordinary bacterial sepsis

In NORTHEAST THAILAND and SE Asia, a DIABETIC with soil/water exposure (e.g. rice farming) presenting with pneumonia, multi-organ ABSCESSES and sepsis should be evaluated for MELIOIDOSIS (Burkholderia pseudomallei) — it needs SPECIFIC prolonged therapy (IV ceftazidime or a carbapenem, then months of oral co-trimoxazole eradication), and standard empiric regimens may miss it, with high mortality and relapse if untreated

pseudomonas-burkholderia-nonfermenters.explanation: Melioidosis is endemic and often overlooked, yet it demands a specific, prolonged regimen distinct from ordinary sepsis cover; recognising the diabetic + soil-exposure + abscess picture in the endemic region is life-saving.

pseudomonas-burkholderia-nonfermenters.stem: What best explains the finding: “Blue-green pigmented, fruity-smelling Gram-negative rod from a burn wound”?
pseudomonas-burkholderia-nonfermenters.explanation: Blue-green pigmented, fruity-smelling Gram-negative rod from a burn wound → Pseudomonas aeruginosa (pyocyanin).

pseudomonas-burkholderia-nonfermenters.stem: What best explains the finding: “Chronic mucoid Pseudomonas colonisation in cystic fibrosis”?
pseudomonas-burkholderia-nonfermenters.explanation: Chronic mucoid Pseudomonas colonisation in cystic fibrosis → Biofilm adaptation.

pseudomonas-burkholderia-nonfermenters.stem: Which should you review before “Pseudomonas, Burkholderia & Non-Fermenters”?
pseudomonas-burkholderia-nonfermenters.explanation: Understanding resistance mechanisms is crucial for managing non-fermenters.

neisseria-meningitidis-gonorrhoeae.stem: A teenager presents with fever, headache, hypotension and a rapidly spreading non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash. The most likely organism is:
neisseria-meningitidis-gonorrhoeae.explanation: Fever with a non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash and shock is meningococcaemia (N. meningitidis); it can progress to Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (adrenal haemorrhage from DIC). It is a medical emergency requiring immediate ceftriaxone and contact chemoprophylaxis.

neisseria-meningitidis-gonorrhoeae.stem: In the laboratory, Neisseria meningitidis is distinguished from N. gonorrhoeae because meningitidis ferments:

options.text: Both glucose and maltose (gonorrhoeae ferments glucose only)

neisseria-meningitidis-gonorrhoeae.explanation: Both Neisseria are oxidase-positive Gram-negative diplococci, but N. meningitidis ferments glucose AND maltose, whereas N. gonorrhoeae ferments glucose only — "Maltose = Meningitidis" is the classic mnemonic.

neisseria-meningitidis-gonorrhoeae.stem: Regarding recurrent neisseria infection — which is correct?

options.text: Recurrent meningococcal or gonococcal infections just reflect repeated exposure

RECURRENT Neisseria infections should prompt evaluation for a TERMINAL COMPLEMENT (C5–C9, membrane-attack-complex) deficiency — the MAC is essential for killing Neisseria, so its deficiency uniquely predisposes to recurrent meningococcal (and gonococcal) disease; asplenia also increases risk of encapsulated meningococcal infection

neisseria-meningitidis-gonorrhoeae.explanation: Recurrent Neisseria disease is a classic clue to terminal complement deficiency; missing this overlooks a diagnosable immunodeficiency (and the need for vaccination/prophylaxis), attributing it merely to bad luck.

neisseria-meningitidis-gonorrhoeae.stem: What best explains the finding: “Non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash with fever and shock”?
neisseria-meningitidis-gonorrhoeae.explanation: Non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash with fever and shock → Meningococcaemia (N. meningitidis).

neisseria-meningitidis-gonorrhoeae.stem: What best explains the finding: “Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage with meningococcal sepsis”?
neisseria-meningitidis-gonorrhoeae.explanation: Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage with meningococcal sepsis → Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

neisseria-meningitidis-gonorrhoeae.stem: Which is a clinical application of “Neisseria: meningitidis & gonorrhoeae”?
neisseria-meningitidis-gonorrhoeae.explanation: Chlamydia co-infection is relevant in the context of Neisseria gonorrhoeae treatment.

haemophilus-bordetella-small-gram-negati.stem: A prolonged cough with severe paroxysms, an inspiratory "whoop", post-tussive vomiting and a strikingly high lymphocyte count suggests:
haemophilus-bordetella-small-gram-negati.explanation: Bordetella pertussis causes whooping cough: after a catarrhal phase, paroxysmal coughing fits with an inspiratory whoop and post-tussive vomiting develop, with marked lymphocytosis (from pertussis toxin). It is vaccine-preventable and treated/prophylaxed with macrolides.

haemophilus-bordetella-small-gram-negati.stem: Haemophilus influenzae is cultured on chocolate agar because it requires:

options.text: Growth factors V (NAD) and X (haemin) released by lysed red cells

haemophilus-bordetella-small-gram-negati.explanation: H. influenzae is fastidious, needing factor V (NAD) and factor X (haemin); chocolate (heated blood) agar releases both, and the organism shows satellitism around S. aureus colonies that supply factor V. The Hib capsule mediates invasiveness, not growth.

haemophilus-bordetella-small-gram-negati.stem: Regarding epiglottitis as an airway emergency — which is correct?
